I've been an N fan all my life. Playing 1.4 on the computer, then 2.0, playing through and beating N+ on DS, PSP (my fav version) and 200/200 on Xbox 360. Purchased N++ on PS4 when it released last year and was the primary reason why I purchased the console.
There's a reason why so many people have played and continue to purchase N games throughout the years:
You can not get a more pure platforming experience than N++.
It's pure skill; no powerups, no "the game cheated!!" it's on you - the player - to completely play the way of the ninja.
N++ maintains this pure skill aspect and throws in:
1) Crazy amount of stages
2) Fantastic soundtrack
3) Color customization options that are fun to play around with
4) Local co-op
5) Online sharing and playing
6) Everything is leaderboards
When Metanet say there won't be a sequel I can absolutely believe it: I have no idea how they can further iterate N.
You like platformers? Want to get a ton of value? Like chasing scores? N++ is your jam.
Pick up, play, break your controller,  pop a blood vessel, lose your hair, lose your voice. 10/10

Absolutely flawless. Every aspect of N++ is so clean and sharp whether it's the graphics, music, sound or gameplay. Although it may not seem like much on the surface, N++ is special because of its movement and momentum mechanics. Watching gameplay doesn't do a justice for how this game feels to play: you need to try it for yourself. It's never the game's fault when you die. It's yours. The difficulty can be evil, but it's still fair all throughout. I'd say it's one of the best, if not THE best platformer out there.
Oh yeah, also there's a level editor & community made levels, so basically infinite gameplay.

Finally: the quintessential version of the game I spent so many hours playing in my formative platforming years, back on its home OS! Pros: gorgeous graphics, lovely music, tons of content, global rankings, user maps. Cons: tweaks aside, it's still fundamentally the same game it was 10 years ago. Whether you see that as a good thing or not depends on how much you love the original. As far as I'm concerned, the price is a steal!

After almost 25-30 hours of gameplay, I can say that this game is really, really good. What is this game, though? Well, it takes the MOBA genre and turns it on it's head; for once, finally, we get a MOBA where we have full control of our characters and it's no longer mouse-clicking spam garbage.
It's an actual MOBA that plays a bit like a first person shooter. Funnily enough, it streamlines a few things, while delivering some unique new aspects to this style of game that I haven't really seen anywhere else.
Instead of towers being pre-placed, you can build turrets, traps, and things to help your team and hinder the enemy team. Also, instead of random creeps, there are several mercenary camps (At least in Incursion) where you can hire more, bigger, powerful creeps to assault the enemy.
Characters have true skilltrees in the form of a Helix. Each Helix has 2 sides, and every time you level, you can select one or the other to truly customize how your character will play, and how their kit works. Plus, as you gain character levels (outside of each match) you get mutations for your Helix, which give you a third choice for several of the existing helix choices.
Items in a MOBA are simplified now - you make a loadout with three pieces of gear, and when you select your character, you pick a loadout. Those 3 pieces go with you and you craft them with shards as the battle progresses. Simple. ♥♥♥♥ League's system, anyway.
It's a solid game with a lot of stuff going for it, so if you're into playing a game that involves a bit of strategy and teamwork, this should be a definite buy for people, especially if you enjoy playing it with friends.
NOTE: This game is NOT comparable to Overwatch. OW is Blizzard's attempt at making a TF2 clone that is incredibly light on content. They give you 20-ish heroes that don't have a ton of depth. You can't customize the playstyle of your chosen hero, and your rank-up system is purely cosmetic. Plus, you only have two game modes (which are copied directly from TF2, I might add) and there is NO PvE element. So, if you like co-op more than PvP, good luck with that. (I mean, even TF2 has PvE now.. and has had it forever now. Come on, Blizzard.)
Get this game. You won't regret it.

About 5 hours into this game and I was having so much fun that I thought I would take a break and write a brief review.

That is another great one and I'll end up getting Overwatch as well. We're lucky to get 2 very good games in Battleborn and Overwatch; each different from the other but both offering loads of fun.

Despite the great music and interesting visuals, this has not been a fun game for me to play.
It should be called Bunny-Hop Activity, because if you're going to survive you will be jumping around way more than is either fun or comfortable.
The concept of a bullet-hell FPS with perma-death, randomly-generated floors and item drops sounds great, but the execution here is really rough.  The bullet-hell is way too difficult to be fun for anyone less than a pro FPS player.
Also, I they might think they're being cool by not telling you what the items do, and experimenting to see what is what would normally be okay with me, but it is totally unfeasible when you can almost NEVER get enough money to buy items, making experimenting really slow and unrewarding.  That, on top of the fact that most items have nearly un-observable passive effects that make figuring them our nigh-on impossible.  Couple that with the "usable" items and "super weapons" being unable to use until you go to Google to figure out which key does what, because you're given NO INSTRUCTION OF ANY KIND EVER.
I understand learning by experimentation, and games not taking you by the hand, but it has to be fun and worthwhile, like a Binding of Isaac or Dark Souls.  This game is simply not fun enough, rewarding enough, or well enough explained or made to be worth it.
We'll see what happens when it's finished, but unless you have twitch reflexes, and absolute precision I would avoid this game if I were you.

What a beautiful game. Every now and then I run across a game that just nails its genre. The Age of Wonders series makes me feel that way for example, and more recently, Mark of the Ninja -- a game that's just an absolute pleasure to play because the makers lavished attention on it to make it a joy, and the player wants it to never come to an end.  Dungeon Siege II is one of those games.
Everything that makes a fantasy action strategy game fun to play is in this game -- gorgeous artwork, evocative soundtrack, user-friendly interface, fully customizeable characters, great gear, generous loot drops, secret rooms, interesting and complicated quests, and far more gold than you could possibly need. Dungeon Siege II is like Torchlight's older brother, just as likeable but more grown up. Well, as grown up as a fantasy romp can be.

This is by far the funnest of the Dungeon Siege series! You don't have to play the first game to understand the story (which is pretty decent by the way).
The gameplay: It's similar to that of the Diablo series, it's point and click movement/combat, except that you can control a party of up to 6 characters (it's easier then it sounds). You can set each character to automatically perform a certain attack or spell. So the only character you have to actually worry about controlling is the one you choose to select as the leader. You gain skill points that you can spend on certain active and passive skills: shield block, less mana consumption for casting spells, dual wield extra damage, etc. The active skills you earn are based on what passive skills you choose. Example: by investing skill points into the passive skill "increase cold spell damage" you earn an active skill that blasts several shards of ice that do massive damage.
Adding the skill point system really improved the oversimplicity of the first Dungeon Siege leveling and combat system (don't get me wrong though, the first one was still fun too). Another addition, is that you can enchant items by finding or buying certain ingredients. You can make some really powerful armor/weapons. This feature definately adds more strategy and depth to the gameplay.
Lastly, the environments are very dynamic and beautiful. There are lots of fun extra dungeons/caves to explore.
I definately recommend this game!

The Nazis have come back as zombies led by sentient zombie Hitler and you (and preferably some friends) must gun them all down with sniper rifles, and occasionally shotguns/SMGs/pistols/etc.
Lots of interesting and detailed enemy types, from your standard Wehrmacht shambler to armored spooky skeletons to chainsaw-wielding SS soldiers. There's a lot of them so it might get a bit repetitive after a while: it's designed to be played co-op and whilst difficulty does scale down in solo play there is a certain something missing by playing alone.
Maps are pretty immersive and expansive, from secluded and foggy forests to the ruined heart of Berlin. Since this is a trilogy combining multiple releases, the chapters get more advanced and in-depth as you go along and you can see the jump between the games, although it's worth noting that all of the maps have been remastered in the new engine and have additional features so it's worth playing through them again even if you've played the standalone first or second chapters (the third chapter is new for everyone though, as it's exclusive to the trilogy- and is arguably the best with a lot more story elements).
Sniping mechanics are obviously the highlight of any Sniper Elite game, and it doesn't disappoint- you have to consider aspects such as distance and elevation when shooting unless you're playing on the easiest difficulty where the bullet simply goes wherever the crosshair is. Even though there's a lack of stealth in the zombie games (something that it's often criticised for) there's still plenty of tactical sniping positions and you're forced to utilise them in order to deal with giant hordes that you stumble across (not to mention when you're fighting zombie snipers- yes, some can use weapons).
Honestly it's a game that's best-played with mates in short bursts, but it's good for solo play as well. Hearty recommendation. I notice Sniper Elite 4 came out recently so maybe we'll get a Zombie Army 4. I certainly wouldn't mind.

There's little to be said about this masterpiece. Even being a 12 year old game, it didn't age too badly and still plays fantastically. Possible to launch it in 1080p with a bit of tinkering. Game does have it's flaws. For example: inventory system is really basic and once you start hitting 20-30+ hours into the game, and if you're a hoarder, it gets very difficult to find stuff that you need, since everything is thrown into one pile. Camera can take some getting used to, but overall won't be too much of a trouble. AI pathing is poor, ofter will your AI partners get stuck and you'll have to take control of them to make them move towards you again. Also your AI doesn't use health packs, stimulants, or any other consumable, half the time they don't even use their learned abilities. There is a "Script" option, but it's very basic, since you can't customize it, and it only offers 3 rudimentary options.
Some of the above mentioned negatives are more or less nitpicks, since this is technically a turn-based RPG, so you are encouraged to micromanage everything yourself, rather than let the AI do everything for you. This might be a deal breaker for some, but I personally did not find it too difficult to setup fights with my party, while also controlling my own character. Game does have a pause, so you can always pause and take a breather if things are getting out of hand.
As a 12 year old RPG game, it puts most today's RPG to shame with what it has to offer.
A must have game for any RPG, Star Wars fan, or even if you just like great games.

===
Genetic Disaster is a top-down, 2D twin stick shooter, mainly oriented towards co-op play. In this game, you can impersonate one of the available heroes, each having distinct abilities, and then start your adventure through procedurally-generated dungeons filled with traps and enemies. For some of the gameplay choices, it vaguely reminds me of The Binding Of Isaac, but just vaguely... i have to say, this game is a decent shooter, but lacks some gameplay components and technical polish to really shine.
===
Genetic Disaster comes in with a classic and straightforward top down shooter gameplay: each player controls a character, who is equippable with different weapons, depending what you find through the dungeon, each of them can carry a maximum of two weapons simultaneously. Levels are not particularly articulate and often have a main path and several side ones for additional rewards or access to facilities like shops or arenas, but are more than sufficent anyway, even if sometimes dungeon generation leads to ankward, nonsensical paths like bridges leading in dead ends. Each room of the dungeon will spawn enemies according to the number of players, more players mean more enemies, some rooms are more challenging than others and often lead to reward boxes, containing money or weapons. Note that each run of this game is rogue-like, meaning there are no checkpoints or saves, and when it's over, you have to restart from the beginning of the game; usually in roguelike types of games there is a persistent progression component that rewards players the more runs they accomplish, but in this case we found no such system, meaning each run does not unlock passive rewards or bonuses like it is common in roguelike games, a very debateable gameplay choice.
Combat is the most classic, twin-stick shooter-like you can imagine: enemies spawn alla round you and players have to dodge bullets while shooting back the enemy to defeat them. Each player has a somewhat limited HP pool and healing items are quite rare, so dodging and defeating enemies fast is important to progress and not get overwhelmed, so we can safely say this title is mainly skill-based as far as combat goes, which is good. Each hero has an unique ability to help himself or the team,l though i noticed not all of them are equally useful, some of them are (like the Shield Dome) while some others are near useless (like the Rage Shot). In between some levels, players will be able to access a roster of different passive abilities they can purchase with gold accumulated in previous levels, and use them to upgrade their characters with useful skills, like having more health, faster walk speed and many more, so there is some kind of progression but always limited to the current session and lost on death.
While procedural generation helps in keeping the gameplay fresh, the fact that there is no persistent progression after the sessions (like with, for example, passive unlockable abilities, or new characters and weapons unlockable only through specific requirements, etc.) really limits the experience and the game soon becomes repetitive by losing the sense of "global progression" that is one of the main factors in roguelike games. Also the quite limited variety of enemies, the absence of mini-bosses and such, and the overall not so varied quantity of events and variables present, do not contribute in making this game good content-wise, quite the opposite in fact.
Balancing quality is overall sufficent but just barely so. Some weapons of ven high rarity are pretty much useless or a waste of ammo, while others are largerly overpowered and useful, while some others are in the middle of these two situations. Overall, the game is somewhat balanced by the quantity of enemies and the rarity of healing items / stations, weapons need to be powerful to overcome such difficulties, but in some cases they are too powerful or too useless, this factor only being determined by sheer luck. In my opinion the main thingd that should be adjusted are reworking some weapons to be more efficent, and incresing enemy Ammo drops because running out of ammo in a twin stick shooter is a comic thing to happen.
This game delivers some decent challenge even at the first levels, which increases the more you proceed forward. Mainly the challenge is given by the rarity of healing items, so every bullet you get hit by plays a big part in your eventual defeat. The challenge can be more or less significant also because of luck, finding the right weapons can dramatically improve your odds, while finding useless ones will not. Overall, it fells like a good challenge.
===
Visuals in Genetic Disaster are quite a sight, being fully 2D presumably hand drawn with a remarkable and original style. While there is a visible absence of modern, advanced effects such as shaders, dynamic shadows, projected lights and so on, the style chosen by the developers works in delivering the toon-like, light-hearted atmosphere they probably had in mind with this game.
Sound effects are frankly quite boring and generic, and so is the soundtrack, it does not give that much needed energy and adrenaline any twin stick shooter soundtrack should give out, emphasizing speed and rushing forward towards the unknown. Not very good in this field.
Apart from the game stopping to respond when loading, this leading to gigantic loading times when a run is first started, there are no other mentionable problems about performance.
Nothing to report.
Enemy AI is what you can expect from a twin stick shooter: a simple follow and shoot when in sight script, which is totally alright.
Well, the control system with a gamepad is really not good, i had a very hard time aiming and controlling the character by using a gamepad, after that i resorted to mouse and keyboard which was so much better and did not have particular problems.
When using a gamepad, you cannot resurret your fallen teammates in a run. You can't! Me and my friend tried any button combination (he was using the gamepad) and it just did not work, and is nowhere to be found in any menu. This is quite a big problem. Also, there is NO OPTIONS MENU! This game quite frankly left early access a bit too soon don't you think?

Fantastic Strategy game that really comes into its own when you play multiplayer.
Some of the players are elitist and ex-military, which can be daunting when you first start, this however is due to the transitional period of playing the computer based AI campaign, to a much more aware, skilled and battle hardened multiplayer, especially if you play 1v1, 2v2, 3v3, 4v4, 5v5. Be ready to have someone let you know you are not supporting, or if you are doing things wrong during the first few days, this is a given.
The "deck" creation feature is a gem, this is where you create your armies for battles. You select which one of the decks you created to use before a battle, however the variations are staggering and this will generally dictact the way you approach a battle. If you want a balanced force or a heavily mechanized force, or want to reign air superiority then create the deck for your style and command them to victory! .... but beware, you will find yourself spending hours upon hours creating decks and trying them out to try get the perfect match, I know I have been trying for months because it is so addictive.
The only "con" I have is that 'some' of the multiplayer community are a little childish/abusive, however that can be said about most MMOGs, on the flip side the majority of ex or current serving military personnel that play the game are a good bunch and are quite entertaining to listen/talk to, especially  when they start telling their military stories :)
For me this is my favourite "non-base building RTS", and with the free DLC due to be released in the very near future this game is going from strength to strength!

I played through this game twice. The first time was with the numbers hidden while they still affect your choices; the second time was with the numbers on but still affecting your choices.
At the end of my first playthrough, I felt absolutely broken as if I'd never be happy again. As someone who can relate to the overall theme of the game, I thought I'd do a better job of taking care of the MC. Oops. In comparison to my my second playthrough, my fortitude levels were absolutely abysmal my first time through. I did too much and overextended the MC, and things I thought would affect me negatively actually affected me positively and vice versa.
If you go through the game blind, read through all the text and the various scenes, you'll probably get a solid 2+ hours out of the game. I highly recommend playing The Experience mode, where you can't see how your actions affect the MC until it's time to make a decision.
I really enjoyed this game, although considering how I felt at the end of my first playthrough perhaps "enjoyed" isn't the right word. The narrative makes it incredibly easy to empathize (or sympathize) with the MC. It can be frustrating (in a good way!) to see things unfold from an outsider's perspective, where you have an idea of how Will, Amy and Jenny really feel but the MC may not always see the reality of their feelings because of the situation the MC is in.
Really, it was such a gem. I absolutely loved the narrator, and somehow the second act took me by surprise.
The only negative thing I have to say is about the small handful of grammatical errors here and there. Their presence sometimes pulled me out of the game for a moment or two, but it wasn't anything absolutely terrible. One more readthrough of the game's script by the dev probably wouldn't hurt, though.
tl;dr I went in expecting to play a game with a depressed MC knowing how it would probably end, tried to make good choices, ended up making bad choices but loved every minute of the game anyway!

The first thing I should note about Ms. Splosion Man is if you're turned off by the aesthetic stop reading. Because that's the most notable part of the game.
I personally dislike the aesthetic of the game and find it annoying. But getting beyond that you have yourself a very entertaining sidescroller that focuses on building momentum via propelling yourself with explosions. The game introduces it's systems gradually and it includes a Mario 3-esque overworld. The game also has an extremely good soundtrack that remixes 80's music, and the pause menu music IS just 80s music.
Ms Splosion Man is great for speedrunners or casual enthusiasts to sidescrollers. It also keeps a decent length and is challenging to boot. Bare in mind it's not for everyone and unless you're curious I'd recommend watching a video of the gameplay before purchasing.

Amazingly Impressive.Playing this game reminded me of the days when I played Super Mario World and Donkey Kong Country on the SNES, it's just as addicting, this game is packed to the brim with personality, it's goes from funny to downright hilarious, I couldn't help as Ms. 'Splosion Man quoted famous singers like Beyonce and Lady Gaga and then turned right around and referenced movies like Predator and Willy Wonka, and the ending is probably one of the most funny things of all time, the gameplay is your basic platformer, easy to grasp but difficult to master, and has a lot of content, there are 47 single player levels, tons of unlockables and secret levels, and then 50 multiplayer levels, and shoes to collect in every one of the single player and multiplayer levels, so there is a lot to keep you busy, and just when you think you've seen everything the levels can offer they through in a new twist to keep you on your toes, but with all these good things it does have its flaws, long load times are frequent, while Ms. 'Splosion man's one liners are funny by the hundredth time you hear them they begin to lose their charm, same goes for the soundtrack, and levels could use more variety, and it can be frustratingly difficult at times, where if your even a hair off, or a split second too late or too early it means an instant death, but thankfully they gave you an option to skip sections that are too hard for you, and checkpoints are generally well placed but there are several levels that have awful checkpoints, and one minor complaint is that when you hit certain enemies they slam onto the screen blocking your view of what's happening, I found it incredibly annoying, but even with these flaws I found myself falling into the just one more level trap time and time again, this truly is a great game, and if your looking for a fun platformer and don't mind some punishing difficulty look no further, however the easily frustrated should look elsewhere.

The original Splosion Man on XBox 360 was quite literally...a blast. It was a somewhat masochistic platformer with a great gimmick of blowing yourself up to complete progressively difficult platforming challenges and its only real fault was that  the creativity sorta ran out by the game's midpoint.
At first glance, and even first play, Ms. Splosion Man can look and feel an awful lot like a reskin and rehash of the first game, but Ms. Pink and Sassy brings her own bit of originality to the formula that helps keep the concept flowing and interesting all the way to the end.
While the original game focused almost entirely on platforming, Ms. Splosion Man dashes in a fun bit of puzzle solving, twitch reaction focused speed sections, and fun boss encounters to keep things moving along at a nice pace without ever fizzling out. The stages are much more varied this time around and their scope much larger, which makes hunting down those elusive shoes and secret exits much more fulfilling since the paths to reach them are often fraught with much more danger than a stage's normal path.
All that said, Ms. Splosion Man is still a fairly difficult game, and checkpoints in stages can sometimes be a little too far apart, so if you're averse to not always having a love-love relationship with your games, you may wanna pass. But if you're up for a bright, upbeat, and endlessly endearing bit of hardcore platforming, Ms. Splosion Man's got something that'll keep you nice and charged up.

Project Highrise is a fantastic skyscraper builder, following in the footsteps of SimTower and Hotel Giant. It offers a good amount of replayability (up to a point), and getting your tower up to a sustainable level that you can make profit off of it is a joy to do. As you build up your tower, more and more rooms can be built to generate more income, and each room requires different needs - offices will originally need Courier and Copying services, but will then need Executive Suites in end-game situations.
The graphics follows a simplistic styling, meaning it is not too heavy on older PC's at early stages. From both far away and up close, you can easily tell which rooms are of which room type, and when closer up you can easily tell the different subtypes of room each room is.
Citizens and tourists in the tower will seem to try and find the quickest route to their rooms or shops, and so placing the elevators and stairs at the far end of the 'soon-to-be' skyscraper is one of the best approaches to go. I would, however, prefer that citizens would take the quickest route at the time - if different elevators have more traffic, the citizens would go to less busy elevators. This may already be the case, although I can't tell usually.
There's quite a bit of micromanagement in Project Highrise, like raising and lowering taxes, which has positive and negative effects based on what you do. As well as this, there is quite a bit of randomness in the events that take place, like local businesses shutting down and your tower profiting from increased tourism. It's an interesting concept, albeit not unique, as it can be positive or negative for your tower.
All in all, it's probably worth an 8/10 by reviewer standards, but as a tower builder its definitely up there with the best.

One of the best Star Wars licence game ever made and one of the best RPG games of all time. Period.
There's little to be said about this masterpiece. Even being a 12 year old game, it didn't age too badly and still plays fantastically. Possible to launch it in 1080p with a bit of tinkering. Game is fairly unstable on modern OS and in one playthrough crashed about 7 or 8 times. Still, all technical negatives aside the game still feels wonderfully crafted. Endless dialogs, various quests, different and varied locations and choices with serious consequences - all these elements are only a small part of the whole KOTOR package. HK-47 is probably one of the best video characters BioWare has ever made, or even in general.
Game does have it's flaws. For example: inventory system is really basic and once you start hitting 20-30+ hours into the game, and if you're a hoarder, it gets very difficult to find stuff that you need, since everything is thrown into one pile. Camera can take some getting used to, but overall won't be too much of a trouble. AI pathing is poor, ofter will your AI partners get stuck and you'll have to take control of them to make them move towards you again. Also your AI doesn't use health packs, stimulants, or any other consumable, half the time they don't even use their learned abilities. There is a "Script" option, but it's very basic, since you can't customize it, and it only offers 3 rudimentary options.
Some of the above mentioned negatives are more or less nitpicks, since this is technically a turn-based RPG, so you are encouraged to micromanage everything yourself, rather than let the AI do everything for you. This might be a deal breaker for some, but I personally did not find it too difficult to setup fights with my party, while also controlling my own character. Game does have a pause, so you can always pause and take a breather if things are getting out of hand.
As a 12 year old RPG game, it puts most today's RPG to shame with what it has to offer.
A must have game for any RPG, Star Wars fan, or even if you just like great games.

I don't usually review games, but Please Knock on My Door, to some degree, compels me to.
I will preface this by saying that I did two playthroughs of the game with both playthroughs having very different "stories" and "endings". If you are someone that has suffered anxiety, stress, depression, or a mental illness in general you are going to have a deep connection to this game. As somone who has suffered from depression and anxiety for a very long time I can say that this game hits home...it hit's home in a way that is deep, raw, and unfiltered. It's a summary of what it is like to deal with these issues on a day to day basis. Some of the struggles, the energy that is needed to accomplish tasks, loss, nagging thoughts/emotions, and the frailty of it all. It is a game that is going to make you feel. Cough cough I ugly cried cough cough.
The controls are simple walking around. Left, right, up, and down. Some clicking here and there. There isn't a lot of "gameplay". You are along for the story.
If you have played other story rich indie games like Night in the Woods or The Beginners Guide this is in the same vein.
Would I recommend Please Knock on My Door? I've played through it twice and plan to keep playing for quite a bit more. I would absolutely recommend it
Edit: I think the best way to play this game the first time is "The experience", after that probably "The Story", and then "The Game". Really "The Experience" feels more like a sim where as the others just give you a bit too much information via "stats"

The Good
- Great soundtrack, with each character having a unique theme which you can listen in the armory or after earning kill streak with the character.
- Nice vibrant graphics
- Over 25 characters to play as (should you unlock them).
- People who purchased teh game before the launch to 'free to play' get a unique avatar, extra awesompoints to unlock charters and pics as well as all their previously owned characters avaialble to play as.

The Bad
- Game can crash when you launch it

Ah Awesomenauts, what a ride you've been.
Balance has been a pretty big issue since the release of the game, there are always at least two or three characters who are way ahead of the rest of the cast in terms of viability. Some characters take months to get changed despite complaints, and by the time they do get changed, they can become nerfed to the point of not being viable anymore. This also goes the other way, however; some characters that are considered weak or bad are buffed too much and become quite a nuissance. If you can look past that, and Ronimo's rather slow pacing when it comes to buffing or nerfing characters, you have a really good game that is very fun to play.
Map designs are pretty good, giving every character something to do well at on at least one of them. There aren't very many maps though, which is something that I hope to be addressed in the future. And not every map is perfect, some are blatantly shifted in favor of certain characters with powerful area denial tools. It's not very fun to come through a portal and instantly be snared on Starstorm, for example.
Characters are silly and have good voice acting! Every character has a unique and distinctive personality, along with several funny lines to boot. Whether it be some movie reference or just some silly joke, the lines are pretty great. Some of the newer Nauts have interactions with one another, which is always a treat. TotalBiscuit voices Vinnie and Spike, need I say more?
The controls are easy to use and feel very fluid. WASD and space for all your movement needs! Platforming feels great, everyone is able to make most jumps. Obviously some characters are able to do more than that, but that's part of their kit for the most part, like if you can fly or have a quadruple jump. Some characters have special/unique things that they can do when it comes to movement, but nothing too major that breaks the game. There's anti-flying zones at the top of maps to keep flying characters in check, they don't want you going to the moon.
All microtransactions are purely cosmetic, you can unlock every single character by just playing the game. Playing matches gives you Awesomepoints, which you can use to unlock portraits and new characters! If you want a snazzy new skin though, they aren't that expensive. Like most games, skins do not do anything besides be purely cosmetic. The game is not pay to win by any means. Some Nauts do take longer to unlock than others with their pricing system, but keep in mind that just because a character is higher up in terms of Awesomepoints, it doesn't always mean they're a better character.
Connection can be another issue in the game, as it is peer to peer. Peer to peer has never been a good idea, you will have matches every now and then against people with really high ping. The host will swap around if the ping gets bad enough, which basically pauses the game for a few seconds. This can be a really bad thing if you're in front of a turret... There is thankfully a setting to keep people you get qued with limited to only your region, and while it definitely helps, it can only do so much. Hopefully Ronimo eventually makes some dedicated servers.
The playerbase is like most games, you have a lot of toxic people, but you do have some nice people out there as well. I have been playing this game for about four years and it's nothing new. You can always disable in-game chat if you are getting harassed too much, which I would suggest if you're newer to the game and are just wanting a good experience. You can also invite two other friends for a premade, which is honestly the best experience you can have. So grab your buddies and get in there.

Quite possibly one of the best shoot-em-up games in history.  This game has a unique gameplay twist where you can keep stacking on more and more ships with every 1UP you get.  You can easily have 30 ships under your control.  Using the left and right triggers you can expand your ships to take up a larger area on the screen or you can compress them down to the size of a single ship.  You might not think there would be any reason to expand them but the weapons change a bit once you spread them out, making it very handy in some cases but increasing danger by giving yourself a larger area to get hit.
I've never seen a shmup where the direction will change from moving upwards, to sideways, to backwards, constantly throughout the levels.  You often have a choice of which direction to go as well.  Not only is this mechanic unique, it's also exectuted perfectly.  Truly a benchmark for the genre.
They could have made it a bit longer though.  I was able to beat the entire game (on normal difficulty) on my first playthrough in 20 minutes.  There were quite a few stages and there is even another game mode where you do not have extra ships, just a single one where you can continuously keep upgrading it over time (but you can only get hit once for each stage or you lose that progress).  This mode is more difficult but adds to the replayability factor.  The Steam leaderboards work well too so even if you were a master of the game, you can keep replaying it to get as high on the leaderboard as possible.
I also loved to see the inclusion of the almost-naked girls everywhere in that one level and the boss battle with the giant girl who shoots you from her nipples.  Although it sort of throws the atmosphere off, it is still tastefully implemented.
I can't wait to try some co-op with a friend.  A must-have for any shmup fan!

I finished this game in one sitting of a little over 6 hours, and absolutely loved it!
Pros:
1) The acting is good. Not "Hollywood movie" good, but quirky and entertaining where it needs to be and serious where it doesn't. I loved it. Jenks, Ryan Rand, and Paul Rand were tremendously amusing. Everyone else was fine as well, of course. But they were the stars.
2) The music isn't too bad.
(Though it does have its troubles, mentioned below in the "cons" section.)
3) The scenes are shot well and the transition clips are good.
4) The look of everything is enjoyable.
5) Unpredictable, at least to me. I had no concrete ideas (only educated guesses) regarding who was responsible for what up to the end. Everything about the clues and what it gave you to work with was very interesting, and its narrative weaves an intricate web.
Cons:
1) The UI was a bit buggy a couple times. The first time I spoke to Ryan Rand I couldn't exit and had to restart the game (thus forcing me to do the conversation again). But I never had that issue after and the other minor UI issues I had during interviews weren't game-breaking.
(Be sure you save semi-often! Perhaps after every round of questioning on a new clue.)
2) The ambient noises had a mild sound of compression that I could hear, and being something of an audio engineer, I found it slightly annoying at first, but it stopped bothering me pretty quickly. I also have the EQ set on my PC in such a way that these noises might appear to me when they may not to others (necessary for when I edit audio).
3) The music is cool and mostly fitting, but nothing overly memorable, and while I did also list the music in the "pros" section, I will note that a couple of times the music that started during certain scenes for mood continued into other parts such as interviews and sort of drowned out the actors as they spoke. I tried to correct for this by adjusting the (limited) in-game audio settings, but that didn't actually resolve the issue entirely. The game does have subtitles, however, so at least there's that, and this wasn't that big of a difficulty. It only occurred twice or so. I also found that closing and opening the game once stopped the music from playing. Regardless, I suppose they could've cleaned this up a bit.
Rating:
9/10.
Contradiction is definitely worth the price (I'd pay a little more for it, to be honest), and just the right length for someone like me who doesn't have too much time to devote to games.
I hope there's a sequel!
P.S. This is the first game that I've ever bothered to review on Steam.

While N++ might look simplistic, N++ focuses on what is most important, gameplay. N++ takes your typical platformer and focuses on what is most important, running and jumping. All you do in the game is run and jump avoiding obstacles to open the door and escape the level. This might sound simplistic but N++ works because the gameplay is so satisfying. The controls work really well and I love how the game feels as you need to use momentum while moving and jumping. If you like platformers I don't know why you wouldn't enjoy N++'s gameplay.
N++ also shines in the amount of content you get. The game has thousands of levels and even though they are only around 10-20 seconds long you can expect to get at least 10 hours out of the game. N++ also includes a level editor so the game could end up being close to endless if players develop good levels for the game.
Basically I only have two small complaints about N++. First not all of the levels are created equally. A lot of the levels are really good but there are your occasional levels that are kind of bland. When you have thousands of levels that is to be expected though. Second while I really enjoyed N++ I don't see it as a game to play for hours at a time. I see it more as the type of game that you play for 30 minutes to an hour each day and then come back to another day.
N++ is a very good platformer. If you like platformers I can't see you not enjoying N++.

Battleborn is the newest game from Gearbox games with the same tongue in cheek humor as the Borderlands series.  With 24 heroes and more to come, Battleborn is an arena shooter with the skill building mechanics similar to MOBAs. While not inherently a MOBA itself, Battleborn does take a lot of elemets from many genres and smashes them together. In essence there is a hero for any play type and a whole lot to play in the game. The Story mode is good clean fun that you can play co-op with friends or random strangers that really brings out the games humor. If you keep your mind open to the game your sure to have a lot of fun with it.

Hard to take this game seriously until it gets a balance patch. Miko must have a 90 percent winrate in incursion mode. Games take too long in this mode and rarely do they swing the other way after one team gets an upper hand in the first 10 mins.
Single player involves moving from one defend point to another and fighting waves. You might get thirty minutes into a mission and fail if the point is taken leaving you with nothing but wasted time, this probably wont happen to you more than a few times though once you get a feel for it. Although connection issues in coop might cause other players to dc from a match making it impossible to finish.
The system for creating loadouts is neat, but the items are fairly limited and don't let you specialise as much as you might want.
A positive is the large roster of characters, though many of them feel a little too straight forward. Probably half of them you wont want to play more than a couple of times. In Versus matchmaking you have no knowledge what the other team might pick, so you are kind of playing a guessing game as to how effective the hero you pick might be.
This game has a few things going for it, but at the moment with its current content and state it is hard to recommend.
I could see this being much better in 3-6 months with some balance patches and content releases. Then again maybe no one is playing it by then as overwatch seems to have stolen its thunder (though they seem to be doing different things)

TL;DR - Try to get it for around $40 when you can. For that value it's a great game. Mostly a multiplayer game. Borderlands meets MOBAs (basically FPS League of Legends)!!!

It comes with a short little storyline played in missions with big boss enemies throughout. But what you're really paying for is the multiplayer. It's got first person mechanics (not unlike Overwatch, if you've been following that), but the actually gameplay modes are VERY reminiscent of MOBAs (like League of Legends), complete with equipment to buy as you collect currency and character growth as you collect XP throughout the course of a game. It's got a few extra tower-defense-esqe elements in there, like building/upgradings emplacements around the map, but the focus is mostly on escorting groups of minions through the enemy's fortifications to reach some objective on their side of the map.

Really enjoying my time in this game so far, I think it's been grossly underated, Everyone seem to think that Overwatch is the better game, when really, BOTH titles are good in their own rights, this and Overwatch are not even remotely alike, other than they are FPS. Battleborn actually breathes some new live into the fps genre,by adding moba style PvE/PvP gameplay. So far i have only played the Prologue and Muliplayer aspects so far, but there are plenty of game modes to keep you interested.  If you like Borderlands, it's graphical style and it's humour, this will be right up you street, well written and voiced dialogue.  Recommended Purchase.

+ Compelling plot
+ Dialogues (apart from Aliens' lines)
+ Characters

+ Force powers and skills

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is a well-acclaimed RPG made by Bioware. Its action is set 4000 years before the Galactic Empire. The war between the Republic and the Dark Sith Lord named Malak is raging. The protagonist is merely a Republic soldier at first, but, as the story progresses, he/she starts to play a much more important role. It turns out that the main character has a strong connection to the Force and has to train as a Jedi.
The player can choose between three classes for the protagonist: Soldier (expert in combat), Scoundrel (rogue), Scout (jack of all trades), and, later on, 3 Jedi classes: Guardian (focus on lightsabre combat), Consular (focus on Force powers), and Sentinel (jack of all trades). Every class has its own strengths and weaknesses and require a different approach so choose wisely.
The main hero will not travel alone. There are a few characters who will join him on the journey. Every companion has a story and motives behind them so it is worth to talk with them. Moreover, they add yet another layer to the rich plot.
The gameplay is focused on doing quests, visiting planets, levelling, and, of course, combat. The game's mechanics are based on D&D 3.5. Fortunately, it is made accessible even to the players who are new to RPGs. There is a huge variety of skills, feats, and Force powers at your disposal which definitely contributes to longevity of the game. Most of the time, the player leads a small group (with up to two companions) and ventures forth. All characters are controllable and while they seem to do well enough on their own, there are issues with pathfinding and sometimes the characters get stuck. This is particularly noticeable in locations with tight corridors.
Throughout the game, the player will have make many decisions. The choices can have a huge influence on the outcome. This is one of the biggest strengths of the game. Speaking of the freedom of choice, the player is able to choose between the light and the dark side as they see fit. Earning light side points make using the light Force powers cost less and using the dark ones cost more and vice versa. This is one of the first games where being the bad guy is just as doable as being the saviour of the Galaxy. While remaining relatively neutral is possible, it is not a very viable choice. For instance, there are some items which are restricted to either side of the Force spectrum. Moreover, the player more often than not will be forced to join one side of a conflict or to take some action. Be wary of your choices, for the Galaxy is at stake!
Saving the Galaxy (or dooming it to fall) can be exhausting. Worry no more, for there is a lot to do in your free time. Apart from a myriad of side-quests, there also are minigames, namely pazaak (blackjack on steroids) and swoop racing. Not only they are enjoyable but also can give you extra credits.
However, there are some serious technical issues. The game is utterly crawling with bugs*. For instance, it is not an uncommon occurrence when the dialogues start to skip. Restarting the game and reloading a previous save seems to help, but it is a glitch worth mentioning. What is more, teammates may sometimes stop attacking the foes. While I have not found any gamebreaking bugs, it is very sensible to save often and in different slots** just in case. Speaking of downsides, I am not particularly fond of the camera and movement. It is not bad per se, but it may take a while to get used to. And last but not least, there are few Aliens' dialogue lines so they get extremely repetitive after some time.
Concluding, this is one of the best RPGs I have ever played. Its compelling plot alone makes it outstanding and the decision-making adds to its replay value. If you do not mind dated graphics and are able to get past the technical issues, the game will reward you with a memorable experience. They just do not make games like they used to...
*Yes, I am aware it's a terrible pun. I apologise.
**Yes, you've heard it right: you can save whenever you want and in different slots. It used to be an "industry standard" back in a day. No silly checkpoints and such.

Ryse - Son of Rome is an excellent game. It looks amazing, is superbly acted with great sound design. Everything about this game is AAA with a Hollywood blockbuster Scale.
Its story is one of the best I’ve played in a game in some time. Driving you naturally towards each set piece. From barbarian hordes invading Rome, to Britannia and back to Rome via the colosseum arena. A story of Gods and Mortal man’s revenge and betrayal.
Game play will be instantly familiar to those who have played the likes of Batman Origins or Shadow of Mordor, throwing in just enough of its own magic to set it apart. The game is extremely violent and bloody, befitting the time period. Sword and shield strokes feel like they have real weight in no small part thanks to the sound and art design. The Crytek engine looks fantastic at 2x super sampling. Would love to see this at 4K
But it does have its problems and those are based around the front end. The most glaring of these is the inability to rebind keyboard and mouse. The various set ups might suite your needs but it’s inexcusable when the rest of the game is built with such polish and attention to detail.
Overall Ryse though is a game that deserves a follow up. Hopefully Microsoft and Crytek can sort out their differences with regards to who owns what.

Humanity is on the ropes yet again. What is it with mankind anyway? It seems like every alien race in the universe wants to see us enslaved, obliterated, or pushed into the mud. Once again you're the lone hero who must push back, and you can't stop until the extraterrestial menace is well and truly wiped out. Shoot 1UP starts with the most basic concept imaginable: You shoot, and you collect 1UPs. Since I grew up on arcade 2D shooters, I'm surprised to see any game where more than two or three extra lives can be attained per play-through. In Shoot 1UP, you get a 1UP every two or three seconds. Wow, not only is it Christmas, but I got the cyborg unicorn that I always wanted.
Now hang on a second. What's with this generosity? In this game, you don't control one ship, you control up to 30. That's right, all of those extra lives are under your control at the same time. So let's just say you're in charge of a squadron. The triggers on your Xbox 360 controller expand and contract your squadron. When expanded, the ships can cover more ground, and this increases the multiplier. This also results in a wicked sweet laser. When you need to conserve ships, that's when you contract for that extra space. Note that contracting is a concious decision to place survival over score, which means your multiplier drops. Once you get a handle on the controls, it isn't hard to figure out when and where to spread your squadron.
Now if you want the best of both worlds (survival and scoring) you have to master the shield. By letting go of the fire button, you start building energy for a shield. Hit the fire button again, and all bullets and most enemies are destroyed. Shield-kills result in a HUGE multiplier bonus, so you'll want to go for them whenever possible. Granted, not every situation will allow you to easily shield-kill everything, so you should use your shot/laser weapons to weaken larger enemies before attempting the finishing blow. Shield-kills are risky because they can result in lost ships due to collisions or stray bullets. When your ships are destroyed, they create small explosions that eliminates nearby bullets and enemies. Unfortunately, this means you don't get a fat multiplier bonus. It's like poetry.
Each of the six stages revolves around applying what you've just learned. Enemies will come from multiple angles; all with their own tactics. It's up to you to figure out how to destroy everything, get the highest possible score, but with minimal losses. This aspect of the game can lead to some very inventive play. Since you're controlling multiple ships at once, you have to monitor their positions, making slight movements to avoid dangers. It's very important that you don't spend too much time playing defensively. The harder difficulties make it seem like you're supposed to play it safe. However, if you don't take the initiative, everything becomes increasingly claustrophobic. Since you have to destroy enemies to obtain 1ups, it can mean sacrificing one ship, in order to obtain two ships. Above all, don't forget about the shield. It's actually a very powerful weapon, and can make short work of most enemies when properly timed.
The Score Trek mode takes Shoot 1UP into a different direction. You're given one ship that becomes stronger with each power-up collected. However, since you're limited to a single solitary ship, it's game over if you take a hit. To balance this out, the game saves after the completion of each stage. Once you defeat the last boss, you start again on a harder loop. This continues for I don't know how long. There's an achievement for completing at least five successive loops. The key to scoring in this mode is simple: abuse the shield. With each loop, the shield becomes more effective. Before long, it's faster to destroy bosses with shields than anything else. Conceptually, this is a neat extra, but it's a little too one-dimensional compared to the main game.
Aside from the long-term appeal found in all shmups, which is playing for the hi-score, Shoot 1UP's original ideas and abstract art-style are what give it staying power. Controlling multiple ships at once is a cool idea, and it's thoroughly explored, as opposed to having an idea but never bothering to capitalize on it. The standard level of difficulty isn't too high. This gives players an incentive to really learn how everything works, so they can maximize their score. Mommy's Best Games always has an eye for choosing colors that I never knew existed. While the environments are repetitive, the creature design is well-done, and the art-direction reminds me something found on the Amiga. All in all, I think this game is worth checking out.

In addition to the above disclaimer, though, I should note that I bought Shoot 1Up several years before this on XBox Live Indie Games, and that it quickly became - and still is - one of my personal favorite "homebrew" shooters. As the official description says, in most scrolling "shmups" you control one ship at a time and simply switch in one of your reserve lives when you die, but here 1Up items are not only fairly commonplace but are deployed instantly, to the point where you can control up to 30 onscreen fighters simultaneously, A novel concept, certainly, but more important is how well the developer has implemented his marquee mechanic, and thus created something much more noteworthy than a never-to-be-revisited experiment for its own sake.
While the only "main" buttons you ever have to worry about here are "move", "shoot", and "brake" (which slows you down for more precise positioning), the "expand" and "contract" commands are equally important - hold down the former and your squadron expands outward in a circle formation (but will squish together when pressed against the screen's edge), while the latter will condense everyone down to the size of a single ship. Staying tightly together makes dodging enemies and their attacks, which come from all sides of the screen, much easier, but also limits your firepower to "pea shooter" power - to really wreak some havoc you'll need to get dangerous and spread out, which not only sends shots in additional directions but unleashes the huge "plasma auger" laser, which is great for mowing baddies down.
If you prefer to get more up close and personal with the opposition there's also the "burst" weapon. If you stop shooting for a moment a circle will start to expand around each of your fighters; tap "fire" after this and a short-range blast within the circles' area will heavily damage enemies and cancel bullets too. Your final "weapon" is the explosion left behind when one of your ships eats an attack; like the burst it causes heavy damage and neutralizes enemy fire, giving you a chance to regroup and get back on the offensive.
What really makes all of the above so engaging, however, is the scoring system. It's actually very simple: basically, the more spread-out your formation is, the more valuable the point items destroyed enemies drop. Moreover, finishing baddies off with the "burst" grants an additional bonus, so if you're brave enough to both leave your fighters vulnerable and get right in your targets' faces before unloading at the last second, you'll be swimming in points in no time. That said, extra lives are not point-dependent, so newer players are free to progress more conservatively and get the feel for things, while genre vets can jump right into the heavy risk-reward stuff: it should be noted that just getting to the end isn't particularly difficult or drawn-out, even on the "Hard" difficulty setting, so the real challenge here comes from score attacking and mastering the constant tug-of-war between moving out or falling back.
Mommy's Best Games has always had a knack for creating memorable, irreverent and occasionally disturbing visuals for its releases, and that talent is on full display here: a strange, unnerving combination of the organic and mechanical infuses every sprite and background on offer, from fortress-sized protozoa to militarized orca corpses to the infamous "robo-boob" lady boss, and almost makes you forget that there's a pretty run-of-the-mill "last desperate hope against the alien menace" plot behind it all. The sound takes a similar tack, with most of the music more subdued and foreboding than you usually expect from a shooter, and a good deal of unearthly wailing and bellowing emitting from the bosses in particular, alongside the requisite bevy of explosions.
Finally, if you prefer a slightly more "traditional" shooter experience there's also an easily-unlockable "Score Trek" mode, which limits you to a single ship (this means Game Over after one hit, so be careful) whose power increases in a more traditional fashion via the "1Up" items. Moreover, you can save your progress after every level to mitigate the reduced margin of error, and the game loops upon completion, so your opportunities for climbing up the leaderboards are limited only by your persistence. Two new modes ("Goof-off", which grants loads of extra 1Ups, and "Turn-based", which pauses the action when no buttons are pressed) and numerous tweaks (prettier score medals, incoming enemy warnings, adjusted squadron movement, etc.) have been added for the Steam release, so unless you're really down on "oddball" games or scrolling shooters in general I simply can't think of too many reasons not to recommend this, especially for the asking price.

I was lucky enough to beta test Shoot 1UP.  I offered myself up as a low tech option since I'm still running Vista 64-bit.  The game runs well.  A 1.5x video scale option was even introduced for those with low resolutions.
I'm not the most skilled player, but I managed to 1CC the game on normal difficulty on my first attempt.  I've been a wannabe long enough to know I should spend that time on survival.  However, I often found myself risking a wide formation to earn greater point medals just because it felt so natural... As expected, my meandering was punished on the higher difficulty. ;)
There's room to tweak runs.  Ship spread can be adjusted for multipliers, levels fork, and there's a rechargeable shield mechanism which can result in a score multiplier when used offensively.  For those with casual-intermediate skill like myself, trying to master the basics while taking the harder fork choices on normal difficulty seems a good fit.
Some may believe the game is short.  However, the circles I lurk in have always claimed that roughly 20 minutes is the perfect time for a shmup.  The goal is to continue playing and reaching higher scores.  You're going to get out of it what you put in.  If you're still dedicated to completing it only once, I recommend playing for survival on the highest difficulty to pad the time with your deaths/retries.  There's also an endless mode which trades the fleet for a more traditional lone ship and saves progress.
Loved it.  Played it on my 5 year old desktop no problems.  Harder then I was expecting, but I don't play shootem ups very often.

Shoot 1UP is all about controlling multiple ships at once. When you pick up an extra life (a 1up), instead of just increasing the number of times you can die, it adds another ship to the screen for you to control. Obviously it's a challenge to keep up to 30 ships alive at the same time, but not because of the game's controls, which make controlling a whole squadron of ships surprisingly straightforward.
It's possible to play the game very conservatively by keeping your ships tightly stacked and using the shield mechanic, but if you want to get a high score you'll have to split up your ships and make good use of all the abilities at your disposal.
The game is very short (I beat the normal difficulty in about 20 minutes), but there's plenty of replay value, between two ship types, achievements, optional side paths in levels, several scalable difficulty options, co-op multiplayer, and global score leaderboards. There's also an endless 'score trek' more which gets harder the farther you get, but you only have one ship - which feels a bit lonely after playing the regular mode.
This is a neat little shmup that can be played casually, but which drives you to master its unique mechanics if you want to get a huge high score, or if you just want to kill every enemy on the screen at once.

Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes is an open world, 3rd person Action/Stealth set as the prologue for the full game Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain.  The first question you should ask is should I play this or just skip to the main meal that is Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain? I would recommend playing this, as it will introduce you to many of the game concepts that are used in The Phantom Pain. As someone who hasn’t played any of the Metal Gear games on previous systems it also introduces you a whole host of important characters, lore and the main antagonist of The Phantom Pain. You can also abduct/help certain people on the island that will appear as staff on your main base in The Phantom Pain, which will give you an early game boost to your bases ranking for upgrades.
You control Snake for all of the missions except a side mission which you control Raiden. I found controlling both characters fun (Raiden’s mission was about killing body snatcher aliens and was quite enjoyable). As snake you can slither, sneak, run and gun and hijack enemy vehicles to rescue Chico and Paz from XOF. The emergency evacuation side mission where you rescue Hideo Kojima, was a blast, and if you collect all the badges around the island there’s a funny scene of snake catching them- it’s nice to see these little touches though out the game. Unlike the Phantom Pain, Ground Zeroes rewards you being super quick through the missions, so the optional objects can mostly be skipped (I would recommend doing them to fully complete your experience, unlock the side op’s and pick up the logs to listen to what is happening).
The game itself is short, but since it’s a prologue that is to be expected. By the end of it I was eagerly awaiting the Phantom Pain’s release, as Ground Zeroes ending finishes on a cliff hanger. Some content has been censored as some of Paz’s tortures tapes can be quite distressing to listen to, and the ending is also difficult to watch once you know what Paz has been through.
The graphics and attention to detail look amazing, and the voicework is also really well done. If you are a fan of the series then snake’s main voice actor was replaced with Kiefer Sutherland (that is a different arguments) who does amazing work, and it shouldn’t let you be put off playing this (without giving away vast parts of the plot it makes sense for this to be the case in the Phantom Pain, but not so much in Ground Zeros).
Other than boycotting the Metal Gear series for Konami dreadful treatment of Hideo Kojima (the series creator) and replacing Snakes original voice actor (David Hayter) there is no reason to not own and play this.

If you were thinking of grabbing this game now is a great time, Zombie Army Trilogy is on sale in the Humble Bundle store for their zombie week sale right now for around $9.00.
And incase you've been on the fence here's my little review about the game:
-Excellent gunplay!
Can't stress this point enough, game is plain fun to play because of this. On the hardest setting things like wind and bullet drop are real, though don't be afraid to break out the machine gun or shotty when the need arises (and it will often).
-Zombie killing done right!
Like L4D but WW2 style, but slower zombies, but plenty of them and it often requires a head shot to take them down or they'll rez (you can play 4 player co op, and if someone goes down you can help them back up if you do it before they bleed out/ you can blow a zombie in half and he'll often still keep crawling to get to you and hit you).
-Decent amount of special type zombies
I don't wanna ruin this one for you, but lets just say it's a sniper game so... and if you hear heavy foot steps and machine gun fire get ready ;).
-Cool xray kills in Single Player
You'll see an inside shot of where your bullet hits the zombies -maybe it'll enter his eye and bounce down his spine or maybe you'll blow the teeth out his mouth (in mulitplayer you get a dumbed down quick version of just the bullet cam so that you don't slow down game play when playing with others or desync from them).
-Various different Weapons/ useables/deployables
Ask any 2 people and they may not agree on what the best weapons are -everyone has a fav., for the deployable/useables you can get gernades, trip mines, land mines, and dynamite -most of which you can shoot to make blow up as well (good for setting traps/ clearing huge groups at a time, not to mention there are things you can shoot in the environment that'll explode and useable turrets placed through out).
-2 game modes, Campaign and Horde mode
Horde mode (basically a wave/hold out kind of mode which is fun to play all on it's own) has like 5 maps (well done I might add; they aren't just straight rips from campaign mode), and campaign (this is the story mode where you work your way through Hitler's zombie armies in various areas and try to put a stop to it all) has like 3 episodes with 5 chapters per episode.
-Pretty good amount of gameplay here (I clocked in about 80 hours by the time i beat it having replayed some areas with different friends/horde mode play some as well) esp. if you put it the hardest setting; some areas can be pretty challenging to get past thanks to the Elites that I dub Heavy Gunners.
-Great Gibs
Zombie parts everywhere when explosions blow/ shoot a zombie in the arm/leg/head with a sniper rifle or shot gun and a good chance you'll blow it off (or maybe even blow him in half if you hit him in the right area).
-Great Co Op fun
Took me back to my days of L4D that my team and I played the heck out of.
-Plenty of ways to control the difficulty -you can choose different difficulty settings (on sniper elite bullet drop, wind, stance, and breathing is a real thing to consider for instance not to mention lower health regen rate etc.) and then on top of it choose to set the spawns according to the number of people -for instance if you wanted to make the game easier you could have 4 people playing but set it to spawn zombies for 2 people or you could flop it around and make it spawn enough zombies for 4 people yet only be playing with 2 people, and even further yet you can choose to turn friendly fire on or off.
-it's a good game though a few of the only downsides are:
-xray kills don't work in multiplayer (they are pretty darn cool in single player- when the bullet hits you'll get an xray of the skeleton in the zombie and see what you hit or break, but in multiplayer you get like a quick bullet cam sometimes -only without the xray part)
-the net code is a little wonky so if you aren't host chances are you'll have a little lag, but it's def. dealable and not worth skipping the game over
-some of the monsters will glitch out here or there (only the one part in the one chapter does often, the part where you have to fend off a horde of skellys with a bunker and a turret on either side- a few of the skellys will get half stuck in the ground and times and you'll have to shoot them or maybe restart the check point)
-the one horde map may be glitched out or atleast glitch out on lower end pc's because of the sheer amount of enemies that show (it crashed the game out on me twice in a row at that wave; I've yet to retry that yet)
All in all though I'd say if you enjoy zombie killin' and like the idea of a WW2 setting this game is def. worth a buy and a steal at the sale price on HB's store.

Though this game may look intimidating, it really isn't. In fact, its as far from a grognard (read hex based 100 page manual) game as starcraft 2 is. However, that's the only comparison to Starcraft 2 that this game will get. Wheras in starcraft 2 economy is everything and APM is your life, in this game, strategy, positioning and most importantly, countering, are paramount. If you liked World in Conlict, you'll like this game. Also you might like this game if you are a fan of Magic: the Gathering, because of the deck building mechanic. In each game you play, you choose a deck of units to bring into battle, that you have preconstructed. Decks have various constraints that can be put on them to make them more powerful in certain areas, and the possibilites are endless, from Norwegian Armoured Decks, to Soviet Marine Decks, this game has it all.
The best part? All the DLC is free. Not just for this game, but for every game in the series.
Playing around with the various units, and building, testing, refining then testing your decks again is one of my favorite things in the game to do.
The only downside to this game is that the sequel, Red Dragon is set to come out in March 2014. As of this review, that is less than 4 months away. If you are hurting for money, you may want to save it for Red Dragon. It promises to add naval units and East Asian nations like Japan and North Korea.
All in all, whatever game happens to be the latest in the Wargame series at the time that you read this is a must buy.

I don't remember when am I purchase this game but I have finished it recently.Sadly that I didn't have time to try multiplayer. I just review the Single player.
This game is talking about a man call Marius who save Rome from bandits. I like his father. He seems so kind. However, he died at the beginning of the game :(
Let's talk about the battle, shall we? I use a controller to play this game. I didn't try keyboard.
There 4 common actions, attack, Break, Block and dodge. If you are facing a shield enemy, you need to break it first.
In some situation, Block is more useful. If you block enemy's attack just before he attacking you, he would lose his defense. I finish this game two times in different difficulty, Normal and Legendary. I seldom use dodge in Normal but Legendary. When more than three enemies stand in front of you, dodge is necessary if they are attacking you at the same time.
Also, there is three special action. Execution, Focus and fast tender. Execution will be available if enemy's health is low. And you can choose what will you get after executing. There is four option, Health, XP,  Damage, and Focus. I seldom choose Damage due to the effective time is short. If you are playing on Legendary, the gain of Health will be lower.
Focus will slow the time and shock the enemies. They are unable to defense or attack. However, you cannot use it when you are against Boss. It is very useful when you are fighting with multiple enemies.
Tender can let you break down enemy's shield. I think it doesn't important. I even didn't use it in Normal difficulty because the time you need isn't really short. You will be attacked when you are using a tender.
I love the graphics and the battle. It won't let me feel this game is old and I feel pleasant when I am fighting. However, the frame rate is locked to 60 and some time will drop.
Plus, the lock-on system of tender is not sensitive enough for me. Maybe it is my problem. I just mention it.
- smooth battle
- QTE(Execution) included
- upgradable skill
- Thought-provoking story
- well optimization
- up to 60fps
- insensibly lock-on (Maybe)
- rich hidden item
- not a long story
I give this game 8/10 and recommend to my friend and you guys.

-When it's working like it should and the teams are balanced, the versus mode can be a lot of fun.
The bad:
-Lack of focus in general. The versus mode with only 3 game modes and 2 maps for each is very lackluster in content-size. The story mode is with 8 missions that can all be completed in under 4 hours doesn't fare better.
-For some reason the characters are all locked behind progression, most of which is easy enough to be done, but few of which take more effort than should be required to unlock them.
-Uninteresting loot. Where in a game like Borderlands you would get new fun and interesting guns and equipment that you could see and actually influenced your character, here you only get uninteresting stat bonuses.
-Story mode is supposed to be replayed with multiple characters, but the game offers barely anything new the second time around, even when you play a different character the best you might get is 1 new line of dialogue, and even that doesn't have to be. Grinding for relatively uninteresting loot isn't a great initiative either.
-Story mode feels very rushed. The story starts and ends in a second, without any real motivation or even the villain's plans explained in the end. The missions are also very uncreative, with almost all missions being either wave defense or escort missions. The final boss basically just recycles older bosses before a non-climactic final fight.
-It is also very noticeable in the story mode that the game wasn't made to focus on it. The balance of characters is absurd, in which some characters run through the whole story without a scratch, others barely manage to get through some missions, if they manage at all. It gets even worse when you get timed challenges during these missions to complete for rewards, which depending on the current circumstances and character you play might just be impossible by default.
-Versus mode feels very unbalanced and unfair. It might be too early to say as of writing this, but where in other similar games, be it first person shooters or similar games in objective such as League of Legends or Dota 2, there is more of a feeling of your individual commitment mattering, here a team will based on composition destroy their opposition without any real chance to fight back. You have not yet experienced what it means to have a match devoid of fun until you have lost a match in Battleborn while not being able to do anything but slowly wait for the opponents to win. In the same way there are some very questionably exploitative things you can do in some of these maps, most notably a character who can snipe an enemy turret from across the map.
-The servers are always online and connected to Steam. If Steam decides to go down for 1 second for a routine maintenance, you are thrown out completely. There is also no saving in story missions, which might be a problem for people who do not feel like sitting 20 to 30 minutes to finish one every time they turn on the game.
-The lore challenges are absurd. The game wants you to finish 5 lore challenges for every character and even rewards you with gear and an achievement for doing so for each individual character, but some of them are completely insane. Some challenges want you to act and play in a way that is basically sabotaging yourself, forcing you to kill your opponents in a specific way, which just brings up annoyance. Other challenges will want you to play a number of matches with a specific other character, or kill a specific other character, which can be quite nerve-wrenching. Having to play 5 matches with a character that basically nobody plays while you also have to be able to pick one of the most commonly picked character is just a slap in the face. These challenges do nothing but hinder the enjoyment of people who want to finish them and unlock their rewards.
In conclusion, this feels like a game that has so much potential, but the developers have taken so many steps to try to botch it as hard as they can. The gameplay feels really good, the character selection is impressive and fun, the game looks good, it sounds good. However, as good as the core mechanics and features of the game are, everything around it seems extremely lackluster. From the barebones content in both versus and story mode, to the awful balance in both of those. It is rare to get a fluid and fun matchup in the game where both sides feel like they are having the same chances. The story mode also feels like it was just thrown together at the last minute, and together with some insanely bad decisions about how the characters and gear is being unlocked, and how bad the challenges the game presents you to do are, the game feels like it is deliberately trying to stop you from having fun. The game could be a gem, instead it has so many bad decisions made to how it was handled by the developer that it is currently just a butchered version of what it could be. Here is hoping that this could change in the future.
