Let me preface this by saying I spent somewhere around 50 hours in the last open beta, and have put another 35 in so far.
PvE Content:
While the solo play is fun, I might have burned myself out on it somewhat (Especially the first 2 missions) trying to grind gear and levels in the beta and on launch. The team play, however is fantastic. The humor is a continuation of the borderlands trend, The interplay with characters and the environment is fun. I've enjoyed trying to pull together team comps for advanced and hardcore mode. Overall, well done, however lacking if standalone.
PvP Content:
This is why the game gets the thumbs down. Lets start with when you queue for a match. During peak hours, you're looking at a 5-20 minute queue time, with 15min to 'I gave up after 45 mins'  queues in mornings and late evenings. When queueing with other people, this seems to be much less of an issue, however queuing solo is frustratingly slow.
On to once you get 5 members for YOUR team. If any 1 player dodges while in queue, the system decides to find a whole new 5-set of players rather than replace the 1. This prolongs the experience of waiting for 5 minutes at a time to even find a group.
Next step, the system looks for an opposing team. If you manage to find one, and nobody on your team leaves, resetting the entire process, you get set against an enemy group. At this point, some people Alt+F4 if the opposing team has high level players, people don't choose the map they want, or someone takes their character. Not many super-flamey people, or toxicity, however people just leave. I have only had a small handful of games total that had all 10 people playing.
Once in game (WOOOO! WE MADE IT!), I've been quite dissapointed with I'd say 1/3 to 1/2 of teamates, as many people quit as soon as they die once, or the enemy scores a handful of points. Thus far I'd say this game has a difficult time of retaining players attention for entire matches, which might come from the fact that someone spent 20 minutes in queue for a game (I use caps here for emphasis, not rage....mostly) ON ITS RELEASE WEEK.
Overarching issues:
Currently there is no way to have players rejoin a match if disconnected, or have players join any game time mid-game. I understand that there is the possibility that steam is having issues, however I've been disconnected from probably 10 games total (just self, not including teamates) since launch, with 4 that I can attribute to failed connection to steam with the game, followed by immediate re-endty to the home screen, and innability to rejoin the game (or have someone else join in as that character either, screweing the party too).
________
Closing notes:
Loved the beta. I had trouble describing the game to friends and family without including the word 'fun'. That hasn't happened with a game in a long while, and my hype showed for release. I almost stopped short of buying this game when I first saw the price tag, $100 CDN was stifling for a MOBA with 2/3 of a PvE game attached. I did, however stomach it, as the game had a lot of promise after seeing the beta, and I intrigued to see the other $80 worth of content not seen during that weekend.
- One of the smoothest launches of a game in recent history, however that shouldn't be an achievement, just a standard.
- I honestly feel like I paid $40 too much for how I'd value this game, with the coming DLC included. I'm actually really bummed out to say that. I was hoping for a bit more work put into systems like queuing, group finding, match joining for a "AAA" game.
- I'll continue to play for now, however likely much more casually than I had planned, and less frequently. I almost feel obligated to play it for the money put in, otherwise I'm just broke with nothing to do, which is a slightly worse alternative to waiting in queue.
EDIT:  June 18th '16.
New character artwork was added to the game. Finally some character-specific skin colors and textures, yay! However, instead of making this baseline, or unlockable.... PAY WALL. $100 CDN, not enough apparently for good customer support ( I have had 2 gamebreaking issues that I have tried to file tickets for, and had useless replies to those tickets, and had the tickets closed after they were unable to fix the issue within a week), or baseline character art updates or in game updates to ANYTHING it seems without having to pay extra.
The game is now dead, or so close that the difference is irrelevant. I've never been so dissapointed in a game developper, and this might be where I stop buying any product from 2K or Gearbox. Instead of worrying about customer satisfaction, encouraging growth of player base, communicating with the community to discover and fix various bugs and issues, adding a system to fill games that have DCs/RageQuits (this is a major PvP issue especially)... They added character skins, and taunts, and ways to add bank space.... for more money. You now don't have to play the game to expand your bank, or get a skin that means you achieved a level of mastery, you can just pay them more, and then never be able to get 10 people online in the world to play a PvP match with. GJ devs, your logic is flawless.

I wanted to like this game. After reading several other reviews about how "it's not SimTower", I almost didn't buy it. I decided why not, since it's on sale. Unfortunately, I am not happy with the purchase.
The game simply requires too much micromanaging. From having to build each tower floor - tile by tile - and waiting for your construction workers to manually craft every store/office/tile, to building power/plumbing closets on every floor and running all the electric/gas/water/phone/cabletv/hvac lines (phone and cable have been able to be transported over the same line for at least 2 decades, now...), to building trash/recycling/vending/shoeshine/phonebooths, to manually picking each tenant (offices, restaurants, etc), the game is really just not as fun as it could have been. Earning prestige, influence, and buzz does not feel as rewarding as it should. There are fireworks each time you earn prestige, but they're so non-descript that I didn't even notice them until I was at 4 prestige.
In addition to providing all the above, all the hotel/office/apartment tenants have numerous
that require you to build additional services/utilities such as Courier Services or Plumber Services or Copy Services or Helicopter Charter (seriously?) or Handyman or Dogwalkers or Executive Club or a Gym or Laundromat...the list goes on. If you don't build these, the tenants move out. In some cases, they move out in less than a business day. Oh, and if you don't happen to have enough backup power, and your grid blows, good luck getting it repaired before half your tower moves out.
Some of these items could have been made far more interesting. Helicopter Charter could have instead been a Helipad on the roof of your tower, which
high-profile visitors to your tower (along with an actual Helicopter fly-in/out animation) instead of being a requirement for lazy, wasteful executives ("you expect us to DRIVE to the airport"...yes, yes I do, jackass). The Metro is smaller than a large office or HQ; it should have been an exciting, monolithic addition to your tower. Instead it was a "meh, that's it?". Before you can get the Metro, you have to build a lobbyist office, which itself in turn requires some number of influence.
Essentially the game is all about ticking boxes on a requirements checklist. Before you select a tenant to move in, you have to make sure you have all the utilities & services they require, else they will just move out. It's too much micro to satisfy the casual itch, and not enough challenge to feel rewarding for accomplishing anything in the game.
If checklists sound fun to you, more power to you; but it's not for me.

*I've completed the campaign on the original PS4 release, so add about 40 hours to the play time of this review if it's relevant to you.*
Since its origins as a shareware flash game, the N series has consistently impressed me with its minimalistic design which conceals finely tuned, complex mechanics. N++, the third and purportedly final entry, takes all of the strengths of the previous entries and distills them into the definitive experience.
If you've ever enjoyed an N game or some of thier descendants (Super Meat Boy, Dustforce,) then your money and time will be well-spent here. If dubious, just download the free original and get a feel for the basics, knowing that in ++ the developers have strengthened and refined that design.
Though it offers a breadth of content (over 2000 levels, user created content, cooperative and competetive local-mulitplayer,) N+++ sacrifices no attention to detail. The spartan, vector-based aesthetic exemplifies and serves the minimalist design well, always putting concise, clear communication above extravagance without coming at the cost of sleek style.
N++'s physics-based controls (which are at times more like piloting a graceful glider than running and jumping) may not come as intuitively as a Super Mario or Rayman Legends, but once you grow accustomed to them, you'll likely find they reward practice and patience more than any competitor.
And that's NumberWang.

Very great game that I've been waiting on for quite some time. As a fan of the original N, having this version on the PC is like a homecoming of sorts. This is truly the perfection of platforming and of movement. Might as well write some pros and cons for anyone who wants to read them.
Pros:
Great Soundtrack
Many different color schemes
Genuinely challenging levels (generally not due to "troll design" or controls being difficult)
Intuitive controls
Sublime level design
Local Multiplayer can be extremely fun
Hundreds of hours of content
Minimalist aesthetic makes it easy to understand what's going on, even when many things can be happening.
It "feels" great: the momentum, the movement, the platforming, the design all come together for one cohesive, fun experience.
Neutrals:
Can take a bit of getting used to the momentum and basic mechanics (a bit different from most platformers) if you haven't played N (which is free on the web), but N++ has a series of tutorial levels that help you grasp the core mechanics and features of the game much better than N did. Pro-tip: read the level titles!
Cons:

- Some colour schemes are so vibrant they simply hurt my eyes.

- players can make levels, that might sound like a pro, but it's mostly a con to me. The game has only been out a few hours and I already found a golden swastika.

I've played this game on and off (mostly off) for about four years now and I have alot of mixed feelings I want to share about it. Again, these are my own feelings and opinions based on my personal experience with the game and in no way reflect those of the community or anyone else but me.
First off, it's not perfect... still. There are still lots of balancing issues that need to be, are being and have been addressed. There is also a limited amount of synergy between frameworks (powersets) and even less outside of broader framework groups (Elemental, Technology, Martial Arts, etc.) There are still tons of combination possibilties!
The game is quite long in the tooth and as the player base decreases, the amount of current information is harder to come by. Even on Steam, some of the guides have not been updated in five years.
They do use (poorly) the trinity of role-based gameplay; tank, healer(support), dps. The F2P support options are pretty bad and there is little to no healing and usually not until leveling into the mid teens.
The F2P (Silver) restrictions are pretty bad. I think you only get two character slots and you only have access to the free archetypes. Personally I feel adding a "freeform" slot to F2P would have made this much more popular. You also cannot access your free characters while you are subbed, which I feel is dumb, or vice versa.
The character customization is really good and you can make pretty much anything you can imagine, even spending NO money.
If you play, I recommend subbing (Gold) or if you just want to try it out - make free characters you really won't miss. If you like it, then sub. Only Lifetime members have unfettered access to all costumes; past, present and future but it is SO expensive! $300 at full price! They usually have a sale or two each year but I've never had that much money to spend on a game at one time. Over the years I have spent way more than that in the cash shop on costumes, character slots (which you still have to pay for no matter what your sub status), vehicles, heirlooms, etc. spending $10 here, $20 there and even ocassional $50+. If you go F2P, try and bring some friends, archetpyes work much better in a group.
There really is no end-game content, there are level 40 Alerts which are very short and quick group instances can grind for in-game currencies to purchase top-tier gear from vendors. There are also world and event bosses to grind which are raid-level content but there aren't many and the grind gets really stale.
I personally like the game, but I do not like the way it has been and is being managed. We'll see once some of the newer superhero genre MMO's start launching, but they will probably use CO more as a guide of what NOT to do in their games, that's my hope at least.
I've tried to be as fair and open as I can about the game and set expecations accordingly. Hopefully you found it helpful! Peace and game on!

Let me preface this by saying I spent somewhere around 50 hours in the last open beta, and have put another 35 in so far.
PvE Content:
While the solo play is fun, I might have burned myself out on it somewhat (Especially the first 2 missions) trying to grind gear and levels in the beta and on launch. The team play, however is fantastic. The humor is a continuation of the borderlands trend, The interplay with characters and the environment is fun. I've enjoyed trying to pull together team comps for advanced and hardcore mode. Overall, well done, however lacking if standalone.
PvP Content:
This is why the game gets the thumbs down. Lets start with when you queue for a match. During peak hours, you're looking at a 5-20 minute queue time, with 15min to 'I gave up after 45 mins'  queues in mornings and late evenings. When queueing with other people, this seems to be much less of an issue, however queuing solo is frustratingly slow.
On to once you get 5 members for YOUR team. If any 1 player dodges while in queue, the system decides to find a whole new 5-set of players rather than replace the 1. This prolongs the experience of waiting for 5 minutes at a time to even find a group.
Next step, the system looks for an opposing team. If you manage to find one, and nobody on your team leaves, resetting the entire process, you get set against an enemy group. At this point, some people Alt+F4 if the opposing team has high level players, people don't choose the map they want, or someone takes their character. Not many super-flamey people, or toxicity, however people just leave. I have only had a small handful of games total that had all 10 people playing.
Once in game (WOOOO! WE MADE IT!), I've been quite dissapointed with I'd say 1/3 to 1/2 of teamates, as many people quit as soon as they die once, or the enemy scores a handful of points. Thus far I'd say this game has a difficult time of retaining players attention for entire matches, which might come from the fact that someone spent 20 minutes in queue for a game (I use caps here for emphasis, not rage....mostly) ON ITS RELEASE WEEK.
Overarching issues:
Currently there is no way to have players rejoin a match if disconnected, or have players join any game time mid-game. I understand that there is the possibility that steam is having issues, however I've been disconnected from probably 10 games total (just self, not including teamates) since launch, with 4 that I can attribute to failed connection to steam with the game, followed by immediate re-endty to the home screen, and innability to rejoin the game (or have someone else join in as that character either, screweing the party too).
________
Closing notes:
Loved the beta. I had trouble describing the game to friends and family without including the word 'fun'. That hasn't happened with a game in a long while, and my hype showed for release. I almost stopped short of buying this game when I first saw the price tag, $100 CDN was stifling for a MOBA with 2/3 of a PvE game attached. I did, however stomach it, as the game had a lot of promise after seeing the beta, and I intrigued to see the other $80 worth of content not seen during that weekend.
- One of the smoothest launches of a game in recent history, however that shouldn't be an achievement, just a standard.
- I honestly feel like I paid $40 too much for how I'd value this game, with the coming DLC included. I'm actually really bummed out to say that. I was hoping for a bit more work put into systems like queuing, group finding, match joining for a "AAA" game.
- I'll continue to play for now, however likely much more casually than I had planned, and less frequently. I almost feel obligated to play it for the money put in, otherwise I'm just broke with nothing to do, which is a slightly worse alternative to waiting in queue.
EDIT:  June 18th '16.
New character artwork was added to the game. Finally some character-specific skin colors and textures, yay! However, instead of making this baseline, or unlockable.... PAY WALL. $100 CDN, not enough apparently for good customer support ( I have had 2 gamebreaking issues that I have tried to file tickets for, and had useless replies to those tickets, and had the tickets closed after they were unable to fix the issue within a week), or baseline character art updates or in game updates to ANYTHING it seems without having to pay extra.
The game is now dead, or so close that the difference is irrelevant. I've never been so dissapointed in a game developper, and this might be where I stop buying any product from 2K or Gearbox. Instead of worrying about customer satisfaction, encouraging growth of player base, communicating with the community to discover and fix various bugs and issues, adding a system to fill games that have DCs/RageQuits (this is a major PvP issue especially)... They added character skins, and taunts, and ways to add bank space.... for more money. You now don't have to play the game to expand your bank, or get a skin that means you achieved a level of mastery, you can just pay them more, and then never be able to get 10 people online in the world to play a PvP match with. GJ devs, your logic is flawless.

There is a bit of a shortage of casual relaxing games on Steam - ones that can last a really decent amount of time.  This looks like it has the potential.
It is built to have the look and feel of Stardew Valley.  The artwork style isn't my favourite, but it is nice enough.
The premis is to go around stations delivering passangers and buying and selling cargo.  You get to put different carriages that have different statistics - such as better entertainment / cargo capacity / passanger capacity etc.
The progression speed is about right in the game - I still haven't reached 50% competion in the first area after 10 hours and I'm fine with that.  I do want the game to last, and I'm not in a hurry.  This is a game I want to play in the evening to relax and switch off.
A few problems:
- Going between stations is a bit too slow, although it gets better with time as you buy speed upgrades
- There isn't enough active things to do while the train is rolling between stations.  You click the repair and clean buttons sometimes, and if you have money collecting carriages you click on them now and then to collect coins.  There are some special things to click such as rare passing helicopters, but it gives you a reward the first time and then never again.
I feel like I need more things going on to enjoy this as an active casual game.  Such as some birds landing on the carriages that need to be shooed away otherwise they make it dirty at a faster rate, perhaps mopping dirty spots that I can see rather than one button to click, clicking individual wheels that make sparks etc.  And some small bonus things to collect in the background such as clicking flying geese to collect some eggs that have some sort of long-term collection bonus.
- There are passanger conversations that pop up.  One face appears and say 1-2 words and another face appears to give a 1 word response.  I don't really think much of them - they seem to detract rather than add to the game.
Despite those problems it's enjoyable enough to play in the current state.  There are a few obvious bugs around, but from developer responses it looks like they will be cleaned up soon enough.

Overall this was an engaging game.  A simple interface, good audio/visual quality, and pretty well written.  The idea of comparing pieces of interviews to catch people in a lie was new and interesting, although sometimes some of the "contradictions" seemed a bit of a stretch, while other times something that seemed clearly out of place didn't count as one.
I do have a couple complaints.  For one, you can't skip any of the video transitions between locations, which can start to grate your nerves if you go back and forth a lot between some locations.  Also, most of the acting is very well done.  Most of the suspects' testimonies feel very natural, and a couple feel comfortably heightened (a bit of moustache-twirling, without being fully cheesy).  The protagonist, on the other hand, is irritatingly exaggerated.  As an inspector looking into a potential murder, he almost comes across like he's having a good time and not taking any of it seriously.  Everyone else is playing it straight, while he's hamming it up.  I called him many bad names in my head while playing.
Without giving anything away, the door is left open for potential sequels, which I'd be glad to see.

This game is a cosy investigation played out in gorgeous FMV segments. You progress the story by walking between locations in a sort of Google Maps fashion, and interviewing the characters you find in the hopes of making them contradict themselves. The overall feeling is one that players in the UK will recognize if I say "weekend evening ITV murder mystery". It's a police procedural that has more in common with Poirot than The Bill.
The core mechanic gets a bit wobbly once you're a couple of hours in, because the list  of available topics is so long that it's impossible to hold it all in your head at once, and spotting contradictions is a matter of scrolling up and down the list, reading off each point at a time until something you spot something. And them hoping that the game recognizes it as a contradiction, because not every instance of contradictory text is necessarily something that will move the game forward.
It's charming in setting and cinematography, and the acting is winningly hammy, so the niggles with the problem-solving fade away, especially since a lot of it is easy enough that you can just keep propelling the story forward.

This is one of the best FMV games that I've played, if not THE best one. That isn't to say this is a flawless masterpiece, there are many problems, but there are also alot of positives.
I'll start with the negatives - and this is my biggest complaint. The clue/hint system itself. As you progress through the game your list of possible contradictions naturally grow, making it more difficult to scroll through the list and decipher the short, vague descriptions of what the character said. I think to counter this, there needs to be less possible contradictions, perhaps separate them with "interest" notes that act as a reminder of what the character said. Also, there should be more to it than simply selecting and combining two statements; introducing evidence as part of the contradiction adds more variety and, well, sense.
Another problem is the lack of direction... it's as if the game doesn't know whether it wants to be linear or not, forcing yourself to explore every location multiple times throughout the night, or use the hint system (which you will be using ALL the time). I would have preferred if the game was linear, only being able to explore areas that are needed, and introduce a sort of point 'n' click mechanic where you move the mouse over things in the room rather than a generic magnifying glass.
With that, I think the rest of the game is absolutely phenomenal (especially given this is an FMV game). My favourite elements are this game's writing, music and story. Whilst it IS your bog standard murder-mystery detective story, there are certain things this game does that spice it up, adds flavour, makes it more... involving and personal. For example, I just love seeing the short clips as Jenkins walks up to a house, or turns a corner, or up steps; showing his shoes, his hand opening a door, or his awesomely smug face that you can't help but smile at. And speaking of Jenkins, he's a loveable character, acted out well and is my favourite character of the game. However, this isn't to say the acting for every character is amazing, certain actors I feel weren't up to par or tried too hard to the point where their dialogue and execution felt unnatural. I won't name names, and I did on-the-whole enjoy all the acting, but these two characters stuck out to me as being below average.
There's also the "aha" eureka moment when you finally find the contradiction, Jenkins will confirm this with a Tomb Raider 2-esque "aha" that Lara Croft does when she finds an item. Which is awesome. Another game I feel like this is similar to is Scratches, another game set in England, with an English cast, and offers another murder mystery with a plot twist or two. I mean, even in both games you report to your colleague about updates (Scratches was Jerry, here it's the Chief). Then there's the whole British setting to it that I like and can identify with. The village this is set in was a nice change from the typical towering urban American and I like the lighting and the fact the game takes place in the evening 'til night, the idea of hours progressing based on your own actions is a neat, immersive, organic way to approach progress.
I won't spoil the ending, but it does leave some threads hanging, and not in a good way. Certain characters seem to have disappeared off the face of the planet, collected evidence which were completely useless and character statements which are pointless filler. Having said that, some of that unnecessary digester flavour is what makes this game more life-like, as a real detective won't have perfect results with each candidate.
In the end, I loved the game despite its flaws, I wish they offered a downloadable soundtrack as I feel it was put to good use, the tingles and bells as you explore and find out more about the murder sounds great and as if you're making it closer to the truth. I can recommend this game to adventure lovers, movie-goers or people looking for a nice, relaxing, charming, well-written mystery presented in a clean, HD format.

This is the most challenging game I have ever played. It is tough, it makes me scream and cry, it feels impossibly hard at times. But it has earned being like that. It's never truly frustrating. The ridiculous perfectness of the graphics, the soundtrack, the level design, and most importantly the controls is something no other game will ever be able to emulate. So when I fail a level for the 983rd time, I might be done for the day, but I'm not done for good. Because it still feels like a worthwhile challenge, and not something that is just hard for the sake of being hard, which usually just means "unfair" these days. Twitchy controls, stupid level-design, these are things that make me stop playing games, because then it's just insulting to me. N++ makes a fool of me, but it does it in the most eloquent and respectful way and all I can and want to do is return the favor and push myself further when starting the 984th attempt.

Disclaimer: this review is coming from a fan of the original N
This is flat out the most polished platformer I've ever played. The physics and tight controls are wonderfully reactive, and the level design is creative, sadistic, and meticulous (I'd comare it favorably to Super Meat Boy).
Gameplay enhancements from previous entries are subtle (momemntum boosters, laser turrets, and a few other elements), but the aforementioned excellet level design gets a lot of mileage out of different permutations of the new and old elements, adding a lot of depth. Best addition (IMHO) is the soudtrack, which is extensive for the first time in the series, and quite good. The level editor (a major draw for me) is also substantially improved over the previous entries, and is a good deal easier to use.
I've seen a few folks questioning the pricing of this game, cosidering it is very similar to the original, free version that is available. TBH, the free version is still awesome, and you should totally play it if you're not sure about dropping $15, though in my oppition this updated version is totally worth the 15 dollar price tag, considering the 2000+ levels it comes with, the extra layes of polish, and the soundtrack (which would easily be worth $10 itself).
So yeah, get it, it's good.

As the Game of the Year in 2003 for a multitude of publications and standing the last twelve years as one of the most highly-regarded games ever within the Star Wars universe, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is an RPG experience that, quite frankly, you'd be a fool to miss out on. Featuring a combat system based more on Dungeons and Dragons than the action-based Mass Effect or Skyrim, the round-based combat effectively delivers on the lightsaber and blaster battles anyone who loves the films craves, while offering a unique and captivating storyline set in its own special corner of Star Wars.
If I'd impart one piece of advice before sending you off to purchase what is admittedly one of my favorite games of all time, it would be this: Persevere. Do not let Taris intimidate you, and for goodness sake, savor the few hours before you delve into the flash and hum of lightsabers and Force Powers to get to know the place. Quite frankly, this is one of the most in-depth and immersive games out there, especially from Bioware, and woe be to the gamer who sees the dice roll mechanics and whines because he can't aim down a scope or he has to listen to actual character. This is an RPG, and a fine one at that. Give it time, and it will give you a phenomenal experience.

CO can and will provide endless hours of fun. If you get fun out of creating characters, that is. The character creator is the most extensive I have ever seen and beats even The Sims with variety. You can make anything from an average Joe with superpowers to animals and aliens. Many costumes have to be bought, but there are also many that can be earned/bought with in game currency or unlocked with perks. Paying for cosmetic items is no issue. However, it's not where things end.
Unlike in Cryptic's Star Trek Online, non-subscribers are second class citizens in CO. While the free visual options for toons are more than enough, the free power options are quite limited. First, free players can't pick their powers as they see fit and have to select an archetype (which has a preset power progression and only few choices between A or B on the way). A freeform slot (which can pick freely from all powers in the game) costs a fortune, compared to other store items. Many archetypes have to be purchased as well, so the final list to pick from is somewhat short. It does include 2 options for each role (ranged dps, tank, melee dps, support, plus 1 option for hybrid) and some are pretty good. Some archetypes can also be unlocked through gameplay during events.
And events are a testament to how delusional the devs are about the population. Most events are unplayable for people who don't play during US evening. A European afternoon to evening player will often wait in queues for ages, or simply be unable to complete a daily due to a lack of players. To name an example, the High Noon in Snake Gulch event needed about 30 players to have a chance at success. Before 2 am GMT, that was the case maybe on weekends, so the 12 - 20 EU players stood around waiting and hoping to do this daily. Other events recommended teams of 3 for a daily, but would take hours to finish if it was a team of 3 doing it alone, and not with a bunch of other trios around at the same time. This may not be an issue for players who are online during US evening though, but the low population makes it frustrating for people in other time zones.
The enemy design ranges from "fun and diverse" (the gangs of Westside and Vibora Bay stand out) to "bland and forgettable" (the various "heavily armed militia-terrorist-whatever"). The voice acting throughout the game is atrocious. At times, it gets so cringy, it's painful. Any worse and it might fall under "so bad it's good", but sadly that fine line is never crossed.
New content is occassionally added, but mostly, it's a new sparkly eye aura or some minor cosmetic thing, rather than new missions, queues or powers. I haven't seen any significant PvP activity, which may be due to my time zone, but from what I can tell, it's deader than disco. PvE queues fill, but again, slowly. Waiting 30 minutes to play a 5 minutes daily isn't very efficient. Most missions can be played solo, but when it comes to earning Questionite and end game gear, it gets frustrating as nearly everything requires a team or a serious time investment to solo (with cute reminders that you can only play this 2 - 3 hours adventure pack 4 times a day). And a team may not be easy to get together, even if you play with friends.
I'm reluctant to recommend this game, because it certainly has issues and just doesn't get close to Cryptic/PWE's Star Trek Online. STO has a better F2P model, better story missions and voice acting, and gets way, way more love from the devs. I have blown money at Champions Online, for archetypes, freeform and cosmetics, and it definitely makes a difference. If you are looking for something casual, something to solo, something truly F2P... you may want to pass on this though. I recommend it solely out of hope for a larger player base, because the game has potential.

Where to begin?  Champions Online at one point was a good game.  I started playing this way back in closed beta all the way through launch.  Back when it was a subscription based it was great.  The freedom of being able to choose what powers you wanted and shape your character was great.  Being able to build a Rogue's Gallery of your own custom super villains was also great.
Once perfect world bought and it went free to play it slowly went downhill.  The freedom of of choosing your powers was locked behind either a optional subscription or dropping $50 on a freeform slot.  Instead Archetypes were introduced and you powers were automatically selected for you and you had fewer powers than a freeform.  Lockboxes infested the game and you were either forced to spend money to buy keys to open them with a chance to get good gear or trash them.
Costumes were locked behind a cash shop unless your subbed or you spent money to permanently unlock them.  Now and days people just login to roleplay or you may still find those dedicated players but it's not what it was years ago when it launched.  You would think with two other superhero MMOs out there they would have some money thrown there way to improve the game and compete but that doesn't seem to be the case.

Now lets get to the hot topic of this game.
Is this game a free to play game?
Before i answer this question i just want you guys to know that this game is heavily based on luck and the following answer is based on players who are just normal players with normal luck going into the game.
This game is a free to play game if you don't mind having a bunch of durable weapons and items. Being killed by other players with better weapons. Being killed by zombies in the zombie hero mode or zombie scenario. However you can still enjoy the different modes and maps without paying a single penny! This is what you will experience if you are willing to invest in at around 15 hours into this game.
This however can be changed but it requires a large amount of grinding and a few hundred hours invested into the game. Now lemme explain the systems in this game and how it works.
This game like i said before offers a lot of durable weapons and items. However if you do want permeant weapons and don't want to pay a single penny it is still very possible. This method will require you to invest at least a few hundred hours if you are a player who has a average luck like i do. Now the ways you can earn permeant weapons are through events (Do know that many events don't offer permeant weapons), crafting, extension coupons, mileage decoders and by bingo boards. Now lemme go through briefly each of these systems.
Events:
Events in this game sometimes offer decoders and supreme decoders (Most are really few to nothing) and gives out weapons at times depending on the month. Some of the weapons given like the christmas weapons have a duration. Other events like the spell the weapon name event gives permeant weapons however doesn't have much of a difference compared to the default weapons (This is changed due to some new updates like the serpeant blade or the fire axe... The weapons depends on the event so if you manage to play on a good event then there are good weapons out there for you to get) Also i just want to add that Nexon is being more and more generous with the events on counter strike nexon zombies. The most recent event lets players get 10 decoders everyday for playing one and a half hour + the 3 you can get everyday and 3 you can get every week. This event will last for more than a month so you can end up with more than 400+ decoders. Nexon has also been giving out free premium decoders to the users lately which is why Nexon's events are getting better and they are being more generous.
The crafting system:
This system is mostly used when you complete daily missions, grind zombie kills and decomposing your weapons (Most popular one) Now to actually have a chance of even getting a permeant weapon you need to sythensize and combine your durables to 72 days - permeant. Do know that this process can fail and result you with nothing left. Now if you were lucky enough to go through that you also have to do the same with the blueprints. After all that is done you still aren't offered a 100% chance at getting a permeant craft you still have the chance to fail. From my hours and i may just have been a really unlucky guy after a few hundred hours into the game i have only crafted one permeant weapon. This is just one way to earn a permeant weapon. However you can also stack up your duration of the weapon so for example if you have dual infinity for 100 days if you open another decoder with dual infinity 100 days it will stack on top of each other untill it becomes permeant which is 999 days.
Extension coupons:
Now to earn extension coupons you can either get this from decoders or by disasembling weapons. When you disasemble weapons and if you are doing this right with a large amount of weapons you have the chance of earning a few extension coupons. When you open decoders you have the chance to win around 20 extension coupons ++ and the max you can earn i believe is around 500. With that you need to save up to 999 extension coupons with that you can then make one permeant weapon.
Mileage decoders:
Mileage decoders are like buying lottery or opening lottery the chances of earning permeant weapons can be scarce at times and won't get you much. If you are lucky you can get some permeant weapon at your first opening. However if you are unlucky you can open a hundred decoders and not get a single permeant weapon.
Bingo board:
In the bingo board you can pick up some really good permeant weapons. However to be able to use the bingo board you will need to open decoders which will grant you 30 to around 50 mileage points. Now you are only able to earn 3 mileage decoders a day which requires you to play a total of 3 hours. With these mileage points you can choose to reset your board to get good permeant weapons which requires 50 mileage points and changing the grand prize for 350. Now as you advance in the bingo board your opening special numbers will increase and so will opening random numbers making you need to grind and farm more for permeant weapons. In general if you are a free to play player it will require a large amount of game time and investment.
Weapon upgrade event:
When the weapon upgrade event comes around you can upgrade non permeant weapons into permeant weapons but with a even stronger form then its previous. This event usually brings 4 weapons that can be upgraded into the game. All you have to do is just open a few mileage decoders or craft the weapon which is quite easy if you save up alot of mileage decoders or blue prints and is another way to earn powerful and permeant weapons.
If you can endure everything i have just mentioned above, install and play away it is indeed a free to play game if done right. I just want to say that i do enjoy this game and i really like it and would recommend it to my friend. However i just wanted to do a honest in depth review of the game. I still love this game though! It is still part of my favorites! Anyway thanks for reading! I also just wanted to add that this game is getting much better and Nexon is being way more generous in the events they have recently.

Battleborn is a good game that got released at the wrong time, for the wrong price, with the wrong marketing. However I do believe it still has a chance for success, since they made the PvP part free, and it doesn't rely on any scam tactics (p2w), it's competition is now other free games... and here we have one [Battleborn] made by a AAA company.
______________________________________________________________
If you ever wanted to play a competitive game without being a twitchy shooter or a highly complex moba, this game is for you. It's a great balance of strategy and action that is easy to learn yet cohesive strategies can trump skilled players. And when you're not feeling competitive the co-op campaign is a load of fun too.
Above all it's fun, At the very least you should give it a try; the characters are so varied that there is sure to be one you enjoy.

Good fun, the Story misisons difficulty balance needs looking at however and it can take a nit of time to get matches at the moment, with a lot of people connecting and disconnecting while searching.
Now I have played some more - I found the issue with matchmaking to be that I am in Europe. A good fix for this is to switch your download location to a US Server in Steam, after donig so finding games was fine.

In short: It's great and well worth the money.
It has it all: a PvE singleplayer / coop story campaign with fun-to-fight enemies, 3 different PvP multiplayer modes, tons of very unique and varied heroes to play. The humor is typical Borderlands style and hilarious. You'll discover jokes and references everywhere, even in the menu. It is well done and truly a labor of love, Gearbox made sure you'll discover new jokes and character responses on multiple mission play-throughs. The story may not be very deep, but the setting is cool and interesting and ties it all together.
The skills have punch and feel great, the movement is perfect. The music is lovely, the voice acting on a high level, even the german voices did a movie-quality performance!
The game blends multiple RPG / MOBA elements into the first person shooter at its core, which adds a lot of depth and things to discover. This adds a lot of replay value, as you can not only mix up your team composition, but also skill your selected hero differently each match, to adapt to the game.
The core mechanics are highly addicting, be it destroying those orange shards and collecting their pieces, searching the map for chests or simply the fluid combat and movement.
Yes, the graphical style might put some of you off, but it is like the Saturday morning cartoons we all loved to watch in our childhood. You'll get used to it, and in combination with the humor and the fun atmosphere, you'll enjoy your stay.
A word about the endless comparison to Overwatch: As thousands of people told you before me: These two games are very different. Overwatch is like Team Fortress 2 with heroes, a super simple and fast-paced shooter with hero classes.
Battleborn has much more depth to its gameplay and complexity, it is more tactical and varied. It also offers you solo or coop PvE gameplay, which Overwatch doesn't.
So: Go get Battleborn - You were born for this.

I'm still calling it Slime in 8-bit.
Slime in 8-bit 2 is a sequel to Slime in 8-bit 1, and retains the same genre, art style, sound design and approach to designing levels. The game expands with much more levels and mechanics, and explores all of them just as well. If you're just joining us, Slime and 8-bit 1 and 2 are 2d arcade platformers where you need to navigate to the level exit before the time limit passes with simplistic sound and visual design that is just enough to be the good foundation for solid platforming.
A lot of my annoyances repeat themselves. You can pause the game now, but the screen gets blacked out when you do and can't see the levels, so strategic thinking isn't fit for the game. What it's really crying out for is forcing a button input to start a level, or a 3-5 second time out before it starts, where you can see the screen. You still can't rebind controls and the game still doesn't stop you from moving around the level before you can see it.
Also, there's a level editor now. As much as I'd enjoy having a theoretically infinite amount of levels, at least in theory, the game already explores all its mechanics to a very large degree and I wouldn't expect much beyond an endless string of kaizos. But for better or worse, there is no option to share your levels with others, rendering this option basically useless.
Still, great and fun arcade platformer that would definitely be worth more than nothing, and above all, it's totally worth your interest.

To start off with something simple. This game is an very in-depth space based empire management game where you build an empire and try to defend it.
Distant worlds has been around for a while now and in many ways it was never really a graphically stunning game to begin with. That however should not keep you from buying this game, because this game is all about the in-depth management of your space empire and in practical terms the visuals are really little more than placeholders or chess pieces that tell you what is going on in your empire's space.
The space ship graphics look a bit simplistic and ugly for those who would expect graphical fidelity, but you do not really spend all that much time looking at your ships up close anyway. Much of the time you will end up zooming way back to look at the big picture of your empire to evaluate your options and your empire's logistics on a much larger scale so the graphical simplicity, for me atleast, is a non-issue. This game is all about information on your empire's resources, logistics, fleets, territory and management and considering the thousands of ships your empire and other empires will end up having, simplicity in marking those ships in very simple and straightforward way with icons is actually a good thing considering how complex the game already is.
This game is perfect for those who really prefer management style games because that is to a large degree what you will be doing in this game. It is up to you how much of the management you want to automate and how much you want to control manually. You are given very in-depth options on various automation features which will come in very handy for beginners due to the size your empire will become and how many things are going on simultaneously later on.
Most other 4x games or strategy games have quite simplistic resource management systems where you may have your money and a couple other resources to gather. That is not the case here.
In this game you have 41 different resources and every single one of them is important for different reasons, serves different purposes for your economy and industry and they are randomly found scattered around the galaxy in varying quantities. Each time you begin a game the resources and systems are randomised based on your settings so every start will be different and you will find that you will have to take different approaches and use different tactics and prioritize different materials based on what you have available to you near your starting location. If you get lucky, you'll have plenty of fuel and core materials nearby to build ships and equipment with. If you are less lucky, you may find that you will run into production shortages in constructing or maintaining your fleets if the resources you want are on someone else's territory. Any resources you do not have access to, you will have to buy from your competitors or from pirates. This will make it necessary for you to consider whether you should go to war for that resource and how much that war will cost you in effort and resources. Is that opponent stronger or weaker than you? Is that opponent part of an alliance which could lead to more problems for you or a war on two fronts? Everything you spend on something is away from from something else. If a war drags on and drains your resources (and they will), you will have less of them to invest in expanding your empire and territory.
In that regard logistics and the control of space and material flows is an immensely important aspect in this game. All resources you have are tracked and stored in specific space station cargo holds and nothing can be built without freighters first transporting the necessary equipment to the required building location. Constuction is divided to two parts. One is the construction of vast amounts of different components built with mined raw materials and the other is the constuction of more complicated structures like space stations and ships built from those components. Components are built in production facilities which are located in your or your competitors' space stations. These components then need to be shipped to construction sites or facilities of new space stations or other locations by your construction ships or by civilian freighters that are not under your control.
Also the economy in this game has more depth than any other 4x game I know of. In this game you do not have just one economy but two. One of those economies is your empire economy where you make money from taxes and services you provide to civilian entities. You make money by selling fuels, luxury resources and providing repair and construction services to civilian passenger ships and freighters. Every time a civilian builds a ship in your ship yard, you make money. You also get to tax the civilians who exist in your space. The other economy is the civilian economy that exists as a separate entity and is only affected by you indirectly. It is still important for you to protect the civilian economy so you can gather taxes and they can afford to invest and purchase ships. If your situation becomes dire, you can appoint an authoritarian governing model and outright rob the money and wealth of your civilian sector, but this is obviously a desperate temporary measure that will kill both of your economies if you persist with it. After all, if you rob them blind, they can't afford to repair their ships anymore and then who's going to freight all of your stuff and fuel around.
The economic and logistical model really make this game a great experience to anyone who likes a deeper economic model in an empire game.
The game has a vast amount of different races/empires with different goals, bonuses and play styles and the pirate factions are interesting as well, as you can sometimes use them in interesting ways. They can be a real pain to you as they blackmail you, but they can also end up saving you.
I'll give a simple example about the pirates. In most 4x games when the game advances and starts to turn into someones favour, it's effectively all over and there is no recovery once someone gets the upper hand over you. You begin to lose, you become increasingly overwhelmed and then that momentum just leads to you losing more ground to a certain defeat.
In Distant Worlds I ended up with a very different experience. I had been in an exhausting war with two empires. My resources were depleted, I couldn't protect my systems anymore, my civilian fleets were being destroyed, that lead to logistical problems, fuel delivery problems, whatever fleets I had in the region could not refuel. I had no fuel sources as the enemy had stolen my last fuel source system which was vital to me. I did not have the resources to take it back. I had plenty of money, but a severe resource and ship shortage. I could not build new ships, could not refuel others. The situation looked like an unavoidable, certain defeat. I was bombarded by the enemy fleets and couldn't do anything to resist them really. Not alone.
So I started paying money to different pirate factions to defend my systems. In fact, I paid so much money to the pirates in protection deals and bribes that I ended up developing excellent relationships with the pirate factions. So much so, that I got them to start an all out war with my enemy and to attack my enemies' systems and fleets. This gave me an opportunity to regroup and deal with the resource shortages. I took over couple of his key resource systems, strangled his economy and ended up destroying him with the help of my pirate allies. Grand.
There is so much more to this game, like immigration, tourism, rebellions caused by populations on your planets if you start a war with that population's empire, invasions, scientific research, special event locations, ship and station design customization and more.

This is one of the best space games. It was originally sold for $60, and is worth it at that price. I've got over 300 hours out of this game, which is far more than I get from most full-price games.
Why is this game so good? Three things.
First, you can automate whatever you like about your star empire. Ship design? Yes. Construction of mining bases? Sure. Espionage? Yup. War and peace? Yes. Fleets, both attack and defense? You got it. You can also handle any of these things manually, handle them manually with an advisor, or have the AI handle them according to policies you set. In short, you can *customize* the game to play exactly the way you want. If you only want to worry about the big stuff, you can set it up that way. If you want to micro it, you can do that too. And anything in between. It is up to you!
Second, the ship designer allows a great degree of freedom. Not quite as much as the first Star Ruler, but still a great deal more than most games. You can customize everything, including the AI. You can design stations (everything from star ports to monitoring stations, mining stations, resort bases, etc) too.
Third, there is an interesting historical aspect to the game. Galaxies of different ages have different central stories. Pirates may be weak or strong, ancient threats may emerge, etc. It can force a galaxy to unite against a common threat, fight among themselves, or simply try to survive versus the pirate hordes. Again, you can set it up however you want.
The game isn't perfect, but it is arguably the best 4X game out there.

First, I want to clarify that I beat the game in less than seven hours (Mostly because I thought it would get better).  I found the combat to be unpolished and chain together poorly.  The story was very short and lacked both depth of characters and the events of the game.  There were a multitude of what I would describe as "mini-games" in which you would control troops in Testudo formation (shield wall) and fend off archers.  There was even a "frogger-like" sequence in which if you were hit you died instantly.  The designers didn't seem to stick with what the players knew.  Throwing a new toy or ability into the mix is delightful and refreshing when done right.  Instead they throw in new elements that do not fit within the game and expect you to not be frustrated.
TLDR:
Pros:
Graphics
Hack and slash combat (for the most part)
Satisfying killcams and deaths
Cons:
Unpolished Combat
- Unresponsive commands
- Finicky targeting
- VERY bad aiming mechanic for javelins
- Poor defense against archers or dealing with them quickly
Very short game
Unnecessary mechanics (command of troops)
Weird "mini-games"
Overall, I would not recommend this game.  I bought it during the steam sale hoping it would be a refreshing game.  For me, at least, it was not that at all.

This is a great semi-idle game. I enjoy playing it while browsing Reddit, and sometimes even just play it without multi-tasking. It has many new features over th mobile version and no microtransactions. You can manage the ticket prices, all upgrades are unlockable with coins, etc.
$10 is definitely a reasonable price for this game, and I don't regret buying it at all.

After spending way too much time playing the mobile version, I decided to drop the $10 into the Steam version.
TL:DR- If you liked the mobile version, you will love the Steam version.
This version of the game massively improves upon it. The waiting system is gone, so upgrades are applied automatically. Also gone are the in-app purchases. It's very easy to build up the money you need to buy any upgrades. There is also now a maintenance system, which requires you to keep your cars repaired and clean. I don't have a problem with this new system, as in my opinion, it gives you something to focus on in between your long journeys. Some cars, such as the food cars also generate money now, giving you a little extra to go along with the money you make from passengers. You can also now change your ticket prices, but it seems like you don't have as many passengers at full price. I've played around with it and it seems like 20 gold is the sweet spot between number of passengers and profit. The market system is still there, and has not changed from the mobile version. Also it seems so far that the story is exactly the same.
My only gripe with this version is the gumball system. In order to buy the upgrade that allows you to add more cars to your train, you need to level the gumball machine, which requires you to buy 5 gumballs and an engine and caboose. The prices of which go up with each level. I have noticed a few bugs here and there, but with this still being Early Acess that's to be expected. The bugs aren't game-breaking (that I've seen so far), they usually just require the game to be restarted.
With that being said, the steam version is in my opinion much better than the mobile version, and I don't regret my purchase one bit. 10/10 would train again.

I got this game as part of a Humble Monthly Bundle.  Considering that, I would say this game is worth your attention if you get it for $5 or less.  More than that is a stretch.
This game is certainly a looker, no question about that.  Originally a launch title for the XBox One, it has some pretty textures and a very good atmosphere.  It is a few years old now so by no means the best looking game you will find but with regards to graphical fidelity I would say it holds up and will continue to do so well for years to come.
The gameplay mechanics are very basic.  Scratch that, EXTREMELY basic.  Combat is very easy to get the hang of and even if you don't learn to fight properly you will likely be able to cheese your way through the game.  The combat is "Arkham" in nature with cues as to which enemy is about to strike prompting you to counter before you get hit.  Health regeneration upon a kill is an option the player can select meaning that you, the player will likely never get killed fighting the majority of enemies.
On that note, the controls for combat I found a little sludgey (due to the swinging in the attacks) as well there were a few times where the game forgot to tell me (or my own forgetfulness) what to do in an instance causing me to die repeatedly until I figured out which button or move was needed to get past a certain stage.  I remember fighting a boss called "Glott".  About halfway through the encounter his moveset changed, as these games tend to divide bossfights into stages.  It took me about 20 minutes to figure out Right Mouse Button was the correct response when he turned yellow.  An onscreen hint would have been nice here.
I had difficulty getting the controls working using Steam Controller/ Steamlink.  I ended up just playing it on my PC.  A shame since this would have been a fun couch game.  Especially since as I am writing this review I can see a picture of the Steam controller with "CHECK IT OUT IN BIG PICTURE" right here on the game's store page.
This game is poorly optimized.  The PC port at least.  A common complaint on the forums is framerates dropping all over the place and my experience is no exception.  There are solutions online runing the game in windowed mode then editing a config file to make it borderless windowed, vsync/framecap off etc.  I didn't mess around with this because the game was over before I bothered to look...
I am a bit of a history nerd so I really love the setting of this game.  FAR too few games use this era/setting especially in the action/adventure genres.  The actual story was extremely basic.  Borderline crap but it didn't matter because it facilitated the journey to Roman-occupied Brittain, a place many westerners forget was part of the empire for centuries.  I consider a mark of a good history piece to be something that causes me to search up Wikipedia to learn more about a topic.  This game had me online a few times searching up Celtic barbarians, Wickermen & re-reading up on Hadrian's Wall.  It may not be perfectly accurate from a historical sense, but Crytek did at least do a decent job of putting some fun history and folklore into the game.
I normally wouldn't bother mentioning but this game is REALLY short.  That is not a bad thing outside of value proposition (I already said worth $5 at most) given that it is about 5 hours of fun.  It doesn't outstay it's welcome, and I can forgive shallow gameplay and combat. The combat is still at least somewhat varied with phalanx system which despite being simplified gave me the satisfaction of being a badass Roman commander defeating hoardes of enemies by launching a barrage of pila from a tank made out of dudes stacking their shields.
Solid fun.  Won't be the best game you ever play, nor will it be the worst.  If you dig nice visuals, like the historical period and are looking for a quick game to play and beat fairly easily, I would give it a solid recommend.  Not worth more than $5

A fun, charming FMV adventure game with a focus on dialogue and spotting contradictions in people's stories rather than traditional item logic puzzles. The ending is abrupt and a bit of a cliffhanger, but it's better to be left wanting more than wanting less!

TLDR: Highly entertaining, worth the price, well crafted, something we looked forward to playing, Took a little patience at first.
Being completely honest, I was not impressed by this game at first. My SO and I bought this as something to play together at night after the wee one went to sleep.  The main character didn't strike me as fitting the bill at first and some of the acting was so cheesed up it made me think I was going to regret my purchase.
We were quickly persuaded to continue, however, after a few well placed lines here and there. Deliveries that perfectly tied in to the mild frustration experienced early on while trying to ask everyone everything.
"If i were to do THIS would it mean anything to you?".  As if the inspector knows in advance that it's a waste of time...
There are many aspects of the acting and deliveries that made us cringe, being lovers of Brittish murder mysteries, but after playing for a bit the humor of the game become a bit more obvious. The hammed up lines here and there, the over- acted reactions, and the characters that were briefly thought of as out of place become perfectly suited to their roles.  After the first night of playing we were hooked, looking forward to an hour or so here and there of playing and talking to each other about our theories of what is going on.
I would highly recommend this to anyone looking for an entertaining escape from adventure games of late, anyone who enjoys BBC mytery dramas that can also stand some humor, and anyone just looking to be entertained.

I have no experience with the main Sniper Elite series, but I felt inspired to get Zombie Army Trilogy for myself and my friends some time ago after watching Mr. Sark's amusing playthrough of it. While shooting nazis, zombies and even nazi zombies is nothing new, I think ZAT represents a refinement of such. ZAT has the soul of a cooperative game, unlike Call of Duty's zombies spinoff, which still tries to shoehorn competitive elements in to the gameplay.
As a spinoff of a game about sniping, ZAT has the unique quality of having you use a sniper rifle as your primary weapon, with a choice of secondarys from among various submachine guns, shotguns and the panzerfaust, and a choice of pistols for backup. I recommend the Webley. Depending on the difficulity you're playing on, you must take into account things like bullet drop, wind speed and your character's heartrate when shooting, and giving you prone stance as well as crouching. You can also adjust the density of the zombies.
This standalone release of Zombie Army includes the first two episodes that were add-ons to Sniper Elite 2, as well as a new third episode with new enemies, more interesting level design and better writing, and is overall a superior experience, though the first two are hardly bad, just very straightforward.
Overall, ZAT is not a flashy or unique game, but it offers solid four-player coop third-person shooting, lots of explosives and multi-kill opportunities, and the ability to play as the cast of the Left 4 Dead games if that floats your boat. And, well, you get to shoot zombie Hitler in the face. I'd say that's worth the asking price.

Add to that the character animations being weird, a card game that is the only way for you to grind for money, and dialogue trees that you plow through patiently while looking for hidden options.
The story is pretty decent, though. It's just that how hard and long can you go on about the force? This game goes on about the light side and the dark side of the force from start to finish. ...and I get it: That's the point of Star Wars. It's just that when the force concept can be summed up in about five minutes, it tends to get repetitive after a couple of hours.
...so once I'm done with this game, if I'll ever manage to get through the finale, then I'm done with KotOR, and done with Star Wars games in general.

I have been thinking about how to sum up this game in a review for the past couple days. Usually after playing something for a few hours I can form an ok opinion on it, and then after more time with it I only have to refine that... so obviously there's a thing weird from the start. hm. let’s try again.
Leap of Fate is a hack and slash/roguelike with a storyline that is revealed as you complete missions. The style is very based in the cyberpunk/occult style. There are some RPG elements, as you can gain mana to buy new powers as you fight your way on various roof tops and libraries. There are four characters available to play, each with different powers, and you gain access to them through completing the aforementioned missions – tasks that you try to complete during gameplay. And right there is what I fully understood about the game. I played it for six whole hours - Steam told me so.
The reason why I’m so confused is because the game is all over the place. As a gamer I could learn most of what was going on through play, but if I didn’t have a background in this sort of thing I would be completely lost.
There is no manual, no menu option to explain different aspects of the game, the snippets of advice thrown in during loading screens are barely helpful, and the tutorial mission is threadbare. Every time something new happened I just threw up my hands and thought “whelp, it’s happening again.”
Not to say that once I found my rhythm it wasn’t fun; the mechanics of each character keep everything interesting, the different powers are fun to mix and match, and the random level generator doesn’t seem punishing like it does with other games of this type. I didn’t feel like I was going through the exact same generated room every time. I don’t really go in for roguelikes all that much, so this was a relief. It felt like rogue legacy in a way. The story and how the game was presented as a whole made the generated arenas make sense. And you can tell that the art, the story, the mechanics, and the voice acting were all made to work in sync. It definitely shows.
While I’m on the subject – the voice acting is honestly really good for an indie game. The actors they got for the parts really get into their roles. This is also something that is nice to see.
This review might sound like its bouncing back and forth on opinions, or that I’m trying to reach for good things to say... well that is because I was just in a constant haze of confusing the whole time. Why does this happen? Why are these guys moving like this? What does this power do again? Why are there little lightning bolts? I answered some of these questions three hours into playing the game. Hell maybe I missed the awesome tutorial levels somehow? But then a cut scene would happen and the story would distract me for a bit and then right back into the fighting.
The weirdest part is when I got to the last of the four playable characters… and then everything went bananas. The mechanics I spent hours figuring out went out the window. The way this guy could buy new powers, his special abilities, even the actual stuff he collected changed from mana to skulls for some reason? And he had some sort of meter to fill with said skulls? Nothing made sense anymore. My mind was in shambles. I am typing this from my hospital room.
Honestly, if this game weren’t so damn confusing at times I would rate this a buy. If at some point they add some sort of manual in the pause menu, a better tutorial, or someone coming over to tell me what the hell is going on would improve my disposition, but until then I would suggest only this if you loved roguelikes, steampunk and magic elements, and have a real and deep love of learning new things. Because you will, again and again.

Champions Online, a detailed review.
I'm not much for MMOs.  I purchased this on a whim before it was F2P because the setting attracted me (as power fantasies go, I find superheroes more appealing than, say, warriors or people with guns, and as the current landscape of cinema shows, this is a popular opinion).  And I was glad to have done it.  The game was super fun.
GAMEPLAY:
This is where the game differentiates itself from other MMOs.  The combat is action-oriented.  As a superhero game it's ideal.  Furthermore, you don't really depend much of other players, if playing with others is not your thing (it's not my thing, I prefer single player).  95% of the PVE game can be played solo, and if you have the right character there's only one mission in the game in which you need at least an extra player (due to having to do two things at once).  It's, to me, the ideal online game.  You're not FORCED to play with others, but it you want to, you can easily do it.  There's also PVP, which I won't get into because it's not my thing, so I haven't tried it, but there are a lot of different options for it.
CUSTOMIZATION:
This is where the game really shines.  Practically anything you can imagine you can create, with very few constraints.  You can't, for instance, make a four-armed character, and obviously you're not SUPPOSED to use trademarked characters (not that it stops people from doing it, mind you).  Your character looks are not tied to equipment, you create the look and either keep it as much as you want or change whenever you want (the only thing you cannot change once chosen at the start is a character's gender).  You can even unlock lots more costume pieces just by playing (or purchasing them).
As for powers, there's a large enough array of them to choose that you'll rarely feel wanting.  Elemental, magical, technological, physical, weapon-based, etc.  Wanna specialize exclusively on something or be a jack of all trades?  You can (well, with the obvious Silver constraint, more on that later).  And always with more abilities becoming available as you level up.  Travel powers are not tied to your chosen powerset, which means you can make a perfectly normal guy who shoots guns... and flies around leaving a rainbow on his trail.  Your looks are also not tied to your powers.  You can make a guy that looks like a fiery ghost but has ice-based powers and travels using a grappling gun.
As a bonus, there's no naming restriction (save for, again, use of trademarked names and profanity).  You can name your character "Dave" and it won't matter if there already is a Dave, the game will accept it.  I've even seen a Super Group (this game's version of a Guild) in which all members have the same name.  Surreal.
GRAPHICS:
This is where the game might lose points for some people.  It doesn't look bad.  At all.  It uses a slightly cel-shaded cartoonish style, it doesn't go for photorealism.  But... it's a game from 2008, and it's noticeable.  And you know how some people declare everything that doesn't have the latest in graphic technology as "looking terrible".  Don't listen to those people.
DIFFERENCES BETWEEN FREE AND PAID:
Let's get this out of the way first: this game is NOT "Pay to Win".  The game is perfectly playable and fun without paying.  I've played a lot as both a Gold (paid) and a Silver (free) player and really the only thing I miss in the latter are customization options.  In fact, if you're willing to grind, you can get almost everything a paid costumer gets, except for the Freeform characters.
See, if you are a Silver player you can still customize the looks of your characters as you like, but rather than choose from the complete array of available powers, you're forced to pick a powerset (called "Archetypes" here).  You can choose, for instance, a character that specializes in punches, another that has fire powers, another that uses guns, etc.  And some of them are locked under the game store's currency (called "Zen").  A Gold player, though, can choose from all archetypes right from the start or create a Freeform character, which can pick abilities from all powersets (and customize other things, like power colors).
Here's the thing, though.  Playing the game you can obtain an in-game currency called Questionite.  This can be used to purchase items or abilities or can be exchanged for Zen, which in turn allows you to purchase more Archetypes, costumes, devices and even Freeform slots (a Freeform slot allows you to have a Freeform character in a Silver account).  Yeah, it takes a lot of grinding, but it's perfectly doable.  There's also the fact that equipment is such as important to your character as your available powers are, and there's really no advantage here for Gold players, as everyone has to get equipment by playing.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
It's really simple, the game is free.  You can try it to see if you like it or not, and then see if you deem it worth it to pay for more options (which, AGAIN, is a choice, not a necessity).  If you like customizing characters, this is right up your alley.  If you're not much into online gaming and just want a large-scale single-player game, this is great too.  If you DO want to play with friends, this is just as good for that too.
See the playtime I have on record up there?  I guarantee you the real number is easily double that (1,274.4 hrs on record at the point of writing this review), because I was playing before the game became available on Steam, so it didn't measure my playing time.  I also guarantee you that at the very least a third of the total (I'd say about 800 hours) was spent playing free.  I find the game fun both as a paid and free customer, and that's because it really is.

I was super mega excited when this game came out, because I wasted a great deal of my life playing Sim Tower and Yoot Tower as a young teenager. I made the rookie mistake of comparing a timeless classic with an indie -- and I hate to say it -- immitator.
Sim Tower was basically about building, and building, and building like crazy. It had a real charm to it for being minimalistic but still with fun things to discover all the time, and a really epic "completion" condition. In that respect it was much like Sim City 2000, the endgame being the "exodus" easter egg after you build a bunch of launch arcos.
In any case, this isn't 90's Maxis. There are of course a lot more features and management considerations to make in PH, but to be quite frank, they're just tedious. There are a lot of 'unlockables' that exist purely for aesthetic reasons, which are about as useful as a Steam achievement (except you can at least pick up chicks in bars with Steam acheivements). This is also a question of taste, but I really don't like the "Mad Men" aesthetic of the whole thing.
