TL:DR - Fun game with or without friends if you don't mind the 1 minute lobby wait, no real bad community compared to other games similar to it. Download and enjoy.
+ Fun
+ Many characters/playstyles
+ Different modes
+ Weekly Nauts (characters)
+ Free skins
- Lag
- Too easy for other teammates ruin your stats
- Low reward for winning
This game is very fun, each match lasts around 10-20 minutes depending on the mode and difficulty you picked.
Learning how each character plays is easy to pickup and understand within around 5 minutes and you can test out the characters before you buy them incase they are not what you really expected.
Each week 3 Nauts are free to play as so you can try them out against other players/bots to get a better feel for them compared to the test-mode.
The skins are nice, I would not buy them to be honest but the developers have given some skins a way to be unlocked for simple tasks such as following the game on steam or subscribing to their newsletter.
If you hate playing online games against other players right away, there is a mode to play against just bots but with players on your team, I like this, it is more casual and lets you practice and get better without some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s complaining or shouting at you if you are not up to their standards.
However playing against other players is very fun and so far not met any real angry players, so far this game tends to have a relaxed community/playerbase.
However there is a downside to this, 3 times I have waited 1 minute to be put into a lobby for a match and my team were bots, not actual players. With bots the matches are boring and tend to go on longer because I found myself babysitting the bots. Even if I left the match in the lobby before the match even started, I would be punished and it would still count as a loss.
Sorry but this should be fixed, do not let me go on an ONLINE match and my team be bots, that is what singleplayer should be for. If it takes a little longer to find players so be it but don't let me be punished because you found a lobby with bots for me in an online match. If anything you should not be punished for leaving a lobby with just bots on your team.
Specially since the bots on your team tend to not attack the turrents nor the drill but stay near base even when it is not needed. Yet the enemy bots will attack turrents none-stop so how is that fair?
Secondly, even if you got most kills and killed a turrent or two, if you lose the match (and I have due to team mates leaving or just being horrible and using characters wrong) you won't get ANY exp or rewards. So 10-20 minutes wasted. This should not be the case, give us some reward for our time and efforts, make it be based off kills or turrent damage, not just if you won or not. I really hate making it seem like my time was wasted because one player decided to leave and let us get steam-rolled by Hard/Very Hard bots. Other players have complained about this issue of low-rewards after each match and it should be changed to reward those with higher kills/damage to turrents. Instead the reward is based of how long the match goes on but after the 4th turrent is killed no one is really going to hang around and delay the match.
Lastly is the lag. I only been in 3 matches (out of 31) where every 5-10 seconds I would get RECONNECT error and wait a little bit to be able to move, this happened to the bots and other players. Yet in some matches if this happened it said it was mirgating the host? and fixed itself. Not sure why in some matches it does nothing about the lag but other matches it does.
Otherwise this game plays smoothly online, at least for me, only when I been in matches with players in Russia or something it has gone a bit laggy.
I wish we could create lobbies for this reason, the match making is non-existant, you can be put in the match with someone who just joined or been playing for a long time or is crap with your connection and vise-versa but again if you leave, it counts as a loss and I hate unfair losses like that.
Part from those minor set-backs, I do enjoy the game, simple to pick up and really, no real mean players or what I found yet. If my teammate killed me by mistake with a trap, they said sorry but if I killed someone with the trap  (and they literally stood on it so their fault) they would insult me but that is it, they wouldn't carry on they would go back to fighting the enemy.
So give it a shot, play it with friends or with randoms it looks promising.

Ok after seeing some of the stupid reviews this game is getting, i had to put in my two cents. For starters ANY review that is comparing this to Overwatch is completely pointless. Do your research and see that they are both two different games that people are trying to lump in the same category. Anyway....
A key point about battleborn:
-If you don't like Mobas such as league of legends, smite, heroes of the storm, or Dota 2, then you're going to want to reconsider buying this game. Everything about this game is in the moba styling even in Story Missions (which i've played mobas for almost 5-6 years now so i have no problems with this) but it's incredibly important to know what you're getting yourself into. Competitive players that curse you out when they are also failing, balancing issues at times, lack of teamwork, lack of direction towards objectives, and meta picking champs are all going to be part of the multiplayer in this game. As much as i hate what i just mentioned, it's sadly part of the community. So if you dont like minion killing along lanes, cant deal with toxic players, or don't like repetitive matches on the same maps, then stray away from battleborn. Last thing we need is the reviews plummeting because some kid didn't do his research, thought about gearbox and borderlands, then writes a review saying it sucks.
Battleborn~
Pros:
-Wonderful and creative character roster. Very unique with lots of different play styles. Want to be a gentleman robot sniper who calls people hobos? Marquis is right there for you! Want to cut people down with swords and have a skill calling "Totally not a vampire"? Rath is for you. Want some stealth with holo decoys? Deande is perfect for you!
-Fun art style. Somethign about the art in this game is delightful. From the character design, to level design, and of course how could anyone hate that beautiful hand drawn intro!
-High replay value in missions. Every time you go into a new mission, depending on the characters in your team, the dialogue will change accordingly. here's an example:
Wolf MK1 sentry: so guys what are we gonna do after this whole portal thing that i am totally not going to die to?
Marquis: MOURN YOUR LOSS YOU BEAUTIFUL SENTRY!! *sobbing*
Wolf Mk1 sentry: *same line as before*
Shayne: Uh...ugh....look dude....we're gonna blow you up. I'm sorry.....
Wolf MK1: sounds fun!
-Meltdown is incredibly addicting
-The loadout system gives you ways of altering your play style. Make sure to choose much in the same way you'd choose runes on League. Putting a tanky loadout build on Orendi or Thorn...and well you're gonna have low damage. High health, but lower damage compared to more damage based builds
-Gearbox humor. The first time you hear isic, you're going to be laughing pretty hard. It only gets better from there.
-Cons
-Sabotuer is probably the hardest mission in the game. Your team could be stellar the whole way, but once you get to that last defense point, the target you have to defend (no spoilers of course) seems to just melt. There's talk that they're making it easier, but time will tell. The challenge is welcoming to me, just alot of people have been complaining about it so fair warning.
-Community. As with every moba, the community is a wonderful utopia of teamwork and motivation (can you sense the sarcasm?). Majority of your teammates would rather suck♥♥♥♥♥♥through a straw then attempt to work with you. Though this is a problem plaguing almost every moba.
-Connection issues. Sometimes you're gonna wanna bash your head against the wall when steam maintenance pops up. Almost beat the saboteur and then steam lost connection. Turns out scheduled maintenance came and went. If you have a crappy connection to steam, reconsider this game. It's better than not connecting. Also some computers for what ever reason have port issues where they cant connect to the game at the login screen. It was a common problem in beta, though i havent heard anything about it recently. just passing on info.
-Repetitive gameplay. As i specified before, even though the dialogue changes in hilarious ways, some people just hate doing the same thing over and over (resident raccoon city was a good example. Great game, halfway decent story, but people hated the multiplayer heavy gun toting re feel and doing the same thign over and over). If you dislike doing the same story missions or multiplayer heavy games, stray away from this one. It'll save your money and save the time you'd take writing a salty review.
Conclusion:
-Like mobas? Like crude humor? Like hearing rendain giving a voicemail to Mellka? then drop the 60 and buy it! If 60 isnt your thing, just wait for a sale! i know a gearbox sale is probably coming some time this year or better yet steam summer wallet apocalypse. You wont be sorry!

Hi there folks!
Battleborn, Released on may the 2nd. (PC(STEAM)/XBONE/PS4)
Created by Gearbox Software, the ones who brought you Half-Life expansions ( e.g. Opposing Force, Blue Shift,... ), Borderlands series and Duke Nukem series.
Battleborn is a game, a mix between "moba" gameplay and a bit of Borderlands. This game is an exciting FPS, whereas like a moba game, has 25 playable "heroes" to choose from. Characters ranging from melee to long-range weaponary. (with different skills/traits) Ofcourse most of these "heroes" are locked and you can unlock them by doing challenges or by rank/level. You can level up your player rank, but also your "heroes" can be leveled.
My first impressions are that this game is not a MOBA at all. It's just "based" on. Meaning, if you are not so into moba's (like me), you can still enjoy this game to the fullest. With a humour in style of Borderlands, this game is pretty fun. There are enough characters to explore and after checking them all, i'm sure you'll find the character you want to play with.
This game has a story-mode game. Although in my opinion, the story isn't really interesting. It does give some sort of clue, in what kind of universe you are playing in. The cinematics are a mix of animated american manga/cartoons.
The game has a very fast matchmaking, so if you do not want to play alone, you can easily join up with up to 4 other players. Storymode can be played in co-op with friends or other random players. There are 3 other PVP modes: Meltdown (arena mode), Incursion (destroy enemy base) and Devastion (capture the flag).
Also a part of the game are lootboxes. You can find them after defeating bosses in storymode, leveling up and ofcourse by buying them. These lootboxes includes Items that enrich your character's skills. You can only choose 3 active "powers" that you can activate while playing. These are not character-bound.
This game offers a decent gameplay, loads to explore and a lot of choice in playable characters. Music & voices are great. Although I missed a good story here, the gameplay is as great as playing Borderlands (loads of shooting). And the good/fast matchmaking is really something.
I give this game a 8/10

I've been waiting for this sequel for over 10 years, and it's everything I could have hoped for. N++ is a brilliant, unique style of platformer that has sometimes rage-inducing, sometimes epic moments. The game is easy to learn, has
simple and satisfying controls, (left and right movement keys and a jump button which you can hold down for a lengthier leap) but is still challenging as a proper platformer should be. The basic premise of the game is to complete levels, by going through doors while collecting gold to increase your points. There are 5 levels in one group and completing them will unlock you the next set of levels. Pretty simple, right?
In later stages you will have to manipulate the map perfectly to get that slight boost in your jump, weave through tight areas to evade a missile on your tail, or use a ramp to break an otherwise fatal fall. The gold littered around each level is a neat feature which adds a bit of a gamble into the game. Do you go the route brimming with gold, but also traps, or do you take the easier route and try and finish as quickly and surely as possible...
Multiplayer and interaction with the rest of the community is now bigger. There is a leaderboard which competitive players will like, and adds to the reward of finishing a level perfectly. If you have a friend along for the ride, you can either play with, or against each other. Co-op will have you working together, sometimes sacrificing yourself so that your buddy can finish the level. The Race mode on the other hand adds a tense competition between who can finish the level with the most points, and will have you shouting as you near the door to your victory.
Sometimes you will ragequit a level and come back to it later to finish it with that sweet taste of revenge. Veteran players will recognise some of the classic hazards, redefined, and a whole load of new threats are also introduced, like ghosts of yourself running around, detonating you into a million pieces if they touch you. Laser turrets, mines, drones, and electric blocks are just some of the other obstacles you will face.
The levels are now brightly colored and you can change the music and color palette to your liking. It's a nice change to the constant gray of the previous games. The animations and textures of everything are also more pleasant and sharp. The new level editor has improved by miles. It's more intuitive, much easier to use and enables better made community levels, which there are tons of.
I highly recommend N++ if you liked the older versions and ESPECIALLY if you've never played an N game.

We've all heard of N. It may have been as exactly that, just N, the flash version of the platformer you got good at for bragging rights, or the 360 version, that didn't change a whole lot but did have more of N. It stands to reason that the latest version, N++, is exactly that: it's still very much N, but with more of everything. You'll still have to dash around levels collecting gold - you're a greedy ninja who can't resist its allure - and avoiding enemies and hazards, but instead of ten or a hundred levels, there's thousands of 'em.
The tools given to you are simple enough, with running and jumping being the only things your ninja can do, but as the suggestive name levels will tell you - they range between outright mocking your capacity to cluing you in as to what you have to do - it's how you interact that matters. N++ is a momentum-based platformer, and learning when to jump from a slope, how far you can fall before you go splat and how far up you need to leap is key to success. While at first things may seem simple enough, in the first row of levels you'll already be confronted with the fact that you're bad at this game, as a particular level has golden pieces just out of reach, with only a few slopes near them, and knowing how to maximize your leaps by using these slopes is still something you haven't learned.
While it might initially seem similar to other platformers, such as Super Meat Boy, N++ takes an entirely different approach to its design: finishing the levels themselves isn't that difficult, what is hard is mastering the game to the point you can complete them in a quick fashion or while gathering all the gold nuggets. This reflects in the mood of the game, as while death can be frustrating in other platformers, in N++ it's similar to the loss of a pole vaulter who sets his bar a tad higher than he can and knocks it down because of it: you could have completed the level if you hadn't tried to get all the pieces of gold, or if you hadn't tried to get a specific time. There's still difficulty in N++, it just seems to be an option rather than a roadblock.
For those who had grown used to, and perhaps tired of, the greyscale background of the original games, N++ has an offering of different filters for you to change its looks. While I enjoyed some of them and loathed others, at time with colors too bright, I found myself going back to the easy-on-the-eyes standard filter due to how unobtrusive it was. This is also true of the soundtrack, which went from a more pulsing beat to the amalgamation of trip-hop and trance present in this version, whose soothing tones likely played a role in my lack of frustration upon death.
N++ is a distilled platformer, simple and lightweight, something that some might equate to lacking, some to clever design. For those with a competitive vein, N++ has leaderboards and score tracking, as well as a co-op mode and competitive racing, but it was in taking my own time with the single-player levels that I found the most fun. I didn't find motive to play it for long stretches of time, but N++ makes for a good game to visit every day for a couple of stages, chipping away at the massive roster of intelligently designed levels.

N++ is a 2d platform game in which the player guides a stick ninja to a switch, and then to a door. Along the way, gamers can choose whether to collect coins that will extend the level’s timer or not, and have to dodge various obstacles that can kill the stick ninja in one hit.
The game’s controls seem as simple as N++‘s premise, though level after level, the game’s designers go out of their way to make the player think about more advanced movement techniques in order to advance. Gamers start N++ thinking that it’s a game about pressing a button and jumping, but they quickly discover that jumps depend on acceleration and positioning, turning a task that wouldn’t normally require much thought into something far more interesting.
Coin collection is something that most platformers feature, and it’s another classic trope that N++ quickly turns into something else, as players discover that grabbing all the coins in a level isn’t always a good idea, and that greed can turn an otherwise incredibly easy level into a nigthtmarish adventure.
Later levels introduce enemies that can move and even shoot homing projectiles at the player, upping the stakes, as many of those new hazards can be bypassed if gamers don’t go after the tantalizing gold coins.
If players ever get tired of the game’s 2,360 solo levels (yes, that’s not a typo, the game actually features more than two THOUSAND hand made levels) there is a race mode and a local cooperative experience (which requires real cooperation, as one of the players may need to die in order for the other to progress in some cases, among other interesting cooperative interactions)
Hopefully the developer will be able to add an online mode in the future, though it will all depend on the game’s success.
Gamers interested in creating their own levels can also engage in that activity, as the game features a robust level editor which also lets players upload their creations so others may play them.
Visually, N++ is a minimalist experience, which is something that works on its favor at all times, letting gamers see hazards clearly.
The game’s audio design is also quite clean, and the soundtrack features a selection of techno music tracks that fit N++‘s minimalist visuals perfectly.
N++ is a challenging platformer that every fan of the genre should play. Few games can be so rewarding for those who take the time to understand their mechanics, and even fewer can claim to be as focused and pure as Metanet Software‘s masterpiece is.

N++ is a platformer with a focus on momentum and not dying.
This is a sequel to N and N+. If you enjoyed those previous games, you will feel right at home with this installment in the series. The game feels almost identical, with the exception of new aesthetics, enemies, music etc.
If you've played previous games in the series, feel free to skip this section where I just explain how the game works. Read from "What's New?"
I think this game is a great example of "Simple to pick up, hard to master". It might look like any old platformer, but once you really start to get a feel for the mechanics of the game, you learn all sorts of techniques that are necessary to beat later levels.
Using momentum is something very important in this game, which is what makes playing it feel so good. Depending on your speed, what walls you hit and the angle you jump at, you can go flying through the stage. You also need to be careful with your descents. If you hit the floor from too high up, you will die, unless you can slow yourself down by sliding down a wall or landing on a ramp.
Due to all this stuff, you never feel cheated out of a death. If you die, it's your fault.
Although the game can get hard at times, I never felt that it was unfair. The difficulty curve is really good!
You play the game in chapters. Each chapter has a few levels you need to complete under a shared timer. It's quite a generous amount of time, so don't feel stressed. While you progress through levels, you collect little golden blocks that increase your timer and score. You don't need to collect them all, since they can sometimes be very tricky, but if you enjoy seeing yourself on the leaderboard, it's an option.
In N++, you get a few new things to the series. You can change the colour palette of the game. For the most part, I think a lot of these are too eye-straining to enjoy, although they are pretty, I'd rather stick to some of the darker ones. It's nice that you can unlock these as you play though.
I LOVE the soundtrack. The game hosts music from many different artists, all of them quite chill electronic music. Although the game is difficult, it can also be very relaxing with this soundtrack.
There are a few new obstacles and enemy types to the series that mix things up a bit.
Obviously you also get tonnes of new levels, which will keep you playing for a very long time.
The game also comes with a level creator, as the series has had before. It's relatively easy to use, and will allow the community to keep the game alive through making some pretty fun and creative levels to play.
The game still has Solo, Co-op and Race modes which allow for some fun times. Co-op relies a lot on teamwork, and sometimes you will need to sacrifice yourself so your teammate can complete the level.
Race is a competitive game mode where you get to race against your friends (or by yourself). Pretty self-explanatory.
All modes are playable with 1-4 players, although if you play solo level with multiple people, you forfeit your spot on the leaderboard. Still, it's a nice option to have!
Overall, I strongly recommend this game to any platformer fan. The movement feels so good, and it's just super satisfying to land perfect jumps while listening to the great soundtrack. The only downside I can really think of is that there's no online co-op, which I'm hoping will change in the future. While I agree that it's more fun to have my friend on the couch next to me, it isn't always an option. Other than that, great game. Recommended!

Just about everything is perfect on Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic. But, there are a few nagging exceptions however. There are some MAJOR resolution problems. One of these problems is that everything becomes much smaller when you use a higher resolution. Movement feels a bit too awkward, as though movi9ng and navigating the protagonist is slippery. These problems combined just ruins the game for me.

So this is pretty much Bioware's normal MO for a game, third person actiony rpg with a pause button used in lieu of rounds and being able to plan your characters actions while paused. No other company does this and it's honestly a terrible mechanic. It always feels like they wanted to make a real time action game but just couldn't figure out how to do it right, so they put in this unweildy plan while paused. Alternatively I would have loved to see them add enough abilities to actually make a real turn based rpg out of this, but it seems that is too much work in balancing and planning for Bioware. If you've played DragonAge or Mass Effect you've seen this before cause they are exactly the same gameplay.
I did like the exploration and not being hooked by arrows pointing which way to go or having it constantly spelled out for me. Fighting waves of enemies while I hunt around through every nook and cranny was fun, despite the somewhat repetative areas, but the problem I kept frequently running into were insta kill mobs. See rather than wall off an area you're not supposed to progress through or even put a really tough enemy there, the game puts instant death of some type with zero warning, forcing you to lose progress. The rest of the time enemies will likely pose zero challenge. This zero challenge followed by instant unavoidable death gets real old as the story wears on and it happens again and again.
Graphics were dated, old, but to be expected and the high resolutions were nice.
Sound was Star Wars, impossible to really do wrong since everyone knows what a lightsaber sounds like.
Controls were easy enough to understand but there was no game worth playing them with.
Final verdict: into the trash it goes.
Note: SWTOR is so much better than this, storywise and in gameplay... even though it's a MMO you can pretty much play it as a single player game if MMO's aren't your thing. And it's free with optional pay to unlock more things if you want more content.

I was pleasantly surprised by this game. I read many reviews, pros and cons, and decided to take a chance. The game plays out like many twin-stick, arena, rogue-like shooters with rpg elements. There are six levels (chapters is a better word) to each play thru. In each chapter, you will enter a dozen or more cards that can be combat rooms, shops, mystery (which is a bonus item room), upgrade room, or guardian room. There are also other variances, such as gold rooms (which are regular rooms modified to be more beneficial - shops have two shops or upgrade rooms give one free upgrade). There are also cursed rooms which do the opposite (upgrade room becomes downgrade). You can also find various bonus cards to help you navigate each chapter (such as the skip room card).
There are four different heroes which start out with set abilities. The two active abilities are shadow walk and glyph. Each hero's shadow walk varies partly, but they all allow you to blink or shadow step about 10 meters in the direction you aim. The starting glyphs are useful, but I often trade them for new glyphs when possible. You can unlock all four heroes within a few hours of play.
To access unlocks and permanent upgrades, you have to complete varied extra missions with each character. The upgrades you unlock are upgrades you would normally have to pay for during the run. This allows a small, but useful boost to the beginning of each run. The missions are not hard, but they often require you to play differently than you normally would (such as a mission to kill the level 4 boss with a reflected projectile).
To acquire mana (money), you must kill mobs with your shadow walk, glyph, explosive objects, or sometimes basic attacks (if you have that upgrade). You also get a good amount of mana from chests at the end of combat rooms, as well as from mystery room chests). You also acquire a global currency (used across all play thrus) as loot from some chests or destructible objects (if you have that upgrade). The global currency can allow you to revive once per run if you die or to buy some items from the shops or skip challenge rooms (combat rooms with special objectives).
It must be noted that the story is lacking (though I haven't seen the end), but that is to be expected. However, as you accomplish more with each character, you will unlock new story cutscenes which you can watch from the character select screen. That being said, I do rather enjoy the cutscenes.
I have yet to beat a run. I've made it to the 5th chapter on the third character (I forget her name, but she's real good). I am glad I purchased this game, and I do believe I will continue to enjoy this game.
Update:
I have beaten normal mode on three of the four characters now. After you beat all normal mode missions, hard mode missions become available, allowing you to unlock a few more permanent upgrades. Hard mode is actually fun. The enemy seems to have more health, and an elite enemy (kind of like a mini boss) spawns with the normal enemies. With the extra upgrades, you should be able to tackle hard mode, but a lot of kiting is often involved.
I'm still enjoying the game a lot. I like the cutscenes I unlock as I play (and it gives you extra goals to accomplish to unlock them. After beating it the last time, I almost wish there was another floor of three levels. But, hard mode will keep me busy for a while.
Two concerns though. Sometimes when the chest at the end of a combat appears near the edge of the level, items that spawn from the chest can drop off the map. This has only happened once or twice to me, and I didn't need the items at the time. The other concern is that if you get the upgrade that allows you to float over holes in the battle field, you can often just sit over that hole and shoot non flying characters wtihout danger (this includes some bosses). Now, with many enemies and bosses having ranged or flying capabilities, this "exploit" isn't all that useful. I don't know a solution, or if there needs to be one. I like the upgrade for the ability to cross chasms to get away from runners, and I generally don't sit over a chasm and shoot at melees.
I hope many of you will give this game a try. It really is good (though may not be good for all).

Leap of Fate is a top-down, twin-stick shooter with rogue-lite elements. Set in a urban fantasy version of New York City, the player takes the role of one of four powerful magic users who have entered pocket dimension known as the Crucible of Fates, in order to find their destinies.
Combat is extremely fast and frenetic and the difficulty level ramps up extremely quickly, in later levels it's almost impossible to avoid taking damage without judicious use of your Shadow Walk, which allows you to quickly change location, and your Glyph, which is a powerful offensive spell. The problem there is that these abilities have only limited uses per fight, and using them further will consume energy cells, which are somewhat rare. Further complicating matters is that mana, which is needed to purchase passive skill upgrades, only drops if you kill an enemy using Shadow Walk or a Glyph, though there is a passive that gives your basic attack a chance to knock mana out of enemies.
You can earn permanent upgrades for each character by accomplishing certain objectives given to you during runs, this is also how you unlock new characters, and hard mode, which must be unlocked seperately for each character.
Uniquely, in Leap of Fate your passive skill trees are randomized in each playthrough. Veteran players advise restarting a run if you do not like your tree's layout. These passives are split into three trees: basic attack upgrades, shadow walk upgrades, and general-purpose passives. I advise grabbing the "Third Eye" skill where possible, it makes planning your run much easier.
You begin with only Aeon, the Shadow Mage, and can unlock Big Mo the Technomancer, Mukai the Spirit Channeler and Rasimov the Rogue Occultist. Each has a different basic attack, a different starting buff for Shadow Walk, and unique glyph. Aeon has a spread shot, a simple shadow bolt glyph, and can damage enemies by Shadow Walking through them. Big Mo has a continous-fire beam that can overheat, an aoe damage grenade, and can turn invisible when Shadow Walking, leaving a holographic decoy behind. Mukai has a close range cleaving attack, a glyph that stuns an enemy, and can fire a projectile when Shadow Walking. She also has a shield that intercepts the first hit she takes in each fight, to compensate for her alarmingly low starting health of just 3. Rasimov is perhaps the most interesting character, as he does not spend mana to purchase upgrades, but instead speands health. He has a conical damage attack that will instead fire a large projectile if he does not attack for a short time, a glyph that places an explosive trap that sucks enemies in, and can slow down time for enemies when Shadow Walking. Enemies Rasimov kills with his skills drop souls, and when he collects enough souls he recieves an upgrade and a health pickup.
Considering this is also a cellphone game, Leap of Fate's asthetics are impressive. Music, visual effects, and sound are all good, but notably I thought the voice acting was of unusually good quality for a game like this. Each of the four characters has five possible endings, greatly increasing the lifespan of a game you could otherwise beat in less then an hour... if you're lucky.

Excellent game, highly recommended. It's a fast paced isometric (top-down?) shooter with RPG/roguelite elements. I'm really surprised I haven't heard many people talk about this game, it is very good.
Gameplay is run and gun, you have a default attack and 2 special skills, one of which you can upgrade/change (if you get lucky). You can unlock per-run character buffs from a randomized skill tree, you get one buff whenever you beat a level and you can find others via cards.
Levels are a card layout sort of like solitaire - when you beat a card you get access to the cards it was covering. Each card can be an arena (fight and kill) or buffs/shops/etc.
Roguelite elements are: if you die you have to start over at the beginning (game level 1 of 6, no buffs from last run, etc), and by completing multiple missions (basically mini-achievements) you unlock permanent character buffs.
The combat is fast paced and smooth, there's a great variety of interesting enemies, managing spells is really fun, the randomized skill tree works surprisingly well, and I really really liked the music.
It's taken me 5.5 hours to beat the game on normal with the first char, and I'm definitely going back for more with the other chars. If you're really good at this type of game you might find normal easy, but there is a hard mode which I won't be trying haha - I am terrible at iso/top-down shooters so I'm happy that normal is doable for me.
Very highly recommended if you enjoy roguelites, isometric shooters, or action/combat RPGs.

Alright, so I always hate to make the inevitable comparison to other games in a series, and this game really is pretty similar to the first one, but I'm going to go ahead and not recommend this one in favor of just recommending the first. If you really like the first, sure play this one too, but honestly you'd probably be better off just replaying the first one a few extra times.
The main problem I had with this game was that you had infinite lives. It gave it a much more trial-and-error sort of feel (not to mention the literal trial-and-error levels later on). This changes the pacing and feel of the game dramatically, I would argue for the worse.
The first game threw mechanics at you, and you didn't necessarily know how to handle them at first, but once you got it figured out there were no surprises. In this game, there are lots of surprises. For this sort of micro-level, optimization/speedrun platformer, that's very frustrating.
Furthermore, there's a small animation that covers the entire level for, say, the first half a second, for every level. This, too, gets very frustrating for this sort of game. (For the record, I don't recall if this was the case in the first game or not. However, I did play the first one immediately before this one, so the fact that it didn't stick out means it probably didn't matter so much then if it was there.)
While I appreciate improvements to the physics (there were a couple frustrations with the first game related to the physics), I think they went a little overboard and made it too easy. Too many levels could be completed by just spamming jump and blowing through every obstacle without having to worry about your timing.
Finally, too many of the levels were just too easy. Infinite lives means it doesn't matter if you die a couple times figuring out where things are in the level. There are no consequences. So you die a couple times, and if you take too long getting to the exit, so what, you'll get there again next life. Speaking of taking too long, I think this game relied too heavily on just having longer levels where you went back and forth a bunch. Another consequence of infinite lives, one of the few ways to ramp difficulty is just to make it harder to do everything in the allotted time. In the first game, the time pressure didn't generally act as a way to kill you before reaching the end of the level, just a way to make sure you didn't stop to catch your breath for very long in any one place.
I guess all of this is just to say that this is a very different game from the first one. I found it much less enjoyable overall. Beating an area I was having trouble with in the first game provided me with a sense of accomplishment. With this game, I just didn't get stuck period, there was no real difficulty, just took a little longer.
On a side note, the music is still cool, the graphics are alright, though I thought they were a bit worse in this one than the first (less is more).
Anyway, I would really only recommend this if you're interested in trying out the level editor, seems neat.

I originally recommended Battleborn, but cannot any longer do so. It's been a little bit after launch, and Gearbox still has plenty of time to fix the gripes I have with this game, but matchmaking seems purely random, matching newbies with veterans more often than not; the game is poorly optimized for graphics (my friend is unable to play 2 out of the 3 PVP gamemodes with a GPU considered within the game's specs), and there are exploits which have been around since beta.
Although I consider Battleborn a very enjoyable game when both teams are equally matched and when the game runs, Gearbox needs badly to fix its matchmaking & optimization, as these two conditions are infrequent at best.
For reference, here is my original review:
Battleborn is what you could call a MOBA with FPS elements (or the other way around), typically called a "hero shooter." With 25 playable characters at release, 3 PVP modes with 2 maps each, and a singleplayer/co-op campaign, Battleborn has a lot of gameplay to offer--which is necessary, considering its Triple-A pricetag.
Matches usually run anywhere from 5 to 20 minutes, depending on the gamemode. There's also a surrender option, and close matches may stall to timeout.
You'll hear bad things about any MOBA community, and yes, there are flamers, trolls, and ragequitters in Battleborn too. I've had a net positive experience in my first 20 hours with the official release (and more in the beta), and if you foresee having issues with other players, you can mute them quickly and easily with Tab-E (Mute All).
Character progression outside of individual matches boils down to grinding for Gear, Battleborn's equivalent of items or equipment for your character. You'll earn currency to purchase packs of (randomly-assorted) Gear by playing matches, purchase new Gear in the main menu, and thus be able to use your shiny new Gear in battle.
There's also a boatload of achievements, titles, lore, and skin to unlock. Completionists rejoice!
For those who enjoy competitive or casual multiplayer, I would absolutely recommend Battleborn. Bring some friends along or make some friends for optimum enjoyment, and remember the mute function.
As a disclaimer to my recommendation of this game, be informed that Battleborn apparently runs like♥♥♥♥♥on any computer with an AMD card. Here's hoping this issue gets fixed.

In a nutshell:  "Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney" meets live action profesional UK production.  With decent story and gameplay.
The basic mechanism is really just typical "Ace Attorney" gameplay (i.e. finding contradictions) with high quality FMVs story clips.  But unlike games associated with either features, it is not campy.  In fact, its presentation is top-notch.  The cinematics have been framed, edited and treated with exceptional care.  No green screens or CG effects.  No explosions or major action scenes.  The movies avoids the usual trap of taking on a too big of a scope.  It actually looks like a TV movie.  Except that it is not.  It is a game.
But behind the clips lie a writting team that produced a story that, although quite simple at its core, keeps you engaged like a typical page-turner.  The rich scripts are delivered by superb acting.  Your avatar, Inspector Jenks, at first appears to be a bit too expressive, an over-actor if you will.  But, much like Columbo, his quirks grows on you, and you come to accept his maneurisms (which is good, since you see him all the time...).  Then, unavoidably, there is the sinister Paul Rand, expertly played by veteran actor Paul Darrow.  If you have come to love "Kerr Avon" for his cynicism and egomania, rest asured that Paul Darrow has not lost any of his reptilian flair from his "Blake's 7" days.  The rest of the cast also handles themselves up to par.  No one acts "amateurish"... Well except one "dazed" person, but that could have been intentional...
Gameplay-wise, one feature that is THANKFULLY lacking is the dreaded "pixel hunt".  There is none.  When a location needs to be investigated, you do not need to smash the mouse button around the screen like a maniac.  You just simply click the magnifying glass that appears at the bottom of the screen, and Inspector Jenks will then handle the rest.  This allows you to focus on solving the contradictions.  In fact, gameplay can be summarized with A) walking around ( with some fast-travel points to instantly move between locations that are far apart), B) talking to people, and obviously C) finding contradictions (i.e. match two items from a conversation with a character that contradicts each other, exposing a lie...).  There are very little "use-item-here" situations, and when there are, they are quite obvious.  Also, there are no time-based or reflex-based situations either.
However, there have been times when I wanted to scream at the game that "THERE IS A CONTRADICTION RIGH THERE", but that being said, I only needed some external help only 3 times along the way, once being my complete ignorance on a certain subject that prevented me from knowing that "such" with "such" was an impossibility.
Also, although the case do have a sense of closure, you do get hinted that there are more at stake.  So you could say that the ending is... "partial".
However, these problems do not diminished the fact that I thoroughly enjoyed my journey through this game.  This is one of the first of recent "serious" FMV games.  Solid production, engaging story and acting, fun gameplay.

A really wonderful and fantastic game, with a heaping helping of hilarious cheese. The main premise of the game is to investigate the accidental(?) death of a young woman in a small town, but mysteries quickly pile on and turn into more mysteries, as your character interviews people left and right (some of them high as a kite) and turning up increasingly bizarre pieces of evidence.
The real meat of the game is the interviews -- you have to actually pay attention to what people are saying and try to catch them in a lie. It's super fun, as most games tend to lead you around by the nose these days. It's also quite difficult at times, especially when your list of topics and suspects grows longer and longer and you have a hard time determining what is a lie versus a merely ambiguous statement. Rarely, though, I would discover someone had made a clear contradiction, only to have the game dismiss it, but it only happened two or three times the entire game.
This is honestly the most fun I've had with a game in a long, long time. I played it with my significant other, and we had a million times more fun deducing (and occasionally laughing) together than we would have if we'd played it apart. This game is worth it at full price.

Played this through with my roomate. Took about seven hours with the two of us thinking on everything, no cheats used. It's a wonderful challenge, and none of it particularly unfair; often with these kinds of games you get into a situation where you're lost in the verbage, trying to figure out which exact lines the game wants you to choose, even if it's not the most logical. This game doesn't suffer from that at all, and we were generally able to single out the exact choices we had to make when hit with inspiration.
Acting is spot-on; my only real complaint is about how jarringly hammy the lead detective is, but it's so over-the-top that it eventually becomes strangely endearing. Might not be that way for everyone, but I've come to love Jenks' great facial expressions.

'Contradiction - Spot the Liar' had my attention as soon as I started it. You play as a detective who is inspecting a suicide of a college girl named Girl, who happens to be enrolled in a business course of an organization called Atlas which has all the right amounts of shady. It’s a brilliant setup and is very engrossing. I started playing this with my mom, who had never ever played any sort of video game. She immediately liked it and that’s saying a lot!
Coming to the mechanics, I really loved it. I think it has got its roots from the very famous board game 'Cluedo' and it works on the same principle of questioning the suspects and finding a contradicting statements they have made and so spotting their lies. It’s a really neat mechanic and it meshes in perfectly with this game.
The presentation is well laid out and the menus are easy to traverse. I really loved the little cut scenes which play out when switching between areas but it got a little monotonous in the end and I wished there was an option to skip it. But it’s not a very major gripe that it will keep you from playing the game at all.
Speaking about cut scenes, the main cut scenes are quite enjoyable. Mainly due to the over the top acting of Detective Jenks with his ridiculous outfit, with the more serious acting by the rest of the cast. There were some time where I felt that the acting was not up to the mark but it was negligible. I really enjoyed the acting of Mr. Paul Rynd who had a tone very similar to Professor Snape from the Harry Potter Series.
The story, wow it did grip me all the way from the beginning till the last bit. The ending for me was a letdown, I feel it was rushed and left many questions which I wanted to know unanswered. They introduced a lot of supernatural and horror elements which was fantastic for the brief about of time it lasted, but they shied away from it towards the end. Maybe due to the time restrictions they had to rush the final bits of the game. But I’m sure if they had given more time it would have been a 10/10 experience. This was one of the two issues I had with the game.
The other issue was some of the contradiction puzzles seemed easy, it may also be because I was always in track with all the replies given by each and every suspect for each and every evidence, but some contradictions are very hard to find.
Overall I had a lot of fun playing this game, it kept me hooked throughout until the end bit. They did throw a hint for a sequel in the end which would solve all the mysteries. I hope they manage to come out with it in the future. Finally saying that I do not recommend this game to anyone will be a contradiction itself, so yes go and play this game, its good! I want more of this please!

Note that I only recommend you getting this game during a sale, and here's why:
Son of Rome is in itself not a bad game, the gameplay mechanics are relatively solid, graphics are great and the story with its bombastic presentation will hopefully "keep you entertained"! Each level also includes several collectibles (comics, character backgrounds, artwork, etc.) for you to find and some of them aren't that easy to find.
Unfortunately, this is where the good stuff ends and the ugly begins:
- Combat is technically fine, but there's absolutely NO progression here. You will periodically gain enough XP to upgrade stuff like health, focus and so on as well as the "infamous" executions. Be advised, Son of Rome is not for the faint of heart, since after having dealt enough damage you can (and should) execute enemies, which is portrayed quite viscerally. After executing an enemy you will either get increased XP, health back, increase your damage for a short time or gain more focus. Focus is the resource to enter a kind of god mode in which even the toughest enemies (apart from bosses) will quickly fall. Your soldier has 4 basic abilites: block, shield bash, hit and dodge roll. Different enemies require different combat approaches, shields have to be knocked aside, enemies dazed to avoid dodging your attacks, some attacks cannot be blocked but have to be dodged, and some enemies can only be damaged by successfully blocking their attacks. Sounds like a robust foundation. Unfortunately, this is what you're going to do for the whole game. There is no variation here, which means combat gets stale quickly, especially since you can get your health back after every enemy you execute. And speaking of these executions, they get annoying quickly if they happen for almost every enemy in the game.
- Other than that you will simply follow the level path (there is barely any exploration) and sometimes use a scorpio, pilae, command your soldiers or walk in formation. All of this is well presented, but once again gets old rather quickly.
And that's basically the game...well the 5 hours you'll need to finish it anyway. Son of Rome is a VERY short game with interesting mechanics that are never expanded, which makes the game boring rather quickly. However, the presentation and story are quite well done, My only other real gripe is that the camera is following the character way too closely, which can cause nausea. It's done for a more "visceral feel", but I'm not a fan of it. Get it for 5 or 10 bucks.
Edit: No idea about the multiplayer or if there even IS a MP scene anymore. The game initially released in 2013 after all and was only ported to PC in 2016 or 2017, can't remember.

The developers have compared this game numerous times to The Binding of Isaac and Nuclear Throne and I can say that while the game may be similar it has quite a bit more content to make it stand out and apart from those titles.
The game plays similar to a twin-stick shooter, where are your arenas are designed for fast paced combat that keeps you on your toes with each encounter. As always there's a little Randomness and these kind of games to make each playthrough feel different and it never felt like to me that it detracted from the fun Factor. It was always a joy to unlock a new skill and to see how my play style would change a little bit based on my unlocks. The four different characters also demand different play styles based on their skill sets.
Designed to give challenging short play sessions I find myself coming back to the game over and over again learning from my mistakes and tweaking my character in a slightly different way each time in order to get that edge to win. Graphically the game remind me of a Diablo/ Torchlight combination and feels very aesthetically pleasing for the cyberpunk setting. The music is fittingly intense for the situations of combat and just as fittingly Mystikal went out of it.
As with most roguelike games there is a decent amount of challenge to be had here and the fun Factor will have me coming back for more for a long time to come. Though I picked this game up during a sale, I feel it was worth every penny even if I paid full price. I look forward to seeing what these Developers have up their sleeve in the future.

Due to Metal Gear being a narrative-heavy series, I won't be including any major spoilers in this review, as, with this game being focused on setting up for the narrative for The Phantom Pain, that alone would sour the entire experience and purpose of purchasing this game.
Having completed the game, I can say that I enjoyed my time with it, thanks to my past with the series and the replayability that the game offers.
I can definitely say that I will be playing this game in the future, even though I have The Phantom Pain.
However, this being said, I can say that I would only recommend buying this game on sale at a reduced price or as a part of the MGSV bundle, as the short length of the game may put some people off and the ending leaves some questions unanswered, obviously setting up for The Phantom Pain, which you will likely be hungry for after this game.

It is very easy to dismiss this game with a negative review as it only has one location where its missions take place. On the other hand, the description on the store page emphasises that Ground Zeroes is meant to be a prologue to the now available Phantom Pain. Basically, Ground Zeroes showcases the engine developed for Phantom Pain as well as its stealth gameplay.
We are in the '70s and Snake's job is to infiltrate a camp controlled by a paramilitary group where two hostages are being held. Basically, both are children and need to be exfiltrated before the enemy can get any information out of them. The intro looks great with the appearance of Skull Face - he looks quite menacing; he is basically the MGS version of Marvel's Red Skull. The ending gives us a rewarding cutscene that is also meant to be a sort of trailer for Phantom Pain.
Controlling Snake is very easy and we have the option to do a lot of things (in terms of movement, that is). The game focuses on stealth-based gameplay so if you prefer a more action-oriented approach this is not really for you. Imagine it as a kind of Splinter Cell game. Ending a mission results in an evaluation screen - not killing anybody and being unnoticed all the time can yield us the best score (labelled "S").
The game is not difficult. A so-called Reflex mode allows us to quickly react if we are noticed. The camera even directs us in the right way - doing a quick headshot (with a silencer on) can still save the day. I like how you can interrogate enemies making sure you get more information on the camp. This includes the location of ammo storage or information on where certain enemy types (e.g. snipers) are positioned. What I like about the main mission is how the order in which we save the children can be decided.
This is the controversial part of Ground Zeroes. Once the main mission is completed (in roughly 2 hours) you realise you have seen everything. Although additional missions (4 of them, so-called Side Ops) are available they all take place in the same camp. Objectives are different, though. Some are easier (the Intel Op Rescue is action heavy where stealth is hardly an option), while some require several reloads (Destroy AA Emplacements can be quite tough).
The above are varied and interesting but do not provide much additional information to the story. They do not change the fact that it is still not a full game; it is more like a stripped down AAA game which is not necessarily a problem, however, when you look at the regular price (20 EURs) it is understandable that some might see this as insulting.
If I remember correctly I purchased the game with a 75% discount. This was the correct price for something that can be completed in a mere 2 hours of playtime. I was happy to keep playing to complete the extra missions for more achievements. Overall, the game looks and plays like an AAA game: it looks great, voice acting is also very good (I understand Kiefer Sutherland is a regular when it comes to Solid Snake's voice) and completing the Side Ops can be very challenging (with an "S" rank in mind). It wouldn't be a Kojima / Konami game without all the hidden easter eggs, collectibles and extra gameplay modes / levels.
If you don't mind playing a "prologue" title then Ground Zeroes can be fun. Otherwise watch a playthrough on YouTube and head for Phantom Pain immediately.

Time for a review with what I call "The hierarchy of what matters in a game" the first being the most important and bottom the least important
~Story: The game doesn't seem to have any story, or perhaps it's less of a spoken story and more of a "your guess is as good as mine" story, but the feel of the game and the environment as you climb higher and higher is great.
~Gameplay: Smooth controls, great aiming, sensical spread to the damage and the enemies remain difficult despite your improvement at the game, ensuring that every game is fun and interesting
~Sound: The audio is simply amazing, the music is addictive on it's own even worth listening to on it's own! The guns have a nice sound to them making them feel quite real
~Replayability: I can see stacking up voer a hundred hours in this game before I grow bored of it and that's if the game doesn't get more content through updates. With the updates I forsee 300+ hours.
~Graphics: Greatly stylised old-school look, taking in the old pixelated guns and making it the style to make this game quite beautiful and always pleasing to look it. The dark theme keeps everything intense in feel and makes sure your eyes focus on what is moving.
All in all: Despite my love for a great story and this game lacking an obvious one, I don't typically expect one out of shooters or most games I buy to lose a few minutes here and there. Adding that to the rest of the game simply being this addictive I can't say much more than it is a must try, the game is lots of fun and can even startle you at times and despite some of the enemies feeling a tiny bit cheap I associate that to my innability at aiming than the enemy itself being cheap.
I do recommend!

This title aspires to be a throwback to the '90s with an emphasis on constantly moving, strafing around enemies and shooting from the hip. Champions Online is a great game that suffers under its management and monetization.
CO has some of the best character customization, and power customization, I've ever seen in a video game.  With City of Heroes by-and-large gone save for its community, it's one of the only decent superhero MMOs still in existence.  As someone coming from CoH, having a superhero MMO with numeric stats, and not governed entirely by power choices is something that requires adjustment, but I can live with it.
Now, that's under ideal situations.  When Perfect World took over, power customization, and even the right to pick your own powers, became a thing of the past unless you either bought a freeform character slot or became a paying subscriber.  Free players are limited to pre-set archetypes, which not only have fewer powers than freeforms, but have all but a few of their powers pre-selected, with only advantages remaining for players to choose.  Even then, a good half of the archetypes available are
paywalled.  The crafting system, once a robust and nuanced part of the game that added a lot of depth and versatility to your character build, was gutted, and is now limited almost entirely to combining mods.  Vehicles, probably the most anticipated addition to the game from the moment they were announced, were limited solely to being obtained from the cash shop or lockboxes.
Speaking of lockboxes, they're probably the single most onerous addition to the game.  Many times, the sole loot you'll get from an enemy will consist of lockboxes.  You'll pick up hundreds of these things over the course of one character's career, and the only way to get rid of them is to trash them, sell them to other players for a pittance (and good luck with that, by the way), or pay real money for a key to open one.  When you do open one, you have the
to get rare equipment, rare equipment mods, or a vehicle, but usually you'll just get a consolation prize consisting of questionite and drifter salvage - and while questionite doesn't suck as a reward, it's a far cry from the other things you're probably opening the lockbox for.
Barring the rare few costume unlocks you can find in-game, most costume options are barred behind either cash shop purchases or subscriptions.  I'd say a good 80% of costume options are only available via the cash shop, with the rest either being from limited-time events or other PvE sources. Similarly, alternative travel powers are typically only available from either the Questionite store or as cash shop purchases.
In the interest of fairness, I will say that you can
earn most things, even cash shop things, in game.  Questionite can be earned from defeating signature enemies and doing certain missions, and questionite can be sold to other players on the Questionite Exchange in exchange for cash shop currency.  The exchange rate, however, is god-awful and gets worse all the time, and it will take months, even years of farming to make any significant purchases.  Moreover, many cash shop items are priced at rates that can only be described as 'extortionate' - for example, purchasing a *single* freeform character slot costs more than a purchasing a month's subscription to the game.
All in all, if it wasn't weighed down by PWE/Arc Game's predatory monetization strategies, CO would be a fantastic superhero MMO.  As it stands though, expect to be nickle-and-dimed by the cash shop, purchase a sub, or farm for months to get anything worthwhile.

Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic:
With a game published in 2003, there isn't much new to say.  SWKOTOR is part of a game series played in the days long before the original trilogy. The story is rich and the interactions are impressive even today how ever, for a game  from 2003, its age is beginning to show in the graphics department.   Still, an incredibly enjoyable experience to play the game even after all of these ( 12) years.
Though alot of the secondary models such as background charcters and environments are noticably blocky and the graphics over all  have aged much as one would expect them too, the graphics are still not too hard on the modern eyes.  Though low-poly, most of the models are smooth enough.  [5/10]
The Sound track is specially composed for this game and it is quite plesent to listen to, suiting both the style and classical star wars; music feel.  How ever, though impressive for its time; major annoyances exist. Secondary sound packs such as Alien-speaking sound bites  are rather annoying, and they loop..which you startto notice real fast, and it gets grating.  [7/10]
As mentioned above, the Story is rich and the charcter interactions are likwise rich and immersive. This is a game you can really be comfertable role playing in if you can get past the areas where the game is so obviously aged.   A number of dialogue options  allow for interesting twists in side their own mini-story archs.  Though, the main story suffers a little bit from having binary endings... and  the main arche  ultimately doesnt care how you act through the game, your ending depends ona choice you make at the very end...  which is a bit off setting.
Rich in content none the less and worthy of mention in the same breath as ElderScroll series  in terms of content, lore and ability to interact with that content in game.  [8/10]
I recomend this game, especially for young fans of the StarWars francise... though be warned, the game is aged and the interface as well the graphics are below what you would consider standard for todays games.

This game is a gem !
Very cute, very fun and litteraly a wonder to play with friends !
It's simple, easy to learn and the harder difficulty levels offer quite a challenge.
You can upgrade your ship as you wish, using various combination and powerups and unlocking different ships layouts.
Each level I've seen so far were different from one another, with their own particular settings and challenges.
The game succeed in giving you the feeling that you're on a journey through various distant bits of space.
Playing with friends is incredible ! Co-op is where this game really shines. It's good to mention that you and your friend(s) get to play side by side, using controllers or the same keyboard. Attempting to work as an efficient team, running between the various stations of the ship to counter every challenges with good timing, trying to synergize as best as you can with your friends, it feels great, especialy when you beat some tough boss or especialy difficult level.
The different types of stations you can control requires different skills and offer different challenges. As a team you get to learn how to use everyone's skills in the most efficient way. As an exemple : I might not be good with turrets, I can still pilot the ship very well or use the shields to intercept as many projectiles as possible, making the ship much more resilient while my friends gun down everything. This make co-op interesting even with friends who are not aquainted with the game, as some stations are easier than others.
Even if you don't play with friends, the game is still very fun. You can choose a lovely AI pet that you can order to switch stations at will. You'll end up being the pilot since it's almost the only thing the AI won't do, yet it will be a different challenge than co-op since you'll have to manage your pet between the turrets, shield and map while attempting to navigate through various threats.
It's one of these rare games with a fun/price ratio where the amount of fun outweights the price by far !

Ryse: Son of Rome is a third person game with a lot of quick-time events during the Roman Empire. Originally made for Xbox One to show off its wonderful graphics, it got ported to the pc eventually. Visuals are the game's greatest strength: Characters, animation and environment all look great. Combat is mostly about rightly timed mouse button clicks which takes some time to get used to. Keep in mind that if the enemy changes his colour to blue, you need to press your left mouse button. And if the enemy changes to yellow, you need to press your right mouse button. Somehow, the developers made a bad job to explain this better.
The biggest gripe I have with this game is the wasted potential. It could have been a masterpiece about the Roman Empire where you are fighting endless hordes of savage barbarians. Yet the game ended up being a bad console port with a somewhat fun experience as long as it lasts.
+ great visuals
+ memorable scenes and scenery
+ you are a Roman soldier who fights for civilization
+ many interesting cutscenes
+ developers have guts to show a lot of blood, gore, nudity and other things I won't mention here.
+ testudo formation
+ some kill streaks are very nice
-- bad console port where you will often experience sudden fps drops even if your pc is very strong.
- you can't remap the controls. inexcusable
- no fov slider. it's just too zoomed in. you could fix it with the cheat engine though.
- too linear
- combat could be more complex
- very easy
- NOT historically accurate and it gets worse later on
- lasts about 5-6 hours
- Romans have a British accent. please hire some Italians next time.

Bugs and other informations:
- I fell through the ground once. Loading the last checkpoint helped me.
- cheat engine for fov fix
- best advice to reduce sudden frame drops with nvidia cards is to turn off vsync in the game settings. Leave the game and go to your nvidia control panel. Add ryse.exe to its game list. After adding ryse.exe, go to vertical sync and change it to "adaptive". It still not perfect, but it will improve a bit.
Replay value: low (too linear, combat isn't complex enough, bad console port)
Rating: 7/10
Recommendation: Yes, but only if you tolerate sudden frame drops and no remapping of controls.
Worth: don't pay more than 5 bucks since it only lasts for about 5-6 hours

FIRST IMPRESSION, I WILL GIVE IT ANOTHER CHANCE AND MAY CHANGE MY MIND DRASTICALLY:
The game is advertised as being a roguelike version of Doom/Quake, but ironically Doom and Quake actually feel more dungeon crawl-y thanks to their intricate maze like level designs and emphasis on strategy and resource management.
Paranautical Activity is basically just a first person Binding of Isaac, in that it just lays out some square rooms at random, populates them with enemies, and calls it a day. In essence, there's really no reason to brag about this game being procedurally generated, because all it really does is switch up the order in which you face the games small pool of monsters while throwing slightly different stats at you.
PA also locks you into every room once you enter it, and won't let you out till you kill every monster inside.  This might have worked for Binding of Isaac since that game was essentially just an arena shooter pretending to be a roguelike, but here it just makes things more mindless. Unlike Doom and Quake where a large part of victory was not only reflexes but picking your battles, escaping at the right time, and thinking strategicly, PA instead reduces things to a guessing game by forcing you to blindly pick which room you enter and than not letting you leave if it turns out doing so might be the smarter strategy.
The controls feel a bit clunky also. I think you have to move for a bit before you accelerate, which feels like♥♥♥♥♥♥in a game where moving and turning fast could be the difference between life and death. The enemy designs are decent, but nothing special and are never put to much interesting use thanks to the arena based structure of the game.
Aestheticly it's of course as bleh as it looks. Same not-memorable chiptunes you've heard in a million retro indie games, same cuby graphics you've seen in a ton of Minecraft rip offs. I also have no idea why they thought it was a good idea to name their game a pun based on some dumb horror film people will have forgotten about in a few years.
I think the point of all these action roguelikes is that people want a game that feels like a dungeon crawl but with enjoyable skill based combat and that feels new each time. The combat here may be be skill based, but it's rather bland and the games structure doesn't make it feel like a dungeon crawl at all, it also starts to feel repetitive even on the same playthrough. Doom and Quake did every aspect of this game better, and PA doesn't bring anything worthwhile to the table.

$60 for a 90s-looking game seems a little bit steep but this is easily the best 4x space strategy ever made. I hate to disparage the work of so many awesome dev teams out there but nothing else comes close to this. Main reasons why IMHO.. some other games have a couple of these but none has it all:
-Real time (can pause/speed up/slow down)
-No monolithic race/empire system - you can often have many empires of the same race, and/or multiple races in the same empire. When you find some bird people they might be divided into 3-4+ separate nations and fighting each other across ideological lines. It's not just going to be the single united BigBirdian Empire every time.
-No toggling between galaxy/system views - you can zoom in/out SMOOTHLY from the entire galaxy to a single freighter ship in the middle of nowhere -- this more than makes up for any relative deficiencies in the 2d graphics (which look a lot better ingame than in the Steam store screenshots btw). Also the planets actually rotate around their suns, and satellites around their planets!
-Incredible depth of automation options. You can choose what and where to automate, whether it's taxes and immigration or entire systems and fleets. You can put the whole Federation on autopilot and just control the USS Enterprise and go explore♥♥♥♥♥♥ Even if you love micromanaging, at some point you will get so big that you basically have to start automating certain things to get♥♥♥♥♥♥done, but you can always toggle back and forth freely or override your AI; there are no "sector system" penalties a la Stellaris. Coolest thing about this is the advisor-mode which is a compromise where the AI just asks you for permission to do things (colonize a new planet, build 3 more carrier groups to fight the pirates, massacre the opposition on planet Z with a mech force, etc.) ... really makes you feel like a boss.
-Private sector economy - civilian ships flying around all over the place, and pirates trying to jack them and blow them up. Instead of arbitrary "trade" and "piracy" and "tourism" modifiers to your income, you can actually see the♥♥♥♥♥♥loads of individual ships trading cargo etc. The big numbers are a sum of each of their separate, observably simulated activities - and you can try to protect them or rob any one of them yourself.
-Mod-friendly, several great mods available (more races, more techs, more ships, total conversions for Star Trek and Star Wars, etc). Also, unlike the 90s-era games it looks like, it's stable AF and never crashed to desktop on me.. even with a bunch of weird mods :P

Pros:
- Really well acted and directed FMV adventure game. Decent soundtrack, too. It's incredible that all this was accomplished on a short budget.
- Interesting way of navigating around the locations.
- Virtually no pixel hunting.
- The UI helps a lot in order not to get stuck - and if you use up hints and chief calls and still don't have clue, there is also a "cheat" system to power through your predicament.
- It is not really a short game, or at least doesn't feel like it. It takes its time and you get to meet and get to know most of its (multiple) characters quite well.

- The gameplay is mostly backtracking over locations to interrogate/ ask questions based on new info you discover. However, there is a three-level hint system integrated in the game that assures that you will never get stuck
- 1 or 2 of the (several) contradictions that you are required to spot seemed a bit far fetched.
A definite recommendation from me to anyone who enjoys FMV adventures.

I really should not like the game. I dont like roguelike games and I am not that much into Twin-Stick Shooter. Based on those two facts, I shouldnt like the game.
But I do.
Dont be confused because I dont have many hours on record, because I bought the game first on iPad and played most of my time on this device. It actually took me a while until I realized: There is a PC version!
So why do I enjoy a game I really shouldnt enjoy?
Is it the artstyle? Like a darker version of Shadowrun, mixing technology with magic you feel like there is a whole world to explore. Honestly, there isnt, because it is an arenashooter, but there are bits of lore and character backstory that suck you in, even though the world isnt that fleshed out. But your imagination fills in the blanks and then you are suprisingly immeresed in a world you know nearly nothing about. Thats something not many games can actually do.
Is it because of the characters? Four characters, a modern version of a young mage, a superpowered cyborg, a powerful medium with dark and twisted entities in her mind, and a century-old blood mage. They all are so different, and they all are enjoyable as hell. How surprised I was when I played the medium and suddenly: Melee attacks. Melee?! I use a katana in a twinstick shooter? And it works?! What magic is this?
Is it because the pogression is steady even if you kinda suck? You progress through randomized mission which are, most of the time, easy enough to do. Even when you have a really terrible run, you can at least complete a single mission. And with this, you get permanent skills and buffs for your character on another run. Or you unlock a new character. Your progression is steady, and even a mediocre player will come to the point where a run works so much in your favor that you blast through all six stages and finish a run. Lets see if your next run will be as awesome as the last.
Well, perhaps its all of the above reason. I really enjoy the game and as a mediocre player, I really like how I have to think to get trough the game: Which challenge should I take on now? Try that arena with the three waves of enemies to get more mana for upgrades, or buy a cheaper upgrade now? Use mana to buy health at a shop, or can I blast through the boss with only 2 points of health?
I had fantastic victories, and jaw dropping defeats. You know, those defeats where you have to close the game and do something else, because right now, you dont even wanna know this game exists. But I took my iPad in my hands half an hour later and continued. There is a certain magic to games that invoke so many feelings in you just with gameplay.
The verdict is clear: If you like roguelikes and/or twinstick shooter, there is zero reason not to invest in this game. Heck, even if those arent your favorite genres, you could still take a look at it. Perhaps get the 3.99€ iOs version, like I did at first. If you are anything like me, you will purchase the PC version shortly after. Its a hell of a game.

The risk reward systems are among the best I have seen in any game.
LOF is not a beautiful game. The art is compitent and does a good enough job to clearly convey the gameplay. From a system design standpoint, Leap of Fate is a fantastic achievment and a high bar for others to chase. Absolutely worth the price of admission. This is a must play for all fans of rogue-like action games. GG!

This game is one of the best hidden gems on steam. It's a game about flying a spaceship and rescuing space critters, with every player manning a different station. For example, someone might be stearing, while another is on shields, and another on a turret. It's such a cool concept, and it's executed phenomenally well. Switching between stations is fast and easy, and all of the controls are simple and intuitive.
The three difficulties encompass pretty much every playstyle there is; with easy being almost impossible to die in, normal being challenging but fair, and hard/veteran being hard enough that you're almost guaranteed to die a few times.
The music in this game is incredible. This game would have been perfectly fine if there was some generic, relaxing "space" music in the background, but they decided to do more than that. Some of the tracks are reminiscent of Hotline Miami. Almost kind of odd considering how cutsy this game is, but it works and sounds great (look up "ost Crystal C"). And the boss themes are intense and get the heart pounding (my favourite is "Orion").
The graphics are beautiful to look at and everything animates extremely smooth. It can be eye candy in some parts. I should also mention that while this game is meant to be played with a friend or significant other, it's still fun to play the game by yourself. If played solo, you get an npc that you can tell to man different stations. The AI is good enough that you never get frustrated with it; it's honestly better than most real people I've played this with.
In conclusion, this game is well worth the $15 asking price, and a steal when it goes on sale. So do yourself a favor and pick this up. You won't regret it! (probably)
