I want to like this game, as it's a pretty cool take to the intergalactic crew management genre.  However, I eventually had to stop playing because it was crashing too much and I didn't see anything to look forward to at the end of the grind.
The crew management aspect is fairly rapidly solved to the point where player involvement ceases.  Each crew member can be assigned what to do in four quarter shifts.  You can assign a crew member to any shift they have skills for, and they will spend that time doing that job.  If you instead give them that shift for leisure time, they'll take care of their needs.  So basically all you have to do is set up your ship's facilities so they can take care of their needs during leisure time, make sure they get enough leisure time shifts, and you're done.  There are some random events such as crew members getting sick or being demoralized by something, but these are annoying exceptions.
Making progress starts out difficult but ends up monotonous.  It is not at all difficult to make money running cargo: buy commodities where they are produced and sell them literally anywhere else for a profit, an extremely rudimentary and easy trading model.  However, the earnings of simply trading are small and it gets monotonous fast.  So the player is encouraged to try to do missions to hasten income and introduce a bit more intresting variety of activities.  Big mistake!  Missions have a high tendency to backfire horribly in repair costs, contraband fees, and failure fees!  Once you suffer a major setback, you have no choice but to do boring cargo missions.
Random events have a tendency to give you random money or take it away, which helps keep things interesting, but in an way that's annoyingly completely outside of player control.  Every mistake you make is autosaved, so you're stuck with it.  I'm not normally in favor of save scumming, but when the missions have a high tendency to backfire this badly (and sometimes due to bugs) I think it would have made for a more enjoyable experience for the player.
Overall, Cosmonautica needs an economy rebalance,  a crew management rebalance, and its technical glitches fixed.   It's been released for years, and they've yet to patch out crashing bugs, buggy missions, and other technical issues (such as the shower curtain not animating, displaying contorted polygons).  Did the guy who originally coded it leave? I think the developers probably gave up.  That's a shame, because these are some pretty great assets here, they just need to be utilized properly.

OK -  So, Are you looking for SimTower?  Well This game, is sorta like SimTower.
I was feeling nostalgic and was truely missing the old days of playing SimTower when I was a kid (ironically 20 years later- I go to work everyday as an architect).  The nostalgia.  The feeling of getting taller and taller as your economy grows.  I remember just LOVING that opening sound with SimTower that epic (kong/kong) that to this day... I have no idea what it really was;  But mannn I sure loved hearing it as people poured in from my metros every morning and flooded my tower;
THE REVIEW;
Project Highrise is very much simular to SimTower,  It harks back to the wonderful days of 1990's when graphics cards wern't a thing.  And your game could have 42 colors.  It sounds like it It looks like it, but some of the gameplay elements that I so dearly loved.  Were changed (how... why?... Whyyy?)
ELEVATORS+GOING VERTICAL:
Going vertical in Project Highrise just doesn't feel like a challege.  Which, for some people may be cool.  But for me.  It was definately not a cool thing.  I loved how SimTower had a somewhat challenging elevator managment system;  Elevators had a maximum number of cars and you could see them do their little dance every morning-  completely removed in Project Highrise.  It's like people go into the wall and pop out somewhere else.  Which, is so depressing.  The mechanic isn't challenging and there isn't a feeling of diversity in creating spaces.  I would love to see a more challenging elevator system worked in;  Limited number of elevator cars, cars that skip stop on levels, stairs, esclators, elevator height limits- those were the BREAD AND BUTTER of SimTower; Removed...  What WAS added however was a rather complex "closet" system.  Where players are challenged to manage the vertical movement of resources up the tower.  You provide, water/cable/phones (which is suprizingly realistic to how real towers work) - And I was actually quite exicted to see this worked into the game;  Although.  It didn't feel very complex.  it was more or less.  Build it.  Have enough of it. and keep buildling more of it.  Which.  left me with a very luke warm...
Score: 4/10
Verdict; Not challenging.  Boring even.   And actually borderline FRUSTRATING.  As this mechanic seems so VITAL to get right in a tower building game.
CUSTOMIZATION:
Ok.  Project Highrise takes the cake here.  There's LOTS you can fit in your tower.  Copy Rooms, Computer Service Rooms, Florists, Cafes, Fast Food, Sports Bars.  The list goes on.  Which is great.  I particularly loved how the Lobbies can be customized and you can bling out your tower good ole' Donald Trump Style.  It feels cool.  Although. going back to the vertical transportation diversity issue.  Organizations of what goes were: sorta matters.  But sorta doesn't.  You can place the office service/maids room 50 floors away from your best executive offices.  And they fly up the magic elevators like they are only the next door over.  I felt very much not challenged.   It was fun seeing how Storage space is required for your shops, but their relationship in the tower to the shops didn't matter much;  So long as there was an elevator somewhere to that floor, everyone seemed to think that 1 elevator was enough.
Score: 8/10
Virdict; I'll give some bonus points in this genre, because it genuinely made the game really fun to play for about a day or so; and then I got bored.  Placing chairs in a lobby isn't really worth 20.00. Not to mention that after playing 10 or so hours I had money up the wazzoo.  So although the feeling of being able to build ANTYHING (workshop?! heck yes) is cool.  It's pretty boring in the grand scheme of things when there's not much challenge of making it work.
POPULATION / GAME MECHANICS / ECONOMY
Ok.  The metro station;  THE METRO STATION!  It was the collest thing in SimTower.  You could see all the little sprites buzzing around your basements and it felt like a little New York City maze down there.  Unfortunately.  Project Highrise.  Missed the mark again.  The metro connection takes up something like 8 or so tiles.  It's not animated very "interestingly"... It's just some gates that brings people to the tower.  And it's not even very many people!   I wanted to create a great subterranian metroplex full of shops and buzzing with people.  Instead.  It felt more like... a bombshelter with storage rooms and IT support closets... It Just wasn't as glamourus as I expected.  Not to mention that Luxury shops arn't very luxurious underground in Project Highrise so tennants just kept leaving.  It didn't feel very well thoughtout.  My underground megamall just wasn't going to happen  under my mile high office tower. and my office tower wanted food and dining.  But they didnt' want to eat undergound (next to the metro station).
Economy;  What economy.  I suppose to be fair;  SimTower wasn't exactly challenging to make money.  If you wait, money will come.  But Project Highrise didn't really offer any challenges with organizing my tower.  The game managment didn't really offer anything more than picking some wallpapers for my lobby... which.  Like I said before, was slightly cool.  But... the coolness wore off fast.  And the feeling of "being challenged" was non-existant.
Score: 2/10
Verdict; Snore.  And starting to regret paying as much as I did for a game that missed the mark in so many places.
Final Verdict;
Is the game worth 25 dollars?  well. Sure. considering that going to a movie and being entertained for 1 hour costs 12.00 these days.  Sure.  Project highrise is about as exctiing as that overpriced craft beer that you bought to impress that hotty totty date you brought along.  It was cool for about 2 seconds.  Your friends were like; Oh.  Well- I didn't order that one...  And the next day you're left thinking.  Wow.   Why didn't I just order a water.
Is the game worth a good review?
Eh. Nah.  When I started, I was thinking oh, hopefully they address this... and after a while I thought... Yeah. No.  they're not going to change it.  So It's just kinda a bummer to see such a good attempt to hit a home run and instead just get a face full of dirt.

this game has somewhat the same problem as Cities: Skylines, in that there is little structure to the game, making it heavily sandboxy, while at the same time no significant benefit or motivation to going for the more advanced, complex features like luxury stores, large offices, and high end apartments, especially once you've stabilized your income with a hundred small offices/studio apartments.  Since so much of the higher end office/housing/store spaces require a certain number of Prestige stars, the process of getting more stores contributes more to your building's income and attention than actually having the high end offices to begin with.
Basically, it's the sort of game where you can have a giant tower filled with a handful of mega offices, or a giant tower filled with hundreds of tiny offices, or a giant tower with a mix of both, and there is almost no effect on gameplay beyond the mind-numbingly repetitive task of needing to wire up every single floor with electrical wires, water pipes, cable TV, phone lines, and gas lines, along with a special room for each of these that can only be placed underground.
Once you're about 20-30 days in, barring some self-imposed challenge or a major catastrophe, you're basically done with the game, making huge income and with everything running smoothly, and not have much more than small and medium offices/apartments/restaurants.  There's an entire tier of large and elite office and housing units you can go for, but which are no longer a challenge to acquire.  At this point, you're no longer personally invested in making your tower nice or neat or particularly special; you're just laying down office/apartment suites, then dumping all their required stuff nearby (trash bins, janitorial services, copy services, etc) so they won't whine and complain.
Some gameplay features that are frustrating:
- The Buzz/Influence system.  It's very slow in coming early on, and can be a treat to have enough early on to spend on ad campaigns for increased foot traffic or decreased maintenance costs.  Soon after that, you've got thousands of Buzz points to spare and no use for any of the services provided except to unlock more contracts.  The Influence chart only unlocks like 5-6 different things in 3 different sections, after which you have no more use for Influence points at all.
- Art.  The system in use here is incredibly clumsy and messy.  An entire section of the aforementioned Influence points section is devoted solely to art, yet there's essentially no use for art nor any space for it unless you've pre-planned everything or forcibly evict tenants to make room.  You end up needing to spend lots of money and fill in precious space with multiple different "Art Dealer" suites which generate no income and do nothing other than give you the ABILITY to buy and set down art.
The art itself is limited to the same 3 or 4 objects per category (small, medium, large, outdoor, lobby), tend to be extremely expensive, and can only be placed in empty spaces.  It's unclear how people are even interacting with the art or decorations, nor is there any indication that decorating the empty spaces in your building do anything with regards to tenants' comfort or aesthetics.  I only wallpapered the first two floors' empty spaces, and left the rest in their default "Construction Site" look, with no boost or penalty either way.  Setting down Art basically amounts to having a tiny empty hallway with a fist-sized sculpture on a pedestal in the middle of it.
- Plazas.  The game doesn't tell you until too late that you need at least 5 plaza tiles in order to unlock the Influence choice needed to boost your available building space.  By that time, I had filled in my entire lot area with building.  I ended up having to remove my lobby and a portion of the back of the building just to fit 5 plaza tiles.  On top of that, I find that the available Plaza Art was comparatively massive compared to the plaza tiles, meaning the game apparently expected me to have a much narrower tower in order to pretty up the outside.
- Noise/Smell.  Some of this tends to be common sense (Restaurants generate noise and smell), but there is an immense lack of detail put into this that would be expecting too much, but at the same time would add a bit of special uniqueness to gameplay.  For example; the category of Restaurant includes everything from restaurants, fast food, diners, and bars.  All of them generate Noise and Smell, even bars which do not serve food.  Stores universally generate noise, even book stores and luxury jewellers, which arguably should not generate enough noise to disturb someone 2 stories down from them.
Which leads to another issue; the bleed effect of Noise/Smell is excessive, reaching sometimes 2 or more stories up or down, and in some cases bleeding to the suite directly above them, but somehow not having any effect on the suite situated diagonally from them.
- Information.  It would be nice to know what objects or buildings generate noise/smell, or what makes an area High Traffic.  This doesn't become too big of an issue, but it becomes redundant when you have suites that like high traffic, versus suites that like high traffic and like being near elevators, and no discernable difference in tenant happiness.  You also end up with things like having a luxury jewelry store being built 10 stories underground, with no other suites in the area, right next to an elevator, and the business booming and having no problems with traffic.
Basically, it's a rich and compelling game experience for about 6 hours, after which time there's nothing new left to do.  You've figured out the game by then and realize nothing you do in it really matters, so long as you manage to turn a profit.

There are a lot of really long review about this game so I'll try to keep it short. Yes, there is a pretty big learning curve and the UI doesn't help matters at all, and end game can get pretty slow if you prefer to micromanage EVERYTHING. There are tons of super useful player-made guides online to help you dive into the game, and the in game encyclopedia is very useful as well. There is also a fairly strong modding community that warrents playing the game more if you're bored with the vanilla version (apparently there is an AI mod out there that fixes a ton of the games AI problems, I've yet to check it out). The graphics are dated of course, but there are mods for those too. Or, if you really want to, you can mod it yourself. After digging through the code for 30 minutes, I felt confident enough to create my first race. If you wanna mess with the engine, however, that takes a bit more work (I want to create naturally spawning Mass Relays from Mass Effect that are linked to a partner across the galaxy and catapult ships instantly from one end to the other, still working on that). My only real con is that I cannot enable Return of the Shakturi story events when starting the game as a pirate faction, because I'd love to have to fight them with my upstart pirate empire.

Not worth plowing through the learning curve. After spending much time figuring out the mechanics and complex features, the game shows its shallow core gameplay despite many complex and deep features. The contrast of depth between features is high, some are just underdeveloped. At one point, after the 50 hour mark, I was thinking this was probably the best 4x I've played, but as time went by its flaws and limited gameplay became apparent. In the end this game turned out to be a map painter for me.
The scope is something I've never experienced in other 4x games. It is possible to create a galaxy with 1400 star systems. Each star sytem can house planets, gas giants, asteroids and all have their real time Orbital trajectories. Planets are able to contain multiple moons, so we are talking about thousands of planets in total, really impressive.
This game does a tremendous job turning boring space into a living galaxy full of mining, trading and transport ships doing their routines like busy ants.

There are some interesting choices to be made. For example you can research a reactor which is efficient in the fuel to energy conversion but has relatively low power output or do you go for the reactor that has more power output but inefficient in fuel to energy conversion. Or do you go for one that has a middle grounnd but runs on a different resource. There is a great variety in weapons; Ions, lasers, torpedo's, hangars for fighters with their subclasses, gravitic you name it, it's there. Do you go for the fast shield regeneration or for a slower one but higher shield capacity? The most interesting tech tree I've encountered in the genre.

Some options which are available: Steal territory map, steal galaxy map, Steal operations map, Sabotage structures and ships, assassinate characters, counter espionage and more. Pretty deep feature and there is a wide range of options.
Hands down for the ship customization. The depth is second to none. You need a proper reactor to match the power output of your engines, weapons, hyperdrives. All equipment uses static energy, when weapons, engines or hyperdrives are being activated you will get a peak in your energy output that has to be covered. There even is a Speed vs energy curve for the engines alone which gives incredible details about your energy usage at speed X. The more mass your ship carries the more engines and vector engines you need to keep your acceleration constant.

You have to take into account if a ship has enough fuel to complete a round trip, Ship components need specific resources and so on.
Race X can have a victory condition like; Mine 25% of the galaxy's total of resource A. Race Y can have something like; Lose the least amount of ships or/and have the biggest trade volume.
I like the uniqueness of this system. The economy is split into a state sector (=you) and a private sector (the AI). The problem I have with this system is that trading is entirely located in the private sector. The private sector is responsible for trading, mining and transporting and will build ships at your spaceport if they require more. So with other words the AI handles the trading. You have zero influence on trading. For example, when you need resources A from race B you can't ask a X amount from race B and send a Z amount of freighters to transport it...The private sector will get that resource for you, but from what race? How much and how many freighters will they send? I don't know. This is a factor contributing to the shallow overall gameplay. I really would like to see some manual involvement in trading.
A very cool feature with its problems. The whole idea of offering missions to blow up spaceports, ships and smuggling resources at your request is great. You set a starting price and pirates factions are able to offer prices below the starting price. The pirate faction with the lowest offer will get the mission. They will not get paid by you when they fail to achieve their mission. The frustrating part about pirates is the continues invasions of them into your empire. Troops will get rid of them but the broken AI troop recruitment makes manual recruiting so cumbersome for big empires that it is just utter frustration.
Sooner or later you will have to turn on some elements of automatization to prevent micromanagement from getting tiresome. The AI makes such weird decisions like sending your ships halfway through the galaxy for refueling or creating inefficient ship designs. AI Troop recruitment didn't function at all in any of my games. I'm sorry but the AI is incompetent , you just can't let the AI take it over without sheer frustration.
Got a new tech unlocked? Let's update our 15 ship designs. After a few tech unlocks this becomes a chore. You will try turning on the AI automated ship designs for relieve only to discover useless designs leading to more frustration. Updating ship designs takes too much time relative to other features.

Transport ships will not always load up troops for 100%. It will often take multiple commands individually before they fully load up. AI automatization of troop recruitement at your planets is broken.
Strategy boils down to attacking the nearest planet with your blob of ships. There is hardly any tactical gameplay battle-wise. Battles are oftentimes clusters of ships attacking the nearest ship, formations don't play a role in this game.

You don't get the feel of interacting with races and I'm missing personality of races reflecting in gameplay.
Relations detoriate continuously, meaning you will have to give money periodically to prevent them from decreasing. When your border makes contact with your neighbour's border relations deteriorate so fast that war is just inevitable.

This is by far my favorite of impulse buys this Steam Summer Sale Season. There's been a glut of rogue-lites lately, but Leap of Fate oozes style and cool flavor, great twinstick gameplay, little downtime, and genuinely interesting characters! There's a ton to unlock, from permanent bonuses to costumes and alternate endings. It is also *snappy!* You move from scene to scene with rapid succession, with no back-tracking unless you suddenly need to *instantly* teleport into a previous room to grab that discarded health pack. Hell, the game even leaves you little icons so you can quickly see where you left old drops!
As a warning, I was a little confused at first until I noticed that the game makes use of 4:3 screen size in certain scenes, but full 16:9 in others. Also, the aiming of some special attacks can feel a little floaty at times with my Xbox controller (since you control and place a radial crosshair with your right thumbstick), but the main attack was perfectly accurate.

There's a lot of roguelike/roguelite games. This trend is becoming a little annoying. It seems this genre is exploited to the maximum and personally I'm tired of it. I was hoping to take a loooong break from such games - making Enter The Gungeon my last expierence with roguelikes. Then I saw Leap of Fate. I'm a sci fi/cyberpunk junkie, so i just could not resist. To hell with it, I'm buying the game! Damn it, i said to myself - why am I so hot-headed? I WILL regret that.
The thing is - i don't regret it. Leap of Fate is one of my favorite roguelite's of 2016. Starting from the story and aesthetics - sweet mixture of sci-fi, magic, mysticsm and cyberpunk. Nothing can go wrong here! Suprisingly, the storyline is pretty decent too. You unveil fates of your 4 main protagonists by playing them and achieving character goals. It's all well voice-acted, even if cutscenes are just stills - it's impressive.
The core gameplay is very fast and satyfsying. You play levels - inside randomized tarot decks. Each cards is a encouter or a bonus. Its all very fluid - transitionst between choosing cards and fight scenes are instant. Battles are similar to common hack&slash games, like Diablo. It's all quick and full of explosions. Also - the music keeps you immersed.
Completing all 6 levels in one go... is a huge task. But this games gives You small bonuses for trying. You can earn permament upgrades for your guys, you don't lose everything upon death. This is comforting, but if you cringe at idea of losing most of your stuff with death - this won't help You much. It's still a roguelike game! Only a little more forgiving.
Leap of Fate is fair, immersive and really well designed. It gets though eventually, but that's what we like about roguelikes!

Let's break down why Champions online has the potential to be a far better game than it is.
Firstly I'll say this.   Unless you're looking to waste a day on something different and then you'll uninstall and never play again, bring your wallet.  You don't HAVE to purchase anything, the base power sets and character creator are fine for playing the game and even getting to level cap, so long as you avoid the multiplayer dungeon missions (adventure packs) that can't really be solo'd by a standard character.
However  If you mess around for a bit then buy a freeform character slot and a couple of cosmetic pieces to make the character YOU want to play as, you'll have a far better time.  It's the same as pretty much any F2P MMO nowadays and even some sub and B2P games.  Spending more money = more fun and convenience. Even the juggernaughts of the MMO industry do this.   Champions has the benefit that it WON'T screw you for cash.  Everything CAN be earned in game by currency trading and farming even if that can take months but you'll never have to pony up real money to equip that upgrade or enter the next tier of content.
On to the nitty-gritty. Graphically and technically, CO is a mess,  It's an old game and desperately needs an overhaul.   Bugs are common and usually hilarious with character models being flung all over the place by explosions and getting stuck in ludicrous positions , physics on stacked objects don't seem to have been implimented with floating bits of scenery present after nearly every battle.  The game also suffers from lag, server issues and a nasty memory leak that usually crashes the game after an indeterminate amount of time.
Sound design is also bare bones basic.  half a dozen music tracks, shooty and explodey noises with the odd sound glitch thrown in.  Nothing even remotely notable.
All of this can and should be fixed, but PW spend their time and effort on their favoured son Star trek Online instead which is a crying shame considering Champions has so much potential since, even in it's current state it's a roleplayer's and powergamer's wet dream.
Other games let you play as Tim the wizard, or Gronk the orc warrior.  You need to fit in with the settings, theme and lore and you'll never be a more standout character than the golden boys and girls of that world.  *coughThrallcough*  Hell , in many MMO's even NPC guards have better stats than your characters.
In CO, you can play as Timgronk the orc ninja pirate robot wizard and YOU take center stage, frequently saving everyone else's♥♥♥♥♥and being the general badass you've always wanted to be.  Going freeform lets you create characters capable of soloing all accessible content (Including the 5-10 man adventure packs) and even standard archetypes feel empowering and fun to play.  NPC's refer to you by name, they remember you, sing your praises and hold grudges in rare cases.  You get to design a personal supervillain Nemesis to battle against and can even play raid instances where they can show up as a boss!  This is the game's strength, It's personalization, customization and focus on the PC as the star of the show are on a level no other MMO can even touch.
This is why the technical issues and dated designs are so grating.  Updated , this game could be an utter shameless joy to experience and it's why even with these problems I'm giving it a recommend.  You'll either fall in love with it despite it's faults or despise it outright for them.  Try it and see which category you fit in to.

The main reason people respect the name Bioware.

I will always remember the first time Jolee Bindo told me the 'boy and the snake' story. It was a perfect bit of writing, ending with my very dodgy-looking Jedi (pale skin, yellowing eyes, red lightsaber) asking him, 'Am I supposed to be the snake?' He says, 'Well now, that's what I came to find out'.
--
KotOR is mostly an interactive story, and a really magical one. The writing is slightly dated by the standards set by Bioware's more recent hits, often slightly 'videogame-y' and always less cinematic than the likes of Mass Effect, but it's still just amazing. The combat is semi-turn based - very similar to Dragon Age: Origins or the recent Pillars of Eternity - but it's a lot of fun. And if you've ever wanted to play a game where Bioware absolutely live up to their promises and potential for once, then this is it. It's the one that put them on the map.
It's also the game to play if you're looking for that 'feel like you're in Star Wars' quality that games like Battlefront and Jedi Knight come so close to capturing but don't quite get. In an average 30-40 hour playthrough of KotOR you can expect to save / condemn the galaxy, ride swoop bikes, manipulate beaurocats and dodge docking fees with the Jedi mind trick, leap halfway across a map to cut sand-people in half, convert a lost dark Jedi back to the light (or the opposite), buy an assassin droid who calmly tells you how every single one of his former owners died by his hands and just how much he enjoyed it, and argue with all manner of space-Nazis about every facet of space-racism. It feels very 'Star Wars' and very 'Bioware' at the same time, but the two never clash.
What the game does best is in breathing life and weight into the 'good versus evil' meter that so many RPGs had back then, and some still maintain shadows of (i.e. Mass Effect, The Walking Dead). KotOR's devs and writers were aware that they had the Star Wars licence for this one and that their story was supposed to be about Jedi knights. They took full advantage of the 'lure of the dark side' angle, allowing the cruelty or generosity of your actions to be meaningful and to form the centre of a game's story and theme. Who your character becomes is crucial to the plot, so deciding who to torture with lightning and who to donate money to makes all the difference in the world. It all builds up to a single brilliant decision and two very distinct, very satisfying endings. The game knows exactly what was so great about Star Wars and The Empire Strikes Back (Vader, Yoda, the hero's journey, the dark side, the Falcon, the love story, the big twist, the world-building, the witty banter) and it lovingly packs it all in.

I remember all the hype there was for this game before its release and all the people praising it for the graphics...and I also remember how people bashed this game for it's really short lifetime and it's annoying story when it came out.. So I finally decided to buy it in 2017 to see how good or bad that game actually is, here is my review.
Graphics:
It is one of the strength of the game, Ryse is just incredibly beautiful, still better looking than most of the games today.
The textures, the characters animations, the faces (the emotions are well reflected), all the light,shadow,smoke effects etc (especially the forest in the great britain mission was truly stunning, I spent like 10 minutes watching the grass) and all the cinematic scenes. From a technical point of view Ryse is impressive, it is 10/10 success.
But at the end I am not THAT surprised knowing that the guys who made this also made Crysis 3...
Gameplay:
It is very (too?) simple but there could be a justification for that because of the context of the game. This is not like God Of War where we were controlling a god but here we are controlling a real soldier from the Antique Rome's time (well okay Ryse is as credible as an Asterix's comic book and Marius is way too OP I will give you that), therefore we cannot have a sh!tload of combos and different strikes. Here we got a button for attack, one for block & another one to dodge and that makes the game more realist, at least in my opinion. Furthermore the execution scenes are really impressing which spices things a little more. But I must agree that with time it gets really repetitive and annoying.
The game also needs more variation in the design of the ennemy units, there is like only 5 different designs for briton soldiers, I always felt like fighting the same people.
Storyline:
Well it really is not that bad. Even though the revenge story is really cliché and has nothing original to offer, there is another element that comes and makes the game more interesting and it can make us think of a probable outcome (I won't say anything more to not spoil you).
The story is served by a very pleasant epic staging...but 6 hours is very short (And I know right one could say that given the gameplay it should not be too long)
Note that you can play as many times as you want the campaign in different levels of difficulty if you are looking for some challenge.
Obviously I recall that from a historical point of view this game has the credibility of an Asterix and still ...
Soundtracks:
One word: E P I C
Multiplayer:
The multiplayer is basically the same gameplay as the one we find in the story mode but the difference is that we are always fighting in the Coliseum, nothing really interesting there. Anyway there is almost never anyone online playing this, I personally could not find anyone in the matchmaking.
All in all Ryse is definitely not a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game, on the contrary it's a pretty good game, not very nor excellent, just a good game worth a shot for less than 15 bucks. It fulfills its role of games, it entertains us and despite of its repetitive side the epic and powerful atmosphere that it releases is such that one is caught by the history and cannot leave it before finishing the campaign mode. In short the game is fun and I had a good time on Ryse.

Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes, basically a way to get a quick look at what The Phantom Pain is going to be like, it is recommended that you pick this game up while it's on sale or as part  of the MGSV Definitive experience pack.
Ground Zeroes begins some time after the events of Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker, giving the player a quick recap of what happened during that game as well as Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater. Spoilers ahead for those two games. You have been warned.
Naked Snake (also known as Big Boss) enters "Camp Omega", a place based on Guantanamo Bay, in order to rescue the child soldier Chico and Paz, a 16-year-old girl who studied peace.
Players can approach the Mission in many different ways, all of them more or less efficient in one way or another, but since this is Metal Gear Solid, stealth is usually the best way to go.
Big Boss is usually armed with a lethal assault rifle and a non-lethal handgun, both suppressed, but suppressors on fully-automatic weapons will wear out after some time, requiring the player to carefully place his shots or avoid firing his guns whatsoever.
The secondary weapon for most missions is a handgun that fires tranquilizer rounds. If the player shoots an enemy with this gun, said enemy will fall asleep after some time. How long exactly the enemy takes to fall asleep depends on how close the shot was to the head: a headshot will cause the enemy to fall asleep immediately, a shot in the arm or the torso takes a few seconds and a shot in the foot will take quite some time.
This forces the player to be very cautious, since an enemy spotting them at long range will probably not allow them to land a perfect headshot, since bullet drop will kick in as soon as a shot leaves the weapon's effective range.
If the main mission itself wasn't enough for you, you can also unlock additional side ops that, upon completion, will net you some nice rewards you can use in The Phantom Pain.
However, be warned: The port isn't exactly perfect.
For about one or two seconds after leaving the pause menu, your mouse will still be moving along the screen, i. e. you can't look around or aim for that time. The sensitivity also actually causes the mouse to simply skip a few pixels, which makes using a sniper rifle very frustrating. The CQC mechanic allows you to grab an enemy by holding the left mouse button, holding Q and then hitting up, down, left or right on your keyboard (only up and left are used in CQC, down works only if your target has dropped his gun because you sneaked up on him and pointed your gun at him, right is unused as far as I know).
However, if you can see past that, you get quite an amazing "tech demo" that might just be enough to properly hype you up for The Phantom Pain.
Also, please insert obligatory joke about violins here.

The best introduction to MSG V: The Phantom Pain, take this as a demo, a very well done demo that will keep you busy while you try to complete it at 100%, if you do that the save can be uploaded to The Phantom Pain and you'll unlock awesome stuff.

I would only reccomend buying this if you really want to get the full Metal Gear Solid V experience, or just want to experience the FOX Engine in a new environment. The only story mission is fairly short, but there are a few different side ops that you can find seemingly infinite ways to complete.
If you think about it, Ground Zeroes is like if they made a "Metal Gear Solid 3: Virtuous Mission" as a sort of demo before releasing Snake Eater.

Sometimes it is not possible to change the cursor to a hand and one needs to watch one of the former dialogues to fix the issue and exit. This game is simply not designed to run on monitors made since the game came out. You'll need a microscope to read the text on even a 1080p monitor. Completely unreadable and, as a result, completely unplayable.
These complaints have been made in the past. The developers have always claimed that this could not be fixed because of the engine they used. This response is unacceptable for a game selling for $60. Fix your engine. Patch your engine. The game is written in C#, you can and should perform that sort of runtime patching to fix fundamental usability issues that prevents your game from working at all.
If you want to play this game, you should have one of those old 1024x768 CRT monitors; you should be able to handle the interface on that. If you have a 1080p monitor or (shudder) a 1440p monitor though, go play one of the many other space 4x games instead. Distant Worlds: Universe is one of the best 4x strategy games i've played. The main concern people have when deciding if to buy this game is the difficulty curve; which is, to be frank, rather big. Don't fear, there is a way to get around it with the automation system in game that allows the player to set every aspect of the game to automatic. This makes the game both vivable for the casuale player, and gives it depth for the player looking for a game with complexity.
Distant Worlds: Universe does suffer from a complex and hard to use UI, but after using it for some time using it becomes less of a challenge.
The price tag is a turn off, but you get a lot of content. How much? For only sixty-dollars your getting a game with huge varying galaxies, a decent (but simple) espionage system, a rather interesting story that can be turned off or on according to your preference, the choice to play as a space empire or pirate, characters that get better at their jobs over time, a three branch reasearch system, and a decent selection of races to play.
The game, sadly, lacks multiplayer. A missed oppertunity if there ever was one.

It's an interesting game to say the least. Heavy on the information though and sometimes can get overwhelming when your empire gets too large. That being said, that's where the game's automation shines. But if you're a micromanager like me, it can be a challenge to let the AI take care of the micro so you can focus on the bigger picture. Still, the game has its merits in terms of its gameplay. The graphics is not great (the ships remind me of Star Sector, I wonder if it's the same graphic designer) but this game is not about looking pretty. I got this game on sale as I'm loathe to buy games at full price if they don't get all the checks in my personal checklist. We're spoiled like that. So yeah, I recommend getting this game on sale as it's still worth the gaming experience (just not a "must-have").

I’m unabashedly going to tell you before I get any further into this feature that I love this game. Love. Love. Love. Then again that’s nothing entirely new. So did The Escapist, Kotaku and Gaming Trend. It’s a brilliant action rogue-like game that is played entirely from an isometric perspective. The game is simply a winner.
With the beginning of the game telling such an interesting story about the first player controlled character, Aeon, I would have figured that the game would have had a heavy focus on its story. Instead, the developers decided to push the game’s action gameplay. This was an interesting decision but one that I believe works out extremely well. There is still a vivid story to be discovered but it is up to the player to discover it.
Combat is exciting even if it’s not entirely unique. Reminds me of a slimmed down action RPG such as Diablo or Torchlight. There’s a bit of room for strategy and intelligent decision making as you are constanly forced to think on your feet. The game and therefore the action is far from easy but feels very fair. I have yet to get hit let alone die in a situation where I didn’t immediately realize what I had done incorrectly. Sometimes a bad mistake can snowball dependent upon how much usage of your skills such as shadow walking you have already used in a fight.
I felt that the quality of the graphics are superb. I’ve read elsewhere that others aren’t as enamored with them as what I am but in my opinion the visual effects are on a different level than most indie games. They marry very well with the action at hand and never feel as though they’re in the way or any less than what you would hope to have. The art design is very much in keeping with the tone and the narrative of the game. This is particularly highlighted with the character stories that are told when you first start a game with a new character.
The pyramid of cards reminded me of Hand of Fate albeit the two games are very different. Giving the player the feeling of choice – limited though it may be – was a very nice touch. In fact, it opens up some scope for strategy between levels. When do you allow yourself to go to the shop? Do you wait until you’re low on health and hope that health is able to be purchased when you are desperate for it? DO you go early and see that you should have gone later? The same can apply to the ‘gifts’ and ‘mystery’ cards. Pick the wrong time to click a card and it can spell your future doom.
I was also a fan of the mission system which is directly tied to the character progression system. It’s pretty simple. You need to complete specific set challenges that are given to you at the beginning of each game. Complete enough missions and your character progresses to the next level unlocking more and more powers and abilities. It works really well given how difficult the game actually is. It gave me a feeling of progression even if I didn’t make it as far into the level system as I had hoped I would.
Those who adore a challenge will find plenty within Leap of Fate. It’s a wonderfully presented game that is just begging you to sink your teeth into it.

Leap of Fate is a top down rogue-like with fast paced combat. The game takes place in a cyberpunk New York City in which there is a strong presence of the arcane arts.
You start by playing with one of four characters, and as you play and complete missions you’ll unlock the other three. Each character corresponds to a certain card and you’ll be presented with a cutscene that explains how these people came into contact with magic when you choose them for the first time. Each playthrough is divided into several different levels, each of them being more difficult than the last. They are also uniquely designed, each with their own theme and unique enemy types. In each of these levels you’ll be able to complete various missions which can be something like killing X enemies using a special ability. Completing missions will not only allow you to unlock the other characters but it will also unlock permanent upgrades to those characters.
The  game presents you this entire process in the form of you looking to find your fate and thus, you take part in the Trial of Fates. Each level presents you with a deck of cards, and each of these cards represents a different encounter. These can be combat encounters, challenges, shops and so on. Before selecting which card you want to undertake you can see their difficulty and how big is their reward. These rewards come in the form of mana, which can be used to upgrade passive, attack and mobility skills. In the shop you can buy things like health, energy cells (which allow you to use different skills more times) and keys, which you can use to unlock chests or open a different path to go through on your deck.
The randomness of the game, not only in terms of the layout of each level but also in terms of the variety of the various skills and abilities which you can come across, as well as the fact that your fate will not always be the same, make this game highly replayable. And if you add to that a really fast paced combat that plays like a top-down shooter with some special abilities thrown into there, you get a really solid and enjoyable experience.
Leap of Fate is a blast to play and two different playthroughs will probably never be the same. Combat is simple but offers a challenge to most players and the huge variety of abilities that you can get only help the game feel fresh everytime you go for another run. I highly recommend you check this one out if you’re fan of fast paced shooters or rogue-likes in general.

Leap of Fate:
~~~~~~~~~~~

Tarot cards have been used for many moons to tell our fortunes, but in the case of four individuals it is all about the fate of their survival in cyberpunk downtown New York City. You will enter a trial, one of which will reveal your true fate. Equipped with magical abilities and weapons, the fight against your fears will be fast and frantic. After all, it is just a leap of fate!
Leap of Fate is roguelike/ top down shooter type of game. You will take control of one of four characters (you start with one and have to unlock the other three) available to you. Then you will see a cut scene which will tell you the story of the character you have chosen. Right after that you will cross a busy street in downtown New York City and enter your trial. You will have to go through 6 levels to find your fate. Each level is randomised and is set up via a deck of tarot cards. The aim of each level is to discover under which tarot card the Guardian is (Boss of the level) and to defeat him/her. The deck of tarot will have several types of card: Combat cards, from one to three waves to beat the stage and at the end of it you may or may not receive a treasure chest as a reward (the card will tell you if you will receive a reward or not); Mystery card – You may get health regeneration, mana, keys, energy or even some cards to update your deck (or, if you’re lucky, you may even get a card that reveals the whereabouts of the Guardian); Shop cards – where you can purchase goodies with the mana you collected from the stages; Challenge card – you will be given a challenge and if you succeed you might receive an additional health bar (see description of the challenge). On top of that, each character will have missions to achieve within each level which will help you to either unlock well-needed abilities but also unlock your new character.
The combat phase is really fun and addictive but can be really difficult (this is playing on the normal difficulty) especially with the last two characters. You will land on the stage and enemies will come at you from, left, right and centre. Some are easy to destroy and others are very challenging. Your character has a Normal Attack, the Shadow Walk ability and a Glyph (Special abilities, which you can change, by the way, by purchasing another one at the shop with your mana). Depending on how you kill your enemies, (eg. with your Glyph or Shadow Walk) you will receive mana. Here and there, enemies will drop a health regeneration icon upon dying. Make sure to grab them if you need it or save it for later!
There are three Skill Trees available for your characters: passive, attack and mobility. They are basically upgrades during the gameplay and they are also randomised. Well, what I mean is that you can’t choose which one of the three skills to upgrade; it will be done for you (it will be mentioned on the card) but you can choose one of the two options available at the time. Oh, and make sure you collect enough mana to purchase the upgrade!
Graphically this game looks great and the animations are fluid. Control-wise, you can play with your gamepad or your mouse and keyboard. Personally I prefer the mouse and keyboard.

Developer and published by Clever-Plays, Leap of Fate is a roguelike town down shooter that is rather unique than other games that are of this particular genre. What differentiates this game from others is the way that you gain a set of cards with what you can fight with.
As mentioned above, this is a rather unique way of making your game in this genre of gaming. With the way that you gain a set of cards to fight with throughout each stage makes the game that bit more interesting. The best thing about this card system ts that you can choose what cards you want to enter with and therefor pick out the  best cards and create nice decks. Even though this does sound like more of a card game, this game is definatly still sticking to the roguelike genre, with it's sometimes cruel and diffcult stages that you will encounter throughout the game. With the game having some upgrade skills that you can aquire and bosses for you to defeat it really does make the game challenging to play.
Another unique mechanic that is implimented into this game is the randomized skill tree that you have. Playing through the stages that you come across you have a chance to pick up a upgrade token or cards that will allow you to spend on upgradign your skills. The fun thing about this random skill tree is that you don't get to choose which branch you go down (Passive, combat or mobility) but you get to choose a skill you wish to learn from this branch. This feature can soemtimes screw your run up a bit as you may not want to choose from the branch that it randomly picks for you.
There is a nice variety of characters that you can choose to play as, they all have their own types of attacks which really differ from one another making each of them unique to their own play styles. With their different abilities and such they are all very fun to play as, and testing them all out to see what each character has to offer is fun as well. Although it does sound all nice and such, sometiems the game does lack that bit of depth that is needed in this type of game, I would of liked to see more depth in the story to really pull the player into the game more.
When you first enter the game is sets up a great atmosphere that really sets up the game for what it is. The graphics of the game are nice, and I like the different types of areas that you can get into upon entering each stage throughout the game. All of the enemies that you encounter feel like they have had a lot of time put into them, with some of them having some pretty unique attacks. The cutscenes that occur in the game really tell the story well, with the lighting and shadowing of the game really making it the sort of atmosphere you would expect it to be in.
At first the music in this game is rather nice to listen to, but after a couple of hours of listening to the same soundtrack over and over it does get a bit reptivite and boring to listen to. Even though each setting has it's own soundtrack I still found it reptivite to listen to. The sounds of everything are nice, although I feel like there could be a bit more crisp and clearer at times.
+ A unique twist on the type of genre
+ Beautiful graphics
+ Nice variety of character to choose from, with different play styles
+ Decent amount of replay ability
+ Trading cards & Achievements
- Sometimes lack of depth to the game
- Music got a bit reptivite after a few hours of gameplay
In conclusion, I really liked Leap of Fate. It takes a few new types of mechanics and mixes it in with the roguelike top down shooter genre of gaming that really suits it well. There is a nice amount of characters to be with them all having their own unique types of play styles. Although the music can get a bit reptivite at times and the game is missing somewhat lack of depth, I still recommened this to anyone who enjoys roguelikes.

Leap of Fate is an excellent game.  If you like rogue-like top-down shooters, or even just top-down shooters in general, this is a must have.
The controls are your standard WASD to move, left click to do regular attacks, right click to cast your special, and space bar to shadow walk.  There are also 4 different characters you can play (they have to be unlocked though), each one has their own distinct set of attacks and spells.
What separates this from other top-down shooters is that each stage has a set of cards where you can fight, earn rewards, upgrade skills, and fight bosses.  Best part is you get to choose which cards you want to enter, but eventually you have to find the boss/guardian card and beat it to advance to the next stage.
Another unique feature is the randomized skill tree.  As you play the levels within the stages you may enounter upgrade cards or tokens that let you upgrade skills.  There are 3 different branches, passives, combat, and mobility.  You don't get to choose which branch, but you do get to pick a skill within that branch, granted you have enough mana (the currency) to purchase it.
Lastly regarding the unique features, you can find various spells/glyphs within each stage or get a token to get a free random spell.  They are all unique and have awesome effects against enemies.
For the hours:price ratio, you will definitely get your money's worth and more.  There is a lot of replayability in the game with the various unlocks such as character skins, permanent skill upgrades, and extra story regarding the character.  What makes this even better is there's a hard mode which gives you a few additional unlocks.
My only gripe with this game is the levels  are fairly tight, meaning there isn't much maneuvariblity and you can get cornered very easily.  Some levels are just wierdly layed out along with some awkward structure placements, make it sometimes not fun to play.
In conclusion Leap of Fate is a great game to have in your library collection and a game you can always come back to any time and have fun.  I know I did not cover every aspect of this game as this review would turn into a novel.  The points I brought up in this review I feel are the highlights of the game.  If you have any further questions feel free to leave it as a comment and I'll be more than happy to answer them.
I hope this review helps you decide whether to purchase the game or not.

Leap of Fate is a fast-paced twin-stick shooter rogue-lite that juggles many different play elements and mostly succeeds. Where the game is heavy on cyberpunk/urban fantasy style (think Shadowrun), it is light on any actual substance. This is just as well since the very minimal sketchy cutscenes are accompanied by dialog that must have been translated (poorly), only to be delivered by a bored sounding actor.
Leap of Fate isn't about the story, though. We're here for the frantic, colorful combat, the randomized skill trees, the cool, but wildly unbalanced glyphs that grant game breaking super powers and mana, represented by so very many little dots that Pacman would yak at the prospect of consuming so many.
The game is laid out in a series of cards that represent different situations: fights, mysteries, shops, challenges and an assortment of ways to upgrade any of the four very different unlockable characters. This structure of cards is the first of many randomized system that make Leap of Fate great for a quick replay. While these cards create a flowchart through the level, there are other powers available that allow you to change fate, meaning that certain cards can be skipped or altered.
This breaking of the rules, changing how and what you can do spills over into the combat, which plays out very differently depending on which character you're playing, what you've managed to stumble across and excatly which set of creepy, funny, strange baddies you're fighting.
Combat controversially shifts from a 16:9 aspect ratio to 4:3, making me feel like I played a stand up arcade game, maybe some off brand, spruced up Robotron. Some have complained that the black bars at side of the screen make for wasted space. I agree with that observation only so far as the UI elements could have been put into these dark columns, thus clearing the view for the dozens of baddies and their pew-pew-pew. The developers have been responsive on the aspect issue, explaining that the wider view made the game too easy, less fun. I'm fine with that explanation, but any buyer should know that the action portion of the game feels like playing a Sega Genesis on a CRT.
The skill trees for each character are randomized at the start of every game, making for a different progression on each play through. On one play I found myself stacking up effects on my basic attack power, in another I wound up collecting abilities that let me 'cheat' by having unlimited keys to open locked chests, or by looking at the upside down cards in hopes of finding good toys or even just the level boss.
Combat consists of moving by WASD, clicking the left mouse button for a basic attack, the right mouse button for a glyph (nuke) and the space bar for shadow walking (i.e. teleporting/dodging): that's it.
The glyphs are a mixed bag. Some are over-powered nukes, others are whimpering duds. Invariably, drawing a good random replacement glyph on the first level meant the difference between an easy play or an unfortunate, slogging end. While I enjoyed the sheer variety of ways the glyphs could affect the combat environment, I felt they had too great an impact.
The music is glitzy, wanking hair metal guitar, making bombastic flourishes at every turn. Each level also features a different ambient combat track, to keep things from getting stale. The sound effects are also excellent, though the voices (as mentioned earlier) are downright bad.
The graphics are crisp and colorful, effectively rendering imaginative and varied enemies, as well as a mix of environments and lighting effects to keep it all interesting. The techno-magic powers your character wields, along with the weird blasts, rays and barbed-wire wrapped mummies swinging upside down from chains. (yes, that's in the game) are all flashy and fun.
Leap of Fate boasts a host of unlocks, spread across all four characters. Since these special perks are permanent a failed game may still yield a new power for all future play throughs. More cinematics are unlockable, should the introductory movies for each character not be enough to convince you that they're all terrible. Fortunately they're brief, skippable and irrelevant to actually enjoying the gameplay.
In addition to all the glyphs, the skill trees, the unlocks and all that, the game also offers extra missions that can be linked to a particular level or card or tracked over the course of the entire game. If that's not enough, every once in a while you are offered a wager, a special set of rules to complete a particular combat (such as one shot/one kill) that can be declined only at a price.
With the surging music, wild fights, mish-mash of powers and constant spewing of little purple mana dots, Leap of Fate feels like an over-caffienated slot machine imported from a country that no one can find on any map, linked to an obscure comic book franchise that no one has ever read: Leap of Fate is weird, engaging and, most importantly, a ton of fun.

Not the SimTower I was looking for.
I couldn't find fun in the exploration of the systems because they are mainly strict "If X then Y" situations and do not give you the needed information up front. The game defaults to allowing you to build things that your tower cannot support then punishes you within a minute if you are you are unable to support it. There seems to be none of the elevator or transportation routing of SimTower (which was very satisfying when you got it right) and is replaced by routine laying of power, phone, gas, cable, and water lines (which is busywork and all done the same way).
The final straw was when I had a carefully stacked selection of fancy offices and high end apartments then something suddenly caused a line of the high end supporting stores and resturants to leave. It might have been a power transformer that randomly blew out for a very short time (really don't know, I blinked and suddenly half the tower had sad face icons). It ended up being just enough grumpyness to cause the whole system to collapse: not enough high end stores for the fancy apartment dwellers, and not enough high end restaurants for the fancy office workers. Within minutes large sections of the tower were empty with no notice and I could figure out no way to stop it.
That wasn't terrible on its own. I don't mind setbacks. Natural disasters, no problem. But each move out lowered my star rating, taking me from a 30-something into the negatives. That score recovers, but at a glacially slow pace even at the highest speed setting. Without that score it was not possible to rebuild, as any of the high end stores would immediately move out (due, I guess, to not having the score they wanted to move in).
So eight hours of building reduced to ash in minutes. Feels like it would take less time to build a new tower than it would to let the game run and recover the star rating. I wouldn't have minded this if the game gave me the ability to recover, or the information on what went wrong, or opportunities to prevent the collapse. I shut the game down with about 3 million in cash and no way to rebuild.
My suggestions to the devs:
- Allow the player time to correct the problems of tennants. Give them the information that something is wrong before it's at a breaking point.
- Nix the laying of power, phone, water, etc lines. There's no gameplay in it. Include the costs to cover a floor in the connection closets, if you wish.
- Include the information of noise, smells, and traffic needs before you select a tennant to move in. Allow players to make informed decisions of what to build and where.
- Maybe the loss of the SimCity elevator traffic game was done on purpose, maybe modelling that system is very difficult. Don't know. But that gameplay and the puzzle involved was something I missed.

If you don't want to risk it, hopefully Youtube will have the cutscenes and you'll be able to see what I'm talking about.
Final mark for me: 8.5/10

Paranautical Activity is a throwback to the 'old-school' FPS where your reflexes determine your success moreso than your utilization of chest-high walls. Enemies come at you fast and furious from all angles even from the first room you step into, and the increasing variety of enemies each with unique attack patterns keeps you on your toes. Combine that with a dash of random from the procedurally generated layouts along with all sorts of randomized items that can fundamentally alter your playstyle and it makes for an original, highly replayable game.
Though the ultra retro graphics might be a turnoff for some, in reality it goes along way towards making the combat manageable. There are no particle effects or fancy frou-frou textures to distract you, meaning you can easily identify where everyone and every game-ending bullet is, and because of that the game rarely feels like it cheated you. Rather than trying to surprise you with gotcha moments it presents its challenge openly, leaving it to you and your skills alone to survive.
The only major disappointment is in the room sets. While the layout might randomize, each individual room pulls from a fairly limited pool with static monster locations, allowing you to anticipate exactly what you're walking into before the door closes behind you. With any luck, expanding this room pool will be part of the 'more content' the developer is looking to build in before final release.
I greatly enjoyed playing it, and recommend it to anyone looking for a change of pace to the more routine FPS experience. If the lack of overall room and monster variety disturbs you I'd wait and see how the game evolves on its way to a formal release.

Paranautical Activity is a crazy blend of dungeon crawler and first person shooter. If I had to use other games to describe it I would end up using The Binding of Isaac mixed with Borderlands. With that being said the setting of this game pits you against every increasingly difficult enemies and bosses depending on the selection of your rooms. To mix the game up the rooms always have a random enemy spawn rate making it impossible to really prepare for what you will be facing. The bosses offer a great level of difficutly in exchange for an random item that will help you in your journey to clear all the rooms. Eventually you will find a elevator room that will take you to the next level of insanity increasing the spawn rate of enemies and the stats of boss characters. The fast paced action mixed with the frantic dodging of attacks mixes into a great rogue-like formula. The variety of items keeps you wondering what the next thing you pick up will do. Keep on your toes because if your not Paranautical Activity will suck you in and make you press Restart way too many times.

TL:DR Great game hindered by graphical quality, difficulty to newcomers, and light diplomacy. For those who put in the effort, they will be rewarded however with a fantastically deep strategic 4X game that is unmatched in scale (1000 star galaxies that actually feel huge)
Don't let the immense depth and off-putting graphics fool you: This is one of the best 4X games out there. It is light on diplomacy, but apart from that and the previously mentioned bars to newcomers, this game has incredible depth and size. If you do decide to jump in and spend the $60 (yeah its a bunch, but its the full game plus several expansions) there are several guides, tutorials, and excellent mods (which you should definately play with once you are comfortable with the game) that make the game so much better. Especially look up Das Chrome UI mod right away because it makes the UI understandable. If you don't believe me, look at the hours I have. I only have 161 hours, and I'm still playing.
Note that the game is definately oriented towards military so diplomacy is mostly just prolonging war for as long as possible. It is possible to never start a war and play peaceful, but you will need to keep up with military power to avoid being chow for stronger military empires. Or you could just play as the Teekans whom everyone loves and they make tons upon tons of money. Annnnyways great game and stuff.
P.S. Also, Star Trek mods exist and you should play with them

You Have 10 Seconds 2 is the sequel to the popular You Have 10 Seconds game. It's a time based platformer game, where  you have 10 seconds to complete each stage in each level. It has a great soundtrack to it, so you won't get bored of it even after playing it for a while. There are 12 levels in the game, and if you get bored of that, there is a Map editor so you can create your own levels. The game has a great difficulty curve in it, it starts out easy to let you get to know the game, and slowly raises the difficulty as time progresses. There are a couple levels in which players seem to have trouble with, but it should only take a couple attempts to get it. It is mostly glitch/bug free, In all of my time playing it, I have only encountered 1 bug.
This is one of my favorite games on steam so far, 10/10 rating from me.

CSNZ is without a doubt one of the most enjoyable F2P games I have played in a while, there are obvious flaws, ignoring visual fidelity, you can pay for an advantage in the PVE modes, "Gamble to win" and there are spawn issues and bugs, honestly some of the maps are downright awful but it is defiantly enjoyable despite this.
There are multiple game modes, hell even football, and classic CS, for that alone it is worth playing, however there is one thing that bugs me more than anything else and it has more to do with Nexon than the game itself.
In short by playing you allow Nexon to do the following:
"Nexon shall have the right to monitor and/or record your communications when you use the Software, and you acknowledge and agree that when you use the Software, that you have no expectation that your communications will be private. Nexon shall have the right to utilize recorded communications: (a) to satisfy any applicable law, regulation, legal process or governmental request; (b) to enforce the terms of this Agreement or any other Nexon policy; (c) to protect Nexon’s legal rights and remedies; (d) to protect the health or safety of anyone that Nexon believes may be threatened; or (e) to report a crime or other offensive behavior."
Taken from the EULA
This to me is a grey area of security/privacy that I do not appreciate in any way, the intent is obviously to prevent cheaters etc but it goes quite a bit to far, there is no specification of if it means game communications, which previous companies not just game publishers have abused to a great extent, with the monitoring of ALL communication.
I recommend the game itself, but against doing anything else or running any other programs while playing.

The game had a lot of potential. You'd start with a simple ship, could buy modules to deck it out for crew members, passengers and/or crew and could run cargo or complete missions. You'd start in one star system and work your way out. One main mechanic was navigating between planets which you effectively had to chase as they orbited the star(s) at the core of the system so if you were smart, you could plan a trip to a planet that was coming at you to get there faster. Crew were hired, had abilities and quirks and you could manage shifts, tasks, etc.
But all that was moot because the game would crash randomly costing you a lot of time and effort. The developer stated that they were sorry, that they failed, etc. because the game engine just couldn't support what they wanted to do. Instead of picking themselves up and showing some sort of commitment to their customers, they just decided that was that. So we have a broken game with a lot of potential that is for some reason still for sale.
Steer clear. Unless the devs somehow wake up one day and decide to fix this thing to make it what it could have been, there's no point in giving them free money for half-baked abandonware.

So onto the game.  Its a top down/isometric shooter with both rpg and rogue-lite elements.  The rpg elements in a single run consist of different special attacks and a several semi-randomly generated skill trees.  There are also different characters you can unlock as you play each with slightly different play styles.
The gameplay is solid mainly focused on your ability to dodge enemies and projectiles while managing the number of bombs/dashes you have left.  While the game gets progressively harder as you advance you also can accumulate power ups at a pretty fast rate.  My biggest complaint about the in-game progression is the inability to get new challenges after you complete them in a single run(this may have changed since)
The ingame character models, level design, environmental objects are all nicely drawn but nothing specials.  The music got kind of repetitive to me after a few hours even though it changes between level sets.
Overall this is a solid shooter for people who are a fan of the genre and rogue-lite elements.

Doesn't quite have the infinite-arcade feel of Nuclear Throne, or the depth and content of Binding of Isaac. But with these things in mind, the game is still fantastic, even if I'd only recommend it /after/ giving BoI and NT a try first.

While it is quite a linear experience, "Contradiction: Spot the Liar" is still a very enjoyable ride. The story is chock-full of uncooperative characters, all with interesting personality quirks which makes it fun to just question them. In addition, main character Inspector Jenks is such a goofy character, his facial expressions and mannerisms are simply hilarious, reminding me of Columbo in a way. While it might sound like a knock against the game, I find it's quite accurate of the murder-mystery shows on cable TV: the actor does a fine job, as do the various characters.
As for the technical aspect of the game, it simply looks fantastic. The backdrops' quality are beautiful, the indoor shots are for the most part very well done, and the actors all work very hard to obviously show their hand when you're supposed to pick up on a contradiction.
My only real issue with the game is that the audio mix is sometimes odd: the voices sound a bit tinny or distorted. In addition, there is a striking lack of sound effects. I feel foley work would've made it even better, or more ambient noise would've helped bring the world to life.
All things considered, "Contradiction" is a very well crafted game with a strong intrigue and only a few drawbacks. Even the actors, who are quite good at chewing scenery and making the lines about them, manage to turn in a strong performance all-around. It makes them more believable in a way, and more suspicious which is exactly the point of the game. I am definitely looking forward to seeing more FMV (full-motion video) games like this, and I'm hopeful the team at Baggy Cat will have something new for us very soon.

Project Highrise is the kind of game I can launch any time I have a few minutes, or a few hours to spare. It appears complex at first, but helpful hints and intuitive design make it very easy to start playing. However, creating a successful, booming skyscraper will still take time and plenty of forethought.
This game is a careful balance of an ever growing skyrise ecosystem, a balance constantly being tipped by the needs of my tenants. The larger the building's population, the more resources they required and expectations they whined, *ahem*, asked for.
"Will you shut up, I'm trying to build you a dang patio!"
I love that I can build a skyrise the way I want: go all business and build a giant office building, rent luxurious rooms, two-floor apartments, and roof-top penthouses to wealthy tenants, or mix it up! It is a blast experimenting with layouts and attempting to create an efficient, well operated highrise.
If you dig simulation and/or tycoon games, then Project Highrise is worth a look, especially for the tower sim fans.

Imagine a Stellaris made 5 years ago that is now fully realized, fully developed, fully play-tested, and fully modded. Why wait for Stellaris? Play Distant Worlds: Universe now.
I just started and will be happily learning the ropes for quite some time, revisiting this periodically for a decade or so. It's that good.
Not convinced? Here's my final thought... I was playing my first game, leaving everything paused for about an hour looking at menus, reading galactopedia entries (If this does not sound fun to you, walk away...). I unpaused and made my first orders, and then started scrolling around the galaxy. When I scrolled back to my home system, I was immediately disoriented. Where is my home colony? The mining base I spent 10 minutes placing? The ships I put on guard duty at my home spaceport? Then I realized ... IT WAS ALL ORBITING THE STAR IN THE SYSTEM!
I am going to forget about Stellaris for awhile and enjoy this one. Nice work, devs. Nice.

the absolute worst documentation i have ever seen in a game this complex.   finding relevant information on the various systems in the game requires hours upon hours of searching online just to find some post somewhere that talks about some test some other player did some years ago that may or may not be up to date.   i still don't know if energy collectors function worse further from a star, by how much their efficiency decreases if they do, how different stars/energy types may or may not effect efficiency, or if the really don't work when moving.  (i've seen conflicting reports from online posts)  there is just nothing in the game that shows the info on how much energy they are collecting at any given time.
i want to like this game.   all the pieces are there.   but this "steep learning curve" that the fanboys talk about is just a cover for the fact that the game designers don't explain very important aspects of the game and seems to go to great lengths to hide information from players.    the game really isn't all that complex, once you fight your way past the fact that nothing is properly explained.    it's really pretty standard for a game of this sort. Battleborn is a fast-paced and chaotic team shooter that also uses MOBA elements to create a very fluid and dynamic game. The combat as action-packed and hectic, the characters are all recognizeable and memorable, the constant Borderlands-style humor of the game keeps the game from feeling too serious and competitive. Afterall, it's kind of hard to stay hyper-focused and dead serious when you're playing as a bad-mouthed anrthopomorphic cowboy bird armed with a rocket launcher. The story mode is a nice touch and works to give context to everything going on in the game world as well as give players who aren't really in to PvP something to do. The huge amount of challenges and constant unlockables gives you the sense that you are actually accomplishing something no matter how bad your match is going for you, and also keeps tons of goals for players to work towards, which is something that a lot of games should be doing.
All in all, Battleborn is a wacky, cartoonish team shooter that works off one simple concept: games are supposed to be fun and memorable.
I'd highly recommend it to anybody who enjoys first person shooters, as well as anybody who enjoys MOBAs.
