TL;DR: Definitely try it if you only want to Role-Play.
===
This game is at its best for role playing purposes.
It's literally the only reason why I keep coming back to play it (occasionally). When I do, I just role play my characters with their respective story(ies). It's also fun to just click on random players around to check out their BIO (if they happen to have one of course, because not everyone plays this game for RP'ing). I've read some VERY creative stories for all types of characters.
Some stories are so complex that the creator has a full Wiki-styled web page dedicated to detailing their characters. However, he in-game BIO has a character limit and you can't come up with more than about three long paragraphs of text until you hit the limit, and the formatting to create Bold or Colour text and so on also counts towards the characters limit count. So if you want to make a very fancy and elaborate BIO you'll hit the limit very fast at the cost of losing potential space to add details about your character's story.
What's particularly great about this game's world is that - outside of its base / canon lore - you're still very much free at creating almost literally EVERY types of heroes and/or villains that you can imagine. You want to create a Cyborg, Robot, Demon, Angel, generic Metahuman with super strength, miniature butterfly guy who has the power of teleportation, a Vampire or an Alien with bunny ears and a guitar for accessory... just imagine it and you can most likely do it. The sheer number of possible characters from this game's creation system is - quite simply put - out of this world. There are NO other games currently available (MMOs or not) that can come remotely close to that kind of customization (INCLUDING your character's own BIO / back story if you want to invent one too outside of just making his appearance unique).
Not to mention that there's the (in)famous Club Caprice, 'THE' place for Role-Players to meet. And if you're into more... shall I say "complex" RP'ing and need more privacy you can also just invite your partner to your own place. Indeed, there's Hideouts and you can invite players inside, be it a Penthouse or a Moon base, there's quite a good selection (some are smaller than others though).
I'm just speaking about the Role-Playing aspect here, because I myself have pretty much ignored the ACTUAL "game" behind the curtain (to me, the real game in Champions Online IS the role-play, so everything else it offers IS behind the curtain) over the years. I've literally just leveled up ONE character to Level 35 and stopped there for the past two years now (max Level is 40). My other characters are Levels 25 and below. I just literally buy Hideouts, costumes and costume packs, costume Slots for my best characters, character Auras and so on, mostly due to Role-Play.
So, coming from a (rather humble) role-player, I absolutely recommend this game. However, if what you're looking for is a good actual MMORPG and you cannot possibly care and won't even approach its RP capabilities then I do NOT recommend this. Instead I'd go for something else like Elder Scrolls Online, Black Desert or even Blade & Soul.

One of the most unique real-time strategy (RTS) games I have ever experienced. The gameplay of the Wargame franchise allows you to experience the daily headaches of a general. These involve; sustaining logistic lines, ensuring your troops have enough supplies and setting up your anti-aircraft domes.
The game provides quality realism of an escalated cold-war conflict. There are units up to the late 1980s. Only an experienced commander will utilise his limited arsenal of assets in order to achieve maximum efficiency, which is required to complete the objective. However a game does not come without faults; Wargame lacks a good tutorial, a reliable range indicator (unless you have targeted an enemy unit), and requires an extensive knowledge of real life military assets during the cold war era (1950-1991).
Pros:
- Strikes the ‘war-game’ experience (Imagine a general looking over a scaled diorama map, while moving chess pieces)
- Realistic gameplay and units
- Unique experience compared to other RTS
- Very experienced based
Cons:
- Fairly steep learning curve
- Requires a good understanding of real life military asset roles and functionality

Leap of Fate is a game with a tons of potential, and most of it is realized already. This twitch-shooter rogue-like has a surprising amount of depth to it when you pull back the layers of chaotic combat it's wrapped in. Some mechanics, such as only getting mana (the game's currency) when killing enemies a specific way forces you to play with finesse rather than just to survive. It's incredibly satisfying to take down a hoard of enemies while dodging, teleporting, and blasting your way through. I keep finding myself saying "just one more", which is exactly what a rogue-like should be.
All that being said, the game IS in early access and I have many hopes for it before its full release. At the time of writing this there are two playable characters, each with their own variations of playstyle and replayability, but I am already itching to try out different ones. The 6 different zones of the game start to get quite repetative, especially the early ones you are going to go through again and again. The game plays fair for the most part, but every now and then you get screwed by encountering a level which randomly now makes it so you die in one hit - this puts a huge damper on an otherwise great run and can be frustrating.
Still, it's a ton of fun shooting baddies and grabbing upgrades, and each run plays different with the vast amount of power-ups. The price makes it hard to justify a purchase right away, but I've been incredibly pleased with what Clever-Plays has put out so far and look forward to the future additions.
UPDATE: There have been a number of additions to the game since I first tried my hand at it, and I must say I am impressed with how Leap of Fate has evolved. The game has taken the potentially frustrating aspects of being screwed over by random chance and still maintains it's tough level of difficulty. The new level progression system very much rewards you for continued play, even if you are not great. There is a ton of content to unlock that will keep completionists working for a while. I know I'll jump back in to pick this one up every now and then.

As a rogue-like, Leap of Fate succeeds because the game is truly rewarding. It presents its challenges on a gradual, ever-increasing difficulty curve that gives you time to learn the ropes and ramps up all the way into Ninja Gaiden territory. It very rarely feels unfair, though, which is a nice breath of fresh air after the likes of Faster Than Light!
The controls are tight, feel great and the user interface is generally simple and effective. This truly puts the player in the pilot seat and removes a ton of the classic frustrations in rogue-likes. On top of that, the mechanics in the game are easily understood while retaining a good amount of depth, no need to constantly check up a wiki page to stay on track (I'm looking at you Binding of Isaac!), but you do have a chance to experiment with a ton of nifty interactions.
All in all, I feel Leap of Fate is a worthwile game, especially for the big fans of the rogue-like genre. With a ton of replayability and even more content coming out soon(tm), don't hesitate and just dive into your own madness!

I let the Mixed reviews keep me from buying the game sooner and I wish I hadn't. If you're looking for a game like Freelancer, or Sid Meier's Priates!, you'll find that Cosmonautica scratches that hard to reach itch.
The difficulty games is that this is a very specific, niche genre.  A lot of games aim for it but few games hit the mark. Like Cosmonautica, many games let you choose what kind of space captain you'll be: trader, pirate, smuggler, etc. But many of those games (Eve Online or the X series) are too tecnhical as spaceflight simulations and the UI and learning curve is too steep to be fun. They lack the simple fun that more arcadey controls and mechanics give you.
Other games like Rebel Galaxy or Windward are arcadey enough, but they lack depth and immerseive world-building--the sandbox is too shallow and uninteresting. Other games take the economics too far and require either spreadsheet level optimization, or a wiki research project before you fully understand the mechanics (Patrician series, Europa, etc.). Or they keep the economics straightfoward like Tropico but they focus on city- or empire-management (like Civ or Stellaris). They don't have the Firefly sense of adventure that comes from a ship-centric game like Pirates! or Freelancer.
Lastly some games make you feel alone in space and lack the human-element: there's no Sims style management of crew needs. No Space Colony style workforce management. Without any RPG-style progression via crew experience or ship upgrades, some games are just a grind without cool mid- and end-game mechanics.
Cosmonautica balances all these things pretty well. The art-style is warm like a Blizzard game. The economy and world-building is complex enough to be stimulating but straightforward enough not to require spreadsheets or wiki research. The gameplay centers on the ship's adventure through space rather than being city-and empire-centered. The world is populated with life, a human crew that needs your care and feeding. The ship upgrade system isn't a linear grind of getting the same thing with better numbers; it's specializing your ship for trading, combat, smuggling, hacking, etc. and choosing the best gear to fill your limited space with (ship upgrades use a similar system as Fallout Shelter, or whatever the vault-builder thing is called).
It has its flaws. Sometimes a mission or something is game-breakingly good and feels like a cheat because it rewards you much better than anything else. Or the reverse, you may take a mission that is simply unprofitable upon success and feels like a bug for punishing you. Story mode has an instructive mainline quest that plays like a tutorial which is nice. But your inital ship and resources are so lousy that it takes longer than it should to establish yourself and unlock the more interesting gameplay. So you are forced to plow through a more prolonged 'rat-killing' phase before things get richer.
Bottom line, it falls short of Pirates! or Freelancer because those games were polished, big-budget classics and Cosmonautica is an indie game with some rough edges. It scratches your itch but it doesn't quite let you relive your nostaliga for those games.

Sometimes, a game in your Discovery Queue looks so new, so cool, and so much fun that you think "wow, i bet this game is going to be worth every cent!" And sometimes, that game is in Early Access, and comes with big promises from the developers. Usually, games like Factorio, Prison Architect, or Rimworld promise feature lists that are expansive, ever-growing, and representative of a great game to come, and when release day approaches, a community has grown as the game has evolved, sharing tips, tricks, strategies, and sometimes mods. Eventually, release day comes, and early access buyers find themselves satisfied with a well-polished, fully-featured game well worth their investment.
Cosmonautica is *Not* one of those games.
From the beginning of development, Cosmonautica promised to be a fantastic, wacky space-base-survival-simulator game with a fun, intriguing story mode, in-depth tutorials, far-reaching customization options, and in-depth, complex survival/trade mechanics, all presented within a wild and cartoonish world. As development progressed, early-access investors were teased with promises of additional content, expanded options, and the ever-present "we'll fix that bug soon, don't you worry about it." However, as anyone determined enough to look through their news posts could tell you, these promises were never answered.
Cosmonautica:
- Lacks content variety in rooms, tools, and missions, leading players to quickly tire of building minute variations of the minimum requirements
- Lacks sufficient introductory tutorials, requiring players to search online for "just do it this way or you will die" videos and guides
- Is filled with game-breaking, basic-programming bugs, such as non-closing UI and "cash can go negative" bugs, not to mention crash, after crash, after crash. . .
- Is less robust and more boring than even the most basic of ant-farm clickers; Adventure Captialist has more depth.
Certainly, anyone reading this review might be skeptical- i know I was when i heard much the same when i read the reviews. But it wasn't until the dev's themselves officially apologized for "trying to do too much" and "working on other projects" instead of the one they promised to complete that i realized i had made a mistake. THis is a game, and a developer, that does not deliever on their promises, and it is shameful to think that our community could have let someone like this slip into our ranks.

I almost quit this game a couple times, but kept coming back!  I've not played a game quite like this, and really hope they make a sequel.
It's a mixture of The Sims (managing your space crew of pilots, shooters, scientists, hackers, cleaners, repairers, cooks, sorta like Fallout Shelter), spaceship customization (semi-grid based with tons of different options), space exploration, researching, trading, and cooldown based space combat (with shooting, shields, hacking, and maneuvers).  I liked the art style, the music, and especially customizing my ship.  It just needs a bit more polish and they will have a fantastic sequel!  Luckily their sequel should be much easier to polish, it turns out the engine (and dependencies) they locked themselves into had a lot of limitations that they couldn't escape in the end (I saw their post about it).  That makes me even more keen-eyed for a sequel!
Polish you say?  These are some of the things I mean about polish.  They're not game-breaking in and of themselves, but for many people, this would have possibly been a death by a thousand cuts.  I kept with it because I hadn't played a game before that has quite this mixture of elements, and I really hope they make a sequel, so I am listing these things in hopes of seeing it for "Cosmonautica 2":
1) Those gosh darn repairing and cleaning robots are so insanely loud and annoying (especially in speed-up mode) when you are trying to look at your ship (so loud and annoying that I don't really look at my ship that much when they are cleaning and repairing).  This wouldn't be so bad, but when assembling a team, you pretty much have to have them while you are searching for a crew that compliments your ships.
2) We should be able to more easily customize our crew's talents.  Currently, when you level up a crew, you can either increase their current abilities OR choose to add a new ability.  VERY frustatingly, the new ability is RANDOM.  This makes it extremely tedious to find a good combination of people.  For instance, I would never want a hacker/shooter, nor a repairer/cleaning, nor a pilot/cleaner, the list goes on.  There are so many bad combinations.  This forces the player to hire a level 1 character until level 2, add the new ability, hope it's the right one, and then immediately fire them until they get the right combo.
2) Mods:  there could be so many cool new rooms, crews, ships, weapons, systems, materials, and whatnot for people to easily make and plop into the game.
4) Trading and other items become tedious (there should be upgrades that improve the management flow as you go along), because there’s not any built-in way to catalog a list of materials that are created and/or needed in various systems.  You can’t even look at a different solar system without taking two days to travel there.  There should be a fun system of tracking and logging or something, so that way we don’t have to go and click on each planet, over, and over, and over.  Maybe a key that shows an overlay on the solar system if you have a certain skill, or have researched.  There just seems to be a lot of menu clicking and searching that could be done in a more central location (like on the entire solar system).  Another example would be trying to find out the condition of your ship (cleaness and repairedness) you have to click in every single room to get an idea, over-compensate with cleaning/repair, or just waste time and money repairing and cleaning by being tethered to shipyards (because that's the only other way to do it).  There should just be an option for an overlay.  Lots of simulation games use them, and I think it'd be a great addition.  Socialization is another tedious item, where you have to select the room, select the two people, and hit social and babysit it, or else they'll go on strike (you really have to wait until they've socialized enough over a long time sped up, which is silly, and then tell them manually to stop, this should be an automatic thing, and there should be other ways to fix this, like they should quit as soon as they've hit max relationship, which would make sense).  It just seems like a clunky system where almost no other need is manually or tedious (it needs at least SOME automation, again, like stopping when max AND a notification, the system for notifications is there, after all).
5) Better save system, which would also have lessened the problems with crashing.  Other people have mentioned it, but you really have to restart the game every 45mins to an hour if you don’t want to crash.  It does save your game at every station stop (which is pretty often) BUT it is sad that it happens so much.  It should let you load one of the last 5 or so autosaves, autosave after battles, and allow for quick saves and manual saves.  This allows for experiementation and confidence in the system.  I'm not saying that this would make crashing okay, but if it had a better save system, I think it wouldn't have had as much backlash.  For instance, you could finish an awesome fight, grab loot/money and then crash on the way back and have to repeat the (sometimes tedious) battle all over again.
6) Combat is very tedious at the beginning and didn't get semi-interesting until I had two shields, two hackers, 3 shooters, and a bigger ship.  Before this, you had to hit a couple gun buttons over, and over, and over, and over with the mouse waiting for cooldowns.  It's still not that interesting with all those things, but it's definitely good enough as just another aspect of the game, though.  However, it was tedious enough that I avoided it for the longest time.  One of the most annoying aspects of this is that there are no hotkeys for combat.  You have upwards of 8-10 different buttons to press all with the mouse bouncing around the screen (instead of being able to hotkey some or all of them).
7) Better portraits:  yes, they start to look the same after a while, but I'm mostly talking about how these huge portraits at the bottom of the screen are fuzzy with no anti-aliasing (badly upscaled smaller portraits).
8) Some little mechanical things still aren't clear, for instance, should I put a good shooter on my torpedo since it's so powerful and expensive?  It says that it's guided, but it also misses sometimes.  Why is one of my crew sleeping in a bunk, but the portrait says "taking a dump" and it seems to be confused about what it needs to do first?  Another example, I didn't know I could attempt to flee combat until waaay into the game.
9)  There should be an option to tell characters to quickly go satisfy a need (and temporarily ignore their given tasks) if they're really in need, because they don't seem to use their time well.  I have everything fully upgraded, I don't have very high level characters, and I only give them 2/4 assignment slots per day, yet they still can't find enough time to feed, bathroom, and whatnot.
10) More tutorial-like elements better spaced.  It would be nice if all elements were introduced in a safe environment in the first system (combat, smuggling, trading, scanning, person transport, socializing, etc), even if that means that you have to makeup some crazy reason that you get a temporarily powerful ship.  There's a lot of cool things in this game that don't show up (or you have no idea quite how they function) for a long time into the game.
11) I'm not sure the leveling system is increasing XP logically all the time.  It only seems like crew get XP over time, and only when traveling.  This is weird, because then you shooters don't get any increased XP for fighing, hackers for hacking, etc.
I may add some other things that come to mind, but keep in mind, I DO still recommend playing the game, because it’s a nifty idea that I hope they make a polished sequel for!!!  I am only listing these things because I think they should be some of the focuses on the next in the series.

Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes is the opening sequence to Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain.
If you havent played at least Peace Walker, you won't understand a damn thing that goes on.
Gameplay wise, Metal Gear goes absolutely streamlined with full player freedom, allowing players to control how they approach objectives. What this means in this game is you can choose to be classic sneaking action, or ♥♥♥♥in go in there with guns and kill
Both Metal Gear Solid V's make going loud an actual viable option. Where as in the original games being seen was usually a quick death, killing is ♥♥♥♥in fun in this game. Ground Zeroes has 7 missions, 1 Integral to the plot, with the remaining 6 being filler missions in the same location to give players, at the time, a sneak peak at the then in development Phantom Pain.
Mechanics wise, Ground Zeroes is far more loose and clunky than Phantom Pain. CQC is far more responsive and interesting in GZ for whatever reason, despite crawling and diving being really unresponsive and wonky on keyboard.
I pre ordered this game at launch on PS4, it was 39.99 back then. I remember how salty everyone was because of how "short" the game is, but even with the absurd mission count, that didn't bother me. Ground Zeroes isn't intended to be played by itself, it's intended to be played before The Phantom Pain, and now that both games are 20 bucks, this game is worth it.

*IF YOU ARE CONSIDERING A PURCHASE* This game is a must buy title. Buy it for the definitive Metal Gear Solid V experience. It is absolutely loaded with content, features, and levels.
DO NOT BUY the absurdly overpriced "Phantom Pain." GROUND ZEROES is the better of the two, and at $20, it is a steal.

KOTOR is a great game with an amazing story and character development as well as solid voice acting. Bioware has been crafting these aspects of games right for a long time.
This game also has a stellar sense of environment for its time in regards to the planets you visit: each area has a distinctive and memorable atmosphere and adjoining characters. The music, geography, encounters, and side-quests all make each area an amazing experience on its own.
The component that makes this game a must-own and a classic, however, is its story. The fact that you have true agency over certain situations through dialogue is engaging and makes for a unique gaming experience. The parts of the story that you don't have control over still create such a compelling narrative that truly inhibits emotion - something that many games tend to lack.
While no one needs another review to confirm that this game is a classic worthy of any and everyone's library, another voice to support is always helpful.

Well that was a surprisingly excellent game.
I'll do the negatives first, because there's only a couple. Mouse controls are a little buggy. Some of the things that seem contradictory aren't (e.g. I met someone, but I also only heard about them after they died) and equally some are a little off (i.e. the text doesn't give you the full story, so you need to remember it from the interaction) but there's maybe 3 or 4 cases of both overall.
First off, the FMV is excellent. The actor who played Jenks is downright brilliant at it. No cheesy B-movie; it's all solid acting.
The gameplay is spot on. Everything you need to do is logical and not frustrating.
My favourite part was the story. At no point does it suddenly decide that there is some huge worldwide conspiracy where the USA is run by the Illuminati and aliens are taking over the world and it's all hidden in this little village. It's a good murder mystery because it remains a mystery rather than a silly fantasy.
And it does the whole 'quaint English village' thing ABSOLUTELY PERFECTLY. No more of this silly tally ho wot wot tea and crumpets malarkey; it's just a perfect setting.
The story was great through, the ending was (mostly) great, the acting was brilliant, just overall an exceptionally good game I would recommend to everyone. I'd put it at 6 hours for a playthrough.

I don't know how to review this without sounding harsher than I want to. I don't *hate* this game; it just isn't what I wanted, and it tries to pretend to be that too often for me to be comfortable with.
What I wanted was a modern SimTower. For those who don't know, SimTower is a classic mid-90's Maxis game where the core gameplay mechanic is handling elevator traffic: You place offices and apartments, but the basic problem you're always fighting against is handling the massive flood of people trying to get from points A,B,C to points X,Y,Z during rush hour. There are other mechanics around this to throw a wrench in things — offices don't like having heavy traffic outside, hotel rooms need a front desk and cleaning staff, etc. — but it all revolves around that core of dealing with the traffic these units generate.
The issue is Project Highrise has no core: Every mechanic is so shallow that it's basically a mobile game. Every problem you have to solve is either trivial (put a place for garbage near your restaurants, throw one of the various service rooms in the basement if you need another one), waiting (need more money for X), or busywork (go through every unit and pick a tenant, order regular maintenance when the little icon pops up, draw electric/water/phone lines across the floor). Other than trying to keep things pretty or *maybe* going for an optimal layout, there's just no challenge there: The only point of the game is to see the pretty tower grow, but there's no real sense of accomplishment that goes along with it: After fifteen minutes you have all the skills you need to beat the game, and there isn't enough sandboxiness to make it a creative endeavor.
If you want something more meaningful, go find a copy of SimTower (or Yoot Tower, a slightly later version). It's far from perfect and shows its age in a lot of places, but at least there's a little bit of depth to it.

Not recommended: I just tried to play the first mission (after the initial training mission) on hard ("advanced") setting, to gauge the game difficulty. At (what I assume) is the last boss (a giant spider-bot) I was at step 3 of defeating him and things looked good (4 lives left) - when I RAN OUT OF TIME ! I know there are players out there which like to do "speed runs" - I am not one of them, and being told that my mission failed, because I ran out of time, after having invested over an hour into the game is simply ridiculous. Looks like a very transparent trick to extend the playing time of the (anemic) single player mode...
The fact that you sometimes have to wait in cover for your shield/special abilities to recharge makes this even worse, from a game design point of view.
Game also has other issues, like your avatar hanging at 4 inch sloped single steps (you cannot move forward, jumping does not help) - in a game where it takes very little hits to blast away your shields/health bugs like that are a no-go.
Graphics are OK, but look sterile. "Story" so far is forgettable - Gearbox actually seems to have succeeded in creating less story than in "Borderlands 2" and "Borderlands the Pre-Sequel": In the end it is the same "Slightly annoying taunting voice from the off, declaring that its next minions will _surely_ kill you" as in the previous 2 games (which I both did not play through out of acute boredom).

Zombie Army Trilogy is one of those single track focus games that knows EXACTLY what it is and doesn't try to be anything else. Compelling story and character development? There is a story, but it's as hamfisted and corny as a B-movie horror script. And it lets you do it with the full glory of Sniper Elite's X-Ray killcams, 4 player co-op support, and an atmosphere oozing with over the top grindhouse horror. It's ludicrous, indulgent, vapid, and hella fun. Seriously, what more could you ask for from this title? (Did I mention this game has ZOMBIE HITLER)?
Bottom line: Do you like killing Nazi Zombies? Do you like doing that over and over with your friends? Do you like tasteless gore? Do you want some mindless, melon-popping fun? If so, this is the game for you. If not, you aren't missing a thing here, seriously. While the asking price MAY be kinda meh for some, it's totally worth it to pick this up on sale (9 bucks was a steal for me). Grab some buddies and waste the undead Reich!

Think of the Children is fun for a couple levels but ultimately gets repetetive and frustrating. My main issue is that it doesn't seem like there was any effort put into balancing the game for different player counts, the level seemed to be the same level of hectic for 2 players as it was for 1, and it already seemed like too much for 2 players (but by the end, we were sure that if it didn't scale, 4 players would be far too easy). Unfortunately the gameplay isn't all that compelling either. We were hoping it would be our next Overcooked, but there wasn't very much strategy to it. You get an A+ rating basically as long as you can complete a few tasks while keeping all of the children alive, and that just amounts to going wherever some kid is about to die whenever you're alerted to it, and completing tasks along the way. There's no need to think about who should do what when, or what route you'll take throughout the level while the clock ticks down. You just do it all, and it works, A+ (assuming you have at least 2 people). The graphics were nice, and I don't remember the music being offensive, but I also don't remember what it was like. The writing was great, the court room scenes were always fun but I felt like they slowed down the flow of the campaign a little too much with them being between every level. Finally, the game's pretty buggy. We had a 100% repeatable issue where if we started in campaign with two players, moved to party, and then switched back to campaign, the 2nd player would move to the 3rd player slot or take up 2 slots, and then in gameplay would just be replaced by player one's avatar and be unable to move. The final level in the game also bugged out on us at least twice forcing a restart. Also on the optimization front, my PC sounded like it was working much harder than the visuals would make me think is necessary, but I didn't notice any drops in framerate so that was nice.
I've been really harsh, and I'll admit my expectations were higher than they should have been, but I was still disappointed and I don't think the game is all that worth the time. It is at a nice price though, so if you're really looking for some great writing and almost Overcooked like gameplay, you'll find some fun here. Oh, and there's a lot of optional content although I didn't feel compelled at all to go for it after completing the campaign (took 2-3 hours to beat, my playtime on steam isn't representative as I played the drm-free version while waiting for steam key from humble).

I have changed my rating to thumbs-up-with-a-dire-warning (previous comments below just in case anyone wants to read this crazy journey).  Based on the long learning curve, poor UI and inconsistent automation, I do not recommend this game for any 4x gamer who likes things organized, manageable, smooth, or controllable.
My initial rating reflected this, and I still believe some gamers will get more frustration than fun from the game; however, going back to play other 4x games I hold in high regard showed me how refined DW is in many key aspects.  It has superior maps, design capabilities, battle mechanics, and end game options than its predecessors.  And to be fair, the UI and automation issues stem from the epic scope of the game, the sheer magnitude of possibilities, than from any programmer error (with a few minor quibbles as the exceptions).
Though don't mistake this for glowing praise, because the UI can still give you headaches (literally) from the fine print and unwieldy processes, and the automation will still annoy you even as you learn to work around it (the largest learning curve is understanding what the game's helper does well and terribly, and knowing when to use each).  For example, if you use most of the automation in the beginning, it could very well cost you the game in tougher situations; yet, if you manually handle most of your empire by the time your race is sprawling across 5+ sectors, the micromanagement tedium can quickly wear you down.  The game is nearly as vast as actual space, with both the massive challenges and pains that brings with it.
So, I only recommend this game to those who love mental pain, or who thought GalCiv2 or the Endless or Civilization series were too simple.  And even then, they will have to learn an awful lot about the game to be able to play it successfully--I recommend a tailored easy setup with few pirates and no story events for your initial dose.  If that's too easy, then maybe--just maybe--you can survive the madness that is full settings with all the options turned on.
---------------
After redoubling my efforts and spending about 100 hours more in the game, I feel compelled to edit my original review (below).  The game's steep learning curve makes it feel like you're trying to herd cats, with not-a-damn-thing doing what it should.
Most notably, guard ships often won't stay where you put them (and pirates destroy your stuff the moment the guarding force has left to do something else, like refuel or chase a scout ship they cannot possibly catch), and the AI behavior is quite different between fleets and single ships--it took some painful examples to learn that I couldn't make a single ship do what a fleet could do, and vice versa.
Trusting the automation to do the work for you means being terribly inefficient (and often ineffective) which some races simply cannot afford to do.  So this requires a tremendous amount of learning/research to figure out the workarounds--much of the challenge of the game is learning how to accomplish your far-reaching goals despite the "helpful" AI.
Once I got past that stage, I could enjoy a fantastically complex/vast game and still be challenged on a level that Endless Space (and all the others) just can't manage.
So bottom line: if you want a smooth, fun 4x game, then Endless Space is an exceptional offering.  If you want something far more epic to push your limits of management, then this game will probably scratch that itch.
. . . . . . . . . . . . .
(Original review:)
Do NOT buy this game unless you have time for a large micromanagement job.  Your mileage may vary, but I spent about 3 hours watching Let's Play vids (the best way to get up to speed on the complicated UI and other not-so-obvious things), downloaded the must-have mods for UI, graphics, and expansion, and then spent about 30 hours learning the limits of the "Intelligent Automation" (a relative phrase, to be sure).
Various tasks like character placement, build order, ship action are often terribly handled--you know, the important stuff that must go smoothly for you to dominate a competitive galaxy.  If you care for that kind of stuff, you will end up grinding your teeth or removing the automation that's so flawed, like a fleet admiral taking over some backwater fleet (and refusing to stay in a more appropriate fleet), or a scientist with a negative to a certain research picking that type of lab to inhabit; how about scouts that skip many unexplored systems to go for some far away star with no current relevance to your budding empire, or resources that go to civilian ships while the mining facilities that could actually provide the needed resources remain unfinished?
And then there are timing issues, certain things happening out of order that highlight the flaws of a real-time game on this scale.  The particular example that made me write this review: I was at war with an empire and just so happened to have a colony ship filled with that race.  Figuring they would give me trouble, I had marines in orbit to garrison right away.  Proactive of me, yes?  So, I colonize and at the same moment tell the troop carrier to unload onto the planet.  The planet revolts, wins some bogus ground war (where they instantly got 8k troop strength is a mystery--they should still be bleary-eyed from the stasis pods or whatever).  And then the a-holes give the planet to one of my allies--all before the troops who were in orbit could get on the ground?  What kind of idiot operation is this?
All fun aside, there is no way to enjoy this game with the AI screwing you over (whether or not you automate).  This could be an epic, satisfying game if more kinks get ironed out.

The claim that this game is "just a tech demo" is certainly false, but by less of a margin than many players would like.
It is true that the main mission is only about an hour long (and, skipping cutscenes and rushing, i've completed it in well under 10 minutes) and that there are only a handful of other missions available - two of which are non-canon and the canonicity of the others is debatable (though elements of them are provable as canon) - however there is actually a fairly decent amount of engaging content here for completionists.
There are numerous lore-explaining cassette tapes to be found, which is of much interest to MGS fans such as my self but presumably of little importance to most people, as well as numerous routes in which to complete every mission.
S-Ranking missions is difficult and engaging, but for some of the missions it feels as if there is one "correct" way of going about it, breaking from the non-linear approach of the rest of the game.
The most boring section of the game a prospective completionist will have to endure is unlocking all trials for the "Unlocked" achievement. For most missions, the only viable method involves completing the "Fastest Marking of all Enemies" trial to unlock most of the other trials for said mission, and this is a dull affair without the slightest bit of challenge.
So, overall, if you are willing to commit to a completionist mindset this game is most likely worthy of your money - I myself getting 25 hours out of it before getting 100% - but otherwise just read up on the lore from outside sources and buy TPP instead.

I even survived the buyout from PWE.  The game has gone through a lot of changes and not all of them are positive, but there's still plenty of reasons to play.
Some good points:
>Walking through the door, you have access to create your hero's every physical aspect.  Rather than choosing between one of 8 premade faces and skin tones, you have hundreds of options available to you (And yes you have more if you choose to buy them).  On top of that you have thirty odd sliders to change the size, shape, and detail of every choice you've made.
>Also walking through the door, your hero can already fly.  Or have super speed, or teleport.  You don't have to wait until you hit X level before you can get a mount.
> You feel like a super hero.  You can fly, when you punch guys you can send them flying, You can have lazer eyes or breathe ice. You can be indestructable or set yourself on fire.
>You can make just about any hero you can dream up. They have some set archatypes that function as pre-built 'classes' that give you a few choices but have a solid theme or power set, but the real joy is in going freeform and making your very own hero drawing from any power set you want.  You want to make a Speedster that weilds a sword and uses his friction to throw fire? Done. Do you want to be a robot ninja with a shotgun? Done. Psychic Dinosaur from Outer Space? Got you covered. Even the sky isn't the limit.
>The story is very comic booky and has a self-aware sense of humor.
>They are frequently releasing new comic book stories, events, costume parts, and even power sets.
>The player base is friendly and supportive.  More so than any other online game I've played.  Other players are actually happy to help you or tell you how to get the cool thing they have or to talk characters.
A few Bad things:
>Yes, the game is F2P.  That means you 'can' play without giving them money.  No, you will not have access to all the bits and bobs and cool things as some of the other players do. However,  If you are willing to devote time to the game, you can in fact get everything that paying players can by selling in-game currencies for real money.
>The graphics are a little behind what would be considered the norm at the moment. This being said, it dose make it easier to run on older computers.
>The amount of front-loaded personalization can seem intimadating when starting out.  Just jump in, you'll figure it out.  And dont' be afraid to make a mess.
In closing, if you don't like the Super-Hero genre, this game probably isn't for you. If makeing choices or customizing your own character sounds like too much work for you, you'd probably be happier elsewhere.  But if you do love Comic Books and are the creative sort, and spending hours on end designing, redesigning, and playing your very own superheroes sounds like your kind of a fun time, this could be one of the best games you'll ever buy... or not-buy.

Make no mistake, this is the last true RTS. The developer is competent and clearly in love with the source material. Each unit is lovingly crafted. Matches can be long slugfests or blitzkrieg smack-downs. There's not a whole lot that's more satifsying than successfully punching through your enemies defensive line, or prying open weaknesses on the their flank, or strafing a light vehicle column. No RTS does contemporary warfare better than Wargame, and it'll probably be a long time until we see anything that even comes close.
Graphics: Great. All the units look amazing. The level of detail you can get from zooming is phenomenal.
Sound: The music is dull. I recommend playing classical or 70's era Rock and Roll. The sounds are fitting and in the case of the heavier weapons, satisfying.
Gameplay: The UI is unobtrusive and conveys what it needs to to the player... most of the time. Sometimes things get hairy when there's a big engagement happening and it just looks like a mess of squares. There's no unlocking like in European Escalation, and that's a good thing. Airplanes are an amazing edition and well-balanced.
Replayability: Multiplayer is where it's at, and whether you're trying to perfect your strategies or tinkering with a new deck, there's plenty of reason to come back for more.
All in all, if you're a fan of RTS you should pick up this game. It won't disappoint you unless you've been spoiled on directionless, unevolving, slop like Starcraft.

Contradiction is a minimally funded (via Kickstarter) live action (or if you're old school, FMV) point-and-click adventure that you should buy and play so they can make a sequel.  The end.
Okay, so without giving anything away, the game is mostly about listening to suspect interviews and trying to find contradictory statements.  There is minimal use of the traditional adventure item inventory. If you have no interest in the backtracking, reviewing conversations, or getting stuck that is typical of the last 30 years of adventure gaming, stop reading, because this game won't convince you to like those things.
However, if you are still reading, there are only two questions worth considering for whether you should play this game.  Is the acting too cheesy to tolerate, and does it play well as an adventure? As for the acting, I enjoyed it.  The casting is good, the voices are good, and only the main character (the inspector you play) is heavily overacting, but in the most endearing way possible.  Of course realize that I am predisposed to enjoy the genuine British accents and setting, so without that bias, you may not fall as heavily in love with these actors as I did.  You've got some believable ladies, and several appropriately disturbing gentlemen, one of whom stands by a mantelpiece and channels a smarmy Tim Curry while the other sits in a comfy chair and does a condescending Ian McDiarmid.
As for gameplay, I was able to finish (and 100% the game with no cheats) in a couple of days amounting to maybe seven or eight hours without ever getting maddeningly stuck.  Regarding gameplay, here's my breakdown.
The so-so:
You backtrack a lot.
There aren't many locations and only a handful of items of very limited use.
Due to the nature of the writing, you will think of tons of connections that you can't inquire about.
You can only get further info on contradictions (see the name) and no other connections.
You can't inquire about statements from two different characters that contradict each other, only the self-contradictory statements.
The scenes aren't really reshot for different times, just put through a blue filter for darkness (wait, that's not a gameplay element).
There are typos.
The good:
None of the contradictions are impossible to spot, but only a few are totally obvious.
It's satisfying to find a contradiction because you noticed something visual in the scene that isn't really stated in the summaries you choose from. The statements that act as inventory items are helpful enough, but a keen eye helps too.
There are options for hints and cheats, although I didn't use them.
Calls to the police chief serve to summarize where you stand in the case without acting as cheats.
There is no lore-reading necessary.  All of the story is fully acted out or recounted through live interviews.
The feeling of progress is extremely satisfying, and the advancing of hours acts as milestones.
There are red herrings everywhere, which creates a believable atmosphere, fully fleshed out.
I've played a lot of adventure games since the 80s, and I think you should play this one, even at full price.

If the thrill of shooting down enemies only to find a legendary drop out of them is what you're after, you won't find it here.  Also, if you're not at all interested in PvP, I can't recommend this game for the story mode.  As good as it is, with only 8 chapters it's not worth the price tag.  My understanding is that there'll be more campaigns with the season pass, but as it stands don't bother unless you're also interested in the PvP.  Speaking of which . . .
Multiplayer -
Unfortunately, the extent of my MOBA experience is only a few hours in DOTA2 so I can't say how this game compares to that genre, but as a shooter it is every bit as addictive as TF2.  If arena shooters are you thing, you'll have to re-adjust your play style and think more in the mindset of a lanepusher, but I personally found it to be a rather easy transition.  I think it could use a bit more balancing.  Certain characters, namely Galilea, are agonizing to play against, but she has been nerfed since the beta so she's not the unstoppable force she once was.  I also would like to see a sort of ranking system, not in a competitive format, but more so that new players aren't shuffled in with experienced ones.  Also, about half of the roster is locked, which I think it a terrible idea.  New players may find trying to counter a certain Battleborn frustrating if they don't have the ability to play as them and see how they work.  Good thing is that there's no paywall here.  No microtransactions, so this is not a pay-to-win game.
All in all, I'm really enjoying this game, but there's not a whole lot of content at the moment.  Only 8 campaign chapters and maybe 6 maps in total.  However, the gameplay is so addictive that you really won't notice and you may actually enjoy playing on the same map for hours on end.  If PvP is your thing, I highly recommend this game.

Still a fervent player of Sim Tower (through dos box), and I have to say this is a fantastic modern update!!  All the details that Sim Tower lacked have been added to this game.  Rooftops, seasons, building services, etc. The details that have gone into this game are amazing.
It's pretty difficult in the beginning to get your tower going, but after awhile you develop a rhythm that makes it easier.  Then a little while later you have to carefully plan out where you place certain tenants because noise and smells will affect their happinness.
If I had to make one complaint about the game, though, I would say traffic management needs a big upgrade.  Sim Tower had an incredibly complex (for it's time) traffic management system with the elevators: choosing starting floors, which floors to include/exclude, different styles, types, speeds, etc., but the elevator system in PH is just a teleporter.  It breaks down occasionally, but maintenance men take care of it almost immediately.  You can easily get away with just one elevator.  Upgrading the traffic management system would make this already great game even better.
Overall, I definitely got my money's worth!!

I put a lot of time into Sim Tower back in the day, and I was hoping that Project Highrise could recapture that magic. I'm sad to say that wasn't the case, as Project Highrise is substantially different in enough ways to both differentiate it from Sim Tower, and to miss out on some of the aspects that made that game so interesting. Highrise has its own charms for those interested in the simulation/management genre, but overall building a successful tower primarily just requires progressively more nuanced iterations on the same basic principles. Generating an algorithm to build a successful tower doesn't take long, which means a substantial amount of the player's time is spent just laying out the same predictable pattern of floors repetitiously, rather than learning new techniques or exploring possibilities.
I recommend against it, but only barely. There's a solid structure here, and to anyone who plays it, I strongly recommend playing the scenarios over the free-play mode. Sadly, even the challenges provided in that mode fail to keep it from being, essentially, repetitious without much payoff.

MGSV: Ground Zeroes is a prelude to the main game itself, MGSV: The Phantom Pain (TPP). Set 9 years before TPP, this game will answer some of the questions that you might have if you ended up playing the main game first (which was the case for me). Combine that with the great dialogue and superb voice acting, Ground Zeroes will set you up nicely for The Phantom Pain.
Game Elements:
All of the missions can only be done in one small map, which makes sense because the game is just some sort of a demo. The gameplay is smooth and just like The Phantom Pain, this game has a great optimization for PC, so you won't need a high-end PC to play both of them. Controls can be a bit confusing especially if this is the first time you've played a game from the Metal Gear series, but it will become relatively simple once you get used to it. You will also get some staff members that will be of great help for the early game of The Phantom Pain, giving an incentive for players to go for the 100% completion rate for this game.
Buy now? Or wait for a sale?
I do not recommend buying this game at full price, as it is really expensive for the small amount of content it has. It does, however, usually have a 70-80% drop of its current price whenever it goes on sale, so don't hesitate to buy it when its price becomes that low.

One of the best real time strategy games that I have ever played.
Unlike faster paced strategy games, such as Starcraft or Command and Conquer, Wargame forces the player to plan out their actions beforehand. Those who rush into action will quickly find their units dead, armies depleted, and objectives lost. The deck system is an integral part of this, allowing players to create and tailor their decks for specific strategies with a large assortment of units. Want to build a mixed Scandinavian armor deck, or a glorious all-American deck? It's up to you. I've often considered building a deck to be as much of a game as the game itself.
There is something to be said about watching hundreds of Norwegian tanks heroically charging (and getting slaughtered by) a dug-in Soviet force though :D

Pros :
- There is nothing stopping a silver player(A player without a subscription) from achieving the highest level, making a unique character, or enjoying the relatively small, mostly helpful community.
- There are more than enough pre-unlocked costume pieces for you to customize to your hearts content. Ever wondered what Joker would look like dressed as Supes? Go for it. You get more benefits, granted, but nothing which makes you any better PvP-wise, so there is no 'Pay-to-win'. You get access to free monthly premium currency, exclusive clothing options, freeform character slots, among other things. Freeform simply allows you to mix different powers between powersets. This doesn't necessarily mean you're more powerful when you do this, as the standard archetypes have their own advantages.
- Aside from the given trolls that can be found in any game, the community is eager to help, with some recieving the occasional free gear, buffs and in-game currency to assist with getting started. I've done it multiple times myself.
- There are many pros pertaining to this game, but I'm getting quite tired of writing this review, so I'm going to ramble more off, in no particular order of preference. Lore, social instances, numerous powers, powersets, and travel powers, content continuiously added, every time you reach level 40 on a character, you get another character slot, blah blah blah, this that and the other.
Cons :
- This goes for pretty much any MMO, but, grinding. It'll take some blood, sweat and tears to get your hands on the best gear in the game. Oh, and time.
- Its been out a while. Eight years. How much longer can this game last? Probably a lot longer if you'd just download it and fall in love already.
- Dwindling community besides its many faithful regulars.
- Anthropomorphic lions, tigers and bears, oh my!
------------------------------------------------------

There's been a suicide in a village. You play as Inspector Jenks to see if it could be something more sinister. 99% of the game is interviewing suspects and finding logical errors in their statements.
+ Excellent writing. What seems like a simple suicide case becomes more bizarre as the story progresses.
+ Good acting and interesting characters. Some of the actors really delivered a great performance.
+ High-quality full motion video that is very quick to load. Even when switching between locations quickly there is no lag.
+ Music is well done. Whoever directed this game knew how to use the right music to emphasize tension.
+ No pixel-hunting for objects. Any important items are automatically added to your inventory after a search prompt.
- Poor Steam integration. I can't take take screenshots or use the Steam Chat overlay. I played this on Windows 10.
- Conversation buttons don't work sometimes. Annoying but can be fixed by replaying a dialogue or exiting the conversation.
- Although the main mystery can be solved, some loose ends still remain. The developers say this is an experimental game, and a sequel may be made depending on user feedback.

:
* Very Pretty
* Pacing and Weight of character movement feels good
* Objective gametypes are cleverly done, and I think the modes are the best design feature in that sense.
* Interesting character designs and abilities
* Outstanding VO
* Cool Story
* Great cinematics
* Having characters locked is an instant turn-off to me. I don't want to have to grind out a load of characters I don't like using to maybe unlock one that I also don't like and need to spend longer getting to one I do. They should all be available minute 1.
* Gear seems pretty much pointless, as it's a waste of Shards in almost every game mode.
* Matchmaking times leave something to be desired
* Reports of AMD card issues (though that hasn't happened to me).
* A lot of the abilities simply aren't worth using at times, so when you level up, it's annoying that you sometimes have to burn a point into choice a or b, when you would rather have a choice of just upgrading one ability instead. Might just be me on that, but something I've felt a few times.
* UI is a tad clunky (though that's classic Gearbox in that respect).
* Level Design is a tad dull with regards to map layout. The whole 'needing to use an ability to clear some walls' gets a bit tedious if you dare play as a tank or DPS character.
* The scoring system doesn't help with the whole "Don't encourage people to charge in and kill." As it doesn't reward people that play the objective or the character role truely (ie; Healers are made to look useless on the scoreboard mid-game).
* A LOT of quitters and AFK players. Which doesn't help at all.
* Mildly infuriating when the team you play with is obsessed with getting kills, leaving you 1 vs 3 on an objective and you either have to die trying to hold it or surrender it. Perhaps this is just a flaw with MOBA FPS coming to the mainstream. Could bode poorly for Overwatch too, though time will tell there.
* The character balancing has fallen well and truly short. Some characters are just not worth using and as soon as you get through the roster unlocks, they'll never get used again.
* You can already tell that in about 4 weeks time, this will not be a new player friendly game (I wasn't in the Beta, and I already get wooped a lot by people who clearly were, it's taken a lot of patience to keep at it).
* Some healers have too much health. And the rate at which they can heal is insane. Miko is probably the best character in the game because as a Healer, it can still get kills with relative ease, whilst keeping everyone alive and can take a fair few hits before needing to withdraw
* One Story mission is broken and too difficult for the masses (it took me a fair few attempts)
* After a while, you can see everyone abandoning the firearm users for Melee, as its so much easier to control and land hits with them, and they seem to close with almost no real risk to themselves in mid-close range.
However, if you are going to play it, I'd say do it now, as I can't see this outliving the upcoming competition, so get in whilst there's an active crowd. It might get spikes with DLC packs and Steam Sales, but I wouldn't expect to see much of a growth beyond the next 4 weeks.

This 4x game is an amazing acheivement (especially after three or four updates and mods).  There are two sides to a faction, the State and the Commercial side.  A player may have direct control over over the State (Military and some Resource management),  but can only ever have an indirect influence on the Commercial side, taxes and a ship design option.   The Commercial side is mostly run by the AI, leaving the interesting decisions to you.
The game can be tailored  for people of varying levels of experience with 4x games because you can hand over as much of your faction to AI control as you like.  You can start by handing your entire side to the AI and controlling a single ship, watching the Universe unfold around you. Once you've played a little bit, you will probably want to at least some of the reigns,  the diplomacy and war AI in particular make decisions I disagree wtih.  It takes a bit of learning to mold the game to your desires.
One may find the graphics lacking.  The space creatures are a bit silly, but I grew to like them. The interface can be overwhelming at first, but you can do so much.
I have some issues with the game and some caveats.
It isn't immediately clear how you affect the Commercial side, I'm fairly sure I still don't know the whole story.
The game experience you have is very dependent on the set up, and it takes a couple of shots to understand what the setup knobs do and how that affects the game you play.
The vanilla game provides a variety of "races",  but suffers a bit from 10% more this, 15% less that for differentiation.
For good and ill, there is a lot to learn in this game.  Fortunately Let's Plays are a thing.
This game is fantastic.  Please make more expansions or a full sequel!

Like all Bioware games, this game  heavily relies on the story. You wake up in a ship that is under attack and from that on try to save your own skin. . Dont read any spoilers about this game before your first playthrough. There is a moment in the game that is selected The Most JAW BREAKING MOMENT of all time. It is such a moment that made me stop playing the game because of the shock and made me think how that is possible for a week.
Fighting is amazing. There are 3 classes which effect your play stile a lot. Soldier is the typical fighter class while others are a little different. You are a jedi but you are allowed to focus on guns with high dexterity. You can queue 3 actions for each character while fighting for an easier management. I remember the easy difficulty was too easy so avoid that unless you are only into the story.
I still love the graphics and the soundtrack is a piece of art. Character voices are very well done. I am still inlove with Jennifer Hale as the voice of Bastila Shan and it still makes me smile remember HK-47 saying MEATBAGs.
In conclusion if you are a RPG fun, its highly likely that you already bought the game. If not, then this is the game that willl make you a RPG and Bioware fan.

One of the commercial blurbs for this game goes "This is the game Sim Tower should have been".
Well I played Sim Tower back in the days (I had to upgrade from 4Mb to 8Mb of RAM to meet the minimum specs!). It had its flaws but I can clearly say that I wish Project Highrise should have been more like Sim Tower, and not the other way around.
The major mechanic of Sim Tower was elevator management and how it gets tricky to move everyone once you increase the number of floors. It was amazingly complex and sometimes very frustrating; any Sim Tower player will remember the angry lines of people on the lower floors who will never manage to get a lift back down.
Well in Project Highrise, this is gone. Your elevator is just a big teleport unit which gets everyone where they want to be, instantly. You place one shaft in the middle of your 50 story building, boom, job done.
With such complications gone, the only challenge that's left in Project Highrise is making sure you have enough logistics for what you want to build next. For example I want to build 10 more offices, I don't have enough courrier services for that, I build an extra courrier service, then I build my offices.
It's not rocket science and it makes the game get very routine very fast.
You'll soon feel sympathy for the office workers from your tower, as every day you repeat the same cycle: get some money, build and fit out floors, connect utility lines, run out of money, wait for the next day.
Sometimes you run out of money before you can fully complete a unit. This is a mistake you will make often early in the game. When you do the residents get very angry very fast. The cycle goes a bit like this
at 10AM you built the appartment, but you ran out of money to connect water lines
at 11AM new tenants move in, despite knowing there is no water in yet
at 12PM they send you an angry letter how they are thinking of moving out because you never listen to their complaints, so you lower the rent to zero and think that will help
at 1PM they move out, posting on social media what a horrible landlord you are. You lose a prestige star which is needed later to unlock new units (you will get it back but only after several weeks)
These unforgiving and impatient tenants are the only difficulty you will ever encounter. Unfortunately in terms of challenge it's just not fun at all. It's just here to punish your mistakes but doesn't really require any thinking outside the box to resolve.
Oh did I mention that every apartment/office needs (expensive) maintenance every 3 days because the grime and disrepair has become so bad that the NPCs will complain. 3 days!!! I struggle to imagine what these people do to these poor rooms....
I really can't recommend project highrise unless you just love routine, and like getting a new achievement each day for adding a new floor or a new type of restaurant. Even in terms of art, it's generic: all the units look very same-ish so you don't get much pleasure from just watching your creations and there is little replay value.

This game coud have been an easy 8/10, if only...
Ryse is a third person Action game Developed by Crytek (hence the "Y" trick in the title as in most of Crytek games... Ho-ho-ho). You play as Marius, A Roman soldier with good heart and a strong sense of honor and loyalty to the Roman Empire. Of course the game won't be perfectly following historical events but it will tell you a good story during the time of Emperor Nero and the attempted conquest of Britain. Without any spoiler I can say that the story is quite simple and predictable yet is being told and directed really well with very good taste during cinematic scenes, fights, dialogues.
Cryengine is doing a really good job, as usual. And as usual it is quite resource demanding as I've been playing with mid-high settings at around 30-40 FPS with few minor drops down to 20 FPS in the most demanding situations. However the details level in models and locations is really good even nowadays, and many locations show a very good level of attention and artistic touch.
The entire game is accompanied by a beautiful symphonic OST that will improve the feel during the most epic or challenging situations. The most notable and memorable is the menu theme of course, which can be found few times ingame as well as some kind of encore.
As an action game Ryse introduces some interesting mechanics. First, the
: when you fight enemies they can be executed. If you do (through a QTE) you will be rewarded with health, XP, damage bonus or focus, a preventive choice that can be done at any moment of the game so you can execute your first enemy for some health, then you can go to the next one for some XP.
Second,
. Nothing too fancy, in particuar situations you can choose what kind of suport to get from your soldiers. in two ways battlefields you can ask for some ground support on one side while you take care of the other one, in other situations you can ask for archers suport, and in some parts (the best, IMHO) you can call your soldiers in formation and command to proceed, throw pikes or raise shields along with them. This is something so simple yet there's nothing that makes you feel like a Roman Soldier more than this!
There's obviously a Multiplayer section but it doesn't allow classic PvP fights but (more important to me) cooperative modes. Cooperative modes allows you to play with a friend (through steam invite) or via automatic server pairing to different modes, all of them set inside different and  colorful variants of the Coliseum which are meant to represent a "story" to entertain the Roman public, such as barbaric invasions, Ancient Gods defense and so on. Particularly funny (in a good way, I just love it) the commentary during fights in the Gladiator arena mode. At the end of each fight you will add up the experience and "money" to level up you character's abilities and
something you don't have during the single player campaign: inventory. You can buy random packs with ingame money value (never to be paid with real money, just playing) which may contain pieces of armours, swords, shields, potions and all of them can boost your Health, focus stats and more. Very interesting, very underestimated. Underestimated because I wish I could see this piece of gameplay during the SP campaign... Too bad
What didn't work for Ryse to prevent an 8/10 and deserve a low 7/10? Few little things. One of the most annoying things is key binding. Or better, non-key binding as you can only choose between 2 o 3 keyboard+mouse presets which can't be edited to set your own. Luckily they're not too... strange so it was quite easy for me to get used to it. Yet it's pretty ridiculous at this time... I only use Kb+Mouse so I don't know if the same trouble can be found for joypad users.
The story is going towards a precise direction and it's pretty clear as you play. This doesn't mean it's a bad story, nor a bad game as it still is very epic and a pleasure to follow anyways. It's just simple, hence predictable, that's all.
Gameplay gets quite simple as enemies are predictable and can be faced without too much trouble. Going ahead with the game you will meet different new "classes" to face in different ways but they're not that much. Boss fights represent the only real challenge in the game, yet only the last two are noteworthy.
The worst sin of the game however is the  main campaign lenght. I've completed it in about 6/7 hours. Definitely short. Good thing the Multiplayer coop mode is fun enough to entertain after the SP campaign.

A random deck of cards is dealt, each card is one map. Whether it being enemies, an upgrade or just treasure. You can choose which one you take next, untill you reach the point of one of the last cards giving an entrance to the next level.
You can also re-enter cards, to pick up some health (if you didn't need it before), or to get the upgrade you couldn't afford before. So choose wisely before ending a level.
I like the soundtracks used in this game, it fits in pretty well. Even more, I like the story. About a secret organization called cabal. Something you could compare to the illuminati. You get some textures in between the levels, which are written by different kind of persons, like spirit channelers or reporters. Giving more of an indept on whats going on. Besides those textures you unlock destiny videos of your class. Showing a lot of information on your roll into this story.
So far there is just one out of four classes playable, but since its still early access this is understandable.
So if ur into conspiracies, like a fast paced action shooter, with tons of custimozation. I'd say give it a try!

Distant Worlds is a 4X Sci-Fi-Game with an interesting story-line and lots of possible automations.
That's in short, but you can see from my game time, that this game is seriously addictive ;-)
And by the way: I had that game before, which wasn't via Steam
So whats so interesting at Distant Worlds?
Above all other components it's the possible automations.
You can let the AI handle (or not) MANY things, like ship design, ship building, base building, planetary building, diplomatic gifts, diplomatic treaties, espionage, ... well, I could count on other things, but that's not the point.
The AI makes it's job pretty good and as I said: You can toggle on or toggle off that automation-options. Many options can work with "half-automation", so that the AI makes suggestions and don't control that aspect directly.
The technology tree is not too complicated, but leads to interesting new components. Technology is absolutely important.
Distant Worlds uses a wide variety of ressources, many of them needed as building materials for your ships and bases, but also luxury resources, which boosts the development of your colonies, which leads to higher taxes.
There are also some really good mods out there for the game. For example Human Revolution or W40k.
I saw how this game developed from its early states as it was only called "Distant Worlds" to this fine developed state. Maybe it was a long way, but it was totally worth it.

Knights of the Old Republic (Also known as:
) is an RPG that BioWare developed in 2003. KOTOR implements conversational dialogue where choices are made between different interactions the main character can make various ethical decisions, solve puzzles, provoke, chastise, forgive, extort, and more.


You are a crew member of a republic ship named the "Endar Spire", after creating your character you awaken to find that your ship is under siege from the Sith forces, you need to use your class-specific-skills to slice, pew, or sneak your way past the Sith troops.
As you progress through the game there are probably HUNDREDS of sub-stories that you encounter, including 9 different characters with their own unique back stories. When it comes to story time, few do it as well as KOTOR.
For my fellow Star Wars Junkies, this game takes places during the "Old Republic" era, not long after the Sith wars (or Jedi Civil War). The lore on this game is very good, you get to visit Kashyyk, Korriban, Tatooine, Yavin, Manaan, Dantooine, and a few more KOTOR specific planets.

This is the part where I stop praising the wonderful lore and story of the game... I have been replaying this game on steam, I had actually spend many hundreds of hours on this game when I was a kid... I had forgotten that the game is rather buggy, and your character gets stuck often.
There are ways to get around the flaws (teleport back to your ship, or switch characters and run as someone else), but the inconvenience is VERY obnoxious. Others may not encounter these problems, but my point is the game hasn't aged very well at all.
Bug's aside, the auto level up feature in the game is definitely suggested for beginners, however I was an idiot when I first played this game and would create characters who had skills they had no business in specking into.
The Game play really doesn't get rolling until after you've escaped the Endar Spire and Taris, then you get to chose between having Jedi, Droids, or range fighters by your side. The strategies in the game really start to shine once you get into situations you cannot win with default combat alone.
Something should be said for the detail and complexity of the combat system in the KOTOR series, if you don't want to learn how it works, just auto level up and you should be able to get through the story. (However, there are parts and fights that will elude you unless you get creative.)

There are no Steam achievements for  KOTOR, that doesn't mean there is no challenge or difficulty... Someday I'll need to try to speed run and/or try to see if I can beat it without my whole party wiping (game over).

Knights of the Old Republic is priced at $9.99 that's a pretty fair price for most RPG's. Since this game is rather old, I would recommend waiting for a 50-75% off sale, I got my copy from a Humble Bundle.

I cannot speak for everyone, but this has always been one of my most favorite Star Wars games, even with the various bugs while running the game, I still intend to play through the game at least once via steam.
The game should easily take about 25-40 hours... depends on how easily you're side tracked... if you're a completionist like me you'll probably be looking closer to 50 hours, and then if you want to replay to help/screw the NPC's you screwed/helped, you can easily double your time spent.
Let's put it in a simple pro's vs con's list:
Cons: graphics are old, characters get stuck, not much aesthetic customization, combat is more complicated than it needs to be, cheap tactics to get you to replay the game, screen resolution limitations, and lastly Bastila Shan and Carth Onasi as main characters.
Pros: HK-47 and Jolee Bindo... Trust me - they're awesome. Good story telling, skills/talents/stats are highly customizable, multiple endings and multiple endings to sub-stories, props for all the voice recording required for this game, and the appearance of familiar star wars themes/planets/factions.

(CO) is my first MMO game and I've played it since 2011 (with breaks every now and then) before I got myself a Steam-account some years later.
I used to play it a lot before the
update: I loved the old tutorial mission where I got a chance to fight side by side with the original Champions. I enjoyed the story archs, the Hero Games PvP (where lots of players joined the different games) and I really liked the crafting system.
CO changed (a lot) after the update - some people say to the worse, others aren't too affected by it. The Adventure Packs which used to be Premium missions are now free, there are new missions and new features to the Millennium City map while some of the old ones are removed. I miss the Hero Games PvP-duels which are quite abandoned today since players more or less play the co-op Alert-missions instead. But in the end, it's the same game with the same Champions as before.

This game is not the greatest game of the Counter Strike series, but it also is not the worst, and that itself is a review for another time.
I got into the game because I saw that it was free, and for being a free game in the series it isn't that bad. It holds true to the classic 1.6 vibe, in terms of the "original" mode that the game offers. The only difference being the increased armory that the players have with new weapons that are exclusive to this game only. I thought it was a nice touch, with weapons like the "Tar 21," "MP7A1," and "Spas12," just to name a few. Though there are very "op" or "broken" weapons in the game for this mode such as the grenade launchers, ThunderBolt, and Savery.
Guns that are intended for other modes such as the TB, Savery, Skull, Janus, and Balrog series; when used in original can give slight advantages. For example, the Balrog V does good damage but instead of a standard assault rifle 30:90 clip storage it has a 40:240 clip storage allowing the weilder to stay in the battle a little longer if they are smart about ammo expenditure. There is an option to keep weapons to "classic" only, but personally I wish that were the only option.
The game is very P2W, which is why even the best Counter Strike players can be beaten by a mere beginner who paid for better guns, as there are guns with no active recoil and a large hurt box, i.e TB.
If you are looking to play Counter Strike in the competive CS:GO fashion then you should actually play CS:GO and not this game. Even for "zombie mode," all the previous Counter Strike titles have "zombie mods" that are better than the zombie modes offered in this game, especially Counter Strike 1.6, BUT, if you don't want to go through all that hassle and work, then this is the Counter Strike game for you as it tries to offer you everything it can in the Counter Strike Universe and is free.
