Ryse is an Arkham Knight fighting style ARPG. However, they put a ton of effort into the story and no effort into the gameplay. Well not the story, so much as the voice acting and cutscenes. The story is a trope and easily forgettable. The characters are 2 dimensional and the plot plays out exactly the way you figure it will.
The graphics, while not bad, aren't great. Like, not great for a cryengine game great. This is probably the least graphically impressive game I've seen from cryengine. The graphics aren't bad, and the faces are realistic, but as a whole I really expected more.
The combat is not as satisfying as Arkham. The executions are slower and forgive incorrect button presses, at least on Normal difficulty. You only fight 2 guys at once which keeps the action contained. It's enough fun to be fun, but not enough to feel like a total a$$ kicking BA Roman elite solder fun.
They encourage you to upgrade your skills without ever introducing the skill tree. The tree is simplistic at best and after only playing 1.5hrs I had unlocked over 60% of the tree. Basically you have a 2 stats: Health & Focus. As you execute people you increase a stat or you can increase Damage or XP. However, you can only select one execution bonus at a time. Many times you'll be in "the zone" killing barbarians and forget that you've had health selected for 10 minutes and haven't even been hit once in that whole time. Skill selection is delegated to the mouse wheel. Which felt like a bad implemenation. I'd have preferred the number keys so I could memorize what I'm switching to and it would take a load off your mouse hand which is already hitting Left and Right mouse for combat. Overall, the skill tree lacks greatly.
I played until I got to a mini-game where I had to throw spears at archers while the archers were targeting me. You have to hold L-CTRL and select the target, then hold L-Mouse until you get a Red indicator. BUT if an archer targets you, you have to stop all that and hit Space to knock an arrow at the exact right time or you get hit. After the third death, I took stock of what I'd accomplished and decided I had "enjoyed" this title enough.
I only paid 4.99 for this game. The 1.5 hours was worth that, but as a whole, this game just doesn't excite.

Well, I want to keep my review short and precise. This game is probably of the best Indiegames I have played in years. I saw the trailer and I placed it on my wishlist. A nice person gave it to me as a gift and after trying it, I was astonished. While it features basic game mechanics, there are a few aspects where it peeks out of the masses of other games:
Humor: I play in my native language, which is german and it is refreshing that this game is filled with puns, tiny jokes and overall a great sense of humour. It feels like playing games like Theme Hospital, LucasArts Adventures, just filled with the lore of space movies, games, modern TV shows and so on. I love the dialogues and the perks and features the crew members have. Its funny. It just is.
The writing: As said above, I love the dialogues. But not only them. Every character in the game seems to be "handcrafted". N1L the parrot, who might dream of electrical sheep, has is own personality just like the other character you meet. You can feel that alot of love went into this game.
Soundtrack: I really love the spacy soundtrack. The sound in general seems to be of high quality and aesthetics.
Animations: Looking at your crew making funny faces, going nuts, walking around the interior of the spaceship makes it feel alive. And I began to care for my crew which is always a good sign.
Several ways to play the game: When you first start out, you have a basic ship but once you gathered some cash, its up to you which way you want to play. You can become a trader, a bandit or bandit hunter or you can just go for the luxury cruise line that transports partyhoppers and VIPs.
Stability: In my 10 hours of gametime, I have encountered one bug. A strike symbol would not vanish even after the character stopped striking. I went to a spacestation, from there to the main menu, clicked on "continue" and the bug was gone. No gamebreaks. Solved in 30 seconds.
While the game is missing some aspects, especially mod support, I dont regret having it in my library and I really like to play it. New content would be awesome and the possibility to create your own character to get sucked into the game even deeper. Aswell as new areas, space stations, crisises escpecially hitting the traders market and so on. But that could all be added with mod support.
I would recommend this game to people who like space simulation games with tycoonish aspects. Grüße aus NRW nach Stuttgart. Das habt ihr toll gemacht. :)

DWU (Distant Worlds Universe) is simply outstanding in my opinion and I have probably played several hundred hours with it.
The game is a 4X sandbox of unlimited duration or at least until your empire becomes the sole ruler the galaxy. You can sit on high like I do and make the big decisions and let the AI handle the mundane work (economy, research, exploration, war) or micro-manage to your hearts content. AI works reasonably well enough that I am comfortable letting the military do their job with minimal interference and I think it does a better job on the economy than I do. What I do not trust is the diplomats and I micro-manage the relations between the various empires. After all that is what Emperors are for.
Nothing is better than sitting back after you have initiated "trade sanctions" on another empire (it is the key to the AI that you are contemplating war) and watching the fleets move across the universe to attack positions and then declaring war. Which is why you need to micro-manage the diplomatic relations. Diplomats just love trade sanctions and if you are in a disputed system with another empire the military (think Patton or MacArthur)  just might get you involved in a war you don't want to be in.
Pros: Good AI, graphics reasonably good, excellent music in the background, tutorials are good.
Cons: An occasional crash when my empire becomes too big. Restarting the game from the last time I saved it fixes the problem. Slow learning curve in the beginning so it does pay to go through the tutorials and then play the introductory game "at slowest speed" until you can get a handle on the interface, AI options, etc. Interface needs improvement. It is too cluttered.
I do not like Pirates but I can get around those by playing custom games and just removing them from the  game. Pirates are for policemen not Emperors!

One of the best Star Wars games of all time...
What? You want me to explain? Fine. A traditional Star Wars story that captures the heart and soul of the series and is 10 times better than anything Lucas has written since Return of the Jedi. Set a couple 1000 years before Phantom Menace (Lucas wouldn't let them get any further away from it), Bioware was given the creative freedom to write their own narrative, succeeding in creating not just one of the greatest Star Wars games ever made (arguably the greatest, behind a heavily modded KOTOR 2) but one of the greatest Star Wars stories ever told. Helping you on your adventure is a cast of colorful Bioware characters that you'll either love (Bastila) or hate (Carth) but find engaging nonetheless. Possessing classic real time combat that doesn't feel as dated as it should for game that is 12 years old, newcomers will be able to adapt its to Pre-Skyrim style quite easily. Engaging voice acting from some of the best (Jennifer Hale and Kevin Michael Richardson to name a few) just seals the deal. The visuals are a little dated but that just means any modern computer can play this game at full settings. Besides, presentation is everything and Bioware's models are just as Star Wars as the movies.

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is one of the most beloved Star Wars games to date. It takes place about 4000 years before the Rebellion destroyed the first Death Star. The game is an RPG (Based on the D20 system, meaning the game 'rolls' to see how much damage you will do at the current turn). Before you start up, make sure to familiarize yourself with RPG mechanics (For example, you will want to know what Fortitude is, or saves)
The game has an average completion time of about 30 hours, and about 20 if you've played before. The story is one thing that is truly remarkable. If you haven't had the game spoiled for you, drop what you're doing and just invest your time into this, as it has one of the most compelling and unexpected stories you could find in the Star Wars universe.
Pros
-Long story
-Story keeps you invested
-Great variety of planets
-Lot's of variety in playstyles
Cons
-No native 1080p support
-Few bugs on newer OS's (Windows 7 and above)

There are also plenty of bonus missions set on the same map and with very diverse objectives, further increasing the game's potential. The graphics are good, with gorgeous facial art, and it is optimized beautifully on PC. I run it with (mostly?) everything maxed out and I get constant 60 fps on my very modest machine. Does it worth the undiscounted 20€ it asks from you? No, absolutely not. But with a -80% discount, it is more than you could ask for. 87/100.

Each of these give you a power-up, new weapon, boost, etc. that can help you throughout the game. I used to play City of Heroes (CoH) on and off. I suppose I didn't give CO a fair shake, as I only played it for a little over a week.  In a recent fit of nostalgia, I reinstalled this game, and found it to be quite enjoyable, though.  It's not the best MMO out there, but it is far better than DC Universe Online (it is painfully obvious that DCUO was written as a console game, but that's another review for another time).
I'd give Champions Online a solid 7.5 / 10.  It is not the best MMO, but it is currently the best superhero MMO available.
One caveat, though: be prepared to pay a subscription fee.  The game is very stripped down for free-to-play players, and it is prohibitively expensive to purchase the content one piece at a time.  A subscription is your best option.

Hotkeys aside, there are many small tasks like upgrading utilities, checking tenant satisfaction, changing rent, fulfilling prerequisites and acquiring new tenant types which all feel more exhausting than engaging.
Finally, building higher and advancing up the tech tree should be the fun parts of a game about building better and higher, but I find those key component to be bland here. New rooms have new requirements, but filling those requirements feels like I'm just checking off boxes. When I've checked them off, the tenant moves in. Then I have to move in a bunch more of the same tenant until the next higher tier is available. Rinse and repeat, all while clicking hundreds of times to build the same floor and the same utilities up and up and up.
Nowhere near as fun as I'd hoped.

That's it, I'm throwing the towel. The gameplay mechanics do not want you to have fun unless you play exactly the way the game wants you to play it. Now don't get me wrong, the game isn't totaly bad. But there are numerous examples of "anti-fun" mechanics that made me give up on several saves already.
For example, why do all rooms need a renovation every other day? It's unreal how much dirt this tower produces per day. It's managable, but feels weird. And who came up with that noise & smell system? A room will actively complain about things happening on the floor above or below which isn't bad but quite a few examples are heavily unrealistic. Is it really that hard to develop floors that don't let noise or smell pass through? I mean okay, I can understand the noise problems but smell? Really? Are the floors full of holes or what? It gets extremely unrealistic when a room starts to complain about traffic, even though there is NO TRAFFIC on the floor the room is located or the floor directly above/below. What kind of a tower has such thin walls that you can hear people moving 2 floors below you??
And who the hell thought about that prestige downspiral mess? THIS mechanic is the sole reason why I can't recommend the game in its current state. I can accept all other mistakes that I personally dislike but this one I just can't.
Everything that is not a low-tier room will loose you prestige if you want to remove it or if the tenants move out themselves. You CAN'T redesign your own tower once you've put 2+ hours into your game. The game will PUNISH you for doing so. Don't even dare to think you could just destroy those few mid-tier rooms and relocate them so you can do something else with the space or you will loose so much prestige that OTHER rooms will start destroying themselves because the tenants now feel unhappy about your lack of prestige. This new self-destruction due to lack of prestige will cost you - yep, you guessed right - prestige again! And to complete the mess: You do regenerate the prestige you lost thanks to eviction / destruction of rooms, however you only regenerate one prestige per 5 in-game days. That's about 1 prestige every 20min if you're playing on the fastest tempo. The mid-tier and high-tier rooms cost you 1-3 prestige PER ROOM making even the idea of redesigning parts of your tower impossible. Not to mention the underground metro is a room that you can't even destroy after placing it. Sure, the game warns you about the metro. But why is this even a feature to begin with? Are the concepts of customization and identification with your own tower really that bad that the game has to burden the player down just so the player doesn't try to play differently than the game wants him to?
I don't understand how anyone thought that it's a good idea to develop a tower-simulation game that actively wants to punish the user for wanting to redesign mistakes of the past. Almost every type of room has different measurements, for someone new to the game it's almost impossible to plan ahead. And when the game tries to punish me for trying to redesign past mistakes, what else am I supposed to do? Leave them be? Start a new save?

This game is an IOS port and is based on FMV. You are a detective that needs to solve a murder crime by talking to people in the city and collecting objects. You have only a few hours to solve the crime.
This game is structured in hours. After you accomplish everything that is scripted for a segment, the game advances an hour and opens us new places, objects and people to talk to.
What I liked:
The FMV is in full HD glory and well made.
The game is not overpriced.
There is a hint system.
What I did not like:
The acting is campy most of the time.
You are required to visit the same place several times because there might be a new person or object in that location. I hate backtracking.
The game is based on a system that requires you to spot contradictions between dialogues by confronting them. At first, I enjoyed it, however it got old very fast.
Steam only allows me to recommend a game or to not recommend it. I guess "Depends" would be a good recommendation, based on how much you like crime investigations, FMV and lots of backtracing.
Because I did not enjoy and could not care to finish it, I could not recommend it. Instead, I recommend "Her Story" which is also based on FMV and asks you to watch FMV to make sense of a crime. I believe Her Story execution is simply better.

I'm very glad to see the full video adventure games making a come back, thanks to the technology we now have for the actual data storage means and thanks to less expensive video cameras and such. These full video games had emerged eons ago with the CD storage but quickly died because of being terribly expensive to film and because the CD storage wasn't good enough; videos weren't compressed or anything and quickly filled a cd with barely anything. 5 CDs games were legions and were quickly  hated for being cumbersome and annoying to use. Now thanks to a better technology the videos won't rip your eyes out as they did in the past (interlaced mode videos were deadly! ^^) and they can feature more than one hour of filming. And with the digitalized era, we don't have to fiddle with the numerous CDs or DVDs or anything anymore; a couple of clicks on Steam and you're set! Yes, a game all filmed is terribly kitsch but it will have better characters - you do relate more to human beings than to pixels after all.

This game is oustanding fun.
We sat down to try it out and ended up spending 6 hours playing the entire thing in one sitting. The story and characters draw you in almost immediately and you can't help but keep playing as contradictions and evidence gradually get unearthed.
As far as the story goes, it's an engaging murder mystery set in an English village full of quirky characters. It's a very visually satisfying and well made game. The live action video format is really well used here - it doesn't feel at odds with the gameplay at all and most of the scenes are beautifully shot. The whole thing has a great cast - Jenks, Rebecca, Paul and Ryan are particularly well done. The feel is campy whodunit fun with some sinister undertones and the game balances it very well. It's challenging enough to make you feel like you're putting the detective work in, without being frustratingly impossible. The answers are all there if you look for them and you get a huge feeling of satisfaction every time you catch someone out in a lie.
Fantastic and novel game - fingers crossed for a sequel.

Well, if you are reading this then you are in need of help deciding if you should buy this game.  I like most people looking for a new moo2, have my own ideas on what would be the best game in the genre. So this review will start with my ideals.
- complexity
-  the ability to manage things on the grand scale (i.e. just globally order things)
- or to micro manage every aspect of a planet/ship including placement of the parts on the ship design
- difficulty (no cheating AI's and a game that pushes you all the way)
- technologies that make you want to replay as a different type of race and culture
- I like star systems with a multitude of planets and other heavenly bodies (i.e. wormholes, asteroids, etc.)
So from this list of my ideals, which is by no means the complete list, I will now inform you if this game delivers.
With respect to complexity I find that this game delivers.  With the state owned ships and the private ships you never have full control of your suply lines but you can either have the AI manage your escort ships or do it yourself.  You can manage nearly all other aspects of the game.
The grandscale is sometimes my preferred method in this game for the mid to late game. It works well as the ships that are built pick up your grandscale orders (like nearest constructor- fix this ship, or you can have the AI make up your fleets).
You can micromanage most things but this game fails at the ship design.  The player can only choose what parts are on the ship, not where they are on the ship.  I believe that damage that occurs after the shields and armor is done to random parts on the ship.
As for all other ideals this game delivers a good difficulty curve, incorporates multi-planet systems, and has a good research tree that is enjoyable and keeps your desire to replay high.
So,
THIS GAME IS EASY TO RECOMMEND,
because it delivers on nearly all of my biggest desires for a space simulation game.  The main problems are the lack of ship design aspects and decent space monsters that challenge.  The pirates that I have yet to mention fix the challenging monsters.
P.S.     I have deliberately only talked about the game play of a normal nation not as a pirate nation because that is just icing on the cake!!

Distant Worlds is an incredibly open-ended space 4x strategy sandbox game. You can manage huge aspects of your empire, down to ship design, attitude toward migrants/foreign alien races, pirates, economy, etc. The generated maps are huge, and one thing about this game that really makes me drool is the seamless transition between galaxy to sector to star system to planet, as well as the lack of direct paths connecting systems that restrict travel; in other words, you can travel literally anywhere on the map, not just concrete points on a straight line between systems. If you want to have a space battle in middle-of-nowhere-deep-space, you can. Anyways, managing a space empire is not easy when you command nearly everything. Such responsibility requires a rather intense learning experience, satisfied by reading a guide or two, maybe watching a youtube series.
Once you get the hang of the game (I recommend setting nearly every aspect of your empire to manual control, where the magic is) you can start to open up many other avenues of gameplay. The mod support for Distant Worlds is fantastic, albeit quite contained. The small community, however, seems dedicated.
10/10

Stardate 164, the 18th day of the 8th month.
The war with the Tamarians to our Northeast has not progressed to the expectations of the council. What was intended to be a short colonial war to annex the outer-colonies of the Tamarians has turned into a dragging war of attrition. After the unfortunate Invasion of Orto and the loss of the Alliance's Elite Guard, the empire lacks the reserves to assault the colonial militias of our enemy. However, the war progresses in our favor. Our superior naval forces continue to capture and scuttle the mining stations of our enemy, bleeding their navy dry as we hit it hard in our border sorties.
Stardate 165, the 2nd day of the 2nd month.
Hell is upon us. What started as a simple petty war of imperialism between two of the lesser empires has sent shockwaves throughout the galaxy. The delicate system of overlapping and contradicting guarentees and alliances has burst and thrown the galaxy into a haelstrom of practically free-for-all war.  Most empires are at war with at least four others, and many at war with eight or greater. The Ferengi Alliance sits in a tenuous position. With the supreme navy of the galaxy, direct attacks on our systems seem unlikely, however, a deeper threat looms. The empire relies on mining stations in the nebulous border-zones of the empire, which draw the ire and greed of neighbors who wish to see those resources their own. The people are already worn out from the long colonial war with the Tamarians to the north-east, and though that front has been settled, this promises to be a war on a far grander, and more destructive scale. Only the alliance with our strong trading partner to the Southeast, the Federation has held strong. This is to be, I believe, our greatest crutch in this war. As long as the trade routes between us are protected against the vast swaths of enemies, our two nations can continue to hold fast. However, at this very moment, over half a dozen of our outlying mining stations are under attack, and the pirates grow worrisomely powerful, half the galaxy feeding into them for supplies and mercenary services. Trade cut as it has been, and war on several fronts, I look to the hands of fate to decide the future of the Alliance. Hell is upon us.

While there are many games now set in space this is really the only one that makes me actually feel like I am exploring a universe.  It is simply the best 4X I've ever played and its depth puts most other games to shame. Start in a tiny corner of a 1400 star universe, get humiliated by space pirates, slowly map out your little corner of space, secure a few strategic resources and planets, build up your technology slowly, design your ideal fleet in minute detail,make first contact with aliens, send some of your secret agents to steal their secrets and finally you are ready to start building a real space empire.
One thing, you should not play the game on fully automated mode until you know what is going on with it. This is the best way to confuse yourself. Automated mode is great when you want to cut down on micromanagement late in the game, it is not a substitute for actually learning how to play. Best way to learn how to play is to start in a pre-warp universe and just take it slow. Put everything on manual at first with the computer making suggestions of what to do. At the beginning you will only have one planet and a few ships to worry about, it is not too overwhelming. Pay off the pirates when they come as your military is probably not strong enough to fight them, you'll get revenge later. Set your tax rate as low as possible to make your planet grow faster, occasionally raising it back when you need money.

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is one of the most beloved Star Wars games to date. It takes place about 4000 years before the Rebellion destroyed the first Death Star. The game is an RPG (Based on the D20 system, meaning the game 'rolls' to see how much damage you will do at the current turn). Before you start up, make sure to familiarize yourself with RPG mechanics (For example, you will want to know what Fortitude is, or saves)
The game has an average completion time of about 30 hours, and about 20 if you've played before. The story is one thing that is truly remarkable. If you haven't had the game spoiled for you, drop what you're doing and just invest your time into this, as it has one of the most compelling and unexpected stories you could find in the Star Wars universe.
Pros
-Long story
-Story keeps you invested
-Great variety of planets
-Lot's of variety in playstyles
Cons
-No native 1080p support
-Few bugs on newer OS's (Windows 7 and above)

- Most of the populated servers seem to be EU based (or at least from what i've seen) which seemed to give me lag / very high ping.

The problem with this is that your character will auto-pickup the ball if it touches you, so when a player passes the ball to you, you may think to right click to grab it, but you end up mistakingly launching the ball. When you are a goalie, you can press shift to dash back and fourth, and ctrl to put up a shield. The problem with this is that it's hard to press shift and ctrl quickly to move and deflect a ball.

After playing this game more, I find that I don't enjoy it despite really wanting to like it. I'm a huge fan of Gearbox's Borderlands series and you can see that pedigree in the PvE story-mode. . .  except that we dont' really get a full story-mode. Instead, the player is sent on a variety of different PvE group missions that jump around a story and sort of highlight peices of it but with nothing to hold all the bits together. Plus, because the game is built to primarily be a 3rd-person MOBA, the character development in the single player lacks depth or longterm progression. You can eventually unlock more variety in what can be leveled up each match, but the leveling up process was so slow that I grew bored with it. . .  for example, one character I played 5 times and I unlocked a single new option. . .  and not even one I cared about. That's about 3-4 hours of time invested in one of the game numerous characters to unlock a single mutation. If the game was really fun, maybe that kind of time investment would be worth it, but it just isn't.
In both PvE and PvP, it seems to be about team play first and fore-most. Damage is so low that the way to win is to heal. Seriously. A support class played well can keep up their team and lead them to victory. Otherwise, the low damage makes it so that ambush tactics and skill-shots matter very little. What gets kills is combinging on players as a team or bating people to overextend by not healing people for a bit to make them bait and then throwing the heals into overdrive when they over-extend to try to get the heal. Thus, the game requires that you play in teams that have coordinated voice chat or lose to people who have those things. . .  and ultimately, this is boring because: not everyone got the game and I can't ask people to unless I'm willing to buy it (there is no F2P), and the same tactics over and over are boring. Playing a healer over and over is boring. Having to have your friends online to be competitive is boring.
So the game really needs some help. . .  but honestly, I hope they just punt on this and get back to making really great single-player and drop-in/drop-put co-op games. This is a talented game development team and they should have stuck to making things they know how to make well instead of making this camel poorly.

I will be blunt and say I don't recommend this game. The reasons are below, behind is just the TL;DR.
PERSONAL EXPERIENCE: I started playing this game 3 years back, I'd played Guild Wars 2 and SWTOR at that time and found both to be lacking, for a time it filled the void left by City of Heroes when it shut down *Taken too soon.*
Now note I said: For a time, after a while the problems started to pop up, what didn't help the issue was that it was run by PWE *Perfect World Entertainment* at that time and THAT is a massive example of Corporate Greed, they would ignore obvious needs for rebalancing or a reduction of damage for the sake of things you bought with RL Money, never added anything to change the Vapid gameplay and overall they did things that turned me off of it for a while.
Then I returned a year later to a game run by PROPER Devs and I enjoyed it for a short time, even making a whole new character and playing him to 40, then a glitch basically made him unusable...The reason I kept coming back was the RP and that was mainly because a good number of its original community were people from City of Heroes *it was actually a huge draw for me* but the community wasn't enough to excuse the gameplay and its nature...Sure City of Heroes had repettitive gameplay but you could excuse it for two reasons: 1: it was made at the time this was popular and 2: the levels were FUN to play through so people didn't mind this and this was on top of the amazing community.
This game on the other hand is repetitive and BORING...Not even the active bits of the combat could keep me riveted so I started just hamming it up in a sort of 'I REALLY don't care.' matter. And the age of Comics they went with was NOT well done as you have to balance it out proper with comedy in SMALL points, not all over the damn place, your enemy groups need to have MORE threat even under a silly exterior. Comparring the Hunter-Patriots with Malta is an unfair contest in Malta's Favor.
The customization *While far more than DCUO...URGH that's a subject that needs tackling another day* pales in comparrison to City of Heroes, which would be 12 years old now if it were still around, because before it had its many updates, it still had WAY WAY WAY more customization in every aspect. After the updates you could make entire story arcs yourself using Archetect Entertainment and Change how your powers looked not just in color but in some cases how they ANIMATED!
Grouping is almost BEYOND impossible even with a paragon of patience as it takes a while to get people to join you in something that actually REQUIRES people, the PvP could have been handled better *Stupid Queue system mixed with Bad Server Issues meant you could easily miss ALMOST THE ENTIREITY OF THE MATCH YOU QUEUED FOR* The big missions could have had specific people to talk to who wouldn't give you the mission if you didn't have a team of *Insert number of players here* the group limit is rather STUPIDLY low *Unsettlingly so* FINALLY None of the arcs *with the exception of the Victoria Bay Apocalypse arc* have any real investment or worthwhile payoff.
In the end...I would say 'Play City of Heroes instead' but its gone *Damn you NCSoft* so instead I say this: Keep looking, maybe look up City of Titans or other projects in the similar vein of Spiritual Successors, they're looking good and if they rock when they come out and keep rocking, I'm pretty sure this game would DIE a very slow death.

Buy? Maybe. (Note, this reflects an Early Acess game that will likely change over time, potentially negating this review. Dec 23, 2013).
PA is best described as a rogue-lite FPS, where the gameplay mechanics are boiled down to the near most simple understandings of the FPS model. The goal is to reach lower floors, but I'm not sure if there is an end due to my constant dying. Nagivating each floor is much similar to the Binding of Issac and NES Zelda - Enter a rectangular room and clear the are of enemies before you can advance. The game controls near exactly like the original Painkiller and early entries in the Quake and Unreal Series - fast movement, circle strafing, and bunny hopping. The hook of PA is using your skill to stay alive with your limited health and advancing with a mix of your class weaponry, passive power-ups, and active power-ups.
Classes include Crossbow user, Sickle thrower, Grenade Launcher, a Minigun user and a shotgun user (I forget the names of these classes, except Tank for the shotgun user). Each have their advantages and disadvantages in terms of weapon mechanics, secondary weapons (if any), damage output, range, and health. You can also get other weapons from gift shop if you are able to save up enough cash from them, which is often tough (Weapons seem to cost more than I have ever earned early in game, and when I do save up good funds, I'm usually on level 3-4 where I die). Enemies are varied, some which shoot a single a bullet or two every two seconds, some shooting a continuous hail of bullets, or even those that can nearly teleport to you for melee or enemies that can hop towards you and explode on proximity. What most shooting enemies have in common is that their projectiles aren't hit scan, so it takes timing, skill, and room knowledge to be sucessful. Each floor has a miniboss that usually provides a power-up, money, and sometimes health, weaponry, or items.
The art direction is much like 3D Dot Game Heroes with an interesting lighting selection - where there are very few lights but each projectile also emits projectiles. However, most players will simply say something like "DARK MINECRAFT VOXELS WITH GUNS". There is not much sound assets besides gun shots, door openings, item chimes, and the player's "Oof!" from being hit. Much of the sound is in the form of a nearly rave-like techno beats that reminds you of other "Futurisitcky" games like Wipeout, Extreme G, or Forsaken.
I actaully personally enjoy the base mechanics and idea behind the game - it's actually very easy to get a grasp of circle bunny hopping and learning when is a good time to strafe or sometimes stand still. You can skip the majority or at least the remainder of the floor if you desire, provided that you are able to find the boss room quick enough. The game is both easy since I am decent at shooters and because circle strafing the whole room though the entirety of a fight is almost always sucessful, but hard due to limited health, and the unprediticable nature of roguelikes (random enemies, random power ups, random room types).
My main problem with this game is once you reach level 3 or 4, you often encounter enemy flying skulls which are often hard to dodge, can gang up on you and "combo air juggle" you against a wall, and what makes it worse is that they can get so close to you that are behind the point where your bullet will spawn, leaving you literally defenseless (unless maybe you have a melee weapon). This is compounded when you have a group of skulls that for me, seem impossible to deal with unless I'm in a room with a floor plan that will block them or at least slow them down a bit. And of course, like Rogue-lites/like (and Adult Swim games apparently) it needs to be punishingly hard, so despite me doing well up to this point, I die and have to start all over again. Since I'd like to clear my massive Steam backlog, "Ain't nobody got time fo' dat". But unlike other rogue-lites where it seems like patience, skill refinement and a bit of luck will help you beat the game, I hit this brick wall to completion once I meet these skulls and my enjoyment of this game is wiped away, much like my progress once I see that annoying Restart or Quit screen.
Paranautical Activity is very enjoyable, but a fairly shallow experience, which is multiplied by having to constantly restart. If you are into the resurgence of rouge-like style games as well as old schoold FPS games, there's a fun and simple game to be found here. But I fear the skulls will kill many player's enjoyment.

If like me, you've always wanted a game where you and a few friends are the crew of a starship on a harrowing adventure, then this just might be the game for you. In a nutshell, Lovers is a space action game where 1-4 players share the task of running a small spaceship. Your tiny characters run and jump from room to room to man weapon turrets, direct shields, activate special weapons and pilot your space jalopy. If you've played FTL, that will give you a rough idea of how the ship is layed out. As you thrust around the 2D enviorments dodging space rocks and blasting a menagerie of baddies your main goal is to rescue imprisoned space bunnies who annoyingly scream when you get near them. Once you've located and freed enough of them the exit will open and you can blast your way to the next level.
It's a simple formula that stays fresh for a few reasons: Firstly, each module on your ship can be augmented with a gem that changes it's function. For instance a metal gem, turns your gun turret into a tethered spike ball that you launch at enemies and retract. A beam gem placed in your shield generator allows you to deflect enemy projectiles back at them, etc. With upgrades you can add 2 gems to each module for even more varied abilities. Secondly, the enviorments in each level provide just enough in new obstacles to keep from getting stale. A water level might have a rushing current that carries you around a level while sinister pods sticking to the walls will burst unleashing a group of small enemies upon you if you get to close. Lastly, the games core gameplay co-op spaceship action, is simple, fun, frantic and challenging enough that it will keep you and your friends engaged for a long time.
On the minus side, playing with 3-4 people is the ideal number and any less can become frustrating as you will constantly need to run all over your ship. With only 1 or 2 people this means one of your important ship systems will be unmanned, leaving you vulnerable in one way or another in dire situations. For instance, there are several cases where enemies will frantically swarm you and the best course of action is to jet away while your buddies shield to fend them off and blast a trail for you with a weapon turret. With out the manpower to cover all your systems it can be very difficult to survive in these situations. In single player you are given a competent AI partner and you have the option of lowering the difficulty, but the problem still persists. And to compound this problem is the glaring omission of online play. While playing Lovers with a room of friends is a great experience that we don't get enough of these days, the convenience of online play should not have been ignored and would still provide a great co-op experience.
Despite these issues. Lovers manages to provide a unique, charming and visually striking space adventure like no other. As a single player experience it's still an enjoyable game. However, if you have the means to play with 3-4 people, this is when Lovers really shines.

Project Highrise is a very interesting game, it truly is similar to Sim Tower. There are a few things about the game that I didn't like which felt like nitty grity. In Project Highrise, you have to manually connect up the utilities e.g. electricity, phone lines, water, gas. This felt more like a click chore than playing the game. I'll add more as I play the game.
Conclusion, it has potential but it is not Sim Tower. PH makes the whole process overtly complex. It needs to improve before I can approve. I have played Sim Tower before and this feels way over the top.
1. Pretty good Sim Tower
It really feels like the old game where you can rebuild an entire building to look just the way you want it to.
2. Contracts with the City
Very interesting to have objectives to fulfill.
1. The Utilities
Why do I have to manually stretch utility lines?  Why can't they be hidden from the game just like in real life? How does manually laying utility lines make the game more interesting or fun?
2. Additional Utilities Tab
Due to the Utilities, you have more buttons to press, making the game more confusing. I really can't stand having to lay utility lines. I would prefer simplying buying more utilities instead. Can you name me 1 office that only requires electricity and no phone line. They need the whole package, a tap, a toilet, electricity, phone lines, Internet, trash and air-conditioning. It's really dumb to just highlight 1 or 2 extensions.
3. Inefficient Floor Extension Laying
If I place a floor extension on the 1st, 2nd and 3rd floor and repeat the process, the AI will complete the floor extensions in the order I placed them, running around instead of finishing an entire linked floor first.
4. Lousy UI *****
It's so hard to find the requisite service. Why can't you just place all the support services under 1 section? I had such a hard time finding the storage bay. When the drug store needed a storage bay, I had to find it under one tiny tab under construction tiles.
5. Thematic problems
Courier Services, Copy Services and Bottled Water are not provided by the building. They are not suport services, unlike maintenance. Those are private businesses. Put them under Shops. See Suggestion 2.
6. Do we all have to start with offices?
You could start with rentals of apartments in Sim Tower as well. Give players choice. Not pigeon hole them.
1. Automate the Utilities
It doesn't feel fun to have to take multiple steps to deal with utilities. It's like Farmville where you have to manually click every single farm to collect your daily goods. Just automate them. If you build an office, everything comes with it as a package. That simplifies the game.
2. Do a better UI
Here are the suggested headings
1. Offices (Banks, accountants, lawyers, doctors, etc)
2. Shops (Restaurants, Retail stores, Cinemas, Couriers etc)
3. Residential (Only residential)
4. Building Services (Security, Parking, Maintenance, Cleaning, Trash, Transport, Lobby, etc)
That's it. Only 4 headings and you can create symbiotic relationships. Move the freaking Courier Service to Shops. It is not a building service.
3. Skip the Empty Tile Laying
Just like Sim Tower, just place the office and the tiles will automatically be laid. Remove the construction office and just start building. Just lay an office and external contractors will magically appear to decorate the office. Ok?
4. Start with a Lobby
Just begin properly.
5. Remove the utilities
1 whole space to build a utilities closet that can stretch all the way to the end? Get rid of it. Utilities run over head in real life. So, there's not need to know where it goes. There's so much more interesting things you can do rather than building power lines.
6. Subway
You can't go down all the way. The lowest level should be a subway that the City runs to your building.

I would reccommend the game to the people that enjoy the genre. There are no illogical puzzles and although the contradiction system is iffy at times (the contradictions are not hard to spot but some times there are contradictions that the game just doesn't care about) the game is still worth it.
As a highlight of the game for me was the main character Inspector Jenks. The actor was really emotive and funny. Cheesy at times but the good kind.

I usually can never stick to any strategy games too much for one reason or the other, but Distant Worlds has been an exception. This is not just a space strategy game. Its amore of a simulation of an Empire, or writing a story of your race from begining of one planet, building your very first space station to finally spreading out to the stars. Every game i have played, i have had a unique experience, each game  telling a different story. From freighters trasporting goods from one part of your empire to another, to passanger ships transporting migrants to other colonies within your empire, to  tourists visiting that tourist resort you created near a black hole.
There is soo many things you can do in this game. It is only normal the UI would be a wee bit complicated. But once you learn the way the UI works, things get a lot easier. If you are willing to overlook the Graphics, and take the time to learn the game. I assure this game will take away your life assuming you are a space scifi fan like i am.
Gameplay
Starting from Galaxy map, every part of the galaxy si accessable, you can mvoe your ships to any part of the galaxy, build a star base anywhere, as opposed to having access to only the systems and not the area between it. This essentially increases the scale of the Universe immensly as compared to Stellaris if your playing in 1000 star system.
There are nearly 20 different types of resources, each of these resources needs to be mined by your minign stations, transported by freighters over to your space ports. From where these resources will be used to build ships and other thigns necessary. The transportation is handled by the private sector, so you do not need to worry about that. Each ship component uses certian types of resources, So an entire spaceship with hyper drives, proximity sensors, maxos blasters will use a whole host of resources which your spaceports will need an active stock of in its Cargohold. SO there is no automatic teleporatation of resources, its realistic.
Ships and starbases can be custom designed, if you want to leave the designing aspect to the AI, that can be done as well. But it will be a lot more usefull to design your own ships for specefic needs. You could fit exploration ships with long range sensors and place them on the edges of enemy systems, giving active information of ship movements with a sector.  IF you simply want a starbase to give your colonies better access to entertainment  and medicial facilities to improve their happiness and popuilation growth, that can be done as well...
Combat
IF you decide to build on giant fleet, for your entire empire, you are bound to ragequit. You will be attacked by pirates in different star systems, some times by giant fleets, sometimes by small 1 or 2 ships, some times by space bugs. The only way to adequatly defend your self is too create escorts  and automate them to protect your trade lanes, build small strike fleets to defend vulnarable sectors and few bigger fleets for large engagements. Monitering stations are extremely necessary to find out enemy fleet movements and for better defence co-ordination, otherwise this will become a game of whack-a-mole with pirates constantly harassing you.
Ground combat is more or less simple, you have defensive troops which give massive defensive bonus, you have normal troops used for both attack and defence and then you have armoured regiments for purely offensive use,  and then finally you ahve special forces to take out defensive emplacements like shields. There is arduamantry skill system for troops , as more they fight better they will get in combat effectiveness...
Exploration
Exploration is a rather huge aspect of the game, there are plenty of goodies out there to get from death star space weapons, to abaondned ships, to an ancient starship graveyards where you can end your contructors to repair the ships to special anomalies on planets where you can get tech, credits or activate something sinister which you  will later regret.
PIrate bases are surprisingly well hidden, so you will rarely stumble upon them. Its easier to use the charecters to steal their territory map or operations map.
PIrates
PIrates are probably one of the best(As well as the most annoying) features in the game. There are bascially 3 different types.
Smugglers - they basically use indipendent feighters to transport goods into your empire, earning oney from the private sector. you can infact ask smuggling pirates to get the goods that your empire does not have. They are less aggressive, but they will have a few military ships
Mercenries - They basically do what you pay them to do, they will attack other pirate bases, planets, starbases if you pay them enough. Other empires will also use this feature against you. SO if youare getting harassed by a pirate merc faction. Most likely your rival is funding them.
Raiders - They basically raid, burn♥♥♥♥♥♥and pillage. YOU can pay them off to keep them away from you or you can wipe them out. BUt if you pay them off for too long, by mid game Raiders and merc factions can get extremely powerfull. Even far more powerfull than other Empires.
Trade
Trade in the game is a lot more realistic. Private sector will often go to nearby empires and purchase goods your empire might not have. They will even purchase goods from pirate bases assuming you pay them off to not be hostile with you.
The amount of trade done will positivly effect your relationship with another empire. So you might have in MId to late game freighers from several empires trading and traporting goods withint your empire.
Misc
AI is pretty good compared to other games, it certianly is not a walk over if you change all the setting to extreme. There is also an very good AI mod from icemania in Matrix forums which makes the AI a lot better. The AI still surprises many Vtearan players.
The End game threat is possible one of the hardest in any stratgy game history. Wars against the Shakturi are allways EPIC in scale. The size and scale of battle IMHO is unmatched by any other game until now. If you are not carefull, they will wipe out everyone and everything literally.
Final Comments
This game is dream come true for any space stratgy fan, Galaxy is literally alive from pirate attacks, boarding action , freighters, migrants , tourists , smugglers , space creatures. A pretty decent in game back story, with forgotten ships, starship graveyards , starbases and the massive scale of a 1400 star map with 50,000 odd planets and moons give the game an immense sense of scale and mystery.

I was excited by the game, and even more excited by the comments from players, saying that it's somewhat too complex and not very pretty: I thought that it would be a great challenge for an experienced player like myself.
Well, it was a mistake. This game is probably very deep and complex, but I also think that it requires 50 hours just to understand the basics, and I'm not sure it's worth it. I've done every tutorials, and started the first easy game mode, and spent the first 2 hours watching the game being automated, and not understanding how to perform even a few very basic tasks like attacking a target or sending a spy. i've asked a refund.
To conclude : it's probably a well crafted game, but too complex, even for veterans.

Not at all a deep game, and you don't actually get to drive any of the vehicles. So, it's not really anything like HappyWheels, which is a disappointment.
The meat of the game is picking obstacles to put on the map, pick a vehicle, and determine how fast it will go on it's imaginary rail. So, from an interaction standpoint, it's actually a bit dull.
But the reason I've put a few hours into this is that the physics engine is really good (aside from the cars that make up CPU traffic weighing about 5kg's each), and the rag-doll mechanic is consistently funny in at least a minor way. Plus, it's what I'd call a 60-second game: you can play it in the few minutes extra you have between being ready for work and actually having to leave. Really, it's a good way to get a chuckle if you are running ahead of your schedule and have a few minutes. It's the sort of game you can enjoy without needing more than a minute, unlike many games, and it's cheap enough that the lack of depth isn't a problem.
But only if you can get past the lack of interaction. The spectacle is fun, and there's enough options and choices to set-up your crashes and jumps for the vehicles, but my recommendation is only a marginal thumbs-up since there's no actual driving and the spectacle is only going to get you so far.
Again, you can't actually drive the vehicles, and the level of interaction is very low besides just choosing a car, speed, maps, and placing a couple obstacles.
But it's worth it for a game to have when you just want to have a laugh in the minute or two before having to do something else.
(FINAL NOTE: Around 10 of my hours were gained because of forgetting the game was on after I went to bed. As I said before, it's not something you'd expect to put much time into, but the time does add up if you mess around 5 minutes here or there during a work-week or school week. Really, I think I'm at actually a little over a dozen hours).

Simply put, this is a horror movie fan's wet dream. A John Carpenter-esque soundtrack with parts that look specifically designed to match scenes from "The Fog" (1980), this game will be a pleasure to look at and play for any fan of 80's horror. Rebellion hit a homerun on atmosphere with this game, and it's genuinely frightening when you're getting overrun by nazi zombies. The Super Elite zombies—the dreaded big walking zombies with MG42s—are super cool and scary when you see their red eyes affixed on you in the distance, with their stomping footsteps closing in. Very suspenseful.
The gameplay is simple and straightforward where you're just constantly fighting to survive. All the rifles have a great sound and feel, as well as the pistols. My only gripes are with the submachine guns and shotguns, as they're woefully inaccurate and ineffective at shredding through a horde as they should. The game seems designed around encouraging headshots though which is probably the reason for this. Where I'd prefer to take a 12-gauge to a horde to drop them with one shell, it just doesn't work like that in this game. You have to aim for their individual heads to take them out which sort of defeats the purpose for these sorts of weapons.
Got this on sale for $9 and it was well worth it. Recommended.

In the Star-Box folder in your steam Common folder you can edit the config.ini file to matche your desktop resolution. I would also suggest turning on frame rate limit in your graphic cards game profile to limit screen tearing. In the game you can press F1 for the settings menu.
Overall for the price, if you use the tweaks I suggest above, the game is fun but the combat lag can be annoying.

Don't let the number of hours on my account fool you, I've been playing CO since open beta, and have used the non-steam client for a number of years.
Great character customization, fast paced action for a tab target system, dwindling community, lack of sincere content updates. Last notable update was in 2013, and the devs show interest in new content beyond the occasional costume set and lock boxes.
Once upon a time, this game was my pride and joy. I have 4 lv 40's (max level), and 6 other alts that are at least lv 25. Saying the customization is fantastic wouldn't be doing this game any justice. While you can't quite sculpt your character like you can in a game like Black Desert Online, the amount of sliders, costume pieces, and costume slots the game gives is borderline overwhelming. If you have a gold account, or a freeform slot, you can build your character however you want, selecting what powers you want, which allows you to mix and match to your heart's content.
Despite being a tab target game, the combat is quite fluid and fairly fast paced. It's no Tera Online or Black Desert Online, but in my opinion it holds up against action oriented non-tab target systems. There are quite a few combat mechanics, such as charge skills, hold skills, block skills, and high mobility skills to keep combat interesting. Believe me when I say that this puts most other tab target MMOs to shame.
While this may not be a big selling point for some, the game does have player bases and housing of sorts. You can select from a variety of bases, such as a basement, a lofty apartment, a mystical library, a dark cave, and even a moon base. Once you selected your base, you can customize the interior using a variety of different themed objects. For instance, in the high end apartment (my personal favorite), you can choose what carpeting you want, what wallpaper you want, the style of your ceilings, secret rooms and armories, and even the decor such as statues, couches, aquariums, and the likes. When you have your crib all decked out, you can invite your friends inside and chill to your heart's content.
When it comes to character design, there are really only a few flaws that stop it from being as close to perfect as a 7 year old MMO can be. Most of those flaws revolve around some difficulty getting unique skin textures to match properly, if at all. For instance, some costume pieces don't have matching counterparts, and some face textures don't have matching skin textures.
In the game's current state, I'm afraid you'll find PvP quite lacking. That's not to say there isn't PvP content, because there is, but nobody queues for PvP anymore. Nowadays, the most PvP you'll see are duels in Milennium City's Ren Center. It's quite the shame, because Zombie Apocalypse PvP and Heroes PvP was quite enjoyable back in CO's prime years.
If you plan on playing this game at max settings at anything above 1920x1080, and have the hardware to do so, I hate to tell you but that may prove difficult. Even though the game's graphics engine can detect more than 2GB of VRAM on your video card, the game's engine limits the amount of detail down to 1GB of VRAM. If you exceed 1GB, the game's textures will automatically lower itself until you are below the 1GB limit, and there is no command or .ini tweak that removes the 1GB limit. I've brought the issue to the PW forums just to find that not only does it affect CO, but it also affect Star Trek Online (since it uses the same engine), and despite quite a few users reporting the same issue, the developers have not bothered to acknowledge the problem. (For reference, I have a 4GB GTX 980 in my system.)
Unfortunately, this game has fallen off Cryptic's / Perfect World's to do list in favor of other games under their belt. There have been 3 notable updates to the game, an only one of which was somewhat major. The first update was Adventure Packs, which introduces story driven "dungeons" of sorts that are broken up into a series of chapters. The second update, and most notable, was the Vibora Bay update. Vibora Bay was introduced in 2010, and introduced a new area for high level characters to grind quests and dungeons for gear. The last notable update was the 2013 On Alert update, which introduced the alert system that allows people to queue in mini dungeons, and (for better or for worse) revamped the game's crafting system. Occasionally, there will be a new costume or new vehicle to hit the update news, but they are often sealed away behind lock boxes. If they're not in a lock box, then expect to pay for them as if they were DLC. Occasionally the game will sport events such as Destroid Invasion (robots rampaging around the city), Zombie Apocalypse, Blood Moon (werewolves vs vampires), but these really aren't frequent enough to keep the game interesting.
I really really want this game to have new life breathed into it. Needless to say, it is well overdue for new content, especially since City of Heroes has died off and the only other competition Champions Online has is (the much more active) DC Universe Online. Champions Online holds a lot of nostalgic value to me, and nostalgia aside, is still one of the mechanically better MMOs out there that just happened to miss the public radar. As much as I want a new influx of players to hit, I honestly cannot recommend this game to someone who's looking for a long term commitment. However, the game is free and it doesn't take long to download, so there's no reason not to try it. Perhaps one day, Cryptic and Perfect World will get the hint that Champions is in serious need of some TLC.

I have played this game in the open beta and subsequently prepurchased the Digital Deluxe. Usually I don't prepurchase but I was feeling confident in that decision.
The game starts with a prologue-mission, kind of like a "forced" tutorial. However, the opening cinematic as well as the content of the first mission are very well made and pretty cool, I was hooked right from the start.

The multiplayer part has 3 different modes and every game is very unique since you have a nice and diverse character roster where everyone feels like his own character. I'm enjoying this game very much and can see me adding many more hours to my record in the future!
If I had to find any negative aspects, maybe the high amount of effects on the screen can be overwhelming for some but I haven't had any problems with it so far. YMMV.
All in all, it's a very fun and entertaining game and well worth the money. Especially since everything ingame can only be unlocked by playing (NOT including the new story missions which will come with the DLC. And I think every DLC-pack will have a/some(?) taunts and skins which are exclusive to this DLC although I'm not 100% sure about this).
So there you have it, I can really recommend the game, for the singleplayer as well as the multiplayer!

I really enjoy the minimal aesthetics of this game. Interface is solid and gameplay seems polished enough, nothing too complex but not too shallow either: you need to keep noise and traffic flows in control so that they don't bother "the 1%" renting the upper floors. You also need to keep places clean, especially the high traffic areas get worn down pretty quickly. There's no real gameplay reason to do this, as the map function conveniently lets you warp most places. In fact, seeing the same travel animations time and time again becomes a little tedious, so it's somewhat counter-intuitive that this is occasionally required for the sake of progression. Im not really a Fan of Football games. I dont like Fifa or any other kind of "real" football game.

-Graphics
Well, graphics dont really matter that much in Supraball, its amazing though. I like the design of the Characters, the Menu, they put so much effort into detail on different maps, its just amazing.
As i just said, the game is not really about graphics though.
-Gameplay
I really like the gameplay so far, its not really getting boring or anything.
The only thing i hate so far are beginners not passing the ball.
There is a Training Course (which everyone should play), Online Practice, Regular Matches and Ranked Matches. The two main reasons I'm not recommending this game are: Cumbersome interface, and excessive automation.
Whatever great features this game might boast are buried under a needlessly complex user interface, one that appears to plague most modern space 4x games. The game tries to display all the information you need simultaneously on the screen. While many menus are collapsable (much appreciated, btw), unfortunately others are not and prove to be too distracting while I'm trying to figure what systems I own and what my ships are doing on a dizzying map filled with icons of all geometric types.
Every window is crammed to the rim with text that is tiny, uses unpleasant fonts and colors, and provides poor color contrast with backgrounds. I owe my rapidly deteriorating eyesight to the prevalence of this "text syndrome" in this genre. I was forced to reduce my screen resolution to the minimum, and it still didn't help much. The UI in this game makes me long for MOO3 -- you know, the game no one liked due to its excessive menus.
What makes this UI worse is the constant bombardment of text news and pop-up windows dutifully alerting you to largely inconsequential information, such as Civ X and Civ Y thanking each other for a very minor trade deal, one that had nothing to do with you civ whatsoever. Some more important messages are often duplicated several times, once as scrolling text, another as a pop-up window, and finally a separately loaded screen -- just in case you failed to read it the first two times. The last time I screamed "I don't care about this crap!" so loudly and frequently was in Gal Civ 2.
To all 4x developers: When designing a UI, please take lessons from Civ 5 or MOO2. You can make a deeply complex game without using a complex interface. Modularize the info into layers and display only the most pertinent info at a time, but allow players to delve deeper, but only when they want to.
The second issue is automation. While I appreciate the great efforts to relieve the 4x player the terrible burdens of micromanagement, there IS such a thing as too much automation, which unduly robs the player the power of decision-making.  I spent a good hour trying to figure out how to produce a colony ship, or move a prebuilt one, only to realize that all colonization was automated, with zero input from me. Automation + Real Time = Sit back and twiddle that thumb.
There ARE options to turn off a lot of the automation, but much of it remains. After turning it off completely, I was still getting tons of mission reports from my scouts discovering new ruins, even though I never sent them on any mission. I was getting reports that my fleet won a major victory against pirates, even though I never ordered it to attack anyone. Reports that one of my spies got caught in an allied civ, even though I never ordered the spy mission (or even knew the spy existed). Reports that my troops have begun invading -- well, you get the idea.
I suppose this is what a figurehead feels like. While it can be occasionally relaxing and even enjoyable to sit back and watch a whole game play itself out, I would sure love to be able to make SOME decisions -- I am playing a 4x game, after all, and not watching a movie.
Perhaps if I had more than 2 hours to play this game, I'd have a deeper appreciation, but alas that is the time window Steam gives us for returns,

In this game when you destroy something you collect "shards."  Shards are the currency for the match.
You can have passive items in your loadout.  But these arnt active at the start of the game.  You have to choose between building things like turrents or stationary healers with shards- which in turn, this act grants you XP that will help push to level you up in that match.  Or you use shards to help yourself and activate 1 out of the 3 items you can carry in your loadout.  You can activate all three if you have enough.  The cool feature about this choice is that you not only opt out on building things for your team to help win, but you dont gain any XP from choosing to activate your  items.
Everytime you level up till you hit level 10 you get to choose on  a DNA helix; Ability Skill A or Ability Skill B.  But the more you play with a hero you get new abilities in the middle of the Helix called a Mutation: An Ability Skill C.  So say I'm level 3.  DNA Helix comes up.  Instead of choosing left or right I can now choose a newly aquired skill in the middle.  Which is a permanant 3rd option for that hero.

I like this game, despite apparently everyone else hating it. I am really into the economics aspect of it. I travel through space carrying waste from an overpopulated planet to a planet that grows food and bam, money. I sell cigarettes to an outpost planet and swim in credits. Have to figure out what to research and when to keep the crew happy, decide how to make trips cost effective, and I hope to one day get a bigger ship! See boys, size does matter, and any woman who says otherwise is lying.
It's also a game I can keep on in the background while I am at work, and game throughout the day. I adore games like that. They don't run hot, they stay windowed in the background, and no sound is needed. Perfecto.
There are absolutely cons though. There's no manual save, only an autosave, so if you have one bad run, it can lose you hours worth of money. I read the developers did that on purpose, jerks.
The combat system I have yet to get the hang of. I figure I'll wait until I have a bigger ship and can load it with weapons and then I'll start fighting, so I have no real info there. It does remind me a bit of oldschool space shooters so far though.
And why is it, there are times when it will take entire loops around the solar system to get to a planet that is directly next to me? That's one of the worst issues for me. Makes some missions totally worthless and I lose all my profit.
I have also had the game crash twice in the 9 hours I've played so far. Apparently, from what I am reading, that makes me one of the lucky ones.
And lastly, the missions get old. I feel like I am doing the same things, over and over. I'm just hoping that it will change once I get into the out planets I guess.
So, I enjoy it, but I really like making money games. Now, if you don't mind, there's this guy who needs a four-leafed clover, and I have to get it to him, for the 19th time.

It is one of the strength of the game, Ryse is just incredibly beautiful, still better looking than most of the games today.
The textures, the characters animations, the faces (the emotions are well reflected), all the light,shadow,smoke effects etc (especially the forest in the great britain mission was truly stunning, I spent like 10 minutes watching the grass) and all the cinematic scenes. From a technical point of view Ryse is impressive, it is 10/10 success.
But at the end I am not THAT surprised knowing that the guys who made this also made Crysis 3...
It is very (too?) simple but there could be a justification for that because of the context of the game. This is not like God Of War where we were controlling a god but here we are controlling a real soldier from the Antique Rome's time (well okay Ryse is as credible as an Asterix's comic book and Marius is way too OP I will give you that), therefore we cannot have a sh!tload of combos and different strikes. Here we got a button for attack, one for block & another one to dodge and that makes the game more realist, at least in my opinion. Furthermore the execution scenes are really impressing which spices things a little more. But I must agree that with time it gets really repetitive and annoying.
The game also needs more variation in the design of the ennemy units, there is like only 5 different designs for briton soldiers, I always felt like fighting the same people.
Well it really is not that bad. Even though the revenge story is really cliché and has nothing original to offer, there is another element that comes and makes the game more interesting and it can make us think of a probable outcome (I won't say anything more to not spoil you).
The story is served by a very pleasant epic staging...but 6 hours is very short (And I know right one could say that given the gameplay it should not be too long)
Note that you can play as many times as you want the campaign in different levels of difficulty if you are looking for some challenge.
Obviously I recall that from a historical point of view this game has the credibility of an Asterix and still ...
One word: E P I C
The multiplayer is basically the same gameplay as the one we find in the story mode but the difference is that we are always fighting in the Coliseum, nothing really interesting there. Anyway there is almost never anyone online playing this, I personally could not find anyone in the matchmaking.
All in all Ryse is definitely not a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game, on the contrary it's a pretty good game, not very nor excellent, just a good game worth a shot for less than 15 bucks. It fulfills its role of games, it entertains us and despite of its repetitive side the epic and powerful atmosphere that it releases is such that one is caught by the history and cannot leave it before finishing the campaign mode. In short the game is fun and I had a good time on Ryse.

World-renowned Kojima Productions brings the Metal Gear Solid franchise to Steam with METAL GEAR SOLID V: GROUND ZEROES. Play as the legendary hero Snake and infiltrate a Cuban military base to rescue the hostages.
First thing first, MGSV: Ground Zeroes is a prelude to MGSV: The Phantom Pain and a bridge between MGS: Peace Walker and MGS: TPP. It's ok if you don't know Peace Walker, but you might not know who you're rescuing or why. It's normal for MGS games, if you haven't played the previous one you might be lost in the current. Where the full fledged games might tell you what's going on eventually Ground Zeroes is basically one main rescue mission, so not really much time for storytelling. It plays like any other MGS game, so like a military version of Hitman. Sneak or shoot your way around to kill, rescue or demolish in one main and several side missions.
Main mission should take around 1-2hrs, each side mission is 30-45mins long. All in all there should be about 4-6hrs of playtime here if you don't like repeating things. There are several challenges, achievements and a hard mode if you like to replay things though. The game looks nice and plays great, so if you like MGS series, or Hitman series, you might give it a go.
I liked:
* nice graphics
* excellent music
* that murdery sandbox feeling
* it's fun to replay missions
I disliked:
* it's only one main mission
Get this if:
* you like MGS
* you don't know MGS, but military version of Hitman sounds nice to you
* you are aware that this is only a prelude for the main game (MGSV TPP)
Don't get this if:
* you expect the usual MGS amount of content

Since I will be living away from my brother for some time, I decided to take up on the game and offer him the chance to finish a co-op playthrough. It would be nice to play some local co-op games before I leave, and Lovers in a Dangerous Spacetime had given us a enjoyable experience.
The first time we launched the game it was from my brother's Steam account, so we stopped halfway through the first cutscene to change to my account, which owns the game, just so I can get some trading cards and achievements.
Both times we watched to first cutscene, my bother would always tell me that I'm gay. Maybe because it's called "Lovers" in a Dangerous Spacetime, but I had figured it was fine to play with my brother.
The first boss we came across taught us that the game would be a ton more challenging that it seeemed. We had died an enless amount of times to that boss, because we lacked coordination. My brother, a true lover of the Souls franchise (I am one too), complained that the bosses were way too hard, and "I'd rather finish our Kirito and Asuna builds in Dark Souls 2." But I convinced him to keep trying, well, more like I forced him to.
By the time we defeated the second boss, which was suprisingly easy, our coordination had improved signifigantly. We would man the turrents, the shields, and drive at the same time. Still, we often found ourselves rushing to the love portal at the end of the level with the tiniest skimp of health.
In summary, the game has you and your friends working together in different roles to defeat the antilove monsters, and though this shared experience will reinforce relationships as well as build new ones. Of course, it is frustratingly dificult, but that just means you and your friends will feel more acomplished when you win. Don't be fooled by the title of the game, play it with your guy friends or gal friends. Heck, why not all of your friends in 4-player co-op? (assuming you only have four friends, which I totally feel ya). Very fun and frustrating local co-op. 8.5/10
Oh, and by the way, we did play this on two player co-op normal mode.

There is a certain level of charm exclusive to FMV games. I hated them back then, but now they're all endearing in their own special way. With the computer graphics of today, we can achieve practically anything. That really isn't as exciting as it used to be. Maybe I'm just getting old. I'd probably start yelling at clouds, but I never go outside. Whatever the case, Contradiction - Spot the Liar! is a great example of what the medium is capable of.
Detective Inspector Jenks is tasked with solving the mysterious death of a young woman. Over the course of a single night, he will collect evidence, interview suspects, and discover contradictions. In terms of game-design, the process isn't complicated in any way. Take the Phoenix Wright series for example. In those games, your primary method of progression is tied to spotting contradictions. If you mess up, you're punished with a loss of "life". There are no punishments for mistakes in this game. You can even take as much time as you need to solve the mystery. I appreciate the more casual approach to this investigation. Due to my cautious nature, I tend to save every couple minutes in the Ace Attorney games, which really hurts the pacing.
An aspect that I really enjoy about this game is it can feel like nothing is really happening. I compare it to the Gene Hackman movie "The French Connection". If you take out the car/L-train chase and the shoot-out at the end, you're left with nearly an hour and a half of "boring" police work. A lot of attention is paid to the characters, and how their mostly fruitless investigation plays out. You'll go through a similar process in this game. With every new piece of evidence, you'll  end up asking everyone what they might know about it. Some won't know anything at all, but you're still treated to an answer. The person you're questioning might also make an odd quip or comment. Even if they don't have anything to do with the investigation, these character moments add a lot of personality.
That's why I strongly suggest that - unless you're well and truly stuck - you don't use a guide for this game. Aside from spoiling the answers, you're also taking away the immersive qualities of this game. A lot of the detective work in this game could be considered dull, but that's usually how it goes in the real world. Often the evidence won't consist of something significant like a murder weapon or a fingerprint. In any case, since you're essentially working to solve this mystery in a single night, you won't have access to a bunch of CSI gadgets. All you really can do is think about what everyone tells you, and weed out the red herrings.
This game was made on a budget of 3,000 pounds. 3,000! The more I think about it the crazier it sounds. Some of the voice recordings sound a little off, and the "night" scenes were filmed in the day-time, but otherwise there's nothing that really stuck out as cheaply done. The acting is fine as well, though you're liable to remember Rupert Booth's (Jenks) 1,001 facial expressions most of all. He makes even the most banal scenes amusing.
Definitely give this game a look, especially if it's already in your library.

This is an excellent tower sim with a lot more depth than apparent at first. The game is flexible, stretchable, boppable and moddable all in a small file size.  With a moderately active modding community you may not be able to go crazy but there are mods that fulfill many personal preferences and minor game improvements as well as offering game expansions.
The game has a free mode as well as premade scenarios, it has a fairly simple options menu, but due to its minimalist graphics it should run well on many systems with possible dips in performance upon hitting the 80+ building levels point.
Highly suggest any Sim Tower fans at least check out some gameplay footage if not buy the game outright.
