Very fun management simulator. On the easier difficulties, it's pretty simple to successfully run a nice tower. Difficulty curve is not enormous, but steep enough to feel good when you do well on higher difficulties. Mod support is always welcomed, and I have not run into many issues yet.
Graphics are minimal, which is perfectly fine in a sim that has a ton going on at all times. I haven't encountered too many frustrating issues, other than installing lategame several rooftop penthouses. Make sure you automate maintenance on your buildings to ensure crowds of tenants do not move out and destroy your prestige!
Overall, it's a fun experience that lasts anywhere from 6 to 10 hours, and I'm sure it could be expanded through mod support; however, once you do everything there is to do, it starts becoming too grindy without a whole lot of reward. It's really necessary to grab mods to keep your lategame enjoyable (and keep your tower from looking the exact same with the lack of options). I definitely recommend it at a 40-50% off sale price, but can't recommend it at base price.

Very poor, even for a game made in RPG maker (had to dig around the forums to find this out) - very unoptimized to the point the game becomes unplayable after using the first wormhole in the tutorial, i selected "random space" to have an explore before heading to earth faction like the tutorial implied. I was greeted with a background that didnt even stretch to fill my screen, instead it was made up of 4 seperate backgrounds stuck together with obvious and ugly seams, whats worse however is that moving my ship horizontally gave me a bearable (barely - maybe about 20 fps) frame rate, but any movement vertically brought my FPS to under 5 (on an 8 core CPU at 5Ghz, 16GB DDR2400 and GTX 980). ***See link at bottom for explantion of poor performance***
The framerate issues are evident well before that however, from the general walking around your ship feeling very sluggish and choppy, to the game locking up for a few seconds every time you access your inventory or load a different screen.
No graphical options apart from being able to toggle full screen, game doesnt work at a resolution above 1080p, and the resolution can't be changed within the game (ini hacks needed, even by the dev) as that is against RMXP's (RPG Maker) T's and C's, mainly because that engine was only designed to work in 640x480 and frame rate (and user experience) plummets the more you try and push it past that resolution.
***See link at bottom for better explanation on this***
Graphics are taken from multiple freeware space graphics packs and really dont look good all mixed together.
Ship to ship combat is unfortunately only text based which allows you to select 1 action per turn.
Can't tell you much more about the gameplay as i could only bare playing for about 30 minutes due to the very low framerate and associated laggy feel of the controls.
I think, unfortunately that this one is gonna be refunded, may look into picking it up again in the future if it gets the patches and fixes it obviously and desperately needs. The Developer is also in the habit of deleting posts about performance from the steam forums without rhyme or reason.
***
- Very interesting thread on RPG Makers own website about why the T's and C's lock the game engine to 640x480 and how increasing this with non-eula breaking workarounds (like the dev has done in this case) produces major lag ***
Refunding for now, might buy at a later date when more content is added, i will say though that the up-coming "Apocalypse Hotel" game made by the same dev does look interesting.

Likes:

- Does something not really explored for many years - a bit of FTL, a bit of Star Control, a bit of Sun Dog Legacy, a bit of Star Command
Dislikes:
- The interface is woefully inconsistent (on some screens WASD, on some screens arrows, on some screens mouse)
- Oh, and slow. Where you'd like a table perhaps you get a scrolling list of options in a speech bubble.
- It's buggy and inconsistent (which is more a limit of cramming something ambitious into the RPGmaker XP engine)
Overall:
- I rather like it, despite its shonky nature (that's the Star Command influence at work)
- With a better engine and more polish it could concentrate on the bits it does well, and let the engine handle the interface.

I was a really big fan of the first YH10S, despite some notable flaws, but for a free quick game I really enjoyed both casually playing it and speedrunning it.
YH10S2 feels exactly the same, if you liked the first you'll probably like this. And that is the issue for me.
Nothing has really changed. A few blocks got added (most of which aren't very interesting, some just plain bad), and there's a hub world for no apparent reason (it worked nicer as a menu in the first game.
Other issues:
The grey colour scheme in the first game is back, and still clashes with the backgrounds. This is something that should have been improved between the games.
The double jump is now iffy for some reason. Randomly wont work, feels like it was fiddled with unnecessarily when it was perfect in the first game.
The game doesn't flow as well as the first, a lot of levels feel designed to keep you going slowly and impede progress.
The level-start animation is still playing when you first get control of your character, an issue from the first game. I personally like the idea of having a little moment where you can move before being able to fully see your character, but it lasts far too long (you've normally lost a full second of the level by the time the animation is finished).
Related to the above, many levels still have spikes right in front of the starting point, or teleporter exits, creating further cheap deaths.
Speaking of cheap deaths, "Precisely II" and "I'm sorry!" are still not good level designs.
There's no grand 50 second level at the end of the game, something that was a good surprise at the end of the first game.
Invisible blocks are cheap deaths, glue is an awful idea (and again affects the game's flow), ice doesn't really add anything new to the game (there's nowhere that you can really slip off of, all it really does is slow your acceleration, forcing you to jump when you start on it). Lasers were actually pretty neat, although once you figure out that they fire every other second they become too predictable and easy.
The gravitation blocks were actually pretty interesting, but for some reason wasted in an "Extra" world rather than being part of the main worlds. A further annoyance when some of the worlds feel very padded out, like the author ran out of content.
The mini version of your character has an awful misleading hurtbox, which the levels that you use him in seem to be designed around exploiting that (here, jump this now massive spike, but you don't know which bit of you can and can't touch it, have fun).
The forced credits at the end of the game just list a bunch of different things that the sole author did himself, each one getting a whole screen to itself before the next scrolls up (apart from the guy that aparently provided "Extra support". Not sure what that means but I feel like he could have had a real role name or something.)
All in all I'm fairly disapointed. Was hoping for the handful of issues that the first game had (which were easily overlooked because of the games shortness and well designed levels/mechanics) to be removed and for there to be more to go at, instead got the same issues spread out over more levels.

A great premise, but with an overall limited amount of gameplay.  For a space economy game there is nothing but a basic, static economy.   There is little reason/benefit to travel outside the starting system, and it really makes the game quite light.  The different methods of making money (smuggling/combat/trade) are far from even, with trade being the only actual option unless you want to switch later (and combat is incredibly dull and uneventful.  While smuggling is played exactly like trading, but with a chance of having cargo seized.  There is no way of doing it in any other manner).
It looked set to grow into something impressive; however, the developers have had to spend the last two years fixing coding issues and have run into problems trying to expand the game (due to underlying issues with the initial progaming), which prevents them from doing any significant updates without doing a complete overhaul.  They aren't going to do this as they are moving onto a new game.
The early access was promising.  But the game is incomplete and now abandoned.

I grabbed this while it was 50% off since it looked entertaining despite mixed reviews. And it is entertaining, especially at that price. I'd probably be grinding my teeth a bit if I'd paid full for it though.
It does suffer from both bugs and unpolished gameplay, but it is still fun to play. It crashes occasionally, but has so far always reloaded quickly with little loss of progress. It even seems to save more often than advertised "at every station". So the crashes are irksome but not serious as far as playing it goes.
Some more annoying bits are a mission not completing when it detects the tasks out of order, differences between mission requirements and what you actually need for them, and flight paths suddenly changing and making you miss deadlines (particularly on longer ones). They are at least fairly minor though. Not being able to adjust the window size is also a minor annoyance, having it allways about 5 pixels wider than my screen.
Also you can sometimes manage the flightpath issue by selecting other destinations when it goes wrong (usually a huge loop out in front of the planets orbit when half way there) to force a course-change, then change back again. It requires some micro-management.
Ship and tech progression don't match well and it's very easy to run on with the storyline then realise you've progressed yourself into an unwinable situation. Ship combat also isn't well explained. It does feel like it's missing its final polish.
The way you manage your crew however is very nice and creative with the morale system, and when you do upgrade your ship it is fun kitting it out. Building up a ship is rewarding, especially once you start stacking multiple jobs for destinations.
So despite its flaws, it's still a fun game. Get it while it's cheap.

I should mention at the outset that I got this as part of the MGSV Definitive Experience and thus did not pay $20 for it (I knew what it was and did not feel it would be good value for money, as many people have complained).
With that being said, Ground Zeroes is both brilliant and disturbing. The gameplay is excellent and gives you a solid idea of what TPP is going to be like plus leads you (story-wise) into MGSV:TPP.
Without giving away any spoilers; I found elements of the story to be unexpectedly brutal and as yet, in TPP, I have yet to encounter anything nearly as disturbing. Please understand that this is not a complaint about GZ; as someone who is not familiar with the franchise (also my first Hideo Kojima game too!), I had absolutely no idea what to expect and was both surprised and very impressed.
Consequently, I fuly reccomend GZ as a great experience; just dont pay $20 for it!

This review is spoiler-free.
First off, if you're new to the series, get yourself a PS3 and play MGS1-4 and then Peace Walker for the true Metal Gear experience. You may enjoy GZ and TPP for their gameplay even if you don't do this, but you'll be missing out on half the enjoyment of these games which lies in their story.
MGSV:GZ is, as everyone says, a short game. That being said, it is my favourite Metal Gear game in the entire series, when you compare each game relative to its size.
There is only one main mission that affects the story, however for those that are interested there are a couple more that are almost as good, despite their irrelevance towards the Metal Gear story.
It took me 30.2 hours to 100% this game, which shows that it isn't too long, even with all of the content. However the content that is actually there is golden. Metal Gear is one of my favourite game series, however every entry has its flaws, which vary from game to game. GZ has the least out of them all, possibly due to its short length, but it is tight, crisp, and nothing that is actually in the game disappoints. The game is complete, runs well, and is smooth all the way through.
In comparison to The Phantom Pain, which many criticised for its story, GZ is in my opinion actually far better, relatively. TPP did not finish development, and a fair amount of missions were mere filler, which meant just making
of the game's missions a bit harder. GZ on the hand gives you trials (fastest completion time, time for enemies marked, etc) and hard difficulty for
mission. Each mission in GZ is different from the last and the only similarity between them is the actual location itself.
The cutscenes, gameplay, voice acting and story are all beautifully crafted and tie Peace Walker and The Phantom Pain together perfectly. Don't play The Phantom Pain without missing this, lest you miss out on a critical part of the Phantom Pain story.
Overall, the entire game is a wonderful experience. The only flaw I can find apart from its length is the lack of cardboard boxes (a cardinal sin in the Metal Gear universe). Make sure you buy the definitive MGSV experience, giving you GZ for the same price as Phantom Pain alone (???)
If you already have The Phantom Pain for some reason, I'd recommend waiting for a Steam Sale, as most would not think this game is worth it at its full price.

Could also have been titled Ryse: Made for Consoles.
From the giant tile-based menu that starts the game, to the quick-time laden and painfully predictable ending, and through of the Batman-inspired combat in between, every element of the game seems like a tribute to this decade's AAA console titles.
Which makes it perfect if you have a handful of hours to spare between other games. It's an entertaining romp through beautifully rendered visions of ancient Rome and England. The gameplay mechanics are very simple, but the campaign is short enough that it's not a real problem.
Like other console melee games, this was designed to be played with a controller. It would also probably play best on a TV... the extremely close third person camera can be disorienting when playing on a monitor.

Ryse Son of Rome was Xbox One’s supposed flagship title. It failed to garner any attention due to the fact that not many people bought an Xbox One due to Microsoft’s controversy with the console at the time.
One year later the Xbox One exclusive was an exclusive no more and was the first of many Xbox “exclusives” to be ported onto PC via Windows 10 store or Steam. While Ryse Son of Rome ran at 30fps at 900p, the PC version ran at 60+fps in 1080p or 1440p. The PC version even has the option to run at 4k making the PC version the definitive version. It even sold better and had a higher score on PC.
This is the best looking game I’ve played so far with my new rig. Ran the game at 40fps on 4k (70+fps on 1440p) with an AMD Ryzen X1700 CPU, 16GB DDR4 and an Nvidia Gigabyte GeForce GTX 1070 Founders Edition 8GB 256-bit GDDR5 GPU. The ran smoothly with no studdering what so ever, even when things got busy on the screen.
The gameplay gets a bit repetitive at times with the hacking and slashing but is presented quite nicely and never feels boring. The story is good, the soundtrack is amazing as well as the voice acting. Unlike Xbox, Steam did justice for this game and I was happy to go along for the ride while playing.
The story is on average about 6 to 8 hours. I recommend this game, even at full price at $20. If you can, wait for it to go on sale. Usually it’s about $5. It’s a great deal. Overall I rate this at a 7/10. Just a little above average.

This was one of my favourite MMORPGs simply because of the extensive amount of customization.  You could make pretty much anything, whatever powers you basically wished, and change the colours of these powers (as well as animations) in many cases.  I enjoyed this game for a very long time, still have a longing to return...
However, my experiences with the customer support was completely atrocious.  To explain, I had a subscription to Champions and, as with many MMORPGs I played, would unsub when I wasn't going to play much that month or if I hadn't played in a bit.  Let me clarify beforehand that I only unsubbed from Champions this once, this one time, and only did I return and want to play Champions again did my story start.
I initially had unsubbed as I was busy with other things and games.  Months go by and I am suddenly noticing a charge on my account that I'm unable to track down, so I begin to do some inevstigation.  It turns out when I unsubbed from Champions, although I received a confirmation of doing so in my email, they still charged me.  It took me about a year to notice that they had still be charging me monthly actually, and when I contacted their customer service/support they fought tooth and nail in their own defense.
It was mostly a finger pointing game of who dun it, but it was made to be as if it were my fault entirely on either end.  I was very clear and concise, however the people I spoke with were extremely unprofessional, accusative, and insanely defensive.  Basically, it was insisted that since it took me so long to notice they were basically stealing from me, it was my fault and they'd do absolutely zilch to compensate.
Only after I had shown the email with the exact date and time of my cancellation did they cease trying to give me the run around.  I convinced them to reimburse me for half of what they charged me over that time, but they had tried to convince me to take less than a third of that, in addition to offering me a free month or two of subscription (hah, THANKS.)  I figured that was as much as I was going to get at this point after the customer service/support hooligan I was dealing with not only got my account information wrong regularly, but also threatened to "permanently remove me from gold membership."
Now, if you are unfamiliar with Champions and gold membership, it is a permanent subscription in a one-time fee.  It costs $300 and I'd actually known several in-game friends who'd invested in it.  The fact of the matter is that I never bought gold membership in the first place... and had I, that would mean I'd not have to pay a subscription in the first place.  Funny, that.
Please be very, very careful with these people.  The game is wonderful, but watch your bank like a hawk.

I've seen a preview of this game years ago. When I found out it's finally coming out I couldn't wait. I bought it on release without thinking.
Oh man, did this game DELIVER.
I love coop games and this is pretty much the pinnacle of what I've seen. It is currently my No. 1 favourite coop game of all time. It dethroned Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light and that's quite an achivement in my book.
Most games have tacked-on coop modes that many times just don't work. This a true coop experience and everything is built around it. You can play solo but it's rather boring since you'll be flying the ship 90% of the time while an AI partner will do most of the more interesting stuff (like shooting !). I also didn't play 3 or 4-player coop so I can't tell how good that is. The core 2 player experience is insane though.
The game is so action packed you'll forget you had real-life stuff to do. Every level is a constant scramble to man the necessary stations. It's almost like there's not enough people on your ship, but that's what makes it so fun to pull off. You need to fly the ship, angle the shields and shoot 4 guns all at the same time and enemies just keep on coming.
There's a surprising amount of variation on subsystem upgrades (guns, shields etc.) and you can tweak your ship to fit your playstyle.
Levels are semi-randomized. You get the same opponents and similar obstacles but the layout changes. It's not the level of some other games but enough to keep the levels from becoming a chore to repeat if you fail.
Each campaing has a different theme and ends in a pretty cool and challenging boss fight. Each level also has a different twist on the theme.
There's 3 different ships (2 unlock later) plus the one you start with gets a few upgrated versions later on. One of the other ships is kind of weird and not everybody will be able to play it though. I don't wanna spoil here but is a little mind bending. Makes some people dizzy. I'd kind of like some more ships but it's not that big of a deal.
It is local coop only and many people complain about it. It's understandable and a valid point but I would like to add that I feel like this game would not be that fun if you weren't sitting next to your partner. Online coop is great - but it's not the same.
So if you have somebody to play with I'd HIGHLY RECOMMEND buying this. Worth every penny.

There's not a single round I play where I don't learn something/gain experience. The game is also hugely interesting to anyone with a basic interest in the military, politics and warfare. Just pouring over the units in the armoury is a big amount of fun in itself.
The developers do a fantastic job of modelling the strengths and weaknesses of each nation. Armies of large nations such as the USA and the USSR have all the usual units and vehicles you expect, but also many others too. Equal attention is given to the minor countries like East Germany, Denmark, Norway, Poland, etc. All of them are faithfully modelled and recreated.
In short, this game is a must have for any fan of strategy. It rewards proper thinking, cool-headedness and a willingness to learn. One of my all time greats.

If you like any mystery games at all, this is absolutely, without a doubt, the best one you can find right now. The story is a pretty great murder mystery that most people probably won't guess until the end. Some veterans might realize half-way through, but with the characters in the game, and how well they are acted, you can be led down the wrong road pretty easy. You are kept on track without your hands being held, so you will never truly be lost, but it can steer your guess of who is guilty all over the place.
As I mentioned, the acting is pretty damn good. There are some scenes that are just decent, and the main detective, Jenks, is kind of a goofball, but it's intentional. Pretty much every time you need to know if someone is lying, there is the smallest tell in their acting, but not enough to just give it away easily. I hope they make a sequel, and I hope they keep most of the cast.
The graphics are all really well put together live-action scenes. The transitions are perfectly shot and perfectly timed. The games flow is probably the most impressive thing about it. They give you just enough flair without making you wait too long to get where you want to go. There is also a shortcut system if you want to travel to the other side of the map fast. It's a beautiful game all in all, great stills and great video, all in crisp 1080p.
The controls and UI are very good. You have everything you need and it's not in-your-face. The entire game can also be controlled with the mouse. You click where you want to go, and it gives you a 1-3 second scene of the main character, Detective Jenks, heading there. If you don't want/need any clues, you never have to use them, but it has 3 different layers of hints, not counting the acting tells. The first is a lightbulb button that reminds you who you havent talked to yet and lets you know that you need to go find out if someone is lying, without telling you who. The second is a phone call to your Chief, it lets you know who you should be questioning if you need to narrow it down. Lastly, it allows you to cheat and tells you exactly who to ask about what, if you are stuck.
The only complaint I could even muster about the game, is you end up with a LOT of clues over half-way through. This means a lot of remembering and a lot of scrolling. It keeps all your information for you very neatly organized, best it can, but it gets a little tedious to connect the clues, or contradictions, later on. It's not necessarily a bad thing and certainly isn't badly designed, but it's worth mentioning. Actually pooling similar things together would defeat the purpose of finding the contradictions, so it's nothing they can improve, I just feel bad about writing a perfect review without mentioning even something slightly annoying.
TL:DR
I'm not necessarily a fan of mystery games, mostly because so few of them are good, but I loved every minute of this game and it lasted about 7+ hours. I bought it in a bundle, so it was even better deal for me, but it's worth the base price of $10 for sure, I just didn't know about the game beforehand. But even if you aren't sure about the game, at least get it on a bundle/sale if you like mystery games at all, or even mystery books/movies actually, you will love this.

This is a very cautious and very reserved recommendation. This game will not be for "everybody". At all. It is quite rough around the edges and suffers a few frustrating faults. But. I personally enjoyed it immensely and think it is very much worth looking in to. I got this game in a bundle without having heard of it or it's Kickstarter campaign. It wasn't on my radar at all, even when purchasing the bundle I had my eye on other titles in it, this was just going to be a “throw in”. But it was easily the star of the bunch!
The game is impressively well acted, written, and shot. No Oscar performance or anything but also not cheesy in any way. A lot of “FMV” games or live action cutscenes in video games tend to be on the more campy side of things but this finds the balance in between. They're clearly having great fun, but still portraying the characters well. Never a “cringe” moment. The story and writing is solid and deep enough to mostly keep you guessing. And develops a full atmosphere. Then the cinematography or whatever you want to call it is great within the context of it being a game. Exteriors are particularly well framed.
But it is rough around the edges as I mentioned;
-The “along for the ride” straight line story and not being able to accuse anyone or effect outcomes might bother some but I enjoyed it. Nice casual experience. You don't change the story or have options, you just figure out how to keep it going.
-My biggest issues were some of the “contradiction” choices. You progress the story by presenting evidence to different characters you're interviewing and then taking their answers and finding things that contradict. Doing this flusters them and makes them reveal more to the story. I found at least two of the contradictions annoying in the fact I was on the right track but you had to make sure it was the exact right two statements to get it to trigger. Even though very similar (almost identical) answers wouldn't trigger it. The first time this happened to me I was certain I was on the right track but just happened to not match the perfect two. After circling the map and characters multiple times I thought I bugged the game. Which led me to consult a guide. I felt a "oh comeon!" moment knowing I had virtually pointed out the exact same thing with a different answer. And I hate consulting guides! Haha. But searching for these contradictions led me back to a guide once more later in the game... I feel shame. Then some other contradictions just felt a little too buried in the grey area. And then I'd have to glance over a list of the contradictions somewhere but I also seem to recall an early one not even feeling like a contradiction, but don't quote me on that.
-The last chapter has a lot of clues uncovered by stumbling across corners of the map manually. Which is fine because I like checking corners and had developed a habit of it every chapter. But the game up to that point triggered these events automatically when fast traveling over the area. Might get someone stuck/annoyed.
-Ending was fine with me but might leave some asking for more. There was a deliberate attempt to put more information than needed in the game to make the detective work worth it but this led to more story arcs that went nowhere. And some unresolved that did go somewhere for a bit. Which is kind of the point as well... We live in a world of sequels. And with some fine tuning and smoothing out I'd look forward to a sequel from the same team! Though I think an entirely new adventure would be more thrilling. Either way I hope the people involved from the gamemakers to the actors have more up their sleeves in some form.
Its a fair price for the entertainment value if you aren't expecting deep gameplay or any replay value. Me being cheap and the higher percentage chance of the average gamer not enjoying it, I would recommend waiting for a sale or getting it in a bundle of course. But I think $9.99USD is fair for what you get if its in your budget. Check it out!

This is one of those games that may be difficult to start, but even harder to stop. It's addicting, keeps you thinking and planning. There's a lot you can do. This reminds me of the flash game Corporation Inc (with further additions), but with a challenge to make a profit while making sure your business tenants are making a profit as well and any surrounding enviornments aren't hindering them. Corporation Inc will give you a very small taste of what this game is like, but it won't give it much justice in comparison.
You have to monitor your tenants satisfaction, make sure noise or smell doesn't affect them or their business. Everyone can get to their destination efficently. Adjust rents from 0% to 200% (for either tenants convience or profit) individually. Certain rooms have specific requirements like height (base floor, upper floor, underground floor), prerequisites (presige or influence) and more. Can manage an office, retail, restruant, or housing building; or possibly mix of the four.
There are scenarios that offer a challenge and give you goals to aim for. You can start from scratch on different difficulties of starting money and the city's economy, and adjust how big you want your tower to be at max (tall, wide, inbetween, full size).
The last actual Management game I played, that wasn't a flash game, was the first Rollercoaster Tycoon back in Win 95/98 era. The only thing I wish Project Highrise had was a line chart showing the past x days of finances (like 5 to 10) instead of the past 24 hours with no markings.
The loop music blends in very well that I barely notice it ever looping, and when you zoom out it sounds faint, but when you zoom all the way into your building, you can hear the ambience of a certain room/area.
The tutorial helped the game be from overwhelming of options to understanding the basic mechanics.
Despite what the System Requirements say, the game takes little over half a gig of ram for me, and my processor is an i3 instead of the asking i5. Not sure why the game would ask for 2 gigs of ram...
It's not exactly a fun game as it's not entertaining but more towards planning, but it is worth a shot. The $20 price seems a bit high for the game, but $10 may be more suitible if you're willing to wait for a sale.

After 170h+ of gameplay I believe I am capable of giving an honest accounting of this game.
And it is quite a mess. But before I explain why, let us clear basics first.
: 4/10
- Terrible music. We surely need more dance/rock/techno for a strategic game, where we need to pause, think and plan in advance.
- All those woooshes and beeps. Intefrace has limited amount of sounds, reuses the same alert sounds for different events which can be confusing as hell.
- Ship sounds are sub-par. Apparently cheap sounds used from over internet.
- No vocalizes to speak of. Never.
- Sounds lags and distorts many times.
- Ambient noise from starports and while constructing ships. Imagine looking at your homeworld and having to listen to pneumatic drill for a 15 minutes. FFS, I am pretty sure they would use plasma cutters/welders for construction in space!
:7/10
+ Minimalistic graphics, exactly what you need for a large scale strategy.
+ You can mod in your own ships (hello, S.P.A.Z. carriers!)
- Very limited planet graphics. Ugly. There seem to be mod that fixes that
- Game visibly suffers in default settings from too many ships on the map. This problem (solution described at the end) is caused by fighters, each and every one of them processed the same way as other ships. Meaning a fleet of 10 carriers with 100 fighters each will take as much processing power as 1000 destroyers.
- The above mentioned issue is so pronounced, it makes large-scale battles virtually impossible to watch.
- Possibly the worst interface of 4X games released in the last decade.
- - - Why do I need to have 3 buttons doing the same, but have no list of key shortcuts anywhere inside the game? Why cannot I rebind them in menus?
- - - Why not give me resolution setting, so I could actually choose, how about that?
- - - Why the few pixel gaps between buttons and status window, so that I could hit that space and loose selection of my choosen ship/planet?
- - - Why cram the logs above, why not let me rewind it without entering message history?
- - - Why no real message settings, so I could block the annoying popup windows?
- - - Why no central control screen for AI settings with all those automation sliders so that I could actually FUKKEN DECIDE ON THE POLICY FUKKEN AUTOMATED AI IS EXECUTING?!?!?
- - - Agent succes/failure displays american jet fighter pilot picture, SERIOUSLY?!
- - - No mass 'Retire' button for a fleet. Have to search for every ship in ship browser, luckily we can sort by fleet name.
- - - Default character/ship sorting is by some ID that is not visible. You can't restore it if you click any other header.

Regardless of what positive reviews of this title said, single player kinda sucks.
So. Even if you decide to start a pre-warp empire in a brand new galaxy, you cannot research warp technology. Instead you are given an ability to do so, after you are visited few times from a civilisations already having it (!). These are independent (!) planets, not an empires(!) possesing advanced technology(!). You cannot interact with them in any other way than colonizing/invading.
Why is such a thing in the game? Because you require resources to build stuff and you cannot get them in the beginning, therefore independent trading vessels will conveniently supply you with them.
I shook my head in disbelief for this solution.
Now, once you do start building things you will soon realize that:
- construction and colony ships can only be build on planets, not shipyards.
- the planet building capacities cannot be improved except with a single wonder.
- this was deliberate solution to forcibly slow down player progress.
So you build a couple of recon vessels. Little do you know that you cannot group them in a fleet (nope!). They have to go alone. They will be attacked by every single pirate/space monster they meet.
So perhaps you want to arm your recon vessels so they could defend themselves? Sure, but if you do, every time such a vessel enters a system controlled by other race, your diplomatic relations will deteriorate due to "military ships violating territory". Unbelivable.
The same goes for civilian ships that you cannot control. Arm your passenger transport agains pirates only to see it blown to pieces by a race more powerfull than yours as a "lesson" with few million passengers on board! Oh and by the way if the race has greater military rating than you they will blow up every single of your civilian ship armed with a weapon they see as a "military ship violating territory" even if you transport ultra rare spice to their homeworld! FFS whos idea was that??
Possibly the worst aspect of the game is how you expand your territory and build up your empire.
To begin with, you have no control of your civilian fleet transporting goods from one place to the other. You can and should manually design them, as vanila designs are just too slow/too weak/have too little cargo.
But wait, worse things are to come. In order to balance gameplay, the game features very expensive colonisation research (more about "research" later) and you can only build your colony ships planet side, which takes like forever. No, you cannot build industrial buildings on the planet to construct things faster, there is only one, singular wonder that allows you to do that.
There is more. Some genius decided to add a certain parameter, "quality" to the planet. This defines how big population can get on a planet and below certain population levels planet brings no income, only expenses.
Doesn't sound bad yet? Let me explain: you cannot terraform planet into higher quality. Terraform facility only serves to repair battle damage to the maximum quality planet had, does not increase it over time. But why would you want low quality planet in the first place?
Imagine there is legendary building (one of a kind) or an ultra rare resource (the only source in the galaxy) on a planet with quality 2%.
This planet population won't go above 20M and will always generate -3,6k loss.
And what if this is the only habitable planet in a 2 sector radius and in a mineral rich system of 15 planets and 30 moons in total?
More bad things. Due to some weird bugs construction ships will forget the quequed tasks (I think that happens when they are attacked, pretty sure it does when they are destroyed). Fancy ordering of building mining stations few times in the above sectors of 15 planets and 30 moons?

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is a fantastic game.  I have played a lot of Star Wars and this one is easily my favourite one.  The subtle choices that have are posed to the player (male or female) generate Light or Dark Side points which affect how the NPCs react to your character.  The level up system is very customizable, allowing you to craft your character in whichever way you see fit.  The story is very engaging and left me wanting more from each of the characters.  The Pros and Cons list that follows are just general points; it must be said that not having a controller does not detract from the gameplay at all.  It is, in fact, one of the games that got me out of the need to have a controller to play games.
Pros:
-	Great story
-	Excellent combat
-	Well written characters
-	Exploration
Cons:
-	No widescreen support or un-stretched full screen
-	Visually, not a lot of character customization
-	No controller support
-	Graphics can be glitchy at times
All in all, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is a wonderful experience that has a lot of replay value.

SimTower meets Privateer
Interesting combination of game elements in a manner that shouldn't work, but somehow does.  Interesting range of ships (but needs to be bigger and include more classes), the commodity model is reasonable (albeit rather basic), very similar to the Privateer model of base types, except that this game allows for bases to be multiple 'types'.
Crew recruitment and requirements can be counter-intuitive and frustrating, especially with limited options at each base and the need to build up a large crew over time.  I would have thought that having a crew that eats different things would lead to better harmony as they're not all competing for the same subset of the food supply (but that's me I guess).
Upskilling crew has one SERIOUS limitation; you don't get to choose the additional skill you would like a crew member to learn if you want to multi-skill them.  This to me is a massive flaw and not representative of the real world, where bosses have a large say in what development paths you follow.  Additionally, the random assignment of special attributes is great during upskilling except that it introduces negative traits quite a bit.  I understand that as people become more specialised they can become less adept in other areas, but given that it's an upskill, at least have special attributes balanced; +1 something, -1 something else.
Combat (before you're ready for it) is even more frustrating because the flee move doesn't seem to actually allow you to evade combat; it should if the game is to be properly balanced IMHO)
Mission choices are extremely limited (like Privateer) but the class of missions seems to be even smaller.  Combat, smuggling, or delivery (cargo or passengers).  That would be fine if there was a larger range of destinations and missions to choose from, but there isn't.
Finally, I think the biggest concern I have is that the Devs seem to have moved on to new projects, announcing there is no longer full time support going into this game.  Don't get me wrong; I like the game, but it's incomplete.  There are still some crashes that occur semi-regularly in the game, and there needs to be more content developed for the game to increase choice and range.  I'd like to see more effort put into getting this game right before new games receive focus.
Pros:  Reasonably simple trading model, nice touch of ship management with crew, so long as it doesn't impact the flow of the game.
Cons: Frustrating crew recruitment and upskilling, poor range of choice generally (ships, missions, new crew, pretty much everything), and no more full time support from the devs.
While I recommend this game, I'd love a button for 'undecided'.  It's about a 55/45 split for me at the moment, although I intend to put more time into it to see if familiarity and learning curve change the balance somewhat.  Original fusion of ideas, but needs more polish.

Project Highrise scratches the need for SimTower, and gives you a nice back rub afterward.
In sandbox mode, it takes about 10 - 15 hours to unlock everything. You choose a difficulty, how much space you could potentially build into, and have at it. The better your tower (based on factors that influence tenant happiness), the fancier your tower can be. More expansion means more potential issues, so the game's challenge progresses nicely with your skill level.
In scenario mode, you get specific challenges to accomplish, similar to Rollercoaster Tycoon. This gives the game quite a bit of replayability and makes it well worth the $20 cost.
My only complaint is how it manages saves. By default, it autosaves every 5 in-game days that pass, and it also autosaves upon exiting. This is great so you don't lose progress; however, this makes things a bit difficult if more than one person in your home plays the game.
For example: If I play the game, it'll auto save a file called Autosave 1, then 5 days later it'll save a file called Autosave 2, then 5 days later it'll save Autosave 3. Five days after this, it automatically overwrites Autosave 1, then 2, and so on in order, always looping. I can click Save and change the filename to 300 North Lake Shore Drive, but Autosaves 1, 2, and 3 will be my tower. As soon as my wife starts a game, it'll overwrite my Autosave 1 with her tower, then 2, then 3. If she exits the game, it asks "Do you want to autosave and exit the game?" She chooses yes, and then one of those autosaves will be updated with her latest tower. If I load 300 North Lake Shore Drive, it'll overwrite all of her saves after 15 in-game days and she'll completely lose her tower. So even though has what seems to be nice autosave features to prevent losing progress, you WILL lose progress unless you manually save and create your own filename before every Quit Game.
Overall, the game is a lot of fun and is an easy recommendation for fans of SimTower, Rollercoaster Tycoon, and similar games. However, because of the autosave issue, I give it 4/5 stars.

Paranautical Activity is one of those games I picked up during a Steam sale on the grounds of "it's three dollars, why the hell not?" It's pretty much an FPS version of the Binding of Isaac, set in an undersea Nazi fortress (?) populated with demons, mutants, and affiliated scum. Each floor is composed of randomly selected preset rooms, which lock until the player kills all the enemies therein. As you move down the different floors, more hazards are introduced, such as lava and bladed pendulums. Bosses battles are randomized, divided between mandatory (the room with the elevator to the next level) and optional, and an easy way to get free items. The game is fun, in an arcade-y "how far can i make it" sense, though it's not without problems. The dim lighting and voxel-based graphics sometimes make it hard to pick out enemies from the background, and getting movement powerups makes it very easy to run into something dangerous in the often cramped rooms. The different weapons are often more trouble than they're worth-the shotgun and the sickle are your best choices, hands down, and even then, you're at the mercy of whatever powerups are randomly generated in boss rooms or the store in terms of damage or firing rate. That said, the soundtrack is extremely catchy, and it's hugely fun dashing through the levels when you luck out and get the right upgrades. Though I'm not sure I'd pay ten dollars for it, it IS a fun little game.

This is, hands down, the most complex 4x I ever played.
And I've been playing it since the first release, back when it was only Distant Worlds (this version has four, I think, expansions already integrated)
It does things differently from others, and this is a very good thing.
Let me explain
The most notable thing is the existence of the civilian sector. Unlike most 4x, you aren't a god, you control the state, but not the people and you really need the peoplet to sustain your empire and, thus, must protect them and nurture them so that your tax base grows.
Though it is a bit more complex than that.
The first thing you have to understand is that resources? there are lots of those in game, and came in three cathegories, Strategic, Luxury and Super.
Strategic are needed to keep your warmachine going, Luxury enhance the value of your civilians helping their planets grow faster and more devoped (and thus more profitable), supers are technically luxury as in that they are used by your civilians but they have profound effects, are very rare, expensive and desireable that I generally put them appart (specially since all empires can restrict the trading of these resources to other empires).
Not all planets, asteroids, nevula and what not have all resources, so it si important to have multiple mines thoughout your territory and beyond to feed your industrial might.
Not only this allows you to deepen your stockpiles, buti t also lowers the price of the resource in question, which in turn lowers the cost of components that contain that resource .
Ship components are manufactured from the Strategic resources, it is not abstracted, and generally needs several resources, in different quantities, to produce a single components.
Because of this the logistics of the game are complex, but it is generally of little immediate concern to the player, you aren't going to be manually moving resources, the traders are for that (so you better protect our mines, miners and trade ships) and do so more or less automatically, of course, scarcity of the resource modifies its price, and therefore a component might be made cheaper by having multiple mines.
Speaking of which here is where the game shines, see, because you need to protect the civilian sector, the mines and the trade ships you need more than the battleline, you also need cheap, inexpensive and discardable escorts to police your inner lines both from imperial raiders and pirates.
Spaking of which, it is important to note that this means war is more complex than throwing your fleets at the enemy. You have to protect the homefront too.
Or, if the enemy is more dangerous than you and can't fight it head on, you can try to collapse his economy by raiding his soft underbelly or by hiring pirates to do the raiding for you, you can even do that in peace time, but of course, you might just get found out.
Speaking of pirates, dealing with them can be complicated. using them as proxy might be tampting, but they aren't the most loyal of folks, and letting them grow too large might be... unwise.
The game has several modes, but have a basic divide you can be a normal empire or a pirate nation, this changes how you play the game significantly as they have completely different playstyles.
As a Normal empire, you can start at different levels of development, from pre-warp all the way to being an already stablished star nation.
I love Pre-warp start, it is impressive seeing the little ships puttering on your starting system, as you develop and industralize it, turning it into the cornerstone of your empire

Star-Box is a sci-fi, sandbox, RPG, made using RPG maker, developed by FlynnFour Games. The game has you focusing on exploring the stars in your ship, allowing you to fly from planet to asteroid to space station, and even get into space-faring battles with other ships.
The game is made in RPG maker, an engine over the years that has had it's fair share of mediocre and lazy titles. But thankfully, I'm happy to report that this is not the case. As instead of using the typical RPG maker assets and combat system, the developer has opted for their own. The in-game assets are nice to look at and fit the overall sci-fi theme well, so if you're looking for an RPG maker game that likes to put in some effort into their games, this is definitely one for you.
The combat isn't turn based like the usual RPG maker games, but instead has gone for a more action-oriented combat style. While exploring the stars, you are more than likely to come across your fair share of combat on different worlds, asteroids, and what not. You'll beam down, and that's where it all begins! You move around the screen like you normally would, but around you is a number of enemies, who will not hesitate to shoot you in the face the first chance they get. Luckily, you also have access to a form of attack, also known as your laser gun. By pressing 1, you fire a shot in whatever direction you may be facing, although sadly you cannot shoot diagonally, something I would quite like to see in a future update maybe. Thankful though, there is no delay between shots, so feel free to hit that fire button as hard as you please, because you can assume the AI of your opponents are doing the exact same!
One upside to the combat, is you don't need to go it alone all the time. Providing where you're going allows, you can bring down a mech with you, or 6 if you managed to get a ship with that number of mech bays. Mech's are AI partners that work pretty similar to your AI opponents, except on the upside that they work for you. Once you've loaded in to the level, these ruthless killers will go out in search for something that is set to do you harm. The mech's are a wonderful addition to the game, as they help you immensely on almost all missions you go on. Your character is pretty squishy from the get go, so allowing your mech's to deal with the brunt of the enemies on each level is a tactic that is well worth using often. Which is actually why I spent the majority of my money upgrading my mech's, just because they are more or less literal killing machines.
Technically, there's a subsidiary to the combat system, which is the ship on ship combat. This isn't nearly as exciting as the regular combat, as the gist of it is just move closer, or further away, depending on how close you are to the enemy ship you use a different weapon, be it lasers, cannons, or missiles. Along with those attacks, you have tactics, like boost shields (restore health), disable their engines so they can no longer move closer or further away from you, disabling their option to flee from you. Then there's beam aboard once they are below 50 shields, allowing you to go onto their ships and take it out using yourself and the mech's, allowing you to take over and control the ship, something I haven't yet been able to achieve, as the bugger's block me every single time I've tried to do it!!
The game has a rather light-hearted take on itself, which you soon find out when you first try and upgrade your mech's, as your crew-mate says, "You may have noticed the AI is pretty bad, bumping into walls and all that. Probably warrants an upgrade or two." It was nice to see some humour and see that the game didn't take itself too seriously, as I feel it would of subtracted from the overall experience a little if it had.
Now, before I touch upon the story, and a little more meat of the game, I'm just quickly going to mention that there are a couple of spelling and grammatical errors from time to time, most frequent in the tutorial I believe, but I can imagine it's something that will be patched out in an upcoming update or patch. Now, onto the story!
Star-Box has you in search of your Mother's ship. Not a Mothership, literally your Mother's ship. You've taken to the stars in search of your mother (and her ship). I would say more, but the story so far hasn't been a main drawing point for me, that's the sandbox element the game employs.
Just like in any sandbox game, you're free to go and follow the story to your hearts content, but if you're like me, then you're going to ignore it until you've done more or less everything else first, which is exactly what I did. I picked up some quests, and went straight to them, something the game allows you to do, removing the need to explore for them when you can just go straight to them, something I actually quite like in this game, but something I imagine not all players will feel the same about. The exploring and sandbox elements are easily my favourite, as you're free to just go out and do what you want, pretty much from the very get go, something I wholeheartedly recommend to see what the game has to offer. It also allows you to make as much cash as you can fathom, of which I quickly used to upgrade my mech to turn him into one hell of a beast!
Now, before I give you an overall gist of how I feel, there are just a few things I thought were really quite interesting that add something different to the game. First off, there's a little debuff you can get if you explore certain items, which is an alien disease which slowly decreases your stats if you don't deal with it quickly. It's nice to see that there is something a little detrimental when it comes to exploring, as your character is touching test tubes, picking flowers they've never seen before, who knows what in the world they could do to you, so it gives you a reason to think twice before picking up something up that may not be great for your health. As well as the random debuff, there's the tax mechanic. At the main hub of the game, also known as "Earth" is a number of vendors, where you can buy almost whatever you please, but! They have a 100% tax added to them, meaning you will be paying double for whatever it is you want to purchase. You can do a few things to combat this! You can explore the far reaches of space, and look for a black market, where their tax is significantly lowered for you, but will only remain there until you've left the sector. You can either do that, or swallow your pride and just take the 100% tax with your purchase, or!! You can do missions for the military, and lower your tax rate with each mission you complete, which is a mechanic I really enjoy as it gives the player an incentive to go out and do their missions, other than just the original cash promised for completing it.
Overall, Star-Box has quite a bit to offer to anyone this might appeal to. It has some mechanics you don't normally see, gives players a good number of reasons to explore the sandbox elements of it all, and has some light-hearted humour to go along with it. The game isn't without its issues, with a few bugs or glitches here and then, but I have no doubt they will be soon patched out in one of the next few updates. And speaking of updates, the game got updated a day after I started playing, and they've already added new content in the form of drones, which makes ship combat a little more strategic and interesting for the player. Over time, the game is only going to get better, more optimised and more enjoyable by the sounds of things with more content and all sorts. This seems to be a sandbox game that's worth keeping an eye on, and I know it's something I shall be doing, as so far, the game most certainly deserves it.

TLDR: Battleborn is a great competitve FPS, full of various flavors of combat, skill building, and strategy. If you like Borderlands, the humor is there, if you enjoy a fast paced kill-fest, this is for you, if you get off on the MOBA equipment meta-game, you might want to stick with LOL, HON, or Smite. Overall, a fantastic effort by Gearbox. 8/10.
I had had my eye on Battleborn for a number of months before the open beta. As a veteran of numerous FPS's and MOBA's, the combination of the two had me salivating to say the least. In all fairness, I pre-ordered before the open beta; what can I say? I like to roll the dice every once in a while. I'm happy to report that they came up 7s this time! While I'm not too terribly big on co-op multiplayer, the missions offer something to play with my friends that are, and further, it entices them to come into the online arena to use the loot the gather in the co-op missions.
The PvP is fast paced and fun. Though there may be some balance issues to be worked out, and perhaps the overall player "score" should maybe be relabled "threat" (apparently your score has really no value outside of increasing your spawn time when killed, as read on reddit, not confirmed) overall the matches are frentic with an air of strategery that you scarcely can find in any other modern FPS. Match this with the inherent Gearbox style and you have yourself a winner that is bound to eat up at least a hundred hours of my time. If you're on the fence, jump off. This game will grab you and keep you coming back for more.

I've spent around 80 hours more playing this game (as of 5/4/16) than my Steam Profile shows, between the beta, closed technical test, and PS4 versions of the game. That being said, it's probably one of the most entertaining multiplayer games I've ever played. There's a lot of rock paper scissors style matchups among the characters and different strategies you can utilize as far as loadouts for each character go. The single player missions are a nice way to kill time but honestly not what I bought the game for. I got the Digital Deluxe version with no hesitation because I knew I would get my money's worth in SPITE of already having played the game for 80 hours already, which surprised me to be honest. This is a really fun but also really deep game.
There are three multiplayer modes (all objective based) with no "straight up" PvP. At first I groaned a little bit because it would have been nice but having played the game further I found out I really don't notice it's omission because what the game does provide is pretty damn entertaining. The characters all play really uniquely and you could play one character for weeks (go Team Phoebe!) without getting bored or switch it up and play a traditional FPS oriented character like Oscar Mike. There's a some overlap between characters in terms of their roles on each team (healer, melee, burst damage, support, crowd control, etc.) but the skills and intricacies of each character make each of them stand out in some way. The multiplayer is balanced pretty decently with a few exceptions that are definitely being watched and tuned as during each of the tests I played in Gearbox was very responsive in monitoring the data they received based on matches played, which teams had which characters, etc. and if any characters have been too high powered, they adjusted really quickly to bring things back in line so I have a lot of confidence moving forward that this is something they will address on an ongoing basis.
So in spite of the fact that initially what I was really hoping for was something more in the vein of Borderlands, I'm really happy with how this game ended up, and I can see myself playing it for a while. 9/10

Project Highrise is a game that I've been following after I discovered that SimTower would no longer run like I wanted it to, became really difficult. It finally came out on Steam, and so I bought it. After playing for a number of hours and designed 2 or 3 different towers (Haha, rhymes); I decided to write my review.
I love Project Highrise, I think the complexity...or I should say, realism of the game is very well done. When first starting out, if you have plans of getting that "high-rise" status, you have to plan your buildings. Where the wiring/utility closets go, the number of tiles a cafe and an office take up, and so on. The game is very dependent on decisions you make prior to the next event. A very building block kind of theme. Advanced apartments like lost apartments require luxery shops, luxery shops in turn require these utilities and this many of a different shop. Office headquarters requires so many of a type of office along with various amenities. The list of prerequisites grow with the more advanced you get, but have no fear, the more advanced you get, the more money you make a day.
Project Highrise's mechanics apart from being very "building blocky" is very dependent on your ability to manage your monies to spend on something that will benefit the building. Having a maintenance office over building that office will be much better in the long run becuase you'll need those maintenance crews more than that one office. Placing services and various amenities that don't require above ground or ground level can be placed below ground to save space and potentially not worry about the satisfaction of other tenants.
The
of your tenants come from all kinds of variables. Location in the building, how close they are to elevators, how much traffic goes by, how aesthetic the place is, different "smells" that come from different things in the building; and of course, utility connections. If a place requires a utility, you'd better give it to them or else you're going to have an empty space there.
is another interesting mechanic. The more prestige you earn, the more amenities and building services and places you can unlock. More prestige grants more "fame" so to speak. The more fame you have, the more things you can build, and the more things you build unlocks even more services and feature of the game that all the more increase your pretige and economy.
: 9/10 - Pretty much the best out of a 2D game you're going to get, the movements of people might not be fluid like they're actually moving in realtime but the style of the game rules that out.
: 7/10 - the initial learning curve is a little sharp, but apart from that once you figure out what you're doing, it can very easily be overlooked. Some of the things you have to do for your tenants may get repetative.
: 8/10 - Very realistic, job well done. This includes how you can build. You don't build parts of a tower into a little cloud of cement, physics applies.
: 8/10 - This game allows for a very formal kind of art, architecture. The more playful you get with tiles and paintings and wallpapers, and just the general placement of tiles can really make a tower look unique.
8.5/10 - Would highly recommend to strategy/simulation players, and would go back and build another tower any time.

Best 4x game currently on the market. Great balance of depth and beauty. UI will turn some people off but I find it easy to use, all the information I would ever need is one click away.

DWU = Distant World Universe
Sounds from the ships are nearly very good 75%, but music is only good I give it 60%, of course some tracks are excellent but there a few of them, and they do not perfectly visualize space opera for me. Music could be improved. People from Matrix Games should have listened to soundtracks from Hegemonia Legions of Iron and putted something similar instead. They should have also listened to the sound effects in Hegemonia.

In every game it is necessary to learn the interface, DWU is not different in fact it takes more time than usual, but I do not consider this to be a problem, this game is bigger than the average RTS. All the information that the player needs is nicely and intuitively presented on the screen.
I would like to see some improvements on ship design interface. Parts that are necessary to build a specific ship should not only be described as it is now, but they should also be highlighted in the module window.
There is also a problem with fleets, when a ship is clearly slower than the rest of the fleet, the entire fleet would travel with that lower speed. Interface should point out which of the ships is slowing down the entire fleet. It is a big problem when you have up to 40 ships in a fleet.
I think it is perfectly justified, that the game is presented in 2d. The scope of this game is better captured in 2d, 3d would not run even on high-end machines. What I would like to see is improved devastations on ships in form of particles this could be a great eye candy. I would like to see ships being smashed into pieces, which later are orbiting around a planet this could be achieved with particle physics. These pieces can later be removed when they collide with an asteroid or a planet. I will leave the problem of repairing such a destroyed ship to the developers. One thing is for sure even if the game is in 2d; there is still room to improve the graphics.
When then player starts its own custom game in pre-warp era it is necessary to build a space station, then the player must build an exploration ship to search for resources on planets and asteroids. After that the player must build a construction ship to build mining stations on planets and asteroids. The economy is divided between a state sector and private sector, the player controls only the state sector. In order to maintain the state and its expenses, the player has to choose how high the taxes should be on each colony. This is basically the main game mechanics.
There are 21 races in the game. And they all have different goals in the game if you decide to turn on race specific victory conditions. But basically victory conditions can be divided into, trade, exploration, research war, intelligence and diplomacy. When the player has to choose a race from these 21 races, it must firstly choose between quantity and quality of the military ships. A race that can reproduce itself very fast can produce lots of money that can be spent on military ships, but such a race is usually stupid and therefore the military ships would not be very advanced.
In opposition to this, there are races that do not reproduce very fast and therefore does not produce lots of money, but they are very intelligent and therefore they can research new technologies faster. It is a well-known mechanics from other RTS games.
The game is huge and I think that setting things to be operated by the AI was a must in this game, especially units.
I think the AI acts very rationally. The AI knows when there is a good time to declare war, pay the tribute or propose peace for the player.  I was very impressed when I saw that the AI has sent its own military ship to keep an eye on my military ships when they were located in AI’s home system, even if I had good relationships with that opponent. I was also impressed by the rationality the AI had when I proposed many different deals.

I honestly think anyone who's a fan of space 4x and paradox style strategy could find something to love in this game. I got it recently and literally lost my entire weekend to being absorbed it in. That hasn't happened since I was a kid.
The systems are quite complex, it's got a bit of a learning cliff. Sure you can automate everything but if you don't understand what the settings do then everything falls apart a little. My biggest criticism would be how obtuse some things are. I'd highly recommend spending a couple of hours watching guide videos or reading about systems (Das Tactics on youtube has a great series, and the subbreddit is quite helpful).
If that sounds like the kind of effort you're willing to put in to stop being hopelessly confused then this is the game for you. It's scale is amazing, the stories that come out of it are brilliant. You can go from being a civilisation just stretching its wings in a large and hostile universe to deploying planet cracking weapons against intergallactic supervillians. You start as a galaxy spanning empire and police/nuture your favourite empires to greatness. There's really not a lot of "point" to the game, victory is achieved by simply being the most awesome at everything with a little bit of flavour for race. The joy is in the simulation depth and the emergent stories as you set about doing whatever it is you want to do. Hell you can turn victory conditions off and just mess around if you like.
Once you understand how to get things flowing smoothly to create the kind of game you want to play with the automation there's a little bit for every tactics/strategy gamer in this. Diplomacy your way to galactic peace, engineer hyper efficient ships, steal lie and plant chaos, raid, commit genocide, micro to your hearts content and win battles through abusing range mechanics, bored ships, screw with trade lanes, optimise logistics, kill a leader.. the list goes on.
And when you've exhausted all the different starts and play styles that might be fun, play as a pirate nation or install one of the amazing mods and do it all again!

Overall, if you're looking for a 4x itch to scratch, this game scratches it.  Overall 10/10

This game is marginally thumbs down for me. I don't hate it and I spent a lot of time studying it and learning how to play. That said, I really wanted to love this game, however, it just misses being a good game. Considering how many people say its the greatest 4x space game, I guess I'm the odd one out, but I really don't think it deserves those accolades.
The interface looks clunky, but once you understand how to use it, it's actually not too bad, although it is not quite to the standard of polished interfaces in some games.  The text size is a huge problem, unless you have eagle eyes.  Not being able to increase text size is a substantial ommission.
The map and races are all pretty good, although I found there actually wasn't a lot of meaningful differences between them.
The automation is quite good, but again, feels like there is a layer of auto control that is missing for me.  I'm happy to automate, but I want to be able to give a little more specific direction from a strategic perspective to feel like I'm still controlling the game, rather than simply watchng it.  For example, controlling which races I will allow as immigrants.  I might be wrong, it felt like I either blocked it or risked having traitors in my midst.
I think a significant weakness is the difficulty in defending territory from attacks that often have no warning.  If you have the tech for scanners that can see far into space, you can get some warning, but I feel that there is something missing in the design that requires this.  I'm agnostic on space lanes by the way.  I think what's missing is at least some indicator of a contact incoming, even if its unidentified. It really needs something to give you a heads up.  Finding a planet is dead after the fact is annoying.

A game with this much automation and size needs to automate important warning and bring them to your attention BEFORE they hit, so you have time to think about remedial action. To truly appreciate how good this game is, you have to first understand WHAT this game is.  Interactive fiction, yes.  A full-motion video game (FMV), sure.  But more than either of those, it is a modern-day implementation of the age-old tradition of art commission.
A small team of talented and passionate people reached out to the gaming community and humbly petitioned them for support; the help they needed to bring something they truly believed in to life.  In the end, an understandably skeptical KickStarter community offered £4,010.  Let me repeat that.  £4,010.  At that funding level, Contradition is an astonishing achievement; not only in its polish and enjoyability, but also in what had to have been the colossal charity and collaboration of everyone involved in its making.
Contradiction is an interactive fiction experience in the form of a high-definition, full-motion video game.  A young woman has been found dead; drowned in a lake at the outskirts of a charming hamlet in the English country-side.  Detective Jenks arrives on scene at 5:00PM to investigate and finds the inhabitants of the village not nearly as wholesome as their idyllic surroundings.  At the center of it all is an inscrupulous father and son duo and their cut-throat, corporate executive training program, Atlas.  Jenks has until midnight to solve the mystery,  Tour the town, gather the evidence, and interview the witnesses.  Spot the contradictions and help Jenks close the case.  The Chief is counting on you.
This is British Detective Pulp at its finest.  From the quirky and unflappable Detective Jenks to the deliciously villainous patriarch, Paul Rand, great performances throughout elevate the story-telling well past what I would have alllowed a work of this budget and format could deliver.  The settings are lush, but genuine.  The makeup and costumes are "just right" in their tasteful understatement.  The music and sound effects create mood and communicate enviroment in as expert a fashion as I have ever heard.
The game design is both intuitive and innovative.  The control interface is clever and unobstrusive; an asset to he gameplay instead of a necessary evil.  The offering of both a hint system and a full-on "cheat" bailout welcomes players of every commitment level.  Chapter progression marked by advancing hours and subsequent nightfall are perfect for communicating urgency in a natural and realistic way.  The game is altogether worthy as a vehicle for delivering the quality acting and engrossing story.
I ran into only two challenges with the gameplay and those are easily overcome with a couple of no-spoiler hints:
1.  Start every new chapter by walking the entire length of the village, including the nooks and crannies, and entering evey location.  The quick-travel map can result in a vital progress point being missed for a frustratingly long time.
2.  The hourglass symbol that signifies that there is something in the scene for Jenks to investigate is easy to miss.  Watch closely for it, especially when making the aforementioned new-chapter walkthrough.

Overall, it’s hard not to be charmed by the creepy village of Edenton and its delightful cast of suspicious characters. Sure, Contradiction might not be the most complex of games, but through its simplicity it still manages to offer a familiar and engaging point and click experience dressed up in a fantastically entertaining vaudeville drama that’s just a pleasure to witness.

I've never really been one to play shooters. But then again, I was born into the N64/PS era, and didnt get into gaming until the GC/PS2/Xbox era, by which time Doom, Quake, and UT had run its course. So i've never really been able to experiance the "twitch shooter", only the tryhard big-budget military horsecrap.
Until now.
This game has what most modern shooters don't: a sense of speed, INCREDIBLY tight controls, and... dare I say it... fun? This is the most fun I've had in a while, probably since i was a starry-eyed kid playing Sonic Adventure 2 Battle. Enough exposition, let's get into it.
This game doesnt seem to have a story, except what you can glean from the enviroment, the enimies, and the title of the game. Here's what I've discovered (speculated) so far... (i've only made it to level 5 at this point) you are onboard a nazi submarine filled with demons and demonic sea life. Why? Who knows... and who cares? Just stop thinking and shoot what moves.
Speaking of shooting, the gameplay. Its just sublime. Sublime, and insanely difficult. This game follows up on its promise to harken to rogue-like games (is that how you say it?), with randomly generated floors (specific rooms are premade, but increase in variety as you progress), a Spelunky-esque shop, and a powerup system that brings to mind The Binding of Isaac. The game features permadeath, dying will restart you at floor one. Do not pass go. Paranautical Activity has several different classes, each with its own primary gun, maximum health pool, firing rate (an attribute determined more by the gun than the character), and movement speed. From the shotgun toting Tank, to the Insanely quick but flimsy David Bowie (armed only with a crossbow), there is a playstyle for all kinds of people here. Regardless of your class, all of the primary weapons in the game have infinite ammo, which i personally enjoy, as this game is stressful enough without having to manage it.
When you're not shooting in PA, you're going to be running and jumping for your life. All enemy attacks are either projectile attacks with travel time or rushing you down in melee. Mostly the projectiles. You are tasked with avoiding damage at all costs, which can become rather hectic in later stages of this game. Your character, regardless of class can jump a good hight, and changes directions midair on a dime.
The Graphics are kind of minimal, but I really dig the lighting system. All ingame models are voxel-based, with the enviroment textures looking similar to old-school Doom games. The Soundtrack is surprisingly good, and fits the game well, albeit being a bit repetitive.
All this, and the game is still in beta, and it can only go upwards from here. The devs are talking about adding in co-op (PRAISE THE LAWD) as well as finetuning the gameplay experiance.
This game does have a few bugs. Which is to be expected, as it is a beta, but bugs and minimalist graphics cannot hold back this pure, unadultered, virgin, twitch shooter experiance. Even in its current incomplete state, this game is an easy 8/10, and with solid netcode (fingers crossed), greater room variety early, and maybe a few more playable classes (one that starts with the M4!?!?) this could be propelled to a 9.5 to a 10, easily.
THAT BEING SAID. This game is not for everyone. It is difficult. Its inherent mouse acceleration can be very tough to get used to. If you dont like shooters but like Rogue-Likes you wont like this game. If you like shooters but hate Rogue-Likes, you probably wont like this game. In my honest opinion, this game is pointed at a very specific pocket of gamers, which quite honestly I see as a good thing. Too many game devs these days (mostly AAA ones) are spending way too much time trying to appease everyone (which is impossible) which simply results in a watered-down product, a shadow of what it could have been. YOU WILL NOT SEE THIS HERE. If you dig a challenge, love old-school movement-based shooters, AND like the randomless of Rogue-Likes... welcome home.
