Primordia is a great game with a strong atmosphere and characterization, and it explores themes of loss, friendship, and redemption.
You play as Horatio Nullbuilt, Version 5, and supporting you is Horatio's sidekick/son, Crispin. The premise is pretty standard, you are on a journey to reclaim what was taken from you, but the execution is where the game truly shines. Primordia's world is devoid of life, and yet a few machines persist in carrying out what functions were once prescribed to them. Primordia's world, however, is not devoid of feeling or emotion.
The dialog in Primordia is very strong. From Crispin's snarky remarks to Primer's street poetry, every single character in the game is charismatic, memorable, and interesting to interact with. For example, Clarity, a character you meet in the later half of the game, has some fairly amusing dialog. The writer for Primordia, Mark Yohalem, works in the legal field, and Clarity is a robot built with little to no error margin when it comes to matters of law and justice. She is rigid, uncompromising, and she lays the absolute legal beatdown on poor Horatio on matters of property ownership. It was also not surprising that Horatio had to resolve some unrelated ownership disputes later on, but I digress.
Primordia's main antagonist is another example of a well-written character; it truly believes that it is doing the right thing, and in a way, it is. In a world devoid of humanity, right and wrong are just words, and ideals are worth clinging on to. I have to commend the voice work in the game, too, as it is spot-on. Logan Canningham, of the Bastion fame, voices Horatio. Horatio is appropriately raspy, somber, the perfect tone for a religious leading man. Others are similarly well cast, such as Crispin's upbeat attitude that doesn't wane throughout the game, the Legionbuilt, and so on. There is more to mention about the characters in Primordia, but suffice to say, the game strikes gold when it comes to characterization.
The story, which is fairly short, is satisfying: there are emotional moments, there are moments of idle banter that flesh-out the world and the machines “living” in it, and there is an inevitable conclusion that changes everything. There are several endings to Primordia, and I don't think any of them are weak or abrupt, and it was cool to see how certain plot elements were referenced or expanded on. I felt satisfied viewing each individual ending, and that's not something I can say about the majority of games that have multiple endings. My only real concern about the story is that it could have been a little longer, perhaps utilizing some of the cut content, but it's not a big deal. I was just sad that it was over.
The mechanics, on the other hand, I do have some issues with. The game has a really low screen resolution, and while the pixel-styled graphics lend well to the desolate world of Primordia, alt-tabbing or using the Steam overlay can be really jarring on modern systems. On several instances the game would auto-skip all dialog and sound after alt-tabbing or using the overlay; not game breaking, but a little annoying. Another problem, I feel, is that because of the game's screen resolution, item-hunting can be a pain. This really goes for the point-n-click genre in general, but finding stuff on screen can be a chore when you can't highlight everything you can interact with. That said, if you're a veteran of the genre, this shouldn't be much of a problem.
When it comes to gameplay, I never felt like Primordia was unfairly obtuse or poorly designed. Crispin, Horatio's sidekick, can provide some valuable information if you're stuck, though his advice can be fairly vague at times. I did scratch my head several times, completely oblivious to a puzzle's solution, but prevailed eventually. As with other games, trying everything usually resolves the problem in the end. Also, I feel it salient to mention that certain puzzles in Primordia can be failed and the game can proceed regardless. This doesn't have much of an impact other than modifying one ending sequence—the only exception occurs early on in the game, and failing this puzzle locks you out of future content. Keeping several save-states as you're playing through is recommended.
Mark Yohalem originally recommended that I play through Primordia, and I am certainly glad that I did (after much delay though). The dialog, and some of the atmosphere, actually reminded me of Star Control II, probably one of my all-time favorite video games: a game that combines humor, melancholy, and strong characterization. While the gameplay elements may lack in some way or other, the overall experience is rewarding and worth the time. If you've been eying the game, give Primordia a try. I definitely recommend it.

When you reach the conclusion of this game, you'll be left wanting to find all of the many many alternative endings.
You'll feel real tenderness for your fellow robots living in this world post-Man.  Existential questions are natural and logical, mythology and religion are woven into the storyline effortlessly.
Sweeping lines and highly detailed animations make this game worth the price tag, simply as a feast for your eyes.  Great voice acting, challenging puzzles, and an effective atmospheric soundtrack will keep you engaged.  Humor is peppered into this unforgiving environment, making the impending heat death of the universe just a little more bearable.
Excellent game

This is a beautiful game. I found myself completely engrossed in its post-apocalyptic world and soulful characters during my all too brief time with it. The art style is certainly giger-esque but the world itself is much more humourous and warm than this would suggest. The point and click gameplay underneath this is relatively standard for the genre, but for the most part I found the puzzles made absolute sense, and I never found myself in the common "how on earth did they expect me to figure that out" scenario point and click titles are so known for. The voice work and sound fits the world like a glove, and I found the story went to some incredibly interesting places. My only real complaint here is the length of the game; it's incredibly short, and I found myself wanting quite a bit more of it when I'd reached the end. Given the price, this doesn't effect my reccomendation too much and it may be worth some limited replays due to divergent endings, but bear in mind there isn't a huge amount of content here. Nonetheless, what is here is absolutely stellar, and one of the best point and click adventures I've played in a while. Recommended to anyone who counts themselves a fan of the genre and wants something with a little bit of heart.

Primordia is a great classic point&click adventure with a remarkable story.
It's post-apocalyptic world populated by (rusting) robots is captivating throughout the whole relatively short timespan you spend in it.
The philosophical themes are neatly integrated without overextending the scope of a video game.
The art is phenomenal.
From a gameplay standpoint there are some QOL additions to the standard point&click mixture, e.g. a map with a fast travel feature. There are some potentially frustrating puzzles, as is to be expected. Keep a walkthrough handy, if you're not too proud for that.
On the whole, Primordia is worth its money for the story alone. Not often you find such a neat little story in a video game. If you have any interest in point&click games at all, you should check it out.
A wonderful and rich story/setting. It mixes both darkness and humor in a fascinating way.

Primordia has managed to capture the real spirit of point and click games. It has an immersive and well crafted story, with great dialog and awesome characters. The music really sets the tone of this post apocaliptic world quite well, and while playing I was totally transported into the world. I loved every second of it. Hopefully the developers will consider making a sequel (or prequel). For after completing the game, I felt that there could be so much more to this story.
If you love point and click adventure games then don't miss out on this one.

Starting bit by bit after trying to find the crystal and remembering to take the plug/crystal back out of the terminal after using it.  But afterwards, the solutions were both clever and logical.  My reactions were more 'Ohhh, I see! That makes sense" rather than, "Oh...Duh...Why didn't I think of that."  Also, on some of the more difficult puzzles, it looks like there are multiple ways to solve them, so if you do get stumped, you're not completely stuck and need to reach for the guide.  Lastly, just like the Quest Games, you’ll need to click everything and take anything not nailed down.  Unless they tell you otherwise, in which case don’t worry about it, which is nice.
I guess the only thing that differentiates it from the Quest games is the inability to die. Right from the start, you’re clearly a sturdy robot and not some janitor, so that makes sense why they aren’t included. Deaths can be hard to balance in adventure games to make them useful, interesting, or simply hilarious. As such, I can’t honestly say I miss them, as many of the deaths in other titles can range from tedious to downright infuriating.  I suppose it’s better to be stuck on a puzzle but able to move around than to be stuck at a save point dying over and over again due to bad pathfinding, narrow walkways, a simple mis-click, or not having a freaking pie.

Disclaimer: I've played the game much longer, as I owne the non-Steam version as well, since long before the "Universe" addon came out.
Distant Worlds: Universe is an amazing "living galaxy" 4X strategy game. Thinking of it as EU/CK in Space comes maybe closest to describe it in one sentence. It is in real time, but can be paused any time. You can also freely set the pace of the game. Its options for customization are unique: there is a vast amount of options to customize the game to your liking: size of the galaxy, aggressiveness of the enemies and pirates (which can be turned off completely), colonisation range limits ("sphere of influence"), tech progression, "age" of the galaxy and so on. I am not aware of any other game that allows for so many options.
Basically, your goal is to expand, to colonize other planets and to rule the galaxy. But this game is so huge in scope... Simply set yourself any goal you want. You can also turn off victory conditions.
If you want, you can control any tiny little bit of your empire: diplomacy, fleet formation, ship design, space station building, colonisation activities etc. But what makes this game so valuable and is that you can also decide to fully automate one section of your empire. You don't want to deal with ship design? Then let the AI do it for you. This freedom of choice between manual control and automatisation let's you even configure a game mode, where you automate your whole empire and just control a single fleet - play as an Admiral!) or a single ship (play as a captain!). The possibilities are endless.
With Universe, DW has een four expansions an has reached a high level of perfection. However, it is not for everybody. You need to have time and the willingness to undergo the learning curve. I recommend to check out some Let's Plays on Youtube, to see if the game is for you. he atmosphere it creates is simply amazing.
it is also noteworthy that the whole game is made by one guy, who gives an amazing support and is stilll patching this game with a high frequency.

I love the idea of this game, but the implementation leaves a lot to be desired. I can not recommend this game.
Cosmonautica does a lot of things right, unfortunately it does several critical things wrong.  The humor, the graphics, the sound, the visuals are all spot on and to be admired. It's a fun game to get into. But once you do, and get a little bit into the game, the flaws begin to show through and severely limit your ability to play.
The biggest flaw I came across was a severe lack of balance and difficulty. This is a simple change that could be fixed with the addition of a difficulty slider. See, when you have a game where you trade for credits, that economic model needs to be spot on. Unfortunately even if you do everything 100% correct, the profit margins on trading are razor thin.
In two hours of play, making only positive trades, I barely was able to re-attain the amount of capital (20k credits) I started the game with as seed money. Another hour and a half later and I was still only around the 30k. Now on it's own, this might be acceptable for some. A game where you have to micromanage razor thin profit margins and grind out credits might be acceptable. But this was all while I was making perfect trades and always turning profit. If you take a loss, at any time, it's absolutely devastating. After 3.5 hours play I got stopped by a cop and had a 15% chance of getting caught. RNG came up and I got caught. This caused me to fail my current quest, which penalized me credits, lost all my cargo, and was banned from that world for 15 days. The effects of this were absolutely devastating to my game, knocking me down well below the 20k mark just to get to a new planet, refitted, and get a new hold of cargo. IE one random chance event, that could only happen 3 out of 20 times, and I'd lost around two hours of gameplay.
The further issue in the game is in the absolutely horrible combat system. You run out of ammo FAR too quickly, far more quickly than you can possibly take out even the weakest of pirates.  Forget about harder difficulty ships, you don't stand a chance. Ramming doesn’t even work, because the AI can avoid you forever.
I think Cosmonautica has the potential for a good game, but it feels like an unfinished beta at this point.  I would HIGHLY recommend against buying this game at the current state it's in.  (v1.2)

OK so there's plenty of bad and good for this game. Let me lay my opinion on the line here from a couple of hours of initial gameplay (Which I have no doubt will grow to a few more [albeit modest] hours in the future)
This is a casual game by far. In that sense I've personally found it rather zen. You've no doubt gotten a fair idea of what the gameplay is. You manage a crew in a basic sense aboard your vessel. You travel around, first, one solar system trading, smuggling and fighting to accrue money. This cash goes towards bigger vessels and more capability to extend your activities further abroad. Beyond that overall premise, you have to manage the crew you use to staff said craft and their relationships and needs. As they become more skilled they require more effort to keep them satisfied (A feature which, thanks to a recent addition of bonuses, you can come close to bypassing to an extent early on if the money is flowing),
If you are someone like me that's happy to provide a narrative (Other Dwarf Fortress and Paradox Grand Strategy players will understand) for the game you'll enjoy this, but superficially. There's plenty of capacity to do so but it is provided with a quite limited depth.
There's a comedic element to the game which works quite well, but I personally don't take that in too much as (as mentioned above) I enjoy supplying my own narrative to the game. That being said it provides a level of enjoyment to the game even if it can be found to reduce the 'immersion' factor.
To give a TL;DR overview though, if you are looking for a relaxing game set around Captaining a ship and crew while jaunting around getting into whatever adventures you see fit, this is a great game to destress to. If you want more complexity in your zero-G adventuring, check out the X series or EVE online.
All being said and done, with the above caveats, I will recommend this title as a simple, enjoyable and satisfying experience. Additionally, the devs seem to be taking comments on board and working to adjust gameplay in an ongoing fashion.
PS. A couple of things that I think this game requires:
- The ability to speed up time to a greater extent
- More intricate and involved crew requirements and procedural command events (There are some, I hope there will be more as I go on)
Overall, once again, I've found this a relaxing and satisfying game. It will likely get repetative in the future (And I will update my review accordingly) however that's the lot of a ship captain in reality isn't it? Haul cargo, wash rinse and repeat with a dash of combat and smuggling to make it interesting. If the devs continue to update accordingly, it will continue to satisfy unless you're looking for an ultra-deep and complex experience. In that case, look elsewhere.

This is a gratifyingly complex strategy game with satisfying depth and immense replayability. I would highly recommend it for fans of space settings, 4X, and those looking for a deep game that rewards investment.
Distant Worlds: Universe engages with each of the four Xs in a variety of ways. Exploring, for example, is about discovering what your corner of the galaxy is offering you, which is potentially plenty: ruins, abandoned tech and equipment, pirates, planets filled with independent races, other empires, interstellar phenomena (black holes, super nova), glactically-significant locales. What's important is that this isn't just empty variety: there's a range of ways to engage with what you find, depending largely on what victory conditions you're aiming for. For a peaceful race, you might want to bribe the pirates not to attack you and pay them to introduce you to other races with whom you can trade, set up mining bases in unclaimed systems to fuel your expansion, and build resorts at those interesting ruins and exotic locales to both earn income and establish yourself as the predominant tourism empire in the galaxy (an actual race-specific victory condition). For an espionage-focused race, you might protect yourself from pirates through sabotage and defensive firepower rather than bribes, and incite riots and revolution to cripple your opponent's economy while destroying their research bases to prevent a technological advantage. There are more courses of action available to you in Distant Worlds: Universe than in any other strategy game I've played.
The variety of races and victory conditions bears special mention. There's extra attention paid to crafting a race-specific experience: the difference in game play between various races seems far more significant in DW:U than most other games I've played, strategy or otherwise. The experience is shaped by the skills they offer, the kinds of significant figures they attract, the race-specific technology they have access to (which often synergizes well with general play style), and the race-specific victory conditions, which provide each game you play with direction while still allowing for flexibility. You can also tweak the weighting of various victory conditions in the game creation menu (one of many, many customization options) to allow you to shift focus as desired.
With all these options available, the game is clearly complex. But I don't feel as though it's too complex. This is to a degree a matter of preference, but I think it's also helped by the game's useful tutorials and extensive automation options: you can micromanage as much or as little as you want, including providing rules of thumb for the AI to follow as it runs the nitty-gritty. It's a very effective and well-conceived, well-executed facet of the game that enables you to ease into it and calibrate your experience to your own personal level of OCD-ness.
So in short, this is a great game if you don't mind complexity. If you've played the iconic Dwarf Fortress, I'd say this is 3/4s of its intensity, which is to say, deep, but more focused and well-developed in a particular vision of gameplay, rather than the utter sandbox that DF is. I would highly recommend this game to those looking for a game they can log dozens if not hundreds of hours into; I'm sure I'll hit the 100 mark sooner rather than later.

For non-Metal Gear fans:
With prices for The Phantom Pain getting lower and lower, there's really no reason to buy this as a non-fan unless you just want more MGSV content. If that's the case, this game provides an exclusive smaller open world along with several big missions not found in The Phantom Pain. If you're interested in the story, you should buy this along with MGS1-4 and Peace Walker (all can be found on PS3), and play them in release order. Anyway, the game plays really well, looks amazing, has an unmatched atmosphere and superb cinematography and voice acting.
For Metal Gear fans:
While it's definitely the smallest game in the series, fans of the series will see that Ground Zeroes is an essential piece in the story and stands on its own both plot- and gameplay-wise. It directly continues the story of Peace Walker and leads up to The Phantom Pain. The side missions are fun and varied and contain tons of fan service. And as mentioned above, the gameplay is superb (only surpassed by The Phantom Pain, which makes some improvements) and the graphics are possibly the best in the series.
Overall, I'd only recommend this to fans of Metal Gear and/or people who want the complete MGSV experience.

1. Playing the game can be fun and challenging if you're a competative gamer / experienced gamer, but if you're a casual gamer like me, you'll love the game at the beginning, but soon it becames too hard even on the lowest dificulty settings and I simply couldn't enjoy it anymore.
For example there's the part where you defend a church and I simply couldn't defeat the owerpowered zombie with the machine gun and a horde of lesser zombie soldiers comming at you from all sides. Even if it was on Cadet level with the setting of zombies spawning for 1 player, it was still too hard for me and as such a frustrating experience. Maybe I'll come back to it after playing some of the easier games of the same genre - when I get better in third person shooters...
2. The singleplayer is made mostly of ''Go from point A to point B and defend yourself from the incomming waves of zombies.'' If there wasn't a problem with the game difficulty, this in itself wouldn't bother me much, but I have noticed in the forums that some people disliked this about the game, so I thought I'd mention it.
3. This game doesn't have much of a story but doesn't really need one IMO.
1. I don't know why any of the reviews don't mention this, but you cannot normally save when playing this game. People complain a lot about it in the forums, because it's frustrating not to be able to resume a game where you last left off. If you for example play a chapter for half an hour and then decide to exit the game, there is no save option and you lose all progress. Thus when you launch the game again, you must start at the beginning of the chapter, regardless of how far you've made it the last time. This is the same for single player or co-op. But in single player you can at least ''bypass'' this problem by not closing the game untill you finish the chapter. In other words, when you stop playing, you can just put the game on pause and minimize it, so you can later continue where you left off...
Because there is no normal save option (what to speak of autosave), when playing co-op, if for some reason you lose connection with Steam/internet, you will instantly lose all progress and have to restart the whole chapter from the beginning. The same goes for people who are using Steams Family library sharing to play the game - if the owner of the main account starts playing something, Steam will give you 5 min to leave the game. And since you have no save option, you'll lose all proggress.
2. This game has a few unpleasant bugs. For example sometimes when you have to survive an enemy siege, some kind of error occurs and then even if you kill all of the zombies, the level will not let you progress and you will have to restart the mission from the last save point. Some people reported in forums that sometimes even restarting from the last save point didn't help them. If this happens, you can only restart the whole chapter and hope for the best.
If it weren't for the bugs and the problem of not being able to normally save the game, I would have given this game a solid 9/10 rating - with a warning that the game might be too hard for the inexperienced and casual players. But since there are some annoying bugs and most importantly since there is the problem of not being able to normally save the game whenever you'd want, I give it 6/10.
Considdering everything, I would carefully recommend this game, but only if you're not new to the genre or are not a casual gamer.
I also would't recommend buying this game for the current full price of 42 Eur. For a game worth 40+ Eur I'd expect to be able to save my playing proggress. For me this is a really big minus. But if you can get it on sale for half the price or less, I would definitely reccomend it. It is a really good game.

If you enjoyed the first "You Have 10 Seconds" --
(which I also recommend and actually like better, partly because frankly it's not as sadistic) -- then the platforming here will feel familiar, with a lot of additional tricks up the developer's sleeve, such as sections you have to shrink to get through or platforms that are covered in glue.  Most of these tricks are enjoyable, but since one new obstacle involves invisible ceilings and floors that only reflect light when touched, one of their levels requires you to shrink and then to blindly hop between surfaces hoping to land on something, which feels more like trial and error for its own sake than something you actually figure out with logic or skill.
Compared to the first game, "You Have 10 Second 2" brings its own benefits and drawbacks: you can change the color of the box you play as, you don't have a limited supply of lives anymore, the number of levels and worlds is a lot higher, and they don't always grant you a new ability after completing them anymore.  You now have more room to experiment, since dying a handful of times in a world no longer forces you to start the world over, but some levels--two of them in particular, as noted in some other Steam reviews--take advantage of this and crank up the difficulty long past the point of being entertaining.  Imagine a more punishing and confined Flappy Bird, and you'll have the right idea; at least the name of the second one makes fun of itself.  I did enjoy certain batches of levels that felt heavily inspired by VVVVVV, where level tops/bottoms and sides wrapped around like contiguous areas.  World navigation is now done in a hub area instead of being selected from a menu.  This wasn't really necessary, but at least the entrance doors look neat.
My only problem with the game's impressive level count is that it didn't quite know when it wanted to end.  Between the bonus and extra levels, the game effectively has three finales, none of which are as exciting or memorable as the one in the first game.  There is a level editor if you want to try that, but one thing I and others noticed is that (as of this writing) there doesn't seem to be a way to exit back to the main menu while in a world, since the Escape button merely pauses the game.  On another note, the animated backgrounds didn't seem as distracting here, but the music--while fine--didn't seem as interesting as that of the first game.  That's a small quibble, however, and if you enjoyed the first game, you'll probably enjoy this if the notable increase in difficulty doesn't get to you.

Well, I liked it. The contradictions, if sometimes a little far-fetched, are difficult enough to feeling challenging but not so completely off the wall that you rage quit in frustration. The UI is clunky but in a way that strangely adds to the charm. The acting's got plenty of ham going on, which, again, adds to the charm. And I liked the story - including the ending.
The big downside for me is the lack of a proper 'fail state'. You can't really mess this game up - you'll just be left to walking around until the puzzle solution dawns on you. While the story is entertaining enough for that not to be a problem on first playthrough, it does mean the game has next to no replayability value (for me, anyway). Some alternative paths or alternative endings would have been nice. I can't say I didn't enjoy playing (and I may load this up again in the future once my memory has blanked itself enough not to immediately know what to do) but, at the moment, I feel a bit let down that I've completed it so quickly.
For the price of entry this game has great value! I would encourage anyone with a mystery itch to play this game and challenge yourself to complete it with no cheats.

It's a fantastic game. Not perfect, but almost certainly the best FMV game I've ever seen & quite possibly the best FVM game made so far. I made my way through it in just under 6 hours, and feel I got excellent value for money at that, because of the unique nature of the game when compared to most games out there.
I played it solo and it's great fun that way, but I imagine it'd be even more awesome played with friends/family (that's certainly what I'm currently planning if/when there's another one - possibly even with this one once I've had time to forget enough of the specific contradictions).
Anyway: the visual quality is great,  the soundtrack is awesome (both music and environmental sounds) and the acting is pretty much spot on for me. Yes Jenks is rather over the top, but I get the feeling he's meant to be. It certainly worked well for me, because Jenks, being 'my' character, ended up reflecting my sense of triumph at finding a contradiction, or my bafflement at asking about the same mundane thing again, as a result.
There are still things that could be improved. In a future patch, or a next instalment, I'd love to see hybrid keyboard/mouse control added. I preferred the mouse driven interface for questioning, but as things stand that meant also using the mouse to walk around, which I actually liked the keyboard better for. It's not a huge issue though, and the game is certainly quite playable with either.
At times it can also be annoying that the game doesn't permit follow-up questions except by finding contradictions. This is an inevitable limitation of the format, but it can be annoying to have spotted something (or have made a conjecture) and find yourself unable to ask about it for quite a while, until something comes along to create a contradiction that does allow you to ask about it at last.
Coming up: some minor spoilers, you have been warned!
Sorry, don't mean to bother you, but you have been warned about minor spoilers, right?
You're sure?
Quite sure?
Okay then, let's start with the ending. I'm fine with it, but can see where some people would find it annoying. Inspector Jenks gets his alien/man/woman/demon/killer-rabbit (I'm not going to spoil that much) as you would expect from a game like this. But a lot of other loose threads are left unresolved. For me personally there is enough closure this way to let the game stand alone, but quite a lot of it does seem to be setting up/teasing a sequel (and I enjoyed it enough that I hope it does get one).
The story does have a few weak spots, the most obvious one being Jenks having apparently no way to leave the village or call in support when he feels threatened. Or the fact that there's no way to request more information on anyone beyond what you're given in the introduction.
Still, in the end, the story holds up well enough and makes an excellent vehicle for some terrific gameplay, which is what matters in this case.

The main downsides from the game are twofold.
Firstly the story feels incomplete like there needs to be a bit more to give a better conclusion to the Atlas sotryline. While you complete your origianl goal the ending feels somewhat abrupt. Hopefully a sequel or some DLC will fix this.
Secondly the navigation feels clunky - with a lot of clicks to move around the place (a better mini map might be a suggestion, or better placed pins. Also there are a number of areas that are only used once in the entire game, yet remain clickable - there either needs to be things to do there, or they need to dissapear once you discover what you need to.
Overall this was a great game, well worth playing and I eagerly await the sequel so I can rejoin Jenks on his investigations.

--Initial look--
I first found this game on steam after playing 'FTL'(which I got bored of very quickly), then playing 'Space rogue'(which is basically FTL with better graphics but buggy as hell). The pics looked good, adds a trading and exploration element, as well as the ability to change up your ship in ports to suit your needs.
All this combined with the fact that it was a steam greenlight game, the reviews were mixed(most of the bad ones just stupid little gripes about things that didn't even effect game play) and is currently $14.99 USD on steam, meant that it was worth the risk to buy and give it a go.
--Graphics--
At first glance I was disappointed with the graphics.
That was until I took a closer look at the way it was done, the creators of Cosmonautica have taken a large attention to tiny little details and overlaid the entire game with a filter that resembles the horizontal lines you used to get with old LCD screens. Which in my opinion gives the game that old sci fi feel, like you're overseeing the play of the game from your own consol on the ship.
--In game world--
The map is large and unless you're playing in story mode is procedurally generated for that extra replay value. Each solar system map has four rings with a few planets, the starter ring and the next three that you can research to gain access too. Then you have your star chart, you start with one quadrant which usually has three solar systems in it, then you can research further star charts and expand your travels in world.
--Game play/Controls--
Controls are a simple point and click interface, most things are fairly self explanatory and everything else you just need to click on for a explanation or description.
Game play is fun and addictive. You start off with a little ship and some money and have to fit out your ship from the start, choosing either to take a few passengers, a lot of cargo or split the difference. You will need to hire staff based on skills and wages, with added traits which can determine how well your staff actually get along.
It all comes down to managing your staffs well being, meeting deadlines(or suffer a penalty) and making money to improve your ship or just buy and fit out a new one. Then latter on when you have researched a little and have enough crew to man weapons of shields you can ship goods into bad zones(careful of customs and their heavy fines), hunt pirates or just become a pirate yourself.
--Story--
Story mode is fun, you have a slightly psychotic robot parrot as your companion who gives you comical hints on what to do next or just randomly develops red eyes and starts screaming at you, sometimes in command code(and then apologises).
--Overall--
When I first started playing it had some bugs, but nothing that affected game play, usually just little things like a crew member doing one thing and the character tile saying they are doing another, that being said the developers at Chasing Carrots are at the top of their game and have any bugs fixed really fast.
This is a great game and did everything the other games should have done and with a better look, style and with a comical twist(like space ships being modeled after actual ships).
If you have played FTL or Space rogue and just got bored of it being the exact same thing over and over and over, give Cosmonautica a try.

So, I have pretty much no experience with MOBA's. I've never played LoL, DOTA or SMITE and apart from a basic understanding of "lanes" my knowledge of the genre is pretty limited. So when I heard that Battleborn, a MOBA/FPS game with some raid/dungeon elements, was open for testing I had to see what it was all about. My usual genres of choice are FPS / MMORPGS and Battleborn seems to take the most fun elements of both and combines them together with the fundamental nature of the MOBA.
And here we are, and what a glorious place we find ourselves in. The artistic direction of this game is brilliantly conceived. It's almost as though an Anime cartoonist and a LSD enthusiast had a brainstorming session resulting in this gloriously fun and vibrant parallel dimension. The environments, characters, planets, gameplay, AI and overall universe Gearbox have created is both genius and painstakingly consistent. The whole game feels like an epic labour of love with absolutely no room for compromise.
The story campaign, which can be played either solo or co-operatively, is most reminiscent of your typical WoW dungeon and - in some scenarios - raid! The encounters take all the best game mechanics of a top notch instanced experience and combine it with some of the most fast, furious and colourful FPS action you've ever experienced. The result is... Magical...
Then we have the true heart of Battleborn, the versus mode, where players have the choice of three different game modes: Incursion (defend base, attack enemy case) Capture (hold objectives) and Meltdown (escort friendly minions to enemy base). Each gametype is offers a different player experience, but the true magic here is in the variety of characters to choose from, and the way in which you develop them as they level up and eventually rank up.
I could go on and on about the rewarding item system, the in-game level up choices, the individuality of each character and how the game constantly screams quality, reminding me of the best aspects of all the games I love... But I won't.
All I will say is this: Don't expect an Overwatch clone - this is completely different and in the best way possible. Don't expect a typical dungeon/raid experience - Battleborn takes the best mechanical aspects of both and runs with them. Don't expect a MOBA replacement - treat this more as a compliment to the MOBA genre. Above all: Expect a beautifully crafted game, with a stunning landscape, solid characters, compelling gameplay, genius AI enounters and some of the best art direction you've ever experienced.

Beyond the hours I've logged here, I've been playing the game since it came out and I've played a lot of it through PWE's "Arc".
I bought Champions Online on launch several years ago; it was a completely different game than what it is now. It was a true-blooded cRPG, which relied on you making all the right choices when leveling and choosing your gear. You could be any kind of super-hero with any kind of power available, but at the price of truly balanced classes.
Since the game turned f2p and PWE bought it, it has changed and not for the better. Progression is linear, unless you are subscribed and have "Freeform" slots. Everyone else picks an archetype (a great deal of them require money) and the game chooses the progression of the build for you. A lot of the leveling content is boring and mindelessly repetitive. Endgame content may as well be non-existent and, as of the time of writing this, hasn't seen any significant updates in years.
But there is still value in playing and here's why: if you're here for gameplay, get out. Find something else to play, or something else to do with your time entirely. LARPing will yield better results.
But if you're here to satisfy your super-hero fantasies, come right in. Customization is insane, a lot of the costume pieces require money, but they're sensibly-priced (as long as you understand that's mainly what you'll be spending money on, in this game) and it's a fairly largely populated game, despite the lack of content.
My advice, as someone who's had problems with this game in every form it has ever been in, is this: make your hero. Customize them to your heart's content. Have a look at the store for aesthetics or even powers and services. Play as much of the leveling content as you can stomach. Join a Roleplay Supergroup. Get in character. Take your buddies to battle with you. Pretend the random gang-member NPC on that one snow-covered hill in Canada is the guy that bullied your hero when they were in high-school. Shoot the NPC with your laser-eyes. Explain your tragic origin to your fellow heroes over the bully's smoking body. Then you can safely say you "get" what this game is all about.

It's a tough call as to whether to recommend this game, because if you miss City of Heroes as much as I do, this is really your only option.
The problem is that it was taken over by Perfect World Entertainment, who is notorious for buying decent-but-struggling games and then running them into the ground. This is the case here.
No real development in years. No real new content. Very little new art. Mostly just gamble boxes and regurgitated assets on the cash shop. Every system introduced over the past few years has basically just shuffled existing content around, was launched unfinished, and then never fleshed out. And every update introduces new bugs, which are rarely fixed. Balance passes? Oh, you mean nerfs. Yeah they have those.
If you give this a shot, be prepared to feel disappointed about nearly every aspect of it. Their business model is not based on improving and enhancing the game. It's about doing as little as they can get away with, and getting as much money from you as they can before you inevitably leave in disgust.
PWE is where games with potential go to die.
For the love of god, don't blow your money on boxes (well, the RMT keys required to open them). I'd say like 9 out of every 10 costumes, auras, powers, etc. I've ever bought with real money (or even in-game grind currency), I've been disappointed with -- ranging from "mildly let down" to "it just doesn't work at all".
Every time someone gets a rare from a lockbox it gets broadcasted to everyone else. No way to turn it off. So you see the same 5-10 whales spamming dozens of rewards (like 2-3 per second, just filling your screen). The drop rate on this stuff is very low, so this means one of the following things:
1. That person bought literally thousands of dollars of boxes and is somehow opening them at a rate of about 50 per second. Or,
2. That person is being given a higher drop rate than others because they are a frequent big spender.
Open the boxes yourself and you'll find that you can easily go through 20 without getting a single rare. But these folks who just jackpotted 10 of them will now sell them on the AH for in-game money. They have so many that no one can compete with their prices. And they have so much money that they can buy out others' and flip them for more. So they basically own the economy.
Enemies have ridiculous levels of CC. If you're melee, you spend 90% of combat being knocked back, knocked down, stunned, rooted, slowed, and having your powers toggled off (sometimes all at the same time) by even the trash mobs. Then when you run back to the fight, those trash mobs get blasted 100 meters across the map by some other player, so you have to run more to catch up to them. By the time you do, they're either dead or blasting you across the map again. Hope your character's origin involved an accident with a pinball machine.
There are fights where you're up against 3 bosses at once, who all chain-spam knockbacks and stuns. You have no control over your character as it gets stunned and thrown around like a ragdoll until it dies.
If that sounds fun to you, then you're in luck. Because the devs think that's the definition of fun.
Some of the worst group experiences I can remember in over 15 years of MMOs have been in this game. From people AFK leeching in instances, to leaving their team behind to run ahead and activate a cutscene (just so they can be first, or appear in the scene), to pulling the entire map and then threat-wiping... Some of it is stupidity, some is just pathetic griefing. Whatever the case, Alerts are now the main way of leveling and they are a friggin' nightmare for the most part.
Where to even start. There are thousands of bugs, many present since launch, many more added all the time. You read the notes and see that they haven't fixed anything. Then you log in and discover a new bug that they created by messing with something that wasn't bugged. Then the next patch they
fix that bug, but that's the only thing they fixed. So after 2 patches the net amount of fixes they did is zero. That's if they didn't break anything new. Which they did.
Clicking "Report Bug" in-game just crashes the game. Reports on the forum (polite, well-written reports) are never acknowledged, and often just get silently and repeatedly deleted. I don't know how to interpret this other than "abandon all hope that we will ever fix anything, and refrain from inspiring such hope in others".
It's not that the core game loop isn't fun. It's that what little they do is always half-baked, broken, grindy, and nerfed into impotence. Never finished. Never fixed. And each iteration is more oriented to spending cash. Things that used to be achievable in-game get removed and placed behind a pay wall. Greedy to the point of hostility.
These guys are at the bottom of a long spiral to failure, and it would take a miracle to bring them back.

The problem with most 4x games is also what is cool about them.  Everything is discrete.  You build buildings that give you +2 production.  You have "10 units" of population.  There are 5 different types of planets.  Etc.   This requires you to suspend your disbelief, and understand that these are just ways to represent larger quantities of people, economic development, etc. in an easier to understand metaphor.
The developers of DW:U don't believe in metaphors.
On the one hand, this choice makes the game impenetrable at first.  I can totally understand why someone would try the game, and decide it wasn't for them.  But if you stick with it long enough to understand the glorious complexity beneath the fog, the rewards are a 4x game that is so much more realistic and thus engrossing than any other 4x game.  There are flaws, but this game deserves a look for any fan of the genre.

A lovely FMV (Full Motion Video) experience set in a humble environment and a cast of certainly eccentric characters. I really love the delivery from the actors/actresses since that's the meat of the game when interrogating them as suspects (OMG Jenks!!! xD).
Also another aspect of Contradiction that should be praised are the different levels of hints available to you for support. If you get stuck after asking everyone around and collecting any items available at a time, you can call the Police Chief who can give you subtle hints as to where your should focus your attention on to progress through the game. If all else fails, the tips or "cheats" can give you straight answers, meaning the game itself bypasses the need to leave the game and look up the internet for solutions. This means you remain in the experience but also can afford to see solutions to your current problem without spoiling yourself with accidental glances at a whole walkthrough.
The music is subtle but very appropriate to this game with an orchestral flair. Upbeat as it may be at times, I also found that most of the time there seemed to be an overarching sombre atmosphere. This made me feel sad that as fun as playing a detective solving a mystery can be, the story is still dealing with a tragedy. Props to the soundtrack.
Gameplay wise, the choice between using the keyboard or mouse only is very much appreciated. Also the inclusion of an overhead map that is accessible at all times (except when interviewing suspects) really helped to get to places quicker than slowly walking scene by scene to places.
In terms of criticisms, I really don't have any at the moment except for two small things. Without getting into any spoilers, personally the ending was a bit rushed and left a few story threads unresolved. Also there aren't any branching paths in terms of progression meaning progression is rather linear. However having delved into a little history behind the development of this game, it was a marvel that the developer managed to create such a smooth and wonderful FMV gaming experience on such a small budget. Also the way the story is set up, a follow up sequel would definitely make sense to expand upon the intriguing world and characters introduced in Contradiction.
But don't let this intimidate you as I personally felt the majority of the story isn't necessarily left on a major cliff-hanger as this game presents a rather great self contained plotline with a potential for more on the horizon.
All in all, loved playing what is essentially a choose your own adventure game wrapped in a film like presentation.
TL:DR Really fun game with a slick and simple interrogation system accompanied by hilarious characters with entertaining acting.
Great game, would love a sequel.

This kind of games don't usually appeal to me. The other day I did have a urge to simply kill some time and relax, so I bought it on a sale for 3 euros.
I wouldn't say Ryse: Son of Rome is a bad game. It definitely is an overpriced game. I'd expect much much more for 20 euros.
What you'll get, in my opinion, is a very short (you'll need around 6 hours to complete it on Centurion difficulty, which I bet is not a feat anyway), incoherent and cliche story straight from B-rated action "historical" movie and very linear and repetitive gamplay.
You'll see Brittons on elephants, Celtic/Pictish warriors with dreadlocks who use daemonic voices when speaking, kung-fu choreography, lots of uber-macho men, as this is mainly a war/revenge story, in which blood is shed and mouse buttons are torn apart...
Sometimes the story takes its turn in a completely silly way which would never ever happen in similar circumstances in real life. At times your violence is unjustified. For example, you viciously kill praetorians at the end, although you won't have time to develop any kind of antipathy, not to mention hostility, towards them. They are just there for you to perform a dozen more mouse clicks.
Gameplay is basically a click-fest. Combat system is very simple and nondemanding: use mouse buttons + a few keys and wait for an occasion to preform single/double execution + use a few skills to slow down enemies or get some health or focus (required to use skills) back. I only used two skills: health and focus through the entire game. You'll get visual hints on when to hit a mouse button while performing so called executions.
I haven't noticed any performance issues. I got stuck once in a mission, but reloading solved the problem. Otherwise the game runs all right and is quite nice for the eye, although the fact that it is on-rails limits your sightseeing possibilities.
Reassuming: if you just want to kill some time and  the game happens to be on sale, then sure, go ahead, buy it and play it, otherwise don't waste your time.

I personally enjoy this game, having played through it twice on legendary difficulty. The game is more like a movie than a game, and a decent one at that. (It does however borrow heavily from Gladiator, if you've played it, you know what i'm talking about.) The game has great graphics, it just depends on how well your system can run them. Some levels will have camera lag especially in forest levels. Even on my beastly machine, lag is present, but not a major issue, more of an annoyance. The soundtrack is decent, though not on the level of games like The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt or Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain. The Sounds in game are fitting and help with immersion,  with sounds like shields smashing and swords clanking. THE GAME IS NOT LONG! I have about 13 hours clocked into playing the campaign through twice on the hardest difficulty and I still flew through. I imagine a speedrunner could finish the game in 3 hours or maybe even less! Again it feels more like a movie. It's a good movie, but you should know that going in. Gameplay itself feels like a simplified version of the Arkham system. Press spacebar to block, if you can't block, dodge. Left mouse for sword, right for shield. Executions are fun but can get repetitive. You can also get perks for every execution you perform, although the  only one I find useful is the Health Regain perk. The others seem pointless. To make the game last longer I'd say play through on a lower difficulty first and then play on legendary on a second playthrough. (Not because the game is hard, it's really not, just to make the game last longer and to get more out of it.) If you beat it on legendary right off the bat, the game will probably lose it's value. I'll probably play thorgh once or twice more to get all the trinkets I missed in game, but after that, I'll probably be done with it. Maybe dust it off once in a great while just because it takes so little time and is more like a movie.
Overall, I'd say this game is probably around a high 6 out of 10. I could understand if you think it's lower, although I think anything higher is a little too generous. I can't reccomend this for everyone. I reccomend this to those who love Roman history or people who are looking for a hack and slash cinematic experience. If you aren't one of those however I don't think you will enjoy this one. The game is fun enough to warrent a buy, although I reccomend waiting for it to go on sale. I bought it for $7.50 and I'm happy with it for that price. To me $19.99 seems a little high. If you're reading this during a sale and are interested, I'd say go for it. If you enjoy movies like Gladiator, The Eagle, and Centurion, you'll probably like this too.

Primordia is a game about the earth after us, the stuff we leave behind: junk, devastation, and robots. The game readily explores the concept of religion in non-human sapients, which is fresh and unique in sci-fi settings where religions are regulary viewed with disdain and are associated with less advance societies. The humanist religion is based around man the builder, creator of wonders and robots. In this world humans are missing, where they went and how they went are mysteries; but our lovely robots have carried own in our absence. Our inventor protagonist, Horatio Nullbuilt, is trying to reclaim what was stolen from him in the opening scenes of the game. This puts him on path to solve his immediate problems and eventually his quest leads him to the city of Metropol where the secrets are slowing unraveling the city.
The game is not without it's humor from the banter between Crispin and Horatio, references to other famous robots, and Horatio's object commentary.
If your stuck on a puzzle try using Crispin, on an area you can't reach. The game never tells you about this before you have to figure it out.

If you like post-apocalyptic worlds without mankind, adventure games, and robots: this is probably up you alley.

Don't get me wrong.  The game has got a lot going for it.  But some times it's the little things that can really make or break.

Or you could get this game with a bundle called "Metal Gear Solid: The Definitive Experience" which includes this game and Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain and all its DLC. It's hard to talk about this game without talking about it price tag but I'll try to separate the two and babble about the price point at the end.
In short the game is a third person stealth action combat kind of a game. You play as a Snake or as he is referred later on Big Boss - the whole Metal Gear Solid time line is quite confusing but that's something for die hard to keep a track of.
The game consists of a single story mission and a number of side mission's called side ops. The side ops can be treated as a full flagged missions but with just a different objectives and a lot less story following them. They all take place on a single fairly big map. While the atmospheric conditions change and vary a lot - whether it's a day or night with rain and without it you must understand that the map does not change. Though having a sandbox kind of aspect for all missions lets you learn and appreciate it's design a lot more if after a single mission you'd leave to another area. I'm still on the fence if that's good or not. On one hand I really did enjoy playing the same map but discovering new areas and ways of approach - on the other hand the engine seems just too powerful to have a single map.
The "main game" is short. It took me around 70 minutes on the first try to finish the main mission - and that's including time spent learning what I'm allowed to do and what I'm not. You can probably finish it in half of that and that's not rushing. The additional side ops extended the time spent in game to around 8 hours which is fairly decent for such a short game - and I did not replay any of the mission on hard mode - so that's that. Though in order to unlock two bonus missions had to raplay the main one.
The story is interesting though if you're not paying attention it sometimes does not make a lot of sense. The big thing to note is that Ground Zeros is mostly free of the Metal Gear Solid strangeness. This feels like a more traditional war game rather than metal gear title which comes with quite a bit of supernatural and a few metal gears.
The game engine is a beast. It runs smooth, looks amazing and offers a lot of choices of approach and interactions. You can be stealthy, you can go gun blazing, drive a armoured vehicle - it's up to you. The number of things you can do is really high.
There are sometimes games that have extremely memorable moments. Those can be scripted but this one (and this goes for the MGS5: Phantom Pain as well) is a unscripted moment maker. During a rainy mission I climbed on top a small building and started sniping people down - no suppressor - and due to rain/storm they just couldn't work out where the shots were coming. That was so amazing seeing them just run and talk that there's a shooter somewhere but can't make out where.
The little touches like suppressors lasting only for a certain number of shots, luring enemies with clips, even the sentries calling other guards to investigate something make this game a real joy to play.
The controls are a bit finicky - I struggled between mouse/keyboard and controller. For sneaking and moving around the controller is a much more natural fit. For shooting it's pretty bad. Ended up switching between the two when things got hot. Would have liked if the keyboard controls were a bit more thought through.
Finally the price - this feels more as a DLC rather than a full title. Or even more like a demo. In my personal case that would have worked. If this was free and I'd played that - no doubt I would pre-order the Phantom Pain - full price, no questions asked. As it stands I've stayed away from both until I saw them on at least 50% sale - and the only reason I've picked up Ground Zeros is that they've been bundled. At anything more than 3$ this is definitely not worth picking up. Instead you should just buy the Phantom Pain. There is enough content for this game to not matter entirely.
So in summary. Worth a buy for cheap. Fun game but does nothing that would suggest buying this over Phantom Pain which is definitely a money well spent.

I recommend this game loosely based on the hope that they will fix the current logical problems within the game universe. Right now, there are too many convenient losses that stack against your characters in terms of battles and quests.  Literally every single smuggling quest I have taken has resulted in contraband being found by customs, even when my hacking "camouflage" is over 80%.  Just by the sheer law of probability I should have skated through undetected at least a couple of times even without hacking skill.  Additionally, when you're carrying illegal goods there is always someone who engages a spacefight, even if there are no enemy ships in the vacinity - no ships of any kind in some instances.  Then, there's the problem with the bargaining system while fighting, which allows you to call the other ship and negotiate your peaceful surrender - you give them dough, they go on their merry. However, when you're carrying illegal goods, they confiscate these even if you pay them.  The pay is implied as being given in exchange for not boarding or attacking your ship, so why or how would they know those goods are there?  This game is infuriating, half because I like it so much and half because it isn't fun to play when there is no reason to take the big risks specifically because you will ALWAYS get caught.  If this is fixed, this might become a great game, but until then I don't think I'll play anymore.

Have played a fair amount of this pre-release and post-release. There are lots of positives here but not enough currently to keep my interest. Here are a few headlines if you're on the fence:
PRO'S
Decent crossover of SIMS/Space Trader.
A reasonable amount of ships to save up for.
Lots of star systems to explore, though this isn't really encouraged as much as it could be in the story mode.
Graphics are cartoony and bright.
Missions are fairly varied.
CON'S
Lots of crashes - even after 'finished' release.
As mentioned in other reviews - economy is fairly static and doesn't always make sense. A planet that exports robots only has 10 tons at any given time? How is that an export system?
Lots of bugs - trade bugs will regularly put you into a negative balance. Mission text doesn't always reflect mission outcomes,
Combat - DULL, DULL, DULL. No speed up option, most fights end up in either a stalemate or are a simple matter of 'Charge all guns blazing'.
SIMS element is underplayed - characters don't really interact enough.
Trading is incredibly tedious - see above on static economy. So I bought a ship with 80 units of space but the market only has 4 units of what I need? And it only regenerates at 2 units per 2 days? EXCELLENT.
Autosave feature means that if something goes badly wrong (see negative cash balance bugs) then you are completely scuppered.
Some grammatical errors and generally unpolished text entries.
It's a shame - the game tries to shine in two genres but doesn't really take off in either. Hopefully this game will get more patches and content as it goes along - for now I would only pick this up if you want to grab it while its on sale and you don't mind learning the ropes of an unfinished game that has a lot of potential.

Had a few issues running this game on a HD7970 (garbled movie playback and switching screen resolution). Resolved via disabling steam overlay, then opening the config program [swconfig.exe located in \Steam\steamapps\common\swkotor] and disabling Hardware Mouse and Movies.
Another annoying glitch I had was character movement becoming non responsive in the game (happened when combat ends and normal map exploration resumes). Workaround is to switch character and use them to move around, with option two of: make a new save, load that new save file and resume play with restored character movement.
Glitch/semi-spoiler: If you don't equip your main character with the skill of using throw lightsaber or ranged force powers (dark force influence ones) the end battle will be a hard slog. Load up on grenades before hitting the Star Forge or don't feel bad about having to cheat your way out of that game design flaw.
All those annoyances aside, game was otherwise a smooth experience and lots of fun. Good mission progression and plenty of story to keep you interested right up to the (IMO underwhelming) end of the game. Maybe not as smooth today, as it was when I first played the game around time of release, but otherwise I'm happy with how it performed on current era computer hardware.
Note: I purchased this via the Star Wars Humble Bundle pack.

Easily one of the worst games of the year. Sucks on every level, SP, co-op, MP, everything about this game sucks.
EDIT:
Ok, so I've spent more time with this game, and it really sucks. Like, every single aspect of this game is just bad. I've played single player, which would be impossible for some melee characters, and is pretty impossible for Thorn, my preferred character as well. Dying through the levels wasn't fun in Borderlands, and it's just as not fun here too.
So, then co-op? Well, the 8 missions in this game are so friggin' long. I've had good teams that know what to do and the missions are still a 1/2 hour each, and that's rushing. Since it's clear that Gearbox is beating co-op/online play over your head with an anvil, like they did with Borderlands 2, they should have made 16 episodes instead of 8 and split each episode up. Even if you have a good team, it gets really boring playing through a 30-45 minute episode over and over again.
Repitition, thy name is Battleborn. Yes, this game is going to be added to Roger's Thesaurus as a synonym of repetition. 25 playable characters and only 8 episodes. Each character can level up as a character to 15 and it takes quite a bit of XP even if you're cranking out the "challenges."
The other issue is that this is a MOBA through and through. Your character goes back down to level 0 before every match/mission (this level is different than the above level and both are different than command levels, yeah, it couldn't be more complicated if they tried). So you have to level your character back up to 10 to get all the skills back.
The last issue is the MP. You better hope you win. You know how you get 750 points in Rocket League just for finishing and you can gain other points for clearing the ball or taking a shot on goal? Not here. You get diddly squat if you lose. So, if you lose you can kiss those 45 minutes you just played goodbye, they were worthless. The other issue is that the MP modes SUCK. There aren't any traditional MP modes here like team deathmatch. Instead Gearbox tried to be different and cool and come up with lame MP modes that have all kinds of annoying objectives. I just want to shoot someone in the face. Which you can do, but if the person you shot in the face completes an objective then they win and you get nothing but the disapating satisfaction of shooting someone in the face, which is quickly being overtaken by the mounting annoyance of having spent all that time in an MP match and getting nothing for it.
Except for the money wasted, this game will be forgotten fast. It has zero redeeming qualities, at all. I really can't say anything nice about it. From the stupid loot system which is way worse than Borderlands, to the crazy hoops to jump through to unlock characters, to the insane amount of time that would be required to actually get 1/2 way through everything in this game, not to mention 100%'ing it.
Luckily, this game will be forgotten in time. I'm going to delete it from my Steam account thusly. Then I'm going to go play the Forza Apex beta while I wait for DOOM to hit next Friday and be reminded of what a good FPS game is.
Gearbox, stick to Borderlands, every time you branch out, you fail: DNF, Aliens: Colonial Marines and now Battleborn.

If you enjoy the deeply detailed damage, morale, and line of sight rules and encyclopedic breadth of classic figurine-based wargames such as Warhammer but also enjoy the community, pace, and pick-up-and-play aspects of real time strategy video games you will almost definitely enjoy this game.  It is essentially a perfect mix of those two influences.
The game is so deep that I have clocked just about 100 hours of playing time now playing a single game type (destruction) and game size (10v10) almost exclusively. There are so many viable ways to combine units and utilize them in different ways that even without playing different game sizes or modes, the game always manages to feel fresh.
However, not only is the gameplay at root incredibly deep (I'm still learning new things about units after logging almost 100 hours playing the game already), but there's a lot of breadth on offer as well.  When I do tire of the (visually stunning and incredibly enjoyable) chaos of 10v10, there are plenty of other options.
In addition to 10v10, 1v1, 2v2, 3v3, and 4v4 game sizes are also available for skirmishes, each with different maps scaled for the team sizes involved. There are four dynamic campaigns playable in multiplayer as well, containing an entirely different set of maps. A new patch to be released within the next week or so will be adding the Conquest game mode to the existing list of Destruction, Economy, and Total Destruction modes.  Following soon after will be a patch introducing co-op for the campaign mode.
Single player skirmishes and campaigns are also available, however I must warn you that the AI does cheat a bit in terms of knowing where your units are located. This leads to the unfortunate behavior of the AI streaming units to attack your critical command vehicle units no matter how well they've been hidden.  Mostly for this reason I personally would not recommend the game to those who are primarily interested in single player. That said, I do know of some players who actually only play the game for the single player.  The root gameplay rules remain the same, so it's by no means a terrible experience.
Notably, the developers have a track record of releasing free DLC for the preceding entry in the Wargame series, European Escalation.  Between upcoming DLC and the other game modes that I have yet to try I expect this game will keep me interested for a long time to come.
In conclusion, don't be fooled by this game's unimaginative name. It really is an incredible value proposition at its current Steam sale price of $19.99. Go get it if you are even remotely on the fence.

It's 50% off at the time I'm writing this. For $20 you get one of the most detailed real-time strategy games to come out in years. Every single unit (and there are over 800 units to choose from) has its own specific stats making it different from every other unit in the game. There's infantry, armor, recon, artillery, anti-aircraft artillery, helicopters, fighters, fighter-bombers, stealth bombers. It's realistic to the point that you have to know which AA you have relies on radar to track targets because it makes itself visible to your opponent. Multiplayer with up to 10v10. And it isn't like a rock, paper, scissors RTS. You can have an inferior unit "on paper" and use it to destroy something four times the cost of that inferior unit, if you know how to. If multiplayer's not your thing the game features a dynamic single player campaign with a very challenging artificial intelligence (the dynamic campaign can be played against other people too). The worst thing about this game, that I can think of, is in some of the "big money" matches online people will spam, spam, spam everything. So if you choose to play in those big money matches, keep in mind what you're getting yourself into. I prefer playing on low money games so every unit has a feeling of weight to it. If you're a fan of RTS I couldn't recommend this game more.

I played very little this game and even if I have it since the first not really successfully release, since I have hundreds of other titles to try, I did not give this game a chance until now. As you can imagine having so many games my patience is also limited, so after 20 minutes of trying all graphic settings and not being able to do anything my first thought was to delete it and move to something else.
I took my time to write this for everyone like me who felt frustrated from the unresponsive unappealing first few minutes in the game but was still curious about this game.
First experience (roughly less than 20 minutes): load the game in a decent specced computer, go through a not really informative character creation screen, interesting presentation of the game and lore, graphic horrendous, 2/4 seconds of delay from selecting an action and its realization, etc. After changing all possible graphic settings noticed no improvement and I closed the game frustrated.
Second experience (roughly an hour plus another hour of browsing in Internet): I noticed many people enjoyed the game so I thought they must have managed to play it. Some suggested to read the manual, and although if it presents really well the game setting and lore, it helps very little in how to configure the game or in explaining for example the character creation (if you are familiar with RPGs the instructions don’t tell much more than you already know but still leaves doubts regarding some game-specific mechanics). I then decided to change the graphic settings before loading the game. Closed the game and restarted to ensure the settings were applied and then I could load the game and start using it properly. Most commands can be configured but using the mouse to walk can be frustrating as the character will crash on any object on his path without trying to move around it. WASD controls work better especially after I discovered I can move the camera using the right button of the mouse. Conversations are ok and my inventory stuffed up pretty soon. There are several bugs, like the map functionality first time was loaded completely black leaving me wondering, but reopening it fixes the problem and is actually pretty clear and informative.
In summary after an initial frustration I found that the game is not bug-free but playable and the settings are actually really interesting. The developers, which is trying to build a trilogy, from the little I followed them (even through the second kickstarter I did not back) seem honest and caring about their game (they could have left and abandoned the project after the heavy critics of the first game, instead they republished a new version).  It’s not an early access game (although it receives some updates and some content from the second game) and as such it should (and I feel it is) playable. If you like the genre I would recommend to consider it on sale but if you don’t have the patience to configure the game and lose a significant amount of time just to start it avoid it.
I will keep updating this review as I go through the game and I may even change my opinion, but so far I feel the lack of this kind of games and I’m willing to give this one a chance.

This is an easy recommendation. I think anybody with even an elementary interest in building and management games could get several hours of enjoyment out of this, although at time of writing I'm sitting at about 27 myself. Well worth the price of entry.
That's the TL;DR, but allow me to expand on why.
Project Highrise is essentially a game about confronting your own lack of foresight. When you want to put in that new block of apartments, you're going to have to deal with all the choices you made on lower floors, and if the lobby is 30 storeys down, it's going to be tough to fix problems unless you're willing to think outside the box.
Sometimes the progression can feel a bit odd, though. As other have pointed out some of the requirements to get certain businesses can seem a bit esoteric (we need more sports bars before we can build that accountant's office!), and with how the prestige system works you can unlock a lot of the high-end apartments by focusing exclusively on offices (and vice versa), but these aren't huge problems for me.
A few other reviews have pointed out the limited replayability. It is true that there do seem to be a few optimal setups; not in the sense that there is exactly one way to play the game, so much as sets of systems that work well together when you get them running. I don't know if that's too much of a problem. For one thing, the devs have been pushing out the odd gameplay change to help keep things interesting, and a few of the scenarios make for a fun challenge. For another thing, no game is ever infinitely replayable, and for what it cost me? I've already got my money's worth.

Wow! I did *not* expect this game to be so addictive and absolutely satisfying. A long-overdue and well-executed fast-paced, circle-strafing, old school twitch shooter feel with a lot of elements very much like Binding of Isaac (a very good thing, and I mention the likeness only to its credit.) Different starting characters/builds with different stats and starting weapons to choose from, randomized/procedurally generated rooms and floors, health/armor/gold/bomb drops off enemies, shops on each floor, tons of unique personal upgrades to buy or earn at the end of each floor, etc. With even more content to come, and co-op multiplayer on the way (dear god yes!), I haven't been this pleased with and addicted to any indie title since FTL.
Most importantly, the core controls and mechanics are an absolute joy. The pace and precision of the controls and the action feel absolutely spot-on. This is something many games destined for mediocrity have overlooked in lieu of trying to do everything else. When it comes down to it, the core mechanics, the precision and pacing of the controls of any shooter are at *least* half of what we either enjoy or can't stand about them. And more often than not, we barely even consciously realize that, if at all. Paranautical Activity absolutely nails it in terms of *exactly* how a shooter like this should feel, and it's a feel that is too rare these days. As a pure gaming experience, this one is a huge breath of fresh air. Bravo!

I have never been a big fan of real time strategy games. After trying Age of Empires, World in Conflict and Supreme Commander type games I never considered myself a great fan of having to rush building units, dashing them to the front line and then endlessly mass firing at enemies who are doing the same thing.
But this game is nothing like that!
There is real strategy involved in scouting out areas with Gazelle helicopters and Warrior scouts before sending in your MTBs and infantry. I love the way the armour and penetration are protrayed - you can see the shells bouncing off the Abrams hull armour. And then you get realistic things like infantry getting panicked under fire, but managing to be deadly against tanks that are stupid enough to wander through infantry defended villages.
This game is just so addictive, the graphics are superb especially low down - not that you have much timem to watch them, and the command GUI is really well designed. The enemy AI is very good at both defending and attacking, but even better is multiplayer - this game is completely fluid between the solo and multiplayer modes - I havent been much of a multiplayer gamer before but that could well change.
If you have ever wanted to play the Close Combat games in real time with modern units or the Total War games set in the modern day, this game is it.
