Contradiction is a engaging "experimental independent game" where the player interviews characters and uses their statements against them to uncover the mysteries surrounding a young woman's death.  It's a quick but highly engrossing game with plenty of Christie-style twists and turns that should keep any player interested from start to finish.
All game play is HD full motion video with real actors.  This is part of the "experimental" aspect of the game.  The idea is that the player is interacting with a short movie, or possibly a TV show, on a fundamental level.  While I feel like the game missed that intended mark, the FMV added charm and personality to the game that traditional CG graphics wouldn't have achieved.  The acting is on-point.  The characters are stocky but effective.  The writing results in several genuinely heartfelt, menacing, and terrifying moments that make unlocking scenes and finding the next clue exhilarating.  The story is linear--there is one murderer with one motive--and while this doesn't bother me, I would be interested in seeing any future installments playing with a "choose your own adventure" theme.
Mechanically, Contradiction is a simple point-and-click adventure.  You use your mouse (or the arrows on your keyboard) to move around the map, choose clues from a list, and find contradictions.  It doesn't bring anything new to the genre, except for maybe the cut scenes, and it does fall into a lot of the same issues that other traditional adventure games are prone to.  My playthrough involved a lot of walking back and forth between locations whenever I got stuck, easily adding on another hour to an hour and a half to my play time.  There were also a few extended cut scenes that definitely felt like they were intended to be part of a longer interview section, but were gutted to meet the developers' very strict budget.
I can't say that Contradiction is a difficult game.  The contradictions themselves, with an exception here and there, were easy enough to find.  Rather, Contradiction runs the risk of being frustrating.  There is a lot of evidence, a lot of characters, and a lot of dead ends and red herrings to sort through in order to get to the end of the game.  The game keeps track of everything each character has said, but it's on the player to remember what six different characters said about upwards of two dozen pieces of evidence.  Increasing potential frustration is the fact that contradictory statements have to come from the same character to count.  The player can't use what character A said against character B until character B slips up.  And then characters A through F say the exact same thing about a piece of evidence, which doesn't get you anywhere.
And while I found the ending of the story to be satisfying and clever in hindsight, I thought that the last piece of evidence was a little disappointing, if only because it was maybe too obvious, especially after all of the running around we did.
Overall, I would give Contradiction a 9/10.  The developers have done a lot with a simple concept by focusing on what makes the game unique.  By keeping it a relatively short game--5-7 hours tops--Contradiction stands out as an excellent Friday night game to share with friends.  Like any good story, there's room for speculation and growth.  Even if we never return to Edenton, Baggy Cat has succeeded in a lasting and endlessly enjoyable classic mystery.

I got this game on sale a while back, finally got around to playing it.  It is based off one of the Sniper Elite games.  I played the original Sniper Elite about 10 years ago, and don't remember it well enough to compare to it.  I know I wasn't a fan then, and I gave it to a friend who enjoyed it immensely.
I played through the entire game and enjoyed doing it.  I can't tell a difference in the characters skills with the sniper rifle.  The weapons do have differences.
You choose a scoped sniper rifle, machine gun/shotgun, sidearm, and some form of explosive to start.  All the other weapons are available in the levels as youn play, in addition to some others which you can't choose to start with.
Rifles - Some are semiautomatic and have larger magazine capacities while others are bolt action.  The semi-auto/large magazine rifles seem to have less power than the slower bolt action rifles.  I wasn't able to tell a major difference between the scopes.  You can carry 100 rounds of ammunition for your sniper rifle.
Machine Guns / Shotgun - The machine guns are reasonable accurate, and have varying strength as reflected by the amount of ammuntion carried.  The Russian machine gun carries a lot of ammunition, and you will use it.  The shotgun carries very few rounds, and takes a lng time to reload.  It is good for some enemies, and tedious for others.
Sidearms - 3 automatic pistols and a revolver.  The revolver takes longest to reload, but can be reloaded before all 6 shots have been fired and takes correspondingly less time.  The revolver is also the strongest and effective for one-shot kills.
Explosives - Grenades, mines, tripwires, and bundles of dynamite you must shoot or explode.  I don't like using them unless I have to, and there are times when their capabilities shine.  Used correctly, they can get you easy multiple kills.
Other weapons - The ammunition for the rocket launcher and the double barreled shotgun is fairly rare.  The double barrel gun is very unrealistic, and blows crowds of zombies apart.  It's great if you are being swarmed and would rather cheat than die.  The rocket launcher is pretty standard.  Flies straight, goes boom.
The game play - There is a lot of demonic/satanic imagery in this game.  You are fighting through hordes of undead Nazis.  Most of them are slow moving, but they attack in hordes and can only reliably be put down by being exploded or shot through the head.  If you drop one with body shots, he may get back up and attack while you are sniping other zombies.  The kill cam can be excessive at times.  When you are sniping for dear life when a mob of zombies is creeping up on you, the kill-cam can distract you from counting bullets between reloads.
If you reload immediately after a scoped shot, you reload and return immediately to your scoped view.  Not the best situation, as it is more natural to look around after reloads to make sure a zombie you shot in half isn't creeping up on you.
There are some faster zombies, armored zombies, really strong zombies, and zombies that bob their heads on floppy undead necks around as they zombie-walk toward you.  Sometimes it is hard to put a bullet through those bugger's brains.  A very good shot will go through the eye-slit on the armored zombies, but it is more likely that you will have to shoot their faceplate off the get a brain shot.
Overall, I think this is a fun sniper game.  There is usually enough ammunition that you don't have to go close range very often.

Did you ever play the original  Sim Tower?   If so, that might make you a bit of a fossil like me, but you can rejoice in that Project Highrise is a VERY worthy successor - perhaps THE successor we've been waiting for.  The premise is the same: remain profitable while building bigger and better rooms in a tower-shaped space (both above and below ground).  This is not a game about designing nice architecture, but a strategy game of balancing the best number of rooms with services and accessibility to keep your tenants paying rent, the building maintained, and the elevators fast!  The primary objective is simple: make money.  In Sim Tower, this same goal limited the scope and scale of the game (you basically built until you'd built everything and made money) and Project Highrise is no different in sandbox mode.  There are also scenarios you can play which increases the variety of gameplay.  Basically, the developers have taken the concept and expanded it in every way possible to give the game more longevity than its predecessor, but in essence, this is one of those games where you will likely have most fun building, then scrapping your game to start over (rinse and repeat
...).
New to this neglected genre of building management are more granular levels to micro-manage: business types to accommodate (not just 'offices') and who won't thank you for being placed among too many competitors, the need to incorporate often-expensive building and business services that each occupant requires - as well as all the primary utilities, there are money-winning goals to aim for (in the guise of contracts) and a decent level of micro-management for anyone who likes to tweak individual tenant rents, sift through statistical reports and such.  The developers have made a great job in recreating the Sim Tower experience in 21st century clothing with the kind of management and strategy we expect in games today.
While this game sits largely in the 'casual' game genre, expect to lose quite a few hours to it.  Recommended for all tycoon fans!  A must-buy to fellow aging Sim Tower fans!

I've played Project Highrise for about 9 hours and I really have to say that I'm a bit disappointed. I absolutely love SimTower and YootTower and thought that Project Highrise will somewhat connect and to these two games and further improve. But sadly it's not a good successor.
First, let me tell you, the graphics are awesome, I love the style and artwort. There is so much detail in every room and the variety of rooms is astounding. What lacks is a variety in single rooms. If you place an apartment it will always come with this orange wallpaper, all of the same furnitures and it won't change at all. Same goes for the offices but here it is not that crucial.
There are offices and apartments in all kind of sizes and grades. A lot of restaurants that provide different kind of meals for different times like breakfast, lunch, small snacks, coffee etc. Many of the tenants need different meals throughout the day so you need to have everything available. The offices and apartments also need services like a copy room, post offices, warehouses, laundrys, daycares and a lot more. The "better" the room the more services it needs. I think these dependencies are a great addon and add more variety than YootTower or SimTower. It is fun to care about your tenants with different services and keep everyone happy. But there also is a downside. If a office needs 6 different services, you are totally fine with only satisfying two or three of those needs. Sure, the tenants won't be that happy but it doesn't matter - they pay the rent and keep on living.
That leads me to another point which is the level of difficulty. From the beginning I started with the hardest difficulty. There are small changes in the economy and prices to pay to build rooms but other than that there are no changes at all. The first 1-3 hours are hard and you really need to think twice about your budged. But, and that's the biggest let down, if you manage to get cash flow in you really don't need to care about other things at all. You just fast forward and can't lose anymore. There is nothing that is influencing your income or the economy. You basically can activate fast forward, minimize the game and wait until you got enough money to build another 5 floors to fill with more rooms, fast forward and repeat. The only one that can make it difficult for you is yourself. If you're building a bit cautious you won't lose and fly thorugh the game in an instant.
There are some contracts and objectives you can complete. A contract most of the time gives you some money upfront. On completion you get another amount of cash. Most of the time you need to build more rooms or get more tenants. There is nothing bad with this so far BUT: There is no downside or penalty by not completing the contracts. You can leave them (max. 2) open as long as you play after you accept them. There is no timer that says you need to accomplish the contract in a period of time.
Another try to bring in some difficulty are the electricity and water cabinets. Every room you build needs one or more of basic requieremtns: electricity, water, phone, cable TV or gas. In order to satisfy these needs you have to build cabinets on every floor and build every line one tile after another. This is basically a great idea but right now it is annoying as hell to build every line where you need it, a quick "build to this point" or another kind of building-style would've been better.
The game highly lacks of immersion. One thing I absolutely adore from YootTower was the immersion it build up while you play. The sounds, the graphics and the tenants, everything was fitting. In Project Highrise the building is always bright as day, all the lights are turned on at night, the only thing that changes is that Background which slowly fades but that's it. If the tenants are working or living they are static in their room. There is no real animation that show what they're doing. In YootTower there were literally 2-3 frames of people doing stuff, it's not that much but it immersed you to an unbelievably amount. Also the lack of sounds is really depressing. If you turn off the music and play the game you literally can't hear a thing. There is this background-loop of a city going on and on for eternity (it also won't change at night or days, it is always the same). If you zoom in really really far you can hear some sounds from the rooms but they are so decent that if you zoom out a little bit to a normal state you won't be able to hear anything. You can't hear elevators, visitors, tenants, rooms or the workers doing their job. It is a big, depressing and really quiet building. The best example is YootTower: At night the whole tower was dark, no lights were on (only the apartments where people lived but when they went to sleep they also turned down the lights), there was this silly "caw caw" raven sounds in the morning, I can't describe it but this little sound reminded you of a new day and that the tower will go alive in some minutes. You could also hear the tenants work and live, you could hear people talking and chatting which went louder the more people visited your tower. The more elevators you had the more elevator sounds you could hear. These may be very small things but the immersion they build up is incredible. There is sadly nothing in Project Highrise that reminded me of this cozyness that let me feel that my tower is alive.
All in all I can't recommend Project Highrise right now. If you're into challenging simulation or managing games that hook you for many days, wait or look for something else. You will see everything that project highrise has to offer in about 5 hours and there is almost no replayability.

Primordia is a Chandler-esque point and click adventure set in a dystopian wasteland. It does fantastically with art, voice acting and plotting but falls a little short with design and original story. Still it is a fantastic game worth your time.
Wadjet has the production quality down.  While the visuals are still pixel-art, the quality and detail rich world are superb. Visual design is reminiscent of Mad Max, the world is a dystopian nomadic future. However, the color palette does leave you wanting as the game is entirely brown and gray.  This is understandable due to the setting being a post-apocalyptic world, but it makes places feel smaller and objects in the scene indistinguishable from one another.  That said the world is actually full of characters. NPCs move freely about with their own purpose, unrelated to the story but framing the world.
Game design is closer to standard point and click than Wadjet’s previous Blackwell series.  You find objects, rub two of them together and get a new object. But there are a few problems.  Pixel hunting in this game is abundant.  I had to refer to a guide multiple times only to find out there was some inconspicuous spot on screen that was clickable. This is not just a failing of the art but a failing of design. If something is vital for game progression it should be noticeable inside the massively detailed visuals. With the abundances of clickable spots and NPCs that do nothing it is easy for little things to get lost in the details. There are also some awkward quizzes that kind of pop up out of nowhere, but they are mainly for achievements. But despite that there are some interesting choices.  You have multiple solutions to problems. Some are just for variety, but others actually affect the possible endings in the game. With that in mind, choice matter, so save often.
The first part of the story plays out like a dystopian techno-fantasy, but once the setting changes to the city the style changes somewhat sharply.  The second part of the story resembles Raymond Chandler novel.  A gruff character minding his own business gets pulled into a conspiracy that only he can sort out. Also there is a dame and a bunch noir-esque characters. Overall, the themes are nothing new, you can see similar from Planet of the Apes, Mad Max, or Wall-E. Despite the un-originality of the plot, it is well written. The main character Horatio Nullbuilt has a few interesting parallels to the Shakespearian Horatio, but this time playing the lead and foil to man.  The multiple endings are quite varied.  The Characters ultimate choice for his sense of justice is entirely up to the player.
Primordia suffers a bit from pixel hunting but overall is a fantastic game. It has great visuals, great voice acting and an interesting story where choices matter.

A very fun experience. The actor playing Jenks kept the entire story light and fun despite the dark connotations of the events. He might have gone a bit too far with silly faces from time to time but honestly it was refreshing and entertaining given nonstop wicked overtones.
Pros
The acting is well done for such a small budget, Jenks is straight up wacky in some scenes and calm and reflective in others. I cant imagine he takes his job too seriously. Its a shame because I feel like there are some specific scenes where acting more like a professional and being more concerned for his personal safety would add to the character rather then feel disjointed.
The musical score was very involved as well, gave a nonstop air of foreboding that really helped to set the mood and atmosphere of the game. It also sounded like the major plot points and reveals happened to often coincide with heavy piano notes being played. Could be my imagination but I think that it was done intentionally.
Cons
The interface was a bit jarring at first until you got used to it, various topics would highlight as green while others stayed blue but this didnt actually translate to any hints or topics you should try to converse next. It felt random and led to lots of extra time spent re-exploring topics that werent needed to find contradictions that didnt exist
You will find dozens of things that people say that are contradictory by definition that dont lead to cutscenes, this can be  frustrating over time as you feel that you caught a person in their lies but the payoff never results of actually discussing it with them. Likely this was an error of budget contraints or logical omissions in the games story and script. Either way I would highly encourage the developement team to either include cutscenes for each of these in future games, or more carefully write the dialog so that we dont spend half the game pouring over linking contradictions that aren't intended by the developer.

Lovers in a Dangerous Spacetime is the mouthful of a title given to developer Asteroid Base's inaugural game. I actually got to preview this at PAX Prime earlier this year and it was one of the most popular titles in the indie area and with good reason. Lovers is a cooperative space exploration game where two players must cooperate to man various stations on a spaceship to navigate through space and rescue little space critters. In order to complete a level, a certain number of little space critters has to be rescued for the exit to be unlocked but if you and your partner are feeling like completionists, you can collect all of the critters in each stage to get access to different model ships and unlock other powerups faster. The locations of the critters and the entire world as a whole are totally differently systematically generated on each run, giving every playthrough a fresh feel. Once you find a critter, usually some small challenge has to be completed before you can rescue them. For example, you may have to fight several waves of enemies, escape an explosion or fight a mini boss.
There are various stations to man on each ship including weapons, shields, engines and a powerful yamato cannon weapon. There are several campaigns that are made up of 4 levels and a final boss fight. Each level offers upgrade crystals that you can install in your systems that will persist throughout the campaign. Deciding which crystals to place in which systems is initially a fun experimental learning process, but I've found once you know what the crystal combinations do, you usually fall into a pattern of upgrading that results in a familiar ship layout each time. But there are also several ship layouts to unlock in the game, each with their own stats and quirky gameplay rules. For instance, there's one unlockable ship that constantly rotates around while you play, making locating and controlling your character within the ship quite a challenge, but as a tradeoff, the ship is also immune to terrain damage. I'm a sucker for these kinds of unlockable gameplay variations and this game reminded me a bit of my favorite FTL from the space exploration and battles right down to the unlockable ships. Obviously the gameplay is nowhere close to the same, but there are similarities to be drawn between the two roguelike space exploration games
There are only two crew members, making coordination and teamwork a key to success in this game. Communication with your partner is necessary and coming up with a good strategy is vital so that you and your teammate aren't running to the same stations to man the same systems. Once you get that strategy established and you and your partner know how to run the ship like seasoned space travelers, it's a really neat feeling. But it's also just as fun to yell and scream at your partner when things are going horribly wrong and your ship is about to explode
Lovers in a Dangerous Spacetime offers the best experiences for couch co-op play. It's conceptually simple to learn and easy to pick up and play. But there's still a decent amount of strategy, skill and depth to be found here as well, and applying these strategies skill and depth of understanding of the game is especially necessary in the later levels where the difficulty gets ratcheted up quite a bit. I really enjoyed this game; it's one of the best couch cooperative experiences I've had. If you and a friend are looking for something to play, you can't go wrong with Lovers in a Dangerous Spacetime

To really enjoy this game you have to approach it the right way. If you're looking for an insanely complicated game of space chess then you should look elsewhere, because the pawns don't always do as they're told. But if you want to play the role of an evil galactic emperor (or a pathetically benevolent administrator, however you want to look at it) whose minions will occasionally be bumbling and headstrong (or, sometimes choose to exercise their right to free will), then it's just par for the course... simply execute them (or pat them on the head and give them a medal) and move on.
Yes, it can be extremely frustrating to find the cuddly space monkeys carelessly cavorting among my insectoid stormtroopers when I have given *explicit* instructions that they are to be enslaved to work in the iridium mines, but if crushing the galaxy beneath an iron boot was easy then everyone would be doing it.
The galaxy is relatively interesting, and as it evolves it begins to feel like a real, living place, which makes it so much more satisfying to crush it like an insect.
The automation is functional and somewhat customizable, but not perfect. Sometimes an evil overlord must handle things personally rather than leaving it up to bumbling minions. That's just one of the realities of life that we must deal with if we are to to spread sweet, sweet evil throughout the universe.
I have found that on the largest maps in the mid to late game, the game lags to the point of being unplayable (on a mid-range laptop). There is just too much going on. I am attempting to alleviate this problem by researching the technology needed to create and control Silvermists and use them to annhilate all life that is not within my empire, but have so far been unsuccessful. If you look out your window and see your neighbor's house being consumed by gray goo, you will know that my efforts have borne fruit.
Now if you will excuse me, there is a band of space pirates that have outlived their usefulness.

Distant Worlds borrows many concepts from other space based 4X games, but does none of them particularly well. However, the epic scale makes up for it. Distant Worlds truely makes you feel like you are steering a massive interstellar empire towards it's destiny, whether it's conquering the galaxy, or simply staying relevant while the story of the galaxy unfolds.
Pros
-Epic scale, can play a game with thousands of star systems
-Good ship design that is uncomplicated yet makes it easy to see the results of your design choices
-TONS of game customization, you can play in pretty much any manner you choose. For example, you can start as a backwards pre-warp civilization that is barely beginning to explore their own nearby planets, or an already established galactic superpower, or somewhere in between.
-Victory conditions that are unique to each civilization.
-Decent AI to manage aspects of your empire so you can focus your attention on the things you enjoy the most. Or you can control it all.
Cons
-Economy is somewhat obfuscated and hands-off. Not recommended if you enjoy closely managing the financial details of your empire. (Arguably not a con, but for me it is).
-Somewhat clunky interface
-Diplomacy lacks some of the transparency needed to make informed decisions, AI can be somewhat arbritary at times.
Overall if you are a fan of 4x games this is definitely worth playing.

To date, this is my favorite 4x space strategy game on the market. Yes, it beats out even the classic MOO2 in my own opinion. Don't let my Steam record fool you, I've been playing this game for years well before it became available as complete package on Steam. If you are looking for an in-depth empire simulator, this is it. The scale of the game is what really draws you in. Watching your empire grow from a pre-warp civilization on a single planet to something spanning across hundreds of star systems is very enjoyable and immersive. The pausable realtime nature of the gameplay adds a little bit of pressure that makes you feel like you need to be on the edge of your seat when playing, rather than being a more laid back style of play common in most turn-based 4x games.
Don't get me wrong, the game has some draw backs. It certainly isn't the best looking game on the market nor does it have what I would call an easy learning curve. But the graphics work just fine for me and there are some great guides available on the Matrix forums for newbies. After first I felt both overwhelmed and a little bored at the same time when I first played Distant Worlds years ago. I felt like too much was going on and the automation was taking the fun out of things. But, once I learned how to start a game from scratch with the automation turned off, the game just took off for me and became a huge time shink in a good way. The additions over the years of things like end-game giant threats, characters that level up, and so on have only increased the value of this great title. So if you're looking for an in-depth space 4x empire building simulator, this is the game for you.

I've branched out from major titles on Steam just a few times, with less than stellar results. But I definitely don't regret giving Project Highrise a chance. If you're into tycoon/expansion games, this will definitely fit your interests. It's not exceedingly difficult or overly complex, but the optional goals and the ranking up of unit types keep the game interesting and let's you immerse yourself in the balancing act of constructing a profitable yet balanced building.
The main challenge stems from trying to keep all your tenants happy. Some want more restaurants, but most tenants can't bear the smell. The higher the rent and size of the unit, the more elite services they demand, which drives up your daily budget and can get out of hand if you're not supplementing housing with profitable offices and vice-versa. Lastly, it's asthetically pleasing and has a consistent design that unites each of the elements.
I definitely recomment this game for anyone looking for a casual tycoon experience, or those who just want to bulild up fun towers and manage populations.

I'm quite new to the pc gaming department so please bare with me:
This game is beyond fun. It's one of those games that doesn't take itself too seriously but at the same time you must be serious when playing if you want to actually beat the levels (Referring to the story missions). Wih that being said, this game is heavily focused on playing as a team. Maybe i'm wrong and they are quiet or i have some setting not active, but not many people use mics when playing. Of course there is the option to type out stuff but unless you are super quick and can get it in here and there, you wont be able to type out to your teammates in the heat of things.
Now again, none of this is negative against the game, it is just what i've noticed thus far. This game is ridiculously fun and by all means do not play this game if you are prone to seizures lol. (But seriously, lots of flashes and colors galore). Can't wait to unlock all the characters and give them a try. From what i see, all the characters are pretty unique in their own sense, but they are all similar as well. While they all have different powers, lots tend to have this one melee or special attack power while the other is a "Damage in this specific area" type power. The 10 step upgrade tree though is what makes them extremely unique and also fun to constantly go back with the same character multiple times to see if a different set up works for you. You can basically level up 10 times per match and with each level up you choose power up A or B which both do their own unique ability.
While i agree with ign that the enemies just seem to be more so just enemies that charge and shoot and no real AI to them, idk if i would want them to be that smart lol. With as many enemies as they throw at you at once and their difficulty ranging from 2 hits to kill to 10-20+, i dont want them to try and dodge and flank me. Maybe its different on hardcore, i've yet to try it, but i assume it just means they will simply do more damage.
So in summary, just buy the game if you enjoy super fast paced shooter games. I would recommend coming into this with a set group of friend that are also wanting to buy and play it, because you need a very focused team to get through some of these levels, but you might get lucky in matchmaking (As long as im not on your team xD). Easy controls to learn, great graphics, very fluid, and servers seem to not lag or cause any problems (Though i havent played at peak times such as at night and on weekends yet). Hope this gives you some sort of insight to the game. I highly recommend this game for a fun game with friends and just a good time, just dont come looking for something easy or some great story. You'll be a bit disappointed.

First came The Sims, then Sims Medieval, and now it's...SIMS IN SPACE!
Or at least that's what you'll instantly think when you start this game.
It's a relaxing, casual space-faring game of trading, building skills, taking care of the needs of your crew and optional combat missions.
You don't need to fight at all if you don't want to, but as of the time of this review, the Easy Combat mission, which constantly gets offered at various stations is a veritable quick and easy ATM machine to print money for ships and upgrades.
Looking past that one flaw...or feature, depending on how you look at it...the game will easily fill the occassional itch of armchair space captains who just want to wander space completely on their own terms and play style. It has both a storymode and sandbox mode, and all of the ports of call have missions to undertake if you feel so inclined. If not, then just fill you holds with cigarettes and beer and head out.
Has a multitude of solar systems to discover, quite a few ship layouts in three basic styles; trader, cruise ship, or warship and many room types and upgrades.
All in all, a fun, relaxing, casual space-faring romp for those players who just want to play the way they personally enjoy, and really, what can be better than that?

~Performance will gradually decrease until the game crashes after about 2 hours. Fortunately, in only takes about 10 seconds to re-start, and you'll always come back to a fresh auto-save.
~Travelling is a huge time-sink, and you'll be travelling every few minutes. Encouraging the player to get up and walk away from the computer every 3 minutes is a pretty substantial design flaw.

Primordia is probably my 11th personal favorite of all time, if only on style alone. Buy this game.

Watching a good Science fiction movie was always a rare experience to have, even more so an original one....
Playing a good and original Science fiction game....that's even less probable, it feels like finding a very special treasure.
Good words have been around for Primordia since it came out in 2012 (I'm now playing it for the first time in 2017) and i can say it's all pretty much justified.
The game has a good story, with interesting characters, both main and secondary ones. It has an interesting beginning, a well handled middle and an ending ( and a pretty good one at that, although that depends on which ending you get).
Besides been good or bad, it's always satisfying to see that the creator of the game has put as much dedication to the ending(s) of the game as the beginning. The game has a good flow all around and it (almost) never comes down. It's 97% good, which is a rare thing in itself.
The game has a late 1990s graphic adventure style, although it is from 2012. You can either take it or leave it. I know that's not the reason why i was interested in playing this game, and i'm really not nostalgic at all for playing a game like that.
That being said, there is a certain time for "getting used to" the low res graphics and full screen style, but once you are past that and well into the game, it is a very interesting story, you will forget about everything else.
And that's only because the story is good, the voice acting is also good, the script is well written and feels right and compelling. And the design of the game is as much original and though out as the script, you really feel like looking, if not at least reading a visual novel of the future.
Humans have disappeared from the earth. All that survives are machines built by machines from the past, the Primordium. And you are a loner, a robot living in the dunes outside the city in a broken ship that you are fixing, hoping one day,  it will fly away... but all those dreams are put on hold when suddenly one day your ship is sabotaged and the power core stolen from it. You face a slow death until your energy drains out, so you are forced to go out of your comfort zone and into the big city Metropol, in search of your missing link.
It really feels like it could work for any good movie or even a AAA game. The music also fits very nice within the game.
The puzzles are very original, as the story and for the most part are very fun when you find the solution. There are one or two exceptions, especially one certain  game of words....which at least in my case, needed and external reference to be completed, and of course that's not good at all when you have to, go looking for a clue outside the game, that's a total killer, but besides that all the rest of the puzzles are very good.
The pace of the game is very fluid, and the inclusion of a hint system built into your sidekick works very organically without ruining the game experience and the satisfaction of figuring out most of the things by yourself.
The story has even time to be not only serious, and funny, but also a little philosophical , posing real science fiction questions about time , technology and the future of human society.

Short difficult games.
In Twixel, you control two cubes on two screens: one with the left and right arrows keys on the keyboard and the other with the a and d keys. No options to bind the keys to different buttons, if that is your preference.
As shown in the video, you have to dodge obstacles. The obstacles can appear the same on both screens for a while (dodge left or right at the same time on both screens), then the left and right obstacles can be inverted (dodge right on one screen and dodge left on the other screen).
The games are challenging and my left hand is learning to do things I never thought it could. It's strange, but I like it!

Gosh, I wish I was ambidextrous, the things I could do. My work, my fun time, my sex life, all of it would be great. What’s that I hear you say?! No! Ambidextrous is not Dexter driving an ambulance in a killing spree! It is when you equally use your left and right hands. Where the hell was your devious mind?
Like me, if you want to sharpen your Homer-ish mind (the yellow guy, not the greek philosopher) and your Ninja-less reflexes, then lets take a look at Twixel.
Story
There is none, make it up as you go. Live with it.
Game Play
Game play is so simple yet fun. You control two boxes that must traverse a downwards scrolling maze. Sounds so simple it should be a breeze….. guess what princess, it’s not.
You control the left box with your left hand on the A & D keys and the right box with the right hand on left and right arrow keys. You slide the boxes left and right simultaneously, avoiding obstacles as they come down. You can hit the sides walls to you hearts content but hit an obstacle and you might as well throw both your hands in the air and scream “Rimmer is a Smeg-head!”
You must navigate these mazes as long as you can because if you can last for 60 seconds or more, you get to unlock more fiendishly hard levels. If not, then take heed of these words of wisdom from Master Yoda “Do or Do not, there is no Frys….. with Burger of mine, Yes!”
The are 6 levels (or styles) to choose. Pixel, Vector and Polygon with Hyper Pixel/Vector/Polygon being unlock when you last past 60 seconds, and if you last 60 seconds in all of those, you unlock the Twixel (if you can, then your an ambidextrous Super-Sayan or a bloody Vulcan!)
Everything Else
There is no mouse support (it would be nice) so navigation through the game and option is via left and right arrow keys and space bar. You have the option of 2D and 3D graphic and music volume. Music is annoying so turn it off and go with some Def Leppard on this one. Graphics is just simple box style so nothing to get excited over, but it is clean with no unwanted pixeling.
So if your training to throw daggers with both hands, or double wield MG42’s then Twixel by Caesoose Studios is your goto training app, if not, then you better find something else to do with your two hands.

Ryse: Son of Rome looks stunning, but is let down by linear repetitive gameplay and the constant intrusion of cut scenes that didn't end up telling much of a story. The consolation the game offers is that it's short (~6hrs) so that it doesn't get even more repetitive.
The core game mechanic is the beat-em-up that Batman Arkham Asylum did so well. Ryse's addition to the genre was to break free of the combat to perform executions - something that broke the original mechanic while adding little to the game. If it wasn't a way to regain health or collect extra experience, it would be more a hinderance than a feature. The extra gameplay mechanics like advancing a legion or picking off archers with spears never really integrated into the game. Gameplay never really felt organic, which is something other beat-em-up games do much better.
One final thing to note is the story, because a lot of effort went into rendering the tale. This could have been where the game could have set itself apart by being like a graphic novel. But the story was mediocre, and the amount of time taken to tell the story kept breaking the already fractured gameplay up even further.
With a bit more variation in enemies, a more streamlined (and less intrusive) story, and a few tweaks to the core gameplay, Ryse could have been much better. As it stands, it's a gorgeous mess that pales in contrast to the other games in the genre.

Crytek games for some reason have always had the reputation of just being flashy tech demos to show off the graphical capabilities of any given system. Which is weird because all of their games have solid gameplay to back up the gorgeous graphics.
I'm also guilty in upholding this stereotype, because in my mind Ryse was just a flashy qte game which sole purpose was to render the most realistic roman centurions to sell as much Xbones as possible. While in reality the game is a bit more than that.
Nowadays the highlight of Ryse definitely is it's gameplay. The combat system is hevily inspired by the combat from the Arkham games(minus the gadgets, witch sort of limits the variety of the combat) with a slight twist - once an enemy has suffered enough damage you get to execute him with a special animation. All of this on paper seams like it could get repetitive and boring really fast, but the executions are varied enough and the game is on the short side(about 5h) so you don't really get enough time to get bored.
When it comes to graphics there isn't much to say. It's a Crytek game. It's gorgeous. There are more polygons that real life and every single one of them is beautifully animated.
Oh! And there is also a story. So there's that.
In summary. If it's on sale, and you are in the mood for something with high-rez textures and some meaty combat, go for it.

A very good murder mystery with a spot-the-liar mechanic.
So this game is exactly what you expect from it, you're gradually advancing dialogs by spotting two arguments that contradict each other. That's really the meat of the game. Basically if you enjoy murder mysteries and instead of getting the solution served on a platter as the non-interactive-movies do, you want to be the detective who spots the contradiction, this is the game for you. If you don't there's nothing here for you.
Question is, is it good?
The short answer to that is yes.
The story is excellent. It's interesting and at every part you know what's going on, there's no real plotholes or things that seem too far fetched.
The acting is just lovable. It's serious, but it got charme and actually that charme keeps you playing. You just want to see the next line of dialoge. You want to see inspector Jenks asking "what do you know about this?". You want to see the response from the the villains. This could easily become a boring experience with the wrong actors, luckily they are just perfect, with Rupert Booth (Jenks) and Paul Darrow (Paul) easily the best. Everything also is also very fitting, the scenery, the directing, the edeting. Everything that is film in this game is just very good.
Are the riddles good? - Yes they are. Without any more spoilers all the dialog riddles are good. It's enjoyable.
So are there any downsides? Certainly there are
Character have a habit of conveniently dropping stuff on the floor - to the point of it beeing so ridicoulous, it's almost a running gag, seriously, if a character drops one item accidentally, it's believable, if it's rougly 10 items... it's a bit less believable.
The items are used to unlock sites and further conversation, These little item riddles are more for the immersion and the feeling of doing investigation outside the dialogs, but are real no-brainers. It's all very conveniently placed and the feeling of accomplishment isn't there in those moments, the meat is really in the dialog, not the item-riddles.
The interface isn't the best either, but the game can get away with it and my biggest complaint. The interface tends to bug out. Sometimes you can't click on stuff, have to go to the menu and come back. Really guys, in a game with such minimalistic gameplay, you can still do bugs?
Also there are several contradictions in the game, which you can't spot or can only spot later. There's a guy drinking whiskey and claiming there's no alcohol around. One guy claims to have known the victim, yet claims she was blonde, when the was in fact brunette and a couple more of these and most infamously, the last contradiction, which I won't give away at this point.
All in all the pros largly outweigh the cons for this game. Yes there is stuff I expect to be made better in a hopefully comming sequel, but nothing that diminishes the experience of this game. It's a niché game and if you aren't into this, it's certainly not for you, but it's one of these projects where the lacking budget had to be compensated with even more passion for the project and it shows. I had about 10 hours of fun out of this 10 bucks game. I was uncertain about the purchase at first, because it looks like a game that really easily could have failed at so many points. Luckily it didn't and has been one of the best games of the year for me this far.

I play video games pretty much exclusively on the PC, so I had no hands-on experience with 'Metal Gear Solid' gameplay mechanics and deep knowledge about the backstory. Although 'Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes' expects you to know the story so far, you do not need to know 'MGS' lore to enjoy it. All you really need to know to enjoy 'Ground Zeroes' is that the playable character, Snake, has a very particular set of skills that he has acquired over a very long career, and the said skills make a nightmare for people who cross him. :)
Fans of stealth action video games will definitely enjoy 'Ground Zeroes' for the gameplay. The setting of the game, Camp Omega, is a "sandbox" in which you can explore and exploit its terrain to complete your mission objectives. Throw in different weather conditions, variations to the time of the day, mission restrictions, and some of the best enemy AI in video games to date, the same setting can present new challenges each time you play.
As you may have read elsewhere, the main campaign in 'Ground Zeroes' is very short. As a (very) cautious stealth action gamer, I tend to take my time with my objectives. Having said that, in my first 2 in-game hours, I managed to complete the main campaign in about 90 minutes, and I spent the remainder 30 minutes calibrating game settings, reading the background story, and watching cutscenes and end credits.
However, side-ops are unlocked after completing the main campaign, and they present new mission objectives for you to complete. These side-ops are actually quite fun and are worth trying. Despite my endorsement for this game, I recommend paying no more than $10 for it because not everyone will find completing side missions worthwhile, especially if you are not sure whether or not you will end up liking 'MGS' games. Paying $20 for 'Ground Zeroes' may be worth it if you are already a fan of the 'MGS' series, tend to take on side missions for a challenge, or are a game completionist.
Technically, 'Ground Zeroes' is quite an achievement and is something to behold. At the highest graphical settings, it features some of the best rendering of weather effects. The cutscenes match actual gameplay very seamlessly, providing a cinematic gaming experience. The smart enemy AI is both predictable and unpredictable when it should be, which keeps you on your toes without thoroughly frustrating you. The level, while small, was designed in such a way to allow for non-linear progression and exploration. That is welcoming considering all missions are set in Camp Omega, and you will be spending a good amount of time there.
Game designer Hideo Kojima's attention to details is evident, even in this short game. The subtlety in character movements, placement of characters in the cutscenes, scene framing, as well as level and sound designs were well thought out. Say what you will about the convoluted plot, Kojima makes sure most, if not every, elements he puts in 'Ground Zeroes' serve a good purpose to the game.
Still, 'Ground Zeroes' is hardly perfect. The game is definitely not optimized for keyboard and mouse control, and instructions could have been explained more clearly. I did not know that I could get into a prone position until I held the "C" key for too long accidentally. Some nuances about the game, such as guards waking up from a knock-out, time for which the tranquilizer wears off, and sound suppressor wearing down, were learned through trial and error.
Fans of 'Splinter Cell' games will find it hard not to compare them to ‘MGS’, particularly between 'Splinter Cell: Blacklist' (2013) and ‘Ground Zeroes’ (2014). These two are different games, but both are fantastic. I say play both; no need to pick sides because there is no reason to! If you enjoy the stealth gameplay in ‘Splinter Cell’ games, you will very likely enjoy 'Ground Zeroes', too.

This is my first review for a Steam product. I thought I'd join the litany of positive remarks for the game.
It's exceptionally complicated, but even the learning process is enjoyable. If you take the time to learn how the game works, you can navigate its manyfold layers to create a deep and compelling narrative for your game that plays out like a story and whose gameplay becomes very rewarding.
A little anecdote from my first game:
I had started in preward era as humans. We could barely travel beyond our home planet, and when we could, only using convential thrust engines - limiting how far and fast we could go.
A few technologies in, I build a space port. It was a great achievement for the entire Human Race. We were entering the space age.
I build the revolutionary Surveyor Mrk I - a formidable little ship that would travel the solar system in search of life and answers. And what it found was pirates. Lots of pirates!
As it is exploring, I'm thoroughly extorted by 3 pirate factions, squeezing me for all my Earf (my planet's name) dollars. As a pacifist by inclination (read: lack of fighting ships), I oblige with a smile.
In the mean time, I continue to expand. Earf being a moon of a gas giant, I build a construction ship to build a mining facility on the behemoth.
Simultaneously, I discover an abandoned, broken down ship orbiting another planet in my solar system. Far enough make me think if it's worth trying to recover and risk whatever ship I'd need to send to recover it.
Human curiosity won, and, after a quick Google Search on how to claim an abandoned ship, sent my construction ship to rebuild it in hopes of... I didn't even know what! Perhaps I'd get a new technology, perhaps a new ship, perhaps a some cool new scrap metals, or (probably) a new alien infection that will turn off even the most accepting of spouses back home.
I send my slow construction ship to repair the abandoned hunk of junk from Earf.
Earf's endeavours were not profitable yet, and the pirates were gouging me, quickly going into deficit. It wouldn't be long before my funds would not be able to sustain placating these barbarous space thugs.
Sure enough, in time deficit turns into debt, and I am forced to cancel treatise with the pirates, raising the ire of the Space Maurauder clan especially.
They attack my fledgling space race, now boasting a spaceport, some science facilities, and a few freighters going back and forth to the mining stations. They open fire on all of my facilities and space ships, like pirate do. I was about to quit the game and start again.
Earf's space days were almost over when, suddenly in the distance, lo and behold! The ship had been recovered and manned by my crew and turned out to be a destroyer of epic size and power; a veritable warship beyond human understanding.
Slowly, the lumbering titan made its way back to Earf, and to my great surprise, devistated the entire pirate fleet of several ships with such a show of might and firepower that none could escape its wrath.
The ship became a staple of homeworld defence from then on, and after several hours of gameplay still had not gone obsolete. No pirate squeezed a cent out of Earflings anymore, though they tried several times to overpower my fleet of one... to their demise time and again!
By the end of that session, I had three planets and was a middling power in the universe and wasn't bothered by a pirate (on my home planet) again.
10/10 would turn wreckage into pirate killer.

I LOVE THIS GAME.
I loved Civ V, and coming to this game was like a breath of fresh air.
The mechanics are fantastic, the lore is brilliant, the combat/heroes/armies/technologies/etc. are impeccable. This game is what happens when Civ V evolves into something much, much sexier.
I can't say much more without repeating myself so, here's my entire review in a few words:
If Civ V was a sexy beast.
I give Endless Legend a 10/10.

TL;DR
Pros:
+Fantasy/Scifi theme
+Beatiful art style
+Unique races
+Quest system
+Workshop/DLC content
+Tech "Tree"/"Wheel"
Cons:
-Combat (I usually just auto-skip cuz it's boring and confusing and takes forever)
-Tons of micromanaging resources within cities near endgame (more of a personal problem though xD)
This is by far one of my favorite games! I'm a big fan of 4x. It's very similar to Civ with a fantasy/scifi theme and a few different mechanics, which is good since it'd be kind of boring if it was exactly the same as Civ.
I love how they have a continuity between all of the Endless games (Endless Legend, Space, and dungeon). It gives it much more depth. Each race is unique and there are lots of customizations, especially with workshop mods. (I've even made a couple maps myself- though kind of difficult). It has lots of replayability with each race having a unique game style accomodating to different victory conditions. There also is a pretty immersive quest system belonging to each race which I find adds even more depth to each playthrough, which I don't believe Civ has. I also really like the simplicity of the tech "trees" (they're more like wheels, and you can even count earlier techs towards advancing to a new era) and the hero/unit customization. But I've never figured out combat and feel like I don't need to, and  the battles feel like they take forever. I just put guys on aggressive and hit auto because it's too hard for me to figure out and I end up messing up my armies when they can just win on auto.
But all in all, 9/10.

I hate the point & click genre, but I decided to give Primordia a shot because the story seemed interesting. After playing through Primordia I can say that I still hate the point & click genre, but... Primordia was wonderful. For about half of the game I played on my own due to it being simple enough
, but after that I desperately needed a walkthrough. You're probably questioning why I would look for a walkthrough after getting so far, or actually using a walkthrough in general, and my answer is because Primordia gave me a feeling of determination, of wanting to complete the game and find out more about what's going on. The story keeps you on the edge of your seat making you desire more info, how to solve things and figure out what the outcome will be. While I did not fully enjoy the OST, I can say that it was fitting for the atmosphere of the game, and finally, the characters were well done and not boring/stale personality wise. If you're thinking of buying Primordia, treat it as a visual novel and it'll be worth your time.

You have to admit this game is beautiful, but at the end of the day, that's all there is to it. For a hack and slash game this is tremendously unsatisfying to play. The game is short, which the gameplay itself is made even shorter because half of the time is unskippable cutscenes. And then there's only a handful of different enemy type to kill so once you learn their moves, it because a chore to kill them and move on to the next area.
The boss aren't any better, if anything, they get more and more tedious towards the end. Several bosses get the so-called "second (or even third) life bar", that in itself isn't a big problem, but it is completely pointless if the refreshed boss still have exactly the same moves. So while the first 45 min of the game is somewhat fun as you slash your way through beautiful sceneries, it quickly falls into the monotony of click-click-click-space bar-shift combos to fight the same enemies over and over again with very little variety. The game tries to add some interesting element in the form of a hybrid type QTE system for some beautiful killing system. But this quickly gets tiring as after the first 10 min as you are seeing similar sequence over and over again. Not only that, entering this QTE system unnecessarily drags the game out longer, making this that much more tedious to play.
The level up systems feels overly ineffective as well. As you gain experience, you can spend your points on various QTE skills or to make your character stronger/resilient. But besides the health increase, the rest of the skills feels almost pointless as you will hardly feels any change for your character or make it stronger. It's still the same click-click-click on the same moves to kill the enemy.
Then there's the AI. While I understand this is a hack and slash game. It feels totally immersion breaking in a war situation where you're fighting a horde of enemies while your soldiers just stare at you forming a circle. And as I said before, the enemies aren't that smart either as the AI relies on the same move sets per enemy type and also an almost cheating ability to deflect your attacks if it fits certain move type (i.e. certain enemy will always able to deflect or dodge certain attack 100% of the time unless you pull a different move on them). This doesn't make the game fun at all because then it all comes down to memorizing the correct moves for each enemy.
Then there's the story, it is a hybrid of Roman history based on the uprising of Boudica, but that is the extent of its historical accuracy. The storyline relies on a few unexplained mysticism to cover up a lot of unexplained events or to just conveniently to move the plot along. But once you finished the game, you quickly realize this story made absolutley no sense at all, especially the ending.
I can't recommend this game if you like hack and slash because it's short, repetitive and ultimately just feels like a drag to play rather than drawing you in. The game doesn't make you feel you're in the warzone as the big Roman hero, but rather you just want to move on quickly to the next level and end the game.

I decided to buy the game after seeing the first two episodes of Jesse Cox & Dodger's playthrough of it, and it's an interesting game if perhaps leaving a lot of decision making out of the equation at times (such as non-interactive cutscenes that could have been timed puzzles/QTEs) and you can't accuse/arrest the wrong person, which I add only for completion as that may or may not be important to you as a player.
I appreciate the HD video, but at times not the acting which can range from being (unintentionally?) comical (especially the player character Inspector Jenks, who also perhaps got his dress sense cues from McCloud rather than Morse, which I find to be diverting) and then the acting being ineffectua throughl to playing the scenes straight. The story is okay, but could have been solved almost immediately with the all-important clue being blatantly obvious and yet the option to compare and contrast the statements given yielded no results.  Not until the final in-game hour anyway.
Then there are the elements of a paranormal/horror plot, which sadly was only touched upon and could have made this much more of a game. More than likely the budget constraints put paid to developing that plot, but at least there were little touches in the form of short scenes informing the player of potential events (one I recall being optional, that being the scene in the Reading Room where you're told to go away because "we're about to start a session").
As it stands, I achieved a 96% completion rate by the end of the game. This says to me that there is a way to solve another murder mystery that crops up, but there isn't any warning box/prompt before selecting the option that ends the game.
You cannot fail to get the murderer of the student that Inspector Jenks is investigating the death of, which for me makes the whole experience feel more like a guided tour that you unlock pieces of if you compare the right choices, but that's it. If Contradiction had much more of a budget? Then we could have had a potential Tex Murphy-esque game to play, but right now I can only recommend this to those who don't want to wait for the aforementioned (or any other) Let's Play to be completed or as a party game given that £6.99 is a fair enough price and I got some enjoyment out of it with about 9 hours of play.
All said and done though, there is potential here and I would like to see the developer take another stab at making a detective adventure game.
ADDITIONAL: This, as per the game's Steam store page, is perhaps best played with two or more people as opposed to solo like I did. In that case, I'd say it would play out like a Cluedo-esque murder mystery evening. Approaching Contradiction in this manner would, in my view, override any qualms about the acting and improve the experience overall.

I had high hopes for this game but unfortunately, despite a shiny exterior, it left me frustrated and bored.  I'll start with the bad and then skip to the good stuff:
1. I quickly tired of circling around and around and around and around asking a handful of characters one or two questions at a time.  I appreciate that the makers *tried* to make it less repetitive by letting us skip around on the map but it was still a couple steps each time - e.g. to get from Simon's to Atlas, you could skip all the way across the map, but then you had to click to get into the grounds, click to get into the entryway, click to get into the next room (forget what it's called), then click to get into Ryan's office.  Every time you wanted to visit.  It just got VERY boring going James-Rebecca-Simon/Emma-Ryan-Ryan-Simon/Emma-Rebecca/James, with the occasional search the woods & call the chief thrown in for, uh... variety?
2. Semi-related to the above, one's pace in the game felt extremely restricted.  I couldn't decide I wanted to ask about "such and such", I had to wait for the game to let me.  I couldn't decide "I want to go further this way", I had to wait for the game to let me.  What was really frustrating was when I looked up the solution and a major clue - as I see someone else in another negative review has already mentioned - shows up almost immediately, and you *can't ask about it*.  I mean it's so bloody obvious that I wasted a lot of time in the beginning trying to *find* a way to ask about it because it seemed impossible that an actual inspector wouldn't take one look at that clue and say "... hey, waitaminute."  I eventually gave up, but throughout the game I felt like the questioning method functioned the way it did just to slow you down and increase the gametime (e.g. you have to find something *one* character has contradicted themselves on, you can't say "hang on, so and so said this about you and that contradicts what you said" - again, what kind of lousy, lousy detective would you have to be...?), and that, well, kind of reinforces that feeling.
Things I did love:
1. The live video idea is a lot of fun and I admired it even as I grew more and more bored with the actual story.  I would like to see this done again, just with a less repetitive, restrictive game behind it.  I especially like the guy playing Jenks (he's very clearly enjoying the hell out of himself) but of all the characters I saw, they were all doing a good job at the acting - which you can't always depend on in smaller games.
2. I really love the system where you can ask for hints or outright 'cheats' without any real punishment (except a 'count' of cheats if you use those).  I've always felt that story-based games might as well let people who aren't as good of players enjoy the game by giving them a helping hand - it's a lot less intrusive to the story to be able to click on a quick 'hint' icon and get a nudge in the right direction than to alt-tab out, go search for a walkthrough, try and find the point you need without spoiling yourself for the rest of the game, alt-tab back in and continue.
3. Despite my complaint above, I do like *some* of how questioning was set up - i.e. you had a list of things you wanted to ask about, it let you know if you'd already asked them and kept a record of their responses, and you could review people's responses by person or by item.  At its heart, that's a nice design.

Star Wars, the RPG...  That's basically what this game is.  I'm not going to do a lengthy review on this game simply because of how old it is.  That said, I will tell you one thing, it's got a pretty big bug (but solvable).
THE MENU BUG!
So, you get in game and suddenly realize that you can't do anything on the main menu.  Hell, you can't even exit the game without killing it via the task manager.  So what do you do?  Well, there are a few different solutions.
1.  When you launch the game, rapidly click the mouse button to skip all intro videos before they play.
2.  Go to the KotOR folder and rename files leclogo.bik, legal.bik, and biologo.bik  (the intro videos)
For some reason, if the intro videos play it will bug the main menu.  If you prevent them from playing then the game will operate normally.  Doesn't affect everyone, but it does affect enough people that's it's considered a big problem.
So, do I recommend this game?  Yea, because the storyline is pretty good and even better if you play #2 right after it.

Overview: This game's okay but has some issues.
Story: The story takes place a few hundred years before the actual series and is a stand alone story. It does have references to the movies, and I still recommend you know about the actual movies before playing this. But, I digress this is still something someone knew to the series can get into. I liked the story overall, but it's not as good as many people say. But, there's a great plot twist towards the end. You might see it coming if you look into the clues well enough, but it's very note-worthy still. Another thing to know is that the characters are a weak thing in this story; if you've seen any of the Star Wars films you'll know these character types. While they mostly do their jobs, there're only a few I actually care about.
Presentation: The game shows its age, but I can say that the game looks great for a game of its year. Which is something I'm proud to say aout this game. The character models look good, but a lot of the enemies don't have much variety. You'll meet one group of enemies on a planet that are different from the other planets, but look the same overall. Still the game looks nice and the Force moves have a nice and satisfying flare to them.
Audio: The audio is something I can say holds up magnificentally. It has great voice acting and the sound effects work well for the most part. But there is a limit to how many beeps I can get from using a medpac before I feel like muting the game and diving off the Eiffel Tower. But the audio's good and keeps the grand scale of music from the movies.
Gameplay: Now this game pretty much setted up the gameplay for the Dragon Age series, and some of the Mass Effect series also. The game consists of you walking around and just getting missions and then soon going off to venture for something. (Don't want to give away any bit of the story.) It's pretty much like any RPG go to the city for jobs, supplies and more. After that, the combat's interesting; it pauses and then you clcik for commands. Now this is something you'll have to know, the game is turn based. Yes, turn based. It might not seem that way, but it is. Enemies and your characters stop mid-combat to let the other attack. Then you get to attack. This is okay seeing as how the combat progresses very quickly so this is forgiveable. And if it goes too quick there's a button for pausing the combat so you can qeue up your character's actions. Please know that you can only give commands to one character; otherwise if you try and set up a grand attack. You'll be horribly upset when your characters don't coordinate into what you want. This is a problem, but hey, what can ya do?
Bug(s): Now I ran into a bug in the game where I couldn't load up one of my saves and had to load up another save prior to that one to access the save I wanted. This is a problem that really bugged me.
Rating: 7/10 The game has terrible characters outside of a few good ones, the combat is a little strange. There's an awful bug for saves and sometimes the gaem just drags on and on.

Game has potential, but currently it's not worth it. It is nearly impossible to survive in this game for a few reasons.
First being that there is no solid crowd control in place for Tank classes. Currently it has a feature that requires to strike an enemy to get their attention and that's not a gaurantee either. This causes squishy characters to die over and over. The game needs a solid AOE taunt power with no recharge time so that the aggro can be placed on the tank until the fight is over.  This way the squishy DPS guys can do what they are designed to--deal damage. Same goes for support characters. In a room full of bad guys, the tank needs to be able to pull aggro off of his teammates and onto him at any given time during combat--currently there is nothing solid like this in the game.
Second, to make things even more difficult, you need to pay for healing patches. So not only it's difficult to survive, but also you have to pay in order to have healing patches. You can hardly call someone a hero when they nearly die killing two or three non-elite bad guys.
Bottom line, if you play this game, be prepared to spend more time dying than actually playing.

Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic is a third person rpg set 4000 years before the events of the first movie. It starts off with you being able to customize your character to be either male of female and choosing your class. Afterwards you get into the actual game as your ship is immediately being attacked and boarded by the Sith. You are quickly overwhelmed and crash land on the starting planet. The planets and environments are one of the best features to the game. They are all very unique and offer lots of room to explore. You can converse with most alien species since your character speaks nearly every language under the Republic's domain. Some speak in their native tongues and you understand via subtitles but man do they talk slow. It could take upwards to 20 seconds for every sentence as they grumble and grunt their language at you which made me very glad there is an option to skip sentences with the click of the mouse. It's usually worth talking to them as they explain their culture, problems and feelings on the war between the Republic and the Sith.
Your companions on the other hand are some of the most annoying and broody bunch of support characters I've ever seen. Don't get me wrong a few are actually really cool but it would be nice to kick most of them out of your base. You can take up to two of them with you on missions and you can equip and dress them however you like. They will sometimes trade quips or add their opinions into a conversation which helps flesh them out more. An alignment system is in place where you can either focus on the light side by doing good deeds or the dark side by evil ones. It's not just a superficial system, being on the light sides makes casting dark side powers a lot more difficult for you to cast. You can also be neutral but it is pretty hard to maintain. Which makes for a lot of interesting circumstances on whether you want to help someone due to being dangerously close to steering toward the light side which has nowhere near the strength of the dark side powers. We don't start of as a jedi and don't have these powers at the start of the game but it is something to keep in mind.
Gameplay consists of auto-attacking and clicking on abilities to either damage or heal. There is an option to pause time and set commands to each of the party members which lets you use plan your battles far easier than trying in real time. At times your character will just freeze up and not do anything while enemies get free shots in. Happens rarely but is infuriating when it happens in a brutal fight. A glitch that happens a lot more occasionally is being unable to move after a battle. It fixes itself after 30 seconds of not doing anything but with the amount of battles in this becomes a real problem. Activating Vsync fixes this problem for some people. You can use a shield a limited amount of times, throw grenades, lay land mines and use force powers which makes for a lot of variety. Never gets old seeing a  Jedi get fed up with fighting a group of enemies and just throws a grenade.  Melee combat is pretty cool as well, they have a preset fighting animations where they kick, dodge and slash at each other. You have no control over it but it definitely adds more action to the fights. Ranged has a single animation where you dodge some blaster rounds but starting off your aim is so bad that it would make a StormTrooper blush.
Outside of combat you can explore, disarm landmines and pick locks considering you have the skill to do so. You can gamble in some kind of modified version of BlackJack but you need to collect the cards of the deck yourself. You can also join Swoop races that play like your modern day runner. There are also turret sections on occasion where you can defend your ship from an attack fleet. On top of all that there are a ton of side quests and having done nothing but what I was required to I still got 31 hours out of the game so as you can see it is a very lengthy game. Most of the time you will be in dialogue with another character and given multiple ways to answer or deal with dilemmas. Unfortunately the voice acting ranges from mediocre to terrible and considering the amount of talking you do it may be a bit of a turn off to some. That is the only thing wrong with the sound side of things. The music has a mix of original Star Wars music and some newly composed music that all sound excellent. The sound of blasters, electrocuting people and lightsaber fights all sound great as well.
Story is kind of dull. It starts off promising but quickly devolves into a treasure hunt for maps.  Occasionally you will get a cut-scene of the villain sending some useless goons to hunt you to remind the player he even exists. The story really picks up near the end of the game though. You'll mostly be interested in the politics of each planet and the troubles they are going through like trying to stay neutral in the war, slavery and criminals controlling everything. Your choices have some pretty big impacts like medicine costing much more credits (money) to everyone, yourself included. It is definitely the type of game you play for the adventure instead of the grand overall plot.  Graphics are obviously dated with character models looking very ancient but the environments themselves look decent.  The menus are awful. You can pick up as much stuff as you want without limits but everything in the inventory is seemingly placed at random,without ways to quickly reach a category of weapon or to sell junk it really becomes a chore. You will have to change weapons since some are much more efficient against certain types of enemies and would have been made so much less frustrating by a decent menu.
It is a good game don't get me wrong but it is not the greatest rpg ever that some people claim it to be. I had quite a bit of fun with it and will immediately play the sequel after this review. I am not a Star Wars fan though so that may be a fact to take into consideration.  Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic is a fun game dragged down by some technical and  user interface issues but still manages to be a game worth considering if you are into the genre.It's also nice to see a Star Wars game not including Obi Wan or Luke like most games and you can tell they put a lot of effort into weaving their own identity into the Star Wars universe. It still holds up against the rpgs of today and shouldn't be dismissed due to it's age.
