Many years after Champions Online was released and I am now going to write this review. First off, I was a player of City of Heroes before this, so I have a pretty good idea of what games to hold this game's standards to. I have at least 4 max-level characters and over 1000+ hours of gametime, so I know a few things about this game.
First off, I have nothing but love for Cryptic/PWE. That being said, I'm going to offer some talking points.
Why I play/played it: Champions Online is THE MOST customizable superhero MMORPG available, hands-down. THE MOST. That means  even over DC Universe Online. There are literally almost a 1000+ costume parts you can build your Champion with. This can be a hindrance for some people, as sometimes the options can overwhelm them. Which brings me to my second point. You can play anything from a Drow Elf to a Vampire, to a furred neko or even a sexy robot.
Freeform vs. Archetype vs. Subscription: Subscription offers way too much to be listed here, it offers things like  unlimited Freeform Character creation, chroma-colored powers that can be colored any color you choose, etc.
Freeform  character slots are purchased from the store for Silver accounts. They offer the same customization as  Subscrition minus the power-coloring.
Archetypes are pre-determined power-choosing paths that are based on classic heroes and villains. Your mileage may vary, some power choices horned into the archetypes are inferior to what you COULD be putting into your build with Freeform.
EDIT, 06/27/2017 - The Archetype system has not aged well and does NOT give you alot of options to start with if you're a brand-new player with no money. PWE had a program that allowed players to test-drive archetypes  for a limited time, then rotated them every two weeks. Why can't they go back to that? My friends don't want to have to wait for a sale everytime they want to make a brand new freeform character, because frankly, the starting archetype options are sorely lacking. I had to buy a few archetypes before I  was able to remake some of my Level 40 Gold characters as Silver, sans the fancy bells and whistles that made them great.
However this game has some caveats.
1. This review is wirtten in 2015. By now City of Heroes has closed down and DC Universe Online is out. Champions Online went free-to-play to compete with other F2P games and the concept has not worked as well as say, Star Trek Online. Alot of the more interesting character components have been cordoned off to people willing to pay Zen, so what you're left with is alot of "basic" Archetypes and costume pieces that can make some basic heroes. HOWEVER There are STILL alot of costume piece choices.
2. The game has not aged well. With the release of Star Trek Online (not a superhero MMO but one of Cryptic's newer games) and DC Universe Online, Champions feels kind of clunky. The graphics, while bright and vibrant, feel inferior to DCUO and STO. The gameplay  feels that way too, mostly because of sporadic latency/syncing issues with the servers.
3. People who unsubscribe may find their characters unavailable to play as Gold Account characters because they must be converted into Silver, meaning they lose their Freeform powers. Buying a Freeform Slot does not fix this, as Cryptic has not programmed the game to make the Freeform Slots retroactive, specifically to existing Gold Account characters. Imagine not being able to play the characters you want because you want to keep their powers as-is!
4.  The game lacks a postgame. Some games have a semblance of a postgame (RIFT has you doing raids, DC Universe Online has you doing dungeons for gear).
EDIT: A new endgame area has been added, but I have not seen it yet.
5. The character creator can be frustrating to people who don't like lots of options or are confused by them.
6. The tutorial area is confusing, I've had many of my friends say. They're unsure of what to do next or where to go, even with a blue arrow telling them where to go. As of this writing, The tutorial area is hidden inside a holodeck simulation, which is now even MORE confusing story-wise.
7. The characters aren't really all that noteworthy. While I could argue that a City of Heroes 2.0 would be in order,  Champions is the result of when a MMO's licensing is cut and they need a fast replacement.
HOWEVER. Let's bring this full circle. Some of the things I can commend Cryptic on:
1. Frequent updates. This shows PWE still cares about the game. However, I wish they would add more free content to experience.
2. Great settings.
3. Wide range of power choices (even when restricted to one powerset).
4. The ability to play my own music from Winamp/iTunes while I slam evil.
5. The story was pretty decent, as limited as it was. Also this game has Easter Eggs abound.
6. The Nemesis system. No other game has it. (DCUO doesn't need it, they have a Villain faction).
So yes, this game has its flaws. But there's alot of good in it too, and worth giving a play for 20 levels or so to see how you like it,  if you like superhero stuff.
The community is a hodgepodge melting pot of furries, comic book fans, artists, and roleplayers.

If you're into WoW or RIFT or D&D, I would avoid it. This game isn't serious enough for your needs.

[Edit: Warning! Recent Windows updates have totally screwed up access to the 3rd and 4th game controller! While this is still a great game with two people, it is even more fun when Windows doesn't break everything...]
Don't let its syrupy sweet exterior fool you: This is a fierce couch-cooperative bullet storm shooter that will drag even the most dubious gamer into its orbit.
The overall design is excellent.  There's a tutorial level that is almost a little bit too long and slow, but effectively gives you the basics.  Once you're fully kitted out, the world is yours to explore, and the game doesn't explain anything to you any longer.  What's neat is that it *doesn't have to*.  The game mechanics are easily discoverable and are almost always a delightful surprise instead of an annoying interruption.
The graphics are bright and attractive.  The music is perfect.  The controls are the perfect mix of smooth and frustrating.
The weapons are nicely balanced so that they never really feel overpowered, never get difficult to use, but still can reward players for their skill.
Now the bad, because there IS bad, I'm afraid:  The game is probably easiest to play with gamepads.  However, in the version shipping when I wrote this, there's some terrible defaults configured, and dual gamepads won't work right.  Gamepad + Keyboard won't work right.  In general, nothing's going to work right with two players right out of the box.  But, if you know that, and are prepared to remap all the controls manually, your patience will be rewarded.
Oh, by the way: The game does have a single-player mode... but you shouldn't really bother with it.  This game should really only be played with two of you side by side.  If you don't have two game pads, and don't have ... uh ... any friends ... then you could skip this game.  Otherwise, you should have this game!

Aesthetically weak and uninspired, unoptimized, stagnant, feature-starved. These are just a few descriptors that I feel accurately represent the state of Supraball.
When buying a new game, I am often curious as to what creative energy went into bringing it to fruition. Supraball is a downgrade from the original mod in terms of art direction. This being the case primarily because Deathball used UT2K4 assets. Deathball had hundreds of user-created maps, a plethora of player models, replays, pausing, and in-game ready system, a more sophisticated kickoff system, better in-game stat tracking, and more gameplay variety. A UT2K4 mod, that had been in development for two years, had far more going on for it feature-wise than a standalone game that has, according to the dev team, been “in the works” for four years. Being a programmer, I understand the challenges behind creating something like this. However, the dev team chose to price the game at $20. Rocket League also costs $20. Rocket League is far ahead of Supraball in almost every area one could think of, and the dev team has invited this comparison via their pricing decision.
Gameplay-wise, Supraball is nearly the perfect type of game for me. That I cannot recommend it to most gamers should be a red flag. If you put in the time, a high-level game of Supraball can be more interesting and enjoyable than perhaps any other game I’ve played. It’s that you have to look past the poor art direction, underdeveloped visuals, missing features, nonsensical rank and lobby system, and the very steep learning curve (assuming you want to play in the higher-level games, which is where Supraball becomes far more interesting). In the hands of the right dev team, this type of game could be very successful, as you’ve seen with something like Rocket League. The Rocket League dev team listens to their community, has been a lot of creative energy into their game, and seems to generally “get it”. I cannot say the same for Supraball’s dev team. If you’re looking for something similar to Rocket League in concept, that gives you more control over what’s going on, and has, in my opinion, superior overall gameplay, buy Supraball. Just know that there are several glaring things that you must overlook, and I don’t feel that the vast majority of players are willing to or should have to. If you’re buying this game based on an expectation that it will continue to evolve, don’t. If the game were priced under $10 USD, I feel it would be easier for me to recommend. At $20… No.

The puzzles aren't extremely difficult, but they're not easy neither; and what it's more important: the puzzles are logical and based in mathematical problems, which gives to the game a deeper sense of immersion.

Finally, the dialogs, the jokes and the OST are immersive and well designed, allowing the player understand what's happening in depth, but in a good fragmented order (which makes you feel curious during the whole adventure).
For these reasons, I highly recommend this game in its full price.

Contradiction was a really interesting game. It definitely had that old school point and click vibe going on, but mostly I was reminded of Phoenix Wright. The investigation segments, and of course the interviews were a lot like cross examining a witness, listening to their statements and presenting them with evidence to the contrary. Inspector Jenks is a clever guy. Everyone settles into their role well, giving the game a good feel.
The soundtrack was good. It was never too invasive, and during some of the interview segments it really served to puncutate statements well. Visually, it's all live action. Some people might gripe that later on in the game as it gets close to midnight, it's really not as dark as it should be outside, but I would argue that what they chose to do for those times is better because you can actually see what's going on, something that I imagine would have been much harder had they filmed at night.
I'd like to see this game get a sequel. There's just so much more to touch on with Atlas, and the Rands. I hope it gets the funding it needs.

Contradiction is essentially a FMV (Full-Motion Video) crime novel with point&click elements. I'm not gonna lie, at first I expected a disaster because the premise reminded me a lot of the FMV fad in the 80's and 90's, where you could get these "interactive movies" that had little prompts pop up on the screen sometimes and you could use the remote to choose what will happen. Haven't heard about those? No wonder, the fad never really caught on, and for good reason: IT WAS HORRIBLE. The story was almost always stupid as hell, the acting was atrocious and the production value usually rivaled a ground school drama play. But it wasn't always just movies, FMV was mixed into video games at the time, which made it even worse. The corny acting and pixelated, low-res video was jarring against the blocky 2D (or faux-3D) graphics of the era. In short, technology just wasn't there yet. Fast-forward 20 years, and we get Contradiction. I'll be honest, I didn't expect much, but the premise of seeing an FMV disaster after so many years just made me itch for nostalgia. It was surprisingly cheap, so I bought it for sh!ts and giggles. Turns out, I was wrong on so many levels.
Apparently, technology advanced far enough to make FMV a pretty damn viable form of storytelling. Contradiction looks very good! High definition video, pretty locations with nice sets and I really liked the little cutscenes of transitioning between shots/scenes. Most of the locations have different views depending on where we arrive from, it's a nice little touch that adds a lot to the immersion I think. The technical aspect is also nice, really good editing, shot composition and angles, it's all unexpectedly high quality work for a pretty low-budget production. But, not matter how pretty the window-dressing is, what makes or breaks a medium like this, is the acting and the story.
The acting is...okay. Which in itself is far better than any FMV thing I've seen back in the day. The actors' performances range from "pretty good" to "don't quit your dayjob". I really liked Paul, Emma and Rebecca was okay, the rest of the cast is kinda forgettable. Except for one guy, Inspector Jenks, who was pretty much a disaster. This is particularly bad, since he is the protagonist, and we have to watch him all the time! His performance is truly cringe-worthy, the guy dreadfully overacts every single line, so he comes off more like a circus clown instead of a police inspector. It really grates on you, it's nails-on-chalkboard level at some parts, so the game becomes more of an endurance test instead of a detective story. (I would criticize Ryan's performance too, but since that character was designed to be a pompous, annoying jerk, I can only say: mission friggin accomplished!)
As for the story: it's better than I expected. It has a few twists and turns, but nothing spectacular. There is more mystery and intensity in an episode of Murder She Wrote, but Contradiction essentially being an amateur garage project, you can't really expect Sherlock-level storytelling, can you? It starts out really strong and keeps the interest up with new reveals and builds momentum constantly, but...there is one huge problem: the ending. I won't spoil anything, but this was without doubt one of the worst, flimsiest endings I've seen in a long while. The story was doing a great job of building up to a potentially grand finale, and at the very end it just goes and throws all that away in favor of a shoddy cop-out. I don't get it, if it's supposed to be sequel-bait or something like that, but it really overshadowed the whole experience for me...
For gameplay, well, there isn't much to tell. It's a sort of "point&click for dummies". The game mainly consists of interrogating people around town about facts or things you've found, and finding contradictions in their answers (hence the title). At first, it's pretty straightforward, but as the story unfolds, your list of clues and answers grows exponentially, to the point you'll be strained to sift through everything when looking for contradictions. Some of them are quite hard to get, so sometimes it devolves into flat out guesswork or the good 'ol "rub everything on everything until something works" method puzzle solving. Thankfully, the game is pretty generous about handing out tips, and there is even a cheat system, when activated, it outright tells you what you should do next...you know, in case you wanna rob yourself of actually playing the game.
Despite all the criticism I leveled at Contradiction, it was truly a nice surprise. It's an FMV video game that DOESN'T SUCK, in fact, it's pretty decent for what it is. It's surprisingly cheap and has plenty of content. It's an enjoyable detective story with a few good twists, and if you can excuse the tedious endgame and the terrible finale, it's a really nice experience! I'll be getting the sequel, if there's ever gonna be one. I really recommend this game if you wanna try something unique, or if you wanna finally wash off that awful taste those old and horrible FMV games left you with all those years ago :)

I was very impressed with this game. If you like mystery TV shows or movies, you will absolutely love this game.
I usually have problems with adventure point-and-click games, I want to like them, but after an hour I usually just stop caring about the story, I end up skipping over all the dialog, I get frustrated with the pointless inventory puzzles, and next thing you know I give up and delete the game. Contradiction didn't have any of these problems and is one of the only adventure games I have ever completely finished. The story was captivating. By using real actors (only two of which had talent, but the rest were decent enough) and very high-quality video, the game made the story feel real and compelling. Inventory puzzles are downplayed (almost non-existent) and are replaced instead by dialog puzzles. Basically, to win the game, you need to interview the towns people, carefully listen to and understand everything that everyone is saying. By cross-interwiewing multiple people, contradictions in their stories emerge and by identifying these contradictions, you unlock new clues, new suspects, and new bits of the story. Despite the fact that that this game feels a lot like a British mystery TV mini-series, the interactivity is still quite high as it is up to you to figure things out. The puzzles are all logical but often not immediatley obvious, making this a satisfying and well-balanced game. I highly recommend this game and I hope that there will be a sequel!

Contradiction is a great mystery game. It uses genre tropes, but they don't feel tired. The acting is largely good. I liked Inspector Jenks, the main character. I felt his hamming it up really lent itself to the portrayal of the eccentric detective. The plot was largely tight. There were a few logical leaps, but they ultimately made sense in the story. I have mixed feelings about the length of the game. Part of me wishes it were longer (I took about 5-6 hours and I played slow to take everything in), but because you have to remember your clues and constantly review them, a shorter length was handy sometimes. The main gameplay mechanic, noticing contradictions in the suspects' stories, could be a little unclear sometimes, but lent itself to an interesting experience.
If you like mystery games or if you like FMV's, I'd recommend Contradiction. I really want to see/play a sequel.

A painfully slowly regenerating shield, mediocre item system that focuses on item quality and stuffing mods in them, and even zombies with so much health they make the lumberjacks in 7 Days To Die look like babies! In summation, don't waste your time on this game. There are tons of other amazing ARPGs that actually respond well and feel satisfying to play. This game is clunky, sluggish, and has a horrible UI. Honestly had high hopes for it that were immediately kicked in the nuts and spat on.

I tried the demo years ago and i thought it was quite good but all the negative reviews made me apprehensive about buying it. Finally bought it when it was on 2017 Summer Sale because i like to experience things for myself rather than rely solely on reviews or videos.
It's actually not too bad, only annoyance is that view rotation function is not very useful; it springs back to default angle as soon as the Ctrl key is released. Additionally the zoom in combination with the rotation function is just shy of making it into a full-fledged 3rd person shooter; the angle is slanted downwards making the view distance extermely limited, again not useful. Finally the game seems to be poorly optimized for AMD GPU; i had to run it at relatively low resolution in order to get close to 60 fps.
Another annoying feature or lack of it is that you can't scroll the screen anywhere unless your avatar moves into the vicinity. That means you can't scout for enemy locations until you're close enough to be fired upon.
Medium difficulty is not too difficult. You have a shield and can run out of danger zone, however some melee enemies will pursue you quite a distance. Zombies are harder to kill than robots but you have unlimited ammo with no cooldowns. Dodge ability has a cooldown meter so you can't dodge as quickly and repeatedly as you want until the meter is full.
Checkpoints are also the only places you can save game progress so it's a little inconvenient; bad design decision i think but it's clearly marked so you can easily find it.
My overall impression is that it's a fun game with some tricky puzzle like or rather harzadous sections. Graphics and sound effects are great. Music is good but a little repetitive i think.

Jk (sort of). In all seriousness though. this has to be one of the greatest games ever made, a fact most major gaming publications have agreed upon. I played it many years ago, but never finished. Now I've returned to the KOTOR universe, and I can't see myself not finishing it this time around.
The gameplay is very strategic and smart. It's addictive no matter your success rate. When you dominate in combat, you want to continue dominating. When you fail, success usually seems so close that you want to try again until you've won. The same can be said of the mini-games... I've put way more time into Pazaak than I care to admit.
However, it's the character development where the game really shines. The slow build towards making significant changes in the Star Wars universe captures the tone and feel of A New Hope way better than most other Staw Wars tie-ins. Most of the voice acting is incredibly strong and reasonably paced. It was actually a pleasure to listen to the voice work, which is a must in a game with this much dialogue.
With a little elbow grease (digitally speaking, of course) you can mod your way to a truly incredible experience. Some of the hi-res textures out there really help modernize the title. There are many, many other gameplay enhancements to be downloaded too, although I've been trying to keep my experience as close to the original as possible.
To that point, I was able to use Pinnacle Profiler to configure my 360 gamepad to play close to the original X-Box version, with a shift mode controlling the mouse pointer when I need it. Again, it took some toying and learning, but I was able to get it to the point where it works extremely well.
Not all is sunny and roses on the planet Taris, though. There are some odd graphical glitches from time to time. Also, some of the NPC's faces repeat or are similar enough to be jarring. In 8 hours of play with a few mods installed, I only experienced one crash to desktop (and of course, this could be related to having modded the files). There was also an annoying glitch in which my character would stop moving after battles, but this was fixed on my machine by enabling V-Sync.
However, the overall quality of the title is so absurdly high that these minor annoyances pale in comparison.
HIghest recommendations on this one. Do yourself a favor and enjoy this masterpiece classic.

Coming from LoL to this game and I can say that I really love the style. The games don't take that long so even if you have a bad team you don't have to sit in a game that is lost already for at least 20 minutes or maybe a lot longer.
If someone leaves you are allowed to leave as well, if he doesn't come back for a few minutes which is also a feature I really like since winning with a bot is pretty much impossible if the enmy team knows what they are doing.
There are also things I don't like tho:
- As a lot of other people said the matchmaking seems like it's not on point. I played against people who were prestige 10 and had played the game for a few hundred of hours while I was just getting started and still learning with my 20 hours.
(The good thing is that mostly people in your team won't flame because they know about the problem and it's not really your fault to lose to people who have 10 times + your playtime.)
- The thing that I hate most is that you have to unlock upgrades for Nauts. So you have to play 2-3 games until you are finally able to buy all of the upgrades for one Naut. If you are unlucky enough to also play against veterans and on top of that you are not even able to buy the good/right upgrades... well I guess you can guess where this leads.

I do have really good internet tho and a game that doesn't have good graphics and is possible to run on pretty much any pc should also run on those that have sub optimal connections.
So there are three main issues they have to fix in my opinion to make the game almost perfect. They will probably not fix the connection stuff in the near future because let's face it servers are pretty expensive but it might be worth the investment if they decide to do so.
I think firt of all they should fix the matchmaking and people would already have a lot less to complain about for thus raising the playercount.

Do not let my "record" time fool you: I've put well over 100 hours into this game.
Pros:
+Bullet Time
+Realistic Weaponry/Age-Appropriate Weaponry
+Realistic Bullet Drop and Air Resistance (on Marksman and Sniper Elite modes, respectively)
+Enemies that pose challenges even when knowing how to defeat them, or even knowing the easiest method for dispatching them
+Zombie Hitler
+Killing Zombie Hitler
+The Preacher (shooting Jesus out of a double-barrel elephant gun has never been more satisfying)
+Multiple ways of dispatching opponents keeps the game from becoming boring fast, and figuring out new ways to lay explosives (you get Land Mines, Trip Mines, and Dynamite, as well as Stielhandgranates) in order to get the most bang for your buck is incredibly satisfying, as well as the subsequent body part showers that follow (Note: Trip Mines can be a little lackluster in power, so pair them with Dynamite, as the Trip Mine detonation will set off the Dynamite, giving you a bigger bang and more damage)
Cons:
-There are 3 Levels of Difficulty: Noob, Marksman, and Sniper Elite. Unless you play Noob, you're going to have to adjust your shots according to the level of difficulty you choose. Marksman introduces your ol' pal Gravity, so the further away your target, the higher you have to angle your shot. Sniper Elite takes this a step further and introduces Air Resistance, which means wind becomes another factor you'll have to account for. Then again, if you're shooting someone in the face with a rifle at point-blank range, neither Gravity nor Air Resistance are going to stop you from burying that bullet into their brainpan.
-I'd wager at least half or so of the 15 levels have some part to them where you simply are going to have to learn through Trial-and-Error. A lot. While there are tutorials on the internet, I'd recommend scoping out as much as possible. Depending on the difficulty you choose, you're going to die. A lot.
-Occasional glitch here and there. Sometimes a zombie will be trapped in a wall, and you can't progress unless you kill all the enemies in a given location, so you'll have to restart at the last checkpoint. It sucks, but it happens.
-Nazi Zombie Snipers rarely miss their target, even on easier difficulties. Plus they can leapfrog entire buildings in a single bound, like Nazi Zombie Superman.
Overall, I'd give this game easily a 9/10. One of the better zombie games out there, and one that actually makes you think on how you're going to beat a level before you do so. Playing on harder difficulties also helps prevent the game from getting too repetitive, and yes, you CAN beat the whole thing on Sniper Elite difficulty while going solo.

With the sheer number of MMORPG's on the market, it's importnat to make sure you find on that fits. Champions Online will fill that role for some people better than others
The GOOD
- Roleplayer's paradise! You can be ANYTHING you can imagine and the lore is set up in such a way that it can make sense. Not to mention the shear number of choices for costumes... The character creator is mind bogglingly open.Time traveller? Sure. Monkey with swords for hands? Go crazy! Wizard from an alternate reality? You could probably start a club. The RP community is very active and it's easy to find partners, even if you don't know anyone.
- Very easy learning curve. Not only does the game show you everything you need to know to play, but the community is actually quite good. Every community has it's bad apples, but this one is mostly friendly.
- Freeform System. You may be noticing that many of the good points are about customization. The skill setup is no different. The freeform class option lets you build a custom class. This means choosing your own stats and even which skills you use. You have to pay for this though. Otherwise you can use a wide selection of premade classess. They are pretty good though.
- Free to play. While there are limitations for free players, which I will discuss below, they do not include anything that prevents you from maxing out. You get two slots for characters for free and you can complete the content all the way to max level.
- Full Controller Support. Yes, you read that correctly. You can simply plug in an Xbox controller and play. The controls are not amazing, but it is posible to play most of the game without using your keyboard for anything but messages. It's a great addition for those of us that prefer a controller.
The Meh
- Graphics, story and sounds are nothing to write home about. I mean, the game looks and sounds great, but there is nothing new going on here. The style leans towards cartoons and comics, which works well for the setting.
The Bad
- To really get the most out of your account, you're gonna wanna subscribe. You get 6 more slots, a bunch of classes and access to the freeform system. Plus, the number of costume parts you have access to jumps up alot. Having said that, you got hundreds of parts to start with so it's not really NEEDED unless you really want to get into it.
- Questing and combat are repettive. It's mostly fetch X or kill Y amount of guys. It's not difficult, just repetetive.
- Roleplayers can be kinda sleezy. Whle there is LOTS of legitamate RP in this game, there is also alot of questionable people. ERP (Erotic Role Play) is rampant. Luckily, it is a rule that this not be done in public so you will likly only deal with these people when turning them down. Still, it's worth noting that for younger players it can lead to some innapropriate and possibly illegal interactions.
Summary
If you're looking for a groundbreaking game with advanced gameplay, take a pass on this one. However if you're okay with a lighthearted romp as a superhero then give it a try. After all, it's free so what's to loose? If you're a Roleplayer though... DO IT. This game is basically made for you. Jump in and fulfill all your awesome character fantasies. (The legal ones I mean.)

This game is really great! It's basically a clone of Civilization 5 but I would argue it's even better. I've played a handful of civilization and sim type games of late including Civilization 4, 5, and 6, SimCity, Cities: Skylines, Anno 2050 and 2205 and I would say I enjoyed this game more than all of those.
If you've played any of the recent Civilization games, this game will feel right at home. The mechanics are virtually identical but with a different setting. What's surprising for a game like this is that it has the same high production values you'd expect from Civilization minus the expensive well-known voice actors and the in-game help is not quite as thorough.
One of the things that sets this game apart from Civilization is that while Civilization is basically fixed in real world history, Engless Legend has a totally fantastic settings complete with magic and technology that makes for some very interesting gameplay mechanics.
You can play the game as one of various factions and I was quite pleasantly surprised to find that each faction has significant differences between them that makes for a very different gaming experience that adds replay value to the game.

Endless Legend (EL) is a 4x strategy game with amazing 3D graphics, but somewhat shallow gameplay. Where the game lacks depth, it makes up for it in originality and those stunning graphics (if your video card can support them).
The game consists of several factions that vary considerably. For example, one faction can only get one city and strives to take over minor factions to use against other major factions. When you conquer a city, you destroy it and turn the province its in back to neutral rather than take it over. Another faction relies on trade and the markets so strongly that they not only control it, but live and die by it. The perfect faction for those bankers, economists, and stock market barons amongst us.
The shallow nature I mentioned earlier comes from the fact that once you learn the basics of the game, its not that hard to win games with any faction. There is not much detail in the way of craftable items, spells/abilities, or even the combat system. While  you can customize your units, the options to do that are very limited. You unlock certain Techs to open a few items to fit them with. That's it.
So, in terms of a recommendation. If you love games with incredible graphic detail, then this is the game for you. + Good story fluff
Cons:
- Extremely imbalanced
- Realies heavily on specific play styles
- Needs all expansions to have sufficient depth
- Puts player customised factions at a disadvantage
- Game outcomes are usually quickly determined in early game by factors such as; position, neighbours, chosen faction, ruins RNG, usually resulting in alot of "restarts".
- Extreme difficulty curve between AI difficulty settings
- Expansion mechanics don't feel finished or thoroughly reviewed.
- The game's imbalances punish drawn out games and rewards quick games (Which is an Oxymoron to me as grand strategy game sessions are generally meant to spand longer than your typical RTS session)
- Broken diplomacy
Overall, the game was fun and enjoyable earlier on in its development, however has become imbalanced and fairly hard to enjoy to the extent that you would expect to. So i will personally not be recommending Endless Legend, even though i find its potential to be great.

Well where to begin? I purchased Primordia initially just because I was captivated by the games art style and aesthetic that I saw on the steam store page. The murky, decayed and organic (almost HR Giger-esque in places) qualities of the scenes and designs caught my eye immediately.
In short summary Primordia is a world run by robots - man has vanished. Everything is slowly decaying and power - the lifeblood of the machines and robots who inhabit this world - is running low.
What first struck me when I first played the game beyond the look of it was the quality of the voice acting - especially of the lead character Horatio Nullbuilt (played by Logan Cunningham who also voice acted the narrator in Bastion). Other stand outs for me included your limb challenged sidekick good ol' Crispin, and my personal favourite the medieval old English speaking Ever-Faithful Leobuilt.
There are some deep theological questions and revelations in this game centring around the relationship between man and machine that I won't spoil here. That there are subtle parallels to our own world I also found to be clever and well executed.
Although the tone of the game is pretty depressing, it is counterbalanced by a ton of humour - usually provided by your best friend and ever complaining sidekick Crispin. Listening to some his dialogue genuinely made me laugh (which is an achievement in itself since I'm generally a miserable b'sod).
As it is a point and click adventure game I best mention the puzzles. On the whole they are fine and make sense with a bit of lateral thinking although I did have to resort to a guide once to get past a particularly tricky one. However, in this genre of game I would accuse the developer of not making it hard enough if I wasn't having at least one instance of  being completely at a loss! I reckon it builds character...
The game has multiple ways of solving particular puzzles and also multiple ending which is nice. If you're anything like me you'll want to play through a couple of times at least to see them all.
In conclusion, I would rate Primordia as one of the best point and click adventure games I've ever played and up there right beside one of my other favourites
. More than that though I would rate it as one of the most enjoyable and involving games I've played for the last couple of years. I just wish there was a sequel in the works! The world, setting and characters of Primordia are too good not to revisit.
In the words of the sad robot:
I highly recommend this game: it has endearingly well-written characters with witty lines, nice puzzles, and it's set in a universe that truly draws you in.

This little game is an absolute masterpiece! I would gladly play an entire series set in this universe.
The art is gorgeous, the voice acting top-notch, and the puzzles are challenging without being ridiculous. The characters and story really lift this above your average point-and-click adventure game - Horatio and Crispin's constant banter is hilarious, and I got a kick out of the other robots they meet along their journey. The fact that this game has a "very positive" on Steam worries me. Is it terrible? No. Is it absolutely mediocre? Yes.
Short version:
Pros: Beautiful graphics, cinamatic story, great design, decent music
Cons: Repetive AF. Once you've played the first 12 minutes, you've played the entire rest of the game, Though told through lovely cinematics, the story unfolds like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ized version of Gladiator with some random mystical parts forced in.
Consensus: 5.5/10.  Tries for the seamless, cinamatic epic like Heavenly Sword. Ends up feeling like a tech demo put on repeat. At 6-7 hours, this game feels 4 hours too long. Arguably worth $5-$10 as a nice tech demo. The critics were right about this one.
Long version:
It's been a long while since I've reviewed a game, but I felt this was necessary. I was pumped when I found out this game was coming to PC because the XBONE trailers looked amazing. Thankfully, I waited till the price dropped really low. How this is the same company that made the original Crysis and Far Cry, I don't know. Crytek has gone full George Lucas, losing their soul in technology.
Think of the freedom, variety, and openness of the first Crysis. This game is the exact opposite.
It might as well be an on-rails game.  I wanted to finish it. Push through to see how the story ends, but honestly, with only an hour left of the game, I can't. That hour could be put to much better use elsewhere.
Combat is a clunky, less responding version of the Arkham/Shadow of Mordor style. It seems cool (though unpolished) at first, and then it goes nowhere. The upgrades and unlocks are laughably shallow. The handful of "boss fights" they throw in are sad and embarrassing.
And this is coming from a guy who never got tired of fighting groups of enemies in Shadow of Mordor and Assassin's Creed.
You have spears that are mostly pointless except when you have to use them. They have random turret sections as if they played Duke Nukem Forever and thought "Hey, this game has some good variety in it".
As for the story, it's a well told, well voiced slice of genericism. The main character is like a Maximus from Gladiator if you replaced him with a wooden muppet. And while I'm all for spiritual/supernatural stuff in games, they come out of nowhere in this game and feel like they don't belong whatsoever.
The writers decided to take random historical characters that lived in entirely different periods and throw them together. Commodus is the son of Nero? I realize Gladiator took serious liberties too, but this plays out like bad fanfiction.
I don't know how it ends. I don't care. Like the Roman Pontius Pilate, I'm washing my hands of this game.
You can like this game. But if you love this game, you need to play better 3rd person action games.

Supraball is a First-Person-Soccer game. It rewards fast paced teamoriented plays. Cons:

-Price and content not matching

The only negative thing I have to say about Supraball is the fact that it's SO GOOD that it has made almost every other game seem boring and mundane to me. I've played this game since August of 2014 and have never experienced a dull moment. If you are into competitive games then Supraball is a must. The amount of teamwork and the infinite amount of strategies you can come up with has made this game an all time favorite for me. It's a great game for both casual and competitive players with some of the most complex and unique game mechanics in any game i've ever played. Playing this game is like entering a time machine. 5 hours feel like 30 minutes and each game plays out differently from the next. Supraball also has a very high skill cap and incredible e-sport potential. I'm telling you guys, this game is a gem and there is no other game like it.

If you are looking for a successor to Sim Tower or Yoot Tower, then this game is not what you are looking for. While there is a semblance to these past games, the challenges in Project Highrise are substantially different. Where the Tower games were elevator focused and for getting Sims from point A to point B, in Project Highrise the focus is on services and very careful management of funds. The placement of your elevators is important but there is very little delay from entry to egress and there is currently no other elevator management. Project Highrise however has very little challenge once you understand its basic rules and tempo. Every challenge in the game is achievable if the player is patient and does not try to move forward too quickly.
An example is constructing a residential only tower devoid of offices where the gameplay will be very slow and methodical. Doing so requires multiple game days of wait time to collect enough money (after your seed money in gone) to build upgraded utilities and services in order to build additional tenants. As long as you have the patience to do that, and provide the services the residents want, there is very little challenge to achieving a large residential tower.
The steepest challenge that I have encountered is keeping enough money to repair what was already built because nearly every area of your tower degrades over time. The more popular your tower and the more visitors travel areas of your building, the quicker areas need to be repaired. This even includes visitors just passing through to their actual destination, such as residents heading home and passing through other resident’s homes. A residential apartment in the upper right corner of the highrise will rarely need to be repaired, but ones on the left of the highrise just to the right of an elevator will have to be repaired more often due to passersby’s.
While I have very much enjoyed playing Project Highrise, the game ceased being entertaining for me personally after just 18 hours. No doubt I will continue to play the game from time to time for ambient gameplay while performing other activities. The developers have been fantastic at patching the game quickly when issues have been brought up and I am looking forward to futures patches which may introduce new activities and challenges.
Some areas of improvement that I hope will be addressed in future patches include bizarre pathing by construction workers taking excessively and unnecessary long routes, and the ability to better control the routes that residents and office workers take such as avoiding elevators right next to where they work or live, for elevators on the other side of their building.
Overall, in my opinion, I think this game is worth your time and I do not regret buying it. To me it is enjoyable to load up a tower I've built and to watch visitors and residents wander around as if they were ants in a giant ant farm.

RTS is a dying breed. That's a statement you may have read on a gaming site recently. Maybe gamers like me were simply waiting for the RTS genre to move into the modern age. WARGAME is the RTS I've been waiting for.
Wargame manages to combine stunningly beautiful graphics with deep tactical gameplay. This isn't a game were you can mob a bunch of units together and throw them at you enemy. You will need to understand the terrain you are fighting in, and the units at your disposal. Heavy tanks can only be defeated with weapons capable of punching through their armor, or tactics clever enough to get you a shot at their weak rear armor. Infantry defending urban settings will need to be dug out house by house, street by street, with infantry of your own.
AirLand Battle is also leaps ahead of its predecessor, European Escalation. Better terrain, more countries, a vastly improved deck building mechanic, air power, and a whole new high level strategic campaign make this the  definitive RTS of this era of gaming.
Total Wargasm...

I would absolutely recommend this to any fan of FMV games, or even point-and-click adventure games.
First, in terms of presentation, this game rocks high res video that looks great. I played it on my 55 inch Sony using my "Steambox" living room PC and the game looked like a movie.
As to the acting, I found the characters to be top-notch and each portrayed a distinct personality. I found them all interesting and compelling. Some of them had me fooled and at times I would go back and forth as to who was the murderer.
The narrative itself was engaging and drew me into the story's web of characters and contradictions. I kept wanting to play more and more to learn about Atlus and the mysterious circumstances of Kate Vine's death. There wasn't really a dull moment. However, there are some red herrings scattered about and some loose ends that don't get tied up by the end. I found these issues to be a double edged sword. On one hand, they leave you wanting more but on the other, it seems that the writers just didn't know where else to go or didn't have the resources to flesh out certain plot points.
Finally, the contradictions: the game is based around finding the contradictions among the witnesses. The system works, for the most part, and really shines when various contradictions jump at you and you have an "Ah-ha!" moment. Some contradictions, however, were tenuous at best. In fact, I think some could be argued not to be contradictions at all, yet the game will not progress unless they are pointed out. I regrettably had to look at a walkthrough after getting stumped two times. I hated the fact that I couldn't find the remaining contradiction those times. When I learned what it was that I missed, I found myself rolling my eyes because the contradiction was a little too convoluted to have spotted and wasn't really intuitive. I guess that's the point--contradictions aren't always easy to spot. But this is a game and shouldn't be too taxing!
I really recommend this game and hope there's a sequel.

After playing for a few hours and trying out the campaign and the multiplayer of the game I've realized that I've completely fallen in love with the game. While the singleplayer portion could be improved upon a bit more and not be so restrictive with the time frame (I'd enjoy bidding my time against a hard opponent), the multilayer is where it shines the most.
In the original Wargame I've played quite a bit of multiplayer but it didn't captivate me that much as it was restricted to only 4v4 on rather small maps. In this one they've added a 10v10 map (only 1 so far, hopefully more will come) and at times it can get incredibly chaotic and tense. This is where I've had the most fun so far.
To top that is using your own custom Decks (army builds), finding the best combinations for the majority of situations and watching how effective or ineffective your deck is. Even when loosing I never really felt bothered, it only opened a new window on how I could create a new deck by learning on what happened during battle.
I fully recommand this game, even if you are new to Wargame, or to large scale RTS in general, this is a good game to start with. Endless posibilities, endless fun.
However, remember that this is not your usual RTS, there is no base building. If you are looking for base building RTS this is not it, but if you are looking for a fun, intense RTS game, then this is it.

Greed: Black Border Review - Raymond KT
All things considered, there is a place for Greed: fans of the point-and-click "Diablo" style of gameplay will find quite a lot to enjoy here, and for all of its quirks, it still does offer a pretty immersive universe to delve into and all for 20 bucks. A bland, by the book action-rpg set in a sci-fi world. With your choice of 3 classes(each with different trainable skill sets) you'll embark on a fairly uneventful dungeon crawler through three forgettable locales each with their own distinct mobs. While the classes and builds make for a bit of intrigue you'll quickly be mired in repetition as you clear room after room without much to distinguish each one from the last. In typical crawler fashion the game is broken into three acts each capped by an uninspiring boss encounter. Scant puzzles do very little to break up what it otherwise a mindless grind that is stretched to a robust +12 hour play time. The game also features an incredibly frustrating lack of responsiveness from the controls. Attempts to pivot and free fire are often ignored as you find yourself running directly into damage(and often death) instead.
While it had the potential to be a good title there just isn't enough there to warrant the time commitment and achievement collectors will also be disappointed at the absence of any. Unless you are a die hard fan of the genre or have a fetish for poor controls I'd suggest spending your time elsewhere

I recommend Greed: Black Border (GBB) but it's a borderline decision. I recommend it if you feel for a 10h quick action zombie smashing fix! It felt short and I usually spend ages in games like these selling every piece of unwanted loot and backtracking and checking out every corner of every map.  So with all of that, I finished GBB in roughly 15h and you might say: "It's not that bad..." But compare that with many other games where I easily have 80+ hours if not outright in the few hundreds and 15h is short.
Also there is a lack of weapon, armor variety and monster types. So I guess, in general, the game lacked some content. Now maybe, if you continue after beating the end boss (because you can restart the game at a higher difficulty level), maybe do you get new item images for armor and weapons? I'm not sure but I did not feel like doing the campaign again.
I should also mention that because of the way I play, I only assigned some of my skill points, as a ranged damage dealer and finished the game easily on normal difficulty.
With those negative aspects behind, let's look at the positives:
+ It's an isometric ARPG (Diablo style) but set in a sci-fi futuristic environment.
+ Dropped items are randomized
+ Nice environments (maps) and nice unit animations
+ Good sounds
Negatives:
- Not enough content
- Lacks a bit of polish
- Not enough replayability
So overall, unforatunately, I have to say that if Mass Effect 1 or 2, Diablo 1 or 2, Company of Heroes 1 or 2, Titan Quest, Path of Exile, Dawn of War 1 or 2, etc. are on sale at around the same price as this title, then buy that other title. These games are each worth about 6 times GBB!

I had high expectations for Cosmonautica because its cartoonish art style and the space exploration gameplay were very attractive. However, after playing the game for 12 hours, I must say that the gameplay mechanics are huge disappointments because they seriously lack tactical depth and variety.
This game is mainly composed of 2 gameplay components: 1) space combat and 2) interplanetary trading. The mechanics of these 2 components, unfortunately, are completely broken.
First of all, for space combat, I can simply use 2 words to summarize it: Use torpedoes. That's it. I'm not kidding. You just need to equip your space ship with tons of torpedoes and you'll win every space combat in this game. Don't waste your time and money on other types of weapons.
For space trading, I can just use 4 words to summarize it: Trade high-priced goods. That's it. The profits from trading expensive goods are so high that there's literally no reason at all to trade mid- and low-priced commodities in this game.
So, if you want to be successful in Cosmonautica, it's just very very simple: use torpedoes (in combats) and trade high-priced commodities (in trading). The gameplay mechanics are just overly simplistic and broken. Honestly, after playing this game for about 5 hours, I already got very bored. I kept playing for another 7 hours because I didn't want to waste my $15 spent on the game. I wish the new Steam refund policy had been in effect when I bought this disappointing title.
Conclusion: Cosmonautica has beautiful graphics, but its gameplay mechanics fail miserably.

I can't in good conscience recommend a "finished" game that has such a huge stability issue.
To be clear, the gameplay itself is enjoyable if a bit repetitive. You sail across different galaxies transporting various goods, passengers, while occasionally (or quite often if you decide to become a pirate/warship) fighting other ships for missions/loot.
So, gameplay aside, this Not Recommended is more to do with the fact that you can't play the game for any real length of time. It crashes, A LOT, every half hour or so for me, sometimes more often. Thankfully (or perhaps because of this issue?) the game designers used an auto-save function that saves your game after every major (or minor) interaction, pretty much. It saves it before you enter battle, when you get to, and when you leave a space station. Which is pretty much all you do in this game.
The game also has a bad habit of corrupting save files, making them unloadable. This happens rarely, but when you've put 10-12 hours into a game and all of a sudden you can't access it, it's frustrating to say the least.
Bacially, unless you have a burning desire to support the developers and their company, I recommend you stay away from this game until such time as they've fixed the game crash issues, or pick the game up at a deep discount. And keep in mind that you only have 2 hours (as per Steams' refund policy) to determine wheather or not you want to keep the game, because chances are you won't get a refund from them past that mark no matter how horrible your game plays. Or doesn't play...
EDIT: I went ahead and changed my review to recommended after giving the game another try. While the game did crash a couple times, it did not crash repeatedly minutes after starting. So, as stated above, the gameplay is solid, and now that the game is stable, I would recommend this game if you're into third person space adventure.

Battleborn is an excellent game, the art style and gameplay is great, almost similar to Gearbox's borderlands games, but with a more unique touch to it.  Must have for those who like first-person shooters.
The gameplay is standard first-person shooter, but you also have 3 abilities that you can cast.  Every character has their own skillset.  Every character also has their own unique "skill tree", as you level up you get points to upgrade your character; these are not persistent and will reset every match.
Each player can equip 3 different items.  These items contain various stats that you can bring into each match to help boost your power.  Items come in selected rarities, all the way up to legendary, and the stats are random in the amounts they give, so not one is the same.

I have played Sid Meier's Civilization since the beginning. That is important context into which to place this review of Endless Legend. Many hours have been lost to "just one more turn" late into the night playing Civilization. But my favorite game (in the series) was Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri. That was truly an amazng game, filled with a fascinating and dangerous world, a strange ecosystem, amazing technologies and absorbing, smart story telling. I've been waiting for a sequel to Alpha Centauri for a long, long time.
Endless Legend ticks all of those boxes. Auriga is a fascinating and dangerous world, filled with strange anomalies and creatures. All of the lore and technology, the story telling and myth making, the diverse factions and their quests place Endless Legend squarely on the path to glory in the manner of Alpha Centauri. It's weird at first for a Civ fan--so many gameplay elements seem familiar but play out so differently.
Like Civilization there is a learning curve for a novice to overcome in order to become comfortable and knowledgeable enough to plan ahead and achieve a particularly sought after victory, whether it's a single battle or the completion of a faction quest. But it is totally and absolutely worth every turn played late into the night.
Endless Legend is a beautiful game to look at. It's expansions have rendered it almost as complete as Civilization V. It is possible to play each and every campaign differently from others before it. Amplitude have invested a huge amount of thought and imagination to create a completely new IP that gets better and better as it is polished by successive updates. (And it helps that the complete Endless Legend is half the price of the complete Civ V on Steam.)
I still dream of Alpha Centauri 2 but if I have to wait forever, at least I have Endless Legend to keep me company.

I came into Ryze expecting a repetitive, hack and slash Batman Arkham clone and don't get me wrong, in some ways it is all of these things but the full package is something definitely worth playing. The major criticisms of this game at launchwere the repetitive combat as I stated earlier and the short game length however the length of the game actually works in the games favour as it can be completed in one sitting meaning that the combat while a tad samey is bearable for the full length of the game. Where this game truely shines is in the resentation of it's setting. The environments are incredible and the armour is simply incredible. The level of detail in this game is exceptional which makes it such a shame that teh enemy character models are reused over and over. this didn' bother me though as they were so well made. The story of this game is fantastic. it is a twisting story of vengence that takes you from Rome to York in search of revenge for the death of your family. The voice acting, animations and writing are all great however there are a few characters such as the Emperor's son that I would like to have recieved more screen time as he was such a strong character it was a shame to have only seen him a handfull of times int the 6 hour campaign. My fingers are getting a tad sore so I'll finish here. If you can get the game for less than £5 it's a no brainer. If not I would still reccomend it but it is often on sale so it is worthwile to wait.

Contradiction the All-Video Murder Mystery Adventure is a video game tells a story that you play as inspector Jenks to investigate a bright PHD student named Kate Vine who drowned in a lake at the midnight in a small village called Edenton in England.
The police force committed it as suicide case, but there are unusual questionable facts lying beneath it.  And you’re the one who is willing to unveil the truth, and bring the justice to itself.
The game itself may look like very "simple" designed and uninteresting. However, the magic trick is: it turns the very simplest system into a quite brilliant and incredibly addicting experience to really play with. You need to think really hard as a detective in order to find the proofs against dishonest interviewees, and to read their answers again and again to solve the puzzle and uncover the truth.
They introduced a “Contradition System” to match 2 different answers from the same interviewee to reveal whether he/she is lying.  And the successful results  will make your progress go further.
The gameplay is very addicting (might result you can’t stop saying: “Yes! I did it!”). And yet, the price is highly competitive.
Personally, I think the price is fair, far beyond lots of AAA title games that sell twice expensive as this game is, with very forgettable storyline that only worth 1 playing through.
Contradiction is different, for its unique way of unfolding the crime mystery and the ultimate experience that precisely delivers to its audience. It’s certainly one of the fewest games that will make you remember it once for a while.  It is also one of the fewest games that I can seriously recommend and commented as “worth every penny you’ve just spent”.
I write this review mainly because I saw none of my friends have already own this game, and would like to contribute a bit to the community. If you’d interested into crime puzzle solving games and would like to get yourself involved in a decent story, this is a gem for you.
It might be a bit silly to say so, since I am from England, and I’m often supportive to the video-game industry from homeland, because we want to see more people get involved in it and make the industry has a better future tomorrow. But even without this factor, I would still write this review simply for its magnificent content.
I’ve completed this game twice so far, the 1st time for my own play-through, and the 2nd time to show it to a friend. While showing to him, I couldn’t finish the 1st chapter before he stopped me from playing and purchased it to enjoy it himself.
Also from the high percentage of the positive feedbacks you can also tell I am not lying.

The first of two classic sci-fi RPGs that birthed the creation of the popular MMO, it had great graphics and gameplay for it's time.  Combat tends to follow D&D type rules while still providing action-packed fight scenes.  It tends to follow the set formula of most Bioware RPGs (generic hero with obscure origins and special abilities thrust into an on-going war of good vs. evil, add morality meter and companions, etc.), but contains a number of plot twists and a hefty dose of Star Wars lore.  Both the MC and his/her companions tend to expereicne significant character development as the story progresses, a portion of which the player can influence, leading to some intresting scenes and dialogue in-game.  All in all a classic title, and a must-have for those who wish to delve further into those events that helped shape the world setting of SW:tOR the MMO.

Effectively the main inspiration behind the structure of Bioware's Mass Effect, KoTOR to me is one of the greatest RPG's I've ever played. Even ignoring being a fan of Star Wars overall, it seems detached from almost everything else that has been produced (The Old Republic being based off a similar time frame), movies especially, and brings a lot of new things, despite keeping that semi-familiar setting.
It shows it's age, though, with no widescreen video options, and (very surprisingly), no vanilla overhaul mod available to tweak it up. At the same time though, there's a big reason for that, and that is that it has very little in the way of bugs and problems, and looks good enough for a game over ten years old. Another big way of showing age is a lack of functions many have come to expect from RPG's, like some kind of auto-loot, there's no way to heal the entire party automatically.. But the variety of how you can approach situations is rather staggering (But rather expectable from Bioware nowadays)
Definitely a great game, would recommend it to anyone who wants to lose a few weeks to a rather engrossing classic.

This game is buggy.
Just in my limited time of play, I've found so many bugs. I'll list a few that just irritated me.
When setting up your empires policies. I like mine setup so that whenever a new planet is colonized, it immediately starts building a defensive base. However that's not always available from game to game. I've started 7 seven games so far (all with the exact same settings and race). Of those seven, only in 3 I had the option to build defensive bases when a planet is colonized. I think it was games, 1, 4, and 5. How does that make any sense?
Games 2, 3, 4, had to be abandoned due to some weird glitch that caused my population growth to jump to 109%, maxing it out in seconds, then my cash and income showed infinity, my 1 and only planet would build every ship, regardless of how they were queued, except colony ships.
Game 5, my automated explorers would explore a system, but when you clicked on a specific location, it wouldn't tell you how much of a % of that resource there was. So then you had to do it manually. Game abandoned.
Game 6 had to be abandon because all the civilian ships (the ones you can't control) just sat at a starbase and wouldn't move. Since no resources were being delivered, nothing could be built. After messing around with it for 1/2 hour I gave up.
Often times you give your ships orders and they just ignore them. For instance, I wanted a fleet to attack a pirate base that was close, gave the order and it just sat there ignoring the order. Or I order a constructor ship to refit/refuel, but they just ignore the order. Some of my constructor ships were like 10 levels behind on tech, but just refused to upgrade. I remember this problem from when I played this game 5 years ago.
Sometimes there's the option to refuel a ship, other times there isn't.
Sometimes you can build a certain base on a remote or colonized planet (with a constructor), other times you can't. Or it'll accept the order, but won't actually build it.
And the list goes on and on.
And there are some in game mechanics that I just can't stand or don't make sense to me.
For instance, the bigger your empire, the more you have invested in research, the less you research. I read the reason for that was so the smaller empires had a chance of catching up in tech. Yes, lets just pointlessly build money sucking bases that do nothing.
You get leaders (heroes or whatever you want to call them), and then the leaders get dismissed randomly due to incompetence. My empire leader in game 1 was dismissed, never got another. WTF! (actually completed game 1). Game 2 had 2 empire leaders from the start, only one of them had stats. Supposedly some of the buildings you build will attracted new leaders. I had a Science academy (they're supposed to increase the chance of getting a researcher) on 40 planets (game 1), but I had no research leaders thought out the game (the only 1 I had was dismissed early on). One of my fleet leaders was killed in battle, even though I lost no ships and none of them took any damage (except shields halfway). I noticed that for every leader that's dismissed, it also says there were killed.
Looking at the research tree, for some of the items you have no clue why you would want to research them. Like energy collection, I have no idea what it does for you or why I even need it.
For bases you can click on "mercenary defense mission". There's no explanation in the help for it. Clicking on it costs some money. But when the base gets attacked, it makes no difference. I've tried this before, during and after a raid from pirates. I have yet to figure out what it actually does.
One of the expansions added different types of troops, frankly they could have just left that out and just stuck with one type of troop for all the difference it makes.
I read that people who like this game just love the pre-warp option, frankly, that just makes the game even more boring then it already is, waiting for tech to get researched so you can actually get somewhere.
The messages you get flash on by and there's no way to adjust message speed. You can look in to the message history, but it's useless since clicking on messages in there doesn't take you to the location and by the time you look in there, it's too late anyway.
I do like some of the options they've added for the game, like setting a limit on how many sectors out you can colonize out.
Also if you fully automate everything, then the game will play it self and you can go watch tv. Why did I buy this game again?
Depending on your automation settings, either the game is fast to micromanagement from hell. With ship designs, it's either the game makes the designs, or you do, but not both. Just what I want to do, spend hours designing ships only to find out that I have to abandon the game due to some weird bug that was never fixed.
Due to all the bugs that haven't been fixed, and unless they fixed a lot of the issues, the only thing it deserves so far is a negative.
Currently on game 7, wonder if I'll actually be able to finish it.......

This game is strategic Empire Simulation Game. But the automation aspect and detailed system makes it RPG like game. You can literally play off different role in each game. No race has fixed way of playing game.
Automation may sound like turning the small plays off. But no, this game provides more contents and more strategies just by being more familiar with automation. First of all, the bi-income system is new turn on. The balancing between controllable and dependable yet hard to manage income and uncontrollable, undependable and conditional income was just amazing. You can really manage 'what kind of economy' you want to maintain for your empire. Also you can balance this through automation and really form the 'government' you would like to build. I first thought government systems were useless, just get by contents that all the empire management game have. But no, you can actually play out those governments through your own policy making. The extra perks from policy makes those role-playing realistic and manageable too.
Resource system and delivery mechanism was great too. This makes this game very realistic as it requires significant army to maintain significant supply chain. Also this resource supply chain is just sub-system for uncontrollable economic system. You can fully automate this and forget about it. But if you get use to it and how to twist it, it gives you whole different experience of economy building. Also technology isn't just planetary facilities and ships to win the war or colonize more. They actually affect economy itself. Not just retrofitting, but with sufficient tech and supply chain, you can dominate certain trade literally. Hence making trade sanction very effective. (this domination gets harder as map size increases. But still until AI build tier4 propulsion tech, you will have regional dominance)
Also you can manage your sub culture (side-races). It isn't just simple decoration for your empire profile. You can use their population to colonized planets that you don't have technology of. Gaining bonus is mainstream, but enslavement bonus and extermination option was new. If your planet is about to be overthrown by side-race you can manage that. (of course depends on your role-play)
Bad sides are AI and Diplomacy, Tech tree balance, and characters
After a while you will find whatever you do you will always win unless you put yourself in very disadvantaged situation.
Also diplomacy needs more work. It's too simple to even criticize. Trade Sanction or Treaty is great but this is because of Policy and Automation, not Diplomacy. AIs are very passive regarding Economy to begin with.

Distand Worlds: Universe takes the 4X "conquer the galaxy" genre and weaves it into a large-scale RTS game.
How could this even work? In most RTS games, you might get to a point of managing a large empire with 40 colonies or much more, and can devolve into a sadistic routine of micro-management.
To sovle this, the game puts a lot of emphasis on automation. Letting the AI run things for you.
This works and fails at the same time.
Where is works:
-you can tweak what you want to manage yourself vs. what the AI manages
How it fails:
-the AI is stupid, it needs too much hand-holding, fights against your decisions, all the time, leading to micromanagement of the AI
Example:
-the AI will auto-design ships and not make them the best they can be.
-the AI will put ships into a fleets and strike groups and send it out to the middle of nowhere for no reason
-when you override AI control of fleets, ships, strike groups, the AI will re-override with it's own inferior decision making capability
-During a war, you might have 500 ships and the enemy is attacking ONE system. Rather than defend, the AI will send all your ships to patrol your other systems. This leads to constant fighting with the AI where you order your ships to defend the system, they get there, then the AI overrides and sends them away. I'm not joking, even AFTER YOU DISABLE the AI capability, this happens.
-To disable AI, you can set it up where it doesn't form fleets when you build ships, rather, you can do it manually. Or if the AI forms groups, you can go in to each group separately and disable AI command. THIS IS WAY TOO CUMBERSOME, because of the poor interface, is poorly organized, and extremely glitchy/blippy, and sloooooow. Extremely rough and skiddish at best.
Where as in other games, you can pull up a list of all your ships and fleets and issue orders, settings, global settings, this game let's you pull up the ships, but you have to exit the list to focus on the ship/fleet you select, and then work on issuing commands. Then you have to go back and pull up the list again, scroll through the list looking for it, it's soooo incredibly poorly organized and slow, and then wash, rinse, repeat. Total fail.
It's almost best that you form your own 5 kick-butt fleets, that you always will control, and let the AI handle everything else. Even in this scenario, everything will fall apart into disarray when a big war breaks out.
Graphically, the game looks okay, but the weapon effects and ship designs mostly looks like something out of an♥♥♥♥♥♥
I don't mind lacking graphics.
What I DO MIND, is old, simple graphics that run like crap.
This game's graphics would have been appropriate for something 20 years ago.
The ships are just 2D static pictures.
No flashing lights or effects or anything.
*Just a .jpg that flies around and shoots other .jpgs at other .jpgs.*
So why does this run so bad? I fault the developer, bad programming, that sort of thing.
Has nothing to do with your system when you can easily play a Total War game with thousands of soldiers rendered in full 3D bashing each other over the head, but this game struggles with hundreds of flat 2D pictures moving on the screen. It's like they used a cheap game maker engine from the 90s that wasn't designed to handle so many moving pictures.
Diplomacy is a fair attempt to do something more than throw money at the other side for peace or something.

I expect this comparison is what a lot of people will be wanting to know. I'll preface this section by saying I have about 650 ingame hours in Rocket League and about 2,000 in Supraball.
Deep down at their core they are essentially the same game - put the ball in the goal, just with different methods of doing so. Both are very pure, simple games which give you some basic controls and then set you free to do what you wish.
and play the game though to the degree that every second of the game you are holding the ball the tree of your choices branches 100 times: will you do a little rollspin to juke a defender, will you pass to a teammate who is boosted and flying across the map for a volley combo, will you panic and do a horrible pass back to your keeper and score a hilarious own goal or will you do the countless other things available to you?
within 100 hours of play you can be setting up strong charge to volley goals to score 300km/h screamer goals, whereas in Rocket League setting up a pass play like this is far, far more difficult.
Now let's move onto the pro's and con's of Supraball in it's Early Access State.
+++
The monetization now comes from a chest/key system.
+++
There are so many different ways to play that you never end up playing the same game twice.
+++
You can sink thousands of hours into a position and still have room to learn and innovate. Or, don't conform to the meta, you're free to play however you want!
++
, I have sunk probably 2000 hours into goalkeeping in the Alpha/Beta and I'm not even close to the skill cap. The skill floor is pretty high too, but even when you first start playing and have no idea what you're doing it is still really enjoyable
++ Applying curves and combinations of curves to your shots gives huge variety to the gameplay and
++
The game has alot to learn and the tutorial covers all of the basics, with some sections (such as the goalkeeper training) which are even useful to me with a few thousand hours playtime.
++

I have always been a fan of team sports, especially those that involve advancing an object to an opposing goal, like football, basketball, and hockey.  There are constant individual moves and coordinated team strategies going on that make each sport beautiful.  Any amazing effort or foolish mistake can mean success or failure.  This is Supraball.
Supraball can be enjoyed on a casual level, but competitive Supraball really shines.  Your teammates are counting on you.  Your heart is pounding; your adrenaline flowing.  I have never experienced this from any other video game.
The game is in early access.  I look forward to more features, and improved polish.  The gameplay is great, but it still needs features like instant replay to be a great full release.
Regardless, I've had years of fun playing Supraball and it's predecessor, Deathball.  It's a great game and it has huge potential.  It gives lazy, fat gamers like me the same feeling I'm sure professional athletes get.
