Distant Worlds: Universe is one of the best 4X empire builders out there. If you need a comparison to help you imagine how it plays, think Europa Universalis in Space.
Like seemingly all games of any significant depth, Distant Worlds is not exactly a looker. Infact, the graphics were a barrier to my enjoyment for quite some time until I decided to get over it and see why this game excited serious strategy gamer quite so much.
Gameplay puts you in charge of an empire of two halves. The State, which is the government controlled side of things (which you run) and The Private Sector, which is 90-100% automated. The 10% difference brings me to one of Distant Worlds biggest features. The game allows you to automate any aspect of the game you don't enjoy.
If you don't want to fiddle with ship designing, you can leave it to the AI, or taxes, population management, colonisation, genuinely any aspect of the game can be automated. Heck you can automate your entire empire if you really want. This is highly customisable and can be fiddled with on the fly and makes the game a little easier to get into.
The game is, however, still very complex and it took me watching 20, 30 minute episodes of a Let's Play series - something I wouldn't usually even consider doing - before I felt comfortable enough to give Full Manual play a shot. But I'm glad I did.
Distant Worlds: Universe is a hard game to recommend to those with limited patience or time, and that aren't big on complex strategy titles to begin with, but if you are curious it is a top of it's class game well worth exploring.

What do I love about it? It's hard to put a finger on, but I guess it's the depth. Nothing seems to be abstracted by the game, and I think this is its greatest feature.
For example: I want to build a military frigate at a space port near one of my colonies. This frigate is made up of components (like reactors, shields, etc), each one of which must be manufactured using resources (over 40 different resources). Every single one of these resources has to be either:
a) mined by one of your mining ships/mining station.
b) purchased from trade.
c) obtained in a raid.
d) smuggled into your system via pirates.
e) maybe more I don't know?
If you don't have the resource, it doesn't get built. So you can see this adds immensely to the value of strategic resources.
And the resource doesn't just appear at the space port. It has to be shipped there. By freighters. So you can
obstruct supply lines by attacking these freighters... it's not just some malformed bonus tacked on, and I really appreciate that.
I captured a base deep within enemy territory (it had a rare resource I really wanted), but even though my fleet was much better than the ships he could throw at me, he succeeded in disrupting my freighters so well, I couldn't refuel my fleet and I had to abandon the colony before my fleet was wiped out.
Like many people here, I bought the game at $50 and on first playing I thought "Oh god, I think I wasted $50".. but now I know I'm going to get hundreds of hours out of this game.
Best way to think about it :
Most AAA titles - All show, no guts.
DW - All guts, no show (debatable, it's functional.. I like the UI once you get used to it)
I'm an old gamer, I want the depth... give me the guts!

For a free game, definitely worth the download. Awesomenauts is a tug of war game that features heroes with all sorts of different abilities that the player controls.
The
is quite fluid and solid in Awesomenauts. The game is designed as a platformer and does a really good job in its delivery. I'm not a huge fan of platformers so getting me to play it took a bit, but once I tried - I was sold. As I've mentioned, the game follows a tug of war scheme. Generally, there are two levels to the stage (literally two levels, like an upper level and a lower level). Each level has two defensive turrets that the enemies have to break through. Players can choose to attack the top level or bottom level as they see fit. Travelling through the levels is made easy as there is a center level that allows easy access to the top and lower level. There are boosting stations that can also help your character jump to where they need to go quicker. Automatically there are robotic players (sometimes small units or big units) that are assigned to attack the enemy players base. As you defeat more enemies, your hero as well as your team levels up (including the AI). Heroes come in all shapes and sizes and all have different abilities. Some can jump extremely high or fly, some can launch bullets or shoot a bunch of lasers. If you bought the full version of the game, you will have access to ALL players. If you're playing for free like me, you'll have to play to unlock. Choose your characters wisely! Each character will have a basic attack (X), followed by two specials (Y, B) and their method of jump (A).
The
are pretty good for the cartoon theme that they chose. The little details of explosions or jumps are all addressed. All the characters are neatly designed and their attacks are all unique to their characteristics. The
are quite detailed as well. On the character selection screen, they will all have different voices and music that plays as you are seeing what their stats are. The game did a pretty good job in this domain.
Overall, the game is good. There are some people that will definitely jump in nose first into the game and get a huge kick out of it. The leveling system is a little tedious, but for a free game, I guess I can understand. The game also rotates which characters you are able to use week to week. Ensure you save up and buy characters you like! The split screen option is also a huge attraction. Players can play against one another online or battle AI. The AI is definitely no push-over in this game.

This fantastic, little game got a lot of criticism for being a ‘glorified demo’, for Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain. People said that it should have been released for free and that it was just a cheap way to ‘cash in’ on the Metal Gear hype. However, as you would expect from Hideo Kojima and his team, Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes is a masterpiece, in it’s own right.
The layers of detail and purposefully built in replay value, make this ‘single area’ game, well worth your time (and money). It is loaded with ‘fan service’ and ‘Easter eggs’, with lots of references to previous games in the series. This version also includes all the DLC, which were previously exclusive to different consoles, before the PC release. It also runs flawlessly for me on a GTX980 running Windows 10.
I really enjoy the gameplay style of Ground Zeroes which requires you to revisit the same environment, many times, in multiple different ways. It encourages me to further appreciate the immersive atmosphere and attention to detail in this single environment. In fact, I got hooked on Ground Zeroes a lot quicker than I did with Phantom Pain, which I still haven’t finished.
Considering that Kojima’s creative process was interfered with during the completion of Phantom Pain. Ground Zeroes seems more like a sincere Metal Gear experience than Phantom Pain is. I love this game and that’s what Ground Zeroes is in my opinion, a full game, that stands strong on it’s own. It’s an excellent, fully fleshed out masterpiece, which (considering it’s size) is filled with great content.
After such an appetizing hors d'oeuvre, I can't wait for the main course.

Although the name of game is quite dull in my opinion, the game itself is highly polished and completed.
I recommend this mainly because its splendid hand-drawn art style. This characters, weapons, armors, enemies, and backgrounds are very pleasant to the eyes. The music and sound effects fit the environments, although not very impressive.
The combat system is a traditional turn-based RPG mode combined with a card management system, where all items you equipped provide their respective cards to form a drawing pool for use in the battle, and your hand available in the current turn is drawn from the pool. This system is neither innovative nor well-balanced, but it works well for the game. Character building is interesting at first, but becomes monotonic in the late game since you will reach top level at the beginning of the fifth book if you finish all the side quests (only a handful throughout the whole game, and not tightly connect to the main story).
As regards the story, I would say it is quite short, bland, straightforward. Each book took me about one hour to finish.
Overall, the aspect of visual representation is the predominate reason for recommending this game, while the other part are just at an average level.
Since the first book is free to try, if you like the art style after a taste, you can buy the other books during a discount.

Very enjoyable murder mystery adventure game with high production value, good cinematography, a strong story, and genuinely excellent acting.  The game has a novel problem solving engine which involves identifying contradictions in individual character statements.  The interface was a bit unusual, and took some time to get used to, but was also weirdly satisfying once the routines sunk in.  The story is compelling and the characters have the right balance of richness dimensionality for a story of this kind.  A couple complaints would be that the storyline itself has some small internal inconsistencies, which are not identified as contradictions within the gameplay.  This proved to be mildly frustrating at times.  The other complaint would be that the process of finding contradictions only took place character-by-character and not across characters (unless it happened to come up in that context).  This made the game more manageable as a puzzler, and still satisfying.  But there were times when characters would say contradictory things with respect to each other, and there was no way to cross examine suspects and access those kind of conversation threads.  Nevertheless, I strongly recommend it for those who enjoy neat, self-contained, story-driven mystery adventure games.

I'm a big fan of point and click adventure games, and I equally enjoy reading cozy murder mystery books. That said, I jumped at the chance to play through Contradiction, an adventure game with a bit of a twist on the traditional formula -- there's actually no "point and click". The character you control, Inspector Jenks, is controlled entirely via a few keyboard keys. Furthermore, the vast majority of puzzles are dialogue-driven (spotting contradictions in the statements of Edenton village's residents). There are few inventory-based puzzles, but the use of inventory items is very simplified, so just a heads up in case you were expecting more traditional adventure game elements such as combining inventory items.
This different take on adventure gaming is refreshing, and I found myself growing to like Jenks' character quite a lot, as he charmingly asks questions regarding the suspicious death of a university student, Kate Vine. Afternoon turns to evening as Jenks' investigation progresses, and I loved how the atmosphere got a bit more suspenseful as time went on. It's the "little things" that demonstrated so much attention to detail that impressed me -- for example, as Jenks walks past a bush, its leaves rustle in the wind, showing us that as night approaches, things are getting a bit more eery. The camera-work in this adventure game is excellent, as is the music soundtrack. The acting overall isn't bad, and I was very happy with the game interface. I particularly enjoyed being able to fast-travel to hotspots within the village via the map (the "d" key by default), as well as the handy built-in hint system, accessed via "a". The hint system gives the player a gentle nudge in the right direction without any spoilers, and it was a very cool thing to see.
While I could go on about the many things I enjoyed about Contradiction, I want to stress that I don't think the actual storyline was of a very high standard. I've written a bit more about my opinion on the storyline at the end of the review, underneath a MINOR SPOILER warning.
The actual dialogue-driven puzzle-solving is excellent, as is the general atmosphere (to include cinematography and music). However, I think the storyline gets more and more ridiculous as Jenks' evening progresses, to the point where there really is no cohesion in storytelling (in my opinion).
As Jenks' delves deeper into Kate's mysterious death, he stumbles upon the subject matters of hallucinogens, paganism, business ethics, mind control, AND satanism. I felt like in the later stages of the game, writer Tim Follin just threw in whatever seemed "taboo" into the plot, to the point where the story becomes a bit of a disjointed mess.

I rarely, if ever, actually use this software as an actual video game. It's a chat client at this point. Most people will say that the character creator is the highlight of this game -- and they'd be right. The character creator is one of the highest points this game achieves, and it achieves it in style.
...However, don't expect to make anything particularly awesome without first dropping real cash on this thing. Costume sets are quite overpriced, too, sometimes requiring the user to spend up to $10 for a single set (mind you, each set doesn't contain that many costume pieces to begin with). Being under the F2P model, you can expect the game to nickel and dime you, but ever since the takeover from Perfect World Entertainment, they've really gone overboard with the microtransactions, all while the devs have simply stopped caring about the game as a whole.
There's no ambition to be had; anything cool you see upon booting up the game was very likely put there years ago, when the game was in its prime, under the guidance of developers with the drive to make a legitimately good game. The ambition once had by the development team has since dwindled to nothing. As a result, content is largely stagnant. Most of the new content is half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥shlock they expect you to pay top dollar for, and anything that's halfway decent is shuttered away behind a lockbox which is essentially a big gamble that you have to pay $1 a pop to open -- and believe me, it may not sound like much, but that will add up quick.
Beyond the diseased, sickly cash cow Perfect World reduced this game to, it's also not that amazing as a game in itself. Sure, the gameplay can be deceptively nice at first, and may even feel like it has great variety -- and in some aspects, it does. But like everything in this game, it seems to only get worse as time goes on, and you'll find yourself fighting the same classes of reskinned, repurposed bad guys over and over again, doing the same types of objectives passing off as something more interesting, all while running around in relatively uninteresting, mundane locales that only have the passing resemblance to something with inspiration put into them.
You can also largely forget about questing, because an expansion introduced a while back basically made it redundant to do so. Instead of adventuring through the game and leveling your character up through time, dedication, and some approximation of hard work, you can instead just queue yourself up for one of the many "alerts" in the game that takes you and four other players to a self-contained instance to fight a boss and get an easy XP or monetary reward. Rinse, repeat, ad nauseam.
The graphics themselves can be summed up in one word: "Meh". They're not bad, but they're not exactly that great, either. On high settings, the visuals can look crisp and well-defined, with pleasing particle effects scattered about to whet your appetite. But the keen eye will notice that the art design is all over the place. This game has a BIG problem with artistic cohesion: you'll often find high-poly models with highly detailed textures in one place, and as little as five feet away will run into a very low-poly, blurry-textured mess of a model right next to it. It can't decide if it wants to look like a PS3 game or a PS2 game, and can be very distracting.
Furthermore, the actual work put into the environments is lazy at best. There's misaligned and missing textures all over the place, spots where you can see straight through the level, and even simply disgusting corner-cutting measures that one can only assume the developers thought nobody would notice, such as entire buildings being misplaced and left out in the middle of the street, or pieces of level geometry hanging a full meter away from where they're supposed to be placed.
The community is also quite lackluster. The overall population of the game is low at best, so I don't know where they're getting this "thousands of heroes" figure from on the bullet points. Maybe Cryptic means in terms of individual characters created and stored in the database, not even taking into account whether they're still active or not. Anywho, the PvP community is - as you'd expect - largely full of pompous blowhards that gloat over their ability to break this game's move sets or exploit some failure of the lackadaisical developers. On the other hand, the roleplay community is largely full of ERP'ers looking to get a quick fix off similarly horny players, all while roaming the one populated RP zone in scantily clad, large-chested women.
In terms of the general "I'm just here to level" player, I can't really complain there. They usually don't say much unless they want to sell an item in zone, or party up to do an alert.
All in all, I'd say avoid this one, unless you REALLY want to make some characters, like being begged by desperate devs to spend cash, or don't have much else better to do, such is the case for me.

This is a fun, addictive, and surprisingly deep logistics puzzle that promises a lot of playtime and replay potential despite a lack of concrete challenge options.
On its surface, the game appears relatively simple -- place three main types of buildings (apartments, office, and retail) along with the support staff and facilities necessary to keep them happy. The challenge comes in balancing the various rooms and services on both a spatial and logistical level -- the higher-end commercial and residential clients want a greater variety of stores and restaurants, but to build these facilities you have to invest a lot in support services that incur a sizeable daily maintenance fee. Managing these tradeoffs in an expedient manner presents a fulfilling puzzle.
Once you get the hang of the various systems in a sandbox format, the game currently presents 10 scenarios with 3 tiers of challenge conditions. These impose a variety of space constraints or other obstacles and often demand an efficient design and expansion strategy to pull them off. The developers promise more scenarios to come and the day-one modding support promises to enhance the work of this one-designer, one-developer team.
Overall, it's certainly worth the price tag. I watched several hours of pre-release review copies of this game on streaming services and emerged impressed enough to pre-order. I haven't been disappointed.

The galaxy has a life on its on, pirate factions roam around and other empires go on about their business. And the best part, you can choose exactly where to intervene and at what level. You want to add more missile launchers to a specific line of frigates, do that. You want to decide what planet to colonize first, do that instead. Whit an excellent automation tool, you can choose where you want to put your focus. This way you also really feel like you are managing an empire. Distant Worlds is a RTS game where you command either an empire or a pirate faction and attempt to dominate the universe. The universe can be very large with many different possible races interacting. Each race has its own advantages and disadvantages. The gameplay is very deep, and can take quite a while to get the hang of. Thankfully, the game allows you to automate as much of your empire as you wish, while you figure out what and how to play the game. If you should so wish, you can play a purely economic game, letting the AI focus on war, or command your fleets to victory, while the AI handles production. You can also do everything yourself if you should so choose. The game gives great flexibility in how you choose to run your empire.
The game does have a "grand menace" the Shakturi that will come and blow all your planets to smithereens if you are not careful. As such, its also great that you can turn them off! There is a fairly deep storyline for an RTS, and covers a very large timespan.
The game also gives you the freedom to design your own ships, however, there are balancing issues with this. As of writing this, you can simply build ONLY carriers and dominate the universe easily.
The game's diplomacy system is fairly shallow, and interactions with Pirate factions is annoyingly limited. It does give a breakdown of how other factions feel about you, which is great for determining who to kill first. A deep web of alliances however forces you to choose your targets carefully. One empire may look weak, but might be allied to two of the biggest empires in the game. Interestingly, there is a reputation system, and this greatly affects how other empires can react to you.
The spying mechanic is decently well developed for an RTS. Assassinating other factions leaders and commanders can be an excellent way to weaken them. Spies can sabatoge bases, destroying them utterly. This can actually weaken a race's defenses if you use this right, but its random nature is iffy.
The game allows you to create maps as you wish, from the system's star, down to every last asteroid. It also has a random map generator that does a pretty good job. Planets are your typical Earth/Ocean/Desert/Ice/Barren etc... You can find leftover damaged or abandoned ships throughout the universe, and incomplete planet killers can be claimed and finished for your personal useage.
The game has a difficulty slider that affects how the AI plays, however, this can be further modified by how you set up the match. You can make the game a veritable cakewalk, or tool your galaxy to be as hostile to you as possible.
Victory conditions are very customizeable! Decide exactly how you want the game to end! Or not, sandbox is possible too.
A major complaint I have about the game is the lack of an interactive tutorial. The game does have a manual that describes everything IN the game, as well as how to play, however it can amount to a fair bit of reading, and is not particularly well organized.
So, quick summery:
Pros:
Deep gameplay
Research and ship design mechanics
Well developed spy mechanic
Randomly generated maps, as well as designable maps.
Extremely customizeable gameplay
Sandbox or victory conditions.
Cons:
Deep gameplay, so takes time to learn.
No tutorial system

Today, I'm going to write a review for Reassembly, and I hope it reaches everyone who is thinking about purchasing this game.
Where to start...
Reassembly throws you into a hostile universe, riddled with factions that care only about your destruction.
When starting, there is a very gradual, and intuitive learning curve, with just enough complexity to keep you coming back for more. Even after unlocking all factions, and playing with a few which are community created, I still find this game highly replayable. Reason? Space domination of course!
There still seem to be a few balancing issues with several of the factions, but this game is damn well polished.
- Very high replay value. With an endless combination of building possibilities, Reassembly rivals some of the more well known indie games. With multiple universes/galaxies to explore, and constantly discovering new player created enemies. I have to give this game a 9/10 for replayability alone
- Very nice points system (R, C, P). The system seems designed to make you feel very powerful, and like you are accomplishing a lot when playing. However it does not make you feel over powered (except some player created factions). Player factions aside this game makes you feel like you are getting your moneys worth. 10/10
- Excellent use of propulsion/collision, and super cool, almost retro feeling graphics make Reassembly feel very polished. 9/10
- Amazing ecosystems. Reassembly has one of the most organic ecosystems I have ever encountered. From enemies repopulating, to the way a single space plant can launch a seed, stick to another asteroid, and begin growing to produce more seeds and plants, alone, makes this game worth it's price point. ShUT UP AND TAkE MY MUNNY! 10/10
- Music. I don't even know how to explain this one - The soundtrack to Reassembly is one of the absolute best soundtracks you could ever hope for in a space game. It really makes you feel at home in the game, and is extremely well done. Whoever created the music for Reassembly deserves a raise of epic proportions! I would have to say that the soundtrack drew me in more than anything. Usually when playing a game, I like to mute the music volume, and play my own tunes, but with this, I just like to turn the music volume up! Bravo to the Maestro! 10/10
Overall I have to say that I have fully enjoyed the experience bestowed upon me by Reassembly. If you're thinking about getting this game, I absolutely recommend jumping the fence, and going for it! I hope to see updates to this game in the future, but as of right now, the game is amazing as it stands.
Overall score for this game:
9.7/10

Ryse: Son of Rome is decidedly mediocre third person action game.
Ryse was originally released to showcase the graphical prowess of the Xbox One and the Cryengine and the visuals certainly still hold up well. The sound effects and sound track are pretty decent too. Unfortunately these were pretty much the only elements Crytek nailed with the game.
The action combat owes a lot to Batman: Arkham series and starts out decent enough. Unfortunately there's very little depth to the extremely repetitive combat and you spend the whole game fighting against the exact same enemies. Another big problem are the executions. You'll be doing a lot of these QTE takedowns and they really break the flow of the combat without adding anything to the experience.
The story and the writing are extremely weak too. The setting bears little resemblance to the historical Roman empire, instead we are given an unsatisfying hodgepodge of characters and story elements from different eras and locations. The game is full of immersion breaking elements too, from the semi-automatic scorpios and the exploding barrels to the ridiculous rendition of the Colosseum.
Ryse: Son of Rome is an extremely bland and repetitive experience and I wouldn't recommend it unless the only thing you care about in games is great graphics.
I played through the main campaign on centurion difficulty and found the experience rather easy overall.
The good:
- Impressive visuals
- Nice audio
The bad:
- Extremely repetitive and shallow combat
- Terrible QTE executions break the flow of the combat
- Boring boss fights
- Poor blending of combat animations
- Terrible leveling system
- Extremely linear
- Weak writing and story
- Poorly realized setting
The ugly:
- Few low quality models really stand out when the rest of the game looks so good

NEUTRAL - a pretty, but empty shell
Ryse: Son of Rome has mind-blowingly beautiful graphics. This is the prettiest game I have ever seen. Considering it is already over three years old, this is even more astonishing.
Alas the story, the voice actors and the gameplay disappoint. The story is well presented, but ultimately too far from reality and the ending can be guessed half an hour into the game.
Instead of the roman gods and godesses, the seasons summer and winter are the major influencing 'gods' in this game. Why make this game even more unrealistic and waste so much potential on the myriad of classic gods at disposal?
The choice of voice actors is rather odd. The 'roman' soldiers have as heavy of and 'british' accent as the British barbarians itself! This is not acceptable.
The gameplay is the most disappointing element of this game. The rhythm-based combat such as in Arkham is woefully simplistic. There are two heavy and light attacks, which you mash over, over and over again in this game. Even on the highest difficulty which you are allowed to start on (2nd highest), this game is way too easy, as each combat is easily doable with instant blocks, mashing the attack buttons until an execution on an enemy is possible, during which the main character is invulnerable. This goes on for about 6 hours. Over, over, and over again.
Occasional pili throw and ballista segments only distract for a while until it gets back to the repetitive combat system. While the executions are stylish, they don't seem to be important, as, once started, they go through, even if you miss all the QTEs. Also executing almost every single soldier in this game (instead of a few important ones) makes this move appear really mundane.
The beautiful graphical immersion is severely hindered by flashing green collectable objects. Addionally fire ballistas fire almost as fast as machine guns, which is in stark contrast to the realistic graphics.
Occasional glitches (stuttering fellow roman soldier), bugs (one boss randomly not working as intended) and awkward camera movement add to the detriment of this game.
Not recommended! Strikingly beautiful game, albeit ruined the a boring and highly repetitive combat system, dull story and camera issues. Possibly recommended if you like mindless and repetitive action with amazing graphics. If possible I would rate give rather a neutral than a negative review.

7/10. Good game but not great. The setting, the music, the art style, and the writing are all good, but the sameness of the aesthetic does get a bit monotonous by the end of the game. So much brown and gray everywhere. It's also a little on the short side, and has the usual flaws of point-and-click adventure games. You know, like "I'm stuck because I didn't see this tiny object that's barely visible against the monochrome background." If that doesn't bother you then you will probably like Primordia more than I did.

Digging through Wadjet Eye catalogue is a pleasure every time, so when I finally found the time to try Primordia out, I wasn't expecting any less than a great adventure. But wow, I wasn't expecting it to be
great, either.
Obviously, most of the reviewers around here have already described the game much better than a non-native English speaker ever could, though it never hurts to praise a masterpiece. And as with any other masterpiece, it doesn't seem necessary to break it down to individual components and discuss whether the mechanics lack gunplay. The only thing that matters here is the feeling, what it's like to live through the story of Primordia.
You know when you're close to finishing a book so good you almost don't want to read the last few pages? It's as if a significant part of your life is about to be taken, and you try to savor every single word there's left. Oh boy, I still remember the devastation I felt as a kid when 'Pippi Longstocking' ended.
A horrible yet extremely satisfying moment of experiencing something beautiful and important. And it's exactly what a quality adventure game should be – a book you will never forget.
Primordia bears this very feeling in its core logic. Its world, consisting of rust and despair, might not be of the attractive kind, but the minute you dive into it, you'll have enough reasons to stay. It is surprisingly smart, detailed, vivid and, even less expectedly, highly amusing thanks to the characters populating it. Despite the depressing tones, the amount of intelligent humour makes it one of the most likeable worlds in the recent adventure games history.
No wonder leaving it is incredibly hard. I found myself thinking, "This is not enough! Why would you end it so soon? I want more!" and loading random saves to listen to random dialogues once again. But while Primordia surely is a short experience, I doubt making it longer would've made any difference. You just can't have enough of worlds like this one.
Primordia is indeed a hidden gem of the genre. Well, not really hidden anymore, but it definitely is something that deserves more attention. Every piece of attention you can afford, to be precise.

They were trying to fix up a crashed airship, a relic of the long-forgotten War of the Four Cities, so they could at last fly away from the Dunes and go wherever they want. Unfortunately, their progress is halted when a mysterious robot named Scraper shows up and "plunders" their power core--an item they cannot survive without. When trying to find power in the Dunes fails, they have no choice but to travel to Metropol, the last city, where their power core has been taken. To make matters worse, an anceint robot named MetroMind has claimed your power core for the betterment of the city, since it is crumbling under her inept rule and she needs all the power she can get.
From there, it is up to you how the story ends. Choose carefully, your every move has consequences.
The voice-acting is masterfully done. Every character is unique and full of personality. The story and lore are very well-crafted as well. Unraveling the mystery of the world you're in never fails to be fascinating, and if you play through it just right, the ending is beautiful and cathartic.

By the way (this is a bit of a tangent), if people liked the darker undertones of this and was looking for something even more graphic and unsettling while being open to the prospect of digging up a visual novel, Kara no Shoujo is probably my all time favorite among murder mysteries across gaming media.  Higurashi is also up there if you're big on a heavy read, and that is on Steam! I was sort of expecting some super dark twists out of Contradiction considering the age gate, but it doesn't quite get there. For those familiar with FMV games of yore, it is certainly no Phantasmagoria in graphic content; Contradiction is quite tame! Still, it did do an excellent job in satiating my FMV murder mystery hunger.  Speaking of FMV murder myster hunger with respect to Contradiction, however, I'll certainly be hungry for a sequel!

>Simplistic design for easy to pick up gameplay

Cons:
>Card based combat restrictive as it only allows 3 random moves from a pool determines by your equipment
>Characters and enemies are generic and repetitive
>Non-engaging story as there is no voice acting and characters lack movement and have preset emotions
>Animations in battle are almost non-existant and feel clunky (swings sword for a kick attack)
>Lack of depth, very story driven
>Music can get repetitive and is rather forgettable (the battle theme doesn't seem to change, nor is it any good)

Hopefully the developers work upon this beautiful art-style and game design and perhaps expand into something more, engaging and deep.

It is a very unique experience and you will not be disappointed.

So this game is awesome, but not everything about it is good. Strange design choices and weird bugs are plentiful in this game. Thus, this is a list of everything - that I have found - that I did NOT like about this game
Everybody knows the stupid builders from the movies that dropped out of school in grade 10 and couldn't do anything else. Thankfully, however, they actually do their job. In this game they might as well have replaced the workmen with plantpots - even those things work faster.
But it isn't necesarilly how slow they are - though they do want a lunchbreak every five minutes and then complain that the building that they haven't even built yet doesn't have a diner in it - that is the issue. Though certain tasks do seem to take longer than they should - such as the moving of boxes - it is quickly resolved with the speed up button.
No, what absolutely bothers me is that they work as ineficiently as the American government. "Oh let us quickly put up half of this wall and then move on to the next floor and do the other half after that yes that makes complete sense" said no one ever. Except the developers of this game, apparently.
The order in which they build things is extremely simple - you give them the order and they do it. So let's say you decide to build half a bloody building and suddenly you realise you don't have enough power - which, by the way, brings me to another issue I will talk about in a moment. You will have to replace the power thing with a better power thing. You can also instantly build a new one - which is nice - but replacing one is sometimes better for the daily expenses.
So you want to replace it. Well, don't worry. Just remove the power thingy and you can put a new one down. Thankfully you can instantly remove it too. No actual human labour required. Oh, but wait. Apparently the power thingy leaves boxes behind. And although you have the magical power of instantly placing and removing something you cannot move a bloody box.
Oh, and since you only have two workers it will take them a long time to finish the new building. There is no cancel - sort of, I'll get to that later - and your entire building is out of power. You can't place a new one down because the boxes are in the way and if you didn't expand your building so you can place it somewhere else you'll have to wait.
This could easily be fixed with a priority system. You can set which thing you want to prioritise and they'll do that before all the other guff.
There is already some sort of priority system in place - they will for example build elevators before other things so people can at least move around. But if you really want them to finish this copy service so the offices won't complain anymore before finishing three floors, well, too bad.
Remember what I said about there being no way to cancel your tasks? Well, there is. Sort of. It doesn't return your money though which is absolutely stupid and it's bugged. I found that even
I cancel an order it wouldn't actually be canceled. Instead the workers would still do that thing I asked them
to do it just wouldn't actually be there this time. In fact I one time even got my worker stuck on the roof because the room he tried to build/not build was canceled. To get him out I had to build the thing I tried to
in the first place!
So usually it's the landlords that are absolutely merciless, but in this game it's the tenants that are annoying about everything. Apparently we live in some sort of distopian future where the democratic government has given tenants all the rights they could possibly want.
There is no such thing as a contract so if they want to leave they can - though if you want them to leave you have to pay money. Although they are usually very mild - for example a shop can run a loss for days, if not weeks at a time because there are too many competitors in the area taking away their customers and - as long as you don't overrent them - they won't leave.
But the moment you cut out the power,
they'll leave your building extremely quickly. So if you want to replace the power thingy I spoke about earlier you'll find that half of your people have left - leaving only boxes. And as I said earlier, they take extremely long to move. Not just that, the entire office is gone so you'll also have to pay for that.
It's not just with electricity. Water, gas, tv, phone - they all have the same issue. The only difference is that almost every room uses electricity. Especially once you get a big tower going you'll find that replacing ever single office becomes quite a pain.
There are more small things wrong with this that I won't go into major detail with:
So why, despite all its problems, do I recommend this game? I can describe that easily with just a single word:
Satisfaction
This game is pure, pure satisfaction. Despite all the problems it has, it feels so satisfying to build up your tower, to build more offices. It feels extremely satisfying to have to work on a new tower because the last one failed.
Everything you do is for a reason. And I mean everything. Let's say you build an office. You have different options for offices that can enter the space. Legal, accounting, creative - they all come with their own needs and their own money bags to fill your pockets.
The cheaper ones will have fewer requirements but will give you less money. The more expensive ones might want a courier service or a copy service - in some cases both. Or they might want a phone line, which also costs money.
With more offices you can get prestige and you can also get buzz from restaurants and-
This is a deep, though mistakenbly simplistic game. And the best thing about it? You can take your own pace. Although money is an issue, it isn't that big of a deal that you have to keep paying attention to it. Want to hold off making level II appartments? Don't wory, just make the regular ones for now.
I
recommend this game. It's only under the not recommended section because some people want to see why they
buy this game, which you can't really find under the recommended section.

This is NOT a paid review.
A few months ago Kasedo Games contacted our live stream at Diz.tv and asked us to try out this game. It was an early build still, but we were intrigued and so we gave it a try. Almost instantly the Sim Tower nostalgia hit us and everyone in the chat community. We played the game for about 16 hours over four days and really enjoyed it.
The game is sim tower only as something I can compare it to. You build the tower, place the rooms, and the elevators and stairs and manage the finances. There the similarities end. In Project High Rise you must also anticipate the needs of the tenants and provide them everything from copier services to high-speed internet connections.
The higher paying tenants want more from you than the lower paying ones do, and will move out quicker. There is also an economy simulation in the background, this means some types of tenants will be more popular and pay more, or become less popular and pay less. There is so much to cover and balance here its a challenge to keep up.
I am glad to see this game release! If you are a fan of simulation and management games I think you would have a great time with this one.
Thanks again Kasedo Games for pointing me here! If you hadn't I would have never known about this little gem.

One of the deepest 4X space strategies ever finally came to steam with really appealing price (well, their previous publisher prices was real outrage).
Despite lacking some visual appeal the game is unusually deep and replayable. Somewhat hard to learn (read in-game encyclopedia) but surprisingly fun when you master it. At the start you can think it is really slow paced (research is
and hyperjumping takes forever, especially when ship is running out of fuel) but in a half an hour you'll find yourself splitting your last couple of combat-ready warships between defence and offence simultaneously recruiting troops and leading planetary invasion plus planning your mining operations for a couple of wars ahead.
So, sparing details here's my list of pros/cons for this game:
- No jumplanes/wormholes or binding ships to solar systems - your fleets are free to go anywhere.
- Economy model: division to player controlled 'state' ships based and 'private' AI civilians is unique for the whole genre.
- Storyline: no more usual 'exterminate/dominate' endgames.
- Random encounters of epic scale: imagine ancient battlefield with half a hundred damaged ships to claim either for immediate firepower or for tech inside.
- Unforgiving AI: yeah, set your difficulty to max and be gone in first 15 minutes.
- Diplomacy: no more fiddling with 'if I add 1 credit to this deal will it work?'. You get immediate assesment of your demands and possibilities are really diverse.
- Space combat: no micromanagement, no direct controlled ships. Construct your ships, form fleets and watch them burn.
- Ground combat: no micromanagement too, just make sure enough of your troops safely land
- Automation: every single aspect can be automated, starting from planetary taxes, through automatic colonization and even automatic fleet formation and attack/defence missions.
- Visuals: they are from 2000.
- Sound: pew-pew-pew, clang-clang (getting worse when you zoom into busy spaceport).
- In-game help, especially in ship designer: 'what does damage control +40% mean?'
- A bit slow UI (well, it is responsible at least, and doesn't slow down in epic 100-on-100 space battles).

Written October 2 2014: Cosmonautica is still in the Early access stages of its development, but what I've seen so far looks pretty solid:  there's an organic feelling to the local economy, a tongue in cheek sense of humor that feels right with what they're trying to do, and a good vibe to the crew and ship that give it a lot of personality (right down to the religions your crew belong to).
That said:
- The game does crash a fair bit (Probably 4 or 5 times in the last hour)
- Some of the missions you pick up aren't particularly clear on how to resolve them (i.e.: Told to kill a pirate who was coming to the station I was at... waited for a few cycles for the pirate to show up, got bored and left and was then revealed I had to leave the station to engage them).
- Would be nice to see more danger associated with certain cargo. Hauling fertilizer may not yield high profits, but if moving guns meant getting the attention of pirates and grabby governments, I might think twice.
- One mechanic in the game is that a more skilled crew needs more things which is neat (i.e.: the 5 star pilot needs entertainment, exercise, social exchanges, etc... compared to the 1 star who needs a toilet, food, and a place to sleep). That said; I cannot see what the difference is between the 1 star and the 5 star which makes the need for developing your crew a little moot (i.e.: Maybe a 5 star pilot keeps the ship from being hit in combat and plots faster trips, the better mechanic makes the ships engines faster, the medic buffs everyone so everyone does better, etc)
- On the same note, I found that the more skilled my crew was (5 star pilot for instance), the more difficult it was to keep their morale even somewhat positive. There are just too many needs that accumulate and the time it takes to service each one (while the others continue to increase) don't leave a lot of room to do anything but go from one need to the next. Possible solution may be to have certain rooms service multiple needs at the same time (the club could be exercise, social, and entertainment and the chef's lounge could be social, food, and fatigue, etc...), or to slow the rate of need accumulation.
- Despite the variety of planets, would like to see a greater emphasis on more illegal products which might force different paths through space (Weapons could be illegal in a particular area requiring you to step around them, etc...). At the moment, Narcotics is the only product that falls into that category, but its implemented very well.
- Would like to see 'me' in the game. In the sense that I'm a disembodied 'thing' that tells the crew what to do and where to go, yet I'm not an actual crew member. Would be good to create your avatar, pick the skill you start with, then filling in gaps amongst the crew as you proceed.
- Would like to see more ship variety and the ability to rename my own ship.
Now all this said and done; I'm writing this review early into their cycle so I'm guessing lots of the above will get changed or addressed, but for now I'm happy to recommend this game to anyone who wants to bend the 'verse to their whims.

The story is a little predictable, but I suppose it would have to be. We're in Ben Hur, Nero, Hail Caesar- Land, after all. That being said, it feels more like a Greek Tragedy than a Roman Epic... (I hope I'm not spoiling anything for people with a good sense of predicting story-line-dynamics, but let's be honest if you're that good at story-prediction, you've picked the wrong game.) I feel sorry for the Hero. I feel sorry for some, (SOME) of the "villains." I feel sorry for the game. (You'll probly get it once you've completed the campaign.)
The controls aren't hard. They're just a bit tricky. Especially when you scale up or down in difficulty, (yup, you can actually challenge yourself by scaling DOWN the difficulty! The timing shifts EEEEver so slightly, so you have to adjust to it, all over again. Not really much in the way of replayabillity, but there it is...)
The Graphics are pretty. You can probably MAKE them stunning, if your PC has the juice for it, but sooner or later, it's gonna mess with the game if you do. (And even if it doesn't, you'll likely run into issues in multiplayer.)
I'm not gonna go into Pros & Cons on this one. There are equally good and bad factors in this game.
I AM gonna cover one slight Con though... There's a massive "void" that crops up amidst the stunning campaign scenes and epic battles and what-not, the multiplayer Gladiator Arena (Don't bother with The Arena unless you've logged at least 100+ hours in the game on hardest difficulty, or you'll get turned into shish-kebab by those "happy few" who loiter on the servers who have, and live for nothing else than handing your a## to you in any game they can.) - The story is "High Drama" and lots, and lots, and lots of tragedy and insults and doing-wrongs and revenge and what not; and if you enjoy that sort of thing, (which, for the first playthrough, I do,) this is a game for you. However, there's not a whole lot of Funfactor, and as I've said, little to no Replayabillity, unless you enjoy Campagn replay for that "perfect" achivement, or Arena play, for that EPIC REVENGE on that guy who killed you in 3 seconds flat on your first time playing, just because he "could,"  (which I don't) this is not the game for you.
Dear Devs. It's a beautiful game, with an intense dramatic, (and very "Roman") story, but it's a little "open-and-shut," isn't it? I reccomend this game for fans of pretty hack'n'slash games with progressive story with good depth. However, there's room for bigger and better things... (A simple expansion campaign would do wonders. Maybe you could play the role of the "Tragic Villain I mentioned?" Even that would be a step in the right direction, wouldn't it?)

Very nice game, delivers what it advertises on the cover.
As far as MMOs go this one stays true to the typical grind and craft system where most missions come down to killing 10 of this or collecting 20 of that. However the real fun is in the setting and the way the bigger super villain missions are presented.
A lot of the more climactic quests where you finally face of with a super villain is really immersive and well done. You feel like a super hero saving the world from one of it's greatest threats. These are usually instance maps where you don't have to run around with 100 other public players but rather only with your super group.
The customizations and costumes are really great and there is a lot of variety and depth. The power system also allows you to create the hero you want, however this is very limited in free to play. The costume slots also allow you to change the look and feel of your hero on the fly and adds to the immersion.
When you reach a high enough level, you also unlock the ability to create your own nemesis. This is probably my favourite feature of Champions Online, since you use the same creation toolset used to create your own characters. This allows you to really customize your nemesis and put just as much attention and love into making a nemesis as you do making your hero.
The nemesis goes on to generate his own random encounters and missions, where you have to stop him. You really develop a history with the nemesis and look forward to each encounter.
I cannot say much about the PvP, since I am not a fan of it in these sort of MMOs. I think unfortunately it suffers from the same problems as other MMO PvP games in terms of meta and conformity.
Finally, I do need to add that there is a fairly big gap between free to play and subscription. Although you can get most of the main content and experience on f2p, subscription just opens the game up so much more. You are able to create a freeform character, which means you can choose almost any powers from the power pool (depending on skill trees). The expansion missions that are in included with subscription also add hours of fun.
Overall a great game. It has been labelled as dead for quite a few years. But each time I have the money to go back to it, it offers the same level of enjoyment I have grown accustomed to.

Mythic Wonders: The Philosopher's Stone [CE*], is a HOPA* game, developed by Organic 2 Digital and published by Artifex Mundi
*CE - Collector's Edition
*HOPA - Hidden Object Puzzle Adventure.
Since this is an collector's edition game, it comes with some extra features, that aren't available in the regular edition game.
I want to mentioned that the visuals for this game is nicely done. The visuals can be adjusted in the option menu.
I want to mentioned that the audio for this game is well done even if it's simplistic and somewhat repetitive. The audio can be adjusted in the option menu as well.
There are only four difficulty game modes to choose from: Casual, Advanced, Expert and Custom.
Journal Notebook has two sections: Notes and Objectives.
There are interactive items in the game. Interactive items are marked with a symbol. Most of these interactive items do require extra items before they can be interact with.
The interactive map allows the player to fast travel between each location quickly. It also indicates there are tasks that needs to be done at certain locations.
Elemental Artifact is found towards the beginning of the game. But it can't be used immediately because it's elements needs to be found in each of the worlds. Light; Earth; Water; Fire; Air and Aether. Artifact is used in certain situation. Like using the gate portal to access the next world.
Most of the hidden object scenes consists of find "x" amount, traditional word lists, picture items with little or no interaction. Most of the hidden object scenes can be replayed in the extra content section.
Most of the game's puzzles are fairly easy to solve without having the need to skip any of them. Most of the game's puzzles can be replayed in the extra content section.
There's a bonus chapter, but it can be access, only after the main portion of the game is fully completed. The bonus chapter is sequel to the main story.
Seventeen different morphing objects to find throughout the game.
There are twenty-four different achievements that can be unlocked from playing the game. Each of these achievements do has some requirement before they can be unlocked. The achievements are tied to 'Game Story,' 'Hidden Object Scenes,' 'Puzzle/Mini-Games,' 'Collectibles.'
There are total of five different trading cards. You only get the three of those cards from the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading card: Purchased from Steam's Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and it's Booster Pack Creator.
Final thoughts, I've found this game enjoyable to certain extend. The replay value for this game is low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

This is a typical hidden object game, really. If you've played one of these you've played, well, most. I say "most" because I found this one to be very lacking and inferior to other hidden object games.
The positives are what you'd find in any HO game: lots of gorgeous, hand-drawn images, fitting music, puzzles, challenges, etc. This particular game is more enjoyable than more because you can get all of the achievements in one playthrough whereas a lot require you to play through twice to get everything. (I'm looking at you specifically, Harmonia Mundi, with your BS achievements to solve all HO games but then solve all Mahjongg games, which is impossible in one playthrough!) I found it to be relatively bug-free although it does NOT appreciate when you alt-tab to another application.
However, the main storyline left so many questions that never got solved in the bonus area. Don't misunderstand me. HO games rarely have deep plots; but this was lacking even more than that. I can't say more without spoilers, but the main villain in this effectively came out of nowhere with no explanation for his actions. That's the biggest example.
But the voice acting.... holy sweet jumping Jesus! BOTH of the leading ladies' (assuming that they were different actresses) are HORRIBLE! They define the term "wooden acting"! In fact, I wonder if the term "acting" can really apply. There are a lot of HO games out there with actors who at least put in an effort to perform the lines with some degree of accuracy. Not here! "Oh, golly. I'm going to read my lines as though I really don't want to be here and I'm severely caffeine deficient and I just want to go to sleep." Bad, bad, BAD!
I won't say that I don't recommend this because there actually are worse HO games out there -- even worse voice acting, bugs out the wazoo, and so forth. But be aware that you will probably be scratching your head at the ending and the lead VO "actresses" are really bad.

I got game over around 6 times with different equipment combinations until I gave up and changed my game setting to Easy, which felt horrible, to be honest. You can’t really level up much in this game after doing all the side quests, so I was stuck on what to do. I believe I was at the max level with all characters. Anyway, I finally defeated the Enchantress. I don’t know if I messed up somewhere in the story, but the battle system had 3 slots for characters and I only had 2 max at all times, so there’s that tidbit.
When it comes to the story, I really did enjoy this game. The story was a nice fairy tale-like one, not too complicated but good enough, in my opinion. I really liked the main characters—Elizabeth and Marcus. Although, Elizabeth did get on my nerves at times when she kept going against Marcus’s advice.
Yet, she just kept doing her thing, even though it ended up badly most of the time. I’m not sure how much the choices in the game actually affected the story, but I did feel like I messed up a couple of times when making choices. In the end, the game did have a nice ending, although I feel like it was a bit abrupt. I would have liked a bit more closure to it. Overall, this was a fun game and one I’d recommend, especially if you get the season pass! It’s very nice and well worth the price. I hope this developer makes more games like this. Story rich games are fun and the added battle card mechanism was very enjoyable! I’m looking forward to more games like this one.

The easiest way I can describe this is, Project Highrise is to SimTower, as Stardew Valley is to Harvest Moon.
Take a classic formula, and expand upon it without scope creep. I say with no hyperbole I've been waiting for a game like this for years.

Target Audience: SimTower Lovers, or Micromanagers in general
Summary:
Project Highrise knows what it is: a modern day SimTower. And like that old game: it has that addictive quality to it, where a certain reviewer was planning to play the game for 5 hours....and ended up playing it 12. That should give you an indication of how you can get lost in the gameplay: in all of the good ways. The ecosystem that is created is complex: you'll have to watch a variety of factors: noise, trash, etc, in order to keep your various tenants happy, and not paying attention to those factors could bite you if you're not careful. In addition, there's a LOT of information to work with here if you're looking to use it, so you can plan out your own custom tower of perfection, down to the name of each individual shop if you so desire. Add on a modding scene available on day one with actual usable documentation (which in my experience is RARE AS HELL), and you've got a great simulator/management game that will keep you entertained for a good while. I do have concerns about the long run of the game due to the lack of random events that seems to occur: but I also wonder if that will be easily fixed by the modding scene. And most of my other complaints are minor: granted, ones that keep the game from being the top in the genre, but not ones that keep fans of the genre from picking up this game. A worthy buy at the price point.
Lists:
Positives:
The ecosystem created is a bit complex, and it's complex is the best ways. If you don't pay attention to all of the factors, you'll find that no one's happy, and it could end up snowballing into multiple people leaving.
Lots of different rooms and a good variety of things to build. Gives you a bit of freedom.
Addictive quality. A game that's perfect for watching youtube videos in the background. Those who love OCD type placement and organization management will love what the game brings to the table.
UI implementation for the most part is solid: easy to see what's going on in your tower with clear and distinct icons that are appropriate for the level of warnings they give you.
Love the heat map implementation. Simple to show what's going on in your tower, and where you need to improve.
Secondary systems feels substantial, and all work together to improve the main building element. I can't emphasize this enough: this doesn't feel just tacked on for some variety: it feels woven: meaning that you actually feel the effects of when you use these systems in order to improve your building.
Visuals for the most part work, especially if you get in close via the zoom feature. You can see the damage on the walls when you need to repair, and the art style makes things clean to see even at 10000 feet up.
You get a sense of real scale when you get up to the 20/30 floor element, as you zoom out and look at your work. It can feel like you really have created something special.
Scenarios do add some variety to the game and some focus if you have trouble with the sandbox mode.
Modding on day one: and there's good documentation for people who aren't experienced to take up the mantle of module.
Negatives:
Do have concerns in the long run gameplay wise. Most of the issues has to do with random events: most everything plays out the same way if you do the same sequence: there's not a lot of ways to react to it.
Even with all the information that it gives you, there's always information that is missing detail at times. For example, I know that this tenant wants to be close to an elevator....but how close is close? It's small details like that that end up in some trial and error gameplay. Expect your first 2 attempts in the sandbox to just learn the mechanics so you can do it right on your third attempt.
Missing audio cues to tell you if something is going wrong. It's all visual.
Would have liked a 2X Fast forward option. Sometimes, you spend way too much time waiting for the next set of income to come in.
You'll turn the music off and put a YT video on, because it's not only nothing special, it just doesn't have variety.
Let me build overhangs. Let my creative side flourish. The trailer on the store page shows it (seems like a teaser), but I couldn't get that to work.
There's tiny implementation issues. Would like to have seen more keyboard controls for ease of use. Nothing that breaks the game, but for ease of use, would like to see added.

So, The Huntsman: Winter's Curse is essentially a linear visual novel with battles. Looks and feels like something in between Banner Saga and Child of Light. I purchased this game on a discount and I believe those were money well spent. I love the overall style, the visuals, the music too. The game uses a rather unqiue combat system where instead of actions you play cards and those cards are provided by various equipment, so changing equipment allows you to modify your "deck". An interesting idea, it actually shows promise and can be used in other games of similar type.  Although, of the battles themselves I have to say they are not terribly exciting, mostly because all you need to do is click a card once in every 5-10 seconds. Also the very theme of dark fairy tales is getting really, really old. Certain cliches and tropes are very much apparent in the story. However, nothing is entirely new nowadays and the story itself isn't bad at all. It is well written, happily avoiding some common pitfalls like using modern slang or making characters talk like idiots.
All in all, I enjoyed playing this game. Check it out if you're into such things, especially since the first chapter is free, so everyone can make their own opinion.

First off: I don't truly hate this game. In fact, there are quite a few good things about it - the degree to which you can experiment with the numerous obstacles and veichles to get different outcomes can be impressive and the courses themselves well-designed, encouraging maximum destruction and crazy hijinks all throughout. Workshop intergration is well-done, with a bunch of user-created levels to play around in, and of course there is always a good laugh to be had from a crash dummy getting as screwed up as possible.
But the fact of the matter is that it's nowhere near as interesting to crash a car for the 100th time as it is to crash it for the first. After about 3 hours of play, I grew incredibly and extremely bored with the repetition of crashing, the bland style of the game, and with the lack of variety overall. After a while, it starts to all feel like 'same old, same old' - just the same freaking thing over and over again throughout and throughout without much difference. Even the Workshop levels (which tend to blow things up the absolute extreme) can't stop the monotony from breaking through.
You might like this game a lot more than I did. You might find the game's explosive antics a lot more amusing than I ever would. You might be crashing cars way more times than I could ever bear. But for me, this game is nothing more - and nothing less - than what it is: a virtual way to crash cars. Over and over and over and over and over again.

Very Nice strategy game.
This game is in the style of Master of Orion, but with quite a bit of difference. You start with one planet pre or post warp as you choose. You try to expand in the universe by colonizing and conquering other planets.
The difference is that there are a crapload of planets in the universe. At least 50% or more are not colonizable, but it still leaves an immense possibility of an empire! You can have around 16 opponents against you(just to show you how biiiiig the universe is) and your'e not even crowded! Plus the damn pirates who makes your life interesting until you stamp them out. And they are tough!
You can design all the ships and bases in the game. You can research new technologies which improve or add new components to the ships. Some special teks are race specific to give some flavor to each race. You can change your government, which actually matters a big deal and there are a lot to choose from. You also got a boatload of ressources (i think there are more than 15 of them) that you need to get to build your bases and ships. For that you must build mining bases.
Now the big peculiarity in this game is that EVERYTHING can be automated. Actually, you can put the game on full automatic and just watch it play itself! All ships can be automated to play their role, to be included in fleets as they are built and to attack or defend automatically without your intervention! Even the colonisation can be fully automated. They actually colonise better than you would manually. The idea here is that when you start playing the game, you're better off with most things automated and as you become more acquainted with it, you can decide what to keep automated and what to put on manual. You even have an in-between step that suggest to you if you want to do something(i use it for colonization and spying). You have to understand that you can eventually have more than 1000 ships in hundred of fleets so just managing them all manually would drive most peeps insane, so the automatisation is there for you!
The other big thing in this game is that you don't go fetch the ressources you need! You got private sector ships to do the job for you but they build their ships at your starport (and pay you for building those ships with your designs!). You only build and control the state ships which include warships, constructor, colony, explorer and troops ships. Bases too can be built by the constructors and colonies. So you pay maintenance only on those ships. The private sector will pay its maintenance on their ships. What you do when you reaaaaally want a ressource is to build a mining base on the planet of that resource. The private sector will send cargo hauler to it to fetch that resource.
So the game is played mostly at a grand strategy level and not at a ship level. The battles are quite simple affairs that basically come down to who got the bigger guns, shields and armor = win. The graphics are 2-D for all the ships and bases. The view is top down. You don't play this game for graphics. The music is actually pretty good. The game is tough to learn and can last a very long time if you want to conquer everything (but you don't have to there are victory conditions that make you win the game much earlier than total conquest). the diplomacy is pretty good with lots of choice and the ai is not completely insane either compared to other games diplomacy.
Also, with universe, you get something close to 4 games in one! You can even play as a pirate faction which function quite differently from the other empires! You can also play a fleet admiral or captain of a single ship. You can also play the game mode for spying only!!! That one is quite intriguing i must say.
The game is well supported with many patches already since i bought the game so this is very nice.

This game could've been something pretty great, but it turned out just so damn mediocre, sort of playing it safe at every turn. I almost feel like only thing saving the game is it's graphical fidelity (and the atmosphere achieved thanks to it).
The setting is in the time of Nero's rule of the Roman Empire, focusing on the invasion of Britain. Sadly, this part of the game is mostly non-sense. The main characters in the game have either never existed or aren't portrayed very well. Sadly they even missed the spot with portraying landmarks-something that the Assassin's Creed series handled greatly (especially the earlier games), Ryse gives you a nice sense of what Rome might've looked like, but majority of the events and characters are made up. Not just in the sense that history doesn't say anything about them (ie playable character), which would be okay, but the worse offense that it makes up facts about real people (ie. Boudicca, Nero and his non-existent sons).
This seems like a seriously missed opportunity, especially since this is a very interesting part of history and one that would've been very easy to portrait realistically-it already contains excessive ammounts of violence, betrayal, intrique and everything we love in videogames.
The story is..well..stupid. It's about as much of a cliché as it can get, and you'll probably be able to predict it right from the start. Here's a summary (it's short, but there isn't much more to it).
Yup, not very revolutionary nor interesting. There are a few good bites hidden in there though. At least the story cutscenes are rendered pretty nicely though.
So far I've been bashing to for the history, but it does get some things right. First of: the vicousness of the combat. It's a brutal and satisfying, somewhat similiar to a batman game with more limb amputation. It is very repetitive, but seeing as the game is pretty short, it's not that big of an issue. Combat being repetitive is only amplified by the fact that enemy variety is close to non-existent. Throughout the game, you wont face anything else than
, with a few bosses sprinkled through the game, but those sadly behave very closely to normal enemies, only with longer health bars. The ammount of designs for the enemy classes is very tiny, so you'll be freaquently in a fight with multiple clones. The AI does nothing that you wouldn't expect it to.
This is easily the strongest point of the game. It was developed by Crytek, with a huge budget thanks to their cooperation with Microsoft, so it has the visual fidelity we've come to expect from the studio, this especially shines in the battle scenes or my favourite part,
It's one of the moments where the atmosphere of the game really shines through.
If you're planning to run the game on ultra, bring a solid machine, with my overclocked (4,3ghz) i5 6600K and a GTX1070, I was getting around 50 fps, with some drops even below 40. You can optimize the game to get significantly better performance on lower hardware, but I simply haven't bothered with it, so take my fps results with a large grain of salt.

Mythic Wonders does a good job at delivering a modern fantasy tale with some sci-fi elements in the mix, but it feels a little dated for a hidden object game, despite its 2014 release.
After playing Mythic Wonders: The Philosopher's Stone, I couldn’t shake the feeling that this is some attempt at a high-definition remake of an early 2010 hidden object game. But no; this is an early 2014 title that can be either considered a little dated for its age—or pleasantly nostalgic about that short period where the usual HOG tropes still didn’t fully bloom yet.
To make it more clear: the story follows the usual cliché of a female protagonist who tries to find her missing relative in a fantasy world—where she collects the power of the four (plus one) elements—but the story is less predictable than most would think, and the visual style is a lot closer to 1980s sci-fi/fantasy than the usual enchanted forest backdrop.
The dated feel is also present in picture quality and the reliance of simple puzzles, needlessly complicated item gathering, and the surprisingly challenging hidden object scenes. The latter have three different versions, so at there won’t be any complaints about variety, even if the game may seem a bit boring for newer players.
