The CD-ROM era both birthed and killed the Full Motion Video game. While still in its crib, a generation-long curse was laid upon the genre, dooming all creations branded with the FMV tag to receive nothing but scorn and contempt in every village around the world. And to be honest, the reputation was wholly deserved.
Decades later, hard drive space is now cheap and the codecs plentiful. The creators also seem wiser this time around, focusing on small and intimate, non-branching storylines and cutting the flashy sizzle reel tricks and animations altogether.
Contradiction is, like other recent FMV games such as Her Story and Tesla Effect, a detective mystery: A girl has been found dead in a small rural British town. You play as Inspector Jenks who's been sent to investigate, mostly interviewing the residents about the incident and doing some minor inventory-based sleuthing.
Chats with people open up more points of discussion, and the idea is to find contradictions in the statements of the suspects. This is easier said than done, since the conversations always bring up dozens of possible subjects and pinpointing the slips of the tongue requires attention and thought. Just randomly trying things will get you nowhere.
I was surprised at how engrossed in the game I got. The characters are intriguing and I have no major problems with the acting (Jenks himself can get a bit over the top on occasion, though). The setting and the plot are also atmospheric, with a lot of hints towards something truly sinister. The music properly sets the mood, and the village itself is visually a rather charmingly beautiful little slice of English countryside.
Pacing around the town can get slightly frustrating if you get stuck, but the game has its own elegantly integrated hint system so you're never truly lost. The game is definitely no walk in the park either, so expect your little grey cells to get an outing they probably deserve in this day and age.
The only downside of Contradiction is that you can sometimes see a few corners cut where budget limitations apparently came into play, however, cheapo after effects are blessedly kept to a minimum. Biggest bummer is that some of the major story strands are never brought into conclusion after the case is cracked, but are left to be resolved in a potential sequel.
Anyhow, this is FMV gaming done right. I finished the game in one nine-hour sitting and had fun the whole time. That's more than I can say for most games, FMV or not.

Full motion video was quite the rage for a brief time in the mid 90's. Outside of Tex Murphy though few developers got it right. Contradiction brings back everything that was good about FMV gaming while avoiding most if not all of its negatives. For a low budget game this has very good acting and a fairly polished and easy to use interface. There is just something very appealing about getting to play the detective and this story has a lot of interesting clues and sub plots that keep you driving to a solution. The basic gameplay premise works very well. Collect clues, interview subjects and spot contradictions in their testimony. This is much more challenging than you would think as you end up with a large amount of testimony from several suspects throughout the 7 to 8 hour experience and finding the contradictions as you get towards the end can be very challenging. You also end up with a large number of red herrings that can distract you from what is important in the information you uncover. There are a couple of hint systems available in the game, but it's very satisfying to work through the testimony on your own to find the solution.
Pros:
HD quality video and solid acting
Smooth interface that is easy to navigate once you get the key commands down.
Backtracking is helped by map that allows you to quickly return to locations
Very interesting mystery that keeps you pushing towards the solution
Cons:
Audio is a bit over compressed causing it to be tinny. Hopefully this is fixed in a later update.
Story ends with many of the subplots unresolved, but open to a possible sequel.
Controller support broken on Windows currently.
You will have to backtrack and speak to suspects over and over as you unlock more clues. This part does have some of the downsides of old 90’s games, but I enjoyed Inspector Jenks so much I didn’t mind and was willing to overlook this. Also, over the course of the many in game hours of interviews the suspects will mostly be in the same places. Drinks will stay the same level and suspects will stare into the same fireplaces. This can take you a bit out of the experience, but I’m sure all the dialog was recorded at the same time and this was necessary for the game design.
Overall this is one of the best FMV and Mystery titles ever made and is quite the achievement on the very small budget the game was made with. I can only hope the game does well enough to make a sequel possible. Game is well worth the asking price.

Turbo Dismount is a gem of a game.
The premise is simple: you control a crash dummy and your goal is to toss it against vehicles, obstacles and objects to get a high score. There is a fair ammount of customization in the game. The dummy can be strapped to a variety of vehicles (including rides from an office chair to a monster truck). Each of these vehicles allows you to select from different poses in which the dummy can be positioned. You can even upload a photo of a friend/enemy and paste it onto the dummy's head!
There are also different stages, which range from simple straightways to huge intersections of heavy traffic meant to maximize carnage. These stages can also be customized with different obstacles like turbo pads, roadblocks or minefieds. The game also has steam workshop support, allowing you to download additional stages.
After you finish customizing your dummy and stage, you choose a speed and direction and let the physics engine do its thing. The dummy and vehicle can be broken down in multiple itty bitty parts, each increasing your score based on how hard they hit objects in the stage. After things settle down the replay feature kicks in and you can see the carnage in slow motion. As far as I know there's no option to save replays in game. But you'll be creating so many spectacular crashes that it's not a big deal.
While the premise of Turbo Dismount is basic, it has it down right. It calls to the simple pleasures of childhood, in which throwing your toy cars against makeshift buildings or laughing at people falling in America's Funniest Home Videos was all the entertaiment you needed. You always knew what was coming, but you couldn't help but laugh or wince everytime it happened. You may not put hundreds of hours into this game. Yet you'll be glad that when you want you can throw your toy car against traffic and watch the parts fly.

Pretty fantastic if you're a fan of 4X games.  In terms of gameplay, it's closest to Star Ruler without 3 dimensions. DW:U does everything as well as Star Ruler (and all the other greats), but then adds one killer feature to seperate it from all other space 4X games: a private economy appears and interlocks with your state economy once you have a spaceport built.
Each Ship, Structure and Component in the game has a specific set of resources required to produce it.  There are something like 80 resources throughout the galaxy, some quite rare.  Once you have a space port, a private economy comes to life and does almost all of the work to mine and transport these resources.  It's fun to watch the little mining vessels and transport ships zip around your first star system, mining resources and transporting them back to spaceport or to a needy new colony.
It is hard to overstate how much having a private economy operating independent of the player-run economy makes this game standout in the genre.  Play a few minutes and you'll love it: the game has modeled the boring and repetitive tasks (transporting goods, gathering resources), taken them out of your hands, and explained it in such a way that makes the game more feel more realistic.  Encouraging this private economy to grow (by building mining stations and colonizing planets for them to service) not only gives your Empire more ships to move things about, and each new private ship provides you with money since the private sector buys them from the state.  This gives DW:U that little feeling that has usually been the domain of City Builder games A-Train and SimCity.  You nurture the citizens, they go about their business, and if they thrive then you will benefit greatly.
In just about every way this game equals the best of the genre: the Research Trees are great, the combat is great, the diplomacy and trade are great, new games are absurdly configurable, automated/manual options exist for just about every game concept, species are quite different and fairly balanced, ship design is very detailed, leaders are varied and interesting, espionage system is well done, etc.  Take all that and then completely improve a major aspect of the 4X genre by making the productive economy more meaningful and more fun and you have the best game ever in the genre.  If you loved things like Master of Orion, Galactic Civilizations, and Star Ruler, DW:U is the game for you.
Pros:
Absurdly good in pretty much every way relative to previous games in the genre.

Cons:
Learning curve is steep.  This will be difficult if you haven't played previous games in this genre before.  I'd recommned looking for the guide written by Timotheus for manual gameplay -- he's done a pretty good job of walking you through controlling everything.  In-game tutorials are just so-so.

26/12/16: EDIT - I've honestly been feeling a bit differently about this game recently - And I've come to actually feel like I can recommend this game.  Namely due to elements (like Crispin) helping you piece together the puzzles and story.
OLD REVIEW
All my problems with the game are equally balanced with the things I liked.
I can't recommend it, because I just didn't like more.
Credit where credit is due, the 'witty sidekick' is actually funny, and that can be really hard to do.  He is surprisingly not annoying.
However, in a post-human, desolate wasteland planet earth.... how did they get so many planks of wood?  How have they not all rotted and decomposed away?

I really liked the game. The best thing about this game is the story which is great and interesting. As for puzzles, they are a bit on the easy side, but with a few that may force you to consult a walkthrough if you're not paying close attention.
Since the game is quite short, I recommend getting this on sale.

Each place you visit during the game offers very well-drawn and thematic pixel art with a good animation quality. More importantly, everything offers a feel of authenticity, which keeps you immersed in this post-apocalyptic sci-fi world.
The soundeffects are very decent for a point & click game. What really outshines all else are the soundtrack and the narration. The soundtrack is the most immersive and fitting I've ever encountered in this genre. It has around 40 (!) different tracks, which is very rare to see for such a game. The narration of the two main characters is very well done and their lines vary between fitting, serene and often amusing. In fact, it was so well done that I had to listen to the hints despite having solved a puzzle, just to hear all they had to say!
You control two robot companions, stranded in a post-apocalyptic world, where man has perished and become a myth. Your task is to solve different puzzles in the typical point & click style. Your goal is to repair your broken down ship and leave this world. You will visit different locations within the gameworld to find objects and solve puzzles which consist in many cases of applying one or two items to a certain location. Many of the puzzles are challenging but fair. Only for a few I had to go 'pixel hunting' and click everything on the screen to find what I was looking for. Should you have trouble solving a puzzle, your trusty robot companion at your side will always have a few hints for you ready!
The world is incredibly well built and the story kept me glued to the screen until I reached one of the many endings after around 12 hours.
I enjoyed this game more than any other point & click adventure game I have ever played. In my opinion it even outshines the well praised Machinarium. Minor gripes were some technical issue while trying to launch the game for the first time.
Amazing world, story, pixel art, narration and soundtrack. If you have not played this game yet, it is my personal favourite point & click of all times. A must to play!

This game is, in my opinion, an absolute classic RPG. I played the original for Xbox for many hours and continued to do so on PC.
The story is strong and unique from the rest of the Star Wars universe, the plot is engaging and the characters are unique and develop as you interact with them on their own personal stories with the main character.
Knights of the Old Republic was released in 2003 and the graphics are nothing special by today's standards however they have aged far better than other comparable RPGs that were released around the same time. The 3D models are smooth and the environments are noticably smoothed by the anti-aliasing.
I would strongly recommend this game to any long-time BioWare fans, although the chances of a long time Bio-Ware fan not experiencing this game are slim! The recommendation is also to those who enjoy a RPG with a well-structured plot and turn-based style combat system.
A word of warning to users with HD monitors - Without modification and third-party programs this game has a max resolution of 1280x1024 however, at this resolution the game looks by no means bad, just not ideal. It has been quite a while since a game has held my interest for so long.  This has become my new addiction in gaming.
The concept of this game is simple:
1. Build your spaceship using guns, armor, and various other parts depending on your play preference.
2. Pilot your spaceship in real time on a 2d plane against A.I. faction ships.
3. Kill other ships and collect what is essentially their XP orbs.
4. Turn in XP for money.
5. Increase your build capacity and unlock guns and blocks with your money.
6. Improve on your ship or make an entirely new one to add to your growing roster of ships for your current faction and watch the A.I. build your new creations to use against your enemies!
It is so satisfying to see your own ship builds being made and used by your own faction in just the ways you intended.
Make a farming ship to cultivate plants for resource orbs.
Create a ship designed with massive cargo holds solely to collect resource orbs to turn in for massive profits.
Create a ship with the ability to heal other ships using beams and drones.
Focus on shields and beams to burst your opponent down from close up.
Make high armored missle-clad monsters to take out your enemies from a distance.
Cover your ship in drone launchers and swarm your enemies with mosquitos!
You can do all of this and so much more, your imagination is really the limit.
The modding scene with this game is surprizingly great and the community is very welcoming and also surprizingly large.
Hopefully, this game gets much more attention.  It certainly flew under the radar for me but once I picked it up I was easily hooked without intending to be.  I've already put in 25 hours in just a few days and I guarantee that will rise steadily over the next few days as well.

Short version: I feel pretty good about Evoland. It is a nice little game.
+ nice various mechanics
+ fun references and good humor / parody
+ very nostalgic
0 short
0 uses intentionally annoying mechanics and and settings from back in the day. (adds to the feeling but is even after all
these years as annoying as ever ^^'')
- probably no fun if your too young to know at least some of the old stuff and/or are not interested in "gaming history"
- lacks a little on background information here and there.
It is a very short game however so if that's a no-no to you... well paws off of that one. I've got like 5 hours on the clock with this one and that is including a while AFK and playing that one minigame a couple of times... and according to the ending screen I have the game 95.6% complete. (just a little collectable left if your the type of player for it)
That game is more for people who know all the old games... I myself didn't know all the stages from experience but most of 'em. So I had a pretty good time. The references to Zelda, Diablo and co as well as the parody-elements and the mechanics and mockery of them... all the "in your face" of the old games... liked it. Had a blast for an afternoon.
Also it was sometimes a little sudden but fun whenever they just up and switched the game mechanics fo that you basically play something like the old final fantasy games in one moment and click. now you're playing diablo.
Of course some of the old mechanics like making you run in circles all day or throwing a random encouter at you every three steps are still annoying but they were pretty obvious about that being intentional so that the veterans fell right back at home.
Story is a little weak overall but it is not about a story in the sense of plot. the game obviously focuses around telling a story about the old games and their evolution. Granted that it would've been a nice touch to have a little background to it like when did a certain feature get introduced? or what games used them (just a famous example or two)?
Graphics and music change along with the mechanics and are playing more to the nostalgic elements and less to raw punshing power. so some are not very pretty or something but that's just how it was back in the day. Think that quite some will appreciate them.
If your one of the veterans and want some nostalgic trip lasting you a rainy afternoon or maybe don't even have time for any 80+ hour epic in your day to day life... then Evoland is your go to game.

Evoland is overview of how RPG’s have changed over the last 20 years, ending with the Super Nintendo / Playstation 1 era. While the games plot is a very high overview of Final Fantasy 7 and Zelda (most of the characters names are direct copies of FF7 with a slightly different spelling) the real interesting concept of the game is the Game’s meta, which evolves as you advance further into the game.
You start out with something that looks like it was made in the 80’s, with gameplay styles and menus from the very old-school RPG’s and as you beat each dungeon/boss it upgrades to a new era (I remember playing some of the older RPG’s and it’s just as painful now to look at). Even items bought from shops affects the game in this style, such as more RAM (to make some of the animations more fluid) or another upgrade which reduces the time it takes to save the same.
Each area of the map is heavily influenced by the age it is trying to depict, with the late 80’s early 90’s era having fake walls in dungeons, gaining color and moving from 8 bit sprites with no animation to 16 bit sprites, the late 90’s moving from random turn based battles to real time battles (think Secret of Mana), to something that looks a lot like the Nintendo 3DS graphics used for the Final Fantasy remakes. Hats off to a battle that looks like it uses mode7 (used in Some Super Nintendo games where things focus on the center of the screen and the background/stage rotates around it.)
The music is likewise based on the era, and fits the theme of the game. It’s not going to win any awards, but each map/area’s music fits the stage well, and brings back a sense of nostalgia.
The only gripe I can really think about on this game is it’s not very long, so you will likely finish it in one or two sittings. This is including doing everything for all the achievements (unless you have never played a RPG and have no idea of the methods the older games used like fake walls).
There are some hidden collectables scattered around the world to collect (with a hint much like the old Zelda games), so there is something other than powering through the stages to do, but there isn’t great enemy diversity (I think most areas have 3-4 enemies) so each area gets repetitive quickly.
I would recommend it if you like RPG’s and want to talk a quick walk down nostalgia lane.

I played over 20 hours of Endless Legend in a week, and there's some things I really enjoyed about it. There's also some glaring problems I feel, but I'll get to those later.
To start positive, the music is nothing short of amazing. I also love the visual design of the different factions, the Cultists and Necrophages especially are great. A lot of the concept art/loading screens & backgrounds look fantastic too. I'm also a big fan of how different every class feels, you really do have to play to each classes' strengths and try to circumvent their weaknesses to establish a proper win condition. There are some classes where you pretty much have to focus on a specific victory type, which is good in terms of making them all feel varied but can be annoying when you start a certain way and realise you kinda set yourself up for failure.
Now onto the negatives... there's unfortunately quite a few. Most of my complaints towards Endless Legend come to this - it feels like an exercise in tedium. The default values for a campaign feel INCREDIBLY slow. Fortunately you can change almost all these values before a campaign but during you're completely out of luck. Played a nearly 10 hour campaign getting an economic victory and it was truly mind numbing. I really strongly recommend you don't have combat speed on normal because it is so painful to sit through, I ended up just alt tabbing every time. You can't really use auto-fight either because it sometimes just flips a coin and decides you lose a battle you really have no reason to.
Beyond that, combat itself is not very intuitive or fun. The game assigns orders automatically, which are consistently terrible. You usually have to change the majority of these orders anyway. The fight animations are awfully slow, there's occasions where your units will walk 2 or 3 more spaces than they have to. This pathfinding happens in regular terrain (outside of combat too) and it's honestly difficult to watch sometimes. If you get a warning popup after clicking end turn, you click dismiss and then still have to click end turn again. That's 3 clicks, even if you already knew what the warning would be. Sometimes you don't want to have a construction thing being built, sometimes you can't afford to give your villagers food. If I've already clicked end turn and then dismiss, don't make me press end turn again too.
There's also the winter season which is far more annoying than actually challenging. There's not really much you can do about it other than some hero skills and constructions, and you just lose a bunch of resources for a long time and it also detracts from the game's great OST because you just hear wind noises. I honestly would've preferred there be immediate and more impactful natural disasters than having to spend 20 turns in the winter season. At least then there's room for variation.
Endless Legend is also incredibly addictive, as evidenced by my 20 hours in a week. That's because Endless Legend is an occasionally brilliant game, marred by tedious and frustrating elements. Once you have the ball rolling, it becomes satisfying and fun but I honestly think the most fun you'll find here is in messing around with the gameplay values, having 8 factions in a smallish world all next to each other. Grinding out some of the less fun victory conditions is on the other hand, perhaps a cure for insomnia.
Endless Legend is one of the most difficult games to review for me because I can see why people loved it, but I can also see why people would label this as mostly terrible. I find myself somewhere in the middle. I both love and hate it. I can see myself playing it in the future, but I can also see myself getting so bored or annoyed with it that I just rage uninstall and never visit it again. I think it's a non-recommendation from me, albeit very close to a hesitant recommendation.

This is my favourite 4X game, hands-down. It's an artistic treat, for one thing: it's got a lovely, vaguely ethereal art style, a fantastic score, a slick UI that doesn't get in the way, and a lot of great illustrated art for heroes, units, technologies, and quests.
Quests? Yeah, your average game of Endless Legend probably also has the strongest narrative chops of any 4X experience I've played. There's no one overarching storyline or campaign - the narrative exists within the world in the form of lore text and quests you get from all kinds of different places. Though individual quests do repeat, the combinations of quests and environmental conditions you'll be faced with, and the fact that the quests are fairly unobtrusive, do help make things feel fresh each time. Each faction has its own unique quest, too, which adds a lot to the flavour of the game and the distinction between the factions.
Because the factions, really, are the star of the show here. Each faction has the kind of unique units and artwork you'd expect, some unique technology, musical themes, and quests, and most interestingly, a few radically unique mechanics. A playthrough of a particular game ends up feeling far more unique based on your faction than you'd get in another game.
So really, what I'm saying is: this game oozes character and texture and richness on top of the usual 4X experience. It really stands apart from its competitors in that regard, and it cemented me as a fan of Amplitude's work. Buy this and buy all the DLC - it's worth it.

You, With Me adds to the pool of depressing visual novels we've been enjoying from Japan and abroad for years now. And while its premise sets you up for an easily moving story, the writing doesn't do it justice. With minimal assets and a disturbing lack of sound for the most part, it's up to the story to drive everything, but though it is in every aspect a melodrama, it fails to deliver what makes those kinds of stories memorable and emotional.
There's an overwhelming banality to every event, helped in no part by the stiff, awkward, heavy-handed narration that drags on for far too long. We're lead in circles as the characters struggle over the same problems, only to be fed the point of it all as if we never had a hope of realising it. It's not Afterthought Studios' best (and it's not laughably bad either), so I can only hope it was a stepping stone to a stronger work. As-is, however, the game comes off as a clumsy first draft in dire need of re-writing and editing.

If there was a "neutral" option, I'd use it, because I'm really torn about whether to recommend this or not.
Here's the thing: It's really just a short story with a few graphics. As such, it follows the proper short story formula, in that the main character has hardships/obstracles, and in the end, is changed by them, and learns from them.
On the upside, the message of the story is good.
On the downside, it's REALLY melodramatic, and extremely unrealistic. I've had cancer, and this VN doesn't deal with it in a reailistic way at all. But then, I guess most people wouldn't realize that.
Additionally, at least one major plot twist is foreshadowed so heavily that you can't help but know what is about to be revealed; the writing here is too heavy-handed.
Grammar and such is extremely iffy--I get the feeling this was written by someone whose native language is not English, so for that reason I mostly chose to overlook it, but, I'd recommend that the writer get someone to proofreed future works.
In the end, I guess I'm going to recommend this simply because the message it's trying to get across IS a good one, and, because the flaws in the main character were well-written enough that for a good part of the VN I wanted to slap the guy and tell him to quit being... well... no spoilers..
Graphically, there's nothing too exciting here. The scenes look good, but there are only a few of them and they are re-used a lot.
One character, at the very end, has a weird error in that when the person is talked about, it's a male person named Shawn, but when speaking, it's a female named Natasha. That, and a few other things do need to be cleaned up a bit.
So yeah, I'll recommend, but catch it on sale--even though it's cheap already. I think whoever wrote this can do better, with practice.

I purchased this visual novel after experiencing the outstanding masterpiece produced by the same developer Afterthought Studios "Forgotten, Not Lost" last year.  (The key was purchased rather for the small discount over at
Much like Forgotten, Not Lost dealt with the really tough end-of-life loss of memory that comes with older age, this one deals with perhaps even a tougher real life matter in being told you have cancer and you only have months to live.
While I read this aloud, word for word on my youtube channel to my viewers, and choked up a few times, I discovered that this VN is a heart warming and inspiring tale that I highly recommend!  While this novel isn't quite as well written as the before-mentioned Forgotten, Not Lost, it is still a very heart wrenching at times, and heart warming at other times tale that I enjoyed very much!  It's very much worth the price tag and the time spent reading it, which if read silently should only take 2 to 4 hours depending on your reading speed.  While you can certainly go watch and/or listen to my playlist found linked below, I highly recommend that you read this for yourself first to the maximum effect and experience.
It isn't without its faults, the biggest problem I had was no way to change the text size or window size to allow me to read all of the text that just didn't all fit on some screens, so it left me feeling like I missed something at times.  Other smaller problems were bad grammer or the choice of wording in some places, but in the end, it didn't do much damage to the overall impact of the great story which it seeks to tell us.
Another impressive VN from Afterthought Studios in my book, and I give this one a strong 8.5 out of 10 and want to say right now that this is the kind of story that has the power to change your life!  ..Yes, it really is that good!  :-)
Here is my playlist, but again I highly recommend you purchase it and read it to experience it yourself first!

While I liked Afterthought Studios’ previous works, unfortunately I cannot recommend this title. I wish that Steam had a neutral option on times like this, but since there’s not, my answer is “no”. Also, like it says on the title, this is a kinetic novel meaning that there are no choices and you only read the text.
Jacob is an ordinary man and lives with his wife, Lisa, in Singapore. Everything is pretty much chill until Jacob finds out he’s really sick and will die in a few months. The stress that the couple goes through (especially Jacob) is intense, which makes Jacob act kinda like an a-s-s to his wife. Of course that his behavior is bad, but well, he’s dying and people tend to lose it. I thought that his behavior was very “human”, not the “everything will be alright” kind of cliché (at least at first). He’s a guy who worries about the future of his wife, and he already accepted the fact that he won’t be around for too long. I could feel his frustration of wanting to prepare for the worst, and Lisa acting hopeful bothered him.
You know, at first I actually felt sorry for her.
All she did to make Jacob fell better was flushed down through the toilet because of that crappy act she pulled.
Overall, the story is interesting but I think that its execution wasn’t good. There’s several grammar mistakes (I’m not a native English speaker tho, but they bothered me a little), the narration isn’t that good, and there’s the layout; there are no paragraphs on this novel, it’s just a plain text wall without the proper space. It gets tiring to read, and the text even invades the bottom of the window, surpassing the text box:
4/10. Still, I wish the best of luck to the developers with their next releases.

This visual novel's story had the potential to be interesting and touching, as it explores a man and his wife's differing approaches to handling the man's cancer diagnosis. Unfortunately, it reads like the writer put it through google translate, with plentiful instances of baffling grammar and word choices that don't quite make sense. It's also full of bugs like the text getting cut off sometimes, or sprites appearing on top of each other. I might have been able to overlook some of that if the story was still compelling, but I found it extremely hard to sympathize with the protagonist, who spends most of his time being scornful and patronizing toward his wife as she tries to take care of him. Although I stopped feeling bad for her later on,
Either way, every aspect of this VN was disappointing except for its unintentional comedic value. Go spend your money on better VNs instead.

The game has its flaws, but it's a cute visual novel and a great way to spend a few hours. The writing is a bit awkward and there are some glitches that cause text to repeat/the wrong names to show up, but if you can get past that, the game has a lovely little story. I'd say it takes ~3 hours to complete if you actually read everything (I skimmed through some of the bigger chunks of text) and it's well worth the couple bucks it costs to buy the game. Overall, I'd say... 6.5/10, would recommend.

I pre-purchased "Project Highrise" after watching LGR's review on Youtube.
After completing the tutorials and working on the first scenario, I have to say, I'm hooked. It is reminiscent of "SimTower," and brings me the same appeal that game did. However, it is different, and deeper than the original title. Enough so, that it feels modern, and like more of a proper business management sim. Having to manage utilities and tower services to appeal to different clients is something that really adds a special facet to the game.
The art style is simplistic, but I like that. I feel that simple ideas executed well are better than lofty ideas that are buggy and incoherent. However, when you select an individual tenet, you are greeted with an animalistic or nearly neanderthal "Uh-huh" - all the time. There are male and female tones, and variations for differing levels of satisfaction, but I admit i chuckled when i heard it first. It works though, for an acknowledgement that I have selected them for information, but I hope it's expanded upon in the future.
For the price, I feel "Project Highrise" can't be beat. It really fills an amazingly open void in the gaming library that mixes older, nostalgic gameplay with some newer, modern elements that keep you engrossed for long periods of time.
It's SimTower but streamlined... but complex.... but it's simple. I can see hours being put into this game finetuning my towers. Can not wait to see what the Modding community will do with this gem.

Quality game!

Project Highrise knows what it is: a modern day SimTower. And like that old game: it has that addictive quality to it, where a certain reviewer was planning to play the game for 5 hours....and ended up playing it 12. That should give you an indication of how you can get lost in the gameplay: in all of the good ways. The ecosystem that is created is complex: you'll have to watch a variety of factors: noise, trash, etc, in order to keep your various tenants happy, and not paying attention to those factors could bite you if you're not careful. In addition, there's a LOT of information to work with here if you're looking to use it, so you can plan out your own custom tower of perfection, down to the name of each individual shop if you so desire. Add on a modding scene available on day one with actual usable documentation (which in my experience is RARE AS HELL), and you've got a great simulator/management game that will keep you entertained for a good while. I do have concerns about the long run of the game due to the lack of random events that seems to occur: but I also wonder if that will be easily fixed by the modding scene. And most of my other complaints are minor: granted, ones that keep the game from being the top in the genre, but not ones that keep fans of the genre from picking up this game. A worthy buy at the price point.

I've just finished Book 1 (which is available for free). I find the artstyle quite amazing. The aesthetics got me interested in this game and did not disappoint.
As for the rest - Huntsman: Winter's Curse is a visual novel with turn based battles. While you are quite often presented with a choice, it doesn't matter at all. There is always a "right" answer and the "wrong" answer. If you pick the "wrong" one, you'll just get to read 1-2 extra paragraphs steering you immediately on the right track. The consequences are always the same.
Story is fairly straightforward and predictable. Some of the characters are likeable, but barely fleshed out. Narration seems to be quite shallow.
That's why the addition of combat is really welcome. It's turn based with initiative bar and cards as skills (variations of attacks, heals, aoes, status effects). There is also a character screen where you can allocate points into basic passive traits and equip your group with gear (each equipment piece has its own set of cards = abilities provided). It's not complicated at all, but relatively enjoyable and makes the game less one-dimensional.

Pros:
>Good story - robot society after humans are gone
>Variety of characters with personality
>Easy to get around - you can walk and you have a map that teleports you to key spots.
>Puzzle quality and variety - From building tools to opening doors to judging court cases I can't think of a point that really struck me as needing unintuitive logic to solve.
>Hint system - robot buddy that you can ask for puzzle suggestions, usually helpful
>Takes notes for you - game jots down important information for you, which can help for puzzles. Couple spots you might still need pen and paper to work something out, though.
>Hot keys for menu stuff
>Does a good job getting into your thought processes - a few puzzles with multiple solutions, some puzzles animated to let you try something even though it doesn't actually work.
>Flavor text - if you like subtle characterization and banter, you can look at most everything for description stuff.

Cons:
>Can't easily get out of item use - have to go into inventory to get your regular cursor back (hot key makes it bearable)
>Some pixel hunting - at least one puzzle where you need to notice a small, muddy colored item in a dark, muddy colored area
>Hints aren't always helpful - sometimes it hints what you know you need to find, not how or where to find it. Other times it's so obtuse that it's really no help at all.
>One or two puzzles that use a game feature only once - ran into one that required using the describe feature, which I didn't know was there and which had never been necessary to get info about items or progress puzzles before then.
>Loading issue - due to the chosen game engine, can't load saves past your 20th most recent save. Have to delete saves to get the one you want in that 1-20 section.

Contradiction is a rather unique game that uses full-motion-video to tell an intriguing murder mystery story, where you play the detective and have to not only spot the other characters lying, but actually catch them at it with their own words. The game gets off to a slow start as you rapidly figure out the interface and game conventions, but the initial world to explore is quite small with only a couple of characters which the game slowly widens and adds to as you call out the characters on their lies.
The writing and acting are superb, which really helps bring you into the story, and the sense of achievement when you spot the contradictions is great because the script is intelligent and doesn't dumb things down. The quaint British village setting and the cult/occult storyline make you think of classic British TV.
Only real criticism so far is that sometimes the audio for the actors speaking is a touch distorted. This isn't enough to detract from the gameplay and more of the pointer to the producers so that when they make their next game (yes - this is more than good enough to warrant a number of sequels) they're able to improve on this aspect. The in-game music fits the setting perfectly and has just the right amount of creepiness, adding much to the atmosphere!

This is a really fun FMV murder-mystery, made all the more impressive because it's largely a one-man show - aside from the actors, from what I understand, Tim Follin (who made the music for games like Ecco The Dolphin and Lemmings, and later became a Director of Photography, working mostly in TV) edited, scored, and coded the entire thing despite never having previously released a game on his own.
Tim's background in video work is obvious. He knows how to frame shots, and in almost all of the "idle" screens I've seen, there's something moving without being distracting. This is notable because I haven't seen any compression artifacts, the video is always crisp and sharp whether there's movement or not. Everything looks fantastic. The dialogue is a bit tinny on occasion, but never during suspect interviews, and it's not even close to being distracting or inaudible. The game had a very small budget, and that's really the only time it shows, yet it's still not enough to be considered a detriment. His background in music also shines through, and I hope the soundtrack will be offered as DLC.

Also of note: The hint system of calling back to police headquarters using a phone booth is great. I've been going through the game pretty quickly, but I'd love to play again later and hear all the hints for places where I wasn't stuck.

If you're old enough to have been gaming in the 90's you might remember the emergence (and sad demise) of the FMV sub genre.
Games like Gabriel Knight, Phantasmagoria and the Tex Murphy titles started to embrace Full Motion Video footage.
Initially it was viewed as a novelty, real actors playing out the narrative in all the interlaced video glory the 90's could muster.
FMV seemed liked a perfect fit for cut scenes and narrative heavy titles and I loved it!
Even some real "Hollywood" actors were seduced by the rise of the interactive movie, with the likes of Mark "Skywalker" Hamil heading up the Wing Commander games and Christopher "Pulp Fiction" Walken starring in the 1996 FMV thriller "Ripper"
Unfortunately, my love for all things FMV wasn't shared by my peers,  I was in the minority and the FMV trend had almost died away completely by the end of the 90's.
This was partly due to the technological limitations of the time.
The video was often interlaced or blocky, the frame rates were poor and the amount of space required by the footage used up a huge amount of CD-Rom storage, the game Ripper I mentioned earlier was spread across 6 CD's!
Many FMV games also suffered from cheesy writing and equally bad acting.
"Phoned in" performances were the norm and as such a stigma began to emerge in the media around the whole "interactive movie" genre.
This stigma probably had as much to do with the death of the genre as the technical limitations of the 90's, but whatever the reason, the interactive movie died, I mourned its passing and moved on, but now I've discovered a game which has rekindled my interest, a new, modern FMV experience in all its interactive movie gaming glory.
Contradiction: Spot the Liar! to give it its full (and unnecessarily long title) is a "whodunnit" detective adventure set in the sleepy little English village of Edenton.
Edenton isn't just a stage for the players either, its a character in its own right.
From the village pub to the surrounding woodland, all the locations are beautifully realised and tie together to create a charming and peaceful setting, you'll even see the odd Union Jack fluttering in the breeze.
This rural tranquillity gives Edenton a charm of its own, it feels like a real location that you'd find if you drove out  into the green and pleasant land that is the English countryside.
It's this tranquil charm which makes the recent events in Edenton all the more shocking.
There's been a suspicious death in the village, a young woman, Kate Vine, has drowned but was it suicide? a terrible accident? or something more sinister?
You've got one night to find out, let the investigations begin!
You play as Detective Inspector Jenks, an interestingly likeable character with a compelling interview technique which is sure to make you smile, he's also somewhat of a kleptomaniac and has the added side effect of making me want to start wearing a hat.
As you explore the village you'll come across some equally interesting locals, friends and acquaintances of Kate's all getting on with their lives, each with their own personalities, view of events and secrets to hide.
I can't overstate how well written these characters are, without exception everyone you come across feels like a fleshed out and fully realised person, from the landlady at the village pub to the father and son team who run "Atlas" an exclusive business training course which seems to be popular with the local students, they're all engaging and make each interview a pleasure to play through.
Jenks arrives in the village of Edenton one week after Kate Vines death, it's a Friday evening, the locals are going about their business and it's your job to snoop through their things and interview them regarding the death.
Everything in this game is presented through video footage, from the navigation of the village through to the interviews themselves, but more on that later.
Movement around the village is a simple, go  left, go right affair, each location has its own video loop, there are no static screens here, Edenton is a living, breathing village.
Stand by the lakeside and waves will ripple in the light whilst branches move and creak  in the wind, the level of immersion this creates is undeniably impressive.
You'll find yourself searching through locations, finding clues and interviewing the locals.
These interviews are the meat of the game, initially you'll only have a couple of "conversation pieces"  to enquire about, the dead girl, Kate Vine and her driving license which was discovered some distance away from her body.
Questioning the residents of Edenton quickly opens up your investigative  options as you uncover more information about events leading up to Kate's death and "acquire" items to ask about from your inevitable snooping.
It's not just a case of ask everyone about everything you discover either, that's just part of it.
You actually need to listen to what people say,
Who's lying?
Who's telling the truth?
It's listening out for contradictions in characters answers that will help reveal this information.
The actual mechanic of spotting these contradictions is well implemented too.
As you question a person, notes of their relevant answers are recorded in your journal.
You can go through these notes and if you spot two that contradict each other you can question the person further regarding the holes in their story.
Why did they lie?
What are they hiding?
This game is by no means easy either, you're not going to breeze straight through the story without actually thinking about what people have told you and going through your notes.
Having said that, there is a hint system if you find yourself stuck at a dead end.
The hints are given by going to the phone box in the village (Jenks is an old school kind of guy and doesn't seem to have a mobile) and calling the police chief who will offer an insight to help get you back on track.
If these hints aren't enough there's always the old faithful option of just plain cheating too, but try and avoid it if you can, the satisfaction of catching someone in a lie is what this game is all about.
One thing I wasn't keen on with this game was the snooping investigation mechanic.
When you reach a scene with something interesting for you to discover a giant magnifying glass icon appears in the bottom right corner of the screen.
Click on it and Jenks will investigate whatever it is that he has spotted at that location.
It works fine but I would have enjoyed a little more subtlety here.
This mechanic is likely a throwback to the titles mobile gaming routes but as a PC gamer the ability to scan your mouse over a location to discover something for yourself would have been more rewarding.
I'm just being picky though, this didn't tarnish my enjoyment of the game,  it's a just a change that would have added something to what otherwise was an excellent experience.
Visually this game is hard to fault with high quality full motion video throughout.
This is an FMV title with the production values of a primetime TV show.
From the camera angles to the sets themselves, everything works to draw you into what feels like a real place populated by real people.
The sound is equally impressive, with an excellently appropriate musical score to accompany the ambient sounds found at each location.
The voice recording itself is generally of a high quality, occasionally you'll... [snip]

Steam doesn’t give an option for a middle-ground thumb, which necessitates this disclaimer: I would not recommend this game for its overall quality of gameplay, but for the low price you get a sufficiently impressive six-hour experience. The visuals are stunning, the story—while majorly historically inaccurate—is interesting, and the voice acting is fantastic. So really, you’re playing for the cutscenes and the incredible artistry of the scenery. Everything else is repetition, repetition, repetition. The only thing to break the endless tedium of hack-and-slash battles with innumerable Barbarian clones is the hunt for collectibles, which are few and far between and provide no interactive reward. Don’t count on enjoying those spoils. And on the topic of spoils, there is no variety in equipment, no new weapons or armor to be had along the campaign. Even the fighting, once established in the very beginning of the game, sees no evolution other than increased necessity for rolling out of the way of heavy attacks, which become more frequent as you proceed. The boss fights, while not necessarily easy, consist solely of waiting for your enemy to use a heavy attack, evading it, getting in a strike, and getting out of the way of the next attack. Rinse and repeat twenty times, because any strikes you attempt in between will be blocked. If the repetition of fighting three predictable thugs at once makes you crazy, the bosses will have you praying to Ares for a bit of desperately-needed variety.
From the beginning I had difficulty with the controls, which felt heavy-handed and inaccurate. I had to disable the movement blur, which was so excessive as to be laughable. Marius’ non-combat movements are sometimes iffy and occasionally he ends up walking diagonally into walls when the controls glitch. My favorite movement glitch was getting stuck running in unbreakable circles outside Nero’s palace in the very beginning, which according to a quick Google search has been a problem for numerous players since the game’s release and requires restarting the game. Even interacting with items is a bit of a nightmare, as positioning yourself perfectly in front of something is apparently a requirement. Even after doing so, it often ends in Marius flailing like an idiot instead of interacting with the thing that’s RIGHT THERE, MARIUS. You could spend a minute just trying to break a single pot because he keeps missing what’s directly in front of his nose. Brawn for this guy. Not brains.
If you’re an achievement junkie like I am, you’re going to be extremely disappointed after your first playthrough. There is no accessible counter on achievements for doing something a certain number of times, so you likely won’t know how close you are. Many of the achievements involve playing the game again on various difficulty levels, which I can’t say is a fun time. One playthrough is fun. Four? Not fun. And sure, you’ve got survival and multiplayer and a jaunt through the Colosseum, but most of that requires multiplayer and hoo boy, good luck getting connected with another person.  Plus, in the end even those are the same old, same old (except that you have a very exposed butt in non-campaign mode). (And frankly, it’s not the best butt I’ve ever seen.)
5/5 for the art department.
1.5/5 for whoever designed the playstyle.

I started playing this back during it's closed beta. And the game is fun. Logging in now and then is still something I do even after all this time. But it's not a great game. Don't let that make you think it's a bad game though. It had some issues at launch, and the chat window is typically too small. But the combat mechanics are dynamic. For the most part you aren't just standing there and auto attacking. The missions are entertaining too. And yet the game's rather average as an MMO. Which again, isn't exactly a bad thing.
There's so many MMOs out there that it can be difficult to stand out from the pack. One fantasy MMO plays remarkably like another fantasy MMO. Sci Fi 3rd person shooter MMOs all play rather similarly too. So this isn't a bad thing in and of it's self. City of Heroes was the first one to feature super heroes. Champions tries to  take a slightly different approach to that clasic but now defunct game. So while this isn't a great game, it's still a good game. And to be honest that's the most you can typically expect from an MMO.
The archtypes are interesting, yet in my opinion often underwhelming. They give a good sample of a given framework without giving access to the best abilities in those frameworks. And they shoehorn you into a specific role. Which is fine if that's what you want. But to truely experience the game you want to have access to freeform builds. This is the meat and potatos of character creation after all, and what the game's original claim to fame was. It's where you can pick and chose abilities from any power framework. Want a regenerating dual sword wielder who fires optic blasts and summons robot minions? Go for it. Or maybe it's a psychic sorcerer you want to  build? Again, go for it.
While freeform builds are by far the best character builds, they can equally be horrifiyingly bad. Since you can take any power from any framework with few restrictions, it's possible to royally mess up. But again, this is a part of the fun in Champions Online. In short I'd suggest giving the game a shot. And if you do, maybe pay for one month of Gold membership. At the very least you'll have a fun free game to spend time with on occasion. At best you'll fall in love with the game. Me, I fall somewhere in the middle.

This is the best 4x game ever made.  Actually wait...let me rephrase that.  This is the best strategy game ever made.  Nope, still not right.  One more time, This is the BEST game ever made.  Yeah, sounds about right.  What other game can you build 35 fleets and hundreds/thousands of ships just to kill one insect race or those dang pirates that you have a long hatred for and have since forgotten why.  Yupp, only this one.

THE Definite 4X experience.
Why, let me point out a few reasons.
1.  There is no 4x game in existence that gives the sense of life like DW:U does, all the civilian ships running around, your escort ships, your fleets standing at the ready, gives a definite sense that this is a living universe.
2.  It is almost always challenging in some way.  Earlier games I have played (and I've played down to the oringal Master of Orion) usually have a point where it's no longer a challenge.  This game rarely has that (at least not till very close to the end).  There are always pirates, another empire, or the great destroyers to worry about.
3.  Deep ship design, there are many different types of weapons and other components to place on your ships, that only thing missing here is firing arcs.
4.  Good AI, AI is usually very good, most games I am more middle in the pack for most areas (yet still competitive).
5.  Pirates, there be PIRATES.  LOTS OF PIRATES.
And probably a lot more, but IMHO, this game is amoung the top 3 best space 4x games ever made.  Save your money, it is worth the price!

I picked this up this weekend. $50 is alot, but it comes with ALL the expansions. This is one of the best 4X space games I have played. It is real-time, but can be paused or sped up. Somewhat even the late game is playable, performance-wise. Cool.

So Master of Orion 2 was your holy grail. You spend the better half of your 20s failing to find a worthy successor and alienating women at parties talking about its greatness and how nothing ever came close yadda yadda. And even though you felt it was the best space 4x you ever played, you still thought that certain Ideas or features could have made it even greater...
Oh well my friend, you are in for a treat. Distant Worlds is not only a worthy successor of MoO2. It also implemented every single one of these "oh man it would be sooo cool if i'd be allowed to do that now"-things you always missed and then some more. And it didn't stop there. It made everything bigger. It literally just bumped up the scale of everything. More stars. More ships. More explosions. More opponents. More everything. And then just molded it all together in an enjoyable and extremly well thought out, somewhat steamlined but not at all simplified* and balanced gaming experience.
And this it all does while having the charming graphics of and excel-editor. Which makes the game an even greater achievement.
*Yes this game isn't easy to get into. Yes you can leave most things on automation but then you'd just be playing a non-turn-based, bigger MoO2. The true greatness of this game doesn't get unleashed untill you spend some hours watching youtube tutorials and turn a lot of the automation off (especially research and ship design). It's gonna be a bumpy ride for a few hours but trust me - if you stick with it you will see the light.

Decided to re-review this game after trying out games again with small play time. I think I posted the wrong review originally! Anyway, it's still down as a "Not Recommended" but not because the game is bad but just to highlight some issues. This game is not for those who are new to 4X.
Starting out, it's overwhelming. There's just so much that can be done, as a result, the GUI's are overloaded and inititally unfriendly. Thankfully they've included AI automation. Your empire can pretty much run itself. I would highly recommend starting out letting the AI manage everything, while you get used to the layout. Unfortunately, due to the font being used, and font size, some bits are difficult to read.
The game offers a global currency, and also resources at your various planets and other space features. Lots of different resources, perhaps even too many (Like Gold, Lead, Steel, Helium, Argon, Nitrogen, etc, etc) Everything you build needs both, some are for ships, some are for colonies. You'll always get resource shortages at the start.
I do love that every star is it's own system of planets+moon, that do orbit the star, and that you can zoom in directly (and fairly smoothly) from galaxy view to planet view. Plus, you can have other species in your empire as a result of battles and independant colonies. They provide additional benefits, and allow you the oppertunity to own other planet types you wouldn't normally be able to colonize.
There are some aspects I think were not needed, or need improving:
"Hero's" - your empire produces various hero's/leaders who develop additional skills. When controlling a galaxy wide empire, you don't really need to care about individual people, or as an example, if one of your "hero's" gains the useful skill of being "Drunk".
Troops - all your troop squads (used for defense and attacking planets) are individual entities, that gain experience. Seems overkill again for a game focusing on galaxy wide empires.
Ship Design - I took one look at the GUI and thought, nope. Left that to the AI. It's not a pretty screen.
Real Time - So much happens that you have to frequently keep pausing to keep track of things. Kinda defeats the point of a Real Time experience.
Fleet Selection - I'm finding this clunky at the moment. Have to zoom to galaxy view to be able to select fleet icon, then zoom back in to control the action within a system.
Finally, the price is very excessive. Sure, it's got a lot of fairly good AI within the game, a fairly useful contex sensitive ingame wiki, lots of game modes, etc. But it's a very steep price.

Despite KOTOR's famous twist being up there with "Would You Kindly?" in terms of famous videogame plot points, the fact that this is one of BioWare's earlier RPGs is obvious at a glance. BioWare is famous for its excellent character writing, but apart from everyone's favorite assassin droid none of them really stand out here.
The villains in particular are atrociously written, playing the roll of the bully, the tyrant, the revolutionary, the brute, the corrupter, or whatever stereotypical villain trait was pulled out of their hat for that scene, regardless of consistancy. Pretty much the only thing I could tell you about the Sith from playing KOTOR is that they're evil, as any other trait is played up in one scene and directly contradicted in the other. Your own character doesn't escape this hold either. Regardless of your character motives for turning evil, the moment you do you immediately turn into a shouty, melodramatic sadist whose dialogue choices range for "I'll kill you for the lulz" or "I'll kill you for disagreeing with me."
The gameplay, on the other hand, is inoffensive. An early version of BioWare's standard model there's little to complain about, but has been outdone by their later projects so many times it doesn't get any praise either. It does, however, eventually fall prey to the BioWare Climax, where almost all gameplay vanishes as you fight wave after wave after wave after wave of enemies, with absolutely nothing else to fill your time until you're finally pitted against the villain you've been promised all game. Cue slightly disappointing cutscene and credits.
All that said though, despite all the criticisms I just leveled at it, this was still basically the codifier for the BioWare RPG. And I rather like BioWare RPGs. So while it's not a great game, it's still a good one. Give it a shot.

Yeah, yeah. Metal Gear Solid V: The Two Hour Game. This review contains spoilers for the entirety of Ground Zeroes, the ending of Peace Walker, and certain aspects of The Phantom Pain.
Ground Zeroes is basically a demo for The Phantom Pain, but not playing it leaves you without the (admittedly sparse anyway) full experience of Metal Gear Solid V.
You'll see people argue that GZ is a waste of time and money, but honestly, that's wrong. This is the most well-optimised, polished, handcrafted game in years. It runs on my toaster at graphic settings far better than my original Xbox 360 experience, which is worthy of the extra money spent on it.
Ground Zeroes starts shortly after Peace Walker's true ending, where Paz and Zeke vanish into the ocean. From the opening shot of Snake in the helicopter, the player knows that this is the darkest direction the Metal Gear series has ever gone in - the trailers were bleak, the voice acting far less comedic than previous entries, the music brooding and ominous. Ground Zeroes is the darkest of the series. Within the first five minutes we see prisoners being tortued at Camp Omega (a kind of obvious stand-in for Guantanamo Bay), Snake without the iconic bandana, and a cinematically brilliant introduction consisting of one long, uninterrupted take. Snake's mission is simple enough, considering previous games - break into Camp Omega, retrieve Chico, and confirm Paz's survival.
It's up to the player whether this goes south sooner rather than later; guns blazing is an option here, but it renders the cutscenes completely illogical. We're introduced to the villain of the overall MGSV story - Skull Face. The name sounds ridiculous and honestly the accent does too. But the depravity contained within cassette tapes that fill in the gaps between what we know and what's left to our imagination open up his character as a man willing to do evil to secure his end goals - at least, whatever those are, because we aren't told in Ground Zeroes. All we do know is, he uses Snake's absence from Mother Base to stage a fake nuclear inspection, allowing his unit (XOF, a name choice that seems bizarre until TPP where it either gets even stupider or becomes genius depending on your outlook) to attack MSF without any real resistance. The action resumes nine years later in The Phantom Pain.
One of the complaints Peace Walker received was an awkward control system excused by its initial appearance on the PSP. While the HD release on Xbox and PS3 fixed these, it was still a portable game at heart. Ground Zeroes returns to a far more traditional feel. Snake is more responsive than ever, capable of moving from a low crouched walk to a sprint without fear of accidentally going prone while attempting to stand up. Introduced in Ground Zeroes is a sticky cover system that actually works and a quick dive button that can be used to incapacitate enemies as well as duck out of sight. Holding up enemies in GZ is a simple matter of aiming at them, and utilising a new dialogue wheel to order information, call nearby guards, or force the enemy into submission. Also new to the series is vehicular movement - Snake can commandeer a Jeep, an APC, or transport truck. With these comes new infiltration opportunities - Snake can hide in the bed of a truck for example, or load a Jeep with passengers to make a quick getaway.
The player is free to test their skills in all areas - stealth, shooting and driving.
As with Peace Walker and Guns of the Patriots, the classic Metal Gear Theme is not used here due to copyright issues. In Ground Zeroes, the player is free to use their own tracks in-game as helicopter music or a soundtrack. There isn't much of a soundtrack to go with anyway, as the Harry Gregson-Williams orchestral pieces are gone in favour of more sombre, mysterious music stings. Of particular mention is the Joan Baez version of Here's To You - this song will play at least three times in a normal playthrough of the main mission. A true soundtrack returns mainly in the bonus missions, and alert/combat phases do convey a sense of urgency and danger. It's not bad by any sense, but you'll hear nothing like Yell Dead Cell or Clash With Evil Personified.
Thanks to the FOX Engine (which will never be used again outside of Pro Evo and Pachinko machines), Metal Gear Solid V looks fantastic. It scales to any rig, even looking impressive at low settings. Similar to Half-Life 2, the design of Ground Zeroes ensures that whatever the game is played on, it will be playable and visually appealing regardless of specs. Of particular note is the rain and hair - every surface looks appropriately shiny and slick due to the downpour during the Ground Zeroes mission, and Snake's model is amazingly realistic.
Even if you don't play The Phantom Pain, Ground Zeroes is worth a low price of admission. Who knows; maybe you'll actually like it more than the sequel.

This game is cute, I'll say that. It's more like a youtube video pretending to be a game though, and tha game becomes a chore to play rather quickly.
=====================
Positives:
It's adorable and occasionally a bit tongue-in-cheek, it has some decent music and graphics, it showcases many different genres of games into one main experience, it might give you a bit of nostalgia for some of the games it's emulating, and it shows an psuedo-evolution (haha) of games over time.
=====================
Negatives:
The random encounters were a brainless chore. They're not difficult, fun, or straining to a non-existent mana pool. They're just kind of there since "rpg's have random encounters lol". I quickly found myself in the tap space to continue and heal to full every now and then routine (healing is free and infinite by the way). There's also not many ways you can speed up the process (no multi-hit moves apart from one on a real-world ~5minute cooldown). This wouldn't be THAT bad if it weren't for the encounter rate being way too high. Every couple steps it's another random encounter. They're tedious and really started wasting my time... Yeah that's actually the best description I could give these: a tedious, enourmous waste of time.
False-walls are strewn throughout. The first time you're likely made aware of this is halfway through the game when a fireball clearly goes through one. Sometimes it's obvious that there must be an invisible wall around because you can see a chest off in the distance, but other times you couldn't find it unless you walked through every wall in the game just to check. There's no indicator where any items you are missing are, nor is there an indicator that there are still items in a given area (just 2 global counters letting you know there are items SOMEWHERE in the game that you haven't found), you simply have to walk against every wall in the game to test whether or not you can walk through it... Makes you feel like a game tester, you know, that thing people are paid to do because it's boring as all hell. The false-walls in the real time combat areas aren't that terrible, but good god they are so painful in the random encounter areas.
This game is in deperate need of a run button. Things are too damn far apart and with the trial-and-error exploration that this game makes you do to find secrets, this gets really annoying.
The game is too easy. I beat the game without even finding the extra heart. The bosses might take you a second or two to figure out, but not much more. It's entirely possible  to figure out a boss strategy and defeat it without dying at all. Actually fighting them is never a challenge either. The rpg battles I've already stated were brainless, the puzzles the game has could likely be figured out by a 2 year old just as fast as anyone. The game always states where to go / what to do next in plain english.
There's barely any content honestly. You can probably go through the game in under 2 hours if you really know what you're doing and skip the two optional things (stars and cards). Nothing in the game is particulary challenging (unless you count it's assult on your patience) and it's extremely linear. I went out of my way to get every achievement just because, once I completed the game, I was almost done with all the achievements anyway (and if you know what you're doing finishing everything will probably take an extra hour or two more tops).
There isn't a whole lot of game in this game. It's a cute little showcase of things in video games, but there's no depth to any of it. There's rpg combat, but it's limited to attack, use items, or cast spell/use ability (and the full list of spells and ablities is: heal, ice attack, dragon attack). There's also no resource pools so you can just continually cast. There's 3 total equipment pieces in the game. They're all optional, 2 of them are armour which increses your defense and one of them is a sword which increases your attack. There's only a handful of enemies/layouts and many times you can easily play blindfolded. The rpg combat is just shallow. The hack'n slash combat is even more shallow. It boils down to just clicking space until the enemies fall down. You could strategise and attack the spellcasters first if you want, but it really doesn't matter because you'll still get through even if you don't. Lastly there's legend of zelda style combat which is basically like the diablo style except you have limited hearts.
=====================
If you want to introduce someone to the world of video games but you don't know what genre to pick, this game would probably be of some use. Other than that you might as well ignore even if it's on sale for $1. Play the games this is based off of instead (the legend of zelda series,the diablo series, dragonquest 8, final fantasy 6 and 7, I guess mario technically, and probably more) you'll have more fun with them.

Best game I'll probably never going to play again. For all its greatness it really apalled me that if you beat the game you get one single image celebrating your victory. And a bad one at that, too! No reiteration of your story, no assignment of a title, no scoreboard. Just "You did win, now bugger off." After investing several days into beating the game that's a serious failing.
Still... EL is probably one of the best CIV-style games out there. It's fun to grow your cities and add new regions, at the same time you don't want to randomly overextend your empire either. With mid-to-late-game tech you can, though. Harvesting lots of valuable resources, kicking some AI butt, this was fun. Much more so than CIV has been ever since CIV3, that is.
Some pros and cons:
+ Looks amazing
- You usually toggle away the looks because you need hard info instead
- Pretends to be fantasy, looks like Science Fiction
+ Quests keep the game interesting and varied beyond the normal 4X gameplay
+ Varied ways to boost your civ with resources
+ Great tech system with unlocking tiers, some hard choices
+ Upgrading your cities is fun

Endless Legend turned out to be more than just Civ 5 on an acid trip, but it's eccentricities  are what sets it apart from the other heavy hitters in the fantasy 4x genre.
The game has an amazing soundtrack by FlyByNo. It's not the usual epic score, by a really stellar ambient record that gives the game a dream-like quality that's strangely and powerfully immersive. If music is  important in your gaming experience, this game destroys the competition. Like cheese and wine, this game pairs well with absinthe or jazz cigarettes.
The combat is an aquired taste. It takes place on a kind of transitional map that is a literal interpretation of the area on the strategy map where combat began. You set the AI behavior of your troops before combat begins, and your troops will plan their own moves. This seems strange and hand-holdy at first, and it feels automated if you don't understand the complexities of the game mechanics. Movement is initiative based, but you issue orders to all your troops, which they then execute when you end your turn. Your orders can quickly go out the window though, once units start moving, dying, and fleeing around the battlefield. The AI behavior helps your units adapt to changes on the battlefield during the execution phase of the turn. Once you learn to read the behaviors of your units, the enemy's, and the initiative system, you'll need the AI less and take more control of combat yourself.
The rpg elements are meaningful and deep. You'll outfit and upgrade your line troops, as well as your heroes. You can really tailor your armies to suit your play style, again, if you take the time to learn the mechanics.
The maps are varied and beautiful in a geometric tabletop style. It's hard to overstate how good this game looks. Zoom in on a city and be amazed by the details.
This is a game that gives back what you put into it. You can play it lazily and miss the depth it offers. Be diligent. Learn the mechanics. Read the texts and immerse yourself in the lore. You won't regret it.

This is easily one of the most enjoyable Zombie games I have played in a long time. In a market that has become increasingly saturated over the years, mostly due to the ongoing popularity of Call of Duty's Zombie modes, it is refreshing to play something that feels so balls out ridiculous and designed purely for enjoyment.
There are no deep metaphors about the state of the human race, no morally ambiguous choices to make, just waves and waves of Zombie scum to obliterate in any means you deem fit. Don't get me wrong, there is definitely a place for a deeper exploration of the Zombie theme in gaming, but it's just so refreshing to see something deviate so whole heartedly from that and pull it off without just seeming like a stupid cash in.
Obviously this is not a game that will suit everyones tastes, but if you have any kind of love for classic B movie zombie fare or just want to spend a few hours watching heads explode with a few mates, I can't recommend this highly enough.

Of all the 4X games I've played, this one has had the most reasonable AI governor control. AI control really helps keep the game from getting too micro-managed, but unfortunately it also never really engages in a coherent strategy either and babysitting is always required. The scope of the game is significant though and you really cannot play this game in full hands on mode and maintain your sanity.
The game has some incredibly huge late game balance issues that need resolution badly. Planetary shields are horribly overpowered; instead of mitigating bombardment effects, they completely nullify them altogether, which is just stupid. For 20k (drop in the bucket) you get complete immunity to orbital bombardment of any kind! Whee! Which might not be so bad except that ground assaults are also broken, with tons of stacking bonuses that can make an assault on a heavily guarded planet effectively impossible. Meanwhile, actually loading troops into ships is often incredibly tedious and your AI governors will frequently fight you for control of the ships while you're trying to issue orders to load troops onboard. Meanwhile your ships will just respond to a load troops order by visiting the nearest colony... not the nearest colony with... you know... troops.
I really enjoyed this game and if they could just make invasions not a horribly frustrating experience I think I could recommend it without much reservation. Well, other than the obvious caveat of "Woah, that is a steep learning curve!" But as it currently is, the game is only fun in the early/mid game. It just completely falls over late game once bombardment stops being a viable workaround to homeworlds being immune to invasion.

There are so many ways to enjoy this game. Where to begin?

The user interface is atrociously bad, but I honestly can't think of any other way to get across the vast amount of information needed to play this game to the player. That said, finding buttons requires a freaking map and compass. Keep Google handy if you want to do something the UI doesn't think you'll need to do.
EDIT: After going further into a game, I've noticed a major flaw in the UI that cannot be overstated. The UI starts to look like a Jackson Pollack painting that moves, which is neat and all, but almost completely impossible to understand. You need to pause pretty frequently to understand what's happening, or automate more and more of your empire as you go on in order to keep pace with what's going on.
