Distant worlds is a Realtime 4X which essentially serves as a combination between Stardrive and The Last Federation. Everything you can do you can automate - which means that once your massive galactic empire starts hitting the 2 or 3 digits you can confidently delegate your minor decisions to the AI and policies you set for the empire. At the same time you always need to pay attention as the governor system will often make a decision you wouldn't have made or underutilise available  resources.
The enemy AI has exactly the capabilities of your own, which means that the only thing holding them back from crushing your empire is the input you place on it's path.
Aesthetically, the graphics are primarily functional - the fact that it's 2D is the only thing saving your computer from turning into a pile of melted scrap because once you start hitting several hundred occupied systems even the hardiest rig starts to struggle. It looks reasonable and with one or two exceptions you can generally see what's going on, although sometimes planets with heavy trading can get a bit too clustered to select anything.
The interface is quite plain, like the rest of Distant World's design. I recommend you use the built in tutorials and even practice on the tutorial galaxies as the general layout isn't very intuitive. The game is complex so this is expected, but some icon groups could be a bit easier to spot. I'm also somewhat disappointed in the diplomacy screens and the choice to use 3D models for the races instead of artwork.
The game's sound isn't particularly inspired by any stretch but it does the job, the music is suitably epic but does get grating after a while - you may want to consider muting music and putting on your own. The FX can get quite loud so keep the ingame volume a little lower.
The main storyline is wide in scope and primarily revolves around a hostile alien race called the Shakturi. Several expansions have widened the game lore significantly and there's now a wide variety of starting scenarios as well as custom scenarios containing however much of the main plotline you'd like. The game allows a lot of flexibility with regards to starting conditions and empires, and even takes things a step further by allowing you to edit your galaxy while it's running with a built in game editor (SM mode?). The size of creatable galaxies is impressive, with the advertised 1400 star systems and assorted bodies. There are games that can do larger systems but not as deep.
Gameplay is, in the end, where Distant World really shines - planetary
In the end, Distant World's appeal is in it's gameplay more than anything else. With a bountiful amount of resources, wide tech tree and reasonably deep colonisation system your empire keeps you reasonably occupied from the get go. Once things start building up and you develop a multicolony empire, you start needing to automate the more common decisions - facilities to be built, fleet management, warsand diplomacy. The policies system an AI are powerful enough to do this meaning that instead of feeling like some sort of accountant you can drop the minor chores and simply make the big decisions. At any time, however, you can step in and take over for as long as needed - feel the AI isn't building enough Cruisers? Queue for them to be built and the AI will revert to policy afterwards.
As a last note, I tend to leave ship design on automatic - the system isn't nearly as enjoyable or intuitive as Stardrive's, but perhaps I've just been spoilt for anything worse.
Overall I'd say Distant Worlds is a very good game for anyone who enjoys games like Stardrive or Master of Orion. The automation aspect implies that anyone can play no matter how casual, but the slower early pace - particularly on prewarp games - and unintuitive interface means that some may be scared off.

The character creation isn't all that fancy, but that's definitely not the focus of the game. If you ever even kind of enjoyed the Star Wars series, this is the game for you. You can play as anything you want, from a Sith Lord to a Jedi Master. This game was one of the first to include a reliable and easy to follow Morality system.
As you travel the galaxy, you meet a whole host of characters that can help/hinder your progess. Many of them are based off of common characters in the Movies... from a Han Solo Like smuggler, to a Bounty Hunter, to other master Jedis.
Many of the plot points are a little predictable, but that's also not too much of a problem. The game play is smooth, and fun. The entire game uses a d20 system similar to D&D. It also takes longer than I'd like to gain Force powers, but again it seems it's a necessity of the game.
Not only would I recommend the game to anyone who's a fan of Star Wars, but I'd also recommend it to anyone who's a fan of nice action-oriented RPGs too.

The first Metal Gear Solid game to be given an official PC release (that wasn't a terrible port like Metal Gear Solid 2 was) is here, and thanks to one of my friends being obsessed with the series, I was persuaded into picking this game up. It suffers from a peculiar problem, though; while it is a good game, there's a serious lack of content relative to the price tag.
Ground Zeroes is a little interesting here. While it suffers from some lower-resolution textures and models here and there, usually when it comes to world objects and weapons, the game still looks absolutely gorgeous and feels like a gripping espionage film from start to finish. The characters all look great, something I always like to see. There are some level of detail issues, most prominently with pop-in models, and some of the design elements are rather strange - such as the digital 'bars' that fly across the screen whenever one acquires intel files from the enemy - but that doesn't stop Ground Zeroes from having some simply fantastic graphics. They aren't cutting edge, but they sure are nice to look at.
The sound design in Ground Zeroes is, on the whole, fairly good. Weapons sound distinct, albeit a little bit muted for some reason, the environmental sound effects really help to immerse you in the world, and voice acting is polished and well done. I wasn't not sure how I would feel about Kiefer Sutherland replacing David Hayter as the voice of Snake, but he did a pretty good job in Ground Zeroes, and I think it helped to make the game feel more serious. The soundtrack is also excellent; not quite as distinct as previous games, in my opinion, but it still suits the game very well and helps to increase the emotion of whatever scene it's used in.
Ground Zeroes does very well in this regard. I was getting a constant 60 frames per second on my current system while playing this game, and I had very few issues with frame drops, visual artifacts, or crashing. Loading screens don't take very long, and as long as your system meets the requirements you should have no problems with Ground Zeroes. Thankfully, I also haven't noticed any game-breaking bugs or glitches.
Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes is a third-person 'tactical espionage' shooter game, which revolves around using a variety of tools - from your bare hands to custom-designed equipment which probably violates the Geneva Convention - to complete stealth missions in the pursuit of any number of things; revenge, glory, or just a plain old high score. Compared to its predecessors, Ground Zeroes' controls are
more smooth and polished, and it is very easy to control your character in this title, unlike in some previous ones. There is an easy to use radial inventory system for items, and a variety - albeit not a great one - of ways to interact with elements of the world. Weapons handle nicely, and firefights will take place at longer ranges in Ground Zeroes than they did in previous titles.
Ground Zeroes takes place after Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker, with Snake searching for some associates of his who are being held in a US black site near Guantanamo Bay due to their involvement with his mercenary group, MSF. Snake's company is headquartered on a massive off-shore platform known as Mother Base, and he is trying to find and rescue two hostages before a UN-mandated nuclear materials inspection takes place on their platform. And, that's about it. Honestly, this game was
short. I was able to finish it in about one hour. I'm not sure why they're trying to charge twenty dollars for it; years ago, we used to call something with this much content a demonstration and it would be free. I'm really disappointed with the amount of content here, even if it was very well-polished and played nicely.
I'm not sure what I expected from a company like Konami in this regard. They've done pretty terribly, and are actively working against the interests of community content creators whenever possible. There are no development tools available for the community, and Konami breaks the game's compatibility with existing modifications whenever possible. There are still some content creators which have done an impressive job given our lack of tools, however, so if you aren't happy with the game in its official state, you might want to look into the community's efforts to improve it.
Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes has no business trying to market itself at $19.99. I would never suggest picking this title up for full price, in spite of the fact that it was a fun game. Wait until a sale, and get it for, perhaps, 75% off. If its price tag were under ten dollars, I'd recommend it in a heartbeat, but twenty is outrageous for an hour of story content and only one or two more of side missions.

Definitely pick up during sales if you are interested in getting MGSV The Phantom Pain as well.

Reassembly is an outstanding game, I highly recomend it. Collect resources, buy new parts, design your ship to it's full potential, take over new territory, unlock new factions, and the process repeats itself.
But each time you play there are new challenges and new ways to play, offered by the seven diverse factions included in the game, and the thousands of workshop mods and contributions. The graphics are incredible and really bring the best out of a 2D game, offering vibrant and extensively customisable colour schemes. Arguably the game's best feature, however, is the stunning ship design platform that far out-plays any other vehicle design I've ever seen in a game, allowing you to place, rotate, and resize each individual block of each individual ship that you build. The way you build your ships determine how well they will do in the diversity of space, having to tough out aggressive forests of spiky plants, angered factions, explosive rocks and swarms of teleporting drones.
If you are particularly happy with a fleet you have created, you can pitch them up against your steam friends' fleets in heated Tournament mode, or even export them and send them to the workshop for anyone to try out.
The soundtrack is also very nice, fitting nicely in the background of the game. Whether you are battling a fleet of crystalline ships or spending time tweaking your mothership's design, the music creates a simple yet entertaining space themed aesthetic to suit the game perfectly. (plus you can buy it separatley as DLC; if it's DLC worthy then it's gotta be good m79)
Despite the single-player gem of a game this is, many people including me have been asking for a multiplayer mode for a L O N G  time, so if you are thinking that this is a space-themed MMO, you've come to the wrong place. There also haven't been many major updates of the game for a while, so I think the devs are happy with the game for now; don't expect any major new content being released.
If you want to see some gameplay, I recomend a youtuber called Deluks Gaming, he does very good Let's Plays that teach you the basics of the game (plus many tournament videos) and can give you a feel for it and whether it's a good game for you or not.
The game I think does take a while to get hold of, despite that you can never lose and there are infinite save files for you, and I think it attracts a particular audience, which is why it isn't a lot more popular than it currently is. Hopefully this has been helpful, I really can't stress how good the game is; take advantage of the sales and get it while it's cheaper ;)

Ryse: Son of Rome amazes with stunning graphics, but the pace of the game, and its length doesn't allow a player to enjoy it.
First of all, you have to realize that most negative scores are based on the fact that the game is extremely short. I finished it in 2 evenings - so I played for 7-8 hours maybe. If you take the price of the game, and its length then the score is quite reasonable. My review, however, focuses only on gameplay, and it's AWESOME! If you like the times of ancient Rome and slicing your opponents this is the game for you. I love actions games and taking a break from BF1 to play such a gem was really nice. Let's be honest, there isn't any other game where you could be a Roman soldier apart from i.e. Total War, which is a different genre. It puzzles me however, why the game is so short, why you can't walk (you almost always run), why you can't kill silently and why the creators didn't develop it further. Because of that, it seems as if the product was not finished. They could have gone so much further, because the world of ancient Rome they created is beautiful. I will never forget the feeling I had when I first saw Colosseum - absolutely stunning! Unfortunately, you don't get much chance to admire the views because everything happens too fast. Also, slicing your opponents becomes boring quite quickly. A player has no choice over his actions and there is no stealth option whatsoever.
All in all, Crytek created a beautiful game, which is definitely too short. If they developed it further, created alternative choices of events, enabled stealth kills, using tactics and an open world it would be 9/10 for me.

Evoland was a great concept for a game celebrating the history of games, and the execution wasn't as bad as it could have been. The presentation as a whole is quite nice. Unfortunately, there are several underlying problems that left a bad taste in my mouth back when I put this game down.
To begin with the positives:
-It manages to cover most of the big changes in the game industry that happened between the NES and N64/PS1 era.
-The spritework and 3D models for each "era" are well made, and look the part.
-The music isn't bad, not very memorable in my opinion, but not bad.
-Some mechanics are quite well represented.
-The game has a sense of humor. not a great one, but it's there, and helps keep things light.
-The controls feel okay. Not great, but it's good enough for what it is.
-There are a decent variety of areas to go through.
Moving on to the negatives:
-The game rushes you through the 'upgrades' to the visual and audio stuff so quickly you don't really have enough time to let it sink in. Once you have the 3D stuff you pretty much never see the sprites again apart from a few moments. In similar fashion, while I like that the game has both Active Time Battle rpg mechanics, and overhead action rpg mechanics, the former replaces the latter outside of specific areas.
-The story, while not the focus of the game, is very bare-bones and easily forgettable.
-The combat, especially the overhead action rpg combat, is unpolished, and on occasion feels incomplete.
-Many of the areas that aren't forests are only in 3D. I imagine many of the areas we only see in 3D, such as Laogai City, would be interesting to see in spritework. I understand that this was done to cut back on costs, as it takes time to make sprites, and it's easier and cheaper to just have one type of area be visible in 2D.
All in all, this isn't a bad game, I'd say it was a fun romp for the two hours or so I played it. I just feel it would have been so much better with a bit more time and money put into it. From what I've heard, that's what they did with the sequel. I probably won't play Evoland II though, and due to the issues I brought up, I just can't see myself reccomending this game.

Some puzzles are fairly easy because you know you got everything you need and must make it work somehow.
Others are terrible - the flipped ship, the rag that takes long to discover, the overall logic of the puzzles. One time you try to search the junk and your character says there's nothing in there of interest, next time you find something in there. When I get told: "This is all crap", then I dont expect this to magically transform suddenly to the puzzle solution. Games usually separate between useless and useful. The useless is for decoration mostly. These NPCs are called "workers", so there's not much to gain from them, but one of them has a name, so the player knows he's useful to progress in the story. These items are used to progress, others are just junk, decoration and so on. Usually the main character makes clear quickly what they are. You know you can look at them but never use them. I hate when a game ♥♥♥♥♥ on this and abuses well etablished ways for orientation as some kind of puzzle.
Lots of the stuff in the inventory looks like the weird crap it is, how do I know how I am supposed to use it? So I just try everything with everything until something works, and if nothing does, I just try everything in my inventory on everything in the outside world, which sometimes is a problem because the developers thought it's fun to search for hot spots.
Usually adventure games have a button to reveal them, not here though. I don't like pixelhunting at all, and I think old games, especially adventures, were mostly way too cryptic and way too complicated. I don't even call it hard, for me it's simply bad game design when you are clueless of what to do next once again. I wouldn't use bad game design as example of how to make a game unnecessarily complicated.
Usually in games you can figure out by some logical thinking - where do I go from here? What can I try? What item could go with which item? What am I doing AT ALL and WHY? Why am I accessing a giant robot again? Why like this? Why do I have to access a bomb again that also is a religious shrine somehow AND a powercore? Why again do I have to attach graphite to a cat with granny's panty hose to blow up a mailbox??
It doesn't have to be this way. I've played games where every next step makes sense through the WHOLE GAME and not only a few parts. It's not that the puzzles in Primordia are super hard to solve, it's just an overload of stuff. Especially of numbers. I think using plenty of numbers/codes is the lame way to create difficulty. Add some annoying minigames, like power cord connection and machine assembling. Ugh. Hand me the walkthrough!
Despite that, the game has great atmosphere, really good voice acting, I like the humor and sound design, and I'd still recommend it.

Distant Worlds is a phenomenon in itself; it is already a cult classic. The learning curve is steep and game UI and functions may seem rough at times. Don't let details like that fool you, because underneath, we find the best 4X games ever created and one of the best strategy games in history overall. I've been playing the game since late 2012 and been spending more hours with this than any other strategy title in recent years. I learned the basics of the game through watching YouTube videos and then I did my own epxerimentations to find my preferred gaming style. There is no one single winning gaming style in this game; you can play it however you feel comfortable and there are a thousand different ways.
The game satisfies many of my strategy needs. I can be a ruler of a grand space empire, dealing in politics and diplomacy, and/or I can take direct command of my fleets and see them fight out the battles against opposing space empires in real time. I can pause the action at any time, to take a look at all the details of what is happening; analyze and perfect my ship designs according to how well or not they perform in battle. It is even possible to not deal with battle at all; with a good eye for diplomacy, I could succeed in winning the game by avoiding warfare altogether and playing a peaceful empire. Indeed, if I wanted it, I could let the automation run the whole empire around me, while I controlled only one single ship!
Automation and AI is in focus. I'm not a true micro-manager, so I just leave the AI to handle certain parts of my empire that do not interest me. If the AI screws up, I can easily go in and manually order the building of that mining station on the polymer-rich planet that I need. The galaxies generated by the game are huge: Up to 1400 stars, most with several orbiting planets that may or may not contain valuable, extractable resources or other secrets. Soon, you'll have an empire with thousands of ships buzzing from planet to planet with the private sector taking care of transport of passengers and goods; mining stations, defensive bases, enormous star bases on your most important planets, and military ships and exploration ships going around protecting against pirates, border incursions or just out exploring distant star systems to find new resources. The immersion is immense.
Don't expect the outer polish of an AAA title, but do expect the complex, intricate inner mechanics of a truly great 4X title. The gaming community has been wanting a detailed, sophisticated strategy game for years and has been loudly proclaiming that it's tired of streamlined super-commercial games with focus on graphics and expensive DLC. Well, here it is. If you're not up for a real man's game like DW, then go play some AAA graphics focused COD in space instead, there are lots of them already. Otherwise, come join the cult phenomenon that is Distant Worlds.

Pros:
HUGE games with up to 1400 star systems, each with a star, planets, moons, asteriods, all moving about in orbits. You'll easily get hundreds to thousands of military ships, just in your empire alone.
Unique private sector builds and manages all their ships and moves resources and people around. It's fun to watch all the traffic around your bustling spaceports.
Automation options allow you to manage everything yourself or turn on complete computer control over everything.
You can turn automation on and off at any time during a game for anything, from tax policies for your entire empire down to individual ships.
Ship and base design is totally freeform. Place as many weapons, reactors, thrusters, manuvering jets, as you want on any of your military ships or bases. This isn't like some other 4x games where ship design means filling in a few blanks on an already designed ship class, here you decide everything about how the ship performs.
Cons:
The game engine is somewhat bad. The gameplay runs well enough on my old computer even in a big galaxy. Amazingly well considering all the ships and planets moving around both on the screen and in the galaxy at large.
But the game itself loads slowly, and loading savegames is also a little slow. There can be a noticable delay when bringing up UI screens and popups. There's also the occasional exception popup that allows you to maybe continue the game. I've also had one crash where I had to load an older autosave to continue.
But it's not so bad that it isn't playable, and if past expansion packs for this game are any indication then all the crash bugs should be fixed in updates.
This game is singleplayer only.
Bottom line:
This is absolutely worth the price RIGHT NOW if you're a fan of 4x games.
Tips!
If you have extra money and your population isn't at the planetary max, cutting taxes to zero or as close as possible can be an excellent investment for the future, since lower taxes increase population growth, which leads to more future taxes.
Conversely, if you are at planetary maximum population then move taxes to 50% or as close to it as you possibly can.
Intellegence agents can be extremely powerful sources of research if they have the skills and you can find an empire with weak counter intellegence.

Very good game. If you want a quick comparison, Lost Planet is sorta like Monster Hunter, but with mechs. The mechs themselves aren't the main draw of the game, they're more of a means of transportation. You fight mostly on foot, so this is mainly a 3rd-person FPS instead of a "proper" mecha game. So, keep that in mind when you buy this.
Pros:
- movement of the main character is pretty good, but could be faster
- nice ambientation, the feeling of desolation on open environments was masterfully done
- can get in and out of mechs
- mech sounds and movement are very good, although most are slow
- varied mechs (jumper, jack-of-all-trades, tank, etc)
Cons:
- weapon balancing went out of the window (dual gatlings on a mech do less damage than a handheld plasma rifle)
- no mech customization, except switching weapons during missions
- enemy AI (for humans) is VERY, VERY DUMB
- human enemies near the end are bullet sponges (except if you grab the plasma gun)
- this is a mission-based game, so there's no "sense" of progress at all (you start every mission with the same gun, you don't keep anything)
- the first few missions can be a drag
- sometimes you don't know what you're supposed to do, the onscreen info doesn't help
- if you're fighting out of the mech, it's pretty common to be ragdolled around without being able to do anything
- what the hell is that story

Split Personalities.
We see it in the best of our heroes. Ryse tells two different stories. The one told by the gameplay, about the most brutal demi-god/centurion Rome has ever (*fictionally) seen. And the one told by the writers about a noble and good leader who loved his family, his men, and his nation. Marius is all of the above. Like Nathan Drake, he murders platoons--nay--legions of faceless soldiers ("barbarians," the zombies of historical warfare), and then laments over the blood and carnage. What a well grounded guy.
This game almost earns my recommendation for how it unknowingly tells the story of Rome's final days. The outward nobility and beauty of one of the greatest civilizations that has graced the earth, which also happened to have a colosseum where people decapitated eachother for sport.
The game graces us with tales of honor and courage, even sings about the ideals of fairness and peace, while the menus want you to upgrade your ability to chop off arms, and show gruesome imagery while making silly, roman-esque quips about that sexy new move. Almost as if the developers and writers never had a chat about what the campaign was going to be about.
There are no ideals in the gameplay; It's all about how fast, how brutal, how gory you can make the combat. Marius is your poor puppet, helplessly flinging himself at hoards for your viewing pleasure. And, at least graphically, it is a pleasure to view.

Despite the bad press this game got upon release as a day-one game for the Xbox One/PS4, this game is an enchanting piece of artwork with incredible storytelling match with fantastic voice-acting and incredible gameplay mechanics. It’s no wonder this game is as good as it is given that Crytek are the team behind its development and they take a tried and tested combat formula (seemingly inspired by the likes of the Batman Arkham series) and match that with an encapsulating experience of heroic Romanic combat to produce one of the best action games of 2013 (2014 for PC).
Pros/Cons
+ The fantastically cinematic campaign strikes a perfect balance of longevity vs. repetitiveness.
+ The scale of maps and battles you encounter convey the experience of mass war.
+ Combat is incredibly fluid and upgraded execution paths keep combat fresh and intense.
+ Online multiplayer never seems to get boring thanks to the mix of maps and modes.
- The online multiplayer mode could have been stretched way beyond just co-op arena combat.

TL;DR:
After 17 hours play time, the game does not live up to what is promised in the description. The gameplay is crude, even for an older game, the story has yet to develop any interesting aspects. The game may become more interesting later, but the last 17 hours it kept me waiting. And I'm bored, so I don't really feel like playing any longer.
LONG VERSION:
This game is a bit of an oddity. It's made by Russian developers who apparently had little experience in making RPGs or games in general. I say this because the game is very crude and badly executed in some parts.
It didn't even start on Windows 7, but after upgrading to Windows 10, it actually works, more or less. I have to restart it every now and then because SFX and voice stop working, so only the background music still plays. I'd rather have it the other way around, as the game only seems to have two tracks - normal music and battle music.
I guess the game was originally in Russian, as it has its fair share of translation errors. Some sentences don't make sense, names keep changing (for example, the Merry Tower becomes the Jolly Tower and is also called the Tower of Joy).
Even on easy, the game can become quite hard at times, especially when several enemies suddenly leap at you. It is also made clear on several occasions that you should own a horse - you can take one in the very beginning and have opportunities to buy one in pretty much every area. However, I actually advise against it. The areas aren't that large, you can easily cover the distances by foot. Also, you often run into bandits or hostile fauna, and fighting from your horse is difficult. Not only is it hard to hit an enemy (they have to be in front and to the right of you), the horse also dies rather quickly. And considering how much they cost, this is not worth it.
The character you play seems to have no personality or spine at all. He is the only character in the game that is not voiced in conversations, and judging by his answer choices (mostly there is only one answer to choose from, making this a bit pointless), he is easily intimidated. While you can choose to be unfriendly and scornful to peasants, when talking to someone who outranks you, or has something you want/need, your answers often comprise "But...", "Yes...", "I see..." or "I understand..." (literally).
SPOILERS
After 17 hours of gameplay, I haven't seen much of a story yet. You're sent on a mission to kill someone, and gather information about someone else. The killing proves difficult (you are alone with him and could certainly take him on, but since you're quite spineless, he easily convinces you to do something else instead, and no, you don't get a choice here), and the gathering of information results in rather confusing information. Every so often you're teleported to some ruins where you talk to a stranger who keeps mocking you and telling you what to do. The first time this happened I actually thought a bug had sent me to the wrong scene and I was now watching something that should not take place until later in the game.
The information one receives is meager, at best. For example, you find someone's diary. Then the stranger appears and you start talking about the diary's contents. What is said does not make much sense.
"Did you notice him using thieves can't here and there?" - "Wasn't it cant?" (no typo).
Your first thought is probably "could you let me read the book BEFORE, so I know what you're talking about". However, when you read the book afterwards, it only contains one sentence, which does not really make sense to you.
Apparently the story is quite a drag. So far nothing really interesting happened. Reading the description of the game, I haven't seen much come true after 17 hours.
Let's compare the description with my experience so far.
"He’s strong, sly and intelligent, he is the most powerful person living in Arkanar" - Nope. He's not strong - 3 enemies are enough to overpower him in a sequence. He also does not come across as sly and intelligent at all. He follows orders blindly, is easily intimidated and outsmarted, quite gullible and listens to a stranger who keeps appearing to him in visions, mocking him and telling him what to do, without even questioning or wondering about his nature and intentions.
• Attractive non-liner storyline. - I'm hardly ever offered choices in dialoges, and if I do, it's usually either to accept or refuse a mission (side missions only), ask questions which do not influence the story, or to trade or not trade.
• Interface of medival and alternative future epochs in the game universe. - So far nothing, but the mentioning of a flying machine. Which could have been some delusional fool's fantasy.
• Original character development system. - Sure. Spending points on skills (light/medium/heavy weapons, ranged, some none-battle stuff like diplomacy) is very original, I've never seen that in any other RPG before.
• Interactive game world. - You can talk to NPCs, kill enemies, loot their corpses, loot chests and click on signs to travel. You can also bump into obstacles. I guess that counts as interactive.
• Real-time combat system with active pause includes many different combos and special attacks (stunning, disarming, etc.). - Let's see. So far I can... left-click to attack, right-click to do the same attack, use healing/stamina potions. It doesn't even look like the engine can do anything else.
• Varied managing approach to mercenaries and volunteers of the hero’s party. - I can't say yet, so far there was no way to recruit someone. There also are no signs that this could be done later, so I again wonder if the engine can even do that.
• Sci-fi technologies instead of a traditional magic system. - Not after 17 hours so far. The only thing showing that this is not a normal medieval world is raptors, giant leeches and giant spiders as enemies.
• Free movement through locations and random encounters using global map. - You use the global map to reach different areas, and you have enemies appearing on these areas. That's true. A bit too many enemies, at least I don't like the fact that I'm constantly attacked by bandits, even inside the city.
• Environments created in different style and landscape types affecting the movement speed. - I guess the game needs to advertize that it has different landscapes. So far I've only seen city and forest. I didn't notice any change in movement speed.

One of BioWare's earlier achievements, KOTOR's an easy game to criticize in retrospect. From the release of Baldur's Gate in 1998 to Mass Effect just 10 years later, most every RPG released by BioWare would follow the same mass-produced, literally by-the-books Hero's Quest outline—i.e., each game’s plot felt like a meeting of forced expectations, sometimes satisfying and sometimes mind-numbing in their predicted delivery—a choice that simultaneously made their products restrictive holds against and necessary stepping stones for advancing the depth possible in video game story-telling.
But who cares, right? KOTOR tells a generic Star Wars story with mostly generic Star Wars characters, meeting every generic Star Wars expectation a gamer could ask for right down to the tired, required lines, but it does so almost flawlessly, to such an extent that its seemingly pedestrian qualities make it among the most fun and accessible modern RPG experiences and Star Wars stories. In an age-old formula so noticeable and so repeated some players even refer to it as "the BioWare Cliché," a faceless variable with a background too vague and mysterious to be taken seriously, recognized by everyone around them as vitally important is thrown into the midst of a universal conflict against a threatening Force of Unfathomable Evil. As their life is turned upside down against their better judgment, they’re guided by close mentors friends, one of whose personality’s teeters on the edge of simply being Han Solo before he’s overcome by emotional turmoil (and the personality traits are thusly handed off to a snarky youngster and her wookie companion), the other a sassy, sexy Obi-Wan-Leia hybrid.* Through thick and thin, unsurprising twists and heart-wrenching betrayal, they form a series of close bonds and pass the required tests necessary to rid the galaxy of malice once and for all.
Dropping the vague references to clichés repeated, KOTOR stars a young nobody, canonically male, her past just barely customizable to the point of ineffectuality, being shipped under unspoken circumstances that end under the galaxy-wide Jedi Civil War igniting her hidden potential in the Force (à la Luke Skywalker) over an introduction spent making friends and escaping the occupied planet-city Taris. Under the tutelage of these newfound friends, she hones her skills in the Force, strained physically and morally under four major tests of heroism across beloved planets like Tatooine and Kashyyk. What she and her entourage seek, they seek in the footsteps of the Sith Lord Malak and his former master Revan—deceased: betrayal, Siths, &c.**—, piecing together an alien map in order to understand what massive power source drove those two to Team Slytherin, or, like, whatever.
Their fall is itself a story existing partially outside the game’s bounds, a series of events that took place after the culmination of the Mandalorian Wars—the galaxy’s previous Big Mistake and a war led by the war-mongering culture of Mandalore, a bone-headed, unlikeable civilization modeled after a single facet of humanity, their sole goal to enslave or destroy everyone just because. The backdrop of this war’s aftermath fuels the chaotic political state in KOTOR; it was a war in which the Jedi stood by, watching—idling on the decision of whether their place included interference—and yet a war won almost single-handedly the two previously-mentioned Jedi, rationalizing the need to defend freedoms and lives threatened by Mandalore’s conquest.
Krayt dragons, wookie tribes, life debts, Klingons, Jawas and their sandcrawlers, planets being razed from space, half-naked old men running around star ships, limitless sources of unimaginable power, lost alien civilizations, bland villains—KOTOR has everything you expect and love from a Star Wars tale, wrapped and guided by the massive conflict of good and evil fighting over mythopoeic indulgence. The central theme of mythology itself, abused by Lucas and now by BioWare, here works as a symbol of their aging morality mechanics. Following this game, treading those grey areas became a duty, even if it took a couple stories and universes to figure out how to present believably.
As an RPG born in 2003, it almost can’t help but tread that line between oldschool and new-, providing a strategic (but accessible, simplified) battle-management system that lets you plan the course of every encounter at your own pace, coupled with real-time decision-making and exciting action full of lasers and light sabers and lightning-quick force powers and, uhm, grenades, I guess—just with dice rolls, added and appreciated: beloved mechanic of chance in things past. The leveling system also stands as one of BioWare's most fluid and functional (opposed to, say, Mass Effect’s messy, meaningless overdose of options and numbers), letting players tread lines however customizable they can get to the point of breaking the game, i.e., as with many RPGs prior to this last generation, it’s not exactly difficult to customize your character to the point that whatever plot point is impassibly difficult, i.e., multiple save files are strongly suggested.
And as such an RPG, it took some shocking dares in character design: HK-47, the fan-favorite assassin droid prefaces every delivered line with the emotional intent behind them, creating a stir of always-contemptuous black humor and irony; and Jolee Bindo, whose entire presence—a good man sitting comfortably on the line between the series’ Dark and Light Sides, quick to point out the flaws (and outright stupidity) inherent in the tenets of the Jedi Knight code—hints at the brilliant postmodern deconstruction Star Wars would get in Obsidian's ambitious sequel. They let us know lead-author Drew Karpshyn was capable of a lot more than farting out game-y dialogue and fetch quests by the dozens even when limited by that bullet-point list of Quest-with-a-Q requirements.
That greyed-out line Jolee walks, also brings to the forefront major flaws in BioWare’s championship of the modern RPG format. Areas of grey don’t apply much outside of his character or even BioWare’s RPGs prior to Mass Effect 2, but the forceful impact of choice has been their calling card (& often selling point) since 1998. When choice arises in dialogue or action, the writers strive to bring the sense that you’re calling the shots, that you’re the acting force that shaping its conclusion. Those choices, unfortunately, amount to either following that path of charity and sacrifice defined by the Jedi code, or make your avatar sound like a cartoon jerk tossing out petty insults like candy--maniacal laugh included. Under this system, choices often amount to little more than variations on the lines “I’d love to help clothe and feed you!” or “I don’t have time for your stupid babble.” This never makes sense with whatever narrative is being told: E.g., Why would these characters follow these bad decisions? Why would this person fall in love with this monstrous cliché?
Are these aged mechanics and writing a bad thing? I would definitely argue No, despite the lingering force of Internet backlash BioWare gets from more critical players. The ambition driving this illusion of meaning in player choice has only improved and grown more bewilderingly ambitious with every game BioWare’s released, the massive steps taken between each a necessary movement culminating in (as of 2013) the phenomenon that is the Mass Effect trilogy, a series driven successfully by the player choice and personal involvement all their previous RPGs like KOTOR strived towards. It may have taken a lot of trial-‘n’-error gambits—still ongoing—but it doesn’t mean the errors are necessarily mistakes, and it certainly doesn’t mean they aren’t worth experiencing when they’re this danged fun.

Commonly referred to as the prologue chapter of Metal Gear Solid V, Ground Zeroes offers a variety of objectives and mission types, and a plethora of methods to which players are able to go about carrying them out - all in the game's pseudo-sandbox environment known as Camp Omega. In total, there are seven missions -- each with their own list of objectives and "trials." Without spoiling much, there is the main mission, four Side Ops, and two Extra Ops. The missions themselves are fairly diverse ranging anywhere from your traditional Metal Gear Solid stealth mission to an on-rails chopper-based mission (as the passenger, not pilot, to clarify). Something important to note about the missions packaged with Ground Zeroes is that each one takes place during a different time of day - in various conditions, giving us a nice glimpse of what would be to come by way of The Phantom Pain's day/night cycles and a hint at some of the weather affects (such as rain and snow). That last sentiment itself can be thought of as a microcosm for many who have played Ground Zeroes, in that it gives a great sample of what The Phantom Pain has to offer. That being said, this game has plenty to give in its own right - especially for a fan of the series.
The main mission's intro cutscene is one of -- if not the -- coolest opening sequences I've ever seen in a video game (or any other medium, for that matter). This one-shot cinematic follows a mysterious man paying a visit to a young volunteer in Snake's private army, Chico, before leaving the game's play area. One of the best parts about this scene is that it can actually be used by the players as a route to arrive at their destination. This mission only contains two cutscenes - in bookend form; one to start, one to close. However, there are smaller event-based scenes -- that occur in real-time! What this means is that, depending on whether you skip these scenes or not, the enemy patrols will vary. (Pretty neat!)
The game offers four Side Ops and two Extra Ops. I don't want to say too much, as I would likely spoil some pretty cool details. But I will say that these missions are a nice balance to the tone of the main mission and provide quite a bit of that traditional Metal Gear charm. While the missions are referenced as "pseudo-historical recreations," completing these missions in a certain manner will benefit those planning to play The Phantom Pain!
Kept you waiting, huh? The gameplay in Ground Zeroes is very streamlined and is so fluid that games like Splinter Cell: Blacklist and Hitman: Absolution feel clunky and outdated to me (despite the fact that those are two fantastic games in their own right, which control beautifully). The transition from standing to crawling, and vice versa, is incredibly seamless. If I had to describe how the stealth works in this game, I'd probably compare it most to Metal Gear Solid 2. You use the environment to your advantage, staying out of the light and in the dark. I compare it more so to MGS2 than a game like MGS3 mostly due to the fact that this game offers little-to-no mission preparation. For the most part, weapons and equipment are OSP. One of my favorite features of Ground Zeroes is the sneak peek of The Phantom Pain's "realistic passage of time" and "realtime weather." It is handled a bit differently in Ground Zeroes, but is present in some form. Here, the missions have a set time of day and set weather conditions. (Whereas in TPP, weather and other environmental factors all play out in real time.) It is much easier to be spotted during the day, but it is also much easier for you to spot enemies. As with the rainy night of the main mission, visibility is lower, making it harder for enemies to spot you while, in turn, also works against you for the same reason. Make it your priority to mark your enemies. Doing so will help play a part in planning the best possible route using the in-game navigation system known as the iDroid!
The iDroid is Snake's mobile device that comes in handy in more ways than the one mentioned earlier. Not only can you get real-time updates on marked enemies, you can do all sorts of cool things, such as listen to the cassette tapes picked up throughout Camp Omega - whether they be vital to learning the story of MGSV or tunes to rock out to (which can be done at the main menu or in-game)! Need backup? No problem. Call in Morpho using the "Helicopter" option on your iDroid and he'll be there to extract targets (enemy or friendly), provide cover fire, or help you escape once the mission is complete!
I've 100% completed both Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes and Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain, and wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone.
Imagine you are making a game and it is only one episode. And you pay real deal for it. I don't care how good it is, this is robbery.

I gave Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain a positive review, largely because of the extremely open-ended and organic gameplay. While the core mechanics are identical in both games, it's hard to give Ground Zeroes the same level of recommendation. Metal Gear Solid V should have stayed combined as one title; The Phantom Pain is the main game and is tons of fun, while Ground Zeroes feels like nothing more than a demo you have to pay for.
Gameplay-wise, the game is decent but doesn't measure up to The Phantom Pain. Strong stealth mechanics and intelligent AI make for a tense playthrough, and Camp Omega is a very well-designed set piece. Unfortunately, TPP offers a lot of extra depth that GZ completely lacks. You can't choose your starting point, there's no custom loadouts, enemies don't adapt to your tactics over time, there's no dynamic time and weather system, and a lot of the really interesting tools and weapons in the main game are entirely unavailable here. And there's really not much
here. There's ONE main mission (that's right, one and only one sole mission that has anything to do with the MGS V story), and a number of side ops which are over fairly quickly. There's simply not enough content to justify the game's price.
As for the story, Ground Zeroes take place a mere couple of weeks after the events of Peace Walker. It does a great job of setting the stage for The Phantom Pain, but that's all it does. That's all it
do. It's clearly supposed to be the opening sequence for a much larger game, chopped off and sold as a standalone experience.
You should only buy Ground Zeroes if you're really into the storyline for MGS. Be warned that you are not getting $20 worth of content. Not even close. If you're new to the series and just want to get into the gameplay, skip this and buy The Phantom Pain. It'll easily explain the short events of this game while offering so much more. Ground Zeroes, while enjoyable for a short while, is over far too quickly and it ultimately just seems like a tech demo for the Fox Engine more than anything else. Save your money for something else unless you really
care about MGS.

Not that Steam accurately portrays this as I almost never used it for Champions, but I've been in and out of this game since the beginning. Beta just finished, early start for pre-orders/lifers kicked off, and everyone sat in the start of the tutorial laughing at the characters other people were making. Some of which would probably not make it long before being reported for something or other.
That's still a huge part of things after all this time. Making whatever weird crap you can think of, seeing what weird crap the other guys are making. There are even player run contests related to stuff like that. Anyway, let's get to this.
The good:
If you've payed for such, you can make whatever the hell character you want, from the looks to the powers. If you haven't payed, you can still do a fair bit for free in this regard but if you've ever played as gold it will feel like your experience has been gutted. If you can't consistently be gold, I do not reccomend trying it out. You'll kill off your ability to play it for free.
The combat isn't terribly difficult, but it's pretty fun on average. With the right powers, it can lead to hysterical laughter at the keyboard. I can't recommend the force power set or the sets in the brick school of power sets enough for crits and giggles. Charge up your attacks and watch the henchmen of your enemies go flying to their dooms in the next zip code. The game is generally easy enough that despite how hard it is to get the best equipment you can, you will be able to play PvE with out a problem. Your milage may vary depending on how well you build your characters. Personally, I can tank Alerts without any items on at all with my tanky characters. A few days worth of daily questing at level cap will see your character more than ready to face just about anything.
One of my favorite things is kind of silly to bring up, but it's such a big deal in a Make Your Own Super Hero game. Character names are NOT first come, first served. The way this works out is with your account name being involved. Your characters full name in chat if you have showing this enabled will be Charactername@Accountname. This means you could make, basically, an entire super group full of the same character with your friends to mimic the power of making copies of yourself. It'd even be easy to look the same due to another favorite quality of life thing from Champions: the ability to save your costumes (the specific appearance settings of the character) as image files. You can copy 'em, pass 'em along to a buddy and they just drop the file in the right folder to be able to load it in game.
The not so good:
In a lot of ways, Champions Online had the most potential for any MMO I've seen in a long time. Unfortunately, a lot of that potential was not really lived up to. Due to questionable company mission statements announced in 2009ish with the beta and start of the game, Champions was pretty much always destined to not be Cryptic Entertainment's focus. Cryptic wanted to launch MMOs almost one after the other. What we've seen so far being Champions Online, Star Trek Online and Neverwinter. Each game is using the same base engine, but the more recently made it is, the better it utilizes it and the less deep rooted issues the game had in its basic set up. Splitting the staff up for the different games, Champions just doesn't have the manpower it needs to address some of the things that really need to be addressed for it to flourish.
That aside for the moment, let's talk about micro transactions, lock boxes and the change of the publisher holding Cryptic's leash. When the game launched, it was both buy and pay to play. It still had some micro transactions in the form of additional cosmetic options and the like. Costume sets, costume and character slots being the big money makers. Eventually the game began its shift to free to play, and we saw the precursor to lock boxes in the form of grab bags. The grab bags were cash shop items with randomized loot inside that you purchased. Lock boxes, when they took over would be collected as drops. The purchasing is directed at keys necessary to open them. Both grab bags and the keys to lock boxes are tradable items. Now, there's a whole hell of a lot I don't like about either of them. The least of which to me being the powerful equipment, because again you don't really need to try that hard to have adequate equipment. I'd prefer to just buy stuff I'll spend real money on directly, especially costume sets.
As for the change in publisher I mentioned, this is kind of a not very important point I feel people need to be aware of anyway. Originally published by Atari, Cryptic and its games were bought by Perfect World. A lot of people mistakenly attribute the current state of the cash shop and what have you to Perfect World, but in all honesty the grab bags showed up during Atari's run. Cryptic and them were already on this path, and the one about making an MMO one after the other as fast as they can manage. So when you see, or possibly contribute to, whining in game about PW ruining Champions, just remember Cryptic wanted this business model before they showed up. PW may have contributed to it, but ultimately Cryptic was happy to oblige.
This next con for Champions is mostly a symptom of the deep rooted issues. The code in Champions is all too happy to just break when the mood strikes it. I've seen more bugs come and go and come back later than I could shake a bug report at. There are a lot of nooks and crannies in this games code, and you really just never know when changing one thing is going to break another. Some of these bugs have been around a long time, others are new but will linger. The crew handling this game is doing the best they can in all fairness, but the game seems like it wants to make them look bad. Meanwhile the guys who wrote a lot of what's breaking, are probably working either on a different Cryptic title or at another company, so if something is put together oddly, the new guys have their work cut out for them looking into what the problem is and what to do about it. The debugging is better now than it was in the past though, to be fair to the team.
I think the last con I'm gonna get into is PvP. On its best days, PvP in Champions was unbalanced as hell. With great customization comes great dickery with unintended combos or powers that aren't really tuned well for PvP. On my last visit to Champions, the current problem with PvP was still pretty bad. The proper matches are nearly impossible to get into without arranging for things ahead of time despite having a queue system. The PvP vendors never got properly updated after the big itemization update, and the Alerts (PvE queue content) is just better by miles for leveling. Most of the PvP you'll see nowadays is one on one dueling. Where the massive amount of customization is boiled down to flavor of the month builds because it's impossible to balance for PvP in this game.
As an honorable mention that I feel is a bit of a neutral thing, I'll finish things off with this. The game is pretty campy. The Champions setting itself is kind of like that to begin with, back on the table top. But the area this really shines, or not depending on your view of it, is the voice acting. Everything from the lines to the accents is so cheesy. I've found myself pleased and displeased with this at different times.
Anyway, I do love this game. It's just not one I can play all the time, and I'm definitely not able to enjoy it without being subscribed. Hopefully this review will help some of you.

TL;DR: A fun laid-back shooter (with lotsa MECHS!) in which you don't have to worry about loot, builds, or backtracking. This means, in hard mode you can fully focus on getting good. In normal mode, it's a breeze.
Single player: The characters, the story, atmosphere, and characters are typically bad just like every game from Japan after the 90s.
But I'm actually pretty suprirsed the gameplay still holds up to this day. Blasting enemies in snowy locales still feels cheap, like you can tell the enemies are just cranked out by a director who tells the art team do whatever they think is cool and just cram that in the game without thinking how it integrates with the setting. Typical of Japanese games that try to take themselves seriously and fail, really. The meat is in the gameplay.
+ Pretty good graphics for an old game.
+ Lots of kinds of mecha toys to ride in.
+ Interesting game mechanic (Thermal energy is your life + game time rolled into one. And breaking the environment to earn them is fun)
+ Each mission is play-and-forget, meaning there is no overarching upg system or anything, which is good because I'm not stressed over what builds to plan out. Plus, if such a system was included in a "timed" game like this, it would cause too much pressure.
GG

An amazing 4x game, innovative but very polished. Probably one of the best in the genre lately. For those unfamiliar with the genre, it is somewhat similar to games like Civilization, Stellaris, Fallen Enchantress and others: a turn-based strategy where you build an empire from the ground up.
The asymmetrical factions make for various styles of play and great re-playability, as well as creating interesting situations during the game. It has a great UI and is generally a beautiful game, with a very distinct flavor and story that is communicated not through campaign missions but rather through in-game quests and the very progression of the game - the lengthening winter, the names of the techs from later eras, the rewards you get from quests and so on. It is also interesting that the factions don't quite follow the usual fantasy clichés - it takes some pages from sci-fi to add survivors of a spaceship crash, crazy machine cults and old biological experiments alongside ghost armors that feed on souls, weird forest people and dragon people.
It has some interesting mechanics that make it stand out from other 4x games, like the active use of luxury resources for different benefits, the marketplace where you can buy and sell resources and units, the cycles of winter that drastically affects your plans, the various minor factions that you pacify and assimilate for several different benefits (including new unit types and empire-wide benefits), the unique mechanics of factions and other minor things. Most of the mechanics are well-executed, with few exceptions (stockpiles, for example: an entire system for something very minor). Combat isn't particularly good either, a bit hard to control, but is good enough (and much better than in Endless Space 1 or 2, other games in the same series).
The DLC is also quite cool, in particular the new factions (that each bring new mechanics to the game).

Mystery Of Rivenhallows is a simplistic adventure game that most people probably acquired from a bundle of a famous site. It seemed interesting despite the not so great (pretty bad to be precise) reviews. Unfortunately these reviews are right (once again) and sadly Mystery Of Rivenhallows is not a good, but a very dull game, which fails to be exciting. The game not only disappoints in the adventure section, but also as a thriller (what it is supposed to be) and thus should rather be labelled as Misery of Rivenhallows.
Most people would still give (as I have) this game a chance, because it is a thriller and is supposed to be scary. To spare the reader from disappointment, let me tell you: we won't be dying of mystery overdose while playing (the ending is relatively predictable) and there's only 1 (yes, one) ghost sighting altogether.
According to the story, the game's protagonist, a journalist, was once a student in Rivenhallows Orphanage, from where children have mysteriously disappeared. He returns and decides to uncover the secret and find out what happened to them (why now?). Because if the police did not find anything back then, we sure will now, right?
The game puts us right to the entrance of the orphanage and after succesfully finding a way inside, our "thrilling" (less than an hour long) adventure begins.
Along the way we are going to find plenty of items and clues and this is exactly where the problems start appearing: while we possess a journal, most of our notes and memos are only going be pictures, that seemingly provide no help solving the mysteries and puzzles ahead. Looks can be deceiving though, so they do help us, just not the way anyone would expect. On one occasion we find a book with a page displaying a yellow giraffe, a red fish, a blue(ish) star and a green letter 'e' within the text, only to find out later (after several attempts to find any meaning for it) that this is the colour code combination of an electronic drawer. No there's no indication, no text it's just there and that's it. "Puzzles" like this can cause weird moments, like being able to beat the whole game within a few minutes (an item which is basically the key to the final scene can be found  almost at the beginning rather quickly by clicking around and guessing randomly). Some of the hints aren't bad and are actually useful (like the ones marking the correct positions of the window shutters of the dollhouse), but that's not the case most of the time. This leaves us with many intuitive puzzles and only handful of them can make good use of proper hints and clues.
Mystery Of Rivenhallows also makes the biggest mistake of all adventure games: most of the objects we find are keys for various locks. Searching for codes and passwords become refreshing in comparison.
The controls follow the usual point and click formula, but not without flaws here either: sometimes we have to click more than once on the given object/target so that the action can be registered.
To top it all off, the game isn't a sight to behold: it operates with plain semi-photorealistic scenes with lackluster colours and minimal amount of animations (nothing really, except for a few cutscenes). One could say it builds atmosphere, but in reality it just appears dull. There are also old(ish) black and white photos (and movie clips) presenting us events and people from the past, which is plausible.
There's hardly any sound effects except for the "ping" alert sound of finding clues and the usual door creaking. The music is mysterious sounding, but that's not nearly enough for salvation.
Mystery Of Rivenhallows looked like a promising minimum budget title with an interesting premise, but it failed to meet the expectations. At the end of the story the creators at least chose the only sensible conclusion, so it could be worse I guess. There are so many horror/thriller adventure games with great ambience available on Steam, that I really can't see any reason to recommend this game, not even to hardcore adventure enthusiasts.
PROS
+ ideal environment for a horror/thriller adventure, interesting premise
+ the music is fitting (sort of)
CONS
- clues are sometimes quite vague and don't point at the puzzles
- not thrilling as opposed to what it suggests
- minimalistic graphics, no sound effects basically
- very short
RATING
2.5/10

Wormwood Studios made their introduction onto Steam a memorable one with Primordia, a post-apocalyptic sci-fi point and click title. You will guide Horatio Nullbuilt through the futuristic, rusty dystopian wasteland known as Primordia. Horatio, and his floating comic-relief sidekick Crispin, need to get their stolen power core back; either that, or face death when their charges run dry and they shut down. They soon find out that getting their power core back is the least of their worries, as there's an entire city known as Metropol that's run by a corrupted master computer.
As you wander the lonely, desolate landscape of Primordia, you will come across many robots to interact with. Some of them are self-aware, some of them utter their pre-programmed responses, some will become friends, and some will be enemies. Man has ceased to exist for many years, though the exact timeframe is undetermined, but long enough for them to have vanished into legend. Horatio is a believer in Humanism, a religion that sees man as god; he even carries his copy of the Gospel of Man with him. The story is absolutely stunning, and the same can be said for the dialogue; I will forego delving any further into either so that you may truly enjoy the experience for yourself.
This is another point and click title that is obscure in its puzzle solving. There are many times that you will need an item which is hidden in a place that you'd never think to look. For people like me that completely suck with even the simple point and clicks, a guide will absolutely be necessary. However, for more advanced enthusiasts of the genre, you're in for a real challenge and treat. Every puzzle is a "think outside the box" type, and very few are expected or familiar. Even a large portion of the achievements are enigmatic. With a guide, you're looking at about 5-6 hours of playtime, without one you'll easily approach 10 hours.
The artwork of Primordia is done in a monochromatic rusty theme, for the most part consisting of dark browns and dirty oranges. There are subtle glimpses of neon reds and blues, and some places that are steel grey, but they're few and far between. The art does a fantastic job in bringing out the feeling that everything is coated in thick layers of rust, dirt, and sand, and that humans have been dead for centuries. Likewise, the pockmarks on Horatio and many other characters and places conveys the likelihood of near-constant acid rain. The melancholic, dismal, void-of-life atmosphere of the title is both exceedingly strong and somehow calming. The soundtrack is comprised of ambient, semi-industrial tracks that compliment the art wonderfully.
If you've been holding off on grabbing Primordia, stop waiting and just go for it. You simply cannot rob yourself of a detailed, highly immersive experience such as this one. Truly one of the greatest point and click adventure games of the modern era, Primordia is the complete package; visuals, audio, enjoyable characters, story, dialogue, and challenging gameplay. Even though it's a steal at $10.99 CAD, you can also find it on sale for $2.19 CAD at times, either one is a huge bargain.

Well, it wasn't my first first game. I spent my first hour or so getting mauled by pirates and figuring out how to deal them as well as getting out to colonize some worlds.
It takes a few hours to get used to the interface and the mechanics (Fairly certain I've not even touched 10% of the mechanics) but eventually it clicks and it becomes completely enthralling. Encountering different alliances and races, bullying out poorer empires for resources and kicking back and exploring the galaxies. It's absolutely massive.
The automation is pretty cool as well, there were points were I didn't want to deal with the economic side and just go messing around other peoples territory, there were other times where I got smashed and figured I better know how the economic side works. You have the freedom to automate or determine a lot of your gameplan.
Alas, In my first game I managed to incur the wrath of the Ancient Guardians (I think we had some contested bases) and I was well and truly put in my place (I didn't find/trigger the Shakturi).
Pros -
It's massive. Incredibly indepth, I've not even scratched the surface.
Being aggressive is incredibly fun, but the slow, methodical economic route is also pretty fun too.
You can even be a pirate, rather than a budding empire.
Music was pretty immersive too.
It's currently -17% off and supposedly this game ran for $100+ without the expansions.
Supposedly there's a story, so you get to enjoy that too.
Automation, so you can leave the stuff you don't want to do to the AI and you can get on with what you want.
Cons -
You will get smashed before you figure the basic things out. (Pirates are pretty brutal, do the tutorial!)
The game has a relatively steep learning curve, but it's nothing a few games won't sort out.
The UI can be a little.. messy.
Overall, I'll probably end up spending a ton of time on this. It's pretty fun and especially worth the money now that you get the expansion content at this price.

This review is of the single-player mode only.
Some great graphics (for its time) and drive-able mechs can’t make up for the bare minimum of weapons, linear progression, and boring gameplay. Add to this a poor excuse for a story that is told entirely in cut-scenes via the most basic of dialogue, and Lost Planet: Extreme Conditions is an empty shell of a single player experience that bores after the first mission.
Total size on my hard-drive: 8 GB.
+ Great graphics. Hard to believe Lost Planet: Extreme Condition is 10 years old.
+ Driveable combat mechs that can transform between different modes.
+ Massive monsters. If you like big boss fights, you can have fun.
+ Destructible cover, so stay moving.
+/- Grapple-hook provided, and required. But what could be a great new way to explore the environment is mostly used to “grapple up onto those crates to grab that out-of-reach ammo.” The game never takes full advantage of the mechanic.
+/- Large environments (good) that are strangely empty (not so good). Probably a sign of when it was made.  But what’s with the ruined houses and wreckage of cars lying about? EDN III was supposed to be a frontier site. A wrecked snowcat or two I understand, but a wrecked four-door sedan stands out like a sore thumb.
- No saving within a level. None. If you die, start the level over from the beginning.
- The story starts with a confused mess of an intro and never gets better. Cut-scenes provide some context to the gameplay, but little else. There’s no reason to care about any of it.
- Sniper rifle is over-powered. Picked one up before entering a snow-pirate base. Cleared the entire level in five minutes.
- Enemy AI is stupid as hell. Your buddy drops dead next to you from a well-placed sniper shot, and you just stand there like, “Yeah, whatever, man.” So dumb.
+/- Play the game in DirectX9 mode. As for DX10: apparently Lost Planet was created using an early version of DX10; Microsoft patched DX10 to approach some commands differently, but Lost Planet was never patched to be compatible with the newer version. You’ll have to copy some files from your Windows folder if you want to try it. And even then, there is one particular boss that will always crash the game unless you’re playing in DX9 mode.
- The game runs well enough (aside from the DirectX issue noted above), but the control scheme is a mess. Whoever ported the game clearly didn’t give a damn.
- Camera movement is horrifically slow (and mouse sensitivity cannot be adjusted in the options menu). This makes setting up shots very easy, but if you need to turn the camera quickly to face a suddenly spawning target, you’re in trouble. Press the Shift key + A or D to execute an immediate 50% turn. Makes the gameplay more cumbersome than it needs to be.
- Over-saturated brightness. Even with the brightness turned way down, I had to limit my playtime or risk a headache. And because the brightness was turned down to manage the snow-scapes, the caves seemed unnaturally dark.
- T-Energy count-down. Without a constant supply of T-energy, you won’t stay warm and you’ll die. Wouldn’t be so bad if there was plenty to go around. Sometimes enemies fail to spawn (T-energy can be collected from fallen enemies), meaning there isn’t enough T-energy to finish a level. Wtf.
I have previously played Lost Planet 3, and really enjoyed it. Then I saw so many people saying that Lost Planet 3 isn’t really that good of a game, and the original Lost Planet is “where it’s at.” Well, not sure what they were referring to, because I found Lost Planet: Extreme Condition to be a string of open-ish but ultimately linear levels stitched together with some incredibly trite cut-scenes, while the fun of the boss battles is hurt by the clumsy mechanics. Pass on this one. It’s not even worth the $3 I spent on it.

Evoland is a RPG-parody that leads the player trough different kinds of RPG gameplays during its cliche story.
While game starts off with basic action-adventure gameplay it evolves into turn based combat with leveling and later on into hack and slash. While each gameplay type is really just their most common stereotypical form, it doesnt evolve into anything bigger than that. The action adventure part is a zelda parody, turn based is final fantasy (7) parody and the hack and slash is diablo. Each is just the basic barebones of the games they parody and therefore really unenjoyable after a couple of minutes. It starts to drag on and get boring and the only thing that keeps you going is some new cliche they implement via a new chest that you open. All of the bosses are also just parodies of known bosses and just follow one attack pattern you have to repeat.

The story is a stereotype mix out of zelda and final fantasy 7. Almost all of the jokes werent funny at all because calling your main character Clink and the antagonist Zephyros isnt funny at all. As an example DLC Quest had a similliar structure like the game but was shorter and was based around one single issue with modern gaming.
After i finished the 3 hours of the game i didnt really felt i enjoyed the game in any way because neither the gameplay nor the jokes were any funny.

Easily the best 4X game I've played. It's real-time pausable, and has it all: grand strategy, ship designs, huge research tree, deep modding, everything from fighters up to planet destroyers, random events, diplomacy, economy, troops/invasion, borders/territory, fleets. And you can easily let the AI handle the parts you dislike, and handle the parts you like on your own. I love this game so much.

I cannot recommend this game without significant reservations.  For many people, this game may be ideal, but most people, even most 4X fans, will find it features too much micromanagement with a weak interface.
Distant Worlds is a 4X space game in the mold of Master of Orion and similar games.  It simulates building a space empire including setting up trade, mining asteroids, designing and building your own ships, diplomacy, exploration, and such.  That's a lot of tasks and all of them, to some degree, are interesting.  The problem is they all come at once.
Take mining.  You can mine nearly every planet, moon, and asteroid belt in the game.  This is important because mining provides valuable resources.  A large system may have over a dozen mining points in it.  That's fine and all, but that's a lot of mining potential and you receive an alert every time your mining station is attacked.  By what I would consider mid-game, once I've more or less completed my initial expansion and now press up against other empires, I have scores of mining stations.  Mining as a whole is important, but any single mining station isn't particularly valuable.  Thankfully, the AI automation is very good at setting up new mining systems so you don't need to manually send out your mining units.
However, the alert system is not so nuanced.  I receive alerts for every attack on every mining station.  Little information is provided on these reports and they come in fast and furious.  I can't tell from an alert whether this is a single pirate destroyer skirmishing on the frontier or the initial attack of an alien armada aimed at my home system.  If you click on an alert you should be sent to the area in question, but the game doesn't change the zoom level.  Watching an attack on a single mining station isn't particularly useful at the galaxy zoom level.  Consider that I am getting a ton of these alerts every minute of the game and the alert system becomes unworkable.
The same can be said about nearly every other system in the game: good AI for automation (probably the best I've ever seen in a 4X game), but poor human interface.  Of course once you get used to the AI, which will intelligently colonize planets, choose tech goals, and automate other high-level tasks (and can be turned off or overridden if you want to perform those tasks yourself), you will become frustrated by what the AI doesn't do.
Why the AI can intelligently choose a planet for a colony but wouldn't build planet infrastructure or critical star ports is beyond me.
Probably some of my complaints could be salved through setting up AI priorities and adjusting other settings in the game, but I'll be damned if I can find the right screens to do that.  The interface is just complex and obtuse.
If you are interested in an innovative space 4x with great AI automation then maybe you should give this game a try.  I can't recommend it straight out because it can be really frustrating to work with.  Maybe you will enjoy it, but be warned.
