As far as 4x space strategy games go, Distant Worlds has a surprising amount of depth. All of the components of everything you create require a specific type of recourse witch would create a nice challenge as you try to supply distant bases in an ever expanding empire, except that it is unnecessarily difficult to tell what any given base needs. The game provides no warning if, for example, one of your bases has run out of gas to fuel your ships' reactors until you recieve a warning of an alien attack only to realize the defense fleet you had at the station has no fuel and cant move. While this information can be looked up manually, it requires navigating a confusing, poorly ordered menu system, and browsing static menus for long periods of time just is not fun. The bad menus and lack of warning aren't an issue in the early game when your empire is small, but when your empire takes up a large chunk of the galaxy it can be neigh but impossibl to manage.
Distant Worlds also takes place at a surprisingly fast pace, with three technology trees that are all recearched simultainiously. New technologies are researched fairly quickly, so you will often find your once mighty fleet quickly becoming obsolete. Between your Military Ships, Civilian Ships, and Stations, which can quickly add up to over thrity designs, can quickly become an overwhelming management crisis, which requires tedious menu browsing to solve. This would not be so bad if not for the games terrible AI. If left to its own devices, the AI that manages you ship upgrades, research, and fleet assignements will damn you with the first pirate base you discover. The AI will equip your ships with a single week beam weapon, or if you are lucky, a few missle pods, then hurl them en mass at an infinitely better equiped pirate base. All the while, it will be researching how to upgrade your ground troops while a human fleet is bombing you from space.
I really wanted to like Distant Worlds, but I just couldn't overcome its design flaws. It is a shame, because underneath it all is a  the obvious potential for a really great game. The game looks good, sounds great, and has a level of depth and customization rarely seen in any game. The galaxy really comes alive once you have mad contact with a few neighboring empires, as civilian ships begin to establish trade routes and interact with your intersteallar neighbors, and it can be fun to just kick back and watch things unflod with out your intervention. Acually playing the game however, is a tedious slog down menu lane. If you are a hardcore 4x strategy fan, there may be something here you can salvage, but for anyone else the tedious menu system an terrible AI are just too much.

I bought this on a whim and having been having a lot of fun learning the ins and outs.  You can go for uber-micro where you manage every little aspect of the game... from ship designs, to colony tax rates, to research, to ground troop deployment, to ship maneuvering, to fleet operations, to... well, you name it.  Alternatively, you can play the role of a lone ship captain, turn all management over to the AI, and just manage one... single... ship.  This way, you can get a feel for the game and see what kinds of decisions and operations the AI takes out so you don't feel totally overwhelmed.
My first shot at controlling a minimal amount of ships went like this:
- Set things up in the Age of Shadows, kept pirates weak, went for smaller sectors, played pre-warp Empire
- Took command of the first exploration ship that got produced by the AI
- Bee-lined it for a planet that contained ruins on it (signified by three dots next to the name in the map)
- Uncovered the secrets of warp.  Changed up the research tree to concentrate on warp capabilities
- By this time, the AI popped out a two-ship fleet containing a frigate and a destroyer.  I decided to switch the exploration ship to auto and then assumed command of the fleet
- With this mini-fleet, I was able to fend off some pirate attacks.  Unfortunately, one of my mining stations fell and was taken control by the blasted pirates.
- I destroyed the pirate controlled mining station which kicked out a data core that gave me coordinates to an abandoned ship in a nearby sector.
- I visited that sector and uncovered a Capital ship that was adrift.  I could not believe my luck!  It had a huge warp inhibitor field to prevent enemies from running away, a large squadron of on-board fighters, tractor beams, and massive firepower.  I quickly added that to my fleet.
- The AI sent out several exploration ships which lead to the discovery of the base of operations for a pirate gang.  I brought the Capital ship enabled fleet to the system and was able to wipe that base out.
- Their base in shambles, the pirates quickly thought better of the situation and handed the remnants of their fleet over to me.
Wow.  Is that cool or what???
All of that occurred without much micro-managing.  The AI did the heavy lifting and I was able to engage in the fun of simply being a Fleet Commander.  Very cool stuff.  There is definitely a learning curve, but having a neckbeard is not a hard and fast requirement to enjoy this deep game.
Highly recommended!

Just in case, I started to play when it turned into Free-to-Play. I don't have the experiences with anything before that time either. This is my self explanations and the whole experiences I got during the time I played this game. (Yes, over 5k hours)
When I started out, the game got recently into free-to-play. From me, it was great!  I got into the game, got a hard time to choose my very first archetype (Free build for Free players) and the customization of my very first character, which I finally made a kinda "Lizardman fighter tank" looking for the Tank build (The Behemoth). Back in time, we had 2 primary stats for our character builds. When I played it out, Free Players, on PvP, could do at least to go Toe-to-toe with the subscribed players, which they are Freeform build (making their own powers,etc.) As for the crafting, I do remember the old system, where you needed to gather materials to craft your equipments. It was grindy, but in the end, it worthed it. And if you wanted to continue to do your researches for the crafting, you needed to go to a special location for each branch you wanted to do!
Maybe 1 year later, I went to the lifetime myself, thinking to support the game, like many others too! Then... they started to make one the mistakes I still am not happy with it: The Patch that it changed the whole system: The Champions Online ON ALERT. I was quite neutral with the stuff that it changed that we needed 3 Primary stats, but it was more focused to try to create some "balances" beyond superpower builds. The problem is, that system greatly degenerated about how it was. Instead of you need to focus on two stats and that you needed a teammate to help you out (MMO everyone! not MSO (Massive Singleplayer Online)), they did clearly put that everyone can solo MOSTLY ALL the contents without any other players (Except Therakiel Temple and I don't count the alerts, see below). So yes, a full team instance can be soloes without any problems now!
Where is the MMO feeling in that?
As written in my brackets. We got the Constant farming with the Alerts. The Alerts are instances that they constantly change after a set of time, doing some rotations in fact. The idea at first was quite innovative at first, but it was simply mind grinding them for getting free XP and leveling faster, most of the time. Otherwise, you can do those for gaining Money or Mods (new crafting system). But since most people do Experiences alerts mostly, mainly none does the two others. There is also another type of alert which you do gain another type of ressources that it is called Questionites. It is used for buying stuff in the store for free!
How cool is that! But here's the catchy thing: There is also a Questionite / Zen exchange which you can get Zen (currency from Perfect World by using real money into virtual money) by exchanging your questionites. But the Zen currency are coming from OTHER PLAYERS! So if you want Zen by exchanging your questionites, you should check what the other players has to offer to you IF they want to exchange it. I mean, the Lifetimers get Zen for free each month, so they can do that in the game freely without any problems. If we take another game from Cryptic Studio, for example Neverwinter, there is no such thing in the game! So you can't get Zen for free except if you want to pay on your own with your money from your wallet.
Anyway, I could return another disaprovement if we look toward the Crafting system, right now. Since we changed into 3 primary stats, the old items are not good anymore, so we needed to make our gear to be changed. The materials we used before are now useless. We need to get a Certain mod which it will improve our stats. As simple as that You can do that under 1 specific place. Do you remember when I said that you needed to go to another place to continue your crafting? Those places are no more around. There was a hole with some lights going out near a Prison in the City where you could enter to get into a specific crafting lab. Now you can't! They removed it. I was not happy when I noticed this. Heck, we were able to enter in a library before. But instead of re-opening the library, they made a Door, standing out of nowhere, front of that door, to let us go to a place of an ancient crafting instance: THAT HOLE near the prison, completly at the opposite of the city!
Then we have the famous PvP. The game never been too balance, I must say. The reality is that the PvP is really dead. I don't mean those who enjoys the Duels and such. I am rather more focused the PvP instance, where you do gain Points to get PvP gears too, along with PvP costumes! No one enters in those instances anymore. No one cares about those PvP. Mostly everyone prefer hitting each others in a duel, which it doesn't gives any pvp points. Since the duels are there, 1 vs 1, the Dev made a Team duel during one of the updates, no one wants to do that anyway. So what's the point if the players don't care anymore?
Seriously, I could add much more with my disapointment of the game of its state (My list would go on and such, no kidding), right now, but if I could make a favor for Cryptic Studio, I would say this one:
"Please, remake the game fully. This game is on the verge of being dropped down into the abyss. If you want to see it shiny, I would suggest to make a new one and maybe, just maybe, listen to the players  to those who have a idea to fix all the problems from it. You are too focused on trying to get this game as a money sink. Do like you did for the character editor: Get Creative, dammit!"
I know this isn't much, but to those who read my review, I supported the game fully. But I do feel, since a while, that this game really need a kick in the butt to get up, once again.

I skipped this one back in 2007. Lost Planet came along in a post-Halo-2 era when there was a whole raft of console-focused sci-fi shooters trying to steal Halo 3's thunder. Killzone, Resistance, Crysis, TimeShift, and on and on. It was easy to lose one in the onslaught, though Lost Planet does try for something a little different: a pyrotechnic, anime-inspired third-person adventure that feels like a sloppy mash-up of Metal Gear Solid and Gears of War.
The Good:
* The level design-- where you're often frantically hopping into a stolen mech right in the middle of a pitched battle and then ejecting out again as it gets blown up around you-- is rad. Titanfall obviously cribbed some notes from this one.
* The game still looks faaaaantastic with the graphic settings cranked up. The snow, dynamic shadows, smoky explosions, & even the fur trim on your coat still looks impressive.
* The cut-scenes are anime af, while still telling a story that's way easier to follow than a Metal Gear plotline
The Bad:
* Boss battles often seem more difficult than they're supposed to be, because of sloppy controls or bad camera placement. (Why the hell can't you go first person while piloting a mech? Too often you're blindly firing at an enemy while staring at the back of your own armor.)
* The basic enemy soldiers are laughably bad shots, like stormtrooper-level bad. This is fun in its own way, but can make some stretches a little tedious.
* That straightforward storyline sometimes runs a little *too* obvious, and left me wishing for a bit more Metal Gear weirdness.
Not much else to add. Surprisingly recommendable!

A pretty fantastic game, that is just a bit to heavy on the sandbox side for me. I should clarify, that I just figured I would try this game out last night, since it's been sitting in my library for ahwile. It was almost everything that I hoped it would be:
The Pro's
Awesome space battles, intuitive, fun, chaotic and beatifully designed
Easy ship editor, that is only mildly frustrating to use at times
Interesting factions, and well thought out gameplay
Massive universe: really captures the space adventure feel
Cool faction system
Con's
No goals or mission objectives. For some this is not a con, and I can appreciate this style of pure sandbox gameplay where the goal is to get a bigger ship to destroy bigger enemies, so you can get a bigger ship. However, I usually like my games to have some sort of goal to work towards, otherwise after awhile I lose interest.
There are Bosses, but I haven't had a "fight for my life" or a "holy Sh** that ship is huge! retreat" moment
Ship builder could use some refinement, nothing major, but it can be frustrating
While the world is vast, the terrain isn't very varried.
I started playing around 8:00PM yesterday and binged straight through the night. I went to bed for a few hours around 6am, then woke up and went straight back to it. It felt really great to have that "addicted" feeling in a game, I haven't experienced that in ahwile. That being said, In that 9-13 hours, I feel like I have experienced most of what the game has to offer. There are other factions to explore and unlock (I think I unlocked 4 or 5 during time played so far) but after ahwile without a purpose and when you've built your big bad mothership, you start to wonder what to do next.
Some people were complaining about the grindy nature of the game, and actually I felt that was done quite well. I felt the grind relaxing, and I was always eager to find new enemies, get more resources, and upgrade my ship. I would love to see some DLC that add's proper bosses, Missions, new terrains, new factions, some sort of primitive economy, trading, selling, bounty hunting, different way's to mine, some sort of story line, or anything that adds more of a reason for me to actually *want* a bigger ship. As it stands it is fun to create a bigger fleet just for the fun of it, but the pressure of a more well defined enemy, or additional base mechanics could add a whole new level to gameplay. I really think this game had the potential to be the next terraria, in that the gameplay is a blast, and it's also a unique experience. It's old so I am not hoping for updates, but would gladly pay for some DLC or a sequel.
I think 15 dollars is a bit pricey, considering that after this binge I will likely not pick the game up again, but I just paid 13.75 to go to the movies the other day for 1.5 hours of so/sso entertainment. 15.00 for 9-13 hours of solid entertainment is a good value in my book.
If the dev's are out there, for the love of god make a sequel. Consider adding some sort of endgame, and you'd have a real winner.

The game description reads, "Only by reaching the very end will you unveil the terrible truth to the shocking events that eventually shut down the orphanage."
Well, I obvioulsy did something in the "wrong" order, because, after playing only 15 minutes I found something that triggered the revelation of the "shocking events!"  It was the ending early, because the police were called, and the newspaper headline was about how I, a former resident there, discovered the truth.
I could back out of that scene, and continue to play, and use my inventory, but really, what's the point?  I know what happened.
Is that happening to everyone who is playing?
Or, are players thinking the game's over at that point, and not playing more?  I thought it was over until I realized I hadn't used inventory yet.  "Continue" just repeated the ending, so I used the back button to continue playing.
If that hadn't happened, I was having a lot of fun. I am not big on point and click adventure games, most of them make me sick with movement, but this one was not like that.  I like having to take notes, no hints, etc.
So, I recommend the game if the events play in the right order, but I don't recommend it because the end was ruined for me, and it may be ruined for you.

Rise was a launch XBOX One launch game clearly meant to show off what a next gen console could do. It looks absolutley beautiful, even by todays standards.
Pros:
- Looks incredible.
- Great animation and voice acting.
- Story itself is interesting enough.
Cons:
- The game doesnt really change mechanics at all from the beginning.  Meaning the relatively shallow combat system is the same one you will be using throughout the whole game.
- The upgrades. There are upgrades you buy but they never felt meaningful or useful.  I just bought whichever ones i could afford. There arent many and it is never apparent that they were ever necessary.
Neutral:
- The combat.  I put this as neutral because it in itself isnt awful.  But as i pointed out, it doesnt change,  The combat consists of a shield attack, a sword attack, a roll, and a parry. There are a few heavy attacks which can be performed by holding the sheild or sword attack down.  So you slash your way enough with the same two buttons for the most part until the enemy gets an "instant kill" icon above them.  When this happens, you click a button and perform a series of prompted button presses that play out in a stylized manner. If you click the right buttons, you can regen health.
If you are looking for a pretty game that has dumb redundant combat and no real progression character-wise, Rise may be something you could play to kill off 5-6 hours.  I wouldnt spend a ton of money on it. Like 5 bucks tops.  But there are better games to play for those 5-6 hours.

The Pros and Cons for this game are as followed
Pros:
-Male/Female main character options (romatic relationships relative to opposite genders)
-Custom name and skin tones allowing for varied personal experience
-Best Cinematic Experience gaming has ever given us in 2003.
-Dialog options that constrast from a linear gameplay model (Ie. one choice, one path.)
-Customizible items that improve the weapons as well as increase dialog options further (Ie. headgear or clothes)
-Active combat dueling that allows directional control over multiple units while commanding squad-based tactics
-Rich dialog allowing greater character depths that add fuel to the already brush fire of outstanding RPG fueled quests. (Ie. side missions activated during dialog options.)
-Light/Dark side personalities and perks (Ie Light side Healing/Dark side life drain, Squad buffs, Force Moves, Dark side lighting.)
-Balanced level design/combat (Ie. leveled the maps with the same level NPCs as the player.)
-Change character perspectives to play other character with useful perks/skills
-You can't grab all the perks and beat the endgame in a minute! You need to take a minute and look for the best option
Summary: The gameplay is fluid with the custom dialog options that inturn create a symobic relationship with combat and specialized tasks (Open a door as a robot, hack a computer as a Sneaky ninja, create a destructive path of an unrelentling powerhouse of multiple combat tactics.) Which allows the player to get deeply emersed into their customized hero. This game allows a broadstroke to the overall quest to finish the game with the player's choices deeply rooted into the arc of the story making this a great blend of RPG/Turn-Based Action Adventure,
Cons:
-Failed run cycles forcing uncontrolible camera angles
-Combat sluggish behavour that feels incomplete
-dialog circle options (never-ending conversations can be repeated endlessly)
-Invisible walls in locations that should be allowed to explore but is walled off for pacing purposes
-broken quest options that become active after a point of no return to finish and complete said side quests making for bad game design
-Cinematic graphics unseen in the game but transmit during a factal scene of the game (if you make a cutscene turn it into a loading screen transition to the next level)
-invisible walkpaths that block movement and stop exploration that results in a previous saved file (hereby hindering the exploration of any place an instant roll of the dice to dodge invisible locations that you cannot escape from.)
-The skybox is pretty, I want to go there. (I actually can't so no happy dreams for me.)
-Item textures are almost lego-esc inspired and run cycles on the player mode is almost near robotic (the Machine characters have more physical emotion with every stride.)
-Miss shots or melee swings that divert adventure with needless combat (Ie. Lightsaber should drop all but the strongest enemies.)
-Random number generated hit detections that result in bad combat that cripples pacing of exploration.
-Stuck character paths that break combat and run to unexplained locations, making the feel of combat useless when no one is there to fight.
-Redundant dialog options exist breed and procreate in droves to the point of slow pacing to hinder the RPG adventure.
-Grinding XP to max out player level, can be repeated NPCs in common locations for easy farming and level gain that ultimately ruins game play
-Forced auto-target that throws combat delays for miss queuing tactics and failed assaults.
Summary: This game is a great example of rushed and delayed game mechanics that almost make it unbarable to play but slightly engaging enough to make up for shooty game play for interactive story arcing to force the player to make generic decisions that ultimately have little impact or forgotten meaning behind the main quest, which begs the question "Why did I complete this mission?" Cliche'-like characters with linear direction and little personality that make the game more uncomfortable to play with predictible actions and no independent thought going into their design. There more, the cinematic experience is almost half the game? Why? Also citing sexuality concerns as underware clathed characters can seemlessly walk through combat or exploration losing the important element of adventure and gaining a "neckbeard level" attraction.
In conclusion: There is a library of other elements to this game I can't complete as the list will grow more and more, this review is to get the surface level pros and cons that I remember most about and try to hopelessly translate it to others without addressing the main concerns. So! Buy this game if you want to emerse yourself into a galaxy of planets and quests that make you question the consumation of time that it took to complete every part of the game from - side missions to puzzles and intellectual tests that really  set the pace of the game. However, clunky controls robot run cycles and dorky item textures (aside from god-like lightabers which are cool by the way!) this game is a average 7/10 good but not too good to be any less than an average RPG with dialog options and ques that differ from a simplier RPG with a mono directional path. This game is worth it if you have the patience for Star Wars games and RPG elements similar to Buldar's Gate. (BioWare did a great job expanding the Star Wars extended universe.)

To anyone who has windows 7 or higher and seem to not be able to play the game, heres how.
1. Set the .exe to run in windows xp service pack 2 compatibility mode.
2. Set the .exe to always run as administrator.
3. Added AllowWindowedMode=1 to the ini and set Fullscreen=0 so the game always runs in windows mode.
4. Turned off Frame-buffer effects and soft shadows in adv. graphics options. Also disabled anisotropic filtering and anti-aliasing.
5. Went into sound adv. options and clicked the option to force software.

"Until we realize that things might not be we cannot realize that things are" a great poet once said.
I have to admit that I didn't fully enjoy Primordia on my recently finished first playthrough (there will be more) - it started excellent so the further into the story I got, the more I was waiting for it to disappoint me. But it didn't.
It's somewhat ironic, that game so "retro" - from it's visual form, through mechanics, to themes - feels so fresh. After playing so many contemporary adventure and semi-adventure games it's nice to see that there are people who don't see stories just as shiny boxes filled with emotions. Instead of killing some characters who got a lot of screen time to make viewer shed a tear and considering job well done, Primordia focuses on building an atmosphere, allowing emotions to occur naturally, and, what is recently rare in storytelling, tells a story. Rather than having a bunch of characters hoping from place to place pushed by expendable plot, the game has a topic which it wills to explore.
I might say, that Primordia is philosophical, that it's meditating upon metaphysical themes, but we may not quite understand each other, since the meaning of word "philosophical" has devalued. The game isn't trying to make some "social commentary" or present a political concept, but it asks fundamental questions, questions that, one may say, are ancient. But, as a (great) poet once said, only weighty ideals live long enough to be called ancient.
Every element of Primoridia harmonizes with each other. Unique and rich world isn't original only for originality's sake - a wasteland world where robot's seek their raison d'être, a city ideologically based on vague and hollow Progress, a court where the judge has two advisers - justice and mercy, the Gospel of Man which was given to robots by their creators... Primordia becomes more like a biblical parable than a typical belletristic story.
The meaning of life, the wonder of existence, presence of evil in the world, relationship between creation and creator, between robots and man, between man and God - Primordia not only mentions these themes, but also discusses them. It reminds us why people used to tell each other stories. It was because they had something to say.

It focused mainly on high-level 4x game information, most of which I already knew.  When I tried to interact with the interface, I became flustered immediately.  I told my planet to build a construction facility, as the tutorial suggested, and had to decide which one myself having no real basis for making such a decision.  I then couldn't even verify that it was building until I dug around enough to realize the game was paused.  Once I unpaused it, though, I still couldn't really verify that it was building until I zoomed in really close and saw some construction dust like effects.  There was no progress bar listing the build queue, or active projects, or anything that would show me progress.  I started to explore around to different planets, and was very uninspired by the whole thing.
So I can't really speak to thegame depth, or the features, although they all sounded good to me.  For me, I cannot get past that interface, which really seems to be as bad as I've ever seen.  I found myself getting frustrated really quickly, and I gave up.  I've probably spent more time writing this review than I actually have playing the game.  I'm sorry I couldn't be more complete.

NOTE: I already own the non-steam version without the Universe expansion and have thus invested way more time into the game than steam claims.
This is a seriesI have really tried to like. I have invested money into all of the expansions, hoping each time that the game might become fun. But it just doesn't.
The single biggest problem with the game is the concept. While the idea of controlling a huge empire indirectly through AI automation may sound clever (and I admit that it does), it also means that the player isn't left with much to do (you can try controlling everything by yourself but you won't have any fun because of the insane micro that you will have to suffer) and that the AI's automation will either make or break the game.
I will admit that the AI automation isn't half-bad, but it's really not ideal either. It's really painful when you get attacked and then defeated merely because the AI did not have the good sense to build a strong fleet and an army even though your AI empire setting gives fleet building a high priority.
If you so wish you can only make the AI control certain aspects of the game while taking care of others, but no single aspect is really deep enough to be fun all on it's own. This makes for a dull game.
I will admit that the game has some strong points, like very good game start-up options, and this latest expansion is suppose to make modding even easier than before. But for me this doesn't fix the game's core flaws.
Overall I regret having to say that this series just isn't doing it for me. I am sure others might have fun with it, but it just isn't my cup of tea.

Distant Worlds is a 4X unlike any other, and is unmatched in its variety, gameplay and complexity. Don't let the complexity scare you though. Thanks to intelligent automation, Distant Worlds can be as simple or as complex as you want. Only want to deal with one ship or a fleet? Fine, automate everything except a ship and explore like it was a spaceship game. Only want to deal with ship building? Fine, you can set that to manual and everything else to automated. Want to have advisers suggest certain courses of action, but leave the details to the AI? You can do that too! The galaxies in Distant Worlds are teeming with life, and there's always something out there to discover.
Thanks to an amazing amount of races (even more with modding) and an exceptional amount of game setup options -- including an in-game editor to make changes on the fly -- no two games will ever be alike. If you're looking for a 4X game that makes you feel like an emperor rather than a micromanager, or if you want, a ship builder rather than an emperor or, if you want, and admiral rather than a ship builder, then Distant Worlds is for you. I've played nearly every 4X there is, and this is my all-time favorite.

This was a thiny-veiled cash grab / advertisement for Phantom Pain.
This game features a single "mission" as well as several "side ops" which are played separately.  All of these are played on the same map and, while that map is pretty detailed, it's barely larger or more complex than those in games like Hitman: Absolution or Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
The gameplay was good, what little of it there was.  It took me two hours to beat the "mission."  (Technically, I suppose it was the only one.)  I enjoyed the game mechanics, but not enough to execute them again and again in the same game location.
The designers of the game seem to have no concept as to how technology has changed since 1975.  Snake is outfitted with an "iDroid", which is essentially a telephone, tape player, radar device, electronic map, and PDA.  I normally wouldn't gripe about something like this, but the dissonance between the supposed time period and Snake's equipment handily kills the atmosphere.
The story was *almost* on par for stealth games like this: sufficient to motivate the game but shallow and full of cliches.  (Not too surprising, since there wasn't enough story to fill a 20 minute TV episode.)  I haven't played any MGS games in a long time, though, and this game makes constant references to characters and events that I'd never heard of.  I'm sure it's excellent fanservice, but the game didn't really make itself accessible to stealth game fans from outside the franchise (despite the short, textual exposition made available in the main menu).
Overall, it's quite a shame.  The game is gorgeous and the gameplay was quite enjoyable.  But it's exceedingly short, not very well motivated, and leaves you feeling like you've just been had.  It's definitely not worth the $20 that was being asked when I wrote this.

Metal Gear Solid: The Paid Demo.
Ground Zeroes is a pretty good taste of what MGS is like, right before it turned into MGSV, which is a hell of a lot different. The mission (singular, yes) is tense as ♥♥♥♥ and really gives you the old MGS feeling of infiltrating a massive base and surviving against all the odds (although the odds are slightly higher this time).
The story of GZ is pretty short, just like the game. For those who haven't played Peace Walker, the game preceeding this, you'll have no idea who some of the main characters are, like Chico, Paz and Kaz. It's not fully necessary to play PW, though.
The gameplay of GZ is great. Very neatly put together. Everything works together perfectly, and the game does exactly what you want it to. You're not fighting with controls.
The playtime of the game is short. It comes with Ground Zeroes, the main mission, which lasted a good two hours the first time I played it, and then six smaller side ops, which feature different objectives in the base. They'll take a good 15-30 minutes to complete, each. After that, there's not much left to do beyond collect some stuff and play again on a harder difficulty.
The game runs as well as The Phantom Pain, which is really ♥♥♥♥ing well. You're able to play below minimum specs and most mid-low range cards can still get 60 frames on relatively good settings.
For a purist MGS experience, GZ is pretty good.

Decided to write this one a quick review because at the time of writing it's on sale.
I bought this game a few months back when it was $20 and it was worth it. It's a fairly challenging coop shooter with Zombies and it's a lot of fun. Plus it's 3 games in one, so for $8.99 it's a steal.
This game features the stories from NZA 1 and 2 with updated textures, an exclusive third story continuing on from the other two that you can only buy in this collection, and a decent survival mode which is also exclusive to the trillogy. All are available in 4 player coop.
It has a fairly healthy online community, but it's certainly best with friends, which is why I don't have much time on it. That said, it has a certain dark humour to its story which makes it both endearing, but also a bit terrifying at times. If you're a fan of Call of Duty Zombies, particularly World at War, you'll probably love this.
I have a fairly mid range PC (AMD FX-6300, R9 270x) and I run this at 80 fps 1080p on high with supersampling off and it runs beautifully. The graphics are pretty decent too.
If using an Xbox controller is your thing, the controller support is fantastic. Simply turn it on at any point and it'll work just fine. I use a 360 controller, but the game most certainly supports an Xbone controller too (it's image is used in the controls section of the options).
Basically, buy it now while it's on sale because it's great. If you happen to read this after a sale, it is still worth getting it over the other two if you want both.

What is there is pretty good but also gets dull rather rapidly. I particulary like the graphical style with the intense colors and the kind of 80s computer games like presentation. The designs of the enemy ships are also very cool. From space-bees to space-plants, the factions both playable and unplayable have unique and cool designs. The game shines when you stumble into big conflicts between multiple factions. Its all pretty blood-dragon-hotline-miami-esque if that makes sense :D Or if you are as ancient as me it might remind you of standing in an actual arcade. Only presentationwise though. The scale of the universe and amount of stuff going on on screen is pretty huge.
The ship building is very enjoyable and a lot deeper than I initialy thought. From gunships to carriers to "ramming-devices", there are a lot of feasable designs you can go with. Different factions will also have different equipment.
My two problems with the game are that, for one, while you can test your ship against other ships directly from the build menue, the battle is automated for some reason. This just seems odd. Also the game picks random ships that have a comparable cost to yours. Since I'm not into multiplayer I would preferre it if you could just fight one on one battles agains the AI with a ship of your choosing (Like fight your old ship with your new ship)
While the former is more a nice to have, the end game is where the real problem is. You "can" conquer the universe in this which at first glance seems to be the endgoal of the game. The idea being that you can create stations that in turn can create more ships. In practice this means that you just dump out at least one station in every sector and then move on. There is not really any strategy involved in it. Nor is it interesting. Personally I just discovered the universe and then got bored. It would have been cool if the "empire building" was a lot more fleshed out than it actually is. It seems to be just tagged on and is ultimately boring. Maybe if you're a 100% completion guy that still appeals to you, for me personally the game ended after I discovered everything once. It has been a while since I played but I believe the game is already complete. While it has mod support, I don't imagin core game mechanics are something that is exposed and changeable by mods. It is therefor likely that the basebuilding aspect of the game can be considered final. This is a real shame. In my opinion the game could be interessting for manytimes as long if that would have been done a little better.
At any rate for the price you can expect 20-30 Hours of cool exploration and unlocking higher and higher ship classes. Then it ends anticlimacticly when you discover that you could conquer the universe now but it would also be pretty dull.
Still if the game seems at all interessting to you from the trailers you should get it. Its uniquely pretty and pretty unique.

The only negative I can see to this game is the fact that it does tend to go into a lag fest when you enter a bee infested or thorn infested territory. In those situations, the lag is manageable (it feels a bit like slow mo, so get ready to fight those battles reaaally slow). Otherwise, avoid those territories and that problem never occurs. One of the reasons I bought this game is to get my spaceship building fix, while still being playable on a non-gaming laptop. Evoland is very quirky, offering clever references to classic and popular rpgs while still being original and fresh. The idea of an rpg evolving it's literal gaming elements (I.e.: music, graphics, generational gaming mechanics) while you progress is very well done. The writing for the story and characters is very simple and easy to follow, however it is not well polished and can feel rushed as a result. If you love rpgs and their tropes, and having a heavy or well-written plot does not bother you, then you'll definitely enjoy this game. Even still, Evoland is an easy-going, short (about 10 or so hours long), and has a good sense of humor. I would definitely reccommend it as a game worth playing.
PROS
- Music (has great background music and sound effects)
- Graphics (the different visual styles are all well done)
- Concept (great originality and creative twist on a classic rpg genre game)
CONS
- Plot (very loose, too simple, broad and kind of boring)

Ryse (shudder) is a pretty tried and tested game in terms of styling and mechanics - it's a hack n' slash and it does a pretty damn good job of not making a meal of it. Son of Rome suffers as much as it gains from its simplicity; due to it's simple uncluttered gameplay and small areas the graphical standards can be pushed as high as possible (this was something fo a showcase game for the Xbone after all) and framerates even on lower spec machines should be high. The game is easy to play and enjoyable with a whopping three buttons used - attack, block, bash with shield, oh, make that four; do cool but completely unrealistic finisher that in a real fight would get you killed. That's pretty much it for the whole game - no complicated skill trees, no upgrades, no new combos to learn. Just plain old hack and slash.
Problem is, this makes the game exactly the same at the end as it is at the beginning. Which is bad. Not a deal breaker but it's still bad. Once you figure out that slash-bash-slash-bash-slash-bash-finisher works for 99% of enemies you'll be left struggling to find new ways to make fights interesting.

After a total 11 hours of playing, I've finished Primordia. As a point-and-click the gameplay is mainly based on puzzles and some basic crafting, but its steampunk atmosphere, its hughely charismatic characters and its deep and thought-provoking messages are the strongest part in the game.
In general, Primordia creates a powerful discourse about justice, law, charity, industry and energy, community and knowledge, energy and history. Most importantly, about logic and free will. As a player, you are brought to wander in an environment that is partially an echo of men's life, partially an odd representation of robotic life, where to the decay of humanity is counterposed the need for energy of the last city on earth. Every knowledge is lost in the dust, and Metropol, the city where the two protagonists will find themselves in, is a ghost city whose only side still provided with energy is a long road.
I will be haunted by its finale for a while, also because of its powerful credit OST. It leaves its scars, but worth, worth playing.

I love the writing, atmosphere, characters, and soundtrack of Primordia. It's a sort of post-apocalyptic dystopian future in which "Man" went extinct in the distant past and robots are all that is left on planet Earth. I liked that a lot of the story went unspoken and has to be pieced together as you play the game, and I find it funny that I have come up with my depiction of the "unspoken" backstory in my own mind. I also thought the voice actor for Horatio was excellent.
That being said, the movement is a bit clunky (even considering that it is a 2.5D retro game) and I wish there were more areas to explore. Also, the game being pixellated did not add much to the experience. I often wonder what the game would look like with hand-drawn sprites instead of pixel sprites (probably much cooler).
Overall, I would recommend Primordia if you have the patience for a point-and-click RPG.

A Hideo Kojima Game
Ground Zeroes is short. Ground Zeroes is just a prologue mission for The Phantom Pain. Ground Zeroes is pricey considering the amount of content. And yet, Ground Zeroes is also an amazing experience that stands up to pretty much most of The Phantom Pain, and is better than most missions in that game. Barely any enemy outposts in TPP can be even compared to Camp Omega with its security cameras, numerous guards that can't just be Fultoned out of existance, hidden cassette tapes, and limited resources. If you're planning on playing The Phantom Pain, doing a playthrough of Ground Zeroes is pretty much mandatory, not only to understand the story (as it's the link between Peace Walker and The Phantom Pain), but also to get the first glimpse at the tight gameplay both of the Metal Gear Solid V iterations offer.
Sure, the price-point is a bit high for what is pretty much a 2-hour mission, but getting all secrets, extracting all prisoners and playing through the six Side-Ops will extend that time by quite a large bit. It's definitely worth at least the sale price of 4.99€.

I struggle to understand why some people seem to like this game.  As 4x games go I find it far inferior to any of the other games readily available.  The game itself is automated to the point where a 'player' can just sit back and watch while occaisionally clicking on a confirmation button.  Performance is suprisingly poor with message windows having an odd way of painting in one piece at a time over several seconds.  It is very frustrating just trying to tell what is going on and even more so trying to direct the activities of your empire.  Ships come and go on their own, giving them orders is painfully difficult and even then it seems like there is a good chance the orders will be ignored or superseded by some other automated command.
I find the UI difficult to use and rather unhelpful (and I enjoy Dwarf Fortress!).  In the face of resource shortages simply directing your units to colonize an appropriate planet and build much needed refineries is an exercise in studying the fine print across several spreadsheet like windows.  Budgets for building and research balloon into the 10's or hundreds of thousands one  minute only to disappear again by the time you've decided what to spend it on.  Similarly ships are destroyed and replaced with barely even a blip to bring it to the player's attention.
In short the game feels like it prefers to run itself and almost seems to make it intentionally difficult for players to get involved.  Imagine a game of Galactic Civilizations or Master of Orion where all actions were automated, the player existed only in a sort of spectator /  advisory mode while turns flipped by at the rate of several per minute and you have a glimpse of the chaos and frustration that is Distant Worlds.

Distant Worlds is one of the most enjoyable 4Xs I have ever played.  I have been playing it since the Legends expansion and took part in the Beta for Universe.  When I first started playing it, I had a hard time getting into it and went back and forth from feeling overwhelmed (limited automation) to feeling like the game was boring and basically ran itself (too much automation).  The turning point for me was when I started watching some of the excellent LPs by DAS24680 and Larry Monte.  As I watched more and more of their LPs I gained a better understanding of the game mechanics, many which I didn't even know existed.  I slowly began to switch off parts of the automation and instead of feeling overwhelmed found myself having a great deal of fun.
Pros (IMO):
+ Automation: The fact that you can automate almost every aspect of the game allows for the flexibility to choose what kind of game you want to play.
+ Community:  The community is very friendly and helpful.
+ Private Sector: Having a private sector that is outside of your immediate control is a really neat game mechanic that adds another dimension to the game.  It also makes for a more immersive experience.
+ Resources: The fact that a component that is built for a ship or base requires certain specific resources.  I enjoy that aspect since it adds another dimension to the game and makes you prioritize what planets you set up mines on first or colonize first.
+ Game Setup:  I like the fact that you can change almost everything about a game and that the game remembers your settings.  This allows for the ability to customize the game however you want and leads to substantial replayability.
+ Modability:  I think that it was a really good decision to make the game fully modable and can't wait to see what the community comes up with.
Cons (IMO):
- Graphics:  Initially, I didn't like the graphics very much and my initial impressions of the game were not good.  However, over time I have gotten used to them and have improved them via mods.  I also understand that given the size/complexity of the galaxy you can create a map for (up to 1400 stars), having less system taxing graphics is probably a good design decision.  I will take complexity and the ability to create large 1400 star galaxies over graphics any day.
Mods that I am using:
Distant Worlds Extended Universe 1.0: Adds 18 races to the game bringing the total to 40.
Das Chrome UI: Reskin of the UI
Make sure to watch some of the LPs before/after you purchase the game to get a better understanding and appreciation for the game mechanics and enjoy the game.  This is definitely a diamond in the rough.

There is no other game. There is only Distant Worlds.
Why do you play games? What is their purpose? What can they achieve?
This game answered all those questions for me. I struggled with the learning curve, until I just made the computer do everything, paid attention, and took control of one thing at a time.
You can macro manage the entire game, completely zoomed out and looking at the galaxy map as the computer makes ships, assembles them into fleets, and lets you designate where they form up and take control of worlds for you. You can take control of just a single ship and fly across the galaxy with it as a miniscule speck in the sea of destruction that roars around you. You can be the scientist and let the computer utilize all the research and technology you've acquired. You can just work diplomacy and back door deals. You can do whatever the hell you want in this game, and every aspect of it is incredibly deep to the point that makes you want to curl up, suck your thumb, and cry for your mommy.
I've played over 20 hours the past two days, losing sleep and my mind, and I've barely even got out of pre-warp stage. Buy this game.

I got this game a veeeeeery long time ago (it was still in early access if I remember well), and it is still by far my favorite once-in-a-while game. When I'm not sure what to do, I launch Reassembly and play for a perfectly undetermined amount of time.
Reassembly is the perfect relaxation game. The music is both calm and upbeat, making the transitions between travelling, gathering and fighting almost seemless. Vector graphics also help to the surreal feel, and they allow the game to run very smoothly on most computers (as long as you keep away from the damn spiky plants, spamming projectiles until your computer fries). Fighting is also a spam-festival, but somehow keeps your game running good (and there is never FPS drop: only a physical simulation slowdown), and it is just exciting enough to be fun without making you hyper-active like playing Quake on accelerated speed after injection of pure Montain Dew essence. Death happens a lot, but isn't too punishing most of the time, and you usually tell yourself "oh, well" and keep going. Building is complex enough to make you activate a few brain cells without frying them, and permissive enough to allow for some beautifully shaped motherships,or if you are like me, spamming of pulse lasers to make an one-shot cube. Speaking of absurd powerful weapons, The tech system (a.k.a factions, unlocking weapons and upgrading your ship) is diverse and smooth enough to keep you going for quite some time.
My personnal recommandation is to spam the same mid or end-tier weapon to make your gunships, except for the tinkrel (purple guys) able to make their own weapons: here just make a fat♥♥♥♥♥death-pouring valve, it's hilarious. And of course never forget the anti-missile cannons.
My personnal favourite faction is the Red, because the lack of shields (hardest faction, by the way) forces you in making a swarm of well-designed ships, usually quite cheap and fast to produce. Unless you try to attack a ridiculous player-made gunship, few fleets can compete with a 100 ships army.
The only complain I have is the lack of true multiplayer: you can see other player-made fleets in your world (agents), but that's it.
Otherwise, I highly recommend getting this game.

Introduction
The moment your given control of your ship in this game a terse tutorial quickly shows you the controls and basic mechanics. Then it tells you to kill everyone who is colored differently from you, that's racism. Or is it spacism? Since it's in outer space... I think... for all I know it feels like your a bunch of bacteria fighting for control of someone's stomach. Either way, Reassembly delivers an enjoyably modular destruction sim where you are the only person in your entire race who has something very special, initiative.
TL;DR
+++ Mods
+++ Shooting pieces off of ships
++ Ship Building (Way better than any other I've seen out there IMO)
++ Pretty visuals
+ GENOCIDE!!! (pretending your Alexander the Great!)
- Genocide (knowing your actually like Hitler)
- AI isn't great (especially if you have followers)
- Vanilla game has a total point-cap of 8000 (there is mods that "fix" this)
-- Taking territory can become grindy
--- Lack of reward for taking territory
GAMEPLAY
The game plays like a twin-stick shooter in that the default controls have you aim and shoot with the mouse and control your thrusters with WASD. The controls have several different configurations and can be rebinded if desired. I've found the default controls to be sufficient.
The game starts you off by choosing one of the several factions (more if you have mods) and plops you in some friendly territory equipped with the outer-space (or inner-gastric, I don't know) equivalent of a dingy. You then must use your meager might to collect purple floaty-things called "resources" (creative huh?) to trade in at friendly factories for "credits" (again, the innovation!). The resources usually grow near plants attached to asteroids/food-globs found throughout the galaxy/stomach. You can also get resources by killing black/white/red/yellow/etc colored ships. You will then use the credits you get from trading (aka, going near any friendly factory) to purchase new parts and a higher point-cap (lets you add more pieces) for your ship.
About half of your time spent in Reassembly will be in the ship designer. It's quite easy to use once you get the hang of it. Everything you would expect to need for a ship is present here (as long as you've unlocked the right parts). You build around your core (the part that you should be protecting) with pieces ranging from armor, to point-defence, to generators, to drone-launchers. What is it with games nowadays and drones? Well, just like real life drones these ones break really easily. Unlike real life drones you can keep spamming them out and overwhelm your enemies.
One of the problems with the game is that the ship builder only lets you upgrade you point-cap to 8000. This prevents you from building those giant ships shaped like various things. However, don't fret, there are more than a couple mods that rectify this horrendous hindrance to holocaustic, wholesale, hellenistic, Hitlerism.
Another thing this game gets wrong is that it presents you with a daunting task of occupying every sector of the galaxy/gut with your color. This requires exterminating every single thing that isn't your color. Some would say this exceeds Mount and Blade: Warband levels of grindy conquering. Plus there are wormholes ({sarcastically} wormholes, riiiiggghhhht) scattered through the galaxy/gastric that urge you to go to a different world entirely (or upload the designs you've built).
Despite these flaws, the game excels in letting you shoot everything and watch it break. It is immensely satisfying to watch an enemy capitalship get it's primary weapons turned offline as you separate them from the main body with a giant cutting laser, or any other of the MANY weapons to be found both in the vanilla game and mods.
Story
Once upon a time...
life evolved/someone swallowed
into many races/some bacteria
that fought for control
of the galaxy/of the abdomen
I'm just kidding, there is no story past what you imagine.
Graphics
The graphics in this game are highly modifiable and can be absolutely beautifully (I'm talking like, epileptic levels of lights, shaders, blooms, etc.) or look like a flash game for those of you using potatoes. But hey, that's still fun. I myself played at potato level for several months after a hard drive failure {shudder}.
Conclusion
All in all, this game is definitely worth your time. I bought it at full price, but you could wait for a sale (not that I've ever seen one for this). Even if you just have 15 minutes, Reassembly can satisfy that modular ship shooting itch with it's varied factions, massive possibilities and amazing ship builder. So get this game go have fun taking over the galaxy/belly!

Turbo Dismount is the fourth game in the dismount series, and the most ambitious one. I've played all of them at least once, and the progress Secret Exit has made is impressive. I do have a few gripes, but so far I feel like Turbo Dismount was a worthy purchase.
Turbo Dismount is a physics simulator in which you take one poor little dummy man (or lady), put them in one of a varity of vehicles, and sending them to certain destruction. The game offers a nice varity in regards of vehicles and maps, which helps keeps from growing boring. Most maps also offer you different paths you can take, as well as spots where you can put obsticles in hopes to reach a higher score.
While the game offers a healthy varity, it remains a game much like it predecessors; a game that you play while bored, or for a few minutes at a time. Playing it for too long will numb your mind, no matter how many times you see your little dummy character shatter into pieces. Trying to reach high scores is always fun, but most of the time you won't reach that high of a score unless you know the odds and ends of the system, and what vehicles have the most potential to cause calamity. If you try to score attack every time, you'll end up finding yourself trying the same things over and over again, just awaiting that one situational change to make your score sky rocket.
This aside, the game shows a lot of promise and potential, and at the very least it'll help you kill a few hours while waiting for your friends to log in. Ten dollars might seem like a lot for a time killer, but so far the developers have not dropped this game, and if they continue to support it, then it'll be completely worth the investment.

In
, you play as Max who lives together with his loving girlfriend, Ann. Max lives a pretty care-free life while Ann is the one who works and cooks the meals. However, perhaps everything is not quite what it seems.
This game is a short visual novel. Despite the choices available, the game is fairly linear. The choices only alter the dialogue a bit and achieve different achievements. All choices end up leading to the same ending. As said, this is on the shorter side. Even with backtracking for achievements, this game should not take more than a half-hour to complete.
The art itself is okay, though the short length of the game forces a limitation on how much there is. The music is fairly generic sounding, but the game is not long enough for it to be repetitive.
As with most visual novels, the story and writing is the main thing and this is where the game has issues. The only real purpose of the game is the twist ending, so I will avoid spoiling it. However, that being said, I did not feel the twist was really worth it and, truth be told, I had already pretty much predicted it before the reveal. Other than that, half of this game's short content feels like filler material which is really inexcusable considering the game's short length. There is not much room for character development and I really did not care about the characters nor what happens to them.
The writing also has another issue. The game was apparently originally written in Russian and translated. The translation is often poor with the text being replete with grammatical errors. This really could have used a proofreader.
Overall, with a boring story, limited characterization, and problematic translation, I do not recommend this visual novel. It is free and short, so you do not have much to lose by checking it out if you are curious, but I found it to be a very underwhelming experience.
One final note: When I first tried playing this, it seems to have triggered my anti-virus software. I know I am not the only one who had this issue. However, the warning appears to be erroneous as I have had no issues when the game started running. Still, such an issue should really have been checked and corrected by the developers before being released on Steam.

Awesomenauts, oh how good you could be if your developer fixed the long standing problems this game had before launching F2P.
There are quite a few problems, some of them deeper design decisions, some of them technical.
Let's start with the worse that every player will encounter more often than not. If you think about picking this game up and enjoy a round on your own, well matchmaking will remove that fun for you.
It likes to pit you against premades. Long term player premades on top of that. Yes, you as a new player solo queuing with an characters that cannot even buy every item available in the shop, will be put against veteran premades. And you will get stomped hard. And this will get worse, as the playerbase declines after the F2P release. I cannot imagine how the game will look like in 4 weeks for a new player just joining.
Next up, a technical issue. The game uses Peer-To-Peer for networking. One player is decided to be a host, who controls the basic assets like turrets and droids. Other than that, you have a connection to every player, and the connection between you and the other players decides how fluid those players move around. You can have those with a good connection towards you, and it works fine for the most part. But then there can be a player with a bad connection towards you, and those players will move eradically, with lot's of teleporting. Since hitting it based on their current position, you have to hit those teleporting models. In return, you will most likely also teleport around on their side. But if you know you have a bad connection for the most part, you can just pick a character who requires less aim.
If you ever wondered why your general Moba, even the smallest ones, uses dedicated servers, well this game shows why.
The there are design decisions. Characters, called Awesomenauts or short 'nauts, in this game only have 2 abilities plus a third ability which is their basic attack. There is for the most part no resources either, so skills can be used based on cooldowns, and cooldowns only. That isn't necessarily bad. After all, it's not fun to not be able to use your skill because you have to save mana. Also there are no ultimate abilities which long cooldowns and massive impact, which isn't so bad either. The problem comes from the fact that every 'naut has only 2 abilities. For them to have a unique feel, and impact on the game they must the strong. Like really strong. They basically rolled the power that is normally distributed among 4 skills including the ultimate into just 2 skills. This results in most characters dealing massive amount of damage, with very bloated abilities. Most characters have abilities which allows them to deal burst damage like you would expect assassins to do. Yes, even supports will have abilities which are around 400 damage, just like assassin abilities. With how fast it is to switch lanes (about 1-2 seconds), you are basically always in danger of being ganked if you play offensively. Even when a support switches lane, that's an assassin now.
Abilities are also upgraded with new perks along the match. TLDR and all that:
This game features you hacking your way through the enemies and then the members of the Roman Empire. It ends with you defeating Boudicca, queen of the celts, on a war elephant. In Rome, during a Barbarian invasion. When you also kill emperor Nero. That said, the graphics are neat, and the gameplay is solid enough for the most part. If you can switch your brain off while you play it, and can avoid a brain hemmorhage during the final cutscenes, you might enjoy it. Maybe.
Longish version:
If you enjoyed films like 300, you will enjoy this game.
If you enjoy an Assassin's Creed style gameplay without the hassle of stealth or an open world, you will love it.
If you watched Gladiator and King Arthur and thought, "well, that was nice but could I have less historical stuff and more violence, please?", you will be hopping for joy when you play Ryse.
If you enjoy steering your clichéd overpowered butcher character through an increasingly ridiculous world of violent slaughter, you will be ecstatic.
No, really, I'm not kidding. You might enjoy this game. I know I enjoyed parts of it (the violent parts) - it's a great way of blowing off steam.
If, on the other hand, you like your game stories to make a modicum of sense, you will find this game disappointing.
If you like playing a character that isn't motivated by his family's violent death and is unburdened by any other defining character traits than his finishing moves, you will increasingly be feeling the urge to bite something after the first third of the game.
If you disliked the fascist undertones and pointless glorification of violence as of 300 and the like, you will hate this game.
And if you are the kind of person who thinks games set in the Roman empire should possess at least a tiny smidgen of historical accuracy (as in, having something in common with the Roman Empire), you will be beating your head to a bloody pulp on the keyboard. This game makes the Total War series look like it was written by historians, heck, it makes 300 seem historically sound. Even Game of Thrones has more historical value than this game. I am not kidding. In GoT, at least the armour and swordplay are realistic. Ryse does not even have that going for it.
Essentially, Ryse: Son of Rome is only what I can assume is the product of a game developers' brain storming session that went along the lines of
"Hey, let's make a game like 300, but in Rome!"
"Sounds awesome, we can make some really nice visual effects!"
"Yeah, and we can use gameplay that will make the player feel like a total killing machine!"
"Yeah, we need recognition though. We need stuff any idiot will recognise, you know, Boudicca, War Elephants, Centurions, buzz words."
&quot♥♥♥♥♥♥ we'll have to research that, though."
"Nah, don't sweat that. Just go with what seems awesome."
"Okay... what do we do for story? Should we do something original?"
"No, I got this. Throw the plots of King Arthur, 300 and Gladiator into a word recognition blender and take the most popular results. These guys will buy anything..."

Champions Online is a superhero MMO RPG game, that became Free2Play few years ago and is a spiritual successor of City of Heroes.
You will have to make Perfect World account to play this game. The game isn't exactly at the peak of activity, but is still being updated with small events and new shop stuff. Community is also there, even if some zones are almost completely empty.
Now, as far as gameplay itself goes it's a standart MMO RPG. Well, Superhero theme sure helps to set it aside from usual fantasy trash though. Colorful world and characters, as well as occasional nice action music. And that they got some more sense of gameplay, by having world that doesn't take few hours to travel though, while still giving it nice details. All characters having travel power helps. Gameplay also feels faster and arcadeys, but it's still same old target-based thing you seen before. The main gimmick is that in order to get "mana" (called "energy") you just have to keep using your most basic power on target. There is also Players vs Players duel mechanic, but it's just "abuse the week's most broken powers combinations".
Now, the game is Free 2 Play. And yep, those who pay get gameplay stuff as well. Like, costumes, classes, small boosts. You can farm special "questionite" recources to trade those for in-game shop money, but it takes ages. You also can be a monthly sub, getting all the stuff by default. None the less, what you really should be looking forward are costume pieces and Freeform class. Because the strong point of this MMO is a customization!
Freeform can be said is "the way that game is supposed to be played", as it allows you to pick absolutely any powers available in the game! Water, Thunder, Kung-fu, Dual Pistols, whatever. Sure thing having such broad selection bring problem where are some combinations are clearly more superior than others, as balancing so many powers would be near impossible. Sadly, F2Players only have access from beggining only to Archetypes (read: classes with pre-set powers.) and only to few of them.
And biggest feature this MMO has: One of the best characters costume customizations around. It really is what keeps half of those players, who still play Champions, around, along with RolePlaying. It allows players to do wide arrange of things. Don't think of thousands slides of "how thick is that eyebrow" or "wanna make that single muscle wide". Well, it does have some of such slider. But main focus will be on changing costume pieces of various body parts around, whetever it's belt, cape, head or wings. And there is many of costume pieces to choose from. You can make superhero of your dreams. Actually, what you can do and what many do, is to make a character who doesn't even look like your generic superhero, whetever it's some robot-zombie-pirate, anthro of your choice or, well, troll character that brings acid to your eyes. Though, I wouldn't say that it looks smooth, all non-human heads aren't animated, for example. Clipping is also the thing, but what you would expect from something what has this many choices.
So yes, customization and costume creation is really something what outdoes any MMO and most of other video games, and you are most likely to learn what is "RolePlaying" from this MMO, which is quite common there thanks to features I just told you about. Thus game has great social-part value to it, while having slightly above-average for MMO gameplay part (and below-average compared to non-MMO games).
Unless you don't care of such stuff.
Or want sandbox.
Or just sane videogamer.
Still spent more time with it than I really should have.

SHORT REVIEW: Generic game, great customization, semi-friendly community, bad combat, but worth it.
LONG REVIEW: You will waste about half of your time in character creation. But, it's still a semi-good game. I don't like that the ability/attack system is the number keys so it's kind of just spam it, if you fail level up a bit and come back, it's THAT kind of game, unlike a lot of RPGs, I'll use Skyrim (I hate that game, but it's the best example we all know of) as an example. The spells, Shouts, etc. were all equiped properly so you had to equip them to use them, had to make sure you used them when you really needed them, all that. Warframe, if you've played it, is another great example of what I'm talking about. So, the combat, meh. And, while I know Champions is meant to be a super hero game, it really doesn't feel like it. I really hate super hero games, but this is basically the only exception. The travel powers feel more like just physical attributes or genetic modification that EVERYBODY has, making it more of an upgrade to existence than super heroes, and I quite like that. The movement is phenominal, using the travel powers, especially Super Jump and Mach Speed/Super Speed. Combining those two, or maybe Acrobatics and Super Jump, or Acrobatics and Super Speed... That'd be so damn fun. The game's story is rather meh for me. It's all really generic and bland, but the creation, community (or lack of an active community), and travel powers make it worth the pain of dealing with it. I say lack of active community because most of the people are usually quiet, sticking to themselves and friends, and only teaming up for events and such, at least to me. I don't mind that, really. If you try to talk to them, they'll respond of course. But unless you try to talk to them, they'll not bother you. The skill upgrade system/skill tree seems a bit out of order. I can't explain it, but it's not a BIG issue. The item buffs and slight stat upgrades seems almost pointless, in my opinion, but not a bad or good thing.
PROS:
-Utterly superb customization
-Okay community
-Great travel powers
CONS:
-Rather bad combat
-Rather odd and confusing skill upgrade system

Primordia is a cyberpunk game about faith. Much like in the movie Tron, the main character is a robot with a mission he forgot. A mission given by his own creator, Man.
Primordia is a point-and-click adventure game by Wormwood Studios. The main character is a robot with amnesia, but made for a very significant purpose. It is still his choice to fulfill this purpose. He can be a faithful warrior that defeats the evil progressive mind and unites the robots, or he can run away from it. In the game, the robots live under a totalitarian secularist regime, where the belief that the machines were created by a mysterious being called Man is forbidden. His faith in Man keeps the protagonist alive. It is a very interesting twist for the cyberpunk genre.
The graphics are beautiful, as well as the soundtrack. The voice acting is complete and very well done. The voice of Crispin is the best. The dialogues are funny and the developers opted for a more dynamic gameplay, allowing the player to engage in the story without huge dialogues.
One of the advantages is a map that saves the player a good time that would be wasted wandering around. Another advantage is the "automatic notes", which saves you the trouble of writing down important information. There are several ways to solve the puzzles, and the developers sought to avoid puzzles that are incoherent with the setting. There is a great internal system for tips, preventing players from getting stuck.
If you like games like Beneath a Steel Sky, or games that allow you to immerse in an engaging and deep atmosphere with unique and intriguing stories, you should give a chance to Primordia.
Positive points
* Amazing setting.
* Good writing and voice-acting.
Negative points
* The engine is limited.

I held of on buying this game for a very long time due to how minimal it seemed, but after playing it I wished I hadn't done so.  This game is as close to flawless as an adventure game can ever be.  It has the best writing and the best soundtrack of any video game I've played and has a surprisingly deep setting and lore to it, which is impressive considering the small size of the game world.  With just a few locations, it creates a realistic world that had me immersed for hours.
The story and atmosphere of the game did a remarkable job of drawing me in and building tension, but where I believe the game stands out the most is in its setting.  The game takes place in a future in which life has long been extinct and Man has become a mythical deity worshipped by the remaining robots that now wander the lifeless desert that covers the earth, or even dismissed altogether as nothing more than legend.  Glass and light have become precious resources and what little remains of human invention is constantly scrapped to build new robots.  This is the kind of creativity that is lacking in most adventure games, and the subtlety with which it was presented was refreshing.
It was surprising to see a post-apocalyptic setting in which humans take only a background role and the nature of the world before is long forgotten.  Rather than barrage the player with the history of the world, Primordia puts the story and gameplay first while allowing players to discover the lore on their own, avoiding many (though not quite all) of the tropes that plague post-apocalyptic, dystopian, and robotic science fiction settings.
The game takes itself seriously and the comic relief exists for the amusement of the characters rather than that of the player, which is a skillful way of keeping the story believable, though Crispin's lines did make me cringe in more than a few points.  The primary cause of the chaotic dystopia is the degradation and corruption of the robots' programming, which becomes increasingly apparent as more of them are encountered.  All of the robots from the days of the humans are dead, insane, or rebuilt to the point of having no memories of the previous era, and the world inhabited by the rusting automotons that remain of civilization is chaotic, unpredictable, and bleak.  The dramatic irony of many characters' situations as well as the limited color palette contribute a depressing and hopeless tone that makes this an especially memorable experience.
Primordia is an essential contribution to the adventure genre of computer games, and one that I will gladly recommend to anyone who has an interest in interactive stories.  If you are considering getting Primordia, then please do yourself a favor and don't make the mistake I made of waiting for several years before buying it.
