Zombie Army Trilogy is a third-person shooter and yet another game in a Zombie Army spin-off of Sniper Elite series. But this time it also remasters the first two campaigns, gets an endless horde mode and brings it all to consoles. Made by Rebellion in 2015.
It also was ported to Xbox One and PS4. Nothing you miss.
Technically, it shouldn't explode. But it has some glitches. Mostly, what I remember is that last siege on 4th level never ended when I played coop with 4 people. Maybe some other multiplayer glitches. And it can still stop recognising mouse after some alt-tab'ing.
Multiplayer community is alive, from what it seems. It might take up to five minutes of sitting with opened lobby but it's going to fill out with all 4 people eventually. So yep, got to try out both campaign and horde mode. The only problem is that netcode doesn't amuse a lot of people. It sure can look as if it takes a full second for action to take place with some hosts.
Anyway, you still shoot zombies. Many, many zombies. There is still no stealth like in Sniper Elite, levels are linear. No randomization. Still setting up explosive traps. And the setting is same classic horror theme, with slow zombies against whom headshots are most effective, lots of blood and guts in dark environments and 80s synth horror music. Music, heck yea! Best part.
And it's still annoying to having to check dead bodies of zombies. There are just too many and process is still too long.
It also is now running on new engine and was ported to consoles. They also added ability to dismember zombies. And while it's cool and blood flows out like ketchup, you can see that they had to optimize it more and actually cut some of graphical stuff. Mostly that zombies have same uniform now. Probably because otherwise it would push memory limits with all the gibbing. But on good side, Trilogy actually runs better than older Zombie Armies. So I am happy enough.
One of the thing that this Trilogy does is to make it feel like it's own game and not just mod for Sniper Elite. Useless leftover features from SE like cover system and binoculaurs got removed for example. HUD now always shows what inventory items you still have and is just more comfortable. Two similar grenades types were fused into just one, with you being able to hold up to four of it. You can even select shotgun and revolver from a start.
It also finally balanced things around by realizing that it's more about close range where player moves around a lot. As a result, you recover breath quickly this time around, allowing you to use scoping abilities, like holding breath or even having time slow down in single player, much more often than almost-never. Some also even say that they have to compensate more for bullet drop now, which makes sense as battles now take at much closer range and you gotta keep that challenge of compensating.
They rebalanced things around. Turrets are now weaker, so some zombies can still pass through and you gotta watch out. Weapons that aren't rifles were made weaker. And most importantly, kick attack was made to be strong. It can knock enemies anytime and it now can finish the ones that lay on ground. It's quite powerful on single zombies. But skeletons now dying from one kick is a bit of a drastic changes. So big that they are now a challenge break than the challenge itself.
And yes, these balance changes impact the original two campaign. Not to mentioning that such things as amount of spawning enemies and some other changes were made to them. Most noticeably a single turret was placed into one level of the first campaign, the lighting style of the whole second campaign was changed to be less painfully orange and there are now less of difficulty spikes, somehow. And yea, kick is more powerful so all the skeletons are easy breaks from action. Some people may agrue that it was casualized, but you know what, I actually felt that it was less tedius to beat these levels in Trilogy than in original. And monotomy is the biggest problem of these games, so I welcome these changes.
And then there is a new, the third chapter made out of five levels. A special note should be taken about the first level. It's awesome and gives off a completely different feel from other levels, with a bit of feeling like you are part of NPC town and some basic exploration, setting false expectations for the remaining chapter. After that it goes back to normal traditional Nazi Zombie structured levels. Ah well.
And yep, it's better than previous chapters and even more varied. I actually recommend new players to start with this one. It also introduced a new theme: zombies and skeletons in armor. And chainsaw dudes. And this is where the balance changes show that they were designed for this chapter. Turrets are placed in such way that they would have been overpowered if not made weaker. And kick is countered by skeletons wearing armor and by huge Panzer Zombies who you can't even knock down!
Also, you get to kill zombie Hitler.
And sure thing the multiplayer plays a big part of this game. Don't even try to solo. Not because it's hard, it's actually quite possible, but because it's just plain tedius. It doesn't have any coop bots to fill the team up either. This game was designed for up to four players cooperative play. There isn't much of team-helping tactics aside from reviving each other, but all the combined firepower helps. It's more fun than solo, trust me.
And it also includes Horde mode, where you are locked in a small map with infinite zombies coming. Well, not infinite spawn, it's divided into waves. But there is no proper final wave. Maybe. I didn't research it much. It's completely boring in solo play but becomes fun with four player team as you run around and try to cover everything, only to get surrounded by three elite zombies. Maps are different, there is even one that is nothing but a dead end corridor. The enemies that it uses there also seems to have balance of Trilogy in mind - there are absolutely no skeletons but really really many zombies in armor.
It's pretty nice and fun. But if you already found previous parts too repetetive, then don't bother with this one, it doesn't fix much. As for others who want, please, play the third episode immeditly in 4-player coop. Or else you will end up getting bored due to monotomy before you reach the better part of a game.

Let me start by stating that Distant Worlds is, at the time of writing, THE BEST 4X GAME THAT MONEY CAN BUY!
Whilst new to Steam with the release of the latest expansion (Universe) Distant Worlds has been available elsewhere for good while and has received several large expansions during its life. (All of which had to be purchased seperatley prior to this full release on Steam).
Compared to the cost of buying all the expansions seperatley direct from Matrix, the steam price for the Universe bundle is actually cheap by comparison. (Although pricey compared to most 4x Titles, you get what you pay for!)
Before I talk about the scope of this game, keep in mind that the number of automation options you can set up from the start menu are almost limitless. You can automate almost anything.
Don't like designing your own ships? just automate it and the AI will handle that aspect for you.
Don't want to fiddle around with the false smiles and bribes that pass for deplomacy, then don't. Automate it and the AI will start paying off the other Empires for you.
Hell you could automate the whole game if you wanted and just sit back and watch it unfold like a TV Space Opera.
All the standard 4x bits and pieces are there.
Research - There's a huge tech tree to unlock, resulting in new planetary facilities to build, better components to install to your ship hulls, larger ship hulls to fit all your new tech inside, various orbital facilities etc.
Resources - There are ALOT of different resources in this game. Each planet, moon, asteroid, gas cloud is a potential source of "stuff" you're going to need.
At first you're civilian sector is going to be buying alot of the resources in to build the components you'll need for your ships and station, but before long, you'll have a fleet of civilian ships (all AI controlled) flying around mining asteroids for minerals and mining Gas Giants for the much needed fuel you're going to need to expand further.
Economy - Unlike most other 4x games, Distant Worlds has a fully featured Civilian economy which works independently to you. You can influence it with your actions but you can't control it directly.
You can design civilian ships, freighters, passenger shuttles etc. and then the civilian economy will buy them from you and use them move goods around to complete the building contracts or colonly requirements within your empire. This happens automatically, and you can actually see every single civilian ship flying around, check it's cargo, see what it's carrying and where it's carrying to.
Place a large military ship build order at a space port and watch all the little civilian ships scuttle around sourcing the resources for the project and ferrying them to the construction site.
Of course the civilian ships can be easy prey for pirates, so you might want to protect them with a military escort. This can be automated too!
These are just a few things, there is so much I could type about, Ground based combat, troop recruitment, Espionage, Characters (Ship captains, fleet admirals, generals etc) , minor races that can develop into full space fairing empires if left unchecked. Story events, re-name-able ships, characters  etc. (Want to rename all your spies after the characters in resevoir dogs, you can! Mr Black, Mr Pink etc.)
Don't let the graphics put you off, whilst far from good looking, the graphics are functional, different ship hulls are fairly easy to distinguish between and the planets and moons can be quite pretty in their own flat, 2D way.
The scope and depth of this game is amazing. It always feels like you're playing in a "real" universe. Of course this depth comes with a learning curve which can be punishing at first.
This is a game you're going to want to watch a lets play or two on before you take the plunge (or just automate everything and watch a while to get the jist of what the AI is doing).
I could spend all night writing about this game but i'm itching to get back to playing it again!
I'm so pleased that Distant Worlds has finally made it's way over to Steam and will now get the audience it deserves.
If you have any interest in 4x games, you need this. Simple as that.
I really hope if you've read this far that you'll buy the game and more importantly that you'll enjoy it as much as I have over the years.
Now if the developer could just make a prettier sequel......

Best and most refreshing space strategy I´ve played! Well worth it´s price tag! I´ve wanted to play this game for years, and finally it is on steam! Now, first this review will tell about my first game, then I will tell shortly about gameplay:
FIRST GAME EXPERIENCE:
I just played my first game with 1400 stars galaxy, starting with evil instectoid race. I pretty much grew quietly, while big factions like humans and others (dont remember names yet, first game) lived happily in their peace. First was the other insectoid (I thought them lizards) race, which I conquered except their homeworld, and ever since I have been having them subdued, as a slave race (yummy economic boost) and ignoring their constant pleas for freedom.
Next was same species as me, with another hive mind. Having another as aggressive as me cannot be allowed, and I conquered them under week, since they were pretty much surrounded by my space once I had conquered lizard race. Hive mind is joined to mine pathetically fast.
Third, blue skinned race with close relations to humans. I start war with them, and humans support them for few weeks, conquering few colonies from me, until humans are passive sheeps they are and just sign peace again with me, leaving their friend race to be conquered in next few years. Now blues skins are also subdued, enslaved race with only their homeworld left. *evil snickers*
Fourth, becomes galactic chaos as I start my war with big human empire, which crumbles and divides to now 5 different factions, after their military have failed to defend themselves before my mighty insectoids, as I just raze their worlds instead of conquering them with troops.
Now, I´ve almost finished conquering small fractions that are left of the old, once big human empire, while other races and fractured, new independent human empires just cover in fear, my reputation as race diabolical due to dozens of human worlds I razed. Few of the other races went through fracturing too as they watched me destroy their ally. Could be though it is not because of my actions, but yeah, I have pretty much won, as there is only small races, some fractured, humans especially so. Only one who could now stop me or at least prove a challenge are humans if they´d unite, since they have quite powerful weapons, but I dont see that happening, and other races are constantly sending me money probably to keep me away from them. Or if every race that despise me because of my brutality towards humans (they all do) would start all war with me, that could actually be end of me, since together I think they have small, but probably big enough upper hand in numbers. But no, they are too busy with wars between each other and fearing/hating me.
GAMEPLAY:
This game is very different from other 4x games. It is RTS, which can be stopped. You yourself don´t actually do anything else, except rule, which is pretty much accepting the ideas/suggestions what your empire should do that your army of advisors and generals send you. Wars happen like that your generals plan and do the dirty work, they suggest attacks/invasions/bombardings to locations X with fleet/strike force X. Same kind of system applies to new colonies/bases and new diplomatic moves and refitting your ships and colonies with new technologies, ship building orders too. It is as if you are actually, really some kind of supreme commander sitting at some cozy and mighty throne room, looking at map as your empire grows. You can actually zoom in and see the civilians do their work, live their lives, go from a to b either to mine or transport goods or migrants or whatever.
This game is not about micromanagement, this game is about RULING. Things like assigning civilians/miners/transporters/traders anything like that is BENEATH you, so it happens automatically! which I think is so deliciously realistic, it feels like you are actually governing empire full of people! I just love it... Sorry, I think I´m getting repetitive, but I fear that some people don´t understand why so many things are automated, so I try to explain it as best I can.
I should mention that some of these things automation/adviced can be turned off, so if you want you can assign your build orders, fleet formation, diplomatic actions, strategic fleet movements and attacks, everything except for civilian actions (mining, transportation etc) yourself. You can say "shut up" to your advisors, but I think it´s not humanly possible to micromanage it all, especially towards the endgame.
*** 28.5. EDIT: As I play further and learn more, I´ve discovered that the amount of settings how much and specifically you can make your advisors do things independently, recommend you or shut up about certain things is IMMENSIVE. At "Empire Policies" you can customize so many things, automation on really specific things, and how your advisors do certain things, after which amount of population you build new installation/base to your colony or it´s orbit, etc etc.
So, this deep game is even deeper! ***
...
TL;DR? HERE:
Enslaved two races, forced one to join me, caused galactical era of chaos, war and infighting not to mention countless deaths in process. Divided and conquered a galaxy. No micromanagement, just pure ruling and grand decision making.
BUY IT.

I've played this game and all of it's expansions to date (Not on steam but on the stand-alone version for a few hundred hours, please ignore the steam play time), but now it is finally available as a single package on steam.
This is by far THE BEST 4x strategy game. It has an impressively steep learning curve but the payout is unrivaled. You start as a custom civilization beginning its trek into the solar system and follow your own path to an intergalactic empire. Ships are fully customizable, technology trees are vast and unique, galactic events and alien ruins can change the course of the game, and diplomacy and contact with new races breathes depth into the fictional universe.
Don't be dissuaded by the 2D graphics, the combat and action scales immensely as you expand and soon you will be ordering multiple fleets around the galaxy, conquering star clusters and invading planets across the stellar terrain. All the while you will be managing your government style, taxes, espionage agents, diplomats, scientists and fleet commanders to flex the strengths of your civilization.
If you like the depth of civilization V, galactic civilization 2, or any game along those lines, seriously consider purchasing this game. You might have to watch some "Let's Play's" and do some manual reading with a test game or two to get your feet under you, but after you learn how to play this game will bring hundreds of hours of replayability and strategy. The Distant Worlds Universe expansion also brings about impressive modding capabilities so it is likely that the community will expand this game far beyond what the developers could have imagined.
Do yourself a favor and plunge into your own Universe.

I am a longtime 4X genre fan, but I'm getting very frustrated with this game. I really wanted to like this game and I bought it based on the large number of positive reviews. It has a lot of the things a liked about games such as MOO and Galactic Civilizations. But the learning curve for using the interface is just ridiculous!
The interface is counter-intuitive in so many places. What would you expect to happen if you select 1st Fleet and then click on a target to attack? About 90% of the time, the brave and mighty ships of the 1st Fleet will do nothing. Those rare few times that they actually attack are almost a shock. Sure you can turn off automation of "Fleet Formations", but that's not guaranteed to improve things either. Playing with automation disabled (even just 'mostly' disabled) can be a nightmare itself, with ships just sitting around doing nothing at all. After a few hours of play, I still can't figure out how to send my fully loaded troop transport to recapture an undefended mining base that pirates boarded. Really? Wouldn't you expect to just select the troop transport, and select the mining base as a target and *bam*, job done? Want to choose the best target for a remote mining base? Some scout just found a swampy moon with some kind of age-defying pears growing on it. Great, sign me up! Let's see, I'll click the "Expansion Planning" button... now show me my pears! Hello? WTF is the pear swamp? GRRRR!!!!
Most of my complaints are related to issuing orders to ships/fleets. Some parts of the game do seem to work as expected. You can automate your spies, for example, and then just override individual spies when you want to send someone on an espionage mission. That's an example of something that IS intuitive. Sadly, it is the exception to the rule.
Now I'm sure there will be longtime fans of this game who will vote down my review for love of the game. They probably invested many many hours of play to find the workarounds for the problems (features?) that I describe here. But do YOU want to buy a not-so-cheap game and not be able to play it until you put the time in to learn how to fight the user-interface?
Others have commented that the graphics are not great. Personally, I think the graphics are fine. If I can love Galciv, well... this game is several steps ahead. It's a little annoying that ships crowd around starbases and make it hard to select the starbase itself. Also, the text is hard to read in places on 1920x1200. But I find the battle sequences quite satisfying.
I still want to love this game, but the game makes itself hard to love.

Difficulty-wise, the game might feel tough in the beginning, but once you get the hang of it, it becomes a lot easier.

You might want to go for that once, to get the achievements.
It is still a great game, sadly it lacks one thing that would make it awesome, namely, a boss rush.
Finally, nobody seems to have ever tried speedrunning this, but it definitely would be both entertaining and not too much of a headache.

Great art, engaging story. However, the game has a critical flaw that permeates the entire experience: discovering how to progress is less an exercise in logic and more an exercise in clicking and walking the world. Many of the components of each puzzle are only tangentially related, oftentimes only in the most esoteric ways. Progression is further  hindered by the game's lack of robust programming. Sometimes you will try something that should work, only to find out that you were supposed to perform that action through slightly different mechanisms.
The game also does not handle choices well. Now, there aren't many story-altering choices to make in this game, but the creators should have given the player more indications of what the effects of their actions would be, as well as more indication that certain paths could have been taken. I felt cheated out of the ending I would have chosen because of the problem I mentioned above. I clicked on something, nothing happened, and I went on my way, not realizing that I could have performed the intended action. This changed the ultimate ending.
Still very much recommended, but don't be ashamed to open up a guidebook if you get stuck.
Edit: Also, the save system was bad. They could have easily done it better.

Ah, Tubo Dismount.  The name alone conjures up images of, well, your mom, actually, but this is not the time or the place for that particular tale.
Anyway, Turbo Dismount is the heartbreaking story of Joe Dismount.  A man trapped in a world that seems to want nothing more than to push him down each time he tries to rise, and hobble him every time he tries to walk.  It's a familiar scene, the cycle of repression which seems torn straight from today's geopolitical headlines.
As painful as it is to watch Joe's agonizing struggles, and I must admit it brought a tear to my eye more than once, we have to face the fact that Joe is not entirely a blameless victim here.  Joe appears to be actively seeking his own demise, and every time we see him dangling from the back of a speeding sports car, or rolling off of a cliff in an office chair, we can only wonder what horrors Joe has seen, or dare I say, even participated in, that drive this insatiable lust for the sweet release of death.
We may never know, for as simple as Turbo Dismount may appear on the surface, beneath lies a complex web of tortured emotion and dark secrets best left undisturbed.  Some may view Joe as a hero, others may see him as a villan, but where Turbo Dismount succeeds in uniting us, is that we can all see Joe torn into little pieces strewn across a highway in the middle of a twenty vehicle pileup.  I suppose that in the end, that's all that really matters.

If you want modular ships, then go for it, otherwise... Ehhh. It's fun, but it has limitations, such as the whole universe and world not being constantly active, leading you to go to every place to clear it out yourself, rather than do it Sim Ant style, and build a fleet so powerful, that your allies jsut take everything over through sheer attrition.
Other limitations include:
- A VERY limited Tournament system, only allowing one fleet to engage another person's single fleet. Not one fleet from one save, or faction. One fleet PERIOD. Also you can't manually control ships either in PvP combat, so that's extremely lame.
- No Co-op, which this game could badly use on the "Conquer everything" achievement, which requires you to have a ship in every quadrant, which.... good luck, there's over 2000 of the things and hte map only updates in proximity of another player, let alone triggers and moves normally. Going fast enough can make it painfully obvious, which is possible to do without any mods btw.
- The 8000 Ship size limit is fine, but when you're grinding up to that point (which IS a grind with some factions, with others, it's just plain tedious in every way) the imagination tends to run wild with about a dozen or more ideas that aren't possible without using mods.
- Agents (user-submitted fleets controlled by AI only) sometimes don't spawn correctly and you gotta regen your world to get them to spawn correctly. This doesn't stop Agents from killing stations though, since, if Agents fought any of MY stations, none of them would survive, especially with my terran faction that abuses missiles (Hint: Lasers eventually do nothing)
- Some weapons are just straight-up overpowered if spammed, whilst other weapons are jsut pretty much useless. Case and Point: Photon Lances, Missiles and Drones are 3 overpowered-when-spammed weapons. Everything literally pales in comparison. Missiles can overpowerd and overwhelm literally everything.
- Railguns are useless for the most part, which is sad because Railguns are 50 times more powerful than any lasers, missiles (save for nukes) or fighter/bomber in any amounts irl. Hint: Because Railguns are literally matter shot at the speed of light, or atleast faster than the speed of sound, which is still deadly on that level.
- AI doesn't redesign ships to counter your powerful warships, as a result, you can eventually design ships that nothing has an answer for, at which point the game's no longer challenging, which wears out the fun pretty quickly after a point. Case and Point: Terran Ships literally made up of a couple of shield generators, and literally a hundred missile launchers.
- You can't stop the game from Auto-pausing without pausing, then unpausing as you immediately tab out. Reason why you'd want to do this: You may have a ship that revolves around puking out space stations for the purpose of just flooding the universe with stations that can also slowly puke out ships on it's own.
The game's more or less a 7/10. Good, but not great. Plenty of flaws.

Anyway, there are a lot of things going for EL. One is that each faction really has flavour and sometimes its' own gameplay changes, unlike Civilization's countries which has a few minor bonuses which generally don't affect gameplay much. The other is that EL really mixes up the Civ formula in different ways that actually work, keeping the game feeling fresh. Gamers like to play with new things, after all.
Speaking of playing with new things, one design flaw: the tactics layer. Generally you won't have access to many unit types because new units of your own faction requires research. So the tactics layer gets kind of stale since it's filled with many of the same unit. You can sort of get around this by enlisting minor factions that complement your basic units.

6 hours to beat the campaign in Centurion mode (hardest available on a first run).  I read a few reviews before playing, and probably wouldn't have bought the game, but it came in a bundle. The reviews were pretty accurate, I'd say: great production value; story was a giant cliche arc, riddled with cliches throughout, but still a fun flick; combat was unique but tedious in the end.
At first, I thought the the reviews were exaggerating about the combat. Starting the game, the combat seemed original and interesting. However, it never, ever gets more complex. There are 4-5 routines you'll get into that will SLOWLY get you through the fights.
Basic enemies: Block, bash, slash-slash. Block, bash, slash-slash. Again. Again. Until the execution symbol appears. Now execute.
Shielded enemies: Bash-slash-slash. Bash-slash-slash. Occasionally you'll need to throw a block in there until you get the execution symbol.
Heavy enemies: Dodge until they're open. Major bash. Major Slash. Major Bash. Major Slash. At some point you might need to dodge again, otherwise, just execute when the symbol arrives.
Groups: Perform the same attacks you would on a single enemy, but be willing to interrupt it with a block (against normal attacks) or dodge (against heavier attacks) and restart the cycle on the new target. Groups feel painfully slow.
Bosses: Similar to other enemies, but they take twice as long to kill, and they have more moves that are difficult (or impossible? I never really was sure with some moves) to block, so you may find yourself dodging more.
Now, it's true that the combos are interesting, but you'll do hundreds of each, and it does get old.  The execution quick-time events are just tedious after about 100 of them, and the bosses are merely boring. Dying is a frustration when you have to watch a cutscene again or fight multiple enemies again. The handful of times where the game interrupts a large fight (with a cutscene, so you don't have to bother finishing the fight) it really felt like a relief. I rememer watching my hero killing enemies during the cutscene after one long chain of fights, and I was thinking, "Thank goodness he's killing them so I don't have to." It was just tedious at that point.
Production quality is similar to Quantum Break, I'd say. Top-notch graphics, cool art and effects, overly clean level layouts that occasionally can confuse because you get so used to the obviousness of it all right before it throws a curve ball.  There were two times when I felt like the level design made little sense, and both were associated with the same area.  They also worked too hard to be mildly gory at times - key moments were emphasized with blood on the screen. But this effect just broke the fourth wall and informed us that we were, in fact, watching this on a monitor.  Why?  Why put blood on the screen?  And then the blood faded away.  Why?  If you're going to splash it there, have it drip off or something. Why fade away?  It was only disruptive to the immersion. There were a couple other attempts to be gruesome that were notable for their rather unimpressive break in suspension of disbelief, but none so glaring as the blood on the screen.
I had fun playing the game. If you've got the game, give it a run through. Would I have bought it myself? Nah. But maybe it's your thing, and there are 6 or so hours of excitement.  So even though I thumbs-down this, maybe you'll end up liking it.
Note: I didn't play multiplayer at all, and several reviews recommend the multiplayer co-op.

To be bluntly honest, Champions Online could have really gone the mile for the Heroes/Villians genre of MMORPGs.  At the beginning, they had so much to offer; wardrobe customization, crafting for the crafters out there, missions that were really fun and entertaining, as well as some pretty heroic ideas for your arch nemesis.  Unfortunately, their hay day is, by far, over.  Now, it is a money sink, with their only additions being given to their cash shops.  Missions no longer roll out, most of their codebase is defective (arch-nemesis code is beyond repair, as has been stated by the developer's public relations division), and that's only the tip of the ice berg.  They started adding flying machines (like a mount) into the game where flight-based travel powers already exist.  The fun of hunting down villians has long-since been buried, replaced by an insta-que (or sometimes not instant at all), in which you wait for a team of other players to activate.  This places you in a variety of instances.  The same ones, over and over and over again.  The repetitious missions never change, save for the holiday events.  When Perfect World bought the developing company, they married their money-in-hand with the game.  This has meant that new powers are gone and done.  The broken skills are not being fixed (ask someone about the ice-based powers, the arcane based powers, or even the electric based powers), and the new things rolling into the game are meant to be purchased.  This goes for both the paying 15.00 a month customer, as well as the "free-for-all" customer.
The original draw to this game for many was the PvP scenarios.  I played from original opening date, if anyone remembers Mother Night, Mother Dusk, and Madame Mirage (just to name a few), and the zombie scenario was always a huge hit for most of the players.  However, that is no longer the case.  To ensure I was giving an accurate and detailed synopsis of the condition in which the game now rests in, I signed in and queued for the PvP scenarios.  All of them.  On both freeform characters and the pre-builts.  2.5 hours later, the queue was still going.  I asked around in-game what was the cause of such a long wait, and I was told there was some sort of bug in the PvP system, as well as a lack of attraction to the the PvP system, that has caused it to go the way of the Dodo; right into extinction.  I asked how long this had been going on, and I was told it had been that way for about two years now.
In conclusion, this game is going the same way as City of Heroes, only with a more drawn-out death that's not only painful to, but also just damned out-right depressing.

Like others, I have had this game for a couple years now and have to put it as one of the top 4X games I've ever played.
There is one key thing that keeps drawing me back: the way this game actually makes you feel like the ruler of a space empire. You can micro-manage all you want at the beginning, but as you expand you will shift towards delegating most tasks to the AI while retaining the ability to tweak things or get hands on as you see fit. There is a ton flexibility here, as you can set the AI to do nothing, to do things automatically (with tons of options regarding what you want them to do), or to ask your permission before doing anything drastic. It's really cool to play out this transition from moving indivdual ships around at the beginning, to only handling your warfleets later on. This applies to other aspects like research, espionage, diplomacy, production and so on.
The other unique element is how you can watch your space empire's economy grow in real time. Soon after the game starts you will see a few civilian ships coasting around your planet, before long they will start building mines and transporting goods around. Before long there will be dozens, then hundreds, then thousands of civilian freighters cruising up and down space lanes connecting to your worlds and beyond. What's more, there's aren't just abstract representations of activity, each individual ship has a name, mission, fuel level, cargo, and purpose. If you order a new space station to be built, the resources aren't just magically transported there, they must be transported there by actual ships, which get the resources from specific worlds, which got the resources from the relevant mine/production facility. So if you want to build something in a distant star system and haven't researched FTL travel, don't expect it to get finished anytime soon.
This also ties into the great sense of scale. At first, just going around your home star system takes a long time. If you use the Age of Shadows start (highly recommended), you only have conventional engines very little options for ships. I won't spoil anything but eventually you will research faster travel, which makes travel between local planets pretty fast, but travel outside your home system is still quite slow. Range is also a factor for most ships at this point. Eventually your ships get much faster, but the galaxy is still a very, very big place. Ordering an exploration ship to investigate some signal on the other side of the map means you won't be able to use it for anything else for the next 15-30 minutes it takes to go there and back. This of course becomes very important when you launch a war. Logistical planning using staging grounds and secure rendezvous for refueling/resupply can make all the difference.
Best 4x available atm. Not for the faint hearted.

Having played this game for about 200 hours before coming to Steam, I can say, without any doubt, that this is the king of science fiction 4X games.
If you like Europa Universalis, Master of Orion, Stars!, Galactic Civilizations, Stardrive, Civilization or any other 4X game and are looking for the "next one", look no further.
It takes some getting used to. It does have a learning curve. However, once you've figured it out, there's nothing else like it.
10/10 would pay $100+ again for it. It's a steal at $49.79. If you count the amount of time I've played this and divide it by the money spent, I spent less than $1 per hour of enjoyment. That's a better way to spend your money than any other that I can think of.

Right.... where to start? Well, this is the best 4x since Masters of Orion 2. For a lot of people that's a good enough review, but there's probably someone who wants details, and I can dish those out. I have a (shameful) five hundred or so hours sunk into this game before it came to Steam (and thank god it did, seriously. Or Bhudda. Allah. Whoever. Thank 'em all.)
I can't really say enough good things about this game. The major flaws all went away when it came to Steam and now hopefully we can all enjoy something amazing at a sane, reasonable price that doesn't require the equivalent of an ancient magical ritual just to buy. No longer will you need to fight the Matrix website and its dyslexic captcha generator for hours on end. The age of galactic empires has come to the masses.
Speaking of mass, the game itself is MASSIVE. Seriously. You can not understand how big this game is. It is TITANIC. HUGE. The galaxy maps rival the original xbox as the most massive work forged by the hand of man. On the largest maps you can expect hours of play before you even find another empire. That's not to say you will be bored, because pirates will be coming in thick and fast. These aren't your garden or average variety pirates either, they are all evil, space based empires themselves, with completely different play styles to the planet bound civilisations. You can play as the pirates as well and yeah, you basically get a totally different game.  Research (The tech tree is also HUGE and I have never reached the end of all the three parts of it), expand onto different worlds (or conquer them), make alliances, salvage ancient wrecks, uncover secrets from the dawn of civilisation and look forward to the first time you fly into a new system and spot an odd looking moon. Not gonna spoil it, but you will shout out one particular line from Star Wars when you look closer. The galaxy teems with stuff to do or see or loot or explode before it lays eggs in your head.
There's a massive galaxy editor that is ... well, if it was any easier or simpler to use it would also have a button that would make it feed you cake irl. I haven't dipped into the new enhanced modding functions in Universe though, so I guess you should take this bit with a grain of salt. Maybe someone with more experience will chip in, but I can't imagine them saying it's hard to use to do complex stuff in game.
You can design your own ships and bases, and this is where there's a bit of annoyance. Hopefully I can come back later and edit this out, but if you make civilian mining stations with armor and weapons, the game loves to overwrite them with unarmed, unarmoured ones whenever you get a new tech and it tells itself to update all the avilable ship designs. Other than that, you can make your own designs very easily, though I would like it if there was a bit more information about what the different components do. It tells you, but not clearly.
There's an overarching story built into each game you play as well, which aside from Alpha Centauri makes this a unique game. It can be turned on or off or individual parts can be toggled, and in the end it isn't a super massive thing, but it is fantastic for shaking up the endgame completely. In most 4x games by endgame you are set in and there's nothing to do since you won a long time ago and are just rolling towards the big flashing 'A WINNER IS YOU' screen. Not so if you have the Return of the Shakturi storyline enabled. Endgame is basically hardmode+.

The game's selling point is you can build yhour own spaceships from an array of building blocks, such as a shield block, cannon block, command block, thrusters block, hull blocks and so on. It then uses a physics engine to move it about, so you need to balance the vessel well and provide enough sufficiently powered trusters in all directions to be able to move and turn.
Weapon firing can be set to autotarget, so in effect you just move slowly around while your cannons destroy anything nearby so you can pick up loot that is needed for upgrades and unlocking new building blocks. Enemies will fire back and destroy your ship block by block, but after a while the blocks auto-generate.
You can also build AI controlled ships, based on your own designs. Those ships can in turn build other ships, so you can dominate the galaxy quite soon. Then it is time to enter a black hole for a fresh universe, where you can start over from your current technology level.

A challenge with this game is that controlling your ship is cumbersome. Even if you design it well, it will still handle sluggish, and I found myself getting stuck in space debris a lot. So, if you approach the game as an action game, it will be very irritating. Approach it more like a strategy game, and it makes more sense though.
Another issue with the game, is it has quite limited scope. Once you unlock all upgrades, there is simply not much to do. You will have no use for the money you collect, and you just aimlessly float around to repeat what you did before over and over. Would be nice with some variation, and perhaps some quests. This makes the game a rather short experience.
Overall, it is a fun game with some fresh innovations.

The game of the holidays 2016 for me with 100+ hr and counting...
I have the same amount of fun playing the game than building new ships, mainly because both have been done equally with care...
Once you get the hang of it (and unlocked the pieces you need), building a ship may take time but is a breeze. You can Copy/Paste (old Ctrl-X-C-V) an entire ship, a bunch of pieces or put pieces one at a time... For example, to make a circular ship (think Borg Sphere), I made 1/4 of the ship, then Copy/Paste and snap the 3 other parts together to make the sphere shell of the ship. Next step was to put weapons, shields Generators and such, then try your new creation in space...
Of course, how you can build and what you can put depend on the faction you selected. Some factions has no square hull or no shield module, for example...
Once in the battlefield, you'll notice that all ships are definitely not created equals and you need to adapt your 'piloting' accordingly:
- Like most game of this type, you have to keep a balance (or not) between Firepower, Armor, Speed and Mass of the ship...
- Your pilot square is not only the thing that keep your ship together and mean death if it is destroyed, but also affect the center of gravity of your ship... That means that for a ship of the same shape, you will drive it differently if you put the pilot capsule at the front, center or rear of the ship... Negligeable if you build a small fighter, but more obvious if you build a 'Star Destroyer' kind of ship... And putting it too close to the extremity means the enemy need to punch less shield/armor to hit it... Life if full of compromises...
- And perhaps what surprise me (in a good way) the most is the feeling that you're not alone. Your part of a faction against other factions. Of course, you have a major infuence on your faction progress (you unlock new parts with your hard earned Credits, your faction will spawn and use ship you created, etc...) but when you pass next to an space port, you may see a new ship spawning and going for enemies and/or ressources alone (piloted by the AI, of course...).
- You can fly solo or order others ships of your faction to follow you, giving you the feeling of commanding a small armada. Of course, AI is not the sharpest tool in the shed, but it is competent enough to follow you and attack your target, giving you an numerical advantage against powerful enemies... Just don't expect they'll use asteroids for cover or retreat in time when in trouble.
Add to that mods from Steam Workshop, and you have plenty to see and do...

I played this game a lot back when it came out, and I had to play it on Windows Live.  Those hours are lost to time, and my steam playtime doesn't reflect my actual playtime.
This is important to note because I played a lot of the mutliplayer, and the multiplayer is one of the best parts of this game.  I wish that it was still a part of the Steam version of this game.  Not to say that Steam isn't hosting servers, but that there's nobody playing, so I don't know.
The single player is fun.  This game feels like a 3D version of a Megaman X or ZX game, which makes sense condifering Inafune was one of the heads of the design team.  The core gameplay is rock solid, "arcade" thrid person shooter.  You know what every mechanic in the game does after briefly playing with it, and the game encourages you to push the limits of what you can do with those mechanics.  I'm mainly talking about the grappling hook, which seems to be endlessly functional.  Any other game like this would be rife with glitches, but Lost Planet defies you to throw yourelf up walls and wedge yourself in corners, never once have I encountered a clipping glitch that made me reload or restart.  The game ends levels with boss fights in the same way Megaman does, with unique bosses in unique environments, which makes the game feel even more "arcadey," despite it's serious tone.
The weapon variety herein is absoutely fantastic.  Automatic rifles that will fire with pinpoint accuracy at any range if you stand still.  Shotguns that knock enemies off their feet.  Rockets that deal rediculous damage on hitting a target, and splash damage if you don't, and come in handy pistol sizes.  Sniper rifles that feel extraneous next to the fully automatic ones noted above, but give you a nice zoom-in of yoru enemy flipping backwards when you headshot them.  A laser gun that spits damage.  A ball-lighting gun that paralyzes and still does damage.  And then there are mech versions of each of those weapons.  And then you can take those weapons off of the mechs, and use them yourself as a puny human who's dwarfed by the guns you're weilding.  And mechs get homing laser organ guns, genade launchers that split their projectiles apart in midair, and pile bunkers that you can also use on foot.  They also get automatic lasers and cannons that you can't pick up, but you still have that pile bunker.  Grenades in this game are a treat: the normal frags are satisfying and concussive to enemies, the plasma grenades will stun and eject pilots from their mechs, the stickybombs are shaped charges that wreck mechs and do double-duty as proximity bombs, fuel-air bombs are terrifying and insta-kill deadly in multiplayer, and you also get frisbee grenades.  Why don't other games have frisbee grenades?
As for mechs, every mech feels unique, but all mechs fit into a tier system.  Most mechs have a unique ability, some have several, but some mechs are just better than others.  You can just get "the best mech" and never want to let go of it, because it is just the best.  In single player, this isn't a huge problem because the game progreesively ramps up the power of its drops and spare mechs you can hop into as you go along.  In multiplayer maps with mechs, this becomes a problem, because the first minute of the match turns into a race for the best mech, and then the next minute is one guy surbstomping every player they can find before taking enough damage to be ejected and pulped by gunfire.
Multiplayer is basically the best part of the game (the core run-and-gun gameplay and the weapons), but with and against other players.  Instead of the Imperial Stormtrooper gunners or Starship Troopers bug hordes, the game throws at you into multiplayer maps that are large enough to get lost in, but not large enough that enemies can't find you, and expects you to hold your own against people who are just as grappling-hook-cabable and gun-handy as you are.  Matches come in several varieties, including capture-the-points, deathmatches and team deathmatches, capture-the-flag, humans vs bugs, and maybe some other gamemodes.  Nobody cares much about the others, because deathmatches, CTP, and bugstomping are so much fun!  The maps are far more creative than any military FPS on the market, and I liken them to Battlefront 2 maps because of how huge and varied they are.  The megaman level design shows its face here, with lots of verticality and the expectation of players to grapple around onto towers and ledges.  This is would fall apart in many other games, but because the core game is so refined, it's easy to grapple and run around quickly whilst maintaining situational awareness.
One map in particular, the in-building "two towers" map, was one of the best CTF maps I have ever played, if only because of the diverse weapon design and the wicked chokepoint skybridge between each team's tower.  That's just about the only way to get to the other team's flag, and the game turns into a match to see who can survive the player-made guantlet of sniper fire, grenades of every variety, stickybomb mines, and machinegun fire long enough to make a break and sacrifice themselves as a distraction for the rest of the team to funnel through and overwhelm the enemy.  The pushes back and forth, and the struggle to maintain control over the exits to the skybridge inside the enemy tower so as to avoid the WW1-style entrenchment that happens when the fight hits the bridge, those games are forever burned into my brain.
Why is this game not the best thing ever?  Well, the campaign is short.  And the story, while interesting, is simple and burried beneath bad acting and a horrible engish script.  It's so bad I can't imagine that the translators had much to work with on the Japanese side.  It's laughably bad, and if you like that kind of thing the cutscenes herein will make your day.  There's a weird "Rising Revengeance" vibe to the cutscenes, especially when talking with this game's verison of Sundowner.  The character designs are interesting, but sometimes silly and sometimes forgettable.  The characters themselves aren't terribly memorable either, ironic considering the main protagonist has amnesia.  Also, the gameplay feels very fun and again Megaman-esque, while the story seems very serious and self-sacrificing, leading to some of that good-old-fashioned lugonarrative dissonance.
There's a lot of frustration towards Lost Planet 2 and 3, and from my perspective, that all comes from players of Extreme Condition that didn't get a more polished (and better-scripted) version of this game.  If the multiplayer community was anywhere near as active as it was in the first three years of this game's release, I would say to buy the game right now for full price.  As it stands, the game can only offer its campaign to showcase its gameplay, which is a dead shame.  If you played this game back in the day, and you can get yourself a Steam key from the box or snag the game for 66% off, do it, play it through again, and hope the community can drum up some multiplayer action once in a while.

According to Steam, the strategy game I have played the most is Crusader Kings II, clocking in at 329 hours. There is no record for DW, because it has only just come to Steam, but there's no question I have put at least double that time into DW in the last year or so (I started playing in April 2013).
In my opinion, you will not find a better 4x space game, period. Although it might seem expensive, the game has incredible depth and complexity, while at the same time allowing you to control as much or as little of your empire as you like. Your empire, and the rest of the galaxy, come alive as you are playing it. The other Empires go to war, sometimes with you, sometimes with each other. Some of them will seem very strong at one time, then they will fade to insignificance when they bite off more than they can chew. New empires can rise from almost nothing. The constant ebb and flow tells a different story every time you play the game.
The playing space can be enormous, if you want it to be. How many space 4x do you see with a 'huge' galaxy setting and 250 stars (often with just one planet each). In DW, 250 stars is the second smallest setting. You really can go right up to 1400 stars (and you can edit in more if you want - the game will let you, as long as your system can run it). Each of these stars has planets in orbit, and asteroids, and asteroid fields. Moons orbit the planets. There can be dozens of objects in each star system, each moving around their planet or their star as the game time progresses. It is just immense, and thoroughly involving.
The game is not quite perfect, but it is close.

A couple of years ago I found this game by pure chance.  After many years of playing almost every Space 4X I was desperate to find something better and luckily I found it ... Distant Worlds is best in class and it's since become my most played game.  It's a huge relief to see it on Steam because it's ready for Prime Time.
A couple of key things to keep in mind before you purchase:
1. This is a massive game and it will take some patience to get over the initial learning curve.  You can choose what to automate and what to control, so start with manual control in one or two of your favourite areas only (e.g. for me it was research and fleets) and build from there.
2. Once over the learning curve hump, if you like this type of game, you'll probably be hooked.  In time you will find more layers of the onion to peel away.  My game strategies were still evolving 100's of hours later.
3. It's a real time game but you can pause to make it feel somewhat like a turn based game and to help keep your massive empires under control.  As a result don't be put off by real time if you prefer turn based games.
4. The graphics are average. If this is your primary driver this probably isn't your game.  But if you want plenty of massive battles you'll get them.
5. There is a massive array of setup options and as a result the game has significant longevity.
6. The Universe release has greatly expanded mod capability.  I don't play with many mods but Distant Worlds has some good ones.
7. The Developer has a long track record of providing support and patches.  This game will continue to improve ...
If this sounds like your type of game then I recommend it highly.

Viktor is a 2D Twin Stick Shooter Platformer with minor Metroidvania elements in which you'll be going through levels finding new weapons, upgrades, and killing lots of enemies as you search for everyone who betrayed the legion and the one who turned them so you can kill them.
Story (has no effect on my opinion of any game)
Story isn't anything spectacular it's a run of the mill you were betrayed by your allies and now you're hunting them down to kill them, save the world, and your friend.
Graphics (has no effect on my opinion of any game)
Graphically it's a vey nice looking game. Enemy variety texture wise is lacking as most enemies appear in all the levels without a slight retexturing to make them fit more with the level but otherwise the game looks excellent and the enemy thing is nitpicking.
Gameplay (the only thing that affects my opinions of games)
This game is more or less a clone of Bleed gameplay wise but it does enough to differ itself from Bleed. When it comes to being a twin stick shooter it's excellent the dash to dodge mechanic is well executed and the shooting is enjoyable. The dodge/dash mechanic will allow you to phase through thin walls and dodge all projectiles and attacks quite easily. The Metroidvania elements leave a lot to be desired as the aren't that well hidden and none of the items you find are required to beat levels or find other items there's  also is very little reason to go back to previous levels to find stuff due to the lack of things to find so it's hard to consider this a Metroidvania. Platforming is meh there are a few areas where it does try to change it up but otherwise it isn't going to challenge you so there's no real benefits to using a controller. Now game breaking bugs are a huge issues as they're very easy to accidentally pull off and some will happen randomly and all require a level restart. First I ran into is when dashing into a wall at the wrong angle or if you're not close enough to phase through the other side you'll occasionally you'll be clip out of the map with no way back so you'll be forced to restart the level. One miniboss will (the one who bounces around) will sometimes during the fight vanish rendering the fight unwinable so you'll have to restart the level. On occasion a boss or yourself will get stuck unable to move and unable to take damage forcing you (you guessed it) to restart the level.
In conclusion Viktor is an excellent game and idea but is held back by a myriad of game breaking bugs that you'd expect in a pre alpha that should have been fixed immediately after discovery.
I recommend that you buy heavily discounted or that you get Bleed instead.

I appreciate that this game exists, because it was clearly made by kids who love video games (especially mega man), but it has some unfortunate general design flaws that basically makes it not worth continuing with. It seems like they cloned the mega man meta without realizing why the specific elements they took worked.
- Some bottomless pits are where you are supposed to go, some of them just kill you.
- You can pick up different weapons somehow, but that is never explained anywhere, so there is no direction on where to go next. Is it money based? Are they in maps? The game doesn't say.
- Health and powerups are all RNG based, ensuring you never get health when you need it or weapon powerups when there is anything to shoot.
- After the first mission you unlock a mega-man style world map, but the basic gameplay upgrades are grinding based. So what map should you choose next? At least have a level recommendation on them or something.
- The jumping is fine for parkour-like movement because it contains signfigant momentum. But then they throw jumping puzzles in there which are simply not fun. The main mechanic, your dodge/warp move, has an unpredictable movement distance.
- The maps take too long to go through just to see how hard the boss is.
- Bosses and mid bosses are bullet sponges with way too much health. You end up mastering a strategy or movement pattern by the time you have it at 80% health remaining, and then it's just endurance based. This is the main thing you have to use the levelling up to reduce so you can defeat some of the more hectic boss fights that are impossible to avoid damage from.
- On top of all of this there is a timer which they use to give you a rank afterwords.
You can see that many of these design flaws are the same as mega man. Hower mega man had better platforming mechanics for jumping puzzles, and clearer game design to indicate where to go next. You could grind for health in mega man because enemies constantly respawned. Mega man contained 1up powerups, and powerups that were built into the level design which singificantly offset the 3 lives issue. Finally it was always possible to defeat a boss in mega man even if you didn't have the right weapon.
The TL;DR is the game devolves into trial and error very fast, and punishes you for it. It's basically all punishment
The art is passable, but not that amazing, It looks like it was all done by one 17 year old guy who just didn't have time to do everything since the game is huge.
One positive I can say was the sound design was solid, probably why I kept playing as long as I did. The metal soundtrack is nice and the bullet fire/enemy hit/death sounds have a satisfying punch.
I hope they learn from this one though and keep making games, or continue to work on this one to make it "complete".

If you aren't familiar with this game, you need to know it is a dungeons and dragons style role playing game. You have a three character party. Your party leader is fully customizable, but other party members come with premade builds (poor ones in my opinion) that you can adjust to your play style. There is a pause mechanic during combat so that you can prepare actions for each round of combat. Attacks are made with a roll of a twenty sided die. You hit if your roll plus modifiers equals your opponents defense. The same is true when you are targeted. There are some exploits that make the game much easier. You can save level ups to have an instant full restore mid combat. You can use an item in addition to taking your regular action in any given round of combat by using it in the inventory menu. Some force powers target enemies through walls. If you have the last survivor flee far enough from combat, it will revive your party.

Almost since the decline of professional adventure games, fans have been making their own games.  These have varied wildly in quality, but in more recent years indie studios such as Wadjet Eye Games have managed to churn out charming retro games with regularity.  They generally strike the right balance in difficulty, the hand-painted art is often beautiful, and the stories are often interesting.  These games are not for everyone, of course, as games of this sort may seem "dated" or slow to modern gamers
To me, Primordia exemplifies the best aspects of most retro adventure games, with wonderful graphics (again, in a low res way that some appreciate more than others) and classic point and click exploration.  Primordia, however, distances itself from its peers through superior story, characters, and story structure.  The basic premise is an interesting one, and game designer and writer Mark Yohalem develops that premise expertly and meticulously.  The world unfolds naturally as you join Horatio and Crispin on their adventure.  The themes are more complex and nuanced than what you will see in most games.  The puzzles feel true to the world rather than thrown in just because you have to have them.
This is, in my opinion, the best game published by Wadjet Eye, and one of the best adventure games in recent memory.  If you're interested in going out on a limb and try an adventure game, consider trying this one.  If you're already a fan of retro games or thoughtful sci-fi, this is a no-brainer.

A whimsical tale of mystery and discovery about a robot and his companion forging a path as fate would have it to uncover the blurred grey line between myth and truth through difficult choices, puzzles, and a rich and compelling story line. take a pixelated adventure into Primordia; one of the best games ive played in years.

I’ll do my best to be brief. Ryse: Son of Rome is a visually strong game that stumbles in the gameplay department. I’m really not sure what they were thinking when designing this game. It feels like a showpiece meant to evoke ooo’s and ah’s, but instead, it made me miss Shadow of Mordor’s combat.
In any case, it’s quite the looker. The buildings, the people, the bodies, the blood, the gore, the limbs being lopped off, and the flora all act as candy for the eyes. You can expect to enjoy many gorgeous vistas or terrible scenes of carnage and murder over five and a half hours. The executions are a big part of the visual enjoyment and are a key component of the gameplay. They also happen in slow motion because the developer really, really wanted you to bask in the graphical glory of Ryse.
The story’s tone is gritty and serious. Marius’ family was murdered in their home while he was there. He then embarks on a bloodthirsty quest for revenge and vengeance. I thought some aspects of the story were neat and they did have several heroic scenes for the protagonist that pleased me. I also enjoyed how the ending resolved. They did a good job with making some real scumbag characters that took no effort to hate. I just wish they didn’t make dumb jokes and references in other parts of the game such as the achievement names (Saving Private Marius) and some of the skill descriptions. They don’t mesh well with the somber revenge plot unfolding in the main game.
The gameplay seemed okay for the first hour. It has combat similar to Batman or Shadow of Mordor. With a controller, X is attack, Y is shield bash, B is roll, and A is parry. I enjoyed when the game would let you lead soldiers in sections where it’s your group versus archers. You could raise the shields and turtle up, move forward, or throw a bunch of javelins at the archers.
Now here’s where the game starts to fall apart. The combat after the first hour becomes very repetitive. Despite unlocking new executions, you’ll see the same executions over and over again. They always happen in slow motion and they can have multiple steps. Marius will stab a guy, pull out the sword, and possibly smash the guy’s face with the shield. I’ve seen an execution with four steps. It’s really tiring to watch these animations repeatedly and feel your time being wasted. Obviously, people that enjoy the executions will not be as bothered as me by all of the above, but I grew very tired of them and started questioning my life choices.
I should mention that the executions are quick time events where you have a button press for each step that occurs. Legendary hits are when you press the corresponding button as soon as the enemy lights up with whatever color (Blue means X, yellow means Y). Here’s a secret, you don’t have to press the buttons. You’ll still gain the completed execution bonus you selected which can be health, Focus (slow down time), bonus damage, or bonus experience. I’m not actually sure what pressing the buttons do besides make the executions go by slightly faster and change the rating of the hit (Recruit to Legendary). Other quick time events can be found in one of the earlier chapters where you have to defend against traps. Some sections will have you deflect or dodge arrows as you make your way around a level or close the distance.
To further drive the point home regarding the abundance of quick time event style gameplay, the 1v1 boss fights later in the game could simply be played by parrying and then striking. You don’t have to move around at all. You can’t attack head-on with the sword or shield so you have to be on the defensive. I just stood there pressing A at the correct times and then X to attack. Two buttons. For a boss fight. Which I won.
There are some other issues I have with the game. Believability when it came to the weird shapeshifting arena in a later chapter pulled me right out of the experience. I can appreciate the supernatural elements of the game because they make sense within the world, but the future tech that the emperor possessed that allow the coliseum to completely change the battleground to a new set in the blink of an eye just confused the heck out of me. Seeing a spaceship drop in the middle of battle would have had the same effect on me. Other than that, the javelin aiming can be wonky and it can be difficult to change targets while in combat. Finally, while there is some enemy variety, they could have had more variations for the barbarian character models for those early chapters.
I had to force myself to finish this game and almost stopped several times. If you insist on playing it, maybe take some breaks if the repeated animations start to wear you down. Ryse: Son of Rome is really more of a visual treat than anything else since the gameplay was tedious and boring. I tend to value gameplay mechanics highly which means I can’t recommend this game to people in good conscience. The game could have used faster executions, less quick time events, less slow motion effects, and better boss fights.
If you want to see pretty cutscenes of rome in splendor and QTEs of blood, then this is for you. If you want, you know, a decent game? Not so much.

Overall I enjoyed my 6 or so hour ride through Ryse: Son of Rome. It's gorgeous even 2+ years later and I was able to play it at max settings with minimal framerate dip at 2k resolution on a moderate gaming PC.
The developer really spent a good amount of time on the visuals and it shows as the somewhat historically accurate intrepretation of Rome is a joy to see. I usually don't take the time to stop and check out my environment in games but I found myself doing so quite often in this.
As for the game itself, it's not that long really so there's not a lot of real long-term investment to make. The story is pretty good and there are enough twists and turns to remain engaged. For those that might think (as I did) that there are going to be fantastical elements, I can tell you that there are none that impact gameplay. It's basically a highly visceral blend of hack, slash, stab, chop, repeat. The fighting feels fluid but not as tight as the Batman games or Dark Souls...but then I guess you aren't exactly playing as Batman here but a Roman soldier. I died a few times in the game but a number of times I felt as though I were being punished unfairly for things that were outside of my control.
This game is not particularly challenging and is highly linear. Linear to the point of needing to walk between the correct bushes or between the right soldiers with no alternate route around or through them. Although I didn't play on the higher difficulties, it's mostly just countering various attack patterns of which there are probably around a half dozen in the whole game. There are times in the game when they throw a large amount of enemies at you but, If you've played something like Dark Souls, even the "boss fights" aren't much more challenging than the first 15 minutes of any game in that series. With that, I don't see a lot of replay value here after beating the main campaign.
There is multiplayer but I didn't try it out and doubt I will.

I can't recommend this game, I'll go in depth, but the basis of that decision is that it's an extremely stripped down game that relied solely on the gimmick of graphics improving over time. Once that graphics stuff is pretty much done (first 25% of the game, it becomes a chore to continue - here's why.
Story - It says it's an evolution of 'RPG gaming culture', when really it's just Final Fantasy 7, and Zelda (literally only those 2 games) with graphics that improve over time. Rather then giving you original content representative of the evolution of RPGs, it just gives you hilarious rip-offs of 2 franchises. You summon a creature called 'Babamut' (yea, guess where that's from). As as well the copy paste FF7 time based battles, and 'claude's sword' which is clearly the Buster Sword. The overworld enemies are clearly Zelda rip-offs as well. A character named 'Kaeris', that dies (FF7 plot point) - and the list goes on. Asides from those aspects, the story is sub-par, although I don't imagine anyone playing this game specifically for it in the first place.
Gameplay - What initially gave me the 'uh, this game actually sucks' impression, is the random switch between 2 entirely different battle systems that have no connecting attributes. You start out with the Zelda'esque 'swinging at baddies with a sword' on enemies that wander around while having 3 hearts of health. Then further along you get random turn based battles, and the given the ability to level up. You train and grind thinking you'll need it, but then you get thrown back into that Zelda battle style, with the same 3 hearts, throwing out all progress you've made leveling up. You go back to random battles again and continue your intial progress, then get thrown AGAIN into Zelda style. But this time you deal damage to enemies, and have the ablility to put on about 30 random pieces of equipment. You then get a mini-map, and a health 'sphere' (similar to Diablo I believe) instead of the hearts, but despite this, it has nothing to do with your level from random battles. You get switched (again) to random battles, and grind up again continuing from the level you last achieved, but then (yes) you get switched back to Zelda style. But that equipment you had? Gone, didn't mean anything. The health sphere? Gone - just the 3 hearts you started out with. Doing actual damage to enemies? Gone as well. Remember that minimap you earned? Well it's still there (sometimes), seeming to disappear in random areas with no reason as to why. And then finally the climax comes, and you have to fight the final boss. How?
In f@cking Zelda style, that's how. Right before this ending, you get the chance to get ONE more heart, giving you a total of 4. Who cares how much you leveled up, right? It means nothing, you get thrown back into this basic combat system that makes ALL the progress and work you achieved completely irrelevant - I can't express how terrible that feels. Other then all that, it's just collect some $h!t, end of game.
Controls - Terrible. It says it's the evolution of RPGs, yet from the first minute until the very end, you control like a terrible 80s arcade game. Which makes no sense, because control is something that's frequently been improved since video games first were a thing. Also, there's no running. So enjoy exploring a somewhat large place, with frusteratingly common random battles, while walking as slow as Red in Pokemon Red/Blue/Yellow.
Sound/music - It was pretty catchy, but extremely repetitive. There'll be about 4 tracks, that are just 8 bars on repeat, over, and over.. and over! Quite irritating. A lot of it sounded exactly like Zelda and FF7 music, but with a couple notes changed. No voice acting at all (perfectly fine though, didn't need it).
Other stuff - There were a couple bugs. At ones point textures were broken in a cave level, a sword I apparently recieved just continued floating in the air above the chest, and didn't hit my inventory for about 2 minutes (but once it did, it was still floating in the overworld?). And at another time you could see the black abyss that is the end of the world.
Summary - You get about 3-4 hours of gamplay, MAYBE 5 if you want to find all the collectables. Otherwise, it's not worth the 10.99 (Canadian) it asks for. Nor it is worth the current 5.49 sale price. I'd pay 2.49 for it, tops. After the stellar graphcal gimmicks wear off, you realise you're playing a pathetic FF7 / Zelda rip off, with terrible mechanics that don't make sense or line up with each other. Steer clear of this one folks! -
